Name: concept_language_binding_asymmetry
Title: The Binding Problem in Multilingual Models: When Shared Concepts Fail to Bind to the Right Language
Short Hypothesis: Cross-lingual factual and reasoning inconsistency is not primarily caused by whether a concept is stored in a shared language-agnostic space, but by a failure to *bind* the correct concept to the target-language output channel during the late-layer language-transition phase. We hypothesize the binding failure rate is predictable from a single measurable quantity: the geometric interference between the target-language decoding direction and competing-language decoding directions, which increases with the number of typologically-close 'competitor' languages a model knows, not just with distance from English.
Related Work: Prior work established that multilingual LLMs form a shared concept space in middle layers and transition to language-specific spaces in final layers (Wendler et al. 2024; Dumas et al. 2024; Semantic Hub 2024). Recent work localizes inconsistency to the late-layer transition (Lost in Multilinguality 2025) and proposes bypassing final layers via a linear shortcut, and identifies 'transfer neurons' (2025) that move representations between spaces. However, all these treat the problem as concept-space alignment quality: is the concept shared or English-centric? None isolate the *binding* step — the mechanism that routes a correctly-retrieved shared concept into the correct language decoder — as a distinct, quantifiable failure mode, nor do they explain why interference scales with the number of *typologically similar* languages (competitor pressure) rather than distance from English. Our proposal reframes cross-lingual inconsistency as a binding/routing problem analogous to the neural binding problem, offers a predictive geometric interference metric, and tests a targeted intervention on the binding step rather than the concept representation.
Abstract: Multilingual language models store much factual and conceptual knowledge in a shared, language-agnostic representation space, yet they answer the same question inconsistently across languages. Existing explanations focus on whether the concept space is truly shared or English-centric. We propose a different lens: cross-lingual inconsistency is fundamentally a *binding* problem. A model may correctly retrieve a concept in its shared space, but then fail to bind that concept to the correct target-language output channel during the late-layer language transition. We formalize this with a geometric interference metric measuring overlap between the target-language decoding direction and competing-language directions, and hypothesize that binding failure — not concept-retrieval failure — is the dominant driver of errors. Crucially, we predict interference scales with the number of *typologically close competitor languages* a model knows, producing counterintuitive cases where a language distant from English but with few competitors binds more reliably than a mid-distance language crowded by neighbors. We test this across Llama-3, Aya-23, BLOOM, and Qwen using activation patching to separate concept-retrieval from binding failures, logit-lens tracking of language-direction competition, and a controlled synthetic-multilingual training study varying competitor density. We then propose a lightweight binding intervention that boosts the target-language decoding direction relative to competitors at the transition layer, without altering the concept representation. We evaluate on multilingual factual QA (mLAMA, cross-lingual consistency), reasoning (multilingual MGSM), and translation, measuring consistency, accuracy, and error-type decomposition. Our work recasts multilingual inconsistency as a routing failure with a predictive, actionable signature.
Experiments:
1) Error decomposition via activation patching: For each factual/reasoning query answered correctly in language A but incorrectly in language B, patch (a) the shared-space concept representation from A into B's forward pass, and (b) only B's late-layer language-specific components. If (a) fixes the error, it was concept-retrieval failure; if the concept is present but only (b)-level routing changes the output, it is binding failure. Report the proportion of each error type across mLAMA and MGSM for Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, BLOOM-7B, Qwen2.5-7B, and 5+ target languages spanning script and typology diversity.
2) Interference metric construction: Using logit-lens / tuned-lens, extract per-language decoding directions at the transition layers. Define interference(B) = sum over competitor languages C of alignment(dir_B, dir_C) weighted by C's decoding strength. Correlate interference(B) with per-language binding-failure rate from Exp 1 (Spearman rho, partial correlation controlling for training-data proportion and distance-from-English).
3) Competitor-density test: Rank target languages by number of typologically-close languages the model was trained on. Test the prediction that binding-failure rate is better predicted by competitor density than by distance from English via nested regression / model comparison (AIC, held-out R^2).
4) Controlled synthetic study: Train small (~50M param) transformers from scratch on synthetic multilingual fact datasets, varying the number and closeness of competitor languages while holding data-per-language fixed. Measure how binding-failure rate and interference metric change; test causal claim that adding a close competitor raises interference and binding errors.
5) Binding intervention: At the transition layer, add a steering vector that increases dir_B relative to competitor directions (leaving concept representation untouched). Compare against the linear-shortcut baseline (Lost in Multilinguality 2025) and cross-lingual English-steering baseline. Metrics: cross-lingual consistency (agreement rate across language pairs), target-language accuracy, translation BLEU/COMET, and off-target rate (fraction of outputs in the wrong language). Report gains and any degradation on English.
Evaluation metrics: binding-vs-concept error proportions, Spearman correlation between interference and failure, held-out predictive R^2, consistency@k, accuracy, off-target rate, COMET/BLEU.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The concept-retrieval vs binding distinction may not cleanly separate in practice; patching may have entangled effects. Mitigation: use multiple patching granularities and report ambiguous cases explicitly. 2) The interference metric relies on logit/tuned-lens decoding directions, which are approximate for non-final layers. 3) Typological competitor-density is confounded with training-data quantity and script; the controlled synthetic study is designed to disentangle this but may not transfer to full-scale models. 4) The binding intervention could improve consistency at the cost of accuracy or English performance. 5) Findings may be model-family dependent (e.g., BLOOM's less English-centric space), which we treat as a feature to analyze rather than a bug. 6) Access limited to open ~7-8B models, so conclusions may not extend to frontier-scale models.

Name: shared_concept_reasoning_tax
Title: The Shared-Space Reasoning Tax: When Thinking in a Language-Agnostic Space Costs Culturally-Grounded Knowledge
Short Hypothesis: The shared, largely English-scaffolded concept space that multilingual LLMs use for reasoning is not neutral: routing a query through it systematically strips culture- and language-specific priors. We hypothesize a measurable 'shared-space reasoning tax' whereby forcing a query deeper into the language-agnostic hub improves language-independent facts but degrades culturally-indexed knowledge (facts whose correct answer differs by cultural context), and that this tradeoff is causally controllable by modulating when a representation enters and exits the shared space.
Related Work: Prior work established a shared semantic hub scaffolded by the dominant language (Semantic Hub 2024; Converging to a Lingua Franca 2024; Emergence of Abstract Thought 2025) and transfer/language-specific neurons that move representations in and out of it (Transfer Neurons Hypothesis 2025; Language-Specific Neurons 2024; MWork 2024). Steering toward the shared space is generally treated as beneficial: it improves cross-lingual consistency and reasoning (Language-Specific Latent Process Hinders Cross-Lingual Performance 2025). Knowledge-tracing work distinguishes language-independent vs shared/transferred facts (Zhao et al. 2024; language-agnostic knowledge neurons 2024). What is missing is the recognition that the shared space has a *directional cost*: because it is scaffolded by the dominant language, it may overwrite culturally-conditioned knowledge (e.g., 'the legal drinking age', 'the traditional wedding color', 'the emergency number') that is genuinely different across cultures and should NOT be homogenized. No prior work isolates this as a distinct failure mode, distinguishes it from ordinary inconsistency, or shows that the very mechanism praised for boosting consistency (deeper shared-space routing) is precisely what harms culturally-indexed facts. We reframe the shared space as a double-edged compression that imposes a quantifiable, mechanistically-localizable tax.
Abstract: Multilingual language models process inputs through a shared, largely English-scaffolded concept space in their middle layers, and steering queries deeper into this space is widely reported to improve cross-lingual consistency and reasoning. We argue this narrative is incomplete: the shared space is not a neutral meaning representation but a compression biased toward the dominant language's world model. We hypothesize a 'shared-space reasoning tax'—routing a query through the language-agnostic hub improves language-independent facts (whose correct answer is identical everywhere) while systematically degrading culturally-indexed knowledge (facts whose correct answer legitimately varies by cultural context, such as legal thresholds, customs, defaults, or norms). We introduce a paired benchmark, CultureVsUniversal, contrasting universal facts against culturally-conditioned facts across languages, and use logit-lens/tuned-lens depth tracking plus transfer-neuron and language-specific-neuron interventions to measure how far each query travels into the shared space. We predict a crossover: for universal facts, deeper shared-space engagement raises accuracy and consistency; for culturally-indexed facts, deeper engagement pulls answers toward the dominant-language default, lowering culturally-correct accuracy. We test this on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM, then demonstrate causal control: by modulating transfer neurons to delay shared-space entry or amplify late-layer language-specific re-projection, we can trade consistency for cultural fidelity on a per-query basis. Metrics include universal-vs-cultural accuracy crossover, shared-space depth correlation, dominant-language-default pull rate, and the fidelity-consistency Pareto frontier under interventions. Our work recasts the celebrated shared semantic hub as a double-edged compression and offers a mechanism-aware knob for culturally-faithful multilingual reasoning.
Experiments:
1) CultureVsUniversal benchmark construction: Build a paired dataset of ~600 queries in each of two categories. (a) Universal facts: correct answer identical across cultures (e.g., 'chemical symbol for gold', 'number of continents'). (b) Culturally-indexed facts: correct answer legitimately varies by cultural/national context (e.g., legal voting/drinking age, emergency phone number, traditional mourning color, default date format, tipping norm), where the culturally-correct answer for language L differs from the dominant-language (English/US) default. Each query is templated in 6+ languages spanning scripts and typologies, with per-language gold answers verified from authoritative sources. Release the benchmark.
2) Baseline crossover measurement: Evaluate Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B. Metrics: accuracy on universal vs cultural subsets per language; 'dominant-language-default pull rate' = fraction of culturally-indexed queries answered with the dominant-language default despite a different correct answer for that language.
3) Shared-space depth tracking: Using logit-lens and tuned-lens, quantify for each query how deeply/long the representation resides in the language-agnostic (dominant-language-decodable) region vs language-specific region across layers. Define shared_depth score per query. Test H1: shared_depth positively correlates with universal-fact accuracy but negatively with culturally-correct accuracy (Spearman rho, per model and pooled; report the predicted crossover sign flip).
4) Neuron-level attribution: Identify transfer neurons (Type-1 in / Type-2 out) and language-specific neurons via LAPE. Test whether Type-2 (re-projection to language-specific space) activation predicts culturally-correct answers, and whether Type-1 activation predicts dominant-default errors on cultural facts.
5) Causal control interventions: (a) Suppress Type-1 transfer neurons / delay shared-space entry; (b) amplify Type-2 late-layer language-specific re-projection; (c) as a comparison, apply the standard 'steer toward shared space' intervention from prior work. Measure the effect on culturally-correct accuracy, universal-fact accuracy, and cross-lingual consistency. Predict interventions (a)/(b) improve cultural fidelity at some cost to consistency, tracing a fidelity-consistency Pareto frontier; predict the shared-space steering baseline improves consistency but worsens cultural fidelity.
6) Per-query adaptive knob: Train a lightweight probe to classify a query as universal vs culturally-indexed from early-layer activations, then apply the appropriate intervention. Report joint accuracy on the mixed set vs fixed-policy baselines.
Evaluation metrics: universal-vs-cultural accuracy crossover point, shared_depth-accuracy Spearman correlations (signed), dominant-language-default pull rate, cross-lingual consistency@k, fidelity-consistency Pareto area, adaptive-knob joint accuracy, and degradation on English.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Defining 'culturally-indexed' facts with unambiguous per-language gold answers is hard; some facts have within-language regional variation. Mitigation: restrict to nation-level norms with authoritative sources and native-speaker verification, and report inter-annotator agreement. 2) The dominant-default pull could partly reflect training-data frequency rather than shared-space compression; we control by including cultural facts where the correct answer is well-attested in the target language corpus. 3) Logit/tuned-lens depth estimates are approximate at intermediate layers. 4) Transfer-neuron identification methods may be noisy or model-family dependent; BLOOM's less English-centric space is analyzed as a contrast case. 5) Interventions may harm fluency or over-suppress genuine cross-lingual transfer; we report the full Pareto tradeoff rather than a single operating point. 6) Findings limited to open ~7-8B models and may not extend to frontier scale. 7) The crossover, if weak, would still be a valuable negative result challenging the assumption that deeper shared-space routing is universally beneficial.

Name: latent_compute_depth_gap
Title: Thinking Less in Low-Resource Languages: The Latent Compute-Depth Gap in Multilingual Reasoning
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual reasoning failures in lower-resource languages are driven not (only) by wrong concepts or English-centric routing, but by a language-dependent shortfall in *latent computational depth*: the model performs fewer effective serial reasoning steps internally before committing to an answer when prompted in low-resource languages. The correct answer 'crystallizes' at a shallower relative layer, so the model reaches a premature fixed point and commits early. We hypothesize this compute-depth gap is measurable per language, correlates with resource level and typological distance from the dominant language, and is causally responsible for a substantial fraction of the accuracy gap—recoverable by granting extra latent computation.
Related Work: Recent work shows LLMs route reasoning through an English-centric shared space (Do Llamas Work in English 2024; Do Multilingual LLMs Think In English 2025) and that latent (pre-verbalization) reasoning is consistent across languages but weaker for low-resource ones (Large Reasoning Models Are Not Yet Multilingual Latent Reasoners 2026). Language-reasoning disentanglement (When Less Language is More 2025) and shared-space steering (Language-Specific Latent Process Hinders 2025) improve reasoning by removing language-specific signal. Knowledge-Free Reasoners (2024) show reasoning transfers while knowledge does not. All of these characterize *where* (which space) or *what content* reasoning uses, and treat the amount of internal computation as fixed. None isolate the *depth/amount* of latent serial computation as a language-dependent, causally-manipulable variable, nor test whether low-resource failure is a 'premature commitment' (early crystallization) phenomenon. Our proposal introduces per-language latent compute-depth metrics (answer-crystallization layer, prediction-trajectory settling time) and a causal test: granting extra latent computation (looped/pause tokens / recurrent-depth injection) selectively closes the accuracy gap for languages that crystallize early. This reframes the multilingual gap as an inference-time compute-allocation problem, distinct from representation-alignment and content-transfer framings.
Abstract: Multilingual language models solve the same reasoning problem correctly in high-resource languages but fail in lower-resource ones. Prevailing explanations point to English-centric internal representations or to knowledge that fails to transfer. We propose a complementary and largely overlooked driver: a language-dependent shortfall in *latent computational depth*. Using a truncation- and logit-lens-based analysis, we measure, per language, the layer at which the correct answer first crystallizes and how long the internal prediction trajectory settles before the model commits. We hypothesize that in lower-resource and typologically distant languages the answer crystallizes at a shallower relative depth—the model reaches a premature internal fixed point and commits early—and that this early commitment, rather than concept absence, causes a measurable fraction of errors. We test this on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and a reasoning model across 11 typologically diverse languages using MGSM, XCOPA, and a controlled multi-step arithmetic/logic suite where required serial depth is known. We correlate crystallization depth with resource level and language distance, and separate 'early-commit' errors (concept present but abandoned) from genuine concept-retrieval failures via activation patching. We then run the key causal test: granting extra latent computation at inference—via inserted pause/filler tokens, logit-lens-guided layer-repetition, and recurrent-depth looping—should selectively recover accuracy for languages that crystallize early, with minimal effect on languages that already compute deeply. Metrics include crystallization-depth gaps, early-commit error share, accuracy recovery per language, and compute-recovery elasticity. Our work recasts the multilingual reasoning gap as an inference-time compute-allocation failure and offers a cheap, targeted remedy.
Experiments:
1) Compute-depth measurement: For each problem and language, apply logit-lens/tuned-lens across layers to identify the 'crystallization layer' (first layer at which the correct final answer token becomes and stays top-ranked in the language-agnostic / target-language decoding) and a 'settling time' (layers over which the top prediction stabilizes). Also use hidden-state truncation (early-exit at layer L) to measure the minimal depth at which each language produces the correct answer. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and a reasoning model (e.g., a distilled R1 or Qwen-reasoning variant). Datasets: MGSM (arithmetic reasoning), XCOPA (causal commonsense), and a controlled synthetic multi-step suite (k-hop arithmetic and k-step logic chains, k in 1..6) translated with verified gold answers into 11 typologically diverse languages spanning scripts.
2) Correlation analysis: Test H1 that mean crystallization depth (normalized by model depth) is shallower for lower-resource / more distant languages. Regress crystallization depth and early-exit-minimal-depth against (a) training-data proportion, (b) typological/embedding distance from the dominant language, controlling for tokenizer fertility. Report Spearman rho and partial correlations; on the synthetic k-step suite, test whether required serial depth k interacts with language (does the gap widen with k?).
3) Error-type decomposition (concept vs early-commit): For problems correct in English but wrong in language B, use activation patching: (a) patch the shared-space concept/intermediate-reasoning state from English into B late enough that only 'commitment' remains, and (b) simply force continued computation. If the correct answer is already latently present in B before it commits (recoverable by early-exit at a deeper layer or by patching only the commitment step), classify as 'early-commit'; otherwise 'concept-retrieval failure'. Report the share of each error type per language.
4) Causal compute-injection test (core experiment): Grant extra latent computation at inference via three mechanisms and measure accuracy recovery per language: (i) inserted pause/filler tokens before the answer (train-free prompting variant and, where feasible, light fine-tuning with pause tokens); (ii) logit-lens-guided layer/block repetition (re-run selected middle blocks n extra times); (iii) recurrent-depth looping if architecture permits, else block-recurrence approximation. Predict: languages identified as 'early-crystallizing' in Exp 1-3 gain the most accuracy, while deep-crystallizing languages gain little (interaction test). Report accuracy recovery, and 'compute-recovery elasticity' = accuracy gain per unit extra latent depth, correlated with the Exp-2 crystallization-depth gap.
5) Specificity controls: Verify gains are not from generic extra compute helping all languages equally (compare gap-closing vs uniform-lift), not from extra tokens leaking translation (check off-target/language-mixing rate), and not from simple length. Compare against baselines: shared-space English steering (Language-Specific Latent Process 2025) and language-specific ablation (When Less Language is More 2025).
Evaluation metrics: normalized crystallization-depth and settling-time gaps across languages; early-exit minimal-depth curves; early-commit vs concept-failure error shares; per-language accuracy recovery under each compute-injection method; compute-recovery elasticity and its correlation with the depth gap; language-mixing/off-target rate; and degradation on high-resource languages.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Logit-lens/tuned-lens 'crystallization layer' is an approximation at intermediate layers and may be noisier for non-final layers; we cross-validate with hidden-state early-exit truncation. 2) 'Early-commit' vs 'concept-retrieval failure' may not cleanly separate; we report ambiguous cases and use multiple patching granularities. 3) Crystallization depth may confound with tokenizer fertility (more tokens per word could inflate apparent depth); we control for fertility and include single-token-friendly languages. 4) Compute-injection mechanisms differ across architectures; recurrent-depth looping may only be approximable via block-recurrence, weakening the cleanest causal test. 5) Extra compute might improve accuracy for reasons unrelated to depth (e.g., re-reading), addressed by the specificity controls and the interaction prediction (selective, not uniform, gains). 6) Effects may be model-family dependent and limited to open 7-8B and mid-size reasoning models, not frontier scale. 7) If the depth gap is small or gains are uniform across languages, this is still an informative negative result challenging the 'premature-commitment' account and clarifying that the multilingual gap is primarily representational/content-based rather than a compute-allocation issue.

Name: fact_provenance_asymmetry
Title: Where a Fact Was Born: Linguistic Provenance Predicts Cross-Lingual Knowledge Accessibility and Edit Propagation
Short Hypothesis: Each fact in a multilingual LLM has a measurable 'linguistic provenance' - the language from whose pretraining data it was predominantly acquired. We hypothesize that provenance, not just script or typology, causally governs where the fact is stored (shared vs. language-specific subspace) and how accessibly it can be retrieved or edited from other languages: facts with high-resource (typically English) provenance sit in the shared hub and transfer broadly, whereas facts with low-resource provenance are trapped in shallow, language-entangled subspaces and resist both cross-lingual retrieval and edit propagation. Provenance is estimable from model internals alone (no training-data access) and predicts transfer better than script/typology.
Related Work: Prior work shows cross-lingual factual consistency is low (Cross-Lingual Consistency 2023; Beneath the Surface 2024), that edit vectors across languages are near-orthogonal and edits fail to propagate (CLM-Bench 2026; Cross-Lingual KE 2024), and that language-agnostic factual neurons exist in late layers (LU-LAFNs 2024; One Mind Many Tongues 2024). Transfer is repeatedly correlated with script similarity, typological distance, and resource level (BMIKE-53 2024; MLaKE 2024; Tracing the Roots 2024). Zhao et al. (2024) distinguish independent/shared/transferred facts but do not tie these to *acquisition provenance* or predict them from internals. All of this treats language identity of the *query* or *edit* as the unit of analysis. No prior work assigns each *individual fact* a linguistic provenance signature derived from model internals, nor tests that provenance - rather than the query language's script/typology - is the causal driver of storage location and cross-lingual accessibility. We reframe cross-lingual inconsistency from a query-language property to a per-fact provenance property, providing an internals-only provenance estimator and a causal test that manipulating provenance (via controlled synthetic pretraining) reshapes transfer.
Abstract: Multilingual language models answer the same factual question inconsistently across languages, and edits made in one language rarely propagate to others. Existing explanations attribute this to script similarity, typological distance, and resource level of the query language. We propose a complementary, per-fact account: every fact has a linguistic provenance - the language from whose pretraining data it was predominantly acquired - and this provenance, not the query language's surface properties, causally determines where the fact is stored and how accessible it is across languages. We introduce an internals-only provenance estimator that assigns each fact a provenance signature by measuring which language's early-layer representation the model's answer decodes most directly from and which language's neurons carry its factual computation, without access to pretraining data. We hypothesize that English/high-resource-provenance facts reside in the late-layer shared hub and transfer broadly, while low-resource-provenance facts are trapped in shallow, language-entangled subspaces that resist cross-lingual retrieval and edit propagation. We test this on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using facts native to different languages (e.g., culturally-rooted entities) versus universal facts, measuring per-fact cross-lingual consistency, storage depth via logit-lens, and edit-propagation success. We validate the estimator against a controlled synthetic pretraining study where provenance is known by construction, then show provenance predicts transfer and edit propagation better than script/typology baselines. Finally, we test a provenance-aware editing intervention that first lifts a low-provenance fact into the shared subspace before editing, improving propagation. Metrics include provenance-transfer correlation, held-out predictive R-squared over script/typology, storage-depth gaps, and edit-propagation success rates.
Experiments:
1) Provenance estimator construction: For each fact (subject-relation-object triple) in a multilingual dataset, query the model in every available language and, using logit-lens/tuned-lens, measure (a) at which layer and in which language's decodable space the correct object first crystallizes, and (b) which language-specific neurons (via LAPE) carry the largest attribution for that fact. Combine into a per-fact provenance signature = the language whose early/mid representation the answer decodes most directly from across all query languages. Report signature stability across paraphrases (test-retest reliability).
2) Datasets: Build a fact set spanning (a) universal facts (mLAMA subset, answer identical across cultures), and (b) language-native facts - entities/facts predominantly documented in a single language's cultural sphere (e.g., regional history, local figures, culture-specific concepts) sourced across 6+ languages spanning scripts (English, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, French). Verify native provenance from Wikipedia language-edition presence as an external (non-model) provenance proxy.
3) Provenance vs. storage location: Test H1 that English/high-resource-provenance facts crystallize deeper (in the late-layer shared hub) while low-resource-provenance facts crystallize shallower and in language-specific space. Regress storage-depth on estimated provenance, controlling for query-language script/typology and answer-token frequency (Spearman rho, partial correlations).
4) Provenance vs. cross-lingual accessibility: For each fact, compute cross-lingual consistency (RankC-style agreement across query languages). Test whether estimated provenance predicts consistency better than query-language script/typology via nested regression / model comparison (AIC, held-out R^2). Prediction: low-resource-provenance facts have lower consistency regardless of query language.
5) Controlled synthetic validation: Pretrain small (~50-100M param) transformers from scratch on synthetic multilingual corpora where each fact is injected with a *known* provenance (introduced in only one language, or with controlled cross-language redundancy). Verify the internals-only estimator recovers ground-truth provenance (classification accuracy), and confirm the causal claim that low-provenance facts are stored shallower and transfer worse.
6) Provenance vs. edit propagation: Using ROME/MEMIT-style and in-context editing, edit each fact in a single language and measure propagation to other languages. Test that edit-propagation success is predicted by provenance (low-provenance facts propagate worse). Compare against the near-orthogonality baseline (CLM-Bench) and script-family baselines.
7) Provenance-aware editing intervention: For low-provenance facts, first apply a steering/patching step that lifts the fact's representation into the late-layer shared subspace (using shared-hub directions from high-provenance facts) before performing the edit. Compare propagation success and locality against standard editing and language-anisotropic editing (LiME) baselines.
Evaluation metrics: provenance estimator test-retest reliability and synthetic-ground-truth recovery accuracy; provenance-transfer Spearman correlation; held-out predictive R^2 of provenance over script/typology baselines; storage-depth gaps by provenance; edit-propagation success and locality; intervention gains vs. baselines; degradation on high-provenance facts.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The internals-only provenance estimator may be confounded with answer-token frequency or tokenizer fertility; we control for these and validate against the synthetic ground-truth study. 2) The external Wikipedia-edition provenance proxy is imperfect (a fact may be documented in multiple editions); we treat it as a noisy label and rely primarily on the synthetic validation for causal claims. 3) Logit-lens/tuned-lens depth estimates are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 4) LAPE neuron attribution can be noisy and model-family dependent; BLOOM's less English-centric space is analyzed as a contrast case. 5) Provenance and script/typology are partially correlated, making disentanglement hard at full scale; the controlled synthetic study is designed to break this correlation but may not fully transfer. 6) The provenance-aware editing intervention could harm locality or high-provenance facts; we report the full tradeoff. 7) If provenance does not outpredict script/typology, this is still an informative result clarifying that surface language properties, not acquisition history, drive transfer. 8) Limited to open ~7-8B and small synthetic models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: reassembly_tax_fertility
Title: The Reassembly Tax: How Tokenizer Fertility Delays Concept Formation and Steals Reasoning Compute in Multilingual Models
Short Hypothesis: When a word is shattered into many subword tokens (high tokenizer fertility), a multilingual LLM must spend early-layer compute silently *reassembling* the fragments into a single coherent concept representation before that concept can enter the shared semantic hub and be reasoned over. We hypothesize this 'reassembly tax' is a distinct, measurable mechanism: high-fertility words enter the shared concept space at a *later relative layer*, leaving fewer effective layers for downstream reasoning, and this delay—not raw resource level or typological distance—is a dominant, causally-manipulable driver of cross-lingual performance gaps. Critically, we predict the gap can be closed at inference time by injecting a 'reassembly shortcut' that collapses fragmented tokens early, without any retraining.
Related Work: Prior work shows (a) morphological information is encoded in middle-to-late layers (Multilingual BERT probing 2020/2023; mT5 vs ByT5 2024); (b) tokenizer fertility is unequal across languages and inflates cost / hurts fairness (Equity with Efficiency 2026; Phonemes to the Rescue 2026; Tokenization Matters Indic 2025); (c) token overlap aids transfer (False Friends 2025); and (d) reasoning is routed through an English-centric shared space (Do Multilingual LLMs Think In English 2025). These treat fertility as an efficiency/cost metric and separately study where concepts live, but none tie fertility to a *mechanistic delay in concept formation* that trades off against downstream reasoning depth. No prior work isolates 'reassembly' as a distinct early-layer computation whose length is set by fertility, measures the layer at which a multi-token word becomes a unified concept, or shows that this concept-formation depth—rather than resource level or typology—predicts and causally controls the cross-lingual gap. We reframe fertility from an efficiency nuisance into a mechanistic compute-allocation tax with an inference-time remedy, distinct from tokenizer-redesign approaches (which require retraining) and from resource/typology explanations of transfer.
Abstract: Multilingual language models fragment words from many languages into long chains of subword tokens. This 'tokenizer fertility' is usually discussed as a cost and fairness problem. We propose that fertility has a deeper, mechanistic consequence: a high-fertility word forces the model to spend its early layers silently *reassembling* fragments into a single coherent concept before that concept can enter the shared semantic hub and participate in reasoning. We call this the reassembly tax. We hypothesize that (1) high-fertility words become unified, hub-decodable concepts at a systematically later relative layer than low-fertility words; (2) this later concept-formation depth leaves fewer effective layers for downstream reasoning, causing errors; and (3) concept-formation depth predicts cross-lingual performance gaps better than raw resource level or typological distance, because two languages at similar resource levels can differ sharply in fertility. We measure concept-formation depth using logit-lens/tuned-lens tracking of when a multi-token entity's fragments converge onto a single hub-decodable representation, plus early-exit truncation. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM across typologically diverse languages, correlating fertility, concept-formation depth, resource level, and typological distance with accuracy on multilingual factual QA and reasoning (mLAMA, MGSM). The core causal test injects a train-free 'reassembly shortcut'—a steering/patching operation that collapses fragmented tokens into a merged concept representation at an early layer—and predicts it selectively recovers accuracy for high-fertility languages while barely affecting low-fertility ones. Metrics include concept-formation depth gaps, fertility-vs-typology predictive R-squared, per-language accuracy recovery, and reassembly-recovery elasticity.
Experiments:
1) Concept-formation depth measurement: For a set of entities/words that are single tokens in some languages but split into k>1 tokens in others, use logit-lens/tuned-lens to identify the 'concept-formation layer'—the first layer at which the final subword position's representation decodes to the unified concept (e.g., the entity in the shared/English-decodable hub) and stops changing—and cross-validate with early-exit truncation (probe whether the concept is recoverable at layer L). Compute per-language mean concept-formation depth (normalized by model depth). Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B. Languages: 10+ spanning scripts and fertility levels (e.g., English, French, German, Turkish, Finnish, Hindi, Arabic, Swahili, Chinese, Korean).
2) Fertility-depth relationship: Test H1 that per-word concept-formation depth increases with that word's token count (fertility), controlling for word frequency and answer-token frequency. Report within-language (varying fertility across words) and across-language (mean fertility vs mean depth) Spearman correlations and partial correlations.
3) Predictive comparison (fertility vs resource/typology): Regress per-language accuracy on mLAMA (factual) and MGSM (reasoning) against (a) tokenizer fertility / concept-formation depth, (b) training-data proportion / resource level, (c) typological & embedding distance from English. Use nested regression / model comparison (AIC, held-out R^2) to test whether concept-formation depth adds predictive power beyond resource and typology. Prediction: two similar-resource languages with divergent fertility (e.g., English vs Finnish; French vs Turkish) show accuracy gaps aligned with depth.
4) Reasoning-compute tradeoff test: On MGSM and a controlled synthetic k-step reasoning suite (k in 1..6) translated with verified gold answers, test whether high concept-formation depth interacts with required reasoning depth k—i.e., the accuracy gap for high-fertility languages widens as k grows, consistent with fewer remaining layers for reasoning. Report the depth-by-k interaction.
5) Error decomposition: For problems correct in a low-fertility language but wrong in a high-fertility one, use activation patching to test whether patching only the *reassembled concept representation* (from the low-fertility forward pass) into the high-fertility pass, early, fixes the error—classifying such cases as 'reassembly failures' vs genuine downstream reasoning failures. Report the share of each per language.
6) Core causal intervention—train-free reassembly shortcut: At an early layer, replace the fragmented subword representations of a high-fertility word with a single merged 'concept' representation, obtained by (a) mean/attention-pooling the fragment states, or (b) patching in the corresponding low-fertility (e.g., single-token or English) representation aligned to that position, then continuing the forward pass. Measure per-language accuracy recovery on mLAMA and MGSM. Prediction: high-fertility languages (identified in Exp 1-3) gain most; low-fertility languages gain little (interaction/selectivity test). Compute 'reassembly-recovery elasticity' = accuracy gain per unit fertility, correlated with the Exp-2 depth gap.
7) Specificity controls: Verify gains are not uniform generic help (compare gap-closing vs uniform-lift), not from language leakage (measure off-target/language-mixing rate), and not merely length-driven. Compare against baselines: English shared-space steering (Do Multilingual LLMs Think In English 2025) and a naive first-token-only pooling ablation.
Evaluation metrics: normalized concept-formation-depth gaps across languages; within/across-language fertility-depth Spearman correlations; held-out predictive R^2 of depth/fertility over resource and typology baselines; depth-by-reasoning-depth interaction; reassembly-vs-reasoning error shares; per-language accuracy recovery and reassembly-recovery elasticity under the shortcut; off-target/language-mixing rate; degradation on low-fertility languages and English.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Logit-lens/tuned-lens 'concept-formation layer' is approximate at intermediate layers; we cross-validate with early-exit truncation and report robustness across lens choices. 2) Fertility is correlated with resource level and script, making disentanglement hard; we specifically select similar-resource, divergent-fertility language pairs and use partial correlations, but residual confounding may remain. 3) 'Reassembly failure' vs 'reasoning failure' may not separate cleanly; we report ambiguous cases and use multiple patching granularities. 4) The train-free reassembly shortcut (pooling/patching) may harm fluency or inject wrong concepts for polysemous fragments; we report the full tradeoff and locality effects. 5) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM's less English-centric space is analyzed as a contrast). 6) Concept-formation depth for logographic scripts (Chinese) where tokens are already dense may behave differently, which we treat as an informative contrast rather than a failure. 7) If depth adds no predictive power beyond fertility itself, the mechanistic claim weakens but the fertility-accuracy link plus the causal shortcut remain valuable. 8) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: portable_operators_scope_rebinding
Title: Portable Operators, Local Scope: How Multilingual LLMs Share Logical Operator Directions but Fail to Re-bind Their Scope Across Languages
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs represent logical/pragmatic operators (negation, universal/existential quantifiers, conditionals) as a largely language-agnostic 'operator direction' in the shared semantic hub, but the operator's SCOPE — which content tokens it transforms — must be re-bound per language according to that language's word order and morphology. We hypothesize that cross-lingual operator failures concentrate in the scope-rebinding step, not in operator detection or content representation, and that this rebinding failure scales with word-order distance from the dominant language. Consequently, an operator direction extracted in one language can be transplanted into another to correctly flip meaning, whereas scope errors cannot be fixed this way — revealing a clean dissociation between a portable operator and a local scope mechanism.
Related Work: Prior work on negation in language models is either (a) a cross-lingual NLP task treating negation as token-level scope span classification (multilingual BERT/XLM-R zero-shot scope transfer; Negation typology 2021; multilingual scope detection surveys 2020-2022), or (b) monolingual mechanistic/probing studies localizing negation to particular layers/heads and showing models poorly encode monotonicity and negation scope (Negation Coordination Quantifiers 2022; How does BERT's attention change 2020; Decomposing Natural Logic 2021/2022; MoNLI 2020; Strong hallucinations from negation 2024; How and where does CLIP process negation 2024). None of these examine, in modern multilingual GENERATIVE LLMs, whether the OPERATOR itself lives in a language-agnostic shared subspace separable from its SCOPE, whether operator handling transfers via the shared hub distinctly from content, or whether cross-lingual operator failure is specifically a scope-rebinding failure driven by word-order distance. Our work reframes multilingual operator processing as a two-part mechanism — a portable operator direction plus a language-local scope binder — and provides a causal transplant test that dissociates them. This is orthogonal to my prior proposals (concept-language binding, cultural compression, compute-depth, fact provenance, tokenizer reassembly), which concern content knowledge and reasoning depth, not the representation and transfer of logical operators.
Abstract: Function words such as 'not', 'every', and 'if' are operators: they transform meaning rather than store it. In multilingual language models, how are such operators represented, and does that representation transfer across languages the way content concepts do? We hypothesize a dissociation: the operator itself (e.g., a 'negation direction') is encoded in the largely language-agnostic shared semantic hub and is therefore portable across languages, whereas the operator's scope — which content tokens it applies to — must be re-bound locally according to each language's word order and morphology. Under this account, cross-lingual operator failures concentrate in scope re-binding, not in operator detection, and worsen with word-order distance from the model's dominant language. We test this on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using a controlled multilingual minimal-pair suite for negation, quantifier polarity, and conditionals across typologically diverse languages spanning SVO/SOV/VSO orders. We (1) extract per-language operator directions via difference-in-means between affirmative/negated (or restricted-quantifier) representations and measure their cross-lingual cosine alignment in the shared hub; (2) train scope probes to test whether scope information is more language-specific than the operator direction; (3) decompose errors via activation patching into operator-detection vs scope-rebinding failures; and (4) run the key causal test: transplant an operator direction extracted in language A into language B's forward pass and measure whether it correctly flips meaning, predicting operator transplant succeeds while it cannot repair scope errors. Metrics include operator-direction alignment, scope-probe language-specificity, error-type shares, word-order-distance correlations, and transplant flip-rate versus scope-repair rate.
Experiments:
1) Minimal-pair operator suite: Construct a controlled dataset in 8+ typologically diverse languages (spanning word orders and scripts, e.g., English, German, French, Turkish (SOV), Japanese (SOV), Arabic (VSO), Hindi, Swahili, Chinese) with (a) negation minimal pairs ('The cat is/ is not on the mat'), (b) quantifier-polarity pairs ('every/no student passed'; downward-monotone contexts), and (c) conditionals. Each item has a controlled scope target and a truth-conditional probe question with verified gold answers. Templated and native-speaker-verified.
2) Operator-direction extraction and alignment (H1): For each language, compute the difference-in-means vector between affirmative and negated (and restricted vs. unrestricted quantifier) hidden states at each layer at the operator/predicate positions, yielding a per-language 'operator direction'. Measure cross-lingual cosine alignment of these directions across layers. Test H1a: operator-direction alignment is high and peaks in the middle/shared-hub layers. Compare against content-concept direction alignment (e.g., subject-noun swaps) as a within-model baseline. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
3) Scope probing (scope is more local than operator): Train linear probes to recover the operator's scope (which tokens are within scope) from hidden states, per language and per layer. Test H1b: a scope probe trained on language A transfers WORSE to language B than an operator-detection probe trained on A transfers to B (report cross-lingual probe transfer gap; operator-detection = is-negated classification). Correlate scope-probe cross-lingual transfer degradation with pairwise word-order distance (WALS features / word-order typology).
4) Behavioral failure map and word-order correlation: Evaluate truth-conditional accuracy on the probe questions per language and operator type. Regress per-language operator accuracy on word-order distance from the dominant language, controlling for resource level and tokenizer fertility (partial correlations; nested regression AIC/held-out R^2 to test whether word-order distance predicts operator failure beyond resource/typology-general baselines).
5) Error decomposition via activation patching: For items correct in the dominant language but wrong in language B, patch (a) the operator direction from the dominant-language pass into B, and (b) the scope-related components (positions/heads implementing scope binding). Classify as operator-detection failure (fixed by (a)) vs scope-rebinding failure (only (b) helps or neither helps). Report the share of each error type per language and operator, predicting scope-rebinding dominates for high word-order-distance languages.
6) Core causal transplant test: Extract the negation/quantifier operator direction in language A and ADD it (steering) into language B's forward pass on an affirmative sentence; measure the 'flip rate' (does the model's truth-conditional answer correctly negate?). Prediction: operator transplant achieves high cross-lingual flip rate (operator is portable), but the SAME transplant cannot repair scope errors on items with mismatched scope (scope-repair rate stays low), demonstrating the dissociation. Compare against a shared-hub English-steering baseline and a random-direction control.
7) Specificity controls: verify transplant does not merely degrade fluency or switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), verify effects are operator-specific (transplanting the negation direction flips negation but not quantifier polarity), and report degradation on the dominant language.
Evaluation metrics: cross-lingual operator-direction cosine alignment (and vs content baseline); scope-probe vs operator-probe cross-lingual transfer gap; operator accuracy vs word-order-distance partial correlations and held-out R^2; operator-detection vs scope-rebinding error shares; transplant flip-rate vs scope-repair rate; off-target/language-mixing rate; dominant-language degradation.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Difference-in-means operator directions may be entangled with content or lexical differences; we control with matched minimal pairs and content-swap baselines, and use multiple probe/patching granularities. 2) Scope annotation across languages (especially discontinuous scope in morphologically rich or VSO languages) is nontrivial; we restrict to controlled templated constructions with native-speaker verification and report inter-annotator agreement. 3) Word-order distance is correlated with resource level and script, making disentanglement hard; we use partial correlations and typologically matched language pairs, but residual confounding may remain. 4) The operator/scope dissociation may be partial rather than clean; a weak dissociation is still an informative result about how logical operators are (or are not) shared across languages. 5) Activation patching may have entangled effects distinguishing operator vs scope; ambiguous cases are reported explicitly. 6) Results may be model-family dependent (BLOOM's less English-centric hub analyzed as a contrast). 7) Steering transplant could harm fluency or switch languages; specificity controls address this. 8) Limited to open 7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale. 9) If operator directions do NOT align cross-lingually, this overturns the portability hypothesis and is itself a valuable finding about the language-specific nature of logical operators.

Name: borrowed_boundary_confidence
Title: Borrowed Boundaries: Multilingual Models Express Confidence Calibrated to Their English Knowledge, Not the Language They Are Answering In
Short Hypothesis: A multilingual LLM's expressed (verbal and logit) uncertainty is governed by a largely language-agnostic 'verbal uncertainty' direction, but that direction reads its input primarily from an English-scaffolded knowledge-boundary signal in the shared hub. Consequently, when a model knows a fact in English but not in a low-resource target language (or vice versa), its expressed confidence tracks its ENGLISH knowledge state rather than its actual target-language competence. This 'borrowed boundary' is the mechanistic cause of cross-lingual miscalibration, it is measurable by decomposing the boundary signal by language, and it is causally correctable by re-sourcing the uncertainty feature's input to the target-language boundary signal.
Related Work: Prior work shows (a) multilingual models are worse-calibrated in low-resource languages (On the Calibration of MMLMs 2022; Multilingual QA Calibration 2023; MlingConf 2024; Contrastive Cross-Lingual Calibration 2025), (b) intermediate layers give better multilingual confidence than the English-biased final layer (LACE 2025; Calibration Across Layers 2025), (c) knowledge-boundary perception is encoded in middle-upper layers and is linearly alignable across languages (Knowledge Boundary Cognition Across Languages 2025), (d) abstention transfers via multilingual feedback/consensus (Teaching LLMs to Abstain 2024; MKA 2025), and (e) monolingually, verbal uncertainty is a single linear feature (VUF) only moderately correlated with semantic uncertainty (Calibrating Verbal Uncertainty 2025; Confidence Regulation Neurons 2024). All existing multilingual calibration work is descriptive or applies post-hoc/ensemble fixes; the boundary-transfer work aligns boundary PERCEPTION across languages but assumes each language's boundary is read from its own representation. NO prior work tests the specific mechanistic claim that the confidence-expressing feature is language-agnostic but SOURCES its input from the English boundary signal - i.e., that low-resource confidence is 'borrowed' from English knowledge rather than computed from target-language competence. This reframes cross-lingual miscalibration from a data-scarcity/post-hoc-scaling problem into a routing/sourcing defect in a shared uncertainty circuit, and yields a targeted causal fix (re-sourcing the VUF input) distinct from temperature scaling, ensembling, or fine-tuning.
Abstract: Multilingual language models are systematically overconfident and poorly calibrated in low-resource languages, yet the mechanism remains unknown; existing remedies are post-hoc (temperature scaling, layer ensembling, fine-tuning). We propose a mechanistic account: the model's confidence-expressing circuit is largely language-agnostic, but it reads its input from an English-scaffolded knowledge-boundary signal in the shared semantic hub. As a result, a model expresses confidence that tracks whether it knows a fact in English, not whether it actually knows it in the language it is answering in. We call this the borrowed boundary. We first replicate the monolingual 'verbal uncertainty feature' (VUF) and test whether the same direction governs hedging across languages (language-agnostic feature). We then decompose the knowledge-boundary signal by language using per-language boundary directions and difference-in-means probes, and test the core claim: in cases where English and target-language knowledge states disagree (know-in-EN/not-in-L and vice versa), the model's expressed confidence and its VUF activation follow the English boundary. We build a controlled fact set with per-language ground-truth knowledge (verified by exhaustive multilingual querying and Wikipedia-edition presence), spanning English-native and target-native facts across typologically diverse languages, on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM. Using activation patching we causally test whether swapping the target-language boundary signal into the VUF's input redirects expressed confidence. Finally, we propose a train-free 're-sourcing' intervention that feeds the VUF the target-language boundary signal, and evaluate calibration (ECE, AUROC), overconfidence on known-unknowns, and abstention quality against LACE and temperature-scaling baselines. Our work recasts multilingual miscalibration as a fixable sourcing defect in a shared uncertainty circuit.
Experiments:
1) Ground-truth per-language knowledge set: Construct a fact set (~800 subject-relation-object triples) with (a) English-native facts (well-documented in English, sparse in target languages) and (b) target-native facts (well-documented in a specific language's sphere, sparse in English), sourced across 6+ typologically diverse languages (English, French, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili). Establish per-language ground-truth 'knows-it' labels via exhaustive multilingual querying with paraphrase consistency, log-prob thresholds, and Wikipedia-edition presence as an external proxy; validate with native-speaker spot checks. Key subset: facts where English and target-language knowledge states DISAGREE.
2) VUF replication and cross-lingual language-agnosticism: Extract the verbal uncertainty feature via difference-in-means between hedged and assertive generations, per language. Measure cross-lingual cosine alignment of VUF directions across layers (test: high alignment = language-agnostic feature). Verify VUF causally controls hedging in each language via steering (flip rate hedged<->assertive).
3) Per-language boundary-signal decomposition: Following knowledge-boundary work, extract per-language knowledge-boundary directions (difference-in-means between known and unknown questions) in middle-upper layers. Train boundary probes per language and measure their cross-lingual transfer, and crucially measure which language's boundary signal best predicts the VUF activation at the point where confidence is set.
4) Core borrowed-boundary test: On the disagreement subset (know-in-EN/not-in-L and not-in-EN/know-in-L), test whether the model's expressed confidence (verbalized confidence + answer log-prob + VUF activation) is predicted by the ENGLISH knowledge state or the TARGET-language knowledge state. Prediction: English boundary dominates, especially for low-resource L. Report the fraction of overconfident errors attributable to English-borrowed confidence, and a regression of VUF activation on EN-boundary vs L-boundary probe scores (partial correlations controlling for resource level and answer frequency).
5) Causal re-sourcing via activation patching: At the layer feeding the VUF, patch in the target-language boundary signal (from a case where the target-language boundary is correctly negative) and test whether expressed confidence correctly drops on know-in-EN/not-in-L items (and rises on not-in-EN/know-in-L items). This isolates the sourcing defect from the feature itself.
6) Train-free re-sourcing intervention: Build a lightweight operator that reads the target-language boundary probe and modulates the VUF input accordingly at inference. Evaluate on multilingual QA (translated TriviaQA/mLAMA-style known-unknowns, plus target-native facts): metrics = ECE, AUROC for correctness, overconfidence rate on known-unknowns, abstention F1, and accuracy preservation. Baselines: LACE intermediate-layer ensemble, per-language temperature scaling, multilingual-feedback abstention, and no-intervention.
7) Specificity controls: verify the intervention does not merely make the model uniformly cautious (check it also RAISES confidence on not-in-EN/know-in-L items), does not switch output language (off-target rate), and does not harm English calibration. Analyze BLOOM (less English-centric hub) as a contrast: predict weaker borrowed-boundary effect.
Evaluation metrics: VUF cross-lingual cosine alignment; EN-boundary vs L-boundary predictive weight on VUF (partial correlation, held-out R^2); fraction of overconfident errors explained by English-borrowed confidence; patching-induced confidence-correction rate (both directions); ECE, AUROC, overconfidence-on-known-unknowns, abstention F1, accuracy; off-target rate; English-calibration degradation.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Establishing per-language ground-truth 'knows-it' labels is noisy; we use multiple signals (consistency, log-prob, Wikipedia proxy, native-speaker checks) and report label reliability. 2) The disagreement subset (know-in-EN/not-in-L) may be small for some language pairs; we oversample target-native facts to balance both directions. 3) VUF and boundary directions from difference-in-means may be entangled with content or frequency; we control with matched pairs and report specificity controls. 4) The 'sourcing' claim relies on patching at the correct layer; if the VUF input layer is ambiguous we sweep layers and report robustness. 5) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM analyzed as a deliberate contrast). 6) The re-sourcing intervention could over-suppress or over-inflate confidence; we require it to move confidence in BOTH directions correctly, not just downward. 7) If the confidence feature turns out to already source from target-language boundaries (no borrowing), this is an informative negative result clarifying that multilingual miscalibration is a boundary-perception-accuracy problem, not a sourcing problem. 8) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: switch_point_information_carryover
Title: Does Meaning Cross the Switch? Information Carryover and Switch-Point Cost in Code-Switched Prompts to Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: When a prompt code-switches mid-sentence, the shared semantic hub acts as a language-invariant carrier that lets already-established meaning flow across the switch, but the switch point itself imposes a localized 'recontextualization cost' at the boundary token, where the model must re-anchor accumulated context into the new language's representation. We hypothesize (1) information established before the switch is preserved in the shared hub and remains accessible after the switch (carryover), (2) the cost of switching is concentrated at the switch-boundary position and scales with the language-pair distance and the shared-hub misalignment there (not with how far into the sentence the switch occurs), and (3) this cost is causally reducible by a targeted intervention that lifts the boundary-token representation into the shared hub, without retraining.
Related Work: Prior code-switching work is either (a) NLP-task-oriented (POS/NER/sentiment on code-switched text; multilingual LLMs are 'not yet code-switchers', 2023; minimal-pair CS evaluation, 2025; OLA output-language alignment, 2026), or (b) about *unintended* code-switching / language confusion as a generation failure, mechanistically traced to late-layer transition failures and excessive language-feature pre-activation (SASFT 2025; latent-space language steering 2025; Language Mixing in Reasoning Models 2025; Mechanistic Language Confusion 2025). Foundational work established a shared/language-agnostic middle-layer hub with language-specific decoding (Do Llamas Work in English 2024; MWork 2024; Transfer Neurons 2025; Cross-Layer Transcoders 2025). Crucially, NO prior work asks the *forward* question: when the INPUT deliberately switches language mid-sentence, does semantic content established before the switch survive across the boundary through the shared hub, and is the switch-point processing 'cost' a localized, boundary-position phenomenon that can be measured and causally reduced? Existing CS studies treat code-switched text as a monolithic input to be classified or generated; existing mechanistic work studies OUTPUT language mixing as a defect. We instead treat an intra-sentential input switch as a controlled probe of the shared hub's role as an information carrier, and localize the switch cost to a specific token position with a targeted fix. This is orthogonal to my prior proposals (content binding, cultural compression, compute depth, provenance, tokenizer reassembly, operators, confidence).
Abstract: People routinely switch languages mid-sentence, yet we do not understand how multilingual language models process an input whose language changes partway through. Does meaning established before the switch flow across the boundary, or is the switch a context reset? We propose that the shared, language-agnostic semantic hub acts as a language-invariant carrier: information encoded before an intra-sentential switch is preserved in the hub and remains accessible after it. However, we hypothesize that the switch imposes a *localized recontextualization cost* concentrated at the boundary token, where accumulated context must be re-anchored into the new language's representation. Critically, we predict this cost scales with the language-pair distance and shared-hub misalignment at the boundary, not with how deep into the sentence the switch occurs, distinguishing our account from a naive 'switching is always disruptive' view. We build a controlled bilingual continuation and comprehension suite in which a fact or referent is introduced in language A and must be used after switching to language B (and vice versa), across typologically diverse pairs, and test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM. Using logit-lens/tuned-lens carryover probes and activation patching, we (1) measure whether pre-switch information survives in the hub, (2) localize the switch cost to boundary positions and correlate it with language distance, and (3) run a train-free intervention that lifts the boundary-token representation into the shared hub, predicting selective cost reduction for distant pairs. Metrics include carryover accuracy, boundary-localized cost curves, distance correlations, and intervention recovery.
Experiments:
1) Controlled code-switch suite: Construct minimal-pair items where a piece of information is introduced in language A and must be used after an intra-sentential switch to language B. Three subtasks: (a) referent carryover ('The scientist who discovered X was born in... <switch> ...which country?' where the antecedent is in A and the query in B); (b) fact continuation (a fact stated in A, a cloze completion in B, single-token verifiable answer); (c) instruction carryover (a constraint given in A, content produced in B). Include matched monolingual controls (no switch) and a 'late vs early switch position' manipulation (switch at 25%/50%/75% of the sentence) with the informational content held fixed. Build across 6+ typologically diverse language pairs spanning scripts and word-order/typology distance (e.g., EN-FR, EN-DE, EN-TR, EN-HI, EN-AR, EN-ZH), templated and native-speaker-verified. Release the suite.
2) Carryover measurement (H1): For items where information is introduced in A before the switch, use logit-lens/tuned-lens at post-switch positions to test whether the pre-switch information is decodable in the shared hub and drives the post-switch answer. Compare answer accuracy on switched vs monolingual-control items; a small gap indicates successful carryover. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
3) Switch-cost localization (H2a): Using a sliding logit-lens/entropy and hidden-state 'surprise' (change in representation norm/direction) across token positions, test whether processing disruption spikes at the switch-boundary token and its immediate successors, then recovers, rather than being diffuse. Report per-position cost curves aligned to the switch point; test that the cost is boundary-localized via a position-alignment analysis (peak at boundary vs flat).
4) Distance and hub-misalignment correlation (H2b): Define boundary hub-misalignment = the representational shift needed to re-anchor context at the switch (e.g., cosine change between pre-switch and post-switch shared-hub representations of the carried content). Test that (i) switch cost and (ii) carryover accuracy gap correlate with language-pair distance (typological/embedding/script distance) and with boundary hub-misalignment, controlling for tokenizer fertility and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2). Crucially, test that switch *position* (early/mid/late) does NOT predict cost once content is held fixed, supporting the boundary-localized account over a 'cumulative disruption' account.
5) Causal carryover test via patching: For items answered correctly in the monolingual control but wrong after the switch, patch the shared-hub representation of the carried content from the control (or from the pre-switch positions) into the post-switch pass at the boundary. If this fixes the answer, the failure was a re-anchoring/recontextualization failure (information was present but not carried), not a content-loss failure. Report the share of each failure type per language pair.
6) Core intervention (H3): Apply a train-free 'boundary lift' - at the switch-boundary token, steer/patch the representation toward the shared-hub direction of the carried content (using hub directions estimated from monolingual passes), leaving later positions untouched. Predict selective reduction of switch cost and recovery of carryover accuracy for distant language pairs (high boundary misalignment), with little effect on close pairs. Compute 'carryover-recovery elasticity' = accuracy gain per unit boundary misalignment, correlated with the Exp-4 distance. Baselines: whole-sentence English-hub steering (Do Multilingual LLMs Think In English 2025), latent-space language steering (2025), and a random-direction control.
7) Specificity controls: verify gains are not uniform generic help (gap-closing vs uniform-lift), do not induce output language mixing (measure off-target/language-mixing rate), are content-specific (lifting the carried referent aids referent carryover but not an unrelated fact), and do not harm monolingual-control performance. Analyze BLOOM's more language-diverse hub as a contrast (predict lower boundary misalignment and smaller switch cost).
Evaluation metrics: carryover accuracy and switched-vs-control gap; per-position boundary-localized cost curves and boundary-peak localization score; switch-cost / carryover-gap partial correlations with language distance and boundary hub-misalignment (and non-correlation with switch position); recontextualization-failure vs content-loss failure shares; intervention carryover recovery and recovery elasticity; off-target/language-mixing rate; monolingual-control degradation.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Logit-lens/tuned-lens hub decoding is approximate at intermediate layers; we cross-validate with early-exit truncation and report robustness across lenses. 2) 'Switch cost' from representation-shift metrics may be confounded with tokenizer fertility jumps at script boundaries; we control for fertility and include same-script pairs. 3) Language distance is correlated with resource level and script, complicating disentanglement; we use partial correlations and typologically varied same-resource pairs but residual confounding may remain. 4) Recontextualization-failure vs content-loss failure may not separate cleanly; we use multiple patching granularities and report ambiguous cases. 5) The boundary-lift intervention could harm fluency or inject wrong content for ambiguous referents; we report the full tradeoff and locality. 6) Naturalistic code-switching has sociolinguistic constraints our templated switches may not capture; we focus on the mechanistic carryover question and note that ecological validity is limited. 7) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM analyzed as a deliberate contrast). 8) If pre-switch information does NOT survive across the boundary (no carryover), this is an informative negative result showing the shared hub does not function as a language-invariant carrier for accumulated context, itself a valuable finding. 9) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: inversion_transcoding_tax
Title: Four-and-Twenty Problems: Does Number-Word Inversion Corrupt the Language-Agnostic Number Representation in Multilingual LLMs?
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs converge on a largely language-agnostic number-value representation (digit-wise base-10 / sinusoidal), but when a number is expressed in a language whose number words are morpho-syntactically INVERTED (unit-before-ten, e.g., German 'vierundzwanzig' = 'four-and-twenty' for 24), the model must transcode across a units-tens order mismatch. We hypothesize this imposes a measurable, localized 'transcoding tax': the model forms the correct value representation later (deeper layer) and less accurately for inverted-language number words, digit-transposition errors (24<->42) spike specifically for inverted languages, and this effect is causally attributable to the units-tens binding step rather than to resource level or tokenization. This mirrors a well-documented human bilingual cognition effect and predicts a distinctive, correctable failure signature in LLMs.
Related Work: Two literatures meet here but have never been connected. (1) Interpretability work shows LLMs encode number VALUE in a largely language-agnostic, structured form: digit-wise circular base-10 representations (Number Digit Representations 2024), sinusoidal/helical value encodings (Language Models Use Trigonometry to Do Addition 2025; Encode Numbers Linearly 2024; Unravelling Manipulating Numbers 2025; Accurate Representations of Numbers 2025), and probe precision predicts arithmetic errors. All of this is monolingual/English and treats the number embedding as language-invariant. (2) Cognitive science shows number-word INVERSION (unit-ten order in German/Dutch/Arabic vs. ten-unit in English/French) causes transposition errors, slower transcoding, and language-of-learning effects in bilinguals (Number word structure influences arithmetic 2015; Inversion effects on multi-digit processing 2013; Units-first or tens-first 2019; Multiple number-naming associations 2023). NO prior work asks whether multilingual LLMs, which supposedly share a language-agnostic number representation, are nonetheless taxed by inverted number-word morphology exactly as human bilinguals are. Prior multilingual-LLM work (Knowledge-Free Reasoners 2024; When Less Language is More 2025; MRRE 2025) treats reasoning transfer at a coarse level and never isolates number-word morphology as a mechanism. We uniquely (a) test whether the 'language-agnostic' number representation is actually corrupted by inverted input morphology, (b) localize the corruption to the units-tens binding step via digit-value probes, (c) predict a language-specific transposition-error signature, and (d) offer a train-free 'de-inversion' intervention. This is orthogonal to my prior proposals (facts, reasoning depth, operators, confidence, code-switching).
Abstract: Interpretability research shows that language models encode numeric values in a structured, largely language-agnostic form (digit-wise base-10, sinusoidal helices), and that the precision of this representation predicts arithmetic errors. Separately, cognitive science shows that humans who speak languages with INVERTED number words (unit-before-ten, e.g., German 'four-and-twenty' for 24) make more digit-transposition errors and are slower at transcoding than speakers of ten-first languages. We ask a simple question that bridges these fields: is the 'language-agnostic' number representation in multilingual LLMs actually corrupted when the input number word is inverted? We hypothesize a 'transcoding tax': when a model reads a spelled-out number in an inverted language, it forms the correct value representation at a deeper layer and less accurately, and produces a distinctive spike in units-tens transposition errors (24<->42) not seen for ten-first languages. Using digit-value probes and the helical/sinusoidal number probes from recent work, we track, layer by layer, when and how accurately the correct two- and three-digit value crystallizes for the SAME number written in inverted (German, Dutch, Arabic) versus non-inverted (English, French, Chinese) number words, on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM. We causally test the units-tens binding account via activation patching that swaps only the tens/units digit slots, and we measure whether inverted-language transcoding errors are fixed by patching in the non-inverted representation. Finally, we propose a train-free 'de-inversion' intervention that reorders the digit-slot bindings at an early layer. Metrics include value-crystallization depth gaps, digit-probe accuracy by slot, transposition-error rates by language type, and intervention recovery. Our work tests whether a celebrated language-agnostic representation secretly inherits a language-specific morphological bias, offering a rare LLM-vs-human cognitive convergence.
Experiments:
1) Number-word stimulus suite: For a controlled set of two-digit (10-99) and three-digit (100-999) integers, generate spelled-out number words in inverted languages (German, Dutch, and Arabic where two-digit inversion applies) and non-inverted languages (English, French, Chinese), plus the digit (Arabic-numeral) form as a language-agnostic control. Native-speaker verify. Tasks: (a) transcoding (spelled-out word -> emit digits), (b) magnitude comparison (which of two spelled-out numbers is larger), (c) simple addition of two spelled-out numbers. Verified single/short-token gold answers. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Value-crystallization depth (H1): Apply digit-wise base-10 probes (Number Digit Representations 2024) and sinusoidal/helical probes (Language Models Use Trigonometry 2025; Accurate Representations 2025) at every layer at the final number-word token position, per language. Identify the 'value-crystallization layer' = first layer at which the correct full value (all digit slots) is decodable and stable. Test H1: for the SAME number, inverted-language inputs crystallize at a deeper relative layer and/or with lower peak probe accuracy than non-inverted inputs. Report normalized depth gaps and peak-accuracy gaps, controlling for tokenizer fertility of the number word and word frequency (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test inversion adds predictive power beyond fertility and resource level).
3) Slot-resolved probing (units-tens binding, H2): Train separate probes for the tens digit and the units digit. Test the prediction that for inverted languages the tens-slot value is resolved LATE (since the tens word arrives after the units word) and that tens/units slots are more confusable (higher cross-slot probe leakage) than for non-inverted languages. Report per-slot crystallization depth and a 'slot-confusion' metric (probability mass the tens-probe assigns to the units value and vice versa).
