4) Behavioral transposition-error signature (H3): On the transcoding and comparison tasks, decompose errors into (i) units-tens transposition errors (predicting 42 for 24), (ii) single-digit errors, (iii) magnitude-scale errors. Test that transposition errors are specifically elevated for inverted languages relative to non-inverted and to the digit control, mirroring the human inversion effect. Correlate per-language transposition rate with the Exp-2/3 slot-confusion and depth-gap metrics.
5) Causal units-tens binding test via patching: For a number wrong in an inverted-language pass but correct in the digit/non-inverted pass, patch (a) the full value representation, (b) ONLY the tens-slot representation, (c) ONLY the units-slot representation from the non-inverted pass into the inverted pass at the crystallization layer. If patching the tens slot alone (or swapping the tens/units slot bindings) fixes transposition errors, this localizes the tax to units-tens binding rather than global value corruption. Report the share of errors fixed by each patch type per language.
6) Train-free de-inversion intervention: At an early layer, apply a fixed 'slot-reorder' operation that re-binds the units-word and tens-word contributions into the canonical tens-then-units digit-slot order (estimated from the non-inverted or digit pass). Predict selective reduction of transposition errors and shallower crystallization for inverted languages, with negligible effect on non-inverted languages (selectivity test). Compute 'de-inversion recovery elasticity' = error reduction per unit baseline inversion tax, correlated with the Exp-2 depth gap. Baselines: whole-representation English/digit steering (MRRE 2025) and a random-reorder control.
7) Specificity controls: verify gains are inversion-specific (no benefit on non-inverted languages or on the digit control), do not change output language (off-target rate), do not merely reduce all errors uniformly (transposition-specific vs uniform reduction), and do not harm three-digit numbers where inversion structure differs (German inverts only the last two digits). Analyze whether the effect scales with the number of inverted digit-pairs. Cross-model: test whether more English-centric models (Llama-3) show a larger inversion tax than more multilingual BLOOM (contrast prediction).
Evaluation metrics: value-crystallization depth and peak probe-accuracy gaps (inverted vs non-inverted); per-slot depth and slot-confusion metrics; transposition-error rate by language type and its correlation with internal slot-confusion; share of errors fixed by full/tens/units patching; de-inversion recovery and elasticity; selectivity (non-inverted and digit-control unchanged); off-target rate; three-digit vs two-digit effects; cross-model inversion-tax comparison; correlation of the LLM inversion tax pattern with the human cognitive literature's qualitative signature.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Spelled-out number words in different languages differ in tokenizer fertility and frequency, confounding depth measurements; we control with partial correlations, include the digit-numeral form as a language-agnostic anchor, and match numbers across languages. 2) Inversion is correlated with language family and script (German/Dutch are Germanic; Arabic differs in script), making disentanglement hard; including a within-Germanic non-inverted comparison (English) and the digit control mitigates but does not fully remove confounds. 3) Digit/sinusoidal probes are approximate at intermediate layers; we cross-validate with multiple probe types (digit-wise, linear, sinusoidal) and report robustness. 4) The units-tens binding localization via slot patching may have entangled effects; we report ambiguous cases and use multiple patch granularities. 5) The de-inversion intervention could harm three-digit numbers or fluency; we report the full tradeoff and selectivity. 6) LLMs may simply memorize frequent number words, weakening the transcoding-mechanism interpretation; we test across the full 10-999 range and emphasize less-frequent numbers. 7) The human-LLM convergence is qualitative, not a claim of identical mechanism. 8) If inverted and non-inverted languages show NO crystallization-depth or transposition-error difference, this is an informative positive result strengthening the claim that the LLM number representation is genuinely language-agnostic and robust to input morphology—valuable either way. 9) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: gender_leak_reasoning
Title: The Bridge Is Sturdy or Elegant? Grammatical Gender Leaks Into Cross-Lingual Reasoning About Genderless Objects
Short Hypothesis: The grammatical gender assigned to an inanimate object in a given language causally leaks into a multilingual LLM's downstream semantic characterization and reasoning about that object, producing systematic cross-lingual inconsistency: when the SAME genderless concept has opposite grammatical genders across two languages (e.g., 'bridge' is masculine in Spanish but feminine in German), the model's descriptions, adjective choices, and even judgment tasks about the object shift toward gender-congruent attributes in each language. This leak is mediated by a partially-shared grammatical-gender feature direction that bleeds into the object's shared-hub concept representation, and it is causally suppressible by ablating that direction without harming task competence.
Related Work: Cognitive science and word-embedding work established that grammatical gender biases the distributional semantics of inanimate nouns (Quantifying the Semantic Core of Gender Systems 2019; How Does Grammatical Gender Affect Noun Representations 2019; Grammatical gender associations outweigh topical bias 2020; Distributed semantic representations are gender biased 2024; Testing a Distributional Account 2024) and that this is a source of measurement artifact in bias studies (Measuring Gender Bias Requires Disentangling Grammatical Gender 2022). Interpretability work shows grammatical gender lives in shared+language-specific subspaces (Analyzing Gender Representation in Multilingual Models 2022) and that morphosyntactic concepts including gender are shared across typologically diverse languages with causal features (LLMs Share Representations of Latent Grammatical Concepts 2025; Same Neurons Different Languages 2022). However, ALL prior work stops at static embeddings or probes of the gender *concept itself*; none tests, in modern generative multilingual LLMs, whether grammatical gender causally *leaks into downstream reasoning and generation about the object* (adjective choice, description, comparative judgment), whether this produces measurable *cross-lingual reasoning inconsistency* on the SAME concept, or whether ablating the shared grammatical-gender direction *removes the leak while preserving task performance*. We move from 'is gender encoded and biased in embeddings' to 'does grammatical gender causally corrupt cross-lingual reasoning in generative LLMs, and can we fix it mechanistically'—a distinct, actionable, and previously untested claim, and orthogonal to my prior proposals (binding, cultural compression, compute depth, provenance, tokenizer, operators, confidence, code-switch, number inversion).
Abstract: Many languages assign grammatical gender to genderless objects, and often disagree: a bridge is masculine in Spanish but feminine in German. Classic studies show this grammatical gender leaks into the distributional semantics of nouns, and human speakers describe such objects with gender-congruent adjectives (sturdy vs. elegant). We ask a simple, previously untested question about modern generative multilingual LLMs: does grammatical gender causally leak into a model's downstream reasoning and generation about a genderless object, and does this create systematic cross-lingual inconsistency on the very same concept? We hypothesize that when a concept has opposite grammatical genders across two languages, the model's descriptions, adjective preferences, and comparative judgments shift toward gender-congruent attributes in each language, mediated by a partially-shared grammatical-gender feature direction that bleeds into the object's shared-hub concept representation. We build a controlled cross-lingual object suite of inanimate nouns whose grammatical gender disagrees across language pairs (Spanish/German/French/Italian/Hindi, English as gender-neutral control), verified against typological resources. On Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM, we (1) measure gender-congruent adjective/description bias per language via forced-choice and generation, (2) quantify cross-lingual inconsistency on gender-mismatched vs. gender-matched concept pairs, (3) localize the leak by probing whether the object's mid-layer concept representation carries the language-local grammatical-gender direction, and (4) run the causal test: ablate the shared grammatical-gender feature (via difference-in-means direction removal or an SAE gender feature) and measure whether cross-lingual inconsistency drops while task competence is preserved. Metrics include gender-congruence effect size, cross-lingual inconsistency gap (mismatched minus matched), leak-mediation regression, and ablation recovery with competence controls.
Experiments:
1) Cross-lingual object suite: Assemble ~300 inanimate, genderless-referent nouns with verified grammatical gender in 5 gendered languages (Spanish, German, French, Italian, Hindi) plus English as a gender-neutral control, using authoritative dictionaries/UniMorph/WALS. Key subsets: (a) MISMATCH pairs—concepts whose grammatical gender is opposite across a language pair (e.g., 'bridge' M in Spanish, F in German); (b) MATCH pairs—same grammatical gender across the pair. For each object, prepare (i) a forced-choice adjective task pairing stereotypically-masculine vs. -feminine attributes (sturdy/strong vs. elegant/beautiful) drawn from the cognitive-science literature, native-speaker-verified per language; (ii) an open description prompt; (iii) a comparative-judgment prompt (e.g., 'Is a bridge more X or more Y?'). Release the suite.
2) Behavioral gender-congruence bias (per language): On Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B, measure the rate at which the model selects/generates gender-congruent attributes for each object in each language. Compute a gender-congruence effect size (Cohen's d) per language, and verify it is near zero for English. Test H1: gendered languages show significant congruence bias; magnitude tracks the strength of the language's gender agreement system.
3) Cross-lingual inconsistency (core behavioral test): For MISMATCH pairs, measure whether the model's attribute/description profile for the SAME concept diverges across the two languages in the gender-congruent direction; for MATCH pairs (control), measure divergence when gender agrees. Define the cross-lingual inconsistency GAP = inconsistency(MISMATCH) minus inconsistency(MATCH). Predict a positive gap: grammatical-gender disagreement, not mere language change, drives extra inconsistency. Control for tokenizer fertility, resource level, and topical/cultural differences by matching concepts and including the English-neutral anchor.
4) Representational localization: Extract a per-language grammatical-gender direction via difference-in-means between masculine and feminine noun representations at each layer (following Analyzing Gender Representation 2022; and SAE gender features following LLMs Share Latent Grammatical Concepts 2025). Probe whether the mid-layer shared-hub representation of a MISMATCH object carries the language-LOCAL grammatical-gender signal (i.e., the object's concept vector projects onto masculine in Spanish but feminine in German). Test the mediation: regress behavioral congruence bias on the object-representation's projection onto the gender direction (per language, partial correlation controlling for frequency/fertility).
5) Causal ablation test: Remove the shared grammatical-gender direction from the object's representation at the localizing layer (a) via difference-in-means projection removal / INLP-style nullspace projection, and (b) via ablating the SAE grammatical-gender feature. Measure whether (i) the gender-congruence bias drops, and (ii) the cross-lingual inconsistency GAP shrinks toward the MATCH baseline. Critically, verify TASK COMPETENCE is preserved: the model must still produce sensible descriptions and correct factual judgments about the object (competence probes and fluency/off-target checks). Compare against (a) random-direction ablation and (b) whole-hub English-steering baselines.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify ablation is gender-specific (removes gender-congruence bias but not unrelated attribute preferences), does not switch output language (off-target rate), and does not degrade English (already neutral, should be unaffected). Cross-model contrast: predict BLOOM (less English-centric, more multilingual hub) and models with stronger per-language gender agreement show larger native leaks; test whether leak magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the gender direction.
Evaluation metrics: per-language gender-congruence effect size (Cohen's d); cross-lingual inconsistency GAP (MISMATCH minus MATCH) with significance; mediation regression coefficient / partial correlation of behavioral bias on gender-direction projection (held-out R^2 over frequency/fertility baselines); ablation-induced reduction in congruence bias and inconsistency GAP; task-competence preservation (description quality, factual-judgment accuracy, fluency); off-target/language-mixing rate; English-neutral control unchanged; cross-model leak-magnitude comparison.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Attribute stereotype lists (masculine vs. feminine adjectives) are themselves culturally loaded and language-specific; we source them from the cognitive-science literature and native-speaker verification, report inter-annotator agreement, and treat the English-neutral anchor as the primary confound control. 2) Grammatical gender is correlated with language family, script, and resource level; MATCH/MISMATCH within-concept contrasts and the English control mitigate but may not fully remove confounds. 3) The leak may be small in instruction-tuned models that have learned to suppress overt stereotyping; we test base models where available and interpret small effects as informative. 4) Difference-in-means / SAE gender directions may be entangled with animacy or lexical features; we use multiple extraction methods and specificity controls. 5) Ablation could harm fluency or over-suppress legitimate semantics; we require competence preservation and report the full tradeoff. 6) Cross-lingual inconsistency could stem from genuine cultural/topical differences rather than grammatical gender; the MATCH control and gender-direction mediation are designed to isolate the grammatical-gender pathway. 7) If no leak or no inconsistency gap is found, this is an informative positive result: it would show modern generative LLMs' shared concept representations are robust to grammatical-gender morphology despite the well-documented embedding-level bias—valuable either way. 8) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: tense_imposition_tenseless
Title: Forcing Time Where None Was Marked: How the Shared Temporal Hub Imposes Tense on Tenseless-Language Inputs in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs converge on a shared temporal-reference representation that is scaffolded by tensed languages (English/French/Russian), where grammar obligatorily fixes a time reference. We hypothesize this shared representation causally IMPOSES a definite time reference onto inputs from tenseless languages (Chinese, Indonesian, Yoruba), where temporal reference is legitimately underspecified and context-dependent. The result is systematic 'tense over-specification': the model spuriously commits to a specific past/present/future reading of a genuinely ambiguous tenseless sentence, tracking the tensed-language default rather than the target-language pragmatics, and this over-commitment is causally attributable to a shared tense direction that can be ablated to restore appropriate underspecification without harming competence.
Related Work: Two literatures meet but have never been connected. (1) Interpretability work shows tense and aspect are encoded as distinct, orthogonal, steerable linear directions in residual space (Steering Tense and Aspect 2025; Probing Verbal Aspect 2024; About Time 2022) and that morphosyntactic concepts including tense are represented in feature directions SHARED across typologically diverse languages, with causal multilingual features (LLMs Share Representations of Latent Grammatical Concepts 2025). Multilingual probing shows tense is easy to recover where morphologically marked (French) but drops sharply where it must be inferred (Chinese) (Multilingual Probe for Tense 2021). (2) Linguistic typology establishes that many languages are TENSELESS: temporal reference is not grammaticalized but inferred from aspect, lexical adverbs, and pragmatics, so a bare sentence is often temporally underspecified (Cross-Linguistic Temporal Reference 2015; English-Chinese Tense/Aspect corpus 2005; LLMs Struggle with NLI for Perfect Aspect 2025). Recent multilingual temporal-reasoning work (MultiTempBench 2026; Date Fragments 2025) focuses on date arithmetic/tokenization, not grammaticalized time reference. NO prior work asks whether the celebrated SHARED tense representation, being scaffolded by tensed languages, causally forces an inappropriate definite time reference onto tenseless-language inputs — turning a shared strength into a cross-lingual over-specification bug. We uniquely (a) frame tenselessness as a stress test of the shared temporal hub, (b) predict and measure spurious tense commitment on genuinely ambiguous inputs, (c) causally localize it to a shared tense direction, and (d) offer a train-free ablation that restores underspecification. This is orthogonal to all my prior proposals (binding, cultural compression, compute depth, provenance, tokenizer, operators, confidence, code-switch, number inversion, grammatical gender).
Abstract: Languages differ fundamentally in how they encode time: tensed languages (English, French, Russian) obligatorily grammaticalize a time reference, while many tenseless languages (Chinese, Indonesian, Yoruba) leave temporal reference underspecified, to be inferred from aspect, adverbs, and context. Multilingual language models are known to build a shared, largely English-scaffolded representation of grammatical tense. We ask a simple question this shared representation makes urgent: does that shared temporal hub causally IMPOSE a definite time reference onto tenseless-language inputs that are genuinely ambiguous? We hypothesize a 'tense imposition' effect — the model spuriously commits to a specific past/present/future reading of a temporally underspecified tenseless sentence, tracking the tensed-language default rather than the target-language pragmatics — and that this commitment is mediated by a shared, ablatable tense direction. We build a controlled bilingual suite of temporally underspecified tenseless-language sentences paired with (i) tensed-language translations that force a specific tense and (ii) context manipulations that should license multiple readings, across tenseless (Chinese, Indonesian, Yoruba) and tensed (English, French, Russian) languages, on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM. We measure spurious tense commitment via forced-continuation, entailment, and elicited-time-reference tasks; probe whether the underspecified input carries a definite tense direction in the shared hub; and run the causal test: ablate the shared tense direction and measure whether appropriate temporal underspecification is restored while comprehension competence is preserved. Metrics include tense-over-specification rate, tensed-default pull rate, tense-direction projection on ambiguous inputs, and ablation-induced restoration of underspecification with competence controls.
Experiments:
1) Tenseless underspecification suite: Construct ~400 template items in tenseless languages (Mandarin Chinese, Indonesian, Yoruba) that are temporally UNDERSPECIFIED at the sentence level (no time adverb, aspect-neutral or context-dependent), each with a native-speaker-verified set of licensed temporal readings (e.g., past/present/future all acceptable given no context). Pair each with (a) tensed-language translations (English, French, Russian) that grammar FORCES into a specific tense, and (b) minimal context variants that disambiguate toward a specific reading (adverbial 'yesterday'/'tomorrow', or discourse). Include tensed-language controls (bare sentences whose tense is grammatically fixed). Native-speaker verify licensed-reading sets and report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite.
2) Behavioral tense-over-specification (H1): On Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B, measure via three tasks whether the model spuriously commits to a single time reference on underspecified tenseless inputs: (i) forced continuation ('When did/does/will this happen?' — measure distribution over past/present/future); (ii) temporal-NLI (does the underspecified sentence ENTAIL a specific-time paraphrase? — a correct model should say 'neutral'/underspecified, following LLMs Struggle with Perfect Aspect 2025); (iii) elicited paraphrase in a tensed language (which tense does the model choose, and does it present it as the only option?). Define tense-over-specification rate = fraction of underspecified items on which the model commits to a single reading as if obligatory. Verify near-zero over-specification on the disambiguated-context variants (model should follow context) and appropriate commitment on genuinely tensed controls.
3) Tensed-default pull (H2): Test whether the committed reading tracks the DEFAULT tense of the model's dominant scaffolding language rather than target-language pragmatics. Define tensed-default pull rate = fraction of over-specification cases whose chosen reading matches the tensed-language (English) default paraphrase. Compare across tenseless languages; predict higher pull for lower-resource tenseless languages (Yoruba > Indonesian ~ Chinese). Control for tokenizer fertility and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2).
4) Representational localization: Extract a shared tense direction via difference-in-means / LDA between past/present/future tensed sentences (following Steering Tense and Aspect 2025; LLMs Share Latent Grammatical Concepts 2025) and verify it is shared across the tensed languages (cross-lingual cosine alignment across layers). Probe whether the mid/late-layer representation of an UNDERSPECIFIED tenseless input nonetheless projects strongly onto a definite pole of this tense direction (i.e., the hub assigns it a tense it does not grammatically have). Mediation: regress behavioral over-specification/pull on the underspecified input's projection magnitude onto the tense direction (partial correlation controlling for frequency/fertility; held-out R^2).
5) Causal ablation test (core): Remove/attenuate the shared tense direction from the underspecified input's representation at the localizing layer via difference-in-means projection removal / INLP nullspace projection (and, where available, an SAE tense feature). Measure whether (i) tense-over-specification rate drops toward the licensed-underspecified baseline and (ii) tensed-default pull shrinks. Critically, verify COMPETENCE is preserved: on the disambiguated-context and genuinely-tensed control items the model must still assign the CORRECT specific tense (ablation should restore underspecification only where warranted, not destroy tense comprehension). Compare against random-direction ablation and whole-hub English-steering baselines.
6) Directional causal test (steering, complementary): Steer the underspecified input's representation toward the past/present/future poles and confirm the tense direction causally controls the elicited reading (flip rate), establishing that the same direction that over-specifies is the one carrying tense. Steer in a tenseless language and verify it changes the elicited time reference without switching output language.
7) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify ablation is tense-specific (reduces spurious tense commitment but not unrelated aspectual/lexical content), does not switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), and does not degrade tensed-control performance. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 shows stronger tense imposition than the more multilingual BLOOM; test whether imposition magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the tense direction. Aspect probe: test whether models that correctly track aspect (imperfective/perfective) in tenseless languages show LESS spurious tense imposition (aspect as the appropriate substitute cue).
Evaluation metrics: tense-over-specification rate (underspecified vs disambiguated vs tensed-control); tensed-default pull rate and its partial correlation with resource/fertility; cross-lingual tense-direction alignment; projection magnitude of underspecified inputs onto the tense direction and its mediation of behavioral over-specification (held-out R^2 over baselines); ablation-induced reduction in over-specification and pull; competence preservation (correct tense on disambiguated/tensed controls, comprehension accuracy, fluency, off-target rate); steering flip rate; cross-model imposition-magnitude comparison; aspect-vs-tense interaction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Defining the 'licensed set of temporal readings' for underspecified tenseless sentences is subtle and can vary by pragmatic context; we restrict to carefully controlled templates with native-speaker verification and report inter-annotator agreement, and treat items with low agreement as excluded. 2) Tenselessness vs tensedness is correlated with language family, script, and resource level; the disambiguated-context and tensed-control conditions, plus within-language underspecified-vs-disambiguated contrasts, are designed to isolate the imposition effect but residual confounds may remain. 3) The tense direction from difference-in-means/LDA may entangle aspect or lexical time-adverb cues; we use multiple extraction methods, include an aspect probe, and apply specificity controls. 4) Ablation could harm fluency or over-suppress legitimate tense comprehension; we require competence preservation on disambiguated and genuinely-tensed items and report the full tradeoff. 5) Instruction-tuned models may have learned to hedge ('it could be past or present'), reducing measured over-specification; we test base models where available and treat hedging as a positive comprehension signal rather than a failure. 6) Elicitation tasks may themselves cue a tense (e.g., an English question word); we use tense-neutral elicitation and tenseless-language probes to mitigate. 7) If NO tense imposition is found — tenseless inputs remain appropriately underspecified — this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the shared temporal hub is robust to typological differences in tense grammaticalization, valuable either way. 8) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: evidentiality_flattening
Title: Losing the Source: Does the English-Scaffolded Shared Hub Erase Obligatory Evidentiality in Multilingual LLMs?
Short Hypothesis: Because the shared semantic hub of multilingual LLMs is scaffolded by languages (English) that do NOT grammatically mark evidentiality (the obligatory marking of information source: witnessed vs. inferred vs. hearsay), the model systematically 'flattens' this category when processing evidential languages (Turkish, Quechua, Bulgarian, Tibetan): the source-of-information distinction, which is grammatically mandatory and semantically load-bearing in those languages, is under-represented in the shared hub and lost during cross-lingual transfer. This produces a distinctive, measurable failure: the model conflates witnessed and hearsay readings, mis-tracks speaker certainty/commitment, and fails to preserve evidential meaning when translating or reasoning across the evidential/non-evidential boundary. We further hypothesize the residual evidential signal is carried in a shallow, language-specific subspace rather than the shared hub, and that this asymmetry is causally attributable to hub scaffolding rather than resource level.
Related Work: Two literatures meet but have never been connected. (1) Interpretability work shows multilingual LLMs share representations of morphosyntactic concepts—number, gender, tense—in feature directions that are causal and largely English-scaffolded (LLMs Share Representations of Latent Grammatical Concepts 2025; multilingual morphosyntactic probing 2021-2024; Deep Subjecthood 2021 shows higher-order grammatical alignment leaks across languages). Critically, ALL of this focuses on categories that English DOES mark (or can express), so a shared representation is unsurprising. (2) Linguistic typology establishes that evidentiality—grammaticalized marking of information source—is obligatory in Turkish, Quechua, Bulgarian, Tibetan, Tucanoan languages but only lexical/optional in English/Spanish (Aikhenvald; Evidentiality 2019; Typological variation 2025), and bilingual cognition work shows evidential marking asymmetrically shapes source-tracking and certainty judgments, with directional translation asymmetries (Tosun & Filipović 2025; Relations Between Language and Cognition 2018). NO prior work asks whether the celebrated SHARED grammatical hub, being scaffolded by a NON-evidential language, FAILS to represent an obligatory category—i.e., whether sharing turns from a strength into an erasure bug for categories absent in the dominant language. This is the mirror image of my prior 'tense imposition' proposal (imposing a category the target lacks); here the phenomenon is ERASING a category the target obligatorily marks, and unlike tense/gender/number it targets a category genuinely absent from the scaffolding language—a much sharper test of the shared-hub-as-English hypothesis. We uniquely (a) frame an obligatory-but-English-absent category as a stress test of the shared hub, (b) predict and measure evidential flattening and source conflation, (c) localize residual evidentiality to a shallow language-specific subspace, and (d) offer a causal patching test.
Abstract: Many languages—Turkish, Quechua, Bulgarian, Tibetan—grammatically require speakers to mark the SOURCE of every reported event: did they witness it, infer it, or hear it from someone else? This category, evidentiality, is obligatory and semantically load-bearing in these languages, yet it is not grammaticalized in English, the language that predominantly scaffolds the shared semantic hub of multilingual LLMs. We ask a simple question this asymmetry makes urgent: does the English-scaffolded shared hub FAIL to represent obligatory evidentiality, systematically 'flattening' the source-of-information distinction when the model processes evidential languages? We hypothesize that (1) evidential meaning (witnessed vs. inferred vs. hearsay) is under-represented in the shared hub and instead lingers in a shallow, language-specific subspace; (2) this produces measurable source conflation—the model confuses witnessed and hearsay readings and mis-tracks speaker certainty; and (3) evidential meaning is lost across the evidential/non-evidential boundary in translation and reasoning, in a directional pattern mirroring human bilinguals. We build a controlled multilingual suite of minimal evidential pairs (same event, different information source) in evidential languages (Turkish, Quechua, Bulgarian, Tibetan) versus non-evidential controls (English, Spanish), on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM. Using logit-lens/tuned-lens depth tracking, difference-in-means evidential probes, and activation patching, we measure where evidential information lives, whether it survives cross-lingual transfer, and whether patching the residual language-specific evidential signal restores source-faithful behavior. Metrics include evidential-probe depth and shared-hub accuracy, source-conflation rate, certainty-tracking error, translation evidential-preservation rate, and patching-induced restoration with competence controls.
Experiments:
1) Evidential minimal-pair suite: Construct ~400 minimal pairs in evidential languages (Turkish -mIş/-DI direct-vs-indirect; Bulgarian renarrative; Quechua and Tibetan where native-speaker access permits) where the SAME event is marked as (a) witnessed/firsthand, (b) inferred, or (c) hearsay, differing only in the evidential marker. Pair each with non-evidential controls in English/Spanish that can only express source lexically ('I saw that...', 'apparently...', 'I heard that...'). Tasks: (i) source-identification ('How does the speaker know this?' — forced choice witnessed/inferred/hearsay); (ii) certainty/commitment judgment (Likert-style, does the speaker vouch for the event?); (iii) evidential-NLI (does a witnessed-marked sentence entail/contradict a hearsay-marked one?); (iv) translation (evidential-language sentence -> English and back). Native-speaker verify markers and gold labels; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral flattening (H1): Measure source-conflation rate = fraction of minimal pairs on which the model fails to distinguish witnessed vs. hearsay (same source-identification answer or same certainty judgment despite different evidential markers). Compare against the model's ability to distinguish the LEXICALLY-marked English/Spanish controls (where the distinction is spelled out). Prediction: high conflation for grammatically-marked evidentiality in evidential languages, low conflation for lexically-marked controls—i.e., the model handles source when it is a content word but flattens it when it is an inflectional marker in an evidential language. Control for tokenizer fertility of the evidential morpheme and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2).
3) Representational localization (H2): Extract an evidential direction via difference-in-means between witnessed and hearsay representations at each layer, per language. Test (a) whether this direction is SHARED across evidential languages and with the English lexical-source direction (cross-lingual cosine alignment across layers), and (b) at what depth evidential meaning crystallizes and how strongly it projects into the shared hub (compared with tense/number directions as a within-model shared-category baseline). Prediction: unlike tense/number, the evidential direction is weak/shallow in the shared hub and stronger in early/language-specific layers. Mediation: regress behavioral conflation on shared-hub evidential-projection strength (partial correlation controlling for fertility/resource; held-out R^2).
4) Cross-lingual transfer loss (H3): Measure evidential-preservation rate in translation across the evidential/non-evidential boundary—does a Turkish hearsay-marked sentence get rendered into English with an appropriate source hedge, and does round-trip translation preserve source? Predict directional asymmetry mirroring bilingual humans (Tosun & Filipović 2025): evidential->English loses source more than English->evidential fails to add it, because the hub lacks a slot for the category. Compare source-preservation for evidential languages vs. tense-preservation (a category English marks) as a matched baseline.
5) Causal patching test: For items where source is conflated in the evidential-language pass, patch the residual language-specific evidential signal (extracted from the early/language-specific layers of the correctly-marked pass) into the later computation and measure whether source-faithful behavior is restored (correct source-identification, correct certainty, correct NLI). Complementary: steer along the evidential direction and confirm it causally controls the elicited source reading (flip rate witnessed<->hearsay) without switching output language. This localizes the failure to the shared hub's failure to READ a signal that is present shallowly, rather than to the signal being absent entirely.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify patching/steering is evidential-specific (changes source reading but not unrelated tense/aspect content), does not switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), and preserves general comprehension (competence probes). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 shows stronger flattening than the more multilingual BLOOM and Aya-23 (which see more evidential-language data); test whether flattening magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the evidential direction and with evidential-language training share.
Evaluation metrics: source-conflation rate (grammatical-evidential vs lexical-control); certainty-tracking error; evidential-NLI accuracy; shared-hub evidential-projection strength and crystallization depth (vs tense/number baseline); cross-lingual alignment of the evidential direction; translation evidential-preservation rate and directional asymmetry (vs tense-preservation baseline); mediation regression (held-out R^2); patching-induced restoration and steering flip rate; competence preservation, off-target rate; cross-model flattening comparison and its correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Reliable native-speaker annotation for Quechua/Tibetan may be hard to obtain; we can restrict the core study to Turkish and Bulgarian (well-resourced, clearly grammaticalized evidentiality) and treat Quechua/Tibetan as extensions where access permits. 2) Evidential markers differ in tokenizer fertility and frequency from the stem; we control with partial correlations and matched minimal pairs isolating the marker. 3) Evidentiality is correlated with language family, script, and resource level; the lexical-control (English/Spanish 'I heard that') and the within-model tense/number baselines are designed to isolate the 'grammatical category absent from the scaffolding language' pathway, but residual confounds may remain. 4) Difference-in-means evidential directions may entangle epistemic modality/certainty (which are related but distinct); we use multiple extraction methods and include certainty-only vs source-only probes to disentangle. 5) Instruction-tuned models may hedge ('the speaker may have heard this'), which we treat as a positive source-tracking signal rather than failure; we test base models where available. 6) Elicitation questions posed in English may themselves cue a source frame; we use target-language and neutral elicitation to mitigate. 7) Patching may have entangled effects; we report ambiguous cases and multiple granularities. 8) If NO flattening is found—evidential distinctions are preserved and shared—this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the shared hub represents even categories absent from its scaffolding language, strengthening the language-agnostic view; valuable either way. 9) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: honorific_register_flattening
Title: Who Is Speaking to Whom? Does the English-Scaffolded Shared Hub Flatten Obligatory Honorific Social Deixis in Multilingual LLMs?
Short Hypothesis: Because the shared semantic hub of multilingual LLMs is scaffolded by languages (English) that do NOT grammatically encode honorific social deixis (the obligatory marking of the speaker-addressee/referent social relationship: deferential vs. plain register), the model systematically 'flattens' this relational category when processing honorific languages (Korean, Japanese, Tibetan, Hindi). The speaker-addressee status relation, which is grammatically mandatory and semantically load-bearing in those languages, is under-represented in the shared hub and lost during cross-lingual transfer. This produces a distinctive, measurable failure: the model conflates deferential and plain readings, mis-tracks the encoded social relationship, fails to preserve register when translating or reasoning across the honorific/non-honorific boundary, and cannot maintain a consistent register within an honorific-language generation. We further hypothesize the residual honorific signal is carried in a shallow, language-specific subspace rather than the shared hub, that this asymmetry is causally attributable to hub scaffolding rather than resource level, and that a train-free intervention lifting/patching the honorific direction can restore register-faithful behavior.
Related Work: Two literatures meet but have never been connected. (1) Interpretability work shows multilingual LLMs share representations of morphosyntactic and stylistic concepts in causal, largely English-scaffolded feature directions (LLMs Share Representations of Latent Grammatical Concepts 2025; Analyzing Gender Representation in Multilingual Models 2022; LinguaLens SAE 2025 finds pragmatics in middle layers; Representation of Lexical Stylistic Features incl. formality 2023; The Geometry of Multilingual Representations 2022). Crucially, this work focuses on categories English marks or on formality as a lexical/stylistic gradient, not on RELATIONAL social deixis grammaticalized as obligatory inflection. (2) Honorifics work is either linguistic typology (Honorifics without [hon] 2023; Tibetic honorific register 2023; Korean/Japanese honorific processing 2010-2025), NLP classification (TyDiP politeness in 9 languages 2022), controlled generation (honorific-constrained NMT via side constraints 2016), or MONOLINGUAL model surprisal on Korean honorific mismatches (2024). NO prior work asks whether the celebrated SHARED grammatical/pragmatic hub, being scaffolded by a NON-honorific language, FAILS to represent obligatory honorific social deixis in generative multilingual LLMs, whether this causes register flattening and loss of the speaker-addressee relation, whether the residual signal lives in a shallow language-specific subspace, or whether a causal intervention restores register fidelity. Unlike my prior evidentiality proposal (an EPISTEMIC category: information source of a proposition), honorifics encode a RELATIONAL/interpersonal variable (the social relation between discourse participants), making this a sharper test of whether the hub represents interpersonal/social structure at all rather than only propositional content. This is orthogonal to all my prior proposals (binding, cultural compression, compute depth, provenance, tokenizer, operators, confidence, code-switch, number inversion, gender, tense, evidentiality).
Abstract: Many languages—Korean, Japanese, Tibetan, Hindi—grammatically require speakers to encode the social relationship between discourse participants: is the addressee or referent being addressed deferentially or plainly? This category, honorific social deixis, is obligatory and semantically load-bearing in these languages, yet it is not grammaticalized in English, the language that predominantly scaffolds the shared semantic hub of multilingual LLMs. We ask a simple question this asymmetry makes urgent: does the English-scaffolded shared hub FAIL to represent obligatory honorific social deixis, systematically 'flattening' the speaker-addressee social relation when the model processes honorific languages? We hypothesize that (1) honorific meaning (deferential vs. plain) is under-represented in the shared hub and instead lingers in a shallow, language-specific subspace; (2) this produces measurable register conflation—the model confuses deferential and plain readings and mis-tracks the encoded social relationship; (3) register is lost across the honorific/non-honorific boundary in translation and reasoning; and (4) the model fails to maintain a consistent register within honorific-language generation. We build a controlled multilingual suite of minimal honorific pairs (same propositional content, different register) in honorific languages (Korean, Japanese, Hindi, Tibetan where access permits) versus non-honorific controls (English), on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM. Using logit-lens/tuned-lens depth tracking, difference-in-means honorific probes, and activation patching, we measure where honorific information lives, whether it survives cross-lingual transfer and within-generation consistency, and whether patching the residual language-specific honorific signal restores register-faithful behavior. Metrics include honorific-probe depth and shared-hub accuracy, register-conflation rate, relationship-tracking error, translation register-preservation rate, within-generation register consistency, and patching-induced restoration with competence controls.
Experiments:
1) Honorific minimal-pair suite: Construct ~400 minimal pairs in honorific languages (Korean sentence-enders and subject honorific -si- across the plain/polite/deferential levels; Japanese teineigo/sonkeigo/kenjougo; Hindi tu/tum/aap addressee levels; Tibetan honorific register where native-speaker access permits) where the SAME propositional content is expressed with (a) deferential/honorific and (b) plain register, differing only in the honorific marking. Pair each with English controls that can only express the social relation lexically/periphrastically ('Sir, would you...', 'Hey, ...'). Tasks: (i) relationship-identification ('What is the social relationship between speaker and addressee?' — forced choice higher-status/equal/lower-status or deferential/plain); (ii) register-classification (is this deferential or plain?); (iii) honorific-NLI (does a deferentially-marked sentence entail/contradict a plainly-marked one about the same event, and about the social relation?); (iv) translation (honorific-language sentence -> English -> back, checking register preservation); (v) within-generation consistency (prompt the model to continue an honorific-language dialogue and measure whether it maintains the established register across sentences). Native-speaker verify markers, register levels, and gold labels; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral flattening (H1): Measure register-conflation rate = fraction of minimal pairs on which the model fails to distinguish deferential vs. plain (same relationship-identification answer or same register-classification despite different honorific markers). Compare against the model's ability to distinguish the LEXICALLY-marked English controls (where the relation is spelled out). Prediction: high conflation for grammatically-marked honorifics in honorific languages, low conflation for lexically-marked English controls—i.e., the model handles the social relation when it is a content word/phrase but flattens it when it is an inflectional/register marker in an honorific language. Control for tokenizer fertility of the honorific morpheme and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2).
3) Representational localization (H2): Extract an honorific direction via difference-in-means between deferential and plain representations at each layer, per language. Test (a) whether this direction is SHARED across honorific languages and with the English lexical-register direction (cross-lingual cosine alignment across layers), and (b) at what depth register crystallizes and how strongly it projects into the shared hub (compared with tense/number directions as a within-model shared-category baseline, and formality as a related-but-distinct stylistic baseline). Prediction: unlike tense/number, the honorific direction is weak/shallow in the shared hub and stronger in early/language-specific layers. Mediation: regress behavioral conflation on shared-hub honorific-projection strength (partial correlation controlling for fertility/resource; held-out R^2).
4) Cross-lingual transfer loss and within-generation consistency (H3): Measure register-preservation rate in translation across the honorific/non-honorific boundary—does a Korean deferential sentence get rendered into English with an appropriate deference marker, and does round-trip translation preserve register? Predict a directional asymmetry: honorific->English loses register more than English->honorific fails to add it, because the hub lacks a slot for the relational category. Separately measure within-generation register consistency: after establishing a register, does the model drift toward the plain (English-default-like) register over a multi-sentence continuation? Compare register-preservation against tense-preservation (a category English marks) as a matched baseline.
5) Causal patching test: For items where register is conflated in the honorific-language pass, patch the residual language-specific honorific signal (extracted from the early/language-specific layers of the correctly-marked pass) into the later computation and measure whether register-faithful behavior is restored (correct relationship-identification, correct register-classification, correct NLI, consistent generation). Complementary: steer along the honorific direction and confirm it causally controls the elicited register/relationship reading (flip rate deferential<->plain) without switching output language. This localizes the failure to the shared hub's failure to READ a signal that is present shallowly, rather than to the signal being absent entirely.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify patching/steering is honorific-specific (changes register/relationship reading but not unrelated tense/aspect/propositional content), does not switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), and preserves general comprehension (competence probes). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 shows stronger flattening than the more multilingual Aya-23 and BLOOM (which see more honorific-language data); test whether flattening magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the honorific direction and with honorific-language training share. Formality disentanglement: include a formality-only vs. honorific-only probe to check the model is not merely collapsing honorifics into a generic formality gradient.
Evaluation metrics: register-conflation rate (grammatical-honorific vs lexical-control); relationship-tracking error; honorific-NLI accuracy; shared-hub honorific-projection strength and crystallization depth (vs tense/number and formality baselines); cross-lingual alignment of the honorific direction; translation register-preservation rate and directional asymmetry (vs tense-preservation baseline); within-generation register-drift rate; mediation regression (held-out R^2); patching-induced restoration and steering flip rate; competence preservation, off-target rate; cross-model flattening comparison and its correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Reliable native-speaker annotation for Tibetan may be hard to obtain; we can restrict the core study to Korean, Japanese, and Hindi (well-resourced, clearly grammaticalized honorific systems) and treat Tibetan as an extension where access permits. 2) Honorific markers differ in tokenizer fertility and frequency from the stem; we control with partial correlations and matched minimal pairs isolating the marker. 3) Honorific vs. non-honorific status is correlated with language family, script, and resource level; the English lexical-control condition, the within-model tense/number baselines, and within-language deferential-vs-plain minimal-pair contrasts are designed to isolate the 'relational category absent from the scaffolding language' pathway, but residual confounds may remain. 4) Honorifics are closely related to formality/politeness as a stylistic gradient; we explicitly include a formality-only vs honorific-only probe and treat conflation of the two as an informative finding rather than a confound. 5) Difference-in-means honorific directions may entangle formality or lexical-choice features; we use multiple extraction methods and specificity controls. 6) Instruction-tuned models may have learned to be uniformly polite, reducing measured conflation in one direction; we test base models where available and use the plain-register direction as a symmetric check (the model must also correctly identify PLAIN register, not just default to deferential). 7) Elicitation questions posed in English may themselves cue a register frame; we use target-language and neutral elicitation to mitigate. 8) Patching may have entangled effects; we report ambiguous cases and multiple granularities. 9) If NO flattening is found—honorific distinctions are preserved, shared, and consistently generated—this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the shared hub represents even relational social-deixis categories absent from its scaffolding language, strengthening the language-agnostic view; valuable either way. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: spatial_frame_imposition
Title: Which Way Is Left? Does the English-Scaffolded Shared Hub Impose an Egocentric Spatial Frame of Reference onto Absolute-Frame Languages in Multilingual LLMs?
Short Hypothesis: Languages differ in their default spatial frame of reference (FoR): relative/egocentric (English/Dutch left-right-front-back) vs. absolute/allocentric (Guugu Yimithirr, Tzeltal, Balinese, Hausa use cardinal/geomorphic north-south-uphill-downhill). Because the shared semantic hub of multilingual LLMs is scaffolded by relative-frame languages, we hypothesize the model IMPOSES an egocentric relative frame when processing or generating for absolute-frame languages: it silently re-encodes absolute spatial descriptions into a relative coordinate system, mis-resolves spatial reference, defaults to egocentric readings on genuinely ambiguous scenes, and fails to preserve the absolute frame across translation and reasoning. We further hypothesize this imposition is mediated by a shared, ablatable 'egocentric-frame' direction, is causally attributable to hub scaffolding rather than resource level, and can be steered toward the correct absolute frame without harming spatial competence.
Related Work: Two literatures meet but have never been connected for text-only multilingual LLMs. (1) Cognitive-linguistic typology robustly establishes that languages divide into relative/egocentric vs. absolute/allocentric spatial frames of reference, that this is the domain where Whorfian effects are strongest (Levinson 'Semantic Typology and Spatial Conceptualization' 1998; 'Language and Cognition in Guugu Yimithirr' 1997; 'Uphill/Downhill in Tzeltal' 1993; 'Cultural background shapes reference-frame proclivity' 2015; axis-dependent FoR 2021/2022/2024), and that spatial terms split into functional vs. geometric classes (Spatial Terms in 12 Languages 2025). (2) Interpretability shows LLMs encode space as linear representations and 'space neurons' (Language Models Represent Space and Time 2023; Do LMs Know the Way to Rome 2021; causal space representations 2023) and process non-English inputs through an English-scaffolded shared hub (Do Llamas Work in English 2024; Semantic Hub Hypothesis 2024). The only work touching FoR in models is COMFORT (2024), which behaviorally shows VISION-language models default to English FoR conventions and fail cross-lingual FoR tests. CRITICALLY: (a) COMFORT is vision-language and purely behavioral, offering no mechanistic account; (b) no prior work asks whether TEXT-only multilingual LLMs re-encode absolute-frame descriptions into an egocentric coordinate system inside the shared hub; (c) none localizes an 'egocentric-frame' direction, tests whether it is shared and English-scaffolded, or causally intervenes to restore the absolute frame; and (d) unlike morphosyntactic categories in my prior proposals (tense, gender, evidentiality, honorifics), spatial FoR is a COORDINATE-SYSTEM/reference-frame property, a distinct and previously untested axis. We uniquely frame the relative/absolute FoR split as a mechanistic stress test of the shared hub, predict and localize egocentric-frame imposition, and offer a causal frame-steering fix.
Abstract: Languages encode spatial relations in fundamentally different coordinate systems: relative/egocentric frames (English 'to the left of the tree') versus absolute/allocentric frames (Guugu Yimithirr and Tzeltal say the equivalent of 'to the north of / uphill from the tree'). This is the domain where linguistic relativity effects are strongest in humans. Multilingual language models build a shared semantic hub scaffolded by relative-frame languages like English. We ask a simple question this asymmetry makes urgent: does the English-scaffolded shared hub IMPOSE an egocentric relative frame of reference onto inputs from absolute-frame languages, silently re-encoding absolute spatial descriptions into a relative coordinate system? We hypothesize that (1) the model mis-resolves spatial reference and defaults to egocentric readings on genuinely ambiguous scenes in absolute-frame languages; (2) the absolute frame is under-represented in the shared hub and lingers only in shallow, language-specific layers; (3) the absolute frame is lost across the absolute/relative boundary in translation and reasoning; and (4) an ablatable, shared 'egocentric-frame' direction mediates the imposition. We build a controlled multilingual suite of spatial-scene descriptions and reasoning items contrasting relative-frame languages (English, Dutch, Chinese) with absolute-frame ones (Balinese, Hausa, and Guugu Yimithirr/Tzeltal where native access permits), on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM. Using logit-lens/tuned-lens depth tracking, difference-in-means frame probes, activation patching, and steering, we measure where frame information lives, whether it survives transfer, and whether steering toward the absolute frame restores frame-faithful behavior. Metrics include egocentric-default rate, frame-conflation rate, shared-hub frame-projection, translation frame-preservation, and intervention recovery with competence controls.
Experiments:
1) Spatial FoR suite: Construct ~400 controlled spatial-scene items in which the SAME scene must be described/resolved under a relative (egocentric left-right-front-back) versus absolute (cardinal/geomorphic north-south-uphill-downhill) frame, in relative-frame languages (English, Dutch, Chinese) and absolute-frame languages (Balinese, Hausa; Guugu Yimithirr / Tzeltal as extensions where native-speaker access permits). Tasks: (i) frame-identification (given a spatial description, which coordinate system is it using?); (ii) referent-resolution ('the ball is <spatial-term> the box; where is the ball?' — measure whether the model resolves egocentrically vs. absolutely); (iii) rotation-invariance test (rotate the observer 180 degrees: an absolute description's answer stays fixed, a relative one flips — measure which invariance the model applies); (iv) ambiguous-scene default (a scene resolvable under either frame — measure which the model picks per language); (v) translation (absolute-frame sentence -> English -> back, checking frame preservation); (vi) within-generation frame consistency (continue an absolute-frame spatial narrative and measure drift toward egocentric terms). Native-speaker verify frame assignments and gold answers; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral egocentric imposition (H1): Measure egocentric-default rate on ambiguous scenes and frame-conflation rate = fraction of items where the model applies a relative reading despite absolute-frame marking (e.g., failing the rotation-invariance test by flipping an absolute description). Compare against relative-frame-language controls (where egocentric IS correct). Prediction: high egocentric imposition specifically for absolute-frame languages; correct rotation-invariance in relative-frame controls. Control for tokenizer fertility of spatial terms and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test frame-type adds predictive power beyond resource/fertility).
3) Representational localization (H2): Extract an egocentric-vs-absolute frame direction via difference-in-means between relative-framed and absolute-framed scene representations at each layer, per language. Test (a) whether the egocentric-frame direction is SHARED across languages and English-scaffolded (cross-lingual cosine alignment across layers; strongest in mid/shared-hub layers), and (b) whether the absolute-frame representation is weak/shallow in the hub and stronger in early/language-specific layers (compared with a within-model shared baseline like tense/number). Use the space/geospatial linear probes (Language Models Represent Space and Time 2023) to test whether absolute-frame inputs nonetheless get mapped onto an egocentric coordinate axis in the hub. Mediation: regress behavioral egocentric-default on shared-hub egocentric-frame projection strength (partial correlation controlling for fertility/resource; held-out R^2).
4) Cross-lingual transfer loss and within-generation consistency (H3): Measure frame-preservation rate in translation across the absolute/relative boundary; predict directional asymmetry — absolute->English loses the absolute frame more than English->absolute fails to add it, because the hub lacks a slot for allocentric coordinates. Measure within-generation frame-drift toward egocentric terms over multi-sentence absolute-frame continuations. Compare against a category-English-marks baseline (e.g., tense-preservation) as a matched control.
5) Causal steering/patching test (core): (a) Steer along the frame direction toward the absolute pole for absolute-frame inputs and measure whether frame-faithful behavior is restored (correct rotation-invariance, correct referent resolution, absolute frame-identification, consistent generation), and confirm the direction causally controls the elicited frame (flip rate egocentric<->absolute) without switching output language. (b) For conflated items, patch the residual language-specific absolute-frame signal (from early/language-specific layers of the correctly-framed pass) into later computation and test restoration — localizing the failure to the shared hub's failure to READ a shallowly-present signal rather than to its absence.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify steering/patching is frame-specific (changes coordinate system but not the identity of objects/other spatial content), does not switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), and preserves general spatial competence (competence probes on relative-frame controls, which must remain correct). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 shows stronger egocentric imposition than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether imposition magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the frame direction and with training share of absolute-frame languages. Axis control: following axis-dependent FoR findings (2021/2022), test whether imposition is stronger on the lateral (left-right) axis than the sagittal (front-back) axis.
Evaluation metrics: egocentric-default rate and frame-conflation rate (absolute-frame languages vs relative-frame controls); rotation-invariance error; frame-identification accuracy; shared-hub egocentric-frame projection strength and absolute-frame crystallization depth (vs shared baseline); cross-lingual alignment of the frame direction; translation frame-preservation rate and directional asymmetry (vs tense-preservation baseline); within-generation frame-drift rate; mediation regression (held-out R^2); steering flip rate and patching-induced restoration; competence preservation, off-target rate; cross-model imposition comparison and correlation with training share; lateral-vs-sagittal axis interaction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Native-speaker annotation for Guugu Yimithirr/Tzeltal is very hard to obtain, and these ultra-low-resource languages may be barely represented in the models; we restrict the CORE study to better-attested absolute/mixed-frame contrasts (e.g., Balinese, Hausa, and relative-frame Dutch/Chinese/English) and treat the classic languages as illustrative extensions where access permits, framing the study around the relative-vs-absolute contrast rather than any single exotic language. 2) If absolute-frame languages are essentially absent from pretraining, the model may never have learned their frame at all, confounding 'imposition' with 'ignorance'; we address this by including languages the models plausibly saw (Hausa, Indonesian/Balinese) and by the shallow-language-specific-signal test in Exp 3/5 (imposition requires the absolute signal to be present-but-overwritten, not absent). 3) Frame type is correlated with language family, script, and resource level; the within-scene relative-vs-absolute contrast, rotation-invariance test, and relative-frame controls isolate the frame pathway but residual confounds may remain. 4) Difference-in-means frame directions may entangle lexical spatial-term identity; we use multiple extraction methods, object-identity specificity controls, and the geospatial linear-probe cross-check. 5) Instruction-tuned models may hedge on ambiguous scenes; we test base models where available and treat appropriate hedging as a positive competence signal. 6) Elicitation posed in English may itself cue an egocentric frame; we use target-language and frame-neutral elicitation to mitigate. 7) Steering/patching may harm fluency or over-impose the absolute frame on relative-frame controls; we require competence preservation and report the full tradeoff. 8) If NO imposition is found — absolute frames are preserved, shared, and consistently generated — this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the shared hub represents allocentric coordinate systems absent from its scaffolding language, valuable either way. 9) Limited to open ~7-8B text-only models; may not extend to frontier scale or multimodal models.

Name: individuation_imposition_classifier
Title: One or Many? Does the English-Scaffolded Shared Hub Impose Obligatory Individuation and Number onto Number-Neutral Classifier-Language Nouns?
Short Hypothesis: Classifier languages (Mandarin, Japanese, Korean, Vietnamese, Thai) leave bare nouns NUMBER-NEUTRAL and countability UNDERSPECIFIED (a bare noun can mean one or many; individuation is supplied only by an explicit numeral+classifier), whereas the English that scaffolds the shared semantic hub obligatorily marks singular/plural and forces a count/mass reading. We hypothesize the shared hub IMPOSES obligatory individuation and number onto number-neutral classifier-language inputs: the model spuriously commits to a singular or plural (and count-vs-mass) reading of genuinely underspecified bare nouns, tracking the English default rather than target-language number-neutrality, mis-tracks quantity in downstream reasoning, and loses number-neutrality across translation. This imposition is mediated by a shared, ablatable 'number/individuation' direction, is causally attributable to hub scaffolding rather than resource level, and can be steered back toward number-neutrality without harming quantity competence.
Related Work: Two literatures meet but have never been connected for multilingual reasoning. (1) Interpretability shows grammatical NUMBER is a linear, causal encoding used by models (Probing for the Usage of Grammatical Number 2022), that morphosyntactic number is shared cross-lingually but SAE-biased (multilingual morphosyntactic probing 2020-2023; Universal and Independent 2022 shows mBERT favors Standard-Average-European categories), that models represent COUNTING via an internal counter (Understanding Counting Mechanisms / CountScope 2025), and that Chinese CLASSIFIER prediction is handled poorly by autoregressive LLMs, driven mainly by the head noun (From BERT to LLMs 2025). (2) Typology establishes the classifier-vs-plural-marking trade-off: classifier languages tend to LACK obligatory plural marking and leave bare nouns number-neutral, with countability/individuation supplied by numeral+classifier (Aikhenvald 2000; Defining numeral classifiers / WACL 2022; sortal vs mensural classifiers 2017/2019; distribution/complexity of gender and numeral classifiers 2019; statistical explanation via plural markers 2018). CRITICALLY: all interpretability work on number treats number/count as a property to be recovered where it is marked; none asks whether the shared hub IMPOSES obligatory number/individuation onto languages where bare nouns are legitimately number-neutral, whether this causes spurious singular/plural commitment and quantity errors in reasoning, whether the residual number-neutral signal lives in a shallow language-specific subspace, or whether a causal intervention restores neutrality. Unlike my prior imposition/flattening proposals (tense, gender, evidentiality, honorifics, spatial frames), this targets the COUNT/MASS and NUMBER-NEUTRALITY / individuation axis grounded in the classifier-vs-plural trade-off - a distinct, previously untested category. It is orthogonal to the Chinese-classifier-prediction paper (a monolingual prediction task) because we ask the reverse question: does forcing English-style obligatory number CORRUPT cross-lingual quantity reasoning about number-neutral nouns.
Abstract: Languages differ in how they encode quantity. English obligatorily marks singular vs plural on every noun and forces a count-vs-mass reading. Classifier languages such as Mandarin, Japanese, Korean, Vietnamese and Thai do the opposite: a bare noun is NUMBER-NEUTRAL and its countability is left underspecified, with individuation supplied only by an explicit numeral plus a shape/kind classifier. Multilingual language models build a shared semantic hub scaffolded by English. We ask a simple question this asymmetry makes urgent: does the English-scaffolded hub IMPOSE obligatory individuation and number onto number-neutral classifier-language inputs, silently committing bare nouns to a singular or plural (and count or mass) reading they do not grammatically have? We hypothesize that (1) the model spuriously fixes a specific number/countability reading of genuinely underspecified bare nouns, tracking the English default; (2) number-neutrality is under-represented in the shared hub and lingers only in shallow, language-specific layers; (3) neutrality is lost across the classifier/non-classifier boundary in translation and mis-tracked in quantity reasoning; and (4) a shared, ablatable number/individuation direction mediates the imposition. We build a controlled multilingual suite contrasting classifier languages (Mandarin, Japanese, Korean, Vietnamese) with number-marking controls (English, Spanish, Russian), on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5 and BLOOM. Using logit-lens/tuned-lens depth tracking, difference-in-means number probes, activation patching and steering, we measure where number information lives, whether neutrality survives transfer, and whether steering toward number-neutrality restores faithful behaviour. Metrics include spurious-number-commitment rate, English-default pull, shared-hub number-projection on bare nouns, translation neutrality-preservation, quantity-reasoning error, and intervention recovery with competence controls.
Experiments:
1) Number-neutrality suite: Construct ~400 controlled items in classifier languages (Mandarin, Japanese, Korean, Vietnamese; Thai as an extension where native access permits) each containing a BARE noun that is genuinely number-neutral and countability-underspecified in context (no numeral+classifier, no explicit plural/quantity cue), paired with (a) English/Spanish/Russian number-marking-language translations that grammar FORCES into singular or plural (and count/mass), and (b) minimal disambiguating variants that add an explicit numeral+classifier (or 'many'/'one') licensing a specific number. Native-speaker-verify the licensed readings (that the bare form admits both singular and plural / count and mass) and report inter-annotator agreement. Tasks: (i) number-elicitation ('Is this one thing or more than one?' - measure whether the model commits vs stays neutral/underspecified); (ii) count/mass classification (does the model treat the bare noun as count or mass?); (iii) number-NLI (does a bare-noun sentence ENTAIL its explicitly-singular or explicitly-plural paraphrase? A faithful model should say NEUTRAL for both); (iv) quantity reasoning (a short scenario where the number-neutral noun must be counted/aggregated - does the model impose a wrong default quantity?); (v) translation (classifier-language bare noun -> English -> back, checking whether obligatory number is silently added and whether round-trip preserves neutrality). Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral imposition (H1): Measure spurious-number-commitment rate = fraction of number-neutral items on which the model commits to a single number/countability reading as if obligatory (on elicitation, NLI, or count/mass tasks). Compare against the disambiguated variants (model should follow the numeral+classifier) and the number-marking-language controls (where commitment IS correct). Prediction: high spurious commitment specifically for bare nouns in classifier languages, near-zero on disambiguated variants and appropriate commitment on controls. Control for tokenizer fertility of the noun and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test classifier-language status adds predictive power beyond resource/fertility).
3) English-default pull (H2): Test whether the committed reading tracks the ENGLISH default (e.g., a bare countable noun defaulting to singular, or a bare mass-like noun to mass) rather than target-language pragmatics. Define English-default-pull rate = fraction of commitment cases whose reading matches the English forced paraphrase. Compare across classifier languages; predict higher pull for lower-resource classifier languages (Vietnamese > Korean ~ Japanese ~ Mandarin). Partial correlations controlling for resource/fertility.
4) Representational localization (H3): Extract a singular-vs-plural (and count-vs-mass) number/individuation direction via difference-in-means between explicitly-singular and explicitly-plural representations at each layer, per language (following Probing for the Usage of Grammatical Number 2022). Test (a) whether the direction is SHARED across languages and English-scaffolded (cross-lingual cosine alignment across layers; strongest in mid/shared-hub layers), and (b) whether a BARE number-neutral noun nonetheless projects strongly onto a definite pole of this direction in the shared hub (the hub assigns it a number it lacks), while any residual neutrality signal is stronger in early/language-specific layers. Use CountScope-style counter probes (Understanding Counting Mechanisms 2025) as a cross-check on whether the hub injects a definite count. Baseline: tense/gender directions as a within-model shared-category comparison. Mediation: regress behavioral commitment/pull on shared-hub number-projection strength of the bare noun (partial correlation controlling for fertility/resource; held-out R^2).
5) Cross-lingual transfer loss (H4): Measure neutrality-preservation rate in translation across the classifier/non-classifier boundary; predict a directional asymmetry - classifier->English silently ADDS obligatory number more than English->classifier fails to strip it, because the hub lacks a number-neutral slot. Measure within-generation number-drift: after a number-neutral setup, does the model drift toward committing English-style number over a continuation? Compare neutrality-preservation against a category-English-marks baseline (e.g., tense-preservation) as a matched control.
6) Causal steering/patching test (core): (a) Steer the bare-noun representation toward the NEUTRAL region (e.g., the midpoint / null-projection of the number direction) and measure whether faithful underspecification is restored (correct NEUTRAL on NLI, no spurious count/mass commitment, correct quantity reasoning), and confirm the direction causally controls the elicited number (flip rate singular<->plural) without switching output language. (b) For committed items, patch the residual language-specific number-neutral signal (from early/language-specific layers of the bare-noun pass) into later computation and test restoration - localizing the failure to the shared hub OVERWRITING a shallowly-present neutrality signal rather than to its absence. Compare against random-direction ablation and whole-hub English-steering baselines.
7) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify steering/patching is number-specific (changes number/countability but not the noun's identity or other content), does not switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), and preserves quantity competence (on disambiguated numeral+classifier items and number-marking controls the model must still get the CORRECT specific number - restoring neutrality only where warranted). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 shows stronger imposition than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM/Qwen (which see more classifier-language data); test whether imposition magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the number direction and with classifier-language training share. Additionally test the classifier-obligatoriness interaction: imposition should be strongest for bare nouns and vanish once an overt numeral+classifier is present.
Evaluation metrics: spurious-number-commitment rate (classifier bare nouns vs disambiguated vs number-marking controls); English-default-pull rate and its partial correlation with resource/fertility; count/mass classification error; number-NLI NEUTRAL-accuracy; shared-hub number-projection strength on bare nouns and crystallization depth (vs tense/gender baseline); cross-lingual alignment of the number direction; translation neutrality-preservation rate and directional asymmetry (vs tense-preservation baseline); within-generation number-drift rate; quantity-reasoning error; mediation regression (held-out R^2); steering flip rate and patching-induced restoration; competence preservation, off-target rate; cross-model imposition comparison and correlation with training share; bare-vs-classifier-present interaction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Native-speaker annotation of 'genuine number-neutrality' for bare nouns is subtle and context-dependent; we restrict to carefully controlled contexts with native-speaker verification, report inter-annotator agreement, and exclude low-agreement items. 2) Classifier-language status is correlated with language family, script (logographic Mandarin/Japanese), and resource level; the disambiguated (numeral+classifier) variants, number-marking controls (English/Spanish/Russian), and within-language bare-vs-marked contrasts are designed to isolate the number-neutrality pathway, but residual confounds may remain. 3) Difference-in-means number directions may entangle count/mass, definiteness, or lexical features;
