we use multiple extraction methods, the CountScope counter-probe cross-check, and specificity controls. 4) Some classifier languages DO have optional plural markers (e.g., Mandarin -men on humans, Korean -deul); we restrict bare-noun items to contexts where number is genuinely unmarked and treat optional-plural items as a separate analysis. 5) Instruction-tuned models may hedge ('one or more'), which we treat as a positive neutrality signal rather than failure; we test base models where available. 6) Elicitation posed in English may itself cue obligatory number; we use target-language and number-neutral elicitation to mitigate. 7) Steering toward neutrality could harm quantity competence or fluency; we require competence preservation on disambiguated and control items and report the full tradeoff. 8) Logographic tokenization may complicate depth measurement; we control for fertility and treat logographic vs alphabetic classifier languages (Mandarin/Japanese vs Korean/Vietnamese) as an informative contrast. 9) If NO imposition is found - bare nouns remain appropriately number-neutral and are preserved across transfer - this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the shared hub represents number-neutrality despite its English scaffolding, valuable either way. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: script_direction_mental_timeline
Title: Does the Model Read Time Left-to-Right? Script-Direction Effects on the Spatial Mental Timeline in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs encode an internal spatial mental timeline (mapping earlier/later onto a left-right axis), and its polarity is influenced by the reading direction of the language being processed - just as it is in humans. Crucially, because the shared semantic hub is scaffolded by left-to-right (LTR) languages like English, we hypothesize the model imposes an LTR (past-left/future-right) timeline even when processing right-to-left (RTL) languages such as Arabic and Hebrew, failing to reproduce the reversed RTL timeline that human RTL readers exhibit. This mismatch produces a measurable, script-direction-dependent spatial-temporal bias that is linearly decodable, causally steerable, and predictive of behavioral space-time congruency errors.
Related Work: A large cross-cultural cognitive-science literature robustly establishes that reading/writing direction shapes the human spatial mental timeline: LTR readers (English) map earlier->left/later->right and are faster on left='earlier' responses, whereas RTL readers (Arabic, Hebrew, Farsi) show the reverse, and even generational/orthographic script changes flip the mapping (Ouellet/Fuhrman & Boroditsky 2010/2012; Tversky/Weger 2007; Bergen 2005/2023; Iranian RTL WM 2024; Arabic-English bilingual language-activation 2024; 'Direction of reading not writing' 2025). Separately, interpretability work shows LLMs encode space and time as linear, causal directions with dedicated space/time neurons and temporal heads (Language Models Represent Space and Time 2023; Temporal Heads 2025; The Other Mind 2025; Time Travel Engine 2026 finds cross-lingual topological isomorphism of temporal subspaces), and that directional/reversal biases are intrinsic to causal Transformers (Reversal Curse; Directional Optimization Asymmetry 2025). CLIP-style work even finds a positional-embedding attention gradient that breaks left-right symmetry (2026). BUT no prior work connects these two literatures: none tests whether a multilingual LLM possesses a SPATIAL (left-right) mental timeline, whether its polarity depends on the reading direction of the input language, or whether the English-scaffolded hub IMPOSES an LTR timeline onto RTL languages instead of the reversed timeline human RTL readers show. Unlike my prior proposals (grammatical categories, facts, reasoning depth, spatial frames of reference), this targets the SPACE-TIME MAPPING / script-directionality axis - a distinct, previously untested phenomenon with a rich human baseline for comparison.
Abstract: In humans, the direction in which we read shapes how we spatialize time: left-to-right (LTR) readers place the past on the left and the future on the right, while right-to-left (RTL) readers of Arabic and Hebrew reverse this mapping. Multilingual language models are known to encode linear representations of time, but it is unknown whether they possess an analogous SPATIAL mental timeline and, if so, whether its orientation depends on the reading direction of the language being processed. We ask a simple question: does a multilingual LLM 'read time' left-to-right, and does it do so regardless of language? We hypothesize (1) the model encodes a decodable left-right spatial axis onto which temporal order is mapped; (2) this timeline is LTR-scaffolded by dominant LTR languages; and (3) because the shared hub is LTR-centric, the model IMPOSES an LTR timeline when processing RTL languages, failing to reproduce the reversed timeline human RTL readers show. We build a controlled multilingual space-time congruency suite (temporal-order judgments and spatial-placement tasks) in LTR (English, French, Chinese) and RTL (Arabic, Hebrew, Farsi) languages, on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM. Using linear probes for a temporal-order-vs-left-right axis, behavioral congruency measures, activation patching, and steering, we test whether the space-time mapping is decodable, whether its polarity flips (or fails to flip) with input language, and whether steering the axis causally changes temporal-order behavior. Metrics include probe axis-alignment and polarity, RTL-vs-LTR congruency-effect direction, imposition rate (LTR bias on RTL inputs), steering flip rate, and cross-model comparison against human effect sizes.
Experiments:
1) Space-time congruency suite: Construct ~400 controlled items instantiating classic human paradigms in text form, in LTR (English, French, Chinese) and RTL (Arabic, Hebrew, Farsi) languages, native-speaker verified. Tasks: (i) spatial-placement - given an ordered sequence of events (e.g., tadpole->frog, or dated events), ask the model to place them on a left-right line and record the assigned left/right positions of earlier vs later items; (ii) temporal-order congruency - present a two-alternative response mapping where 'earlier'/'later' are bound to a 'left'/'right' option and measure accuracy/latency-proxy (log-prob margin) as a function of congruent (earlier=left) vs incongruent (earlier=right) mapping; (iii) directional-cue completion - prompts like 'the past is to the ___' / 'the future lies to the ___' and measure left/right token probabilities. Include number-line and generic ordering controls (alphabet ordering) to separate a generic sequence-space mapping from a specifically TEMPORAL one, and non-directional temporal controls (top/bottom) to test axis specificity. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral timeline polarity (H1/H2): Compute a per-language space-time congruency effect = advantage (higher accuracy / log-prob margin) for earlier=left vs earlier=right mappings. Test H1 (a nonzero effect exists) and measure its POLARITY per language. Predict LTR languages show an earlier=left (LTR) advantage. Test H3: RTL languages ALSO show an LTR-polarity advantage (imposition) rather than the reversed earlier=right advantage human RTL readers show. Define imposition rate = fraction of RTL items where the model applies LTR polarity. Compare against the human effect-size direction from the cognitive-science literature as an external benchmark. Control for tokenizer fertility and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test reading-direction adds predictive power beyond resource/fertility).
3) Representational localization (linear timeline probe): Following Language Models Represent Space and Time (2023), train a linear probe to predict temporal ORDER (rank of an event in a sequence) from hidden states, and separately probe for a left-right spatial axis (from explicit left/right descriptions). Test whether the temporal-order direction ALIGNS with the left-right spatial direction (cosine alignment across layers) - i.e., whether time is literally mapped onto the LR spatial axis internally. Measure the POLARITY of this alignment per input language and test whether it is LTR-scaffolded (aligned with the English polarity) even for RTL inputs. Compare against tense/space direction baselines and the alphabet-order control (to show the mapping is temporal-specific, not merely generic-sequence).
4) Cross-lingual sharing vs language-specificity: Measure cross-lingual cosine alignment of the temporal-order-onto-LR direction across languages and layers. Test whether a single shared LTR timeline axis governs all languages (strong alignment, LTR polarity everywhere) versus a language-specific axis that flips for RTL languages (mirroring humans). Correlate any residual RTL-polarity signal with depth (predict: RTL-reversed signal, if present, is shallow/early and language-specific; the imposed LTR signal dominates in the shared hub).
5) Causal steering/patching test (core): (a) Steer along the temporal-order-onto-LR axis (toward the RTL-reversed polarity) for RTL-language inputs and measure whether the model's spatial-placement and congruency behavior flips to the human-RTL pattern (flip rate), confirming the axis causally drives behavior. (b) For RTL items where the model imposes an LTR mapping, patch in any shallow RTL-polarity signal (from early/language-specific layers) into later computation and test whether it corrects the imposition - localizing the imposition to the shared hub OVERWRITING a shallowly-present RTL signal versus the RTL signal being absent. Compare against random-direction steering and whole-hub English-steering baselines. Verify steering does not switch output language (off-target rate) and preserves temporal-ORDER accuracy (the model must still know which event is earlier - only the spatial mapping should change).
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify the effect is (i) temporal-specific (present for time but weaker/absent for the alphabet-order control), (ii) axis-specific (left-right, not top-bottom, unless the model shows a vertical Mandarin-style timeline - itself an informative finding), and (iii) not merely a lexical 'left'/'right' frequency artifact (balance left/right token frequencies). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 shows stronger LTR imposition than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether imposition magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the timeline axis and with RTL-language training share. Bonus: test whether Chinese (LTR-horizontal but historically vertical) shows any vertical-timeline signal.
Evaluation metrics: per-language space-time congruency effect size and polarity (vs human effect-size direction); imposition rate on RTL inputs; temporal-order-onto-LR probe alignment and polarity per language and layer; cross-lingual axis alignment; steering flip rate and patching-induced correction rate; temporal-order accuracy preservation and off-target rate; temporal-vs-alphabet-order specificity; left-right-vs-top-bottom axis specificity; cross-model imposition comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) A text-only LLM has no embodied reading experience, so an internal spatial timeline, if present, arises purely from co-occurrence statistics (e.g., text describing timelines, charts, 'left' associated with past); this is exactly what makes the question interesting, but it means a null result (no spatial timeline) is plausible and would itself be informative about the limits of the LLM-human analogy. 2) Reading direction is confounded with language family, script, and resource level; the LTR/RTL contrast plus the alphabet-order and top-bottom controls and within-language congruent-vs-incongruent manipulation are designed to isolate the reading-direction pathway, but residual confounds may remain. 3) 'Left'/'right' token frequencies and lexical associations differ across languages; we balance and control for these and use log-prob margins rather than raw preferences. 4) Linear probes for a temporal-order-onto-LR axis may capture a generic ordinal-sequence direction rather than a specifically temporal spatialization; the alphabet-order control and tense baselines address this. 5) Instruction-tuned models may verbally hedge or default to conventional 'timelines go left to right' regardless of language, which would itself confirm LTR imposition; we test base models where available. 6) Steering could harm fluency or temporal-order accuracy; we require order accuracy preservation and report the full tradeoff. 7) Human effect sizes are behavioral and embodied; our LLM-human comparison is qualitative (direction/polarity), not a claim of identical mechanism. 8) If RTL languages show the correctly REVERSED timeline (matching human RTL readers) rather than LTR imposition, this is an equally valuable positive result showing the model learns script-direction-specific space-time mappings from text alone. 9) Limited to open ~7-8B text-only models; may not extend to frontier scale or multimodal models.

Name: cross_lingual_idiom_leakage
Title: Wrong Idiom, Right Meaning: Cross-Lingual Figurative Leakage from Translation-Equivalent Idioms in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: When a multilingual LLM reads an idiom in a lower-resource language, its shared semantic hub does not primarily retrieve the *target-language* idiom's figurative meaning; instead it leaks in the figurative interpretation of the nearest *translation-equivalent idiom in a dominant (English) language*. This 'figurative leakage' produces two signature failures: (a) for target-language idioms with a matching English idiom (shared idioms), figurative retrieval succeeds by borrowing from English; (b) for target-language-*unique* idioms with no English equivalent, figurative retrieval fails and the model falls back to a literal (compositional) reading far more than in English — because the hub has no shared idiom to borrow from. This leakage is mechanistically localizable, predicts a distinctive uniqueness-vs-shared error gap, and is causally testable by patching in the target-language idiom's figurative signal.
Related Work: Monolingual mechanistic work localizes idiom comprehension to a figurative-retrieval-vs-literal 'tug of war' in early layers with dedicated 'Idiom Heads' and competing figurative/literal pathways (Tug-of-war 2025; Anatomy of an Idiom 2025; How Are Idioms Processed 2023; Understanding Memorization Recall 2023), all in English. Multilingual/cross-lingual idiom work is behavioral or task-based: PIE disambiguation transfer improves for 'shared idioms' with English lexical overlap (MultiCoPIE 2025), benchmarks show figurative-hallucination and translation failures (FFEHallu 2026; Mediom 2026; IdiomX 2026), and figurative *generation* steering directions transfer across languages (Cross-Lingual Steering 2026). Cognitive science shows bilinguals activate L1 idiom meanings when reading L2 translations, with culture-specific and translatability effects (Cross-language activation 2023; Bilingual idiom processing 2016; tug of war native/bilingual 2019). NO prior work asks the specific mechanistic question: does the shared hub retrieve figurative meaning by *borrowing from a translation-equivalent dominant-language idiom* rather than from the target-language idiom itself, and does this predict a systematic shared-vs-unique idiom failure gap plus an elevated literal-fallback rate for target-unique idioms? We uniquely (a) reframe cross-lingual idiom failure as figurative leakage/borrowing in the shared hub, (b) distinguish shared vs. target-unique idioms as a controlled contrast, (c) mechanistically localize whether the retrieved figurative signal is English-sourced, and (d) offer a causal patching test. This is orthogonal to prior monolingual mechanistic idiom work (no cross-lingual sourcing question) and to cross-lingual steering (which studies generation, not misretrieval of the wrong idiom's meaning).
Abstract: Idioms mean something other than the sum of their words, and their figurative meanings are culturally and linguistically specific. Prior mechanistic work shows that in English, language models retrieve an idiom's figurative meaning early while suppressing its literal reading. We ask a simple cross-lingual question: when a multilingual model reads an idiom in a lower-resource language, where does the figurative meaning come from? We hypothesize 'figurative leakage'—the English-scaffolded shared hub retrieves the figurative meaning of the nearest *translation-equivalent English idiom* rather than the target-language idiom itself. This predicts a sharp contrast: for SHARED idioms (with a matching English idiom, e.g., 'break the ice'), figurative retrieval succeeds by borrowing from English; but for target-language-UNIQUE idioms with no English counterpart, the hub has nothing to borrow, so the model falls back to a literal, compositional reading far more than it would in English. We build a controlled multilingual idiom suite partitioned into shared vs. target-unique idioms across typologically diverse languages, on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM. Using logit-lens/tuned-lens tracking, figurative-vs-literal probes, and activation patching, we (1) measure the shared-vs-unique figurative-retrieval and literal-fallback gap, (2) test whether the retrieved figurative signal decodes into the English idiom's meaning (leakage), and (3) causally patch in the target-language idiom's figurative signal to restore correct interpretation. Metrics include shared-vs-unique figurative-accuracy gap, literal-fallback rate, English-leakage decoding rate, and patching-induced recovery with competence controls. Our work recasts multilingual idiom failure as figurative borrowing in a shared hub.
Experiments:
1) Controlled idiom suite: Assemble ~500 idioms across typologically diverse languages (e.g., Spanish, German, Turkish, Hindi, Arabic, Chinese) partitioned into (a) SHARED idioms with a direct English translation-equivalent (matching form/meaning, e.g., 'break the ice'), (b) EQUIVALENT-MEANING idioms with a different-form English idiom conveying the same figurative meaning, and (c) TARGET-UNIQUE idioms with no English idiom equivalent (culturally specific). Each idiom appears in (i) a figurative-biasing context and (ii) a literal-biasing context, with native-speaker-verified gold figurative and literal paraphrases, and a multiple-choice interpretation probe (figurative / literal / distractor). English idioms serve as the within-model ceiling. Report inter-annotator agreement; release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral shared-vs-unique gap (H1): On figurative-biasing contexts, measure figurative-interpretation accuracy and literal-fallback rate (fraction choosing/generating the literal compositional reading) for SHARED vs. EQUIVALENT-MEANING vs. TARGET-UNIQUE idioms, per language, benchmarked against English. Prediction: figurative accuracy is high for shared idioms and drops sharply for target-unique idioms, while literal-fallback rises specifically for target-unique idioms; the gap widens for lower-resource languages. Control for idiom frequency, tokenizer fertility, and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test idiom-uniqueness adds predictive power beyond frequency/fertility/resource).
3) Figurative leakage decoding (H2, core): Using logit-lens/tuned-lens at the idiom's final token, test whether the retrieved figurative signal for a SHARED target-language idiom decodes preferentially into the ENGLISH idiom's figurative-meaning tokens (leakage) rather than the target-language paraphrase tokens. Define an English-leakage decoding rate = fraction of shared idioms whose mid-layer figurative signal aligns more with the English figurative meaning than the target-language one. Compare against monolingual English idioms (no leakage baseline) and against target-unique idioms (where no English idiom exists, so no leakage is possible and figurative signal should be weak/absent). Extract per-idiom figurative-vs-literal directions via difference-in-means (following the monolingual tug-of-war mechanism) and measure cross-lingual alignment of the figurative direction between the target idiom and its English equivalent.
4) Localization: Identify at which layers the figurative interpretation is retrieved for shared vs. unique idioms, and whether 'Idiom Heads' identified in English also fire for shared target-language idioms but not for target-unique ones (attention-pattern comparison). Test the prediction that target-unique idioms fail to trigger the shared figurative-retrieval mechanism, leaving the literal pathway dominant.
5) Causal patching test: For target-unique idioms where the model falls back to literal, patch in (a) the figurative-vs-literal direction extracted from a matched context, and (b) the correct figurative meaning representation, and test whether figurative interpretation is restored. Conversely, for shared idioms, ablate the English figurative signal and test whether figurative accuracy collapses to the target-unique level (confirming borrowing). Complementary steering: steer along the figurative direction and measure flip rate literal<->figurative without switching output language. Competence controls: the model must still handle the literal-biasing contexts correctly (no over-imposition of figurative readings), preserve fluency, and not switch output language (off-target rate).
6) Cross-model and cognitive-comparison controls: Predict the more English-centric Llama-3 shows stronger leakage and larger shared-vs-unique gaps than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether leakage magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the figurative direction and with target-language training share. Qualitatively compare the shared-vs-unique and translatability pattern against the human bilingual cross-language idiom-activation literature (direction/polarity, not identical mechanism).
Evaluation metrics: shared-vs-unique figurative-accuracy gap and literal-fallback-rate gap (vs English ceiling); English-leakage decoding rate; cross-lingual figurative-direction alignment (shared vs unique); Idiom-Head firing rates (shared vs unique); patching-induced figurative recovery for unique idioms and English-ablation collapse for shared idioms; steering flip rate; competence preservation on literal contexts, off-target rate; cross-model leakage comparison and correlation with training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for idiom-uniqueness over frequency/fertility/resource baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Classifying idioms as SHARED vs. TARGET-UNIQUE is nontrivial (partial overlaps, near-equivalents); we use native-speaker verification with a graded scale, report inter-annotator agreement, and exclude ambiguous items, treating EQUIVALENT-MEANING (same meaning, different form) as an intermediate condition. 2) Idiom uniqueness is correlated with frequency, cultural specificity, and resource level; the shared/equivalent/unique partition, English ceiling, and within-language figurative-vs-literal-context contrast isolate the leakage pathway, but residual confounds may remain. 3) Difference-in-means figurative directions may entangle topical or lexical content; we use multiple extraction methods, matched literal-context controls, and specificity checks. 4) Logit-lens/tuned-lens decoding is approximate at intermediate layers; we cross-validate with early-exit truncation and multiple lenses. 5) Instruction-tuned models may verbally hedge or explain idioms; we test base models where available and use both multiple-choice probes and generation. 6) Idiom-Head transfer analysis may be noisy and model-family dependent; BLOOM's less English-centric hub is analyzed as a contrast. 7) Patching may have entangled effects; we report ambiguous cases and multiple granularities. 8) If NO leakage is found—target-language idioms are retrieved from their own figurative signal regardless of English equivalence, and target-unique idioms are handled as well as shared ones—this is an informative POSITIVE result showing genuinely language-specific figurative competence, valuable either way. 9) Human-LLM comparison is qualitative. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: color_boundary_warp_categorical_perception
Title: Does the Model See Blue Like a Russian? Language-Warped Color Boundaries and Categorical Perception in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: A multilingual LLM carries a single, largely dominant-language-scaffolded internal color geometry, but the language it is queried in causally warps where category boundaries fall and induces language-specific categorical perception (better discrimination across a boundary that exists in that language). Crucially, because the shared hub is scaffolded by high-color-term languages (English/Russian/Chinese), the model IMPOSES their finer boundaries onto low-color-term languages: it hallucinates a boundary (e.g., a light-blue/dark-blue split) where the queried language draws none, and fails to erase a boundary the language merges. This warp is linearly decodable, correlates with each language's empirical naming map, and is causally steerable.
Related Work: Human cognitive science robustly shows language-specific categorical perception of color: Russian's siniy/goluboy distinction speeds discrimination across the light/dark-blue boundary versus English (Winawer et al. 2007), Himba/Berinmo differ from English (Roberson; Franklin 2005), and color naming is a near-optimal information-theoretic compression that varies cross-linguistically (Zaslavsky/Regier IB 2018; WCS motifs 2009; color naming reflects use 2017). Recent work shows LLMs have language-specific color representations and replicate cross-linguistic naming variation and the color wheel (Studying Globalization on Color Perception 2024; LLMs predict sensory judgments 2023; Color Names in VLMs 2025), and that multilingual models encode language-sensitive vs language-neutral orthogonal axes (Geometry of Multilingual Representations 2022) with shared+language-specific gender subspaces (Analyzing Gender Representation 2022). BUT all LLM color work is BEHAVIORAL (naming outputs) and vision-language-focused; none asks the mechanistic questions: (1) does the queried language causally MOVE internal color-category boundaries in a text-only LLM, (2) does this induce language-specific CATEGORICAL PERCEPTION in a non-naming discrimination task (the actual Whorfian signature), (3) is the boundary geometry a single dominant-language-scaffolded structure that IMPOSES fine boundaries onto low-term languages rather than genuinely reshaping per language, and (4) can we causally steer a color's category membership? We uniquely reframe cross-linguistic color variation as a mechanistic boundary-warp / imposition phenomenon in the shared hub, tie it to categorical perception rather than naming, and provide localization plus a causal steering test. This is orthogonal to all my prior proposals (grammatical categories, facts, reasoning depth, spatial frames, timelines, idioms).
Abstract: Languages carve the color spectrum differently: Russian obligatorily distinguishes light blue (goluboy) from dark blue (siniy), while English calls both 'blue', and this shapes human perception, speeding discrimination across boundaries a language marks. Multilingual language models are known to output color names in language-specific ways, but it is unknown whether the language a model is queried in actually WARPS its internal color geometry, and whether this produces the true Whorfian signature: language-specific categorical perception in a non-naming discrimination task. We hypothesize that (1) a multilingual LLM holds a single, largely dominant-language-scaffolded color geometry whose category boundaries shift as a function of the query language; (2) the model shows better cross-boundary than within-category discrimination aligned to each language's naming map (categorical perception); and (3) because the hub is scaffolded by high-color-term languages, it IMPOSES their fine boundaries onto low-color-term languages, hallucinating splits the language merges and failing to erase them. We build a controlled color suite (perceptually spaced chips near cross-linguistically contested boundaries: blue/green, light/dark blue, warm hues) with same/different discrimination and boundary-placement probes in typologically diverse languages differing in color-term inventory (English, Russian, Chinese, Greek, Turkish, Vietnamese, Himba/Berinmo-style low-term via numeral-free descriptions), on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM. Using linear color-boundary probes, behavioral categorical-perception measures, activation patching, and steering, we test whether the query language moves boundaries, induces categorical perception, imposes dominant-language splits, and whether steering flips a chip's category. Metrics include boundary-shift alignment with empirical naming maps, categorical-perception effect size per language, imposition rate on low-term languages, and steering flip rate.
Experiments:
1) Controlled color suite: Represent colors textually (RGB/hex triples and perceptual CIELAB descriptions, plus named-chip references) sampled as perceptually-even continua straddling cross-linguistically contested boundaries: (a) blue/green (English one-vs-two-term contrast with Greek/Turkish/Vietnamese variants), (b) light-blue/dark-blue (Russian goluboy/siniy, Greek), (c) warm-hue splits, and (d) an English-boundary control continuum. Build discrimination triads/pairs and boundary-placement items. Tasks: (i) same/different discrimination ('Are these two colors the same category of color?' or a 2AFC odd-one-out) at fixed perceptual spacing, straddling vs within category; (ii) boundary-placement ('Where along this series does one color name end and another begin?'); (iii) naming (elicit the color term). Instantiate every item in typologically diverse languages differing in color-term inventory (English, Russian, Chinese, Modern Greek, Turkish, Vietnamese, Hindi, plus a low-term condition via periphrastic/basic-term-restricted descriptions modeled on Himba/Berinmo naming). Native-speaker verify color terms and gold boundary locations from World Color Survey / published naming maps; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral categorical perception (H1/H2, core): For each language, measure the discrimination advantage for cross-boundary vs within-category pairs at MATCHED perceptual distance (the categorical-perception effect). Test H2: the effect is larger and located at the boundary that language names (e.g., a light/dark-blue CP peak for Russian/Greek but not English; a blue/green peak for English but not for one-term languages). Compute per-language CP effect size (Cohen's d) and boundary location; compare the location against the empirical naming map (alignment score). Compare against the human effect-size direction (Winawer 2007; WCS) as an external benchmark. Control for chip perceptual distance, tokenizer fertility of color terms, and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test query-language adds predictive power beyond perceptual distance).
3) Representational boundary localization (H1): Train a linear probe to decode a color chip's category label from mid/late-layer hidden states, per query language, and locate the decision boundary along the continuum. Test whether the internal boundary MOVES with query language (boundary-shift), and whether the shift aligns with each language's naming map. Compare cross-lingual cosine alignment of the color-category direction across languages and layers to test whether a single shared geometry (strong alignment) is being re-thresholded per language versus genuinely distinct per-language geometries. Baseline: a language-neutral perceptual-distance direction (should NOT shift with language) as a specificity control.
4) Imposition test (H3, core): For LOW-color-term languages/conditions (that merge a distinction the dominant languages split, e.g., blue=green or a single blue), test whether the model nonetheless (a) places a boundary where the DOMINANT language (English/Russian/Chinese) would, and (b) shows a CP effect at the dominant-language boundary absent in that language. Define imposition rate = fraction of merged-boundary items where the model applies a dominant-language split. Conversely test failure-to-split: for languages that split where English merges (Russian light/dark blue), does the model UNDER-mark it when queried in English relative to Russian? Predict imposition is stronger for lower-resource languages and correlates with the model's dominant-language color-term inventory (English/Chinese heavy per Color Names in VLMs 2025).
5) Causal steering/patching test: (a) Extract the color-category boundary direction (difference-in-means between chips just below vs just above a boundary) and steer a near-boundary chip's representation across the boundary; measure whether its category label and discrimination behavior flip (flip rate), confirming the direction causally controls category membership. (b) For an imposed boundary on a low-term language, patch in the merged (language-specific) representation and test whether the spurious boundary/CP effect is removed. Complementary: steer the query-language signal itself (language-vector) and test whether it moves the boundary toward that language's map. Competence controls: steering must not switch OUTPUT language (off-target rate), must not corrupt clearly-distinct colors (a red must still differ from a blue), and must preserve perceptual-distance ordering.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify effects are color-boundary-specific (moving the boundary does not change unrelated attributes), axis-specific (hue vs lightness boundaries behave per the language's map), and not a lexical color-word frequency artifact (balance term frequencies; use hex/LAB inputs that contain no color word). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English/Chinese-centric Llama-3/Qwen show stronger imposition and English-shaped boundaries than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether imposition magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the color-category direction and with each language's training share. Qualitatively compare the model's per-language CP and boundary maps against the World Color Survey / human naming maps (structural correlation).
Evaluation metrics: per-language categorical-perception effect size and boundary location (vs empirical naming map alignment and human effect-size direction); internal boundary-shift magnitude and its alignment with naming maps; cross-lingual color-category-direction alignment (shared geometry vs per-language); imposition rate on low-term languages and failure-to-split rate; steering flip rate and patching-induced boundary-removal rate; competence preservation (distinct-color discrimination, perceptual-ordering), off-target rate; cross-model imposition comparison and correlation with training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for query-language over perceptual-distance and frequency baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) A text-only LLM has no visual perception, so any 'categorical perception' arises purely from co-occurrence statistics of color words and numeric color descriptions in text; a null result (no CP, no boundary warp) is plausible and would itself be informative about the limits of the LLM-human color analogy. 2) Representing color as hex/RGB/LAB text may be handled inconsistently by tokenizers and may not map cleanly to perceptual space; we include both numeric and named-chip references, control for tokenizer fertility, and validate that models reproduce basic perceptual ordering before running boundary analyses. 3) Query language is confounded with color-term inventory, script, and resource level; the within-continuum boundary-placement contrast, the language-neutral perceptual-distance control direction, and matched-perceptual-distance CP pairs isolate the boundary-warp pathway, but residual confounds may remain. 4) Low-color-term human languages (Himba/Berinmo) are essentially absent from training; we operationalize the low-term condition via basic-term-restricted periphrastic descriptions rather than claiming to test those languages directly, and interpret results as about term-inventory pressure, not those specific languages. 5) Difference-in-means boundary directions may entangle lightness with hue; we probe hue and lightness axes separately and report axis-specificity. 6) Instruction-tuned models may verbally hedge or default to English basic terms regardless of query language, which would itself confirm imposition; we test base models where available. 7) Steering/patching may harm fluency or over-impose boundaries; we require competence preservation on clearly-distinct colors and report the full tradeoff. 8) Human CP is behavioral/embodied; our LLM-human comparison is structural/qualitative (boundary location and effect direction), not a claim of identical mechanism. 9) If the model shows genuinely per-language boundaries and CP that match each language's naming map WITHOUT dominant-language imposition, this is an equally valuable positive result showing text-only models learn language-specific color categorization from distributional statistics alone. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B text-only models; may not extend to frontier scale or multimodal models.

Name: kinship_feature_collapse
Title: Every Aunt Is the Same Aunt: Does the English-Scaffolded Shared Hub Collapse Obligatory Kinship Distinctions in Multilingual LLMs?
Short Hypothesis: Kinship terminologies disagree not on who the relatives are but on which semantic features (generation, gender, relative age/seniority, lineality/side, cross-vs-parallel, consanguineal-vs-affinal) are OBLIGATORY. Because the shared semantic hub of multilingual LLMs is scaffolded by comparatively coarse-grained kinship languages (English merges maternal/paternal, elder/younger, cross/parallel into 'uncle/aunt/cousin/grandmother'), we hypothesize the hub IMPOSES this coarse partition onto languages with finer, obligatory distinctions: the model collapses distinct kin terms into a shared under-specified representation, mis-resolves which specific relative is meant, defaults to the English-merged reading on genuinely finer inputs, and loses the distinction across translation and multi-hop kinship reasoning. This feature-collapse is linearly decodable, predictable from each language's Kinbank feature inventory, causally attributable to hub scaffolding rather than resource level, and steerable by patching in the language-specific kinship-feature signal.
Related Work: Two literatures meet but have never been connected. (1) Interpretability shows LLMs represent genealogical/kinship structure in a tree-like 'cone' subspace that is causal and largely universal across models (Investigating Representation Universality: Genealogical Representations 2024), that relational concepts are located in shallow-layer last-token hidden states and are transplantable (Locating and Extracting Relational Concepts 2024; Relation-Specific Neurons 2025; Linear Relational Decoding of Morphology 2025), and that multilingual models share morphosyntactic feature directions scaffolded by English (LLMs Share Latent Grammatical Concepts 2025; Do Llamas Work in English 2024; Concept Space Alignment 2024). Cross-lingual consistency work traces factual inconsistency to entity-alignment failures in a middle-layer bottleneck (On the Entity-Level Alignment 2025; Are Knowledge and Reference Cross-Lingually Consistent 2025; Tracing the Roots of Facts 2024). (2) A large typology literature (Kinbank: 210k kinterms across 1229 languages 2023; No universals in kinship evolution 2020; Efficient communication drives kinship structure 2025; culture-specific communicative need in Hindi vs English 2023; global recurrence and variability 2023) precisely quantifies WHICH semantic features each language's kinship system encodes. CRITICALLY, no prior work asks whether the celebrated shared/universal kinship representation, being scaffolded by coarse-grained English, FAILS to represent obligatory kinship distinctions in finer languages, whether this causes feature-collapse and mis-resolution of specific relatives, whether the collapse is predictable from each language's Kinbank feature inventory, or whether a causal intervention restores the distinction. Unlike my prior imposition/flattening proposals (tense, gender, evidentiality, honorifics, spatial frames, number/individuation, color, timelines), kinship uniquely offers (a) a RELATIONAL/graph domain rather than a single morphosyntactic feature, (b) a large external typological ground-truth database (Kinbank) that lets us predict per-language collapse from an independent feature inventory, and (c) a graded target: languages vary continuously in how many features they obligatorily encode, giving a dose-response test rather than a binary contrast. This is orthogonal to all prior proposals.
Abstract: Every human language names family members, but languages carve kinship at strikingly different joints: English lumps a mother's brother and a father's brother into one word ('uncle') and all cousins into one, while Mandarin obligatorily distinguishes maternal from paternal grandparents and elder from younger siblings, and Sudanese systems name every cousin distinctly. Which semantic features (generation, gender, relative age, lineality/side, cross-vs-parallel, blood-vs-marriage) are obligatory varies systematically across the world's languages, as catalogued by the Kinbank database. Multilingual language models build a shared semantic hub scaffolded by comparatively coarse-grained kinship languages like English. We ask a simple question this asymmetry makes urgent: does the English-scaffolded hub IMPOSE its coarse kinship partition onto languages with finer, obligatory distinctions, collapsing distinct kin terms into a shared under-specified representation? We hypothesize that (1) the model mis-resolves which specific relative is meant and defaults to the English-merged reading; (2) the distinction is under-represented in the shared hub and lingers only in shallow, language-specific layers; (3) collapse magnitude is predictable from each language's Kinbank feature inventory; and (4) an ablatable, shared 'coarse-kinship' representation mediates it. Using a controlled multilingual kinship-resolution and multi-hop-reasoning suite across languages spanning the kinship-feature spectrum (English, Swedish, Mandarin, Korean, Turkish, Hindi, Arabic), on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5 and BLOOM, we combine kinship-feature probes, the genealogical cone subspace, activation patching and steering to test where the distinction lives, whether it survives transfer, whether collapse tracks Kinbank, and whether patching the language-specific kinship-feature signal restores correct resolution. Metrics include feature-collapse rate, English-merge pull, Kinbank-predicted collapse correlation, shared-hub distinction-projection, translation distinction-preservation, multi-hop kinship accuracy, and steering flip rate with competence controls.
Experiments:
1) Kinship suite grounded in Kinbank: Using Kinbank feature codings, select languages spanning the obligatory-feature spectrum: coarse (English, Swedish), medium (Turkish, Arabic), fine (Mandarin, Korean, Hindi). For each pair of distinct native kin terms that English MERGES (e.g., Mandarin nai-nai [paternal grandmother] vs wai-po [maternal grandmother]; elder-brother vs younger-brother; cross vs parallel cousin), and matched pairs the language itself merges (control), build ~500 items with tasks: (i) referent resolution ('X is my <native-kin-term>; is X my mother's or father's side / elder or younger / blood or marriage?' - forced choice); (ii) distinctness NLI (does '<term A>' entail/contradict '<term B>' referring to the same person? - a faithful model must say CONTRADICT for genuinely distinct terms and NEUTRAL/ENTAIL for merged ones); (iii) multi-hop kinship reasoning (a short genealogy stated with native terms, then a query requiring the obligatory distinction, e.g., inheritance/seating/naming rules that hinge on maternal-vs-paternal side); (iv) generation (describe the family member using the native term and check whether the model preserves the distinctive feature); (v) translation round-trip (native term -> English -> back, checking whether the distinction is silently lost). Native-speaker verify terms, feature codings, and gold answers; cross-check against Kinbank; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral feature-collapse (H1): Measure feature-collapse rate = fraction of English-merged term pairs on which the model fails to distinguish the native distinction (same resolution answer, or NEUTRAL/ENTAIL on the distinctness-NLI despite genuinely distinct terms). Compare against language-internally-merged control pairs (where collapse IS correct) and against the model's ability to handle the same distinction when it is spelled out lexically in English ('mother's elder brother'). Prediction: high collapse specifically for obligatory native distinctions expressed by single terms, low collapse for lexically-spelled-out or language-internally-merged controls. Control for term frequency, tokenizer fertility, and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test kinship-feature status adds predictive power beyond frequency/fertility/resource).
3) Kinbank-predicted collapse (H3, core external validation): Using Kinbank's per-language feature inventory, predict for each distinction whether a given language OBLIGATORILY encodes it, and test whether the model's per-language, per-feature collapse rate is predicted by the Kinbank coding (i.e., the model collapses exactly those distinctions the queried language marks but English does not). Quantify with a per-feature (generation/gender/age/side/cross-parallel/affinal) collapse-vs-Kinbank correlation and a held-out prediction of collapse from Kinbank features alone. This ties an internal model phenomenon to an independent typological ground truth.
4) English-merge pull (H1b): Test whether the collapsed reading tracks the ENGLISH-merged default rather than the target-language distinction. Define English-merge-pull rate = fraction of collapse cases whose resolution matches the English-lumped category. Predict higher pull for lower-resource fine-grained languages. Partial correlations controlling for resource/fertility.
5) Representational localization (H2): Extract a distinction direction via difference-in-means between the two native kin-term representations (e.g., maternal-vs-paternal, elder-vs-younger) at each layer, per language. Test (a) whether the distinction is weak/shallow in the shared hub versus stronger in early/language-specific layers (compared to a within-model shared-category baseline like generation, which English DOES mark); (b) whether the genealogical cone subspace (Investigating Representation Universality 2024) preserves or discards the language-specific feature; and (c) cross-lingual alignment of the distinction direction across fine-grained languages. Use the relational-concept last-token hidden states (Locating and Extracting Relational Concepts 2024) to test whether the relational representation carries the distinctive feature. Mediation: regress behavioral collapse on shared-hub distinction-projection strength (partial correlation controlling for fertility/resource; held-out R^2).
6) Cross-lingual transfer loss (H4): Measure distinction-preservation rate in translation across the fine/coarse boundary; predict directional asymmetry - fine->English silently DROPS the distinction more than English->fine fails to add it, because the hub lacks a slot for the feature. Measure within-generation drift: after establishing a maternal-side context, does the model drift toward side-neutral English-like terms? Compare distinction-preservation against a generation-preservation baseline (a feature English marks) as a matched control.
7) Causal steering/patching test (core): (a) Steer the kin-term representation along the distinction direction (toward the correct pole) for fine-grained-language inputs and measure whether resolution and multi-hop reasoning flip to the correct answer (flip rate), confirming the direction causally drives behavior; steer in the target language and verify no output-language switch. (b) For collapsed items, patch the residual language-specific distinction signal (from early/language-specific layers of the correct pass) into later computation and test restoration - localizing failure to the shared hub OVERWRITING a shallowly-present feature versus its absence. Compare against random-direction steering and whole-hub English-steering baselines. Competence controls: the model must still handle language-internally-merged terms correctly (no over-splitting), preserve fluency, and not switch output language (off-target rate).
8) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify steering/patching is feature-specific (changes side/age but not the person's identity or unrelated attributes), is graded (collapse severity scales with how many features the language marks beyond English), and is not a lexical frequency artifact. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 shows stronger collapse than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM/Qwen (which see more fine-grained-kinship data); test whether collapse magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the distinction direction, with target-language training share, and with each language's Kinbank feature count. Qualitatively compare the model's per-feature collapse pattern against the efficient-communication / communicative-need structure of kinship (Efficient communication drives kinship 2025).
Evaluation metrics: feature-collapse rate (obligatory-native vs lexically-spelled-out vs internally-merged controls); English-merge-pull rate; per-feature collapse-vs-Kinbank correlation and held-out prediction of collapse from Kinbank features; distinctness-NLI accuracy; multi-hop kinship-reasoning accuracy; shared-hub distinction-projection strength and crystallization depth (vs generation baseline); genealogical cone feature-preservation; cross-lingual distinction-direction alignment; translation distinction-preservation rate and directional asymmetry (vs generation-preservation baseline); within-generation drift; mediation regression (held-out R^2); steering flip rate and patching-induced restoration; competence preservation, off-target rate; cross-model collapse comparison and correlation with training share and Kinbank feature count.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Kinship feature codings can be subtle and dialect-dependent (e.g., partial obligatoriness, register variation); we ground items in Kinbank with native-speaker verification, restrict to clearly obligatory single-term distinctions, report inter-annotator agreement, and exclude low-agreement items. 2) Kinship-feature richness is correlated with language family, script, and resource level; the language-internally-merged controls, the lexically-spelled-out English controls, and the within-language distinct-vs-merged contrasts, plus the Kinbank-based per-feature prediction, are designed to isolate the feature-collapse pathway, but residual confounds may remain. 3) Difference-in-means distinction directions may entangle lexical or frequency features; we use multiple extraction methods, the genealogical cone subspace as an independent representation, matched controls, and specificity checks. 4) Multi-hop kinship reasoning conflates the distinction failure with general reasoning failure; we include single-hop resolution items to isolate the distinction, and only count multi-hop errors that hinge on the collapsed feature. 5) Some fine-grained kin terms are multi-token with high fertility, confounding depth measures; we control for fertility and include single-token native terms where available. 6) Instruction-tuned models may hedge ('maternal or paternal'), which we treat as a positive distinction-awareness signal rather than failure; we test base models where available and use both forced-choice and NLI probes. 7) Patching may have entangled effects; we report ambiguous cases and multiple granularities. 8) If NO collapse is found - fine-grained distinctions are preserved, predictable, and consistently resolved - this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the shared/universal kinship representation retains language-specific feature structure absent from its English scaffolding, strengthening the language-agnostic view; valuable either way. 9) The Kinbank-prediction analysis assumes model training data reflects each language's real kinship usage, which may not hold; we treat Kinbank as a noisy predictor and rely on the behavioral and causal tests for the core claims. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: pragmatic_directness_imposition
Title: Reading Between the Lines in the Wrong Language: Does the English-Scaffolded Shared Hub Impose a Directness Default on Cross-Cultural Pragmatic Inference?
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs perform the pragmatic inference step (recovering a speaker's intended meaning that diverges from literal form, e.g. an indirect refusal, a face-saving hedge, or an off-record request) in a largely English-scaffolded shared hub that carries a dominant-culture 'directness prior'. We hypothesize this hub IMPOSES a low-context, literal/direct interpretation onto high-context languages (Japanese, Korean, Hindi, Arabic) where indirectness is the pragmatic default: the model under-infers implicated meaning, mis-resolves indirect speech acts, and defaults to literal readings far more in high-context languages than in English, even when the same implicature is clearly licensed. This imposition is mediated by a shared, ablatable 'implicature-strength' direction, tracks each culture's empirical indirectness norms, is causally attributable to hub scaffolding rather than resource level, and is steerable by amplifying the implicature signal without harming literal comprehension.
Related Work: Two literatures meet but have never been connected mechanistically. (1) Monolingual interpretability shows LLMs encode pragmatic inference signals: scalar-implicature strength is predictable from a sentence encoder and tracks linguistic cues (Harnessing the Linguistic Signal 2020), discourse/implicit-causality is represented and shapes reference (Discourse Structure Interacts with Reference 2020), and social/politeness concepts are linear, steerable directions (Interpreting Politeness Networks 2016; STAR emotional steering 2025; Computational Basis of Social Decision-Making 2025). All are English/monolingual. (2) Cross-cultural pragmatics work is behavioral or task-based: politeness classification transfers imperfectly across nine languages (TyDiP 2022), prompt-politeness effects differ by language (Should We Respect LLMs 2024), indirect-speech-act benchmarks show models struggle as indirectness rises especially in high-context Korean (READI 2026), and cognitive models show cross-cultural interpretation differences arise from politeness/cost weights (Minding the Politeness Gap 2025). Foundational work shows an English-scaffolded shared hub (Do Llamas Work in English 2024; Semantic Hub 2024) and a Cultural-Linguistic Synergy where models do best on English-culture questions (Disentangling Language and Culture 2025; Under the Shadow of Babel 2025). NO prior work asks the mechanistic question: does the shared hub compute pragmatic implicature with a dominant-culture DIRECTNESS PRIOR that it IMPOSES onto high-context languages, causing systematic under-inference of indirect meaning; where does the implicature-strength signal live; is it English-scaffolded; and can it be causally restored per language? Unlike my prior imposition/flattening proposals (grammatical categories, facts, spatial frames, idioms, color, kinship), pragmatic implicature is an INFERENCE over literal meaning (recovering non-literal speaker intent), a distinct cognitive axis, with an external cross-cultural directness ground truth (CCSARP/DCT norms) enabling a dose-response test.
Abstract: Much of human communication is indirect: a refusal is softened into 'that might be difficult', a request is hidden in a question, meaning lives between the lines. How much indirectness is expected, however, varies sharply across cultures—high-context languages like Japanese, Korean, Hindi and Arabic favor off-record, indirect speech acts, while English tends toward directness. Multilingual language models build a shared semantic hub scaffolded by English. We ask a simple question this asymmetry makes urgent: does the English-scaffolded hub compute pragmatic inference with a dominant-culture DIRECTNESS prior that it IMPOSES onto high-context languages, causing the model to systematically under-read indirect meaning? We hypothesize that (1) the model resolves indirect speech acts and implicatures more literally in high-context languages than in English, even when the same implicature is clearly licensed; (2) implicature strength is under-represented in the shared hub for these languages and lingers only in shallow, language-specific layers; (3) the size of this under-inference tracks each culture's empirical indirectness norms; and (4) an ablatable, shared 'implicature-strength' direction mediates it. We build a controlled multilingual suite of indirect speech acts and scalar/conversational implicatures with matched literal-vs-implicated readings across high-context (Japanese, Korean, Hindi, Arabic) and low-context (English, German, Dutch) languages, on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5 and BLOOM. Using implicature-strength probes, logit-lens depth tracking, activation patching and steering, we test where the inference lives, whether it survives transfer, whether under-inference tracks cultural norms, and whether amplifying the implicature signal restores correct pragmatic reading. Metrics include literal-fallback rate, implicature-under-inference gap, norm-prediction correlation, shared-hub implicature-projection, and steering flip rate with competence controls.
Experiments:
1) Controlled pragmatic suite: Construct ~500 items covering (a) indirect speech acts (indirect refusals/requests/complaints, e.g., 'It's already quite late...' as a refusal), (b) conversational/scalar implicatures ('some' -> not all; 'It's warm in here' -> please open the window), and (c) off-record face-saving hedges, each in a context that CLEARLY licenses the implicated (non-literal) reading. Instantiate every item in high-context languages (Japanese, Korean, Hindi, Arabic) and low-context languages (English, German, Dutch), native-speaker-verified, with matched literal-only controls (same surface form in a context licensing only the literal reading). Tasks: (i) intent-resolution forced choice (literal vs implicated meaning); (ii) implicature NLI (does the utterance entail the implicated meaning given context?); (iii) response-selection (choose the addressee's appropriate reaction, which differs for literal vs implicated); (iv) generation (paraphrase the speaker's intended meaning). Ground indirectness expectations in CCSARP/DCT cross-cultural norm data. Report inter-annotator agreement; release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral under-inference (H1): Measure literal-fallback rate = fraction of clearly-licensed implicature items resolved literally, per language, and the implicature-under-inference gap = fallback(high-context) minus fallback(English). Verify near-zero fallback on literal-only controls (no over-inference) and correct implicature reading in English (ceiling). Control for utterance frequency, tokenizer fertility, and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test high-context status adds predictive power beyond fertility/resource).
3) Dominant-directness pull (H1b): Test whether the fallback reading tracks the ENGLISH/low-context DIRECT default rather than target-culture pragmatics. Define directness-pull rate = fraction of fallback cases matching the literal/direct English reading; predict higher pull for higher-context, lower-resource languages.
4) Cultural-norm prediction (H3, external validation): Using CCSARP/DCT indirectness norms per language/situation, test whether per-language, per-situation under-inference is predicted by the culture's empirical indirectness level (held-out prediction of fallback from external norm scores; Spearman correlation), tying the internal phenomenon to independent cross-cultural ground truth.
5) Representational localization (H2): Extract an implicature-strength direction via difference-in-means between implicated-reading and literal-reading representations (following scalar-implicature-strength work) at each layer, per language. Test (a) whether it is shared across languages and English-scaffolded (cross-lingual cosine alignment, strongest in mid/shared-hub layers); (b) whether high-context-language implicature items project WEAKLY onto the implicated pole in the hub while any residual signal is stronger in early/language-specific layers (vs a within-model shared baseline like negation). Track implicature crystallization depth via logit-lens/tuned-lens. Mediation: regress behavioral fallback on shared-hub implicature-projection strength (partial correlation controlling for fertility/resource; held-out R^2).
6) Cross-lingual transfer loss (complementary): Measure implicature-preservation in translation across the high/low-context boundary; predict directional asymmetry—high-context->English flattens indirect intent into direct statements more than English->high-context fails to add indirectness.
7) Causal steering/patching test (core): (a) Steer along the implicature-strength direction (toward the implicated pole) for high-context inputs and measure whether intent-resolution/NLI flips to the correct implicated reading (flip rate), without switching output language; (b) for fallback items, patch the residual language-specific implicature signal (from early/language-specific layers of the correct pass) into later computation and test restoration—localizing failure to the shared hub UNDER-reading a shallowly-present signal versus its absence. Competence controls: literal-only controls must remain literal (no over-inference), fluency preserved, off-target/language-mixing rate low. Baselines: whole-hub English steering, random-direction steering.
8) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify steering is implicature-specific (changes literal/implicated reading but not unrelated content), graded (under-inference scales with cultural indirectness), and not a lexical-frequency artifact. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 shows stronger imposition than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM/Qwen; test whether imposition magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the implicature direction and with target-language training share.
Evaluation metrics: literal-fallback rate and implicature-under-inference gap (high-context vs English; vs literal-only controls); directness-pull rate; under-inference-vs-CCSARP-norm correlation and held-out prediction; implicature NLI accuracy; shared-hub implicature-projection strength and crystallization depth (vs negation baseline); cross-lingual implicature-direction alignment; translation implicature-preservation and directional asymmetry; mediation regression (held-out R^2); steering flip rate and patching-induced restoration; competence preservation, off-target rate; cross-model imposition comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Whether an implicature is 'clearly licensed' is context-dependent and culturally loaded; we use carefully controlled contexts with native-speaker verification, ground licensing in CCSARP/DCT norms, report inter-annotator agreement, and exclude low-agreement items. 2) High-context status is correlated with language family, script, and resource level; the literal-only controls, low-context comparison languages, within-language implicated-vs-literal contrasts, and the external CCSARP-norm prediction isolate the pragmatic-inference pathway, but residual confounds may remain. 3) Difference-in-means implicature directions may entangle topical/lexical content; we use multiple extraction methods, matched literal controls, and specificity checks. 4) Logit-lens/tuned-lens depth is approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 5) Instruction-tuned models may over-explain or hedge ('this could mean X or Y'), which we treat as a positive inference signal, not failure; we test base models where available and use both forced-choice and NLI probes. 6) Some implicatures (scalar 'some') are less culturally variable than others (indirect refusals); we analyze implicature types separately and expect the imposition effect to be strongest for culturally-variable indirect speech acts. 7) Patching may have entangled effects; we report ambiguous cases and multiple granularities. 8) If NO imposition is found—high-context implicatures are inferred as reliably as in English and preserved across transfer—this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the shared hub performs culturally-faithful pragmatic inference despite English scaffolding, valuable either way. 9) CCSARP norms may not reflect the model's training-data pragmatics; we treat them as a noisy predictor and rely on behavioral and causal tests for core claims. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: phonosemantic_leakage_multilingual
Title: The Sound of a Word Is Reasoned With: Phonosemantic Leakage and Cross-Lingual Inconsistency in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: The phonetic FORM of a word (its sound-symbolic properties: e.g. front vowels/voiceless stops -> small/sharp/fast; back vowels/voiced sonorants -> large/round/slow) causally leaks into a text-only multilingual LLM's downstream SEMANTIC reasoning about the word's referent, even for arbitrary content words where form should be irrelevant. Because the same concept has phonetically different names across languages, this produces a distinctive, measurable cross-lingual inconsistency: the model's judgments about a genderless/attribute-neutral referent (its perceived size, sharpness, speed, brightness) shift toward the sound-symbolic bias of the WORD-FORM in whatever language is queried. This phonosemantic leakage is mediated by a shared, decodable phonetic-form direction that bleeds into the shared-hub concept representation, scales with each language's empirical degree of phonosemantic iconicity, and is causally suppressible by ablating the form direction without harming factual competence.
Related Work: Two literatures meet but have never been connected mechanistically for multilingual reasoning. (1) Sound-symbolism work in models is either behavioral bouba-kiki probing in VISION-language models (Kiki or Bouba? 2023; Cross-modal Bouba-Kiki 2025; With Ears to See 2024) or attention/naming analyses in MULTIMODAL LLMs (Do Language Models Associate Sound with Meaning? 2025 introduces LEX-ICON; Sound Symbolism Across Writing Systems 2024). Cross-linguistic databases quantify iconicity at scale (Typology of Sound Symbolism 2020; Sound Symbolism in Basic Vocabulary 2010; Adversarially Probing Cross-Family Sound Symbolism in 27 Languages 2025; Quantifying Phonosemantic Iconicity in 6 Languages 2025; Color Sound Symbolism 2019). Speech-model work shows phonological features are linear, causal directions (Phonological Vector Arithmetic 2026; wav2vec probing 2022). (2) Interpretability establishes an English-scaffolded shared semantic hub (Do Llamas Work in English 2024; Semantic Hub 2024) and static token embeddings encode iconicity as a psycholinguistic attribute (Word Meanings in Transformer LMs 2025). CRITICALLY, all model sound-symbolism work asks 'does the model REPLICATE the bouba-kiki judgment?' as an isolated probe. NO prior work asks whether phonetic form CONTAMINATES downstream semantic reasoning about an ordinary word's referent in a text-only LLM, whether this produces CROSS-LINGUAL INCONSISTENCY because the same concept sounds different across languages, whether the leak scales with each language's iconicity level, whether a shared phonetic-form direction mediates it, or whether ablating it removes the leak while preserving factual knowledge. This reframes sound symbolism from a curiosity the model 'has' into a bias that CORRUPTS multilingual reasoning, and is orthogonal to all my prior proposals (grammatical categories, facts, reasoning depth, spatial/temporal/color/kinship/pragmatic axes), none of which concern phonetic word-form.
Abstract: The link between how a word sounds and what it means is supposedly arbitrary, yet cross-linguistically words for small/sharp/fast things tend to contain front vowels and voiceless stops, while words for large/round/slow things contain back vowels and voiced sonorants. Models are known to replicate this bouba-kiki intuition as an isolated judgment. We ask a sharper, previously untested question: does the phonetic FORM of a word causally LEAK into a text-only multilingual LLM's semantic reasoning about the word's REFERENT, and does this create cross-lingual inconsistency because the same concept is named with phonetically different words across languages? We hypothesize (1) form-driven bias: the model's attribute judgments about a referent (size, sharpness, speed, brightness) shift toward the sound-symbolic bias of the word-form used to name it, even for arbitrary content words where form is irrelevant; (2) cross-lingual inconsistency: for concepts whose translations have OPPOSITE sound-symbolic biases across two languages, the model judges the same referent inconsistently; (3) a shared, decodable phonetic-form direction mediates the leak and bleeds into the shared-hub concept representation; and (4) leak magnitude scales with each language's empirical iconicity level. We build a controlled multilingual suite of concepts with cross-linguistically divergent word-form biases, plus pseudoword controls, across typologically diverse languages, on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5 and BLOOM. Using logit-lens depth tracking, difference-in-means form probes, activation patching and steering, we measure the leak, its cross-lingual inconsistency signature, its scaling with iconicity databases, and whether ablating the form direction removes it while preserving factual competence. Metrics include form-bias effect size, cross-lingual inconsistency gap, iconicity-prediction correlation, and ablation recovery.
Experiments:
1) Phonosemantic suite: (a) Real-concept set (~400): concrete referents with an attribute-neutral or contested perceptual attribute (size, sharpness/roundness, speed, brightness), each named across typologically diverse languages (English, Spanish, German, Turkish, Finnish, Hindi, Japanese, Swahili). For each concept-language pair, compute the word-form's sound-symbolic bias (front/back vowel ratio, voiced/voiceless, sonorant/obstruent) from IPA transcriptions using coefficients from cross-linguistic iconicity databases (Typology of Sound Symbolism 2020; 27-Languages 2025). Key subset: FORM-DIVERGENT concepts whose translations carry OPPOSITE sound-symbolic biases across a language pair (e.g., a small object whose name is phonetically 'large-sounding' in one language, 'small-sounding' in another). (b) Pseudoword control set (~500): constructed nonce words with systematically varied phonetic form and no referent, used to extract clean form directions and to establish the baseline bouba-kiki magnitude. Native-speaker verify IPA and attribute-neutrality; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral form-bias leak (H1): For each real concept in each language, elicit attribute judgments (forced-choice 'Is X more small or more large / more sharp or more round / faster or slower?' and Likert magnitude) about the REFERENT. Test whether judgments shift toward the sound-symbolic bias of the word-FORM after controlling for the concept's true attribute. Compute a form-bias effect size (partial correlation between word-form bias and judgment, controlling for the referent's ground-truth attribute, word frequency, tokenizer fertility, resource level; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test form adds predictive power). Prediction: nonzero form bias for real content words, strongest for perceptually ambiguous referents; verify near-ceiling form bias on the pseudoword control (no referent to anchor).
3) Cross-lingual inconsistency signature (H2, core): For FORM-DIVERGENT concepts, measure whether the model's attribute judgment about the SAME referent diverges across the two languages in the direction predicted by the word-form biases. Define the cross-lingual inconsistency GAP = inconsistency(FORM-DIVERGENT) minus inconsistency(FORM-CONGRUENT control concepts, whose translations share the same bias). Predict a positive gap: phonetic-form disagreement, not mere language change, drives extra inconsistency. Control by matching concepts and including the pseudoword baseline.
4) Iconicity-level scaling (H4, external validation): Using cross-linguistic iconicity databases, assign each language an empirical iconicity level (how strongly its lexicon exhibits sound-meaning correspondences). Test whether per-language form-bias effect size is predicted by the language's iconicity level (Spearman correlation; held-out prediction of leak from iconicity score), tying the internal phenomenon to independent typological ground truth. Predict stronger leak for higher-iconicity languages (e.g., Japanese with rich ideophones).
5) Representational localization (H3): Extract a phonetic-form direction (e.g., a small/sharp vs large/round 'sound' axis) via difference-in-means over the PSEUDOWORD representations at each layer (clean, referent-free). Test (a) cross-lingual cosine alignment of the form direction (shared vs language-specific) across layers; (b) whether a REAL concept's shared-hub representation projects onto the form axis in the direction of its word-form bias (i.e., the sound leaks into the concept vector) using logit-lens/tuned-lens depth tracking of when this projection emerges; and (c) mediation: regress behavioral form bias on the concept representation's projection onto the form direction (partial correlation controlling for frequency/fertility; held-out R^2). Baseline: a genuine-semantic attribute direction (e.g., real size) as a within-model comparison.
6) Causal ablation/steering test (core): (a) Ablate the phonetic-form direction from the real-concept representation at the localizing layer (difference-in-means projection removal / INLP nullspace) and test whether (i) the form-bias effect drops and (ii) the cross-lingual inconsistency GAP shrinks toward the FORM-CONGRUENT baseline. (b) Complementary steering: add the form direction and confirm it causally shifts attribute judgments (flip rate small<->large) without switching output language. Critically verify FACTUAL COMPETENCE is preserved: the model must still report the referent's true, unambiguous attributes and factual knowledge (competence probes, fluency, off-target/language-mixing rate). Baselines: random-direction ablation, whole-hub English-steering.
7) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify ablation is form-specific (removes sound-symbolic bias but not genuine-semantic attribute knowledge), and not a lexical-frequency artifact (balance frequencies; pseudoword direction contains no semantics). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 shows form directions scaffolded by English phonology, while the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM show more language-specific form axes; test whether leak magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the form direction and with training share. Qualitatively compare the model's per-language leak pattern against the human sound-symbolism effect direction from the databases.
Evaluation metrics: form-bias effect size (real content words vs pseudoword ceiling; partial correlation controlling for true attribute/frequency/fertility; held-out R^2 over baselines); cross-lingual inconsistency GAP (FORM-DIVERGENT minus FORM-CONGRUENT); leak-vs-iconicity-level correlation and held-out prediction; cross-lingual form-direction alignment; concept-representation projection onto the form axis and its mediation of behavioral bias (held-out R^2); ablation-induced reduction in form bias and inconsistency GAP; steering flip rate; factual-competence preservation, fluency, off-target rate; cross-model leak comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Sound-symbolic bias coefficients from databases are noisy and language-specific; we use multiple databases, IPA-based features, native-speaker verification, and treat the coefficients as noisy predictors, relying on the pseudoword-derived form directions for clean causal tests. 2) Word-form bias is correlated with etymology, frequency, and semantic field (e.g., real small things may genuinely tend to have small-sounding names via historical iconicity); the FORM-CONGRUENT vs FORM-DIVERGENT contrast, control for true attribute, and pseudoword baseline are designed to isolate the form-driven pathway, but residual confounding may remain and a modest genuine-iconicity signal in the lexicon is itself interesting. 3) Text-only LLMs have no acoustic input, so any phonetic-form effect arises from orthographic/subword co-occurrence statistics and from IPA-adjacent text; this is exactly what makes the leak surprising, but a null result (no leak beyond the isolated bouba-kiki judgment) is plausible and would itself be informative about the limits of phonosemantic contamination. 4) Difference-in-means form directions may entangle orthographic or lexical features; we use pseudoword-derived directions, multiple extraction methods, and a genuine-semantic-attribute control direction. 5) Logit-lens/tuned-lens depth estimates are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 6) Ablation could harm fluency or over-suppress legitimate semantics; we require factual-competence preservation and report the full tradeoff. 7) Instruction-tuned models may suppress overt form-based guessing;
