we test base models where available and interpret small effects as informative. 8) Tokenizer fertility differs across languages and scripts (logographic Japanese vs alphabetic), confounding depth; we control for fertility and treat script contrasts as informative. 9) If NO leak or inconsistency gap is found - attribute judgments are driven only by the referent and are consistent across languages despite divergent word-forms - this is an informative POSITIVE result showing multilingual concept representations are robust to phonetic form, valuable either way. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B text-only models; may not extend to frontier scale or multimodal models.

Name: vigesimal_base_conversion_tax
Title: Four-Twenties-Ten Is Ninety: Does the Decimal Digit Representation Impose a Base-Conversion Tax on Vigesimal Number Words in Multilingual LLMs?
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs converge on a language-agnostic base-10 digit-wise number-value representation, but spoken number words in vigesimal/mixed-base languages (French 'quatre-vingt-dix' = 4x20+10 = 90; Danish 'halvfems'; Welsh, Georgian, Basque) encode value through embedded multiplication and addition over a non-decimal base. We hypothesize this forces the model to perform a silent, layered base-conversion into its decimal representation, imposing a measurable 'base-conversion tax': the correct value crystallizes at a deeper layer and less accurately for vigesimal number words than for value-matched decimal ones, arithmetic-composition errors (e.g., emitting 70 or 410 for 'quatre-vingt-dix') spike specifically for vigesimal words, and this cost is causally attributable to the base-composition (multiply-then-add) step rather than resource level, tokenizer fertility, or mere inversion. It is train-freely reducible by patching in the decimal digit representation before composition.
Related Work: Two literatures meet but have never been connected. (1) Interpretability robustly shows LLMs encode number VALUE in a largely language-agnostic, base-10 digit-wise form (Language Models Encode Numbers Using Digit Representations in Base 10, 2024; causal per-digit interventions), that base-10 is the most data-efficient numeral system for from-scratch training (Scaling Behavior regarding Numeral Systems / Pythia, 2024), and that value/counting representations emerge progressively across layers (Understanding Counting Mechanisms / CountScope 2025; helical/sinusoidal value work). All of this is monolingual/English and treats the number embedding as base-10-native. (2) Numeration typology establishes that many languages have vigesimal or mixed-base spoken number words whose structure embeds explicit multiplication and addition over a non-decimal base (French/Danish/Welsh/Georgian/Basque vigesimal; base transparency effects; The Cognitive Processing of Numerical Bases 2025; When Bases Clash 2025; A Solid Base for Scaling Up 2025), and cognitive science shows base transparency and base-symbol inconsistency measurably affect human numerical processing and learning. My own prior 'inversion_transcoding_tax' proposal isolates the units-tens ORDER mismatch (inverted number words), but does NOT address non-decimal BASE COMPOSITION, which is a distinct mechanism: inversion reorders two decimal digit slots, whereas vigesimal composition requires evaluating an embedded arithmetic expression (multiply a sub-word by 20, add a residue, sometimes subtractively as in Danish) before a decimal value can be formed. NO prior work asks whether the celebrated language-agnostic base-10 number representation is taxed by having to convert from non-decimal base-structured number words, localizes the multiply-then-add composition step, predicts a vigesimal-specific arithmetic-composition error signature, or offers a train-free de-composition fix. We uniquely bridge the base-10-digit interpretability finding with numeration-base typology.
Abstract: Interpretability research shows language models encode numeric values in a largely language-agnostic base-10, digit-wise form, and that base-10 is the most efficient numeral system for these models. Numeration typology, however, shows that many languages express numbers with vigesimal or mixed-base spoken words: French says 'quatre-vingt-dix' (four-twenties-ten = 90), Danish 'halvfems' (via half-of-the-fifth-twenty), and Welsh, Georgian, and Basque similarly build values through embedded multiplication and addition over base 20. We ask a simple question bridging these fields: is the language-agnostic base-10 number representation taxed when the input number word is structured around a non-decimal base? We hypothesize a base-conversion tax: reading a vigesimal number word forces the model to silently evaluate an embedded arithmetic expression (multiply a sub-word by the base, add or subtract a residue) before its decimal value can crystallize, so the correct value forms at a deeper layer and less accurately than for value-matched decimal number words, and produces a distinctive spike in arithmetic-composition errors (e.g., emitting 70 or 410 for 'ninety') absent for decimal words. Using digit-wise and value probes across layers, we track when and how accurately the correct value crystallizes for the SAME number written as vigesimal versus decimal number words, on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM. We causally test the composition account via activation patching that swaps the base-multiplier sub-word or injects the decimal digit representation before composition, and measure whether vigesimal transcoding errors are fixed. We propose a train-free de-composition intervention. Metrics include value-crystallization depth gaps, composition-error rates by base type, patching-induced recovery, and correlation with human base-transparency effects.
Experiments:
1) Number-word stimulus suite: For two- and three-digit integers, generate spelled-out number words in vigesimal / mixed-base languages (French for 70-99 which are vigesimal: 'soixante-dix', 'quatre-vingts', 'quatre-vingt-dix'; Danish full vigesimal 50/60/70/80/90; Welsh traditional vigesimal; Georgian; Basque where native access permits) and in decimal-transparent controls (English, German, Chinese, plus Belgian/Swiss French 'septante/nonante' as a decimalized within-French control). Include the Arabic-numeral digit form as a language-agnostic anchor. Crucially, VALUE-MATCH stimuli: the same target value (e.g., 90) is presented as a vigesimal word ('quatre-vingt-dix'), a decimal word ('ninety'/'nonante'), and digits ('90'). Tasks: (a) transcoding (word -> emit digits), (b) magnitude comparison, (c) simple addition of two spelled-out numbers. Native-speaker verify; verified short-token gold answers. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Value-crystallization depth (H1): Apply digit-wise base-10 probes (Language Models Encode Numbers in Base 10, 2024) and value probes at every layer at the final number-word token position, per language. Identify the 'value-crystallization layer' = first layer at which the correct full decimal value is decodable and stable. Test H1: for the SAME value, vigesimal number words crystallize at a deeper relative layer and/or with lower peak probe accuracy than value-matched decimal words. Report normalized depth gaps and peak-accuracy gaps, controlling for tokenizer fertility of the number word, word frequency, and number of constituent sub-words (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test base-type adds predictive power beyond fertility, resource level, and sub-word count). The decimalized French control ('nonante' vs 'quatre-vingt-dix') isolates base structure from language.
3) Composition-step probing (H2): For vigesimal words, probe intermediate token positions to test whether the base-multiplier sub-word (e.g., 'quatre-vingt' -> 80) is first resolved as its own value and only later combined with the residue ('dix' -> +10). Train probes for the partial value at the multiplier position vs the final position and measure a 'composition lag' = layers between multiplier-value resolution and full-value crystallization. Predict composition lag is large/nonzero for vigesimal words and near-zero for decimal words. Report a 'partial-value leakage' metric (probability mass the final value assigns to the un-composed multiplier value, e.g., 80 or 70 for 90).
4) Behavioral composition-error signature (H3): Decompose transcoding/comparison errors into (i) base-composition errors (predicting the multiplier or residue alone, e.g., 80, 70, or the wrong arithmetic combination like 410 = 4*100+10 for 'quatre-vingt-dix'), (ii) single-digit errors, (iii) magnitude-scale errors. Test that base-composition errors are specifically elevated for vigesimal words relative to value-matched decimal words and the digit control, and that Danish subtractive forms (e.g., 'halvfems') show the largest tax. Correlate per-language/per-item composition-error rate with the Exp-2/3 composition-lag and partial-value-leakage metrics.
5) Causal composition test via patching: For a number wrong in a vigesimal pass but correct in the decimal/digit pass, patch (a) the full value representation, (b) the base-multiplier sub-word representation, and (c) the decimal digit representation injected at an early layer BEFORE the composition step, from the value-matched decimal/digit pass into the vigesimal pass. If injecting the decimal digit representation (bypassing composition) fixes the error while patching the multiplier alone does not, this localizes the tax to the multiply-then-add base-composition step. Report the share of errors fixed by each patch type per language.
6) Train-free de-composition intervention: At an early layer, apply a fixed operation that replaces the vigesimal number-word representation with the decimal digit representation of the same value (estimated from the digit/decimal-control pass aligned to the final number-word position), then continue the forward pass. Predict selective reduction of base-composition errors and shallower crystallization for vigesimal words, with negligible effect on decimal words (selectivity test). Compute 'de-composition recovery elasticity' = error reduction per unit baseline base-conversion tax, correlated with the Exp-2 depth gap. Baselines: whole-representation English/digit steering, a random-substitution control, and the inversion-only de-inversion operation (from prior work) to confirm base composition, not order, is the driver.
7) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify gains are base-composition-specific (no benefit on decimal words or the digit control), do not switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), and do not merely reduce all errors uniformly (composition-specific vs uniform reduction). Cross-model: test whether more English/decimal-centric models show a larger vigesimal tax than more multilingual BLOOM/Aya (contrast prediction), and whether tax magnitude correlates with training share of the vigesimal language. Qualitatively compare the model's base-transparency effect (vigesimal vs decimalized-French, subtractive Danish worst) against the human numerical-cognition base-transparency literature.
Evaluation metrics: value-crystallization depth and peak probe-accuracy gaps (vigesimal vs value-matched decimal vs digit control, incl. within-French nonante vs quatre-vingt-dix); composition-lag and partial-value-leakage metrics; base-composition-error rate by base type and its correlation with internal composition-lag; share of errors fixed by full/multiplier/decimal-digit patching; de-composition recovery and elasticity; selectivity (decimal words and digit control unchanged); off-target rate; Danish-subtractive vs additive-vigesimal contrast; cross-model tax comparison and correlation with training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for base-type over fertility, resource, and sub-word-count baselines; qualitative correspondence with human base-transparency effects.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Vigesimal number words differ in tokenizer fertility, sub-word count, and frequency from decimal ones, confounding depth measurements; we control with partial correlations, include the digit-numeral anchor, value-match every stimulus, and use the within-French decimalized control (nonante vs quatre-vingt-dix) to isolate base structure from language identity, resource, and script. 2) Base structure is correlated with language family and script; the within-French control and the digit anchor mitigate but may not fully remove confounds, and low-resource vigesimal languages (Georgian/Basque/Welsh) may be sparsely trained, confounding 'tax' with 'ignorance' — we therefore center the CORE study on French (well-resourced, with a clean vigesimal-vs-decimalized minimal contrast) and Danish, treating others as extensions. 3) Digit/value probes are approximate at intermediate layers; we cross-validate with multiple probe types and early-exit truncation. 4) The composition-step localization via sub-word patching may have entangled effects; we report ambiguous cases and multiple patch granularities. 5) The de-composition intervention could harm three-digit numbers or fluency; we report the full tradeoff and selectivity. 6) LLMs may memorize frequent vigesimal words (e.g., French 80, 90), weakening the composition interpretation; we test across the full range and emphasize less-frequent composed values. 7) The human-LLM base-transparency comparison is qualitative, not a claim of identical mechanism. 8) If vigesimal and decimal words show NO crystallization-depth or composition-error difference, this is an informative POSITIVE result strengthening the claim that the LLM base-10 number representation is genuinely robust to input base structure — valuable either way. 9) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: telicity_imposition_boundedness
Title: Did It Finish? Does the English-Scaffolded Shared Hub Impose an Endpoint (Telicity) onto Boundedness-Underspecified Languages in Multilingual LLMs?
Short Hypothesis: Languages differ in whether event completion (telicity/boundedness: did the action reach its natural endpoint?) is grammatically forced or left underspecified. English count/mass object marking and Slavic perfective morphology force a bounded, completed reading, whereas Mandarin and other languages with bare-noun objects and no obligatory count/mass or perfective marking leave completion genuinely underspecified. Because the shared semantic hub of multilingual LLMs is scaffolded by boundedness-forcing languages (English), we hypothesize it IMPOSES a definite telic/completed reading onto boundedness-underspecified inputs: the model spuriously commits to a completed-event interpretation of a genuinely open-ended situation, tracking the English default rather than the target-language aktionsart, mis-tracks whether an event culminated in downstream reasoning, and loses the underspecification across translation. This imposition is mediated by a shared, ablatable telicity/boundedness direction, tracks each language's empirical telicity-marking strategy, is causally attributable to hub scaffolding rather than resource level, and is steerable back toward underspecification without harming event comprehension.
Related Work: Two literatures meet but have never been connected mechanistically in generative multilingual LLMs. (1) Interpretability shows transformers encode telicity, duration, and boundedness (About Time 2022; Do pretrained transformers infer telicity like humans 2021 - finding models over-rely on temporal-unit cues), that verbal aspect and boundedness are causally manipulable in the final layers (Probing Verbal Aspect 2024; Steering Tense and Aspect 2025 finds orthogonal steerable aspect directions), that morphosyntactic concepts are shared cross-lingually and English-scaffolded (LLMs Share Latent Grammatical Concepts 2025; Same Neurons Different Languages 2022), and that tense probing collapses where the category is covert (Multilingual Probe for Tense 2021, French easy vs Chinese hard). (2) Linguistics/psycholinguistics establishes that telicity is covert in English but overt (perfective) in Slavic (Classification of telicity via annotation projection 2017; Time and the event: Russian prefixes 2005), that Mandarin's lack of an obligatory count/mass distinction and bare-noun objects leave events boundedness-underspecified so speakers use atelic predicates for both bounded and unbounded events (Do Cross-Linguistic Differences Influence Event Perception 2024), that languages mark telicity by divergent strategies (Telicity in Hungarian 2016), and that even English simple-past telic predicates do NOT obligatorily entail culmination (Temporal Information and Event Bounding 2022). CRITICALLY, all model work either (a) probes whether telicity is ENCODED (monolingual, or as a shared category that English marks), or (b) treats aspect steering as controllable text generation. NO prior work asks whether the shared hub, scaffolded by a boundedness-FORCING language, IMPOSES a definite completed/telic reading onto languages where completion is legitimately underspecified, causing spurious culmination commitment and cross-lingual reasoning inconsistency; none localizes the residual underspecification signal, ties imposition to each language's telicity-marking typology, or offers a causal fix. This differs from my prior tense-imposition proposal: tense encodes temporal LOCATION (past/present/future), whereas telicity encodes event INTERNAL structure / endpoint (whether the event culminated), a distinct aktionsart axis with a different typology and a sharper entailment test (culmination inference). It is orthogonal to all my other proposals.
Abstract: Languages differ in whether they force you to say an event FINISHED. English count/mass object marking and Slavic perfective prefixes grammatically bound events - 'she ate the apple' entails completion - while Mandarin and other languages with bare-noun objects and no obligatory perfective marking leave completion underspecified: the same sentence can describe a finished or an ongoing eating. Multilingual language models build a shared semantic hub scaffolded by boundedness-forcing English. We ask a simple question this asymmetry makes urgent: does the English-scaffolded hub IMPOSE a definite endpoint (telic, completed) reading onto boundedness-underspecified inputs, silently committing genuinely open-ended events to a completed interpretation? We hypothesize that (1) the model spuriously infers culmination for underspecified events in these languages, tracking the English default; (2) boundedness-underspecification is under-represented in the shared hub and lingers only in shallow, language-specific layers; (3) the size of this imposition tracks each language's telicity-marking typology; and (4) a shared, ablatable telicity/boundedness direction mediates it. We build a controlled multilingual suite of minimal event descriptions with matched telic-vs-atelic and completed-vs-ongoing readings across boundedness-underspecified (Mandarin, Indonesian, Thai) and boundedness-forcing (English, Russian, Spanish) languages, on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5 and BLOOM. Using logit-lens/tuned-lens depth tracking, difference-in-means boundedness probes, activation patching and steering, we measure where the completion signal lives, whether underspecification survives transfer, whether imposition tracks typology, and whether steering toward underspecification restores faithful behavior. Metrics include spurious-culmination-commitment rate, English-completed pull, typology-prediction correlation, shared-hub boundedness-projection, translation underspecification-preservation, culmination-NLI accuracy, and steering flip rate with competence controls.
Experiments:
1) Telicity/boundedness minimal-pair suite: Construct ~450 controlled event descriptions each realized in boundedness-underspecified languages (Mandarin with bare-noun objects; Indonesian; Thai where native access permits) and boundedness-forcing languages (English count/mass; Russian perfective/imperfective; Spanish). For each event, prepare (a) a genuinely UNDERSPECIFIED variant (in the underspecified language, no adverbial/aspectual cue fixing completion; native-speaker verified that both completed and ongoing readings are licensed), (b) a DISAMBIGUATED variant adding an explicit cue ('finished'/'was still doing'), and (c) matched boundedness-forcing translations. Tasks: (i) culmination-inference forced choice ('Did the action reach completion, or is it possibly unfinished?' - a faithful model should stay NEUTRAL on underspecified items); (ii) culmination-NLI (does the sentence ENTAIL 'the action was completed'? correct answer = NEUTRAL for underspecified, ENTAIL for telic-forced); (iii) downstream reasoning (a short scenario whose outcome depends on whether the event culminated, e.g., 'she was crossing the street <event>; did she reach the other side?'); (iv) generation paraphrase (does the model impose a completed frame?); (v) translation round-trip (underspecified sentence -> English -> back; does obligatory completion get silently added and does round-trip preserve underspecification?). Native-speaker verify licensed readings and gold labels; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral imposition (H1): Measure spurious-culmination-commitment rate = fraction of underspecified items on which the model commits to a completed (or definitively-not-completed) reading as if obligatory (on culmination-inference, NLI, or reasoning). Verify near-zero commitment on DISAMBIGUATED variants (model should follow the cue) and appropriate commitment on boundedness-forcing controls. Compare against the model's handling of the same completion distinction when spelled out lexically. Control for tokenizer fertility, verb frequency, and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test underspecified-language status adds predictive power beyond fertility/resource).
3) English-completed pull (H1b): Test whether the committed reading tracks the ENGLISH default (typically a completed/telic reading of a count-object event) rather than target-language pragmatics. Define English-completed-pull rate = fraction of commitment cases whose reading matches the English forced paraphrase. Predict higher pull for lower-resource underspecified languages. Partial correlations controlling for resource/fertility.
4) Typology-predicted imposition (H3, external validation): Using the telicity-marking-strategy typology (covert English, overt Slavic perfective, bare-noun Mandarin, particle-based Hungarian-style), assign each language a boundedness-obligatoriness score, and test whether per-language spurious-culmination rate is predicted by that typological score (Spearman correlation; held-out prediction), tying the internal phenomenon to independent linguistic ground truth. Predict imposition is strongest for the most underspecified languages (Mandarin > Indonesian) and near-zero for perfective-forcing Russian.
5) Representational localization (H2): Extract a telicity/boundedness direction via difference-in-means between telic-completed and atelic-ongoing representations at each layer, per language (following About Time 2022; Steering Tense and Aspect 2025). Test (a) whether the direction is SHARED across languages and English-scaffolded (cross-lingual cosine alignment across layers, strongest in mid/shared-hub layers); (b) whether an UNDERSPECIFIED input nonetheless projects strongly onto the telic/completed pole in the shared hub (the hub assigns an endpoint it lacks) while any residual underspecification signal is stronger in early/language-specific layers, using logit-lens/tuned-lens crystallization-depth tracking. Baseline: tense/number directions (categories English marks) as a within-model shared-category comparison. Mediation: regress behavioral commitment on shared-hub telicity-projection strength of the underspecified input (partial correlation controlling for fertility/resource; held-out R^2).
6) Cross-lingual transfer loss (H4): Measure underspecification-preservation rate in translation across the underspecified/forcing boundary; predict directional asymmetry - underspecified->English silently ADDS obligatory completion more than English->underspecified fails to strip it, because the hub lacks an underspecified-boundedness slot. Measure within-generation drift toward committing completion over a continuation. Compare against a tense-preservation baseline (a category English marks) as a matched control.
7) Causal steering/patching test (core): (a) Steer the underspecified input's representation toward the NEUTRAL/underspecified region (null-projection of the telicity direction) and measure whether faithful underspecification is restored (correct NEUTRAL on NLI, no spurious culmination commitment, correct completion-dependent reasoning), and confirm the direction causally controls the elicited completion reading (flip rate completed<->ongoing) without switching output language. (b) For committed items, patch the residual language-specific underspecification signal (from early/language-specific layers of the underspecified pass) into later computation and test restoration - localizing failure to the shared hub OVERWRITING a shallowly-present underspecification signal versus its absence. Compare against random-direction ablation and whole-hub English-steering baselines. Competence controls: on DISAMBIGUATED and boundedness-forcing items the model must still assign the CORRECT specific completion reading (restoring underspecification only where warranted), preserve fluency, and not switch output language (off-target rate).
8) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify steering/patching is telicity-specific (changes completion reading but not the event's identity, tense, or participants), is graded (imposition scales with how underspecified the language is), and is not a lexical-frequency artifact. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 shows stronger imposition than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM/Qwen (which see more underspecified-language data); test whether imposition magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the telicity direction and with target-language training share. Aspect-cue interaction: following Do pretrained transformers infer telicity like humans (2021), test whether the model over-relies on temporal-unit/object-quantity cues to impose telicity, and whether removing those cues increases or decreases imposition.
Evaluation metrics: spurious-culmination-commitment rate (underspecified vs disambiguated vs boundedness-forcing controls); English-completed-pull rate and its partial correlation with resource/fertility; culmination-NLI NEUTRAL-accuracy; completion-dependent reasoning accuracy; shared-hub telicity-projection strength and crystallization depth (vs tense/number baseline); cross-lingual alignment of the telicity direction; imposition-vs-telicity-typology correlation and held-out prediction; translation underspecification-preservation rate and directional asymmetry (vs tense-preservation baseline); within-generation completion-drift rate; mediation regression (held-out R^2); steering flip rate and patching-induced restoration; competence preservation, off-target rate; cross-model imposition comparison and correlation with training share; temporal-cue-reliance interaction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Establishing that an event is GENUINELY boundedness-underspecified (both completed and ongoing readings licensed) is subtle and context-dependent; we restrict to carefully controlled templates with native-speaker verification, report inter-annotator agreement, and exclude low-agreement items. 2) Boundedness-forcing vs underspecified status is correlated with language family, script (logographic Mandarin), and resource level; the DISAMBIGUATED variants, boundedness-forcing controls, within-language underspecified-vs-disambiguated contrasts, and the typology-based prediction are designed to isolate the imposition pathway, but residual confounds may remain, and low-resource underspecified languages (Thai) may confound imposition with sparse training - we therefore center the CORE study on Mandarin (well-resourced, cleanly underspecified) and English/Russian, treating others as extensions. 3) Difference-in-means telicity directions may entangle tense, duration, or lexical-aspect (stativity) features; we use multiple extraction methods, include tense/duration control probes, and apply specificity checks. 4) Logit-lens/tuned-lens depth is approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation and multiple lenses. 5) Even English does not obligatorily entail culmination for all simple-past telic predicates (Temporal Information and Event Bounding 2022), so the 'English default' is a tendency, not an absolute; we calibrate the English baseline empirically rather than assuming full culmination. 6) Instruction-tuned models may hedge ('the action may or may not be finished'), which we treat as a positive underspecification-awareness signal rather than failure; we test base models where available and use both forced-choice and NLI probes. 7) Patching may have entangled effects; we report ambiguous cases and multiple granularities. 8) If NO imposition is found - underspecified events remain appropriately open-ended, predictable from typology, preserved across transfer - this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the shared hub represents boundedness-underspecification despite its English scaffolding, valuable either way. 9) The typology-prediction analysis assumes training data reflects each language's real aspectual usage, which may not hold; we treat typology as a noisy predictor and rely on behavioral and causal tests for core claims. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: shared_number_attraction_miscalibration
Title: Borrowed Attraction: A Shared, English-Scaffolded Number-Feature Circuit Makes Multilingual LLMs Susceptible to Agreement Attraction Even Where Morphology Should Protect Them
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs implement subject-verb (and other) agreement via a largely shared, English-scaffolded number-feature direction that is written by a controller and read by the verb. We hypothesize this shared circuit inherits an English-like 'agreement attraction' susceptibility — a distractor noun's number leaks into the verb decision — and, crucially, that this susceptibility is MIS-CALIBRATED across languages: it fails to be suppressed in languages whose overt morphology (rich case marking, non-concatenative/ablaut plurals) provides cues that should protect against attraction, because the shared direction is retrieved by number similarity in the hub rather than by language-appropriate case/controller cues. The attraction rate is thus predictable from the geometric interference between distractor and controller number signals, and is causally reducible by suppressing the distractor's contribution to the shared number direction.
Related Work: Interpretability work shows subject-verb agreement is driven by a language-independent 'subject number direction' written by one attention head and read by MLP neurons, steerable across languages (On the Similarity of Circuits across Languages 2024), that morphosyntactic/agreement units overlap cross-lingually and scale with syntactic similarity (Same Neurons Different Languages 2022; Different types of syntactic agreement recruit the same units 2025; Causal Analysis of Syntactic Agreement Neurons in Multilingual LMs 2022), and that two distinct mechanisms exist for short- vs long-range agreement. Separately, a rich human psycholinguistics literature documents AGREEMENT ATTRACTION — a distractor noun illusorily attracting the verb's number — and shows it is modulated by plural-formation strategy (suffixal vs ablaut in Arabic; Tucker et al. 2015), morphological richness and structural distance (Spanish/English; Foote 2013; Lago 2014), i.e., that overt morphology can protect against or shape attraction. NO prior work connects these: none tests whether the SHARED, English-scaffolded number circuit inherits English-like attraction, whether attraction susceptibility is MIS-CALIBRATED for morphologically rich languages (attracting where the language's own morphology should not), whether attraction is predictable from geometric interference in the shared number direction, or whether suppressing the distractor's contribution to that direction causally removes the illusion. Cross-lingual syntactic-transfer work (Understanding Cross-Lingual Syntactic Transfer 2020) finds grammatical transfer is limited/interference-prone, motivating a NEGATIVE-TRANSFER account of attraction. We uniquely reframe agreement attraction as a shared-circuit retrieval-interference bug that is inherited across languages and mis-calibrated to morphology, with a mechanistic interference metric and a targeted causal fix.
Abstract: When people process 'the key to the cabinets are...', a plural distractor ('cabinets') illusorily attracts the verb into agreeing with it — a robust human phenomenon called agreement attraction whose strength depends on a language's morphology (e.g., Arabic suffixal vs. ablaut plurals, Spanish morphological richness). Interpretability work shows multilingual LLMs implement agreement via a largely SHARED, English-scaffolded number-feature direction written by a controller and read by the verb. We ask a simple question these two literatures make urgent: does the shared circuit inherit an English-like attraction susceptibility, and is that susceptibility MIS-CALIBRATED across languages — attracting even where a language's own overt morphology (rich case marking, non-concatenative plurals) should protect against it? We hypothesize (1) attraction arises because the shared number direction is retrieved by number similarity in the hub rather than by language-appropriate controller/case cues; (2) per-item attraction is predictable from a geometric interference metric measuring how strongly the distractor writes onto the shared number direction relative to the controller; and (3) attraction is causally reducible by suppressing the distractor's contribution to that direction, without harming correct agreement. We build controlled multilingual attraction minimal-pair suites across languages varying in case-marking and plural-formation strategy (English, German, Russian, Spanish, Arabic, Turkish), on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM. Using activation patching on the shared number direction, logit-lens interference tracking, and cross-lingual direction transplant, we measure attraction rates, interference-attraction correlations, morphology mis-calibration, and causal-suppression recovery. Metrics include attraction-error rate, interference-metric predictive R-squared, morphology-protection gap (human vs. model), suppression-induced recovery, and off-target rate.
Experiments:
1) Multilingual attraction suite: Construct controlled minimal quadruplets (grammatical/ungrammatical x singular/plural distractor) per language, following the human attraction paradigm ('the key to the cabinet(s) is/are...'), with the distractor inside a PP or relative clause (short vs long-range), across languages spanning morphological strategies: English (impoverished), Spanish (rich verbal morphology), German/Russian (overt case marking that disambiguates the controller), Arabic (suffixal vs ABLAUT plural distractors — the key human contrast), Turkish (agglutinative case + optional plural). Native-speaker verified; include nonce-noun variants to rule out lexical confounds; report inter-annotator agreement. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral attraction map (H0): Measure per-language attraction-error rate = the increase in the model's preference for the distractor-agreeing (grammatically incorrect) verb when the distractor mismatches the controller in number, relative to a matched-number baseline (the classic attraction signature). Replicate the human singular/plural asymmetry (plural distractors attract more) and the short vs long-range difference. Establish that the model shows attraction in English (inheritance baseline).
3) Morphology mis-calibration (H2, core): Test whether attraction FAILS to be suppressed where the language's overt morphology should protect it. Specifically, (a) case-marked languages (German/Russian) unambiguously mark the controller as subject and the distractor as non-subject — does the model still attract as if case were absent (English-like)? (b) Arabic ablaut vs suffixal plural distractors — does the model reproduce the human pattern (suffixal attracts more, ablaut less) or flatten it toward an English-like suffixal-default? Quantify a morphology-protection gap = (expected attraction reduction from the language's morphology, from the human literature) minus (observed model reduction). Predict a positive gap (under-protection) that is larger for lower-resource and more English-distant morphology. Control for tokenizer fertility, distractor frequency, and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test morphology-type adds predictive power beyond fertility/resource).
4) Shared number-direction extraction and interference metric (H1): Following On the Similarity of Circuits across Languages (2024), locate the attention head(s) writing the number direction and the reading MLP neurons per model, and extract a per-language number direction via difference-in-means (singular vs plural controllers). Verify cross-lingual cosine alignment (shared direction) and that steering with the English direction flips verb number in each language. Define per-item interference = projection of the DISTRACTOR token's residual contribution onto the shared number direction relative to the controller's contribution at the verb position. Test whether per-item interference predicts attraction-error probability (Spearman, held-out R^2), and whether the number direction is written from the distractor's position at the verb readout on attracted items (logit-lens/attention attribution).
5) Causal decomposition via activation patching: For attracted (illusory) items, (a) patch the shared number direction at the verb readout from a no-distractor control to test that removing the distractor's number contribution fixes agreement (attraction is a number-direction interference, not a separate mechanism); (b) patch/ablate specifically the distractor's write onto the number direction (zero the distractor-position contribution to the head output) and measure attraction reduction; (c) as a specificity check, patch case/controller-identity components in German/Russian and test whether restoring case information (which the model under-uses) reduces attraction — localizing mis-calibration to failure to gate the number direction by case.
6) Cross-lingual transplant test: Transplant the number direction / distractor-suppression operation learned in one language (e.g., English or Spanish) into another language's attracted forward pass and measure whether it removes attraction — confirming the shared, portable nature of the circuit and that attraction is a shared-circuit property. Compare against a random-direction control.
7) Targeted intervention and specificity: Deploy a train-free 'distractor-gating' intervention that suppresses the distractor's contribution to the shared number direction at the verb readout. Metrics: attraction-error-rate reduction; correct-agreement preservation on grammatical items (the intervention must NOT reduce sensitivity to genuine agreement); off-target/language-mixing and fluency checks; degradation on English. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 shows larger mis-calibration (English-like under-protection) than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test correlation of mis-calibration with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the number direction and with training share.
Evaluation metrics: per-language attraction-error rate (with singular/plural and short/long-range asymmetries vs human patterns); morphology-protection gap (model vs human) and its partial correlation with morphology-type over fertility/resource baselines; interference-metric predictive R^2 for attraction; share of attracted items fixed by number-direction vs distractor-suppression vs case-restoration patching; transplant-induced attraction removal; intervention-induced attraction reduction with correct-agreement preservation; off-target rate; cross-model mis-calibration comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Agreement attraction is a well-studied HUMAN phenomenon; the risk is that models simply show it identically to English humans everywhere — but that itself (English-like attraction even in case-rich languages) is exactly the mis-calibration we predict and would be a positive result. 2) Morphology type is correlated with language family, script, and resource level; the ablaut-vs-suffixal WITHIN-Arabic contrast and case-vs-no-case within-language manipulations (e.g., German case-ambiguous vs case-disambiguated distractors) isolate the morphology pathway, but residual confounds may remain — we center the core morphology-protection test on within-language contrasts. 3) Difference-in-means number directions may entangle lexical/gender features; we use nonce nouns, multiple extraction methods, and the established head/neuron circuit from prior work as an anchor. 4) The interference metric relies on attributing residual contributions by token position, which is approximate; we cross-validate with attention attribution and patching. 5) The distractor-suppression intervention could reduce genuine agreement sensitivity; we require correct-agreement preservation on grammatical items as a hard constraint and report the full tradeoff. 6) Human effect sizes (from self-paced reading) are behavioral and not directly comparable to model log-prob preferences; the model-vs-human comparison is qualitative (direction, singular/plural asymmetry, morphology ordering), not a claim of identical mechanism. 7) Case-restoration patching in German/Russian assumes case information is separably represented; if it is not, we report this as evidence the model never encoded case as a gating cue — itself informative. 8) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM's less English-centric hub analyzed as a contrast). 9) If attraction is correctly calibrated to each language's morphology (no protection gap), this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the shared circuit is gated by language-appropriate cues rather than blindly English-scaffolded — valuable either way. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: register_drift_generation
Title: Losing the Register Halfway Through: Generation-Time Register Drift Toward the English Default in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: When a multilingual LLM generates a longer output in a target language whose grammar obligatorily encodes register/politeness (Japanese/Korean sentence-enders, French/German/Hindi T-V, Javanese ngoko/krama), it fails to MAINTAIN the register it established at the start: as the generation proceeds, the accumulating text pulls the model's late-layer 'register direction' toward the register-flattened default of the English-scaffolded shared hub, producing a measurable, position-dependent register-drift that increases with output length and typological distance from English. This drift is a distinct phenomenon from one-shot language confusion or register comprehension errors, is predicted by a decaying 'register-anchor' signal, and is causally correctable by re-injecting the target register direction at each generation step, without retraining.
Related Work: Prior mechanistic work establishes a shared, English-scaffolded hub with late-layer language-specific decoding (Do Llamas Work in English 2024; Semantic Hub 2024; MWork 2024; Cross-Layer Transcoders 2025) and localizes *language* confusion to late-layer transition failures with neuron-level fixes (Mechanistic Language Confusion 2025; Lost in Multilinguality 2025). Human psycholinguistics shows register switching incurs control costs distinct from language switching (Declerck et al. 2019, register vs language switch costs). Monolingual work treats formality/politeness as steerable linear directions (Interpreting Politeness 2016; STAR 2025). NLP register/formality transfer and honorific-constrained generation exist as tasks. My own prior honorific proposal concerns *comprehension* (collapse of honorific distinctions on input). NO prior work studies generation-time, WITHIN-output register CONSISTENCY: whether a model that starts in a correct register progressively drifts toward the hub's flattened English default as the sequence grows, whether this drift is position-dependent and length-scaled, whether a decaying register-anchor signal predicts it, or whether per-step register re-injection fixes it. We reframe register failure as a temporal, autoregressive drift phenomenon with a distinctive signature and a cheap causal remedy, orthogonal to one-shot language-confusion and comprehension accounts.
Abstract: Many languages grammatically require speakers to encode a social register: Japanese and Korean mark politeness on every sentence-ender, French/German/Hindi choose T vs V pronouns, Javanese picks ngoko vs krama. A faithful generator must hold this register CONSTANT across an entire response. We ask a simple, previously untested question about multilingual language models: when asked to generate a longer answer in a register-marking language, does the model MAINTAIN the register it established, or does it drift? We hypothesize register drift: because the shared semantic hub is scaffolded by register-flat English, the accumulating generated context progressively pulls the model's late-layer register direction toward an English-like default, so register consistency degrades with output position and length, most sharply for languages typologically distant from English. We build a controlled multilingual register-generation suite across register-marking languages (Japanese, Korean, Hindi, German, French, Javanese) and elicit long-form outputs whose register is fixed by an initial instruction/context. Using a per-position register classifier, logit-lens/tuned-lens tracking of a difference-in-means register direction at each generated token, and activation patching, we (1) measure position-dependent register-consistency decay and its length/distance scaling; (2) test whether a decaying 'register-anchor' signal from the prompt predicts drift; and (3) run the core causal test: re-inject the target-language register direction at each generation step and measure restored consistency without harming fluency or content. On Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM. Metrics include per-position register-consistency curves, drift slope vs length and typological distance, anchor-decay prediction, and re-injection recovery with competence controls.
Experiments:
1) Register-generation suite: Construct ~400 prompts across register-marking languages (Japanese teineigo/plain, Korean haeyo/hae, Hindi aap/tum, German Sie/du, French vous/tu, Javanese krama/ngoko where native access permits). Each prompt fixes a target register via explicit instruction and/or an established addressee relationship, and elicits a LONG-FORM output (a multi-sentence explanation, story, or dialogue turn, ~150-400 tokens) that contains many obligatory register-marked positions. Include matched short-output controls and a register-flat English control. Native-speaker verify register markers and gold register; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral register-drift map (H1): Train/validate a per-position register classifier (rule-based on obligatory markers plus a learned classifier) that labels each register-marked token in the generation as target-register vs drifted. Compute a per-position register-consistency curve (fraction correct as a function of token position / marker index in the output). Test H1: consistency decays with position and total output length; quantify drift slope per language. Compare against short-output controls (little room to drift) and the English-flat control. Control for tokenizer fertility and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test typological distance predicts drift slope beyond resource/fertility). Predict steepest drift for the most distant, most-obligatory-register languages (Japanese/Korean/Javanese) and shallower for T-V languages (German/French).
3) Representational tracking (H2): Extract a difference-in-means register direction (deferential vs plain) per language at late layers, verify it causally controls emitted register via steering (flip rate). At each generated token, project the residual stream onto this register direction and track its magnitude across generation. Test whether the projection onto the target-register pole decays with position (mirroring behavioral drift) and drifts toward the English-default pole. Define a 'register-anchor decay' = decline in the prompt-established register signal over generated positions; test whether anchor decay predicts per-position behavioral drift (partial correlation; held-out R^2). Compare register-direction cross-lingual alignment (shared vs language-specific) to test whether the drift target is the shared-hub default.
4) Error localization: Test whether drift coincides with a weakening late-layer register signal rather than a wrong concept (activation patching: patch the late-layer register components at a drifted position from an early, still-correct position; if this restores correct register, the failure is register-signal decay, not content).
5) Core causal intervention (H3): At each generation step, re-inject (add a steering vector for) the target register direction into the late-layer residual stream, with strength calibrated to restore the anchor magnitude. Measure restored per-position register consistency and drift-slope reduction. Compare against baselines: (a) prompt-reinforcement (repeat the register instruction), (b) the linear-shortcut / language-confusion neuron-edit approach adapted to register, (c) a random-direction control. Compute 'consistency-recovery elasticity' = consistency gain per unit baseline drift, correlated with drift slope.
6) Specificity and competence controls: Verify re-injection is register-specific (fixes register but does not change content or switch OUTPUT LANGUAGE; measure off-target/language-mixing rate), preserves fluency and task quality (human/auto ratings), and does not over-formalize where a plain register was intended (test both deferential->plain and plain->deferential targets symmetrically). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 drifts more than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether drift magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the register direction and with target-language training share.
Evaluation metrics: per-position register-consistency curves and drift slope; drift-slope vs output-length and typological-distance partial correlations (held-out R^2 over resource/fertility); register-anchor-decay prediction of drift (held-out R^2); share of drifted positions fixed by late-layer register patching; re-injection consistency-recovery and elasticity vs baselines; competence preservation (fluency, task quality), off-target/language-mixing rate, symmetry across deferential/plain targets; cross-model drift comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Automatic per-position register labeling is hard for languages with subtle or optional marking; we combine rule-based marker detection with a learned classifier, restrict to obligatory-marking positions, use native-speaker verification, and report classifier reliability. 2) Register-marking status is correlated with language family, script, and resource level; the short-output controls, English-flat control, within-language deferential-vs-plain symmetry, and typological-distance partial correlations isolate the drift pathway, but residual confounds may remain; low-resource Javanese may confound drift with sparse training, so we center the core study on well-resourced Japanese/Korean/German/Hindi and treat Javanese as an extension. 3) Difference-in-means register directions may entangle formality/lexical features; we use multiple extraction methods, symmetric (both-pole) checks, and specificity controls. 4) Drift could partly reflect content requiring a register shift (e.g., quoting a plain-speech character); we filter to prompts with a single fixed register and exclude reported-speech items. 5) Re-injection could harm fluency or over-formalize; we require competence preservation and symmetric correction in both register directions, and report the full tradeoff. 6) Instruction-tuned models may be trained to hold register better than base models; we test both and treat strong base-model drift with instruction-tuned improvement as an informative training-effect finding. 7) Logit-lens/tuned-lens projections at late layers are approximate; cross-validated with steering flip-rate and patching. 8) If NO drift is found - register stays consistent across long outputs regardless of length - this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the model maintains a language-specific register anchor despite the English-scaffolded hub, valuable either way. 9) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: moral_foundation_gain_reweighting
Title: Turning the Dials, Not the Dilemma: Language Sets a Gain on Shared Moral-Foundation Directions in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Cross-lingual inconsistency in LLM moral judgments is not caused by language-specific moral concepts, but by a language-controlled GAIN that reweights a small set of SHARED, language-agnostic moral-foundation directions (care, fairness, loyalty, authority, purity, liberty). The dilemma is projected onto the same foundation axes regardless of language; what the query/reasoning language changes is the relative amplitude with which each foundation feeds the final judgment, and this gain vector shifts toward the dominant-language (English/US) default. Consequently the judgment shift is predictable from a single per-language foundation-gain vector, is foundation-specific (not uniform), and is causally correctable by rescaling individual foundation directions at inference without retraining.
Related Work: Behavioral work robustly documents that LLM moral judgments vary by prompt language and align best with WEIRD/English-culture norms (Ethical Reasoning Depends on Language 2024; MultiTP 2024; Moral Machine multilingual 2024; MFQ-2 multilingual 2024; One Model Many Morals 2025), and a diagnostic framework shows the REASONING language contributes twice the variance of the input language and maps onto Moral Foundations Theory dimensions (Untangling Input from Reasoning Language 2026). Mechanistic value work identifies value neurons whose ablation reduces value-aligned behavior (ValueExploration 2025), value vectors/neurons shared vs unique across intrinsic/prompted expression (Dual Mechanisms of Value Expression 2025), and steering of political/cultural orientation via center-of-mass activation interventions (Multilingual Political Views 2025; Localized Cultural Knowledge is Controllable 2025; CultureSteer 2025). Cross-lingual alignment work shows a transfer-vs-cultural-erasure tradeoff with layer-separated steering (Rethinking Cross-lingual Alignment / Surgical Steering 2025). NONE of these decomposes moral judgment into a fixed set of SHARED foundation directions read out through a LANGUAGE-CONTROLLED GAIN, nor tests the specific prediction that language reweights (rather than replaces) foundation axes, nor shows that per-foundation gain rescaling causally reproduces and corrects the cross-lingual shift. We reframe moral inconsistency from 'different values per language' to 'same foundation basis, different mixing weights,' yielding a compact, predictive gain vector and a targeted causal fix.
Abstract: Large language models reach different moral conclusions depending on the language they are prompted in, and recent work shows the language of REASONING matters even more than the language of the dilemma. Existing explanations treat this as culturally divergent values or use coarse value-neuron ablations, but none explains the structure of the shift. We propose a compact mechanistic account grounded in Moral Foundations Theory: an LLM judges a moral dilemma by projecting it onto a small set of SHARED, largely language-agnostic moral-foundation directions (care, fairness, loyalty, authority, purity, liberty), and the query/reasoning language sets a GAIN that reweights how strongly each foundation feeds the final judgment. Under this account, language does not change the moral concepts; it turns dials on a fixed set of axes, and the dial settings drift toward the dominant-language (English/US) default. This makes three testable predictions: (1) foundation directions are shared across languages (high cross-lingual alignment); (2) the per-language judgment shift is captured by a low-dimensional, foundation-specific gain vector, not a uniform bias; and (3) rescaling individual foundation directions at inference can causally reproduce another language's judgments and correct cross-lingual inconsistency. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using multilingual moral benchmarks (MFQ-2, MultiTP/Moral Machine, WVS-derived items) across typologically diverse languages, combining difference-in-means foundation-direction extraction, logit-lens readout, activation patching, and gain-steering. Metrics include cross-lingual foundation-direction alignment, gain-vector predictive R-squared for judgment shifts, foundation-specificity of the shift, and steering-induced consistency recovery with competence controls.
Experiments:
1) Foundation-direction extraction and cross-lingual alignment (P1): Using MFQ-2 and curated single-foundation vignettes, extract per-language difference-in-means directions for each of the six moral foundations (care, fairness/equality, loyalty, authority, purity, liberty) at each layer, in typologically diverse languages (English, Spanish, Russian, Chinese, Hindi, Arabic, Swahili). Measure cross-lingual cosine alignment of each foundation direction across layers; test that alignment is high and peaks in middle/shared-hub layers, and compare against a language-identity direction baseline. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Foundation-gain readout (P2, core): For a bank of moral dilemmas (MultiTP/Moral Machine vignettes, WVS-derived justifiability items, UniMoral) presented per language, project the residual stream at the judgment position onto the six shared foundation directions to obtain a per-item, per-language 'foundation activation profile,' and estimate a per-LANGUAGE gain vector g_L (six scalars) via regression of the model's judgment onto foundation activations. Test P2: the cross-lingual judgment shift for each item is predicted by the difference in gain vectors (g_L vs g_English) applied to the SHARED foundation projections (held-out R^2), and this beats (a) a uniform per-language bias baseline and (b) a full per-language relearned readout (i.e., the shift is low-dimensional and foundation-structured). Report which foundations carry the largest language-dependent gain changes (predict authority/purity/loyalty shift most, care/fairness least), and correlate g_L with WVS/MFQ human survey foundation profiles per culture.
3) Input- vs reasoning-language decomposition: Following the input/reasoning-language diagnostic, cross the dilemma language with the reasoning (chain-of-thought) language (matched and mismatched conditions) and test whether the gain vector is set primarily by the reasoning language (predicting reasoning-language gain dominates, consistent with its larger behavioral variance) versus the input language. This localizes WHERE the gain is set.
4) Causal gain-steering test (P3, core): At the readout layer, rescale individual foundation directions (multiply the projection onto a chosen foundation by a scalar) to transform the English gain vector into a target language's gain vector, and measure whether the model's judgments shift toward that language's judgments WITHOUT changing the input language (judgment-transfer rate). Conversely, correct cross-lingual inconsistency by equalizing gain vectors across languages and measure consistency@k gain. Compare against baselines: whole-hub center-of-mass steering (Multilingual Political Views 2025), cultural steering vector (Localized Cultural Knowledge 2025), and a random-direction control. Verify foundation-specificity: steering the authority gain changes authority-driven items but not care-driven items.
5) Specificity and competence controls: Verify gain-steering (a) does not switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), (b) preserves general reasoning and factual competence and fluency, (c) moves judgments symmetrically (can push toward AND away from the English default), and (d) does not merely add a uniform lenience/severity bias (foundation-specific vs uniform). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 has gain vectors more collapsed toward the English default than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether the magnitude of language-dependent gain change correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the foundation directions and with training share.
Evaluation metrics: per-foundation cross-lingual direction alignment; gain-vector held-out predictive R^2 for judgment shifts (vs uniform-bias and full-relearn baselines); foundation-specificity of shifts; input-vs-reasoning-language gain attribution; judgment-transfer rate and consistency@k recovery under gain-steering vs baselines; correlation of g_L with human survey foundation profiles; off-target rate, competence/fluency preservation, symmetry; cross-model gain-collapse comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The six-foundation basis may not cleanly capture the model's moral geometry; if a data-driven basis (e.g., PCA/SAE over moral-item activations) fits better, we report the empirically-best low-dimensional basis and treat MFT as one interpretable option, keeping the core 'shared basis + language gain' claim testable regardless. 2) Foundation directions from difference-in-means may entangle topical/lexical content; we use matched single-foundation vignettes, multiple extraction methods, and specificity controls. 3) Culture and language are confounded (query language is correlated with resource level, script, culture); the input-vs-reasoning-language crossing and within-language item contrasts help isolate the gain mechanism, but residual confounds remain. 4) Instruction-tuned models may hedge or refuse on dilemmas; we test base models where available and use forced-choice and log-prob-based justifiability measures. 5) Gain-steering could harm reasoning or over-impose a target culture; we require competence preservation, symmetry, and foundation-specificity, reporting the full tradeoff. 6) Human survey foundation profiles are noisy and may not reflect training-data morality; we treat them as an external reference, not ground truth, and rely on the internal gain-vector prediction and causal steering for core claims. 7) The account may only partially hold (some genuine per-language concept differences); a partial result still usefully bounds how much cross-lingual moral inconsistency is reweighting versus genuine value divergence. 8) If foundation directions are NOT shared across languages, the hypothesis is refuted, which is itself an informative finding that moral concepts are genuinely language-specific. 9) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: conceptual_metaphor_source_imposition
Title: Anger Is Heat, But Only in English: Does the Shared Hub Impose the Dominant Language's Conceptual-Metaphor Source Domain Cross-Lingually?
Short Hypothesis: When reasoning about an abstract TARGET concept (anger, importance, time, love, argument), a multilingual LLM recruits the SOURCE-domain structure that is conventionalized in its English-scaffolded shared hub (e.g., ANGER IS HEAT, IMPORTANT IS BIG, TIME IS MONEY), and IMPOSES that source-domain inference even when the queried language conventionally maps the same target onto a DIFFERENT source domain (e.g., a language where anger is mapped to 'a swelling stomach' or importance to 'weight'). This produces a distinctive, measurable cross-lingual reasoning inconsistency: the model's inferential entailments, adjective preferences, and image-schema judgments about the target concept track the ENGLISH source domain rather than the target-language one. The imposition is mediated by a shared source-domain feature direction that bleeds into the target concept's shared-hub representation, tracks each language's empirical conceptual-metaphor inventory, and is causally correctable by steering the source-domain direction without harming literal factual competence.
Related Work: Prior work shows (a) pretrained LMs encode metaphoricity in middle layers and it transfers cross-lingually and cross-dataset (Metaphors in PLMs 2022), (b) GPT-style models can identify source domains but far better in English than Spanish (Does GPT-3 Grasp Metaphors 2023), (c) conceptual metaphors can be operationalized cross-lingually via parallel corpora and clustering (Can we Operationalize Conceptual Metaphor Cross-Lingually 2025; High-Precision Abductive Mapping 2015), (d) typological distance affects preservation of metaphorical mappings in translation (Did he lead monologues 2025), and (e) metaphors causally influence LLM reasoning and cross-domain (mis)alignment (Metaphors are a Source of Cross-Domain Misalignment 2026). Foundational interpretability establishes an English-scaffolded shared semantic hub (Semantic Hub 2024; Do Llamas Work in English 2024; Do Multilingual LLMs Think In English 2025; Separating Tongue from Thought 2024). CRITICALLY, all prior metaphor work asks whether models DETECT/REPLICATE metaphor or how it transfers as a coarse label; NONE asks whether the shared hub IMPOSES the dominant language's CONVENTIONALIZED SOURCE DOMAIN onto languages that lexicalize the same target concept via a DIFFERENT source, causing cross-lingual reasoning INCONSISTENCY on the abstract concept; none localizes a shared source-domain direction that bleeds into the target concept, ties imposition to each language's conceptual-metaphor inventory, or offers a causal source-domain steering fix. Unlike my prior 'idiom leakage' proposal (surface figurative expressions), this targets the deeper CONCEPTUAL-METAPHOR level (systematic target->source domain mappings that structure inference), grounded in Conceptual Metaphor Theory with an external mapping-database ground truth, and it is orthogonal to my grammatical-category, spatial, color, kinship, pragmatic, and phonosemantic proposals.
Abstract: People understand abstract concepts through metaphor: anger is heat, importance is size, time is money. Conceptual Metaphor Theory shows that languages often map the SAME abstract target onto DIFFERENT source domains - anger may be a hot fluid in one language and a swelling body in another. Multilingual language models build a shared semantic hub scaffolded by English. We ask a simple, previously untested question: when a model reasons about an abstract concept, does the English-scaffolded hub IMPOSE English's conventionalized source-domain structure, even when the queried language conventionally uses a different source domain? We hypothesize that (1) the model's inferential judgments about a target concept (entailments, adjective/image-schema preferences, magnitude estimates) track the ENGLISH source domain rather than the target-language one; (2) this yields cross-lingual reasoning inconsistency on the abstract concept, concentrated on target concepts whose source domain DIVERGES across languages (versus a matched CONVERGENT baseline); (3) a shared source-domain feature direction bleeds into the target concept's shared-hub representation and mediates the imposition; and (4) imposition tracks each language's empirical conceptual-metaphor inventory. We build a controlled multilingual suite of abstract targets with cross-linguistically divergent versus convergent source domains, grounded in conceptual-metaphor databases and native-speaker verification, on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5 and BLOOM. Using difference-in-means source-domain probes, logit-lens depth tracking, activation patching and steering, we measure the source-imposition bias, its cross-lingual inconsistency signature, its scaling with metaphor inventories, and whether steering the source direction corrects it while preserving literal factual competence. Metrics include source-bias effect size, divergent-minus-convergent inconsistency gap, inventory-prediction correlation, mediation R-squared, and steering-induced consistency recovery.
Experiments:
1) Conceptual-metaphor suite: Assemble ~350 abstract TARGET concepts (e.g., anger, love, importance, time, argument, difficulty, happiness, understanding) each realized across typologically diverse languages (English, Spanish, Russian, Chinese, Hindi, Arabic, Turkish). For each target-language pair, code the conventional SOURCE domain(s) using conceptual-metaphor databases/lexicons and native-speaker verification (e.g., ANGER IS HEAT vs ANGER IS SWELLING; IMPORTANT IS BIG vs IMPORTANT IS HEAVY; TIME IS MONEY vs TIME IS DISTANCE). Key subsets: (a) DIVERGENT targets whose conventional source domain differs between English and the target language; (b) CONVERGENT targets sharing the same source domain (control). Design probes that hinge on source-domain structure but avoid the metaphor's surface words: (i) inferential entailment ('If John's anger is X, what follows?' with options aligned to heat-entailments vs swelling-entailments); (ii) forced-choice source-congruent adjective/image-schema preference; (iii) magnitude/geometry judgments (e.g., is importance more about size or weight?). Native-speaker verify source codings and gold answers; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral source-imposition bias (H1): For each target in each language, measure the rate at which the model's inferential/preference judgments align with the ENGLISH source domain versus the TARGET-LANGUAGE source domain. Compute a per-language source-imposition effect size (Cohen's d / log-odds), controlling for the target concept's literal facts, word frequency, tokenizer fertility, and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test target-language status adds predictive power). Verify near-zero imposition on CONVERGENT targets and near-ceiling English-alignment on English queries.
3) Cross-lingual inconsistency signature (H2, core): For DIVERGENT targets, measure whether the model's judgment about the SAME concept diverges across two languages in the direction predicted by each language's source domain, and define the inconsistency GAP = inconsistency(DIVERGENT) minus inconsistency(CONVERGENT). Predict a positive gap: source-domain divergence, not mere language change, drives extra inconsistency. Predict larger imposition for lower-resource, more English-distant languages.
4) Metaphor-inventory scaling (H4, external validation): Using conceptual-metaphor database coverage, assign each language an English-source-overlap score, and test whether per-language imposition is predicted by how much its conventional source domains diverge from English's (Spearman correlation; held-out prediction), tying the internal phenomenon to independent linguistic ground truth.
5) Representational localization (H3): Extract a SOURCE-domain feature direction (e.g., a HEAT vs non-heat axis, or a SIZE vs WEIGHT axis) via difference-in-means over neutral source-domain exemplars (not the target concept) at each layer, per language. Test (a) cross-lingual alignment of source-domain directions (shared vs language-specific); (b) whether a DIVERGENT target concept's shared-hub representation projects onto the ENGLISH source axis (source structure leaks into the abstract concept) via logit-lens/tuned-lens depth tracking; and (c) mediation: regress behavioral source-imposition on the target representation's projection onto the source direction (partial correlation controlling for frequency/fertility; held-out R^2). Baseline: a genuine literal-attribute direction as a within-model control.
6) Causal steering/patching test (core): (a) Steer the DIVERGENT target concept's representation from the English source pole toward the target-language source pole (e.g., swelling instead of heat) and measure whether inferential judgments flip to the target-language pattern (flip rate) and the inconsistency GAP shrinks toward the CONVERGENT baseline, without switching output language. (b) For imposed items, patch the residual language-specific source signal (from early/language-specific layers) into later computation and test restoration - localizing failure to the shared hub imposing an English source over a shallowly-present target-language source. Critically verify LITERAL FACTUAL COMPETENCE is preserved (the model must still answer literal factual questions about the concept correctly), plus fluency and off-target/language-mixing checks. Baselines: random-direction steering, whole-hub English-steering.
7) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify steering is source-domain-specific (changes metaphor-driven inference but not literal facts or unrelated attributes), graded (imposition scales with divergence), and not a lexical-frequency artifact. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 shows stronger imposition than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether imposition magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the source direction and with target-language training share. Qualitatively compare the model's per-language imposition pattern against the human Conceptual Metaphor Theory inventory.
Evaluation metrics: source-imposition effect size (divergent vs convergent; English-alignment vs target-alignment; partial correlation over frequency/fertility/resource; held-out R^2); cross-lingual inconsistency GAP (DIVERGENT minus CONVERGENT); imposition-vs-inventory-divergence correlation and held-out prediction; cross-lingual source-direction alignment; target-concept projection onto the source axis and its mediation of behavioral bias (held-out R^2); steering flip rate and patching-induced restoration and GAP reduction; literal-competence preservation, fluency, off-target rate; cross-model imposition comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Coding a language's 'conventional source domain' for an abstract target is subtle - languages often have multiple coexisting source domains and gradient conventionality; we ground codings in conceptual-metaphor databases with native-speaker verification, use a graded conventionality scale, report inter-annotator agreement, and restrict DIVERGENT items to cases with clear cross-lingual source contrast, treating mixed cases as a separate analysis. 2) Source-domain divergence is correlated with language family, script, and resource level; the CONVERGENT controls, English-vs-target alignment contrast, within-concept comparisons, and inventory-based prediction isolate the source-imposition pathway, but residual confounds may remain. 3) Probes must hinge on source-domain STRUCTURE without leaking the metaphor's surface words; we design lexically-neutral inferential/geometry probes and validate they cannot be solved by surface cues. 4) Difference-in-means source directions may entangle topical/lexical content; we extract them from neutral source exemplars (not the target), use multiple extraction methods, and a literal-attribute control direction. 5) Logit-lens/tuned-lens depth estimates are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation and multiple lenses. 6) Instruction-tuned models may verbally hedge or explain metaphors; we test base models where available and use forced-choice and log-prob-based inferential probes. 7) Steering could harm literal competence or fluency; we require literal-competence preservation and report the full tradeoff. 8) Database coverage of conceptual metaphors is uneven across languages; we treat inventory scores as noisy predictors and rely on behavioral and causal tests for core claims. 9) Human-LLM comparison is qualitative, not a claim of identical mechanism. 10) If NO imposition is found - inferential judgments track each language's own source domain and are consistent across languages despite divergent conventional metaphors - this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the shared hub represents abstract concepts in a source-domain-neutral or language-appropriate way, valuable either way. 11) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: recall_vs_translation_stage_editing
Title: Edit the Store, Not the Translator: Why Non-English Knowledge Edits Fail to Propagate in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Cross-lingual edit-propagation failure is not fundamentally about edit-vector orthogonality but about WHICH stage of the multilingual factual-recall pipeline an edit lands in. Because multilingual LLMs recall facts via an English-centric shared 'recall store' and then translate to the target language in late layers, an edit injected using a non-English prompt predominantly modifies the late-layer TRANSLATION stage (surface output mapping) rather than the shared recall store, so it cannot propagate to other languages. We predict edit propagation is governed by a measurable 'recall-store engagement' of the edit: edits that write into the early/mid shared recall store propagate broadly regardless of the language they were made in, whereas edits that write only into the late translation stage stay language-local. This yields a targeted fix: force the edit into the recall store.
Related Work: Prior work shows cross-lingual edits fail to propagate and that Chinese/English edit vectors are nearly orthogonal, treating this as a geometric property to be engineered around via null-space constraints (LangEdit 2025), language-agnostic factual neurons (LU-LAFNs 2024; One Mind Many Tongues 2024; MATRICE 2024), retrieval (ReMaKE 2024), or cross-lingual tuning (X-KDE 2025). Separately, 'Paths Not Taken' (2025) and 'How Do Multilingual LLMs Remember Facts' (2024) reveal a two-stage pipeline: English-centric recall (early/mid, language-independent subject enrichment) followed by late-layer, language-dependent object extraction/translation. 'Localization vs Editing' (Hase 2023) shows tracing location does not predict the best EDIT layer monolingually.
