NO prior work connects the two-stage recall/translation pipeline to edit-propagation failure by asking WHERE in the pipeline a non-English edit actually writes, testing that propagation is predicted by recall-store engagement, or showing that redirecting the edit into the shared recall store (rather than making vectors overlap post hoc) causally restores propagation. We reframe orthogonality as a symptom of stage-mislocalized edits and provide a mechanism-level, stage-targeted account and intervention, distinct from parameter-orthogonality and neuron-set methods.
Abstract: Knowledge edits made in one language rarely propagate to others, and recent work attributes this to nearly orthogonal edit vectors across languages. We propose a mechanistic explanation grounded in how multilingual models actually recall facts: they retrieve knowledge through an early/mid-layer, English-centric shared 'recall store' and then translate the answer into the query language in late layers. We hypothesize that an edit injected with a non-English prompt predominantly modifies the late TRANSLATION stage rather than the shared recall store, and that this stage-mislocalization—not orthogonality per se—is the root cause of propagation failure. This makes a sharp prediction: an edit's cross-lingual propagation is governed by how much it engages the shared recall store, so English-made edits (which naturally write into the store) propagate more than target-language edits, and target-language edits that happen to reach the store also propagate. We test this on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using causal tracing to locate, per edit, whether the injected knowledge lives in the early/mid recall store or the late translation stage; we correlate recall-store engagement with cross-lingual propagation across language pairs and scripts. We then run the core causal test: a stage-targeted editing procedure that forces the update into the shared recall store (editing at recall-store layers using an English-aligned key, then relying on the model's own late-layer translation), and compare its propagation, locality, and portability against ROME/MEMIT, language-agnostic-neuron editing, and null-space methods. Metrics include recall-store-engagement vs propagation correlation, per-language propagation success, portability (multi-hop), and locality.
Experiments:
1) Stage-localization of edits: Using CounterFact-style facts edited via ROME/MEMIT/in-context editing with prompts in different languages (English + target languages spanning scripts: French, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili), apply causal tracing / activation patching to determine, per edit, WHERE the new knowledge is stored: early/mid shared recall-store layers (language-independent subject-enrichment site) vs late language-dependent object-extraction/translation site. Define a per-edit 'recall-store engagement' score = fraction of the edit's causal effect mediated by early/mid shared layers. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Engagement-vs-propagation correlation (core prediction): For each edit, measure cross-lingual propagation (accuracy of the edited fact when queried in every other language, RankC-style) and test whether recall-store engagement predicts propagation better than (a) edit-vector orthogonality between source and target language, (b) script similarity, and (c) resource level. Use partial correlations and nested regression (AIC, held-out R^2). Prediction: engagement is the dominant predictor; orthogonality is a downstream symptom (edits with low store-engagement are also more orthogonal).
3) Language-of-edit asymmetry: Test the prediction that editing the SAME fact in English yields higher recall-store engagement and broader propagation than editing it in a low-resource target language; and that the minority of target-language edits that DO engage the store propagate as well as English edits. Report propagation-success curves as a function of engagement, per language-of-edit.
4) Core causal intervention (stage-targeted editing): Implement 'recall-store editing': perform the parameter update at the early/mid shared recall-store layers (identified in Exp 1) using an English-aligned subject key (mapping the target-language subject into the shared store representation), then let the model's own late layers translate. Compare against baselines: standard ROME/MEMIT at their default layer, language-agnostic-neuron editing (LU-LAFNs), and null-space/LangEdit. Metrics: cross-lingual propagation success (all languages), reliability (edit succeeds in the edit language), locality (unrelated facts unchanged, per language), and portability (multi-hop reasoning with the edited fact, MzsRE/MLaKE-style, CROLIN-MQUAKE).
5) Complementary steering test: At inference, patch the target-language edit's late-stage translation signal while restoring the original recall-store signal (and vice versa) to confirm that late-stage-only edits change surface output without changing the underlying recalled entity, and that store-level edits change the recalled entity in all languages.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify recall-store editing does not switch output language (off-target rate) or harm fluency, and that gains are not merely from editing an 'earlier layer' generically (compare to editing early layers with a target-language key, which should engage the store less). Cross-model contrast: predict more English-centric models (Llama-3) show a sharper store/translation split and larger propagation gains from recall-store editing than more multilingual BLOOM/Aya.
Evaluation metrics: recall-store-engagement-vs-propagation Spearman correlation and held-out R^2 over orthogonality/script/resource baselines; per-language propagation success and reliability; locality; portability (multi-hop accuracy); off-target/language-mixing rate; cross-model comparison of split-sharpness and intervention gains.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The recall-store vs translation-stage split may not be cleanly separable for all facts or architectures; we report ambiguous edits and use multiple tracing granularities. 2) Causal-tracing localization is known not to always predict the best monolingual edit layer (Hase 2023); our claim is specifically about the CROSS-LINGUAL propagation consequence of stage placement, which we test directly rather than assuming, and we compare against strong editing baselines. 3) Mapping a target-language subject into an English-aligned recall-store key requires a translation/alignment step that could introduce errors; we test alignment quality and report failure cases. 4) Recall-store editing might harm locality (broader edits could touch related facts); we measure locality explicitly and report the tradeoff. 5) Engagement and orthogonality are correlated by construction; we use partial correlations and the language-of-edit asymmetry (Exp 3) plus the causal intervention (Exp 4) to establish that engagement is the driver, not merely a correlate. 6) Results may be model-family dependent; BLOOM's less English-centric pipeline is analyzed as a contrast that should show weaker effects. 7) If propagation is NOT predicted by store-engagement, this is an informative negative result supporting the pure-orthogonality view and clarifying that stage placement is irrelevant. 8) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: negative_concord_dn_imposition
Title: Two Negatives Make a What? Does the English-Scaffolded Shared Hub Impose a Double-Negation Reading onto Negative-Concord Languages?
Short Hypothesis: Languages split parametrically on how multiple negatives compose: in Double-Negation (DN) languages (English, German, Mandarin) two negatives cancel to an affirmative, whereas in Negative-Concord (NC) languages (Spanish, Italian, Polish, Turkish) multiple negative words express a single, reinforced negation. Because the shared semantic hub of multilingual LLMs is scaffolded by DN English, we hypothesize the model IMPOSES a DN (cancellation) interpretation onto NC-language inputs: it reads a concord sentence like Spanish 'no vi a nadie' ('I didn't see anyone') as a cancelled double negation ('I saw someone'), tracking the English composition rule rather than the target-language grammar. This imposition is mediated by a shared, ablatable 'negation-composition' direction that governs whether a second negative cancels or reinforces, tracks each language's empirical NC/DN typology, is causally attributable to hub scaffolding rather than resource level, and is steerable back to the correct concord reading without harming single-negation comprehension.
Related Work: Two literatures meet but have never been connected in generative multilingual LLMs. (1) Interpretability treats negation as a single English operator: strong-hallucination theory and a latent-operator fix (Strong hallucinations from negation 2024), NLI/monotonicity and negation-scope failures (MoNLI 2020; Decomposing Natural Logic 2022; BERT attention negation scope 2020; It is not True that Transformers are Inductive Learners 2024), NPI licensing (Do Language Models Understand Anything 2018; BERT NPI 2023), ironic rebound (Don't Think of the White Bear 2025), and INLP-based removal of the negation imprint (Controlling the Imprint of Passivization and Negation 2020). All are monolingual/English and never address multiple-negative COMPOSITION cross-lingually. (2) A large typology literature establishes the NC-vs-DN parametric split and its cross-linguistic variation (de Swart & Sag polyadic quantifiers 2002/2010; Modeling typological markedness in negative concord 2006; Crosslinguistic consistency in logical connectives 2023; NC in Turkish/Romance/Basque/Hindi/Greek 2000-2025; The Negative Concord Mystery: Insights from a Language Model 2025, which studies acquisition in a small English LM, not cross-lingual imposition). CRITICALLY, no prior work asks whether the English-scaffolded shared hub, being a DN system, IMPOSES cancellation onto NC-language inputs, causing systematic single-vs-double-negation misinterpretation; none localizes a shared negation-composition direction, ties imposition to the NC/DN typology, or offers a causal fix. Unlike my prior 'portable operators, local scope' proposal (which concerns WHERE a single operator applies), this targets the parametric COMPOSITION RULE for combining multiple negatives (cancel vs reinforce), a distinct logical-semantics axis with external typological ground truth. It is orthogonal to all my other imposition/flattening proposals (tense, gender, evidentiality, honorifics, spatial frames, number, telicity, etc.).
Abstract: Every language can say 'no', but languages disagree on what happens when you say it twice. In Double-Negation (DN) languages like English, German and Mandarin, two negatives cancel ('I didn't see nobody' = I saw somebody); in Negative-Concord (NC) languages like Spanish, Italian, Polish and Turkish, multiple negative words reinforce a single negation ('no vi a nadie' = I saw no one). Multilingual language models build a shared semantic hub scaffolded by DN English. We ask a simple, previously untested question this asymmetry makes urgent: does the English-scaffolded hub IMPOSE a DN cancellation reading onto NC-language inputs, misinterpreting a reinforced single negation as a cancelled affirmative? We hypothesize that (1) the model reads NC sentences with a DN cancellation bias, tracking English composition rather than the target-language grammar; (2) this bias tracks each language's empirical NC/DN typology; (3) a shared, ablatable 'negation-composition' direction (cancel vs reinforce) mediates it; and (4) the correct concord reading is available shallowly in language-specific layers but overwritten in the shared hub. We build a controlled multilingual minimal-pair suite of single- vs multiple-negation sentences with verified truth-conditional readings across NC languages (Spanish, Italian, Polish, Turkish) and DN languages (English, German, Mandarin), on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5 and BLOOM. Using truth-conditional and NLI probes, difference-in-means composition-direction extraction, logit-lens depth tracking, activation patching and steering, we measure the DN-imposition rate, its typology scaling, its mediation, and whether steering restores concord readings without harming single-negation comprehension. Metrics include DN-imposition rate, concord-vs-DN inconsistency gap, typology-prediction correlation, mediation R-squared, and steering flip rate with competence controls.
Experiments:
1) NC/DN minimal-pair suite: Construct ~450 controlled items each realized in NC languages (Spanish, Italian, Polish, Turkish) and DN languages (English, German, Mandarin), grounded in the negation typology literature and native-speaker verified. Each item has (a) a SINGLE-negation control ('I saw no one'), (b) a MULTIPLE-negative target (in NC languages: negative marker + n-word, e.g. Spanish 'no vi a nadie'; in DN languages the matched literal double negative), and (c) matched affirmative controls. For each, the verified truth-conditional reading is either single-negation (concord) or double-negation (cancellation) per the language's grammar. Tasks: (i) truth-conditional forced choice ('Did the speaker see anyone?' -> yes/no); (ii) negation-composition NLI (does the multiple-negative sentence ENTAIL the single-negation paraphrase [concord] or the affirmative paraphrase [DN]?); (iii) question-answering over a short scenario whose outcome depends on the concord-vs-cancellation reading; (iv) paraphrase generation (does the model render the NC sentence as single or double negation?); (v) translation round-trip (NC sentence -> English -> back, checking whether the single-negation meaning survives). Native-speaker verify readings and gold labels; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral DN-imposition (H1): Measure DN-imposition rate = fraction of NC-language multiple-negative items the model interprets as a cancelled affirmative (double negation) rather than the correct reinforced single negation, on the truth-conditional, NLI, and QA tasks. Compare against (a) single-negation controls (where all languages agree), (b) DN-language multiple-negatives (where cancellation IS correct, an English-side ceiling), and (c) the affirmative controls. Prediction: high DN-imposition specifically for NC-language multiple negatives, near-zero misreading on single-negation and DN controls. Control for tokenizer fertility, n-word frequency, and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test NC-status adds predictive power beyond fertility/resource).
3) Typology-predicted imposition (H2, external validation): Using the NC/DN typological classification and NC strictness (strict vs non-strict concord) from the literature, assign each language a concord-obligatoriness score and test whether per-language DN-imposition rate is predicted by that score (Spearman correlation; held-out prediction of imposition from typology alone). Predict imposition is strongest for strict-NC languages (Turkish/Polish) queried through the DN hub and near-zero for DN Mandarin/German.
4) Representational localization (H3): Extract a negation-composition direction via difference-in-means between representations of concord (single-negation) vs cancellation (double-negation) readings at each layer, per language. Test (a) whether a shared composition direction is DN-scaffolded (cross-lingual cosine alignment across layers, aligned with the English cancellation pole); (b) whether an NC-language multiple-negative input projects onto the DN/cancellation pole in the shared hub while any residual concord signal is stronger in early/language-specific layers, via logit-lens/tuned-lens depth tracking of when the (mis)reading crystallizes. Baseline: a single-negation polarity direction (present in all languages) as a within-model control. Mediation: regress behavioral DN-imposition on shared-hub cancellation-pole projection strength (partial correlation controlling for fertility/resource; held-out R^2).
5) Cross-lingual transfer loss (complementary): Measure concord-meaning-preservation rate in translation across the NC/DN boundary; predict directional asymmetry - NC->English silently converts a single negation into a cancelled/affirmative reading more than English->NC fails to produce concord. Compare against a single-negation-preservation baseline.
6) Causal steering/patching test (core): (a) Steer the NC-language multiple-negative representation along the composition direction toward the CONCORD (reinforce) pole and measure whether truth-conditional/NLI judgments flip to the correct single-negation reading (flip rate), without switching output language. (b) For DN-imposed items, patch the residual language-specific concord signal (from early/language-specific layers) into later computation and test restoration - localizing failure to the shared hub OVERWRITING a shallowly-present concord signal versus its absence. Competence controls: single-negation and affirmative controls must remain correctly interpreted (no over-flipping), fluency preserved, off-target/language-mixing rate low. Baselines: whole-hub English-steering, random-direction steering.
7) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify steering/patching is composition-specific (changes concord/cancellation reading but not the identity of the negated event or single-negation polarity), graded (imposition scales with concord strictness), and not a lexical-frequency artifact (use nonce-verb variants). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 shows stronger DN-imposition than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM (which see more NC-language data); test whether imposition magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the composition direction and with target-language training share. Qualitatively compare the model's per-language imposition pattern against the human NC/DN typology.
Evaluation metrics: DN-imposition rate (NC multiple-negatives vs single-negation vs DN-multiple controls); concord-vs-DN inconsistency gap; imposition-vs-typology correlation and held-out prediction; composition NLI accuracy (concord-entailment); shared-hub cancellation-pole projection strength and crystallization depth (vs single-negation-polarity baseline); cross-lingual composition-direction alignment; translation concord-preservation rate and directional asymmetry; mediation regression (held-out R^2); steering flip rate and patching-induced restoration; competence preservation, off-target rate; cross-model imposition comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) NC/DN interpretation is prosody- and context-sensitive even within a language (both readings can surface under special conditions per the typology literature); we restrict to canonical, context-controlled sentences where native speakers agree on the single-negation concord reading, report inter-annotator agreement, and exclude low-agreement items. 2) NC-vs-DN status is correlated with language family, script, and resource level; the single-negation controls (where all languages agree), DN-language multiple-negative controls, within-language single-vs-multiple contrasts, and the typology-based prediction isolate the composition pathway, but residual confounds may remain; we center the core study on well-resourced Spanish/Italian (NC) and English/German (DN) and treat Polish/Turkish/Mandarin as extensions. 3) Difference-in-means composition directions may entangle single-negation polarity or lexical n-word features; we use nonce-verb variants, multiple extraction methods, a single-negation-polarity control direction, and specificity checks. 4) Logit-lens/tuned-lens depth estimates are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation and multiple lenses. 5) Instruction-tuned models may hedge or explain ('this could be single or double negation'), which we treat as a positive composition-awareness signal rather than failure; we test base models where available and use both forced-choice and NLI probes. 6) Some NC languages have non-strict concord where a preverbal n-word alone suffices; we code strictness explicitly and analyze it as a graded predictor rather than a confound. 7) Patching may have entangled effects; we report ambiguous cases and multiple granularities. 8) The typology-prediction analysis assumes training data reflects each language's real NC usage, which may not hold; we treat typology as a noisy predictor and rely on behavioral and causal tests for core claims. 9) If NO imposition is found - NC multiple-negatives are correctly read as single negations, predictable from typology and preserved across transfer - this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the shared hub represents language-specific negation composition despite its DN English scaffolding, valuable either way. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: do_operator_edge_severing_transfer
Title: Does the Do-Operator Transfer? Cross-Lingual Consistency of Causal-Edge Severing in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Interventional/counterfactual reasoning requires a distinctive internal operation absent from associational reasoning: severing a variable from its normal causes (the do-operator), so downstream inference must ignore the now-inconsistent upstream evidence. We hypothesize this edge-severing operation is implemented as a largely language-agnostic mechanism in the shared hub (so it transfers cross-lingually like knowledge-free reasoning), whereas failures cluster not in the severing step but in a language-specific 'suppression' step that must inhibit the still-active associational pathway. Consequently, cross-lingual counterfactual inconsistency is driven by variable suppression strength (how well the model gates the pre-intervention prior in the target language), which we can measure, predict, and causally correct by amplifying a shared severing/suppression direction.
Related Work: CLadder (2023) and Evaluating Causal Reasoning (2024) show LLMs struggle most on interventional/counterfactual (rung 2/3) queries, and Double Counterfactual Consistency (2026) and Counterfactual Sensitivity Regularization (2025) improve faithfulness via inference-time or training-time consistency, all MONOLINGUAL and BEHAVIORAL. 'Under the Shadow of Babel'/BICAUSE (2025) shows LLMs internalize language-specific causal WORD-ORDER attention biases in a two-sentence forward/reversed causal task, but studies attention over connectives, not the do-operator. Knowledge-Free Reasoners (2024) show knowledge-free reasoning transfers near-perfectly across languages while knowledge retrieval does not, but never isolate interventional edge-severing as a reasoning primitive. Cross-lingual consistency work (Lost in Multilinguality 2025; Entity-Level Alignment 2025) localizes FACTUAL inconsistency to late-layer transition/entity alignment, not causal-graph operations. NO prior work asks whether the do-operator (severing a variable from its causes and suppressing the associational prior) is a shared-hub mechanism that transfers cross-lingually, decomposes counterfactual failure into a language-agnostic severing step versus a language-specific suppression step, or offers a mechanistic suppression-direction fix. We uniquely reframe cross-lingual counterfactual inconsistency as a suppression-gating failure on a shared causal primitive, orthogonal to all my prior grammatical/lexical imposition proposals.
Abstract: Counterfactual and interventional reasoning is where large language models fail most, and where the language they are queried in should not matter at all: whether we intervene to set a variable's value, the causal logic is language-independent. Yet multilingual models answer the same intervention query inconsistently across languages. We propose a mechanistic account. Answering an intervention ('given that we FORCE X=1, what is Y?') requires a distinctive operation absent from associational reasoning: severing X from its normal causes and suppressing the associational prior that would otherwise leak upstream evidence into the inference. We hypothesize that (1) the edge-severing operation is implemented in the largely language-agnostic shared hub and therefore transfers cross-lingually, like knowledge-free reasoning; but (2) counterfactual failures cluster in a downstream SUPPRESSION step that must inhibit the still-active associational pathway, and this suppression is language-specific and weaker in lower-resource, English-distant languages; so (3) cross-lingual counterfactual inconsistency is predicted by per-language suppression strength and is causally correctable by amplifying a shared severing/suppression direction. We build a controlled multilingual causal-graph suite (forks, chains, colliders) with matched associational vs interventional vs counterfactual queries across typologically diverse languages, on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM. Using activation patching, logit-lens tracking of the pre-intervention prior, and a difference-in-means suppression direction, we test where severing lives, whether it transfers, whether failures are suppression failures, and whether steering restores consistency. Metrics include severing-transfer rate, prior-leakage magnitude, suppression-strength vs inconsistency correlation, and steering-induced consistency recovery with competence controls.
Experiments:
1) Controlled multilingual causal-graph suite: Construct ~500 items over small structured causal graphs (2-4 node forks, chains, colliders) with explicitly stated causal mechanisms and prior probabilities, each realized as three matched query types: (a) ASSOCIATIONAL (observe X, infer Y), (b) INTERVENTIONAL (do(X), infer Y, requiring edge-severing of X's parents), and (c) COUNTERFACTUAL (given observed world, had X been different, what is Y). Crucially include DIVERGENCE items where the associational answer and the interventional answer DIFFER (e.g., a confounded fork where observing X predicts Y but intervening on X does not), so that leaking the associational prior produces a detectable wrong answer. Instantiate every item in typologically diverse languages (English, French, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish), templated and native-speaker verified with symbolic-oracle gold answers; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral consistency map: Measure per-language accuracy and cross-lingual consistency@k separately for associational, interventional, and counterfactual queries on DIVERGENCE items. Test the prediction that associational accuracy is high and consistent everywhere, while interventional/counterfactual accuracy is lower and MORE cross-lingually inconsistent, with the gap widening for lower-resource/English-distant languages. Control for tokenizer fertility and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test query-type x language interaction beyond fertility/resource).
3) Prior-leakage measurement (core diagnostic): Using logit-lens/tuned-lens, track for each interventional item the internal probability the model assigns to the ASSOCIATIONAL (pre-intervention) answer across layers. Define prior-leakage = how strongly the associational answer remains active at the readout despite the do() instruction. Test whether wrong interventional answers coincide with high prior-leakage (the associational pathway was not suppressed), per language. Predict prior-leakage is higher in lower-resource languages.
4) Severing-vs-suppression error decomposition via activation patching: For interventional items correct in English but wrong in language B, patch (a) the shared-hub representation of the SEVERED causal structure (the do()-modified graph state) from the English pass into B, and (b) only the late/language-specific suppression components. If (a) rarely changes the outcome (because severing already transferred) but (b) fixes it, the failure is a suppression failure, not a severing failure. Report the share of severing failures vs suppression failures per language. Also test the transfer claim directly: extract the severing operation in one language and transplant it into another; measure whether it produces a correct interventional readout (severing-transfer rate).
5) Suppression direction and its predictive power: Extract a difference-in-means 'suppression direction' from (correctly-suppressed interventional) minus (associational-leaked) representations. Verify cross-lingual alignment of this direction (shared vs language-specific) and that steering along it causally reduces prior-leakage. Test whether per-language suppression strength (projection magnitude onto the suppression direction on interventional items) predicts per-language interventional inconsistency (Spearman; held-out R^2 over fertility/resource baselines).
6) Core causal intervention: Amplify the shared suppression direction at the readout on interventional/counterfactual items in the target language and measure (i) reduction in prior-leakage, (ii) improvement in interventional accuracy, and (iii) improvement in cross-lingual consistency@k. Compare against baselines: English shared-space steering (Language-Specific Latent Process 2025), the linear-shortcut factual fix (Lost in Multilinguality 2025) adapted here, and a random-direction control. Compute consistency-recovery elasticity = consistency gain per unit baseline suppression deficit.
7) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify steering is suppression-specific (improves interventional/counterfactual items but does NOT harm associational items, where the prior is the CORRECT answer and must not be suppressed — a symmetric check), does not switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), and preserves fluency and general reasoning. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 shows sharper suppression deficits in distant languages than the more multilingual BLOOM/Aya; test correlation of suppression deficit with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the suppression direction and with training share.
Evaluation metrics: per-language associational/interventional/counterfactual accuracy and consistency@k (and query-type x language interaction); prior-leakage magnitude and its coincidence with interventional errors; severing-failure vs suppression-failure error shares; severing-transfer rate under transplant; cross-lingual suppression-direction alignment; suppression-strength vs inconsistency correlation (held-out R^2); steering-induced prior-leakage reduction, interventional-accuracy gain, and consistency recovery vs baselines; associational-item preservation (symmetric specificity), off-target rate; cross-model suppression-deficit comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The severing step and the suppression step may not cleanly separate; patching may have entangled effects. Mitigation: use multiple patching granularities, report ambiguous cases, and rely on the symmetric associational-preservation check to validate that we isolate suppression rather than a generic answer-shift. 2) Small structured causal graphs may be solved by memorized heuristics or lexical cues rather than genuine do-operator computation (as Failure Modes 2024 and Counterfactual reasoning 2022 warn); we include nonce-variable and anti-commonsensical graphs to block world-knowledge shortcuts and DIVERGENCE items where heuristics fail. 3) Query-type difficulty is confounded with language resource level and fertility; we use partial correlations and matched associational controls, but residual confounds may remain. 4) Logit-lens prior-leakage estimates are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 5) The suppression-steering intervention could over-suppress and harm associational items; the symmetric specificity check is a hard constraint and we report the full tradeoff. 6) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM's less English-centric hub analyzed as a contrast). 7) If the severing operation itself fails to transfer (i.e., failures are severing failures, not suppression failures), the hypothesis is refuted but this is an informative result relocating cross-lingual counterfactual failure to the graph-construction step. 8) If interventional reasoning transfers as well as associational reasoning (little inconsistency), this positive result would show the do-operator is a fully shared primitive, valuable either way. 9) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: language_dependent_validation_deficit
Title: Right Answer, Wrong-Language Alarm: A Language-Dependent Self-Validation Deficit in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs compute their factual/arithmetic answer through a largely language-agnostic shared hub, but the INTERNAL SELF-VALIDATION signal that flags whether an emitted answer is wrong is language-DEPENDENT: it is weaker, later, and mislocalized in lower-resource / English-distant languages. Consequently a model can internally 'know' an answer is wrong (its validation signal fires correctly) when queried in English yet fail to raise that alarm for the exact same error in a low-resource language, mirroring the reduced second-language error-monitoring (ERN) seen in human bilinguals. This validation deficit predicts poor self-correction and miscalibration in those languages and is causally attributable to a shared validation circuit that is under-engaged, not absent, cross-lingually.
Related Work: Monolingual mechanistic work localizes error detection: 'The Validation Gap' (2025) finds arithmetic validation is done by middle-layer 'consistency heads' structurally dissociated from higher-layer computation; 'Probing for Arithmetic Errors' (2025) and 'LLMs Know More Than They Show' (2024) decode correctness from internal states (skill-specific, concentrated in exact-answer tokens); Gnosis (2025) predicts own failures from internal traces. Cross-lingual work localizes factual INCONSISTENCY (not validation) to late-layer transition/translation failures and English-centric recall (Lost in Multilinguality 2025; Paths Not Taken 2025; Can you map it to English 2025). Human psycholinguistics robustly shows internal error-monitoring is weaker/altered in a second language: reduced or reversed ERN for unstable L2 representations, worse detection under language conflict (Verbal Self-Monitoring in L2 2016; Conflicting Representations & ERN in L2 2020; bilingual conflict-monitoring 2016-2018). CRITICALLY, no prior work asks whether the model's own VALIDATION/error-detection circuit is language-dependent: whether the internal 'this answer is wrong' signal that exists monolingually degrades cross-lingually, is decoupled from the language in which the model actually knows the correct answer, tracks resource level, and can be restored by re-engaging a shared validation direction. This reframes cross-lingual self-correction failure as a metacognitive-monitoring deficit (a language-dependent validation circuit) rather than a content-representation or translation problem, and it uniquely ports the human L2 self-monitoring deficit into LLM mechanisms. It is orthogonal to all my prior proposals, which concern WHAT concept is represented, not whether the model can internally CHECK its own output across languages.
Abstract: Human bilinguals monitor their own speech for errors, but this internal error-detection is measurably weaker in a second language: the error-related brain signal is reduced or reversed when representations are unstable. We ask whether multilingual language models exhibit an analogous deficit in their internal SELF-VALIDATION. Recent mechanistic work shows that, monolingually, LLMs carry an internal signal that flags whether their own answer is wrong (middle-layer consistency/validation heads, decodable correctness directions), even when the model still emits the error. We hypothesize this validation signal is LANGUAGE-DEPENDENT: for the same error, the internal 'this is wrong' alarm fires reliably when the model is queried in English but is weaker, later, and less localized in lower-resource, English-distant languages, and is decoupled from the language in which the model actually knows the correct answer. This predicts that cross-lingual self-correction failure and miscalibration are partly a metacognitive-monitoring deficit, not merely a content or translation problem. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5 and BLOOM across typologically diverse languages using matched correct/incorrect factual and arithmetic answers. We train per-language validation probes on internal states, measure how well each language's alarm predicts correctness and where it lives, and use activation patching to test whether the validation signal is a shared circuit that is under-engaged rather than absent cross-lingually. We then test a targeted intervention that re-engages the shared validation direction, measuring gains in error detection, self-correction, and calibration. Metrics include per-language validation-probe AUROC, validation-depth gaps, cross-lingual transfer of the validation direction, and self-correction / ECE improvements with competence controls.
Experiments:
1) Matched correct/incorrect answer suite: Build ~800 items in each of two skills—(a) factual QA (mLAMA / TriviaQA-style, with verified per-language gold answers) and (b) multi-step arithmetic (controlled, verified)—where for each item we obtain both a correct and an incorrect model-produced (or injected) answer completion. Instantiate in typologically diverse languages spanning resource levels and scripts (English, French, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish). Native-speaker verify translations and gold labels. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Per-language validation probe (H1, core): Following 'Probing for Arithmetic Errors' and 'LLMs Know More Than They Show', train linear probes on internal states (residual stream at the exact-answer token, per layer) to predict whether the emitted answer is correct, SEPARATELY per language. Report per-language validation AUROC on held-out items. Test H1: validation AUROC is high in English and degrades with lower resource level / greater English-distance. Crucially, condition on cases where the model KNOWS the correct answer in English (answers correctly in English) but errs in language B—measure whether the internal alarm nonetheless fails to fire in B (the 'knows-it-is-wrong-only-in-English' signature). Control for tokenizer fertility, answer frequency, and base error rate (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test language/resource adds predictive power).
3) Validation-depth and localization (H2): Using logit-lens/tuned-lens and layer-wise probes, identify the layer at which the correctness signal first becomes decodable ('validation-crystallization layer') per language, and locate the consistency/validation heads (following 'The Validation Gap'). Test whether validation crystallizes LATER and is more diffuse (lower peak probe accuracy, weaker head attribution) in lower-resource languages, and whether the same heads carry validation across languages (shared-circuit test via cross-lingual head-attribution overlap).
4) Shared-vs-absent validation direction (H3, causal): Extract a difference-in-means 'validation direction' (correct minus incorrect answer representations) per language at the validation layer. Measure cross-lingual cosine alignment (shared vs language-specific). Core patching test: on language-B items where the internal alarm fails, patch in (a) the English validation signal / consistency-head outputs and (b) the shared validation direction, and test whether the internal correctness signal is restored (probe now flags the error) and whether behavior (e.g., willingness to revise) changes. If patching restores the alarm, the validation circuit is shared-but-under-engaged, not absent, in language B.
5) Behavioral consequences: Test whether per-language validation AUROC predicts (a) intrinsic self-correction success (does the model, when asked to check its answer, actually fix errors it internally 'flagged'?), and (b) calibration (ECE/AUROC of verbalized/logit confidence). Predict languages with weak internal validation show poor self-correction and worse calibration, and that self-correction fails specifically on errors the internal alarm missed.
6) Core intervention: Deploy a train-free intervention that amplifies the shared validation direction / re-engages the consistency heads at the validation layer during the model's self-check pass in the target language. Measure improvements in: internal-alarm AUROC, error-detection accuracy, self-correction success rate, and calibration (ECE). Compare against baselines: English shared-space steering (Can you map it to English 2025), the linear-shortcut factual fix (Lost in Multilinguality 2025) adapted here, and a random-direction control. Compute recovery elasticity = detection gain per unit baseline validation deficit.
7) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify the intervention is validation-specific (improves error detection without changing the underlying answer content or switching output language; measure off-target/language-mixing rate), does not degrade already-correct answers (must not induce spurious 'wrong' alarms on correct outputs—symmetric check), preserves fluency, and does not harm English. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 shows a sharper cross-lingual validation deficit than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether deficit magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the validation direction and with training share. Qualitatively compare the model's language-dependent validation-deficit pattern against the human L2 self-monitoring / reduced-ERN literature (direction, not identical mechanism).
Evaluation metrics: per-language validation-probe AUROC and the knows-only-in-English error share; validation-crystallization-depth and head-diffuseness gaps; cross-lingual validation-direction alignment and head-overlap; patching-induced alarm-restoration rate; correlation of validation AUROC with self-correction success and calibration (held-out R^2 over fertility/resource baselines); intervention-induced detection, self-correction, and ECE gains vs baselines with symmetric specificity (no spurious alarms on correct answers), off-target rate, English preservation; cross-model deficit comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Correctness probes are known to be skill-specific and may not generalize across factual vs arithmetic tasks ('LLMs Know More Than They Show'); we train and evaluate per-skill and report cross-skill transfer explicitly rather than assuming a universal validation signal. 2) Separating a language-dependent VALIDATION deficit from a language-dependent COMPUTATION deficit is subtle—if the model simply does not know the answer in language B, there is no 'correct answer' to validate against; we mitigate by focusing on the diagnostic subset where the model DOES know the answer in English but errs in B, and by including arithmetic (knowledge-free) items where the correct answer is derivable in-language. 3) Language/resource is confounded with script and tokenizer fertility; we use partial correlations and matched items, and the causal patching test (shared-vs-absent) is the primary evidence, not the correlations. 4) Difference-in-means validation directions may entangle content or answer-token features; we use multiple extraction methods, the established consistency-head circuit as an anchor, and symmetric specificity checks. 5) The intervention could induce spurious 'wrong' alarms on correct answers; the symmetric no-false-alarm constraint is a hard requirement and we report the full tradeoff. 6) Logit/tuned-lens depth and head attribution are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 7) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM's less English-centric hub analyzed as a contrast that should show a weaker deficit). 8) The human-LLM comparison (reduced L2 ERN) is qualitative, not a claim of identical mechanism. 9) If validation is equally strong across languages (no deficit), this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the model's self-monitoring is language-agnostic despite an English-centric hub—valuable either way, and it would relocate cross-lingual self-correction failure to a purely behavioral/decoding issue. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: adaptive_pivot_routing
Title: Choosing the Right Pivot: Per-Step Latent-Language Routing and Its Miscalibration in Multilingual Reasoning
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs do not use a single fixed pivot language for an entire reasoning chain; instead they dynamically ROUTE each reasoning sub-step to whichever internal latent language best supports that step's content (an abstract-logic step routes toward the dominant/English pivot; a culturally- or lexically-grounded step routes toward the language most associated with that content). We hypothesize (1) this per-step pivot routing is measurable and content-dependent, not merely input-language-dependent; (2) the routing POLICY is miscalibrated for lower-resource inputs — the model over-routes culturally-grounded steps to the dominant pivot, stripping the target-language grounding needed for a correct step; and (3) a lightweight per-step steering that re-routes only the mis-routed steps improves accuracy more than uniformly steering the whole chain toward English.
Related Work: Prior work established that multilingual LLMs use an English-centric shared/latent 'pivot' space (Do Llamas Work in English 2024; Do Multilingual LLMs Think in English 2025; Semantic Hub 2024) and dual latent languages in non-English-centric models (Beyond English-Centric 2024). Language-reasoning disentanglement and English-steering improve multilingual reasoning by pushing representations toward the shared space (When Less Language is More 2025; Language-Specific Latent Process Hinders 2025; MRRE 2025), and language mixing in reasoning traces is shown to be a strategic, performance-relevant behavior driven by RLVR (Language Mixing in Reasoning 2025; Impact of Language Mixing 2025). Latent reasoning is English-centered and weaker for low-resource languages (Large Reasoning Models Are Not Yet Multilingual Latent Reasoners 2026). Crucially, all prior work treats the pivot/latent language as a GLOBAL property (of the whole forward pass or whole chain) and treats steering toward English as uniformly beneficial. NONE frame the choice of pivot as a per-STEP ROUTING POLICY conditioned on the CONTENT of each reasoning sub-step, none identify a systematic MISROUTING of culturally/lexically-grounded steps to the dominant pivot as a distinct error mode, and none propose content-selective re-routing (as opposed to uniform English-steering). We reframe the latent-language question from 'which language does the model think in?' to 'how does the model DECIDE, step by step, which language to think in, and when is that decision wrong?'
Abstract: Multilingual language models are known to reason through an English-centric internal pivot, and steering representations toward this shared space is widely reported to help. We challenge the assumption that the pivot is a single, global choice. We propose that within one reasoning chain a model ROUTES each sub-step to whichever internal latent language best supports that step: abstract-logical steps (arithmetic, deduction) route toward the dominant/English pivot, while culturally- or lexically-grounded steps (idioms, local facts, language-specific conventions) route toward the language most associated with that content. We hypothesize this per-step routing is content-dependent and measurable, and that its POLICY is miscalibrated for lower-resource inputs: the model over-routes grounded steps to the dominant pivot, discarding the target-language grounding a correct step needs. We test this on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM across typologically diverse languages. Using logit-lens/tuned-lens per-step latent-language decoding on reasoning chains (MGSM for logic-heavy steps; a new mixed 'grounded-reasoning' suite where some steps require culturally/lexically local knowledge), we (1) show that the decoded latent language shifts step-to-step as a function of step content, not just input language; (2) identify a misrouting signature where grounded steps are pulled to the dominant pivot and this coincides with errors; and (3) run the core causal test: a per-step re-routing steering that only redirects mis-routed grounded steps toward the target-language latent space, compared against uniform English-steering. Metrics include per-step latent-language decoding profiles, content-vs-routing correlation, misrouting-error coincidence, and selective-vs-uniform steering accuracy gains with off-target controls.
Experiments:
1) Mixed grounded-reasoning suite: Build ~400 multi-step reasoning problems each containing (a) ABSTRACT-LOGIC steps (arithmetic/deductive sub-computations whose answer is language-independent) and (b) GROUNDED steps that require culturally- or lexically-local knowledge (a local unit/currency conversion, a language-specific idiom or convention, a locally-indexed fact) such that the correct step depends on target-language grounding. Templated across typologically diverse languages spanning resource levels and scripts (English, French, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish), native-speaker-verified per-step gold answers; report inter-annotator agreement. Also use MGSM as a logic-heavy control (few grounded steps). Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Per-step latent-language decoding (H1): For each generated reasoning step, apply logit-lens/tuned-lens at middle layers to decode the dominant latent language of that step's internal representation (fraction of steps whose mid-layer representation decodes to English/dominant vs target vs a related pivot). Test H1: the decoded latent language shifts step-to-step and is predicted by STEP CONTENT (abstract-logic vs grounded), not merely by the fixed input language. Quantify with a mixed-effects model: latent-language(step) ~ step-type + input-language + (1|problem); report the step-type effect size after controlling for input language, tokenizer fertility, and resource level.
3) Misrouting signature (H2): Define a grounded step as MIS-ROUTED if its latent language decodes to the dominant/English pivot rather than the target language. Test whether mis-routing rate on grounded steps (a) is higher for lower-resource inputs (partial correlation with resource level, controlling for fertility), and (b) coincides with step-level errors: compare error rate on mis-routed vs correctly-routed grounded steps. Use activation patching to test causality: patch the grounded step's mid-layer representation from a correctly-routed (e.g., target-language monolingual) pass into the mis-routed pass and check whether the step becomes correct — distinguishing 'grounding-stripped-by-misrouting' errors from genuine knowledge-absence errors.
4) Content-vs-routing dissociation control: Verify that abstract-logic steps route to the dominant pivot MORE than grounded steps within the SAME problem and language (within-problem contrast), ruling out a pure input-language explanation. Report the within-problem step-type routing gap.
5) Core causal intervention (H3) — selective re-routing: At mid layers, apply a per-step steering vector that redirects ONLY mis-routed grounded steps toward the target-language latent space (target-language difference-in-means direction), leaving abstract-logic steps untouched. A lightweight probe (trained on step representations) classifies each step as abstract-logic vs grounded to decide when to intervene. Compare against baselines: (a) uniform English-steering of the whole chain (Language-Specific Latent Process 2025 / MRRE 2025), (b) uniform target-language steering, (c) no intervention, (d) random-direction control. Metrics: overall problem accuracy, grounded-step accuracy, abstract-logic-step accuracy (must not degrade), cross-lingual consistency, off-target/language-mixing rate, fluency. Predict selective re-routing beats uniform English-steering specifically on grounded-step-heavy problems in lower-resource languages, while uniform English-steering may help logic-heavy MGSM.
6) Cross-model contrast: Predict the more English-centric Llama-3 mis-routes grounded steps more than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether mis-routing magnitude correlates with the model's global English-centricity (measured via baseline latent-language decoding) and with target-language training share.
Evaluation metrics: per-step latent-language decoding profiles; step-type effect on routing (mixed-model coefficient, held-out R^2 over input-language/fertility/resource); grounded-step mis-routing rate and its resource-level correlation; error coincidence (mis-routed vs correctly-routed grounded-step accuracy) and patching-induced step-correction rate; within-problem abstract-vs-grounded routing gap; selective-re-routing accuracy gains vs uniform-English-steering and other baselines, with abstract-step preservation, off-target rate, and consistency; cross-model mis-routing comparison and correlation with English-centricity and training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Logit-lens/tuned-lens per-step latent-language decoding is approximate at intermediate layers and noisier per token than for whole-prompt final-token analyses; we cross-validate with tuned-lens, aggregate over step tokens, and report robustness across lenses. 2) Segmenting a chain into 'steps' and labeling each as abstract-logic vs grounded is non-trivial; we use verified templates with pre-annotated step types, a learned step-type probe with reported reliability, and exclude ambiguous steps. 3) 'Grounded' step correctness may confound genuine knowledge absence with misrouting; the patching test (Exp 3) is designed to separate these, and we report the share of each. 4) Step content is correlated with which language is naturally associated with it, and grounded steps may simply be harder; the within-problem abstract-vs-grounded contrast and the target-language patching control mitigate but may not fully remove confounds. 5) Reasoning models may mix languages overtly in the visible chain; we analyze internal (latent) routing via lens decoding, not surface tokens, and treat visible mixing as a separate covariate. 6) Selective re-routing could harm fluency, switch output language, or over-correct; we require abstract-step preservation and low off-target rate as hard constraints and report the full tradeoff. 7) The step-type probe adds a moving part; we report accuracy with an oracle step-type labeling as an upper bound. 8) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM's less English-centric hub analyzed as a contrast that should show less misrouting). 9) If routing turns out to be globally fixed (no content-dependent step-level shifts), this is an informative negative result showing the pivot is a chain-level rather than step-level property. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: grammatical_gender_reasoning_crutch
Title: Grammar as a Crutch: Multilingual LLMs Offload Coreference and Commonsense Reasoning onto Grammatical Gender Cues That English Lacks
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs exploit grammatical-gender agreement morphology as a cheap SCAFFOLD for coreference and referent-tracking reasoning: when the query language marks gender on the entities and their modifiers/pronouns, the model routes the reasoning through a shared gender-agreement circuit rather than through semantic inference, so it solves the SAME reasoning problem more accurately (and via a different mechanism) in gendered languages than in English. This 'grammatical crutch' produces a directional cross-lingual inconsistency and a distinctive fragility: flipping or removing the grammatical-gender cue (while leaving semantic content intact) degrades reasoning far more in gendered languages than the equivalent semantic perturbation does in English, because in English the model was forced to reason semantically all along.
Related Work: Prior work shows (a) LLMs implement subject-verb/gender agreement via a largely language-independent, causal 'number/gender direction' written by an attention head and read by MLP neurons, steerable across languages (On the Similarity of Circuits across Languages 2024; Causal Analysis of Syntactic Agreement Neurons 2022; LLMs Share Latent Grammatical Concepts 2025); (b) models prioritize particular gender cues (first vs last) for agreement (How Language Models Prioritize Contextual Grammatical Cues 2024) and can rely on surface gender clues rather than abstract rules (Do LSTMs See Gender 2022; Default Reasoning in Gender Assignment 2019); and (c) grammatical gender biases distributional semantics and human non-native pronoun resolution (linguistic gender effect 2004; gender in Chinese pronoun resolution 2012). My own prior proposals treated grammatical gender as a CONTAMINANT of attribute judgments (gender_leak) and as a source of agreement-attraction ILLUSIONS (shared_number_attraction). NO prior work asks the opposite, higher-level question: is grammatical gender a HELPFUL SCAFFOLD that the model recruits to OFFLOAD coreference/commonsense reasoning, such that gendered languages get correct answers via GRAMMAR while English must use SEMANTICS, producing (i) a directional cross-lingual accuracy/mechanism asymmetry and (ii) a selective fragility when the grammatical cue is perturbed. We reframe grammatical morphology from noise/illusion into an exploited reasoning crutch, with a causal, cue-perturbation signature and a shared-agreement-circuit locus.
Abstract: English forces you to figure out who 'they' refers to from meaning alone; Spanish, German, Hindi and many languages instead mark gender on nouns, adjectives, and pronouns, so agreement morphology can disambiguate the referent grammatically. We ask a simple, previously untested question about multilingual language models: do they OFFLOAD coreference and referent-tracking reasoning onto grammatical-gender cues when the query language provides them, using grammar as a crutch instead of reasoning semantically? We hypothesize that (1) on matched reasoning problems, models are more accurate in gendered languages precisely when a grammatical-gender cue happens to align with the correct referent; (2) they solve these via a shared gender-agreement circuit rather than semantic inference, so English (which lacks the cue) and gendered languages recruit different internal mechanisms for the same problem; and (3) this crutch is fragile: flipping or neutralizing the grammatical-gender cue (holding semantic content fixed) degrades reasoning far more in gendered languages than the equivalent semantic perturbation does in English. We build a controlled multilingual coreference/commonsense suite where a grammatical-gender cue can be made congruent, incongruent, or neutral with the semantically-correct referent, across gendered languages (Spanish, German, Russian, Hindi) and gender-light English, on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5 and BLOOM. Using behavioral cue-perturbation tests, activation patching to separate grammatical-cue from semantic-cue pathways, and steering of the shared gender-agreement direction, we measure the crutch effect, its mechanism asymmetry, and its selective fragility. Metrics include congruent-vs-incongruent accuracy swing, cross-lingual mechanism divergence, cue-perturbation fragility gap, and causal-pathway attribution.
Experiments:
1) Controlled cue-vs-semantics suite: Construct ~500 coreference/referent-tracking and simple commonsense items in which two candidate referents differ in grammatical gender in gendered languages, and a downstream pronoun/adjective/verb must be resolved. For each item build three conditions: (a) CONGRUENT — the grammatical-gender agreement cue points to the semantically-correct referent; (b) INCONGRUENT — the grammatical cue points to the semantically WRONG referent (created by choosing referents whose genders are swapped relative to the semantics, so grammar and meaning conflict); (c) NEUTRAL — both referents share the same grammatical gender, so grammar gives no cue and the model MUST use semantics. Instantiate every item in gendered languages (Spanish, German, Russian, Hindi) and in English (where grammatical gender is absent, so all items are effectively NEUTRAL). Ensure the SEMANTICALLY-correct answer is fixed and native-speaker-verified across all conditions and languages; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Crutch effect (H1): Measure accuracy per condition and language. Test the signature pattern: in gendered languages, CONGRUENT accuracy > NEUTRAL accuracy > INCONGRUENT accuracy (the model is helped by an aligned grammatical cue and HURT by a conflicting one), while English shows no such swing (flat across the nominally-equivalent conditions). Define the crutch-swing = CONGRUENT minus INCONGRUENT accuracy per gendered language; predict it is large in gendered languages and ~0 in English. Control for tokenizer fertility, referent frequency, and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test grammatical-cue presence adds predictive power).
3) Mechanism asymmetry (H2): Extract the shared gender-agreement direction / locate the agreement head+MLP circuit per model (following On the Similarity of Circuits across Languages 2024; LLMs Share Latent Grammatical Concepts 2025) via difference-in-means and head attribution. Test whether, on CONGRUENT gendered-language items, the correct answer is driven by the gender-agreement circuit (high attribution / patching effect), whereas on English NEUTRAL items the same problem is driven by semantic/content pathways (low gender-circuit attribution). Quantify cross-lingual mechanism divergence = difference in gender-circuit attribution between gendered-language CONGRUENT and English NEUTRAL solving of matched problems.
4) Causal pathway separation via activation patching: On INCONGRUENT items (grammar vs semantics conflict), patch (a) the grammatical-gender cue signal (from the agreement circuit) and (b) the semantic-referent representation, independently, and measure which pathway the final answer follows per language. Predict gendered languages follow the grammatical cue more often (grammar overrides meaning) than English can (no cue to follow), directly demonstrating offloading. Report the fraction of grammar-driven vs semantics-driven resolutions per language.
5) Selective fragility (H3, core): Apply matched perturbations that hold semantic content fixed: (i) FLIP the grammatical-gender cue (swap agreement morphology to point at the wrong referent) in gendered languages; (ii) NEUTRALIZE it (make both referents same-gender); and, as a semantic-perturbation control, weaken the semantic cue by equal amounts in ALL languages including English. Measure the accuracy drop from each perturbation. Predict the grammatical-cue perturbation causes a much larger drop in gendered languages than the equal-magnitude semantic perturbation causes in English — the fragility gap — revealing the crutch. Causally confirm via steering: amplify the gender-agreement direction toward the wrong referent and measure induced errors selectively in gendered languages.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify the effects are gender-cue-specific (perturbing an irrelevant grammatical feature does not produce the swing), not lexical-frequency artifacts (nonce-referent variants), and do not stem from output-language switching (off-target/language-mixing rate). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 leans on the crutch LESS in gendered languages (weaker gender-circuit engagement) than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether crutch-swing magnitude correlates with the strength/engagement of the shared gender-agreement circuit and with each language's training share.
Evaluation metrics: per-condition accuracy and crutch-swing (CONGRUENT minus INCONGRUENT) by language (vs flat English); gender-circuit attribution and cross-lingual mechanism divergence; grammar-driven vs semantics-driven resolution shares on INCONGRUENT items (patching); fragility gap (grammatical-cue-perturbation drop in gendered languages vs semantic-perturbation drop in English); steering-induced selective error rate; specificity controls (irrelevant-feature, nonce, off-target); cross-model crutch-swing comparison and correlation with gender-circuit engagement and training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for grammatical-cue presence over fertility/frequency/resource baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Constructing INCONGRUENT items where grammatical gender genuinely conflicts with a fixed semantic referent is delicate (some referents have inherent/natural gender that resists a grammatical mismatch); we restrict to inanimate or role-based referents where grammatical gender is arbitrary, native-speaker verify that the semantic answer is unambiguous, and report inter-annotator agreement, excluding low-agreement items. 2) Grammatical-gender presence is correlated with language family, script, and resource level; the within-language CONGRUENT/INCONGRUENT/NEUTRAL contrast and the English flat-baseline isolate the crutch pathway, but residual confounds may remain. 3) The gender-agreement circuit / difference-in-means direction may entangle lexical or number features; we use the established agreement head+MLP circuit as an anchor, nonce-referent variants, and specificity controls. 4) Activation patching to separate grammatical from semantic pathways may have entangled effects; we report ambiguous cases and use multiple granularities. 5) A grammatical crutch could also be a legitimate, beneficial reasoning aid rather than a fragile shortcut; the fragility test (H3) and the INCONGRUENT grammar-overrides-meaning result are what distinguish 'helpful reasoning cue' from 'brittle offloading' — we report both interpretations. 6) Instruction-tuned models may be trained to prioritize semantics; we test base models where available and treat a smaller crutch effect in instruction-tuned models as an informative training-effect finding. 7) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM's less English-centric hub analyzed as a contrast). 8) If NO crutch effect is found — accuracy is flat across congruent/incongruent/neutral and gendered languages reason semantically like English — this is an informative POSITIVE result showing multilingual reasoning is grammar-cue-robust, valuable either way. 9) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: language_authority_credibility_prior
Title: Trusting the Messenger, Not the Message: A Language-Conditioned Source-Credibility Prior Governs Cross-Lingual Knowledge-Conflict Resolution in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: When a multilingual LLM faces external evidence that contradicts its parametric belief, its decision to accept or reject that evidence is biased by the LANGUAGE the evidence is written in, independent of the evidence's content: the model applies a language-conditioned 'source-credibility prior' (higher-resource / dominant-language evidence is treated as more authoritative and more readily overrides parametric memory). This credibility prior is mediated by a shared, decodable 'evidence-trust' direction that is set by the evidence's language before the content is even evaluated, causally shifts belief revision, and can be steered to equalize credibility across languages without changing the evidence's meaning.
Related Work: Extensive work localizes context-memory conflict resolution: residual-stream conflict signals in mid-layers (Analysing the Residual Stream 2024; Probing Language Models on Their Knowledge Source 2024), SAE-based knowledge-selection steering (SPARE 2024), context-aware neurons (IRCAN 2024), and memory-vs-context heads (PH3 2024). Cross-lingual knowledge conflict is newly emerging but purely BEHAVIORAL/benchmark: CLEAR (2026) and 'When Abundance Conceals Weakness' (2026) show resolution depends on language-resource abundance (reasoning tasks) or linguistic affinity (entity tasks); CALM/CLC (2025) use cross-lingual voting to improve consistency. Cross-lingual consistency work traces inconsistency to entity alignment and late-layer transitions (Entity-Level Alignment 2025; Lost in Multilinguality 2025; Beneath the Surface 2024). NONE of these ask whether the LANGUAGE OF THE CONFLICTING EVIDENCE functions as a content-independent CREDIBILITY/AUTHORITY prior that mechanistically gates belief revision, whether a shared 'evidence-trust' direction is set by evidence language BEFORE content evaluation, or whether that credibility can be causally decoupled from language via steering. We reframe cross-lingual conflict resolution from a resource/affinity behavioral regularity into a mechanistic language-as-authority bias with a located, steerable credibility direction — orthogonal to source-selection-neuron work (which localizes WHICH source wins) because we isolate WHY a source's language, not its content, tips the decision. This is also distinct from all our prior grammatical/lexical/conceptual imposition proposals, which do not involve evidence credibility under conflict.
Abstract: A fact's truth does not depend on the language it is written in, so when a multilingual language model weighs external evidence that contradicts its parametric memory, the evidence's language should be irrelevant. We hypothesize the opposite: multilingual LLMs apply a content-independent, language-conditioned SOURCE-CREDIBILITY prior — evidence phrased in a higher-resource or dominant language is treated as more authoritative and more readily overrides parametric belief, while the same evidence in a low-resource language is discounted, regardless of its content. We propose this is not merely a resource-abundance behavioral effect but a mechanistic bias: a shared, decodable 'evidence-trust' direction in mid-layers is set by the evidence's language early, before its content is fully evaluated, and causally gates belief revision. We test this on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using controlled knowledge-conflict items where the SAME contradicting evidence is presented in different languages while the query language is held fixed (and vice versa), across typologically diverse languages. We (1) behaviorally isolate a language-credibility effect (override rate as a function of evidence language, controlling content); (2) probe whether an evidence-trust signal is decodable and set by evidence language pre-content; (3) use activation patching to test whether this signal causally drives acceptance/rejection; and (4) steer the evidence-trust direction to equalize credibility across languages without altering evidence meaning. Metrics include language-credibility override swing, trust-signal decodability and timing, causal patching effect, and steering-induced credibility equalization with content-preservation controls.
Experiments:
1) Controlled cross-lingual conflict suite: Build ~500 items where the model holds a parametric belief about a fact (verified per-language) and is given a single piece of external evidence that CONTRADICTS it. Crucially decouple three factors: (a) QUERY language, (b) EVIDENCE language, (c) evidence CONTENT (held identical across evidence-language conditions via verified parallel translation). Core condition: fix query language and the model's parametric belief, and present the SAME contradicting evidence translated into different evidence languages spanning resource levels and scripts (English, French, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish). Include a within-language paraphrase control (same language, different surface form) to separate language identity from surface variation. Native-speaker verify translations and per-language parametric beliefs; report inter-annotator agreement. Build on ConflictQA/CLEAR-style templates. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral language-credibility effect (H1): Measure override rate = fraction of items where the model revises its answer to match the contradicting evidence, as a function of EVIDENCE language, with query language and content fixed. Test whether override rate varies systematically with evidence language (higher for dominant/high-resource evidence). Define language-credibility swing = override(dominant-language evidence) minus override(low-resource-language evidence). Control for evidence tokenizer fertility, translation quality, and the model's baseline competence in the evidence language (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test evidence-language adds predictive power beyond content and query language). Symmetric check: also vary evidence quality (strong vs weak argument) to confirm the language effect is content-independent (present even when content is held strong).
3) Trust-signal decodability and timing (H2): Extract, via difference-in-means between accepted-evidence and rejected-evidence forward passes, a mid-layer 'evidence-trust' direction (following residual-stream conflict-signal work). Test (a) whether the evidence's language is decodable from the trust signal, and (b) whether the trust signal is SET EARLY — before the content is fully processed — by measuring, via logit-lens/tuned-lens across positions and layers, whether the trust magnitude at the evidence's early tokens already predicts eventual override, independent of the evidence's factual content. Compare the trust direction's cross-lingual alignment (is it a single shared credibility axis re-thresholded by language?).
4) Causal patching (H3, core): For items where dominant-language evidence overrides but the same content in a low-resource language does not, patch (a) the mid-layer evidence-trust signal from the dominant-language pass into the low-resource pass (holding content representations fixed) and test whether override is induced; and conversely patch the low-resource trust signal into the dominant pass to test whether override is suppressed. If the trust signal transfers the acceptance decision while leaving content untouched, this isolates a content-independent credibility gate. Report the fraction of decisions flipped by trust-signal patching vs content patching.
5) Steering to equalize credibility (H4): Add a steering vector along the evidence-trust direction, calibrated to raise low-resource-language evidence to dominant-language credibility (and to lower dominant-language over-trust). Measure whether override rates equalize across evidence languages WITHOUT changing which evidence is factually correct. Critically, verify content-preservation and correctness: steering must raise acceptance of TRUE contradicting evidence in low-resource languages while NOT increasing acceptance of FALSE/misleading evidence (include a false-evidence subset as a hard symmetric control — the goal is language-neutral credibility, not blind gullibility). Compare against baselines: SPARE-style knowledge-selection steering, English-pivot translation of the evidence, and a random-direction control.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify steering is credibility-specific (changes acceptance of contradicting evidence but not unrelated content or output language; measure off-target/language-mixing rate), preserves fluency, and does not harm no-conflict items. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 shows a larger language-credibility swing than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether swing magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the trust direction and with each evidence language's training share. Qualitatively relate the effect to CLEAR's resource-abundance finding, but demonstrate the mechanistic credibility-gate account goes beyond it (the effect persists with content and query language fixed, and is causally steerable).
Evaluation metrics: language-credibility override swing (dominant vs low-resource evidence, content fixed); content-independence check (swing present with content held strong; within-language paraphrase null); trust-signal decodability of evidence language and its early-timing predictiveness of override; fraction of decisions flipped by trust-signal patching vs content patching; steering-induced credibility equalization with true-evidence-acceptance gain AND false-evidence-acceptance non-increase (symmetric); off-target rate, fluency, no-conflict preservation; cross-model swing comparison and correlation with training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for evidence-language over content/query-language/fertility baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The evidence-language effect could be confounded with the model's competence in that language (it may accept dominant-language evidence simply because it understands it better, not because it trusts it more); we control for evidence-language competence, hold content identical via verified parallel translation, and use the trust-signal patching test (which transfers the decision while holding content representations fixed) as the primary causal evidence separating credibility from comprehension. 2) Parametric beliefs must be established per language and per fact, which is noisy; we verify beliefs via paraphrase-consistent multilingual probing and restrict to facts the model reliably holds. 3) Translation quality differences across evidence languages could drive apparent credibility; we measure and control for translation quality and include a within-language paraphrase null control. 4) Difference-in-means trust directions may entangle language-identity or content features; we use multiple extraction methods, the within-language paraphrase control, and specificity checks. 5) The false-evidence symmetric control is essential — if steering merely makes the model more gullible in low-resource languages, that is a failure, not a fix; we require true-evidence gains WITHOUT false-evidence gains and report the full tradeoff. 6) Early-timing (trust set before content) is hard to establish cleanly since content and language co-occur; we use position-resolved logit-lens and truncation and report this as suggestive rather than definitive. 7) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM's less English-centric hub analyzed as a contrast that should show a smaller swing). 8) If NO language-credibility effect is found — override depends only on content, not evidence language, with query language and content fixed — this is an informative POSITIVE result showing multilingual conflict resolution is language-neutral, valuable either way (and would sharpen the CLEAR resource-abundance finding as a comprehension rather than credibility effect). 9) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: language_dependent_temporal_anchor
