Title: What Year Does the Model Think It Is? A Language-Dependent Temporal Anchor Governs Cross-Lingual Recency of Knowledge
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs carry an internal 'temporal anchor' — an implicit present-time reference from which they date time-sensitive facts — and this anchor is LANGUAGE-DEPENDENT: it sits at an earlier (more outdated) effective year when the model is queried in a lower-resource / English-distant language than in English, because that language's pretraining data is older and sparser. Consequently, for facts that CHANGE over time (current officeholders, champions, prices), the model returns systematically more OUTDATED answers in those languages, not merely less accurate ones, and this staleness is predictable from a decodable, steerable temporal-anchor signal set by query language before the content is retrieved.
Related Work: Prior work establishes (a) knowledge cutoffs are not uniform and differ by sub-resource ('Dated Data' 2024; temporal misalignment / fact-duration prediction 2023; 'Time-Aware LMs' 2022; FreshBench 2024), (b) attention 'Temporal Heads' recall time-specific facts and can be edited (Temporal Heads 2025), (c) multilingual factual recall runs through an English-centric pipeline with language-independent subject enrichment and language-dependent object extraction (Paths Not Taken 2025; How Do Multilingual LLMs Remember Facts 2025; Lost in Multilinguality 2025), and (d) benchmarks show geographic/language recall disparities (TiEBe 2025) and evergreen-vs-mutable question temporality (EverGreenQA 2025; LiveCLKTBench 2025). CRITICALLY, all temporal work is monolingual/English and treats the effective cutoff as a single model-level property; all multilingual recall work treats cross-lingual gaps as accuracy/consistency deficits without a TEMPORAL direction. NO prior work asks whether the model's implicit present-time reference (temporal anchor) itself varies by QUERY LANGUAGE, whether this produces a directional STALENESS (outdated but internally-consistent answers) rather than random error, whether a shared temporal-anchor direction is set by language before content retrieval, or whether steering that anchor equalizes recency across languages. We reframe cross-lingual temporal failure from 'less accurate' to 'anchored to an earlier year', a distinct, mechanistically-localizable, steerable phenomenon.
Abstract: A time-sensitive fact — who leads a country, who holds a title, what a thing costs — has different correct answers at different times, so answering it requires an implicit sense of 'now'. Multilingual language models are known to be less accurate on non-English queries, but we ask a sharper, previously untested question: does the model's internal reference point for 'now' — its temporal anchor — depend on the language it is queried in? Because a language's pretraining data is typically older and sparser than English's, we hypothesize the anchor sits at an earlier effective year in lower-resource, English-distant languages, so the model returns systematically OUTDATED (but internally date-consistent) answers to mutable questions in those languages, rather than merely random errors. We further hypothesize a shared, decodable temporal-anchor direction is set by the query language before the fact is retrieved, causally shifting which time-slice of a fact is recalled, and that steering it can equalize recency across languages. We test this on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using time-stamped mutable facts (leaders, sports champions, record holders) whose correct answer is known per year, translated into typologically diverse languages. We (1) estimate each language's effective temporal anchor from the years its answers correspond to; (2) test that the staleness is directional (older answers), not random; (3) decode a temporal-anchor signal set by query language; and (4) steer the anchor to recover recent answers. Metrics include per-language effective-anchor year, staleness-vs-error decomposition, anchor-direction decodability, and steering-induced recency recovery with competence controls.
Experiments:
1) Time-stamped mutable-fact suite: Build ~600 mutable facts whose correct answer is a dated sequence of values (e.g., head of state of country X by year, world/continental champions by year, record holders, populations, current CEOs), with verified per-year gold answers spanning ~2005–2023 from Wikidata. Include an EVERGREEN control set (facts whose answer never changes, e.g., capital, chemical symbol) to separate temporal anchoring from general accuracy. Instantiate every query in typologically diverse languages spanning resource levels and scripts (English, French, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish), templated with NO year specified (so the model must supply its own 'now'). Native-speaker verify translations; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Effective temporal anchor per language (H1, core): For each mutable fact answered in each language, map the model's answer to the YEAR(S) for which that answer was correct, yielding a per-answer 'implied year'. Aggregate to a per-LANGUAGE effective-anchor year (median implied year across facts). Test H1: the effective anchor is earlier (more outdated) for lower-resource / English-distant languages than for English. Regress effective-anchor year on resource level and typological/script distance from English, controlling for the model's overall accuracy in that language (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2). Key: the anchor gap should persist even among facts the model answers CORRECTLY-for-some-year (i.e., it knows *an* answer, just an older one).
3) Directional-staleness decomposition (H2): Decompose errors on mutable facts into (a) STALE errors = the answer was correct in an EARLIER year than the true current answer (right entity, wrong time-slice), (b) FUTURE/anachronistic errors, and (c) random/unrelated errors. Test that lower-resource languages show a disproportionate share of STALE errors (directional outdatedness), not just more random errors. Report per-language stale-vs-random error ratio, benchmarked against English and against the evergreen control (which should show no staleness axis). Cross-check per-language anchor against external recall-disparity data (TiEBe) and effective-cutoff findings (Dated Data).
4) Anchor decodability and timing (H3): Extract a temporal-anchor direction via difference-in-means between representations of queries the model answers with recent vs old values (and via a probe predicting the implied year from hidden states) at middle layers, per language. Test (a) whether the query LANGUAGE is decodable from an early anchor signal and (b) whether that signal is set BEFORE fact retrieval — using logit-lens/tuned-lens across layers/positions, test whether the anchor magnitude at early tokens predicts the eventual implied year, independent of the specific fact. Measure cross-lingual alignment of the anchor direction (single shared temporal axis re-thresholded per language vs language-specific). Relate to the known Temporal Heads (do the same heads carry the anchor, and is their activation language-modulated?).
5) Causal steering test (H4, core): Add a steering vector along the temporal-anchor direction to push a low-resource-language query's anchor toward the recent (English-like) pole, and measure whether the model returns the more RECENT correct answer (recency-recovery rate) — holding the fact and query language fixed. Conversely, steer English toward an earlier anchor and verify it induces stale answers (bidirectional control). Activation-patching complement: patch the English anchor signal into the low-resource pass and test recency recovery. Compare against baselines: English-pivot recall steering (Paths Not Taken 2025 translation/recall vectors), SubInj entity-alignment prompting (Entity-Level Alignment 2025), and a random-direction control.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify steering is anchor-specific (shifts the time-slice recalled but does not change the ENTITY type, switch output language, or harm evergreen facts; measure off-target/language-mixing rate and evergreen accuracy), and moves recency in BOTH directions (recover recent AND induce stale on demand). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 shows a larger per-language anchor gap than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether the anchor gap correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the anchor direction and with each language's training share / data recency.
Evaluation metrics: per-language effective-anchor year and anchor gap vs English (partial correlation with resource/distance controlling for accuracy; held-out R^2); stale-vs-random error ratio (mutable vs evergreen control); anchor-direction decodability of query language and early-timing predictiveness of implied year; cross-lingual anchor-direction alignment and Temporal-Head language-modulation; steering recency-recovery rate and bidirectional control; specificity (evergreen preserved, entity-type unchanged, off-target rate); cross-model anchor-gap comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Mapping an answer to an 'implied year' requires facts with clean dated answer sequences; ambiguous or slowly-changing facts blur the anchor. Mitigation: restrict to facts with sharp yearly transitions (elections, championships) and verified Wikidata timelines, and report items where the implied year is unambiguous. 2) Language resource level is confounded with data recency, script, and overall competence; the key control is conditioning on facts where the model knows *an* answer (isolating time-slice from knowledge absence), plus the evergreen control and partial correlations, but residual confounding may remain. 3) A low-resource answer could be older simply because the recent value was never seen in that language (knowledge absence, not anchoring); the STALE-vs-random decomposition and the steering/patching test (which recovers a recent answer the model demonstrably CAN produce) distinguish anchoring from absence. 4) Difference-in-means anchor directions may entangle language-identity or content features; we use probe-based year decoding, the within-fact bidirectional steering check, and specificity controls. 5) Early-timing (anchor set before retrieval) is hard to establish since language and content co-occur; we use position-resolved lenses and report it as suggestive. 6) Steering could harm fluency or over-shift to anachronistic answers; we require evergreen preservation and bidirectional control and report the full tradeoff. 7) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM's less English-centric hub analyzed as a contrast expected to show a smaller anchor gap). 8) If NO language-dependent anchor is found — implied years are equal across languages once accuracy is controlled — this is an informative POSITIVE result showing temporal grounding is language-agnostic despite uneven data recency, valuable either way. 9) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: translation_equivalent_attrition
Title: New Language In, Old Fact Out: Retroactive Interference from Translation Equivalents Drives Cross-Lingual Knowledge Attrition in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: When a multilingual LLM continually learns new facts in one language, it selectively FORGETS the SAME facts it already knew in OTHER languages, and this forgetting is not uniform catastrophic forgetting but a targeted retroactive-interference effect concentrated on facts whose newly-learned answer is a TRANSLATION EQUIVALENT of the old answer, mirroring the documented human foreign-language-attrition phenomenon. We hypothesize the interference is mediated by overwriting of a shared, language-agnostic answer representation in the middle-layer concept hub (not the language-specific decoders), so attrition is (a) predicted by the pre-training cross-lingual sharedness of the fact, (b) strongest for facts learned via cross-lingual transfer rather than in-language frequency, and (c) causally attributable to shared-hub overwrite, which a shared-representation-protecting update can prevent.
Related Work: Human memory science robustly documents that learning new-language translation equivalents retroactively impairs retrieval of the old-language word (Isurin 2001 'Retroactive interference from translation equivalents'; de Bot; Mickan et al. 2023 'New in, old out'; Bridging SLA and Memory Science 2019), attributing foreign-language attrition to inter-language interference rather than passive decay. On the LLM side, prior work establishes (a) a shared, English-centric concept hub with late-layer language-specific decoding (Do Llamas Work in English 2024; Lost in Multilinguality 2025; Paths Not Taken 2025); (b) multilingual factual knowledge is acquired via frequency-driven learning vs limited cross-lingual transfer (Tracing Multilingual Factual Knowledge Acquisition 2025; Tracing the Roots of Facts 2024); and (c) continual-learning/catastrophic-forgetting and language-transfer forgetting studied at a coarse capability level (Branch-and-Merge 2024; Unveiling Linguistic Regions 2024; FOREVER 2026). CRITICALLY, no prior work asks whether learning a fact in a NEW language selectively erases the SAME fact in OTHER languages, whether this is a targeted TRANSLATION-EQUIVALENT interference effect (as in humans) rather than generic catastrophic forgetting, whether it is mediated by overwriting the shared concept-hub answer representation, or whether pre-training sharedness/transfer-origin predicts which facts attrite. We reframe cross-lingual forgetting from a generic continual-learning nuisance into a structured, human-mirroring retroactive-interference phenomenon with a localizable mechanistic cause and a targeted preventive fix. This is orthogonal to all prior inference-time representation studies and to coarse catastrophic-forgetting work.
Abstract: Bilingual humans forget: learning a new-language word for a concept measurably impairs later retrieval of that concept's word in an already-known language, a retroactive-interference effect at the heart of foreign-language attrition. We ask whether multilingual language models exhibit the same phenomenon when they continually learn new facts. We hypothesize that fine-tuning a model on facts in one language selectively erases the SAME facts it already answered correctly in OTHER languages, and that this is not uniform catastrophic forgetting but a targeted interference effect concentrated on facts whose newly-learned answer is a translation equivalent of the old one. We further hypothesize a mechanism: the update overwrites a shared, language-agnostic answer representation in the middle-layer concept hub rather than the language-specific decoders, so attrition is predicted by how cross-lingually shared a fact was before the update and is strongest for facts originally acquired via cross-lingual transfer. We test this on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM by continually fine-tuning on multilingual factual updates (counterfactual and new facts) in a source language and measuring per-fact accuracy drops in held-out languages, decomposing generic forgetting from translation-equivalent-specific interference via matched control facts. Using logit-lens/tuned-lens hub tracking and activation patching, we localize whether attrition reflects shared-hub overwrite versus decoder disruption, and test a shared-representation-protecting update (freezing/regularizing the hub answer subspace) that should prevent the cross-lingual attrition while preserving learning. Metrics include translation-equivalent attrition rate, sharedness/transfer-origin prediction, hub-overwrite localization, and protective-update recovery with learning preserved.
Experiments:
1) Continual-learning attrition suite: Assemble ~800 subject-relation-object facts (mLAMA/CounterFact-style) that the base model answers CORRECTLY in multiple languages (verified per-language), spanning typologically diverse languages/scripts (English, French, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili). For each fact create an UPDATE (a new/counterfactual object) taught in a SOURCE language via light fine-tuning (LoRA), and measure per-fact accuracy on the ORIGINAL fact in every OTHER (target) language before vs after. Include matched CONTROL facts NOT updated to establish baseline drift. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral attrition and translation-equivalent specificity (H1): Measure per-language attrition rate = fraction of previously-correct target-language answers now lost after the source-language update. Test that attrition is TARGETED: compare (a) facts whose old target-language answer is a translation equivalent of the newly-learned source answer (interference-prone) vs (b) unrelated facts of similar frequency (generic-forgetting baseline). Predict attrition >> baseline drift specifically for translation-equivalent facts. Control for tokenizer fertility, fact frequency, and target-language resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test translation-equivalence adds predictive power). Also test the human-mirroring asymmetry: does the target-language answer that is the direct translation equivalent of the updated answer attrite more than a semantically-related-but-non-equivalent one?
3) Pre-training sharedness / transfer-origin prediction (H2): Using pre-update representations, estimate each fact's cross-lingual SHAREDNESS (RankC-style consistency + shared-hub crystallization depth) and, where a checkpoint-traced signal is available (or via a frequency-vs-transfer proxy following Tracing Multilingual Factual Knowledge Acquisition 2025), its acquisition origin (in-language frequency vs cross-lingual transfer). Test that attrition is higher for facts that were more cross-lingually shared and for facts originally acquired via transfer (held-out prediction of attrition from sharedness/origin, controlling for frequency/fertility).
4) Mechanistic localization (H3): Using logit-lens/tuned-lens, track for attrited vs surviving facts whether the correct target-language answer is still present in the middle-layer shared hub after the update (decoder-only failure) or has been OVERWRITTEN in the hub (shared-representation overwrite). Via activation patching, patch the pre-update shared-hub answer representation into the post-update pass: if it restores the target-language answer, the loss was decoder-level; if the hub itself now encodes the new answer, it is a genuine shared-hub overwrite. Report the share of hub-overwrite vs decoder-disruption attrition per language, and test that translation-equivalent interference is disproportionately hub-overwrite.
5) Protective-update intervention (core causal test): Prevent cross-lingual attrition by protecting the shared answer subspace during the update: (a) freeze/regularize the middle-layer hub directions carrying the old fact (identified in Exp 4) while updating late/language-specific layers, and (b) a projection-based update that constrains the weight change to be orthogonal to the shared-hub answer direction. Predict this reduces translation-equivalent attrition in target languages while STILL successfully teaching the new fact in the source language. Compare against baselines: naive full/LoRA fine-tuning, Branch-and-Merge, EWC-style regularization, and linguistic-region freezing (Unveiling Linguistic Regions 2024). Metrics: source-language edit success (reliability), target-language attrition reduction, locality (unrelated facts), and portability.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify the protective update is attrition-specific (does not block legitimate cross-lingual propagation of the new fact where desired), does not switch output language (off-target rate), and preserves fluency. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 (more shared hub) shows STRONGER translation-equivalent attrition than the more linguistically-diverse BLOOM; test whether attrition magnitude correlates with the model's hub-sharedness and each fact's sharedness.
Evaluation metrics: translation-equivalent attrition rate vs generic-forgetting baseline (and human-mirroring equivalent-vs-related asymmetry); sharedness/transfer-origin prediction of attrition (held-out R^2 over frequency/fertility); hub-overwrite vs decoder-disruption attrition shares and patching-restoration rate; protective-update attrition reduction WITH source-language learning preserved, locality, off-target rate; cross-model attrition comparison and correlation with hub-sharedness.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Continual updates via fine-tuning may cause broad drift that swamps the targeted translation-equivalent signal; we use matched control facts, light LoRA updates, and report the attrition SURPLUS over generic drift rather than raw drops. 2) Establishing per-language 'previously correct' labels is noisy; we use paraphrase-consistent multilingual verification and restrict to reliably-known facts. 3) Translation-equivalence, sharedness, frequency, and resource level are correlated; matched controls, partial correlations, and the causal patching/protective-update tests are designed to isolate the interference pathway, but residual confounds may remain. 4) Hub-overwrite vs decoder-disruption may not separate cleanly; we use multiple patching granularities and report ambiguous cases. 5) The protective update could reduce genuine desirable cross-lingual propagation of the new fact; we measure this tradeoff explicitly (attrition-specificity control). 6) Acquisition-origin (frequency vs transfer) is hard to establish without pretraining-checkpoint access; we use a proxy and, where possible, an open checkpoint-traced model (e.g., OLMo) as validation. 7) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM analyzed as a less-shared-hub contrast expected to show weaker attrition). 8) The human-LLM comparison (translation-equivalent retroactive interference) is qualitative, not a claim of identical mechanism. 9) If NO targeted attrition is found — learning new-language facts does not selectively erase old-language equivalents beyond generic drift — this is an informative POSITIVE result showing multilingual knowledge is robustly compartmentalized, valuable either way. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: gender_congruency_crosslingual
Title: The Gender Congruency Effect in Multilingual LLMs: A Non-Query Language's Grammatical Gender Leaks Into Agreement in the Query Language
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs exhibit a mechanistic analogue of the human bilingual gender-congruency (GC) effect: when producing gender agreement for a noun in a query language, the model co-activates the grammatical gender that the noun's TRANSLATION EQUIVALENT carries in another (non-query) gendered language, so agreement is facilitated when the two languages assign the same gender (congruent) and interfered with when they disagree (incongruent). We hypothesize this leakage is mediated by a partially-shared gender direction that carries the non-query-language gender signal into the query-language agreement computation, is measurable as a congruent-minus-incongruent agreement-accuracy/log-prob swing, scales with cross-lingual sharedness of the gender subspace, and is causally attributable to (and removable by) that shared direction.
Related Work: A large bilingual-cognition literature documents the gender-congruency (GC) effect: translation-equivalent nouns sharing grammatical gender across a bilingual's languages are produced/recognized faster than gender-mismatched ones, with the effect modulated by cognate status and gender-system similarity (Paolieri/Grammatical Gender Inhibition 2011; grammatical-gender processing review 2019; GC meta-analysis 2020; morphosyntactic gender features 2004), and inhibitory control resolves the cross-language competition. Some work argues the two gender systems are functionally autonomous (Costa 2003), making the LLM test genuinely open. Interpretability shows gender lives in shared+language-specific subspaces (Analyzing Gender Representation 2022), agreement is driven by a largely language-independent number/gender direction written by a head and read by MLPs (On the Similarity of Circuits across Languages 2024; Causal Analysis of Syntactic Agreement Neurons 2022; Same Neurons Different Languages 2022), and LMs simulate crosslinguistic influence with L1 co-activation during L2 processing (Language Models as Artificial Learners 2026; From Monolingual to Bilingual 2025). CRITICALLY, no prior work tests whether multilingual LLMs show a GC effect: whether the grammatical gender a noun carries in a NON-QUERY language leaks into and facilitates/interferes with gender AGREEMENT in the query language, whether this is a distinct behavioral swing predicted by cross-lingual gender-subspace sharedness, or whether a shared gender direction causally mediates and can remove it. This differs from my prior gender proposals (gender leaking into ATTRIBUTE reasoning about referents; agreement-ATTRACTION illusions from a within-sentence distractor) because here the interfering cue is the SAME noun's gender in a DIFFERENT LANGUAGE (a translation-equivalent competition), directly porting the human GC paradigm into LLM mechanisms.
Abstract: In bilingual humans, a noun's grammatical gender in one language influences how they process its translation equivalent in the other: agreement is faster when the two languages assign the SAME gender (congruent) and slower when they disagree (incongruent) - the gender-congruency effect. We ask a simple, previously untested question about multilingual language models: when a model produces gender agreement for a noun in a query language, does the grammatical gender that noun's translation equivalent carries in ANOTHER gendered language leak into the computation? We hypothesize a mechanistic GC effect: for translation-equivalent nouns whose gender DIFFERS across two gendered languages, the model's agreement (adjective/determiner/participle inflection) in the query language is facilitated when the other language agrees and interfered with when it disagrees, producing a congruent-minus-incongruent agreement swing absent when the other language shares the same gender. We further hypothesize this leakage is mediated by a partially-shared gender direction carrying the non-query-language gender signal, scales with cross-lingual gender-subspace sharedness, and is causally removable by ablating that direction without harming within-language agreement. We test this on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM across gendered language pairs with divergent gender assignments (Spanish/German, Spanish/French, Italian/Russian, Hindi as a two-gender case), using controlled agreement minimal pairs. Combining behavioral congruency measurement, difference-in-means gender-direction extraction, activation patching, and steering, we measure the GC swing, its sharedness scaling, its causal locus, and whether ablating the shared gender direction removes the cross-language interference. Metrics include congruent-vs-incongruent agreement swing, sharedness prediction, causal-mediation attribution, and ablation-induced interference removal with within-language competence controls.
Experiments:
1) Cross-lingual gender-congruency suite: Assemble ~500 concrete inanimate nouns whose grammatical gender is verified in multiple gendered languages (Spanish, German, French, Italian, Russian, Hindi), partitioned into CONGRUENT pairs (same gender across the two languages of interest) and INCONGRUENT pairs (opposite gender), sourced from authoritative dictionaries/UniMorph and native-speaker verified. For each noun build gender-agreement probe contexts in the QUERY language where a determiner/adjective/participle must inflect for the noun's gender (e.g., Spanish 'la mesa blanca' vs 'el ...'). Also include cognate vs non-cognate splits (to test the human cognate modulation) and a two-gender contrast (Hindi) as a system-similarity variant. Report inter-annotator agreement; release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral GC effect (H1, core): For each noun, measure query-language agreement accuracy and the log-prob margin of the correct gender-inflected form. Compute the GC swing = agreement performance on CONGRUENT (the noun's gender in a second gendered language matches the query language) minus INCONGRUENT (it mismatches) items. Predict a positive swing: incongruent items show degraded agreement / smaller correct-form margin and more gender errors, mirroring humans. Establish that within a single language (no second language cued) there is no such swing. Control for noun frequency, tokenizer fertility, and query-language resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test congruency adds predictive power). Test the human-documented cognate modulation (larger GC swing for cognates) and gender-system-similarity modulation.
3) Sharedness scaling (H2): Extract a per-language grammatical-gender direction via difference-in-means (masculine vs feminine noun representations) at each layer (following Analyzing Gender Representation 2022), and measure cross-lingual cosine alignment (shared vs language-specific gender subspace) per language pair. Test whether the GC swing is larger for language pairs with more SHARED gender subspaces (held-out prediction of swing from sharedness, controlling for frequency/fertility), and correlate with the Interference-Matrix-style expectation that more-aligned systems interfere more.
4) Causal localization via activation patching (H3, core): For INCONGRUENT items where the model makes a gender-agreement error in the query language, test whether the ERROR follows the non-query-language gender. Patch (a) the shared gender direction toward the query-language-correct gender and (b) the noun's mid-layer gender representation from a monolingual (single-language) pass, and measure whether agreement is restored. Conversely, INJECT the second language's opposite-gender signal into a congruent/monolingual pass and test whether it induces an incongruent-style error (bidirectional causal test). This isolates whether the interference is carried by the partially-shared gender direction rather than a separate mechanism.
5) Ablation / removal test: Ablate the shared gender direction (difference-in-means projection removal / INLP nullspace) so the query-language agreement can no longer read the non-query-language gender signal, and test whether the GC swing collapses toward zero. Critically verify WITHIN-LANGUAGE agreement competence is preserved (the model must still inflect correctly using the query language's own gender) and that the ablation does not switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate) or harm fluency. Compare against random-direction ablation and whole-hub English-steering baselines.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify the effect is gender-specific (a congruency manipulation on an irrelevant feature produces no swing) and not a lexical-frequency artifact (nonce-noun variants with assigned genders). Cross-model contrast: predict the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM (more shared gender subspace across many gendered languages) show LARGER GC swings than the more English-centric Llama-3 (English lacks grammatical gender, so less competing signal); test whether swing magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the gender direction and with each language pair's training share. Qualitatively compare the model's GC-swing pattern (cognate boost, system-similarity modulation) against the human GC meta-analysis.
Evaluation metrics: GC swing (congruent minus incongruent agreement accuracy and correct-form log-prob margin; vs no-swing within-language baseline); cognate and gender-system-similarity modulation; sharedness prediction of swing (held-out R^2 over frequency/fertility); share of incongruent errors that follow the non-query-language gender; patching-induced restoration and injection-induced interference (bidirectional causal test); ablation-induced GC-swing collapse WITH within-language agreement preserved; off-target rate, fluency; cross-model swing comparison and correlation with gender-subspace sharedness and training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The human GC effect is a PRODUCTION/latency phenomenon (reaction time), not directly comparable to LLM log-prob margins; our model-vs-human comparison is qualitative (direction, cognate and system-similarity modulation), not a claim of identical mechanism. 2) Some bilingual work argues gender systems are functionally autonomous (Costa 2003), so a null GC swing is a live possibility - but that itself would be an informative result showing LLM gender systems are language-local despite shared subspaces. 3) Grammatical gender is correlated with language family, script, and resource level; the within-noun congruent/incongruent contrast, nonce-noun variants, and within-language no-swing baseline isolate the congruency pathway, but residual confounds may remain. 4) Difference-in-means gender directions may entangle animacy or lexical features; we use multiple extraction methods, the established agreement circuit as an anchor, and specificity controls. 5) The ablation could harm legitimate within-language agreement; we require within-language competence preservation as a hard constraint and report the full tradeoff. 6) Activation patching to separate the shared-gender pathway from query-language gender may have entangled effects; we use the bidirectional injection test and multiple granularities. 7) English lacks grammatical gender, so cross-language competition requires two gendered languages - we center on gendered pairs (Spanish/German/French/Italian/Russian/Hindi) and treat English-centric models as a lower-competition contrast. 8) Instruction-tuned models may suppress errors; we test base models where available and interpret small swings as informative. 9) If NO GC effect is found, this is a valuable positive result on cross-lingual gender autonomy in LLMs. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: language_conditioned_effort_miscalibration
Title: Overthinking in One Language, Underthinking in Another: A Language-Conditioned Reasoning-Effort Setpoint in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual reasoning models carry a language-conditioned 'reasoning-effort setpoint' — an internal target for how much serial computation to spend before committing to an answer — and this setpoint is MISCALIBRATED relative to each language's accuracy-optimal effort: for the SAME problem the model systematically overshoots the optimal effort (overthinking) in some languages while undershooting it (underthinking) in others, so both too-much and too-little effort coexist across languages and both cost accuracy. The setpoint is set early by a decodable, steerable language signal before problem content is processed, and per-language accuracy loss is predictable from the signed effort-mismatch and correctable by steering the setpoint toward each language's optimum.
Related Work: Two lines meet but are never connected. (1) 'When More is Less' (2025) establishes that accuracy vs CoT length follows an inverted-U with an OPTIMAL length that scales with task difficulty and (inversely) model capability, and that RL drives models toward it — but this is MONOLINGUAL and treats effort as content-driven, not language-driven. (2) Multilingual work shows non-English reasoning can be MORE token-efficient at equal accuracy (EfficientXLang 2025; 'Less Data Less Tokens' 2025), that models default to English/high-resource reasoning and lose accuracy when forced into the input language ('When Models Reason in Your Language' 2025; 'Language Matters' 2025; Cross-lingual Collapse 2025), and that latent (pre-verbalization) reasoning is English-centered and weaker for low-resource languages ('Large Reasoning Models Are Not Yet Multilingual Latent Reasoners' 2026). All of these treat verbalized token count as an efficiency/fidelity metric and per-language accuracy as a competence gap. NONE frames the amount of internal reasoning effort as a language-CONDITIONED SETPOINT that can be simultaneously ABOVE optimum (overthinking) in one language and BELOW it (underthinking) in another for the same problem, none measures a signed per-language effort-mismatch against each language's own inverted-U optimum, and none locates/steers a pre-content language-set effort signal to move each language to its optimum. This differs from my prior 'latent compute-depth gap' proposal (which posits only UNDER-computation / premature commitment in low-resource languages); the novel, sharper claim here is a BIDIRECTIONAL miscalibration — overthinking is as real and harmful as underthinking, and both are governed by one steerable setpoint.
Abstract: Reasoning models spend variable internal effort before answering, and monolingual work shows accuracy follows an inverted-U in reasoning length with a task-specific optimum. We ask a simple question this makes urgent for multilingual models: is the amount of reasoning effort a language-CONDITIONED setpoint, and is it miscalibrated relative to each language's accuracy-optimal effort? We hypothesize that for the SAME problem a multilingual model overshoots the optimum (overthinking) in some languages and undershoots it (underthinking) in others, so both errors coexist across languages and both reduce accuracy; that this setpoint is fixed early by a decodable, steerable language signal before the problem is processed; and that per-language accuracy loss is predicted by the signed effort-mismatch and corrected by steering the setpoint toward each language's optimum. We test on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1-distilled Qwen/Llama, Qwen-reasoning) across typologically diverse languages using MGSM, a controlled k-step synthetic suite where required depth is known, and PolyMath. For each language we trace the inverted-U to locate its optimal effort, measure the model's default effort (verbalized length plus a truncation/early-exit-based latent-effort estimate), and compute a signed mismatch. Using logit-lens decoding of an early effort/language signal and a difference-in-means effort-setpoint direction, we test whether the setpoint is set pre-content, whether mismatch predicts accuracy loss, and whether steering the setpoint (train-free) moves each language to its optimum, closing gaps for BOTH overthinking and underthinking languages. Metrics include per-language optimal vs default effort, signed-mismatch-vs-accuracy correlation, and setpoint-steering recovery with specificity controls.
Experiments: 1) Per-language inverted-U and optimal effort: For each problem and language, sweep reasoning effort at inference (budget-forcing via 'wait'/stop-token control, forced max-thinking-tokens, and length-controlled prompts) and record accuracy vs effort, recovering each LANGUAGE's accuracy-optimal effort per difficulty bin. Effort is measured two ways: (a) verbalized reasoning tokens; (b) a latent-effort estimate = the truncation depth / number of internal steps at which the correct answer first crystallizes (logit-lens/early-exit on hidden states), following the latent-reasoning truncation paradigm. Datasets: MGSM, a controlled synthetic k-step arithmetic/logic suite (k=1..6, verified gold, translated), and PolyMath. Languages: 10+ spanning scripts/resource levels (English, French, German, Chinese, Russian, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish, Bengali). Models: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, Qwen2.5/Qwen3-reasoning variant. 2) Default effort and signed mismatch (H1, core): Measure each language's DEFAULT effort (unconstrained) and compute signed mismatch = default minus optimal, per language and difficulty. Test the bidirectional prediction: some languages have positive mismatch (overthinking) and others negative (underthinking) for the SAME problems, and both deviate from their optimum. Control for tokenizer fertility and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test language adds predictive power beyond difficulty and fertility). Verify overthinking is genuine (extra steps degrade accuracy, e.g., self-doubt/answer-flipping) not merely verbose. 3) Mismatch predicts accuracy loss (H2): Test whether per-language accuracy loss (relative to the language's own optimal-effort accuracy and to English) is predicted by the ABSOLUTE signed mismatch (Spearman; held-out R^2), and whether the direction of loss matches the sign (overthinking languages lose via late-step corruption; underthinking via premature commitment) using an error-type decomposition (answer present-then-abandoned vs never-formed) via activation patching. 4) Setpoint is language-set and pre-content (H3): Extract a difference-in-means 'effort-setpoint' direction (high-effort vs low-effort passes) and test (a) that the query LANGUAGE is decodable from an early signal, and (b) via position-resolved logit-lens/truncation, that the effort magnitude at early tokens (before problem content) predicts eventual default effort. Measure cross-lingual alignment of the setpoint direction (shared axis re-thresholded per language). 5) Core causal intervention — setpoint steering: Steer along the effort-setpoint direction to push each language's setpoint toward ITS optimum (up for underthinking languages, down for overthinking), train-free, and measure per-language accuracy recovery. Crucially predict SELECTIVE, BIDIRECTIONAL gains: raising effort helps underthinking languages, lowering effort helps overthinking languages, and mis-signed steering hurts (dose-response). Compare against baselines: uniform English-steering (MRRE 2025), fixed longer/shorter budget for all languages, and random-direction control. Compute recovery elasticity = accuracy gain per unit mismatch corrected, correlated with the H2 mismatch. 6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify steering changes effort without switching output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), preserves fluency, and does not help languages already near their optimum. Cross-model contrast: predict more English-centric distilled models overthink in low-resource languages more (English-anchored high setpoint) while under-resourced-language competence causes underthinking elsewhere; test whether mismatch magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the setpoint direction and with training share. Evaluation metrics: per-language optimal vs default effort (verbalized and latent); fraction of languages overthinking vs underthinking on shared problems; signed-mismatch-vs-accuracy-loss correlation and held-out R^2 over difficulty/fertility; error-type shares by mismatch sign; early-signal language-decodability and pre-content predictiveness; setpoint cross-lingual alignment; bidirectional steering recovery and elasticity with dose-response and mis-sign penalty; off-target rate; cross-model mismatch comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The inverted-U optimal effort is noisy per language/difficulty and depends on how effort is controlled; we use multiple effort-control mechanisms (budget forcing, max-token caps, length prompts), average over difficulty bins, and report robustness across control methods. 2) Verbalized length and latent effort may diverge (a model can crystallize the answer early yet keep verbalizing); we report both and treat their divergence as itself informative, using the latent-effort estimate for the core setpoint claims. 3) Overthinking vs verbose-but-harmless is hard to separate; we require that extra effort actually DEGRADES accuracy (via answer-flip/late-corruption analysis) before labeling a language 'overthinking'. 4) Language is confounded with resource level, script, and tokenizer fertility; partial correlations, the synthetic k-step suite (difficulty controlled), and the causal steering test mitigate but may not fully remove confounds. 5) 'Pre-content' setpoint timing is hard to establish since language and content co-occur; we use position-resolved lenses/truncation and report it as suggestive. 6) Setpoint steering could harm fluency or induce language switching; we require selectivity, bidirectionality, dose-response, and low off-target rate as hard checks and report the full tradeoff. 7) Budget-forcing controls differ across model families and may only approximate the true internal setpoint; recurrent-depth control is not available, weakening the cleanest latent manipulation. 8) Effects may be model-family dependent and limited to open ~7-8B reasoning models; may not extend to frontier scale. 9) If default effort already sits at each language's optimum (no bidirectional mismatch), this is an informative negative result showing multilingual effort allocation is well-calibrated and relocating the multilingual gap to pure competence rather than effort mis-setpointing — valuable either way.

Name: loanword_donor_leakage
Title: Once Borrowed, Never Neutral: A Loanword's Donor Language Leaks Into Cross-Lingual Reasoning in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: A loanword is a word that lives in two languages at once: it is a fully integrated item of the recipient language, yet it entered from a donor language. We hypothesize that when a multilingual LLM reasons about a loanword in its recipient language, its English-scaffolded shared hub routes the word through the DONOR language's associations rather than treating it as a native recipient-language item, so the model's judgments about the loanword (its register/formality, cultural associations, sense disambiguation, and typicality) leak toward the donor language. This produces a distinctive, measurable inconsistency: a loanword is reasoned about differently from a native synonym of the SAME meaning in the SAME recipient-language context, and the size of this donor-leakage tracks each word's empirical borrowing depth (how integrated vs. foreign it is), is mediated by a decodable donor-language signal, and is causally suppressible without harming literal comprehension.
Related Work: Two literatures meet but have never been connected mechanistically. (1) NLP work shows multilingual LLMs are 'borrowing-blind' — they fail to behaviorally distinguish loanwords from native words and are biased toward loanwords over native equivalents (Language Models Are Borrowing-Blind 2025), that vocabulary/token overlap and cognate-like sharing drive cross-lingual transfer and interference (False Friends Are Not Foes 2025; Hyperpolyglot LLMs 2023; It's not Greek to mBERT 2020), and that non-Roman scripts are internally bridged via latent romanization (RomanLens 2025). (2) A large loanword-phonology and language-contact literature establishes that borrowed words retain donor-language phonological, etymological, and sociolinguistic traces and vary in 'borrowing depth'/integration (Loan Phonology 2009; Models of Phonological Loanword Adaptation 2023; Loanwords in Basic Vocabulary 2024; Cross-Lingual Bridges with Models of Lexical Borrowing, Tsvetkov & Dyer 2016; the World Loanword Database). CRITICALLY, all model work either tests whether a model can LABEL a word as borrowed or studies token overlap as a transfer aid; NONE asks whether a loanword's DONOR ORIGIN causally LEAKS into downstream SEMANTIC REASONING about the word's referent in its recipient language, whether this produces a native-synonym vs loanword reasoning inconsistency, whether the leak scales with empirical borrowing depth, whether a shared donor-language signal mediates it, or whether it can be causally suppressed. This reframes lexical borrowing from a transfer/labeling curiosity into a source of reasoning contamination, and is orthogonal to my prior proposals (grammatical categories, facts, idioms, phonosemantics, color, kinship), none of which concern loanwords as a two-languages-at-once natural experiment.
Abstract: Every language borrows words: Swahili's vocabulary is ~40% from Arabic, Japanese is saturated with English loanwords, and English itself is full of French and Latin. A loanword is peculiar: it is a fully integrated item of the recipient language, yet it entered from a donor language and, linguists show, keeps donor-language traces. Multilingual language models build a shared, English-scaffolded semantic hub. We ask a simple, previously untested question: when a model reasons about a loanword in its recipient language, does the DONOR language's associations leak into that reasoning, so the model does not treat the loanword as a native recipient-language item? We hypothesize (1) donor leakage: the model's judgments about a loanword (register/formality, cultural associations, sense, typicality) shift toward the donor language relative to a native recipient-language synonym of the SAME meaning in the SAME context; (2) the leak scales with each word's empirical borrowing depth (deeply integrated loanwords leak less than superficially borrowed ones); (3) a decodable donor-language signal in the shared hub mediates the leak; and (4) suppressing that signal removes the leak without harming literal comprehension. We build a controlled suite of loanword/native-synonym minimal pairs grounded in the World Loanword Database across recipient languages (Swahili, Japanese, Turkish, Hindi, English), on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM. Using difference-in-means donor-signal probes, logit-lens depth tracking, activation patching, and steering, we measure the leak, its borrowing-depth scaling, its mediation, and its causal suppression. Metrics include loanword-vs-native reasoning gap, borrowing-depth-prediction correlation, donor-signal decodability, mediation R-squared, and suppression-induced leak removal with competence controls.
Experiments:
1) Loanword/native-synonym suite grounded in WOLD: Using the World Loanword Database (WOLD) and native-speaker verification, assemble ~400 loanwords across recipient languages with well-documented borrowing (Swahili<-Arabic, Japanese<-English, Turkish<-Arabic/French, Hindi<-Persian/English, English<-French), each paired with (a) a NATIVE recipient-language synonym of the same core meaning and (b) the DONOR-language source word. Attach WOLD borrowing-depth/integration scores per loanword. Design reasoning probes that hinge on associations, NOT on recognizing foreignness: (i) register/formality judgment; (ii) cultural-association forced choice (which cultural sphere the referent belongs to); (iii) sense/collocation disambiguation; (iv) typicality/prototypicality ratings. Present loanword and native synonym in the SAME recipient-language sentence frames with matched meaning. Native-speaker verify meanings, synonymy, and gold labels; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral donor-leakage (H1): For each loanword/native-synonym pair, measure whether the model's reasoning judgments about the loanword shift toward the DONOR language's profile relative to the native synonym (e.g., a loanword judged more formal/foreign-cultural even when the meaning and context are identical to the native synonym). Compute a per-language donor-leakage effect size (loanword judgment minus native-synonym judgment, signed toward donor), controlling for word frequency, tokenizer fertility, and script (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test loanword status adds predictive power). Verify near-zero gap on matched native-native synonym control pairs (both native, same meaning) to rule out a generic synonym-difference artifact.
3) Borrowing-depth scaling (H2, external validation): Using WOLD integration scores, test whether per-word donor-leakage is predicted by borrowing depth — superficially borrowed / recently-borrowed words leak more toward the donor; deeply integrated basic-vocabulary loanwords leak least (Spearman correlation; held-out prediction of leakage from WOLD depth alone), tying the internal phenomenon to independent linguistic ground truth.
4) Representational localization (H3): Extract a donor-language signal via difference-in-means / a language-identity probe (following It's not Greek to mBERT 2020; Hyperpolyglot LLMs 2023) at each layer. Test whether a loanword's shared-hub representation carries a residual DONOR-language signal (i.e., the loanword decodes partly as its donor language) that a native synonym does not, using logit-lens/tuned-lens depth tracking of when and how strongly this donor signal appears (also checking latent romanization for non-Roman scripts per RomanLens). Mediation: regress behavioral donor-leakage on the loanword representation's donor-signal strength (partial correlation controlling for frequency/fertility; held-out R^2). Baseline: a native-synonym control (no donor signal).
5) Causal suppression/steering test (core): (a) Ablate the donor-language signal from the loanword's representation (difference-in-means projection removal / INLP nullspace toward the recipient language) and test whether the donor-leakage effect drops toward the native-synonym baseline; (b) conversely, INJECT the donor signal into the native synonym and test whether it induces loanword-like leakage (bidirectional causal test); (c) for individual leaked judgments, patch the recipient-language representation from the native synonym into the loanword pass and test restoration. Critically verify LITERAL COMPREHENSION is preserved (the model must still answer literal factual/definitional questions about the loanword correctly), plus fluency and off-target/language-mixing checks. Baselines: random-direction ablation, whole-hub English-steering.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify suppression is donor-specific (removes donor-leakage but not genuine meaning or unrelated attributes), graded (leak scales with borrowing depth), and not a lexical-frequency artifact (frequency-matched loanword/native pairs). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 leaks more for English-donor loanwords (e.g., Japanese<-English), while the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM leak less; test whether leak magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the donor signal and with each donor language's training share. Qualitatively compare the model's per-word leakage pattern against the WOLD borrowing-depth structure.
Evaluation metrics: loanword-vs-native-synonym donor-leakage effect size (vs native-native control); donor-leakage-vs-WOLD-borrowing-depth correlation and held-out prediction; donor-signal decodability and crystallization depth for loanwords vs native synonyms; mediation regression (held-out R^2); ablation-induced leak reduction and injection-induced leak (bidirectional); patching-induced restoration; literal-comprehension preservation, fluency, off-target rate; cross-model leak comparison and correlation with donor training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for loanword status over frequency/fertility/script baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Constructing true loanword/native-synonym minimal pairs with identical core meaning is delicate — loanwords and native synonyms often diverge in nuance/register precisely because of borrowing; we native-speaker verify near-synonymy, report inter-annotator agreement, exclude low-agreement pairs, and treat register divergence itself as one measured outcome rather than a confound (with the native-native control isolating generic synonym differences). 2) Loanword status is correlated with word frequency, script (donor-script residue), and recipient-language resource level; frequency-matched pairs, the native-native control, WOLD-based depth prediction, and partial correlations isolate the donor-leakage pathway, but residual confounds may remain. 3) Some donor-leakage may reflect genuine, correct sociolinguistic knowledge (a loanword really IS more formal/foreign) rather than a reasoning bug; we frame the phenomenon descriptively (does donor origin shape reasoning?), use the WOLD-depth and native-synonym contrasts to separate warranted from spurious leakage, and report both interpretations. 4) Difference-in-means donor-language directions may entangle script/orthographic features; we use multiple extraction methods, latent-romanization checks for non-Roman scripts, frequency-matched controls, and a native-synonym baseline. 5) Logit-lens/tuned-lens depth estimates are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 6) Suppression could harm fluency or legitimate meaning; we require literal-comprehension preservation and the bidirectional injection test, and report the full tradeoff. 7) WOLD coverage and borrowing-depth codings are uneven and language-specific; we treat depth scores as noisy predictors and rely on behavioral and causal tests for core claims. 8) Instruction-tuned models may suppress overt foreignness cues; we test base models where available and interpret small effects as informative. 9) If NO donor-leakage is found — loanwords are reasoned about identically to native synonyms — this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the shared hub fully nativizes borrowed vocabulary, valuable either way and complementary to the borrowing-blindness finding. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: portable_relation_local_retrieval_analogy
Title: The Relation Travels, the Answer Doesn't: A Portable Analogy Operator but Language-Local Target Retrieval in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: In multilingual A:B::C:D analogical reasoning, the relational mapping operation (the abstract 'R' that turns C into D) is encoded as a largely language-agnostic operator direction in the shared semantic hub and therefore transfers across languages, whereas the final RETRIEVAL of the target word D is a language-specific step that fails in lower-resource / typologically-distant languages. Cross-lingual analogy inconsistency is thus dominated by target-retrieval failure, not relation-encoding failure, mirroring the human L1/L2 analogy asymmetry where relations are grasped but lexical retrieval in L2 is the bottleneck. Consequently, an analogy operator extracted in a high-resource language can be transplanted into a low-resource-language forward pass to correctly complete the analogy, while the retrieval failure cannot be fixed this way.
Related Work: Interpretability work shows relational/analogy operations are encoded as compact, causal, transplantable representations: concept vectors for verbal relations emerge in early-to-mid layers and can be causally inserted (Analogical Reasoning Inside LLMs 2025; Concept Vectors and the Limits of Abstraction 2025), function vectors and fine-tuned/composite function vectors extract and steer relational knowledge (Relational Knowledge Distillation Using Fine-tuned Function Vectors 2026), and relational information propagates through mid-upper layers with successful analogy marked by structural alignment (The Curious Case of Analogies 2025). Multilingual work establishes a shared, English-scaffolded semantic hub with high cross-lingual concept alignment (Semantic Hub 2024; Concept Space Alignment 2024; Structural Concepts Are Universal 2023) and that larger models drift into language-specific subspaces, hurting cross-lingual consistency (Language-Specific Latent Process Hinders 2025). Cognitive science shows humans solve analogies worse in L2 specifically because relational processing completes but lexical retrieval is costly in L2 (Analogical reasoning in first and second languages 2025; Do LLMs solve verbal analogies like children 2023). CRITICALLY, all analogy-mechanism work is monolingual (English), and all multilingual-hub work concerns static concepts/facts, not the analogy OPERATOR. NO prior work asks whether the relational-mapping operation is a portable cross-lingual operator dissociable from a language-local target-retrieval step, whether cross-lingual analogy inconsistency is a retrieval (not relation-encoding) failure, or whether transplanting the operator across languages completes the analogy. This reframes cross-lingual analogy failure as a portable-relation / local-retrieval dissociation, orthogonal to my prior proposals (which concern grammatical categories, facts, idioms, and lexical form, never the analogy operator itself).
Abstract: Analogical reasoning—mapping A:B onto C to infer D—is a core of cognition, and interpretability work shows language models encode the relational mapping as a compact, causally transplantable direction. Humans, however, solve analogies worse in their second language, and cognitive studies pinpoint the bottleneck not in grasping the relation but in retrieving the target word in L2. We ask whether multilingual LLMs show the same dissociation: is the analogy operator (the abstract relation R) a language-agnostic portable direction in the shared semantic hub, while the retrieval of the target D is a language-specific step that fails cross-lingually? We hypothesize that (1) the relation-encoding operator is shared across languages and transfers, so cross-lingual analogy inconsistency is dominated by target-RETRIEVAL failure, not relation-encoding failure; and (2) an operator extracted in a high-resource language can be transplanted into a low-resource-language forward pass to correctly complete the analogy, whereas retrieval failures cannot be fixed this way. We build a controlled multilingual A:B::C:D analogy suite (spanning semantic and morphological relations) across typologically diverse languages, on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM. Using function/concept-vector extraction, logit-lens tracking, activation patching to separate relation-encoding from target-retrieval failures, and cross-lingual operator transplant, we test where analogy computation lives, which step fails cross-lingually, and whether transplanting the operator restores correct completion. Metrics include relation-encoding vs retrieval error shares, cross-lingual operator-direction alignment, transplant success rate, and correlation with the human L1/L2 analogy asymmetry.
Experiments:
1) Multilingual analogy suite: Construct ~500 A:B::C:D analogy items spanning (a) semantic relations (capital-country, part-whole, antonym, category-member, cause-effect) and (b) morphological relations (comparative, plural, verb-tense), each with a single verified target D, templated across typologically diverse languages spanning scripts and resource levels (English, French, German, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish). Native-speaker verify translations and gold targets; include distractor options for a forced-choice variant and an open-generation variant. Control for target-word frequency and tokenizer fertility. Report inter-annotator agreement; release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral cross-lingual analogy map: Measure per-language analogy accuracy (open-generation and forced-choice) and cross-lingual consistency (agreement on the SAME item across languages). Establish the expected pattern: accuracy is high and consistent in high-resource languages and degrades for lower-resource/English-distant languages. Control for tokenizer fertility, target frequency, and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2).
3) Operator extraction and cross-lingual alignment (H1a): For each relation, extract a per-language analogy-operator direction (function/concept vector) via difference-in-means / causal-mediation over correct A:B pairs at the relation-encoding layers (following Concept Vectors 2025; Fine-tuned Function Vectors 2026). Measure cross-lingual cosine alignment of the operator direction across layers; test that alignment is high and peaks in early-to-mid (shared-hub) layers, comparable to within-model relation baselines. Verify each operator causally completes analogies within its language (insertion flip rate).
4) Relation-encoding vs target-retrieval error decomposition (H1b, core): For items solved correctly in English but wrong in language B, use activation patching to test: (a) patch the shared-hub RELATION operator from the English pass into B; (b) patch only the late-layer target-retrieval/decoding components. Classify as relation-encoding failure (fixed by (a) at the relation stage) vs target-retrieval failure (relation is correctly present but the target is not retrieved/decoded in B). Also use logit-lens to check whether the correct target D is latently present in the shared hub before B's language-specific decoder fails to surface it. Report the share of each error type per language, predicting retrieval failures dominate and grow with resource-distance.
5) Core cross-lingual transplant test (H2): Extract the analogy operator in a high-resource language (English) and TRANSPLANT it (steering/insertion) into a low-resource-language forward pass on the C token; measure whether the model correctly completes the analogy in the target language (transplant success rate). Prediction: operator transplant substantially raises accuracy for relation-encoding failures but CANNOT repair genuine target-retrieval failures (where the language-specific decoder lacks/mis-surfaces D), demonstrating the portable-relation / local-retrieval dissociation. Compare against a shared-hub English-steering baseline, a random-direction control, and a target-retrieval-boosting intervention (steer the target-decoding direction) to show retrieval failures need a different fix.
6) Specificity, human-comparison, and cross-model controls: Verify transplant is relation-specific (transplanting the antonym operator completes antonym analogies but not part-whole), does not switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), and preserves fluency. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 shows sharper retrieval-failure dominance and larger transplant gains than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether the operator-alignment / retrieval-failure split correlates with training share. Qualitatively compare the model's relation-grasped-but-target-not-retrieved pattern against the human L1/L2 analogy asymmetry (relations complete, lexical retrieval is the L2 bottleneck).
Evaluation metrics: per-language analogy accuracy and cross-lingual consistency; cross-lingual operator-direction alignment (and vs within-model relation baseline); relation-encoding vs target-retrieval error shares per language; latent-target-presence-before-decoder-failure rate; transplant success rate (overall and split by error type) vs baselines; relation-specificity of transplant; off-target rate; cross-model comparison and correlation with training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for resource-distance over frequency/fertility baselines; qualitative correspondence with the human L1/L2 asymmetry.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Relation-encoding and target-retrieval steps may not separate cleanly; patching may have entangled effects. Mitigation: use multiple patching granularities, cross-validate with logit-lens latent-target-presence checks, and report ambiguous cases explicitly. 2) Word-analogy tasks can be solved by lexical association rather than genuine relational mapping (Do LLMs solve analogies like children 2023); we include far/cross-domain and morphological relations, distractor-controlled forced-choice items, and low-association targets to reduce association shortcuts. 3) Operator directions from difference-in-means / causal mediation may entangle content or format (Concept Vectors 2025 shows function vectors are format-sensitive); we use format-invariant concept-vector extraction, multiple relation types, and specificity controls. 4) Resource-distance is confounded with tokenizer fertility, script, and target frequency; we use partial correlations and matched targets, but residual confounds may remain. 5) Transplant could harm fluency or switch output language; specificity and off-target checks address this and we report the full tradeoff. 6) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM's less English-centric hub analyzed as a contrast expected to show weaker retrieval-failure dominance). 7) The human-LLM comparison (L1/L2 analogy asymmetry) is qualitative, not a claim of identical mechanism. 8) If the operator does NOT transfer cross-lingually (low alignment, transplant fails), the portability hypothesis is refuted—itself an informative result showing analogy operators are language-specific. Conversely, if failures are relation-encoding rather than retrieval failures, this relocates the cross-lingual analogy bottleneck and is equally valuable. 9) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: language_dependent_memory_span
Title: Fewer Slots in Some Tongues: A Language-Dependent Working-Memory Span Governs Multi-Hop Reasoning in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs have an effective working-memory span — how many intermediate items they can reliably hold and track across a reasoning chain — that is LANGUAGE-DEPENDENT: it is smaller when the model reasons in lower-resource / English-distant languages, so multi-hop and state-tracking failures in those languages arise from a reduced number of usable memory slots, not (only) from missing knowledge or wrong concepts. This span shrinkage is measurable as an earlier accuracy cliff as the number of items-to-track grows, is mechanistically driven by more dispersed (higher-entropy) attention over the to-be-retrieved items in those languages, and is causally attributable to attention-dispersion rather than resource level per se — predicting that sharpening the retrieval attention selectively restores span for low-span languages.
Related Work: Two literatures meet but have never been connected for multilingual reasoning. (1) Interpretability shows transformer self-attention imposes a working-memory capacity limit: N-back accuracy drops as N grows because attention over the N-back position disperses (higher entropy), mirroring human executive-attention limits (Self-Attention Limits Working Memory Capacity 2024; A Language Model with Limited Memory Capacity Captures Interference 2023), and agreement-attraction/interference reflects cue-based retrieval competition in attention (Causal Analysis of Syntactic Agreement Neurons 2022; Gender attraction in comprehension 2021). Human WM work shows L2 processing has reduced usable WM and higher retrieval interference (Interference Hypothesis; L2 gender/number agreement under WM load 2019-2024). (2) Multilingual reasoning work attributes low-resource failures to English-centric latent reasoning, premature commitment, or language-specific subspaces (Do Multilingual LLMs Think In English 2025; Large Reasoning Models Are Not Yet Multilingual Latent Reasoners 2026; Language-Specific Latent Process Hinders 2025; When Less Language is More 2025). CRITICALLY, all WM-capacity work is monolingual (English N-back) and never asks whether the capacity limit itself is LANGUAGE-DEPENDENT; all multilingual-reasoning work characterizes WHERE reasoning is routed or WHETHER it commits early, never framing the low-resource gap as a reduced number of trackable MEMORY SLOTS with an attention-dispersion cause. This is also distinct from my prior 'latent compute-depth gap' proposal (serial DEPTH / premature commitment) and 'effort setpoint' proposal (how much compute): span is a capacity/WIDTH axis — how many items can be held at once — orthogonal to depth and effort. We uniquely reframe the multilingual reasoning gap as a language-dependent working-memory-span limit with a measurable attention-dispersion mechanism and a targeted attention-sharpening fix.
Abstract: Solving a multi-step problem requires holding several intermediate results in mind at once; humans have a limited working-memory span, and recent interpretability work shows transformer self-attention imposes an analogous capacity limit that appears as an accuracy cliff on N-back tasks. We ask a simple, previously untested question about multilingual language models: is this working-memory span LANGUAGE-DEPENDENT? We hypothesize that when a model reasons in a lower-resource or English-distant language it has fewer usable memory slots — it can reliably track fewer intermediate items — so its multi-hop and state-tracking accuracy cliffs earlier than in English, and this span shrinkage, rather than missing knowledge, causes a substantial share of the low-resource reasoning gap. We further hypothesize the shrinkage is mechanistically driven by more dispersed (higher-entropy) attention over the to-be-retrieved items in those languages, and is causally attributable to attention-dispersion: sharpening the retrieval attention should selectively restore span for low-span languages. We test this on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using controlled load-parametric tasks — multilingual N-back, variable-binding/state-tracking, and k-item multi-hop reasoning where the number of items-to-track is dialed independently of difficulty — across typologically diverse languages. We measure per-language span (the load at which accuracy falls to chance), correlate it with attention-entropy over the retrieval positions, decompose failures into span-exceeded vs knowledge-absence via logit-lens item-tracking, and run a train-free attention-sharpening intervention. Metrics include per-language span, span-vs-attention-entropy correlation, span-exceeded error share, and selective span recovery with specificity controls.
Experiments:
1) Load-parametric multilingual suite: Build three families of tasks where the number of items to HOLD/TRACK (the memory load, L) is dialed independently of surface difficulty and knowledge: (a) N-back over sequences of symbols/words (N=1..5); (b) variable-binding/state-tracking (assign L variables values, apply updates, query a final value; L=1..6); (c) k-item multi-hop reasoning (chains where L intermediate results must be carried; L=1..6). All items have symbolic-oracle gold answers and use nonce/low-knowledge content to minimize reliance on world knowledge. Instantiate every item in typologically diverse languages spanning scripts and resource levels (English, French, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish, Bengali). Native-speaker verify templates; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Per-language span measurement (H1, core): For each language and task family, plot accuracy vs load L and estimate the SPAN = the load at which accuracy falls to a fixed threshold (e.g., halfway to chance). Test H1: span is smaller for lower-resource / English-distant languages, for the SAME tasks. Regress span on resource level and typological/embedding distance from English, controlling for tokenizer fertility (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2). Crucially, verify the effect is a WIDTH (load) effect, not a depth/length effect, by holding the number of serial steps fixed while varying L, and vice versa.
3) Attention-dispersion mechanism (H2): Following Self-Attention Limits Working Memory (2024), measure attention entropy over the to-be-retrieved item positions at the query/answer token, per language and load. Test whether (a) attention over the relevant items is more DISPERSED (higher entropy) in low-span languages at matched load, and (b) per-item attention concentration predicts per-item retrieval success. Correlate per-language span with per-language mean retrieval-attention entropy (Spearman; held-out R^2 over fertility/resource).
4) Span-exceeded vs knowledge-absence error decomposition: For items correct in English but wrong in language B, use logit-lens/tuned-lens to check whether the required intermediate items are latently PRESENT but not correctly retrieved/bound at the query (span-exceeded: the model held them but lost track under load) versus never formed (knowledge/computation absence). Also use activation patching: patch the retrieved-item representation from a low-load or English pass into the high-load B pass and test whether the answer is fixed. Report span-exceeded vs absence error shares per language and load, predicting span-exceeded errors dominate the low-resource gap at high load.
5) Core causal intervention — attention sharpening: Apply a train-free intervention that sharpens (lowers the entropy of) the retrieval attention over the relevant item positions at the query token (e.g., temperature-scaling / top-mass renormalization of the relevant heads' attention, identified via Exp 3). Predict SELECTIVE span recovery: accuracy at high load improves most for low-span (low-resource) languages and little for already-high-span languages (interaction test). Compute span-recovery elasticity = span gain per unit baseline attention-dispersion, correlated with the Exp-2 entropy gap. Compare against baselines: uniform English shared-space steering (Language-Specific Latent Process 2025), a generic attention-temperature change applied to all heads, and a random-head control.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify the intervention is span-specific (improves high-load items but not low-load items where span is not the bottleneck — a symmetric check), does not switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), preserves fluency, and does not harm English. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 shows a sharper per-language span drop than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether span-drop magnitude correlates with retrieval-attention entropy and each language's training share. Qualitatively compare the language-dependent span pattern against the human L2 reduced-WM / interference literature (direction, not identical mechanism).
Evaluation metrics: per-language span (load at accuracy threshold) and span drop vs English (partial correlation with resource/distance over fertility; held-out R^2); width-vs-depth dissociation; retrieval-attention entropy and its correlation with span (held-out R^2); span-exceeded vs knowledge-absence error shares and patching-fix rate; selective span recovery under attention sharpening with low-load preservation (symmetric specificity), recovery elasticity, off-target rate, English preservation; cross-model span-drop comparison and correlation with entropy and training share.
