Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) 'Span' estimated from an accuracy-vs-load curve is noisy and threshold-dependent; we use multiple thresholds, three task families, and report robustness. 2) Load (width) is hard to fully decouple from serial depth and from tokenizer fertility (more tokens per item inflates apparent load); the width-vs-depth dissociation (Exp 2) and fertility controls mitigate but may not fully remove confounds. 3) Span-exceeded vs knowledge-absence may not separate cleanly; we use nonce/low-knowledge content, logit-lens item-tracking, and patching, and report ambiguous cases. 4) Attention entropy over 'relevant item positions' requires identifying those positions and heads; we use multiple head-selection methods and report sensitivity. 5) The attention-sharpening intervention could harm fluency, over-concentrate attention, or help all loads uniformly (not selectively); we require the low-load-preservation symmetric check and a selective (interaction) gain, and report the full tradeoff. 6) Language is confounded with script and resource level; partial correlations and the cross-model contrast help, but residual confounds remain. 7) The human L2-WM comparison is qualitative, not a claim of identical mechanism. 8) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM's less English-centric hub analyzed as a contrast expected to show a smaller span drop). 9) If span is equal across languages once fertility is controlled, this is an informative POSITIVE result showing working-memory capacity is language-agnostic and relocating the multilingual reasoning gap to knowledge/routing rather than memory-width — valuable either way. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: language_warped_number_line
Title: A Language-Warped Mental Number Line: Query Language Bends the Log-Compression of the Shared Magnitude Representation in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs encode numeric magnitude on a shared, sublinear (log-compressed) 'mental number line', but the CURVATURE of that line — how much resolution is allocated to which magnitude range — is LANGUAGE-DEPENDENT: querying the same number in a lower-resource / English-distant language yields a more compressed (steeper log) representation with coarser resolution, producing measurably worse magnitude-comparison acuity (larger distance/ratio-effect Weber fractions) for the SAME numbers. This warp is carried by a shared magnitude direction whose scaling is modulated by an early language signal, and is causally correctable by rescaling that direction toward the English-calibrated curvature without changing the number's identity.
Related Work: Interpretability robustly shows LLMs encode numeric magnitude in structured, largely language-agnostic subspaces: sublinear/logarithmic 'mental number line' compression detectable by PCA (Number Representations as Computational Parallel to Human Perception 2025; Internal Numeracy in ALBERT 2024), low-dimensional MONOTONIC and causally-editable numeric-property directions (Monotonic Representation of Numeric Properties 2024; Geometry of Numerical Reasoning 2024; The Representational Geometry of Number 2026), and linearly-encoded log-magnitudes that models fail to fully verbalize (LLMs Know More About Numbers than They Can Say 2026). The Semantic Hub Hypothesis (2024) establishes a shared, English-scaffolded magnitude space (arithmetic included). Human cognitive science shows number-magnitude processing carries language-of-learning imprints: Basque base-20 vs base-10 gamma synchronization in magnitude comparison (Oscillatory Brain Activity 2015), Chinese-German ANS speed differences (2017), and cross-cultural exact-number effects (Frank 2012). CRITICALLY, every LLM number-representation paper treats the log-compressed magnitude line as a SINGLE, language-agnostic geometry and never asks whether its CURVATURE / resolution is modulated by the QUERY LANGUAGE, whether this warps cross-lingual magnitude-comparison acuity (distance/ratio effects) on the SAME numbers, or whether rescaling a shared magnitude direction can equalize acuity across languages. This is orthogonal to my prior number proposals (units-tens inversion order; vigesimal base composition), which concern transcoding number WORDS, not the geometry/resolution of the underlying magnitude line as a function of query language.
Abstract: Humans represent number on a compressed 'mental number line' where small values get finer resolution than large ones, and this compression carries traces of the language in which one learned to count. Interpretability work shows multilingual language models likewise encode numeric magnitude on a shared, sublinear (log-compressed) line and use it causally for numerical reasoning. But every study treats this line as a single, language-agnostic geometry. We ask a simple, previously untested question: does the QUERY LANGUAGE bend the curvature of the model's mental number line? We hypothesize that querying the same numbers in a lower-resource, English-distant language yields a more compressed magnitude representation with coarser resolution, and that this internal warp produces measurably worse magnitude-comparison acuity — larger distance- and ratio-effect Weber fractions — on identical number pairs, mirroring the language-of-learning imprints seen in human bilinguals. We further hypothesize the warp is carried by a shared magnitude direction whose scaling is set by an early language signal, so rescaling that direction toward the English-calibrated curvature causally equalizes acuity across languages without changing which number is represented. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM across typologically diverse languages, using magnitude-comparison tasks over matched numbers presented as spelled-out words and (as a language-agnostic control) Arabic digits. Combining PCA/probe recovery of the magnitude line, behavioral distance/ratio acuity measures, activation patching, and steering, we measure per-language curvature, curvature-vs-acuity coupling, and steering-induced acuity equalization with specificity controls. Metrics include per-language log-compression rate, Weber-fraction acuity gaps, curvature-acuity correlation, and rescaling-induced recovery.
Experiments: 1) Magnitude-comparison suite: For integers spanning several orders of magnitude (e.g., 1–9999), build matched pairwise magnitude-comparison items ('Which is larger, A or B?') with controlled numeric distance and ratio between A and B, presented (a) as SPELLED-OUT number words in typologically diverse languages spanning scripts and resource levels (English, French, German, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish) and (b) as Arabic-DIGIT forms as a shared, language-agnostic anchor. Native-speaker verify number words. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B. 2) Per-language mental-number-line curvature (H1): At the number token position, recover the magnitude representation per language using PCA (unsupervised, following Number Representations as Computational Parallel 2025) and a monotonic-subspace probe (following Monotonic Representation 2024). Fit a geometric/log regression to obtain a per-language Scaling Rate Index (β, log-compression steepness) and resolution (embedding distance per unit magnitude) across layers. Test H1: lower-resource / English-distant languages show more compression (lower β / steeper log) and coarser resolution than English for the SAME numbers, while the digit-anchor form shows the least language-dependence. Control for tokenizer fertility and number-word frequency (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test query language adds predictive power beyond fertility/frequency). 3) Behavioral acuity and curvature-acuity coupling (H2, core): Measure per-language comparison accuracy and log-prob margin as a function of numeric distance and ratio, extracting distance/ratio-effect slopes and a Weber-fraction-like acuity per language. Test that (a) acuity is worse (larger Weber fraction, steeper distance effect) in the languages with more compressed lines, on identical number pairs, and (b) per-language internal curvature (β/resolution from Exp 2) predicts per-language behavioral acuity (Spearman; held-out R^2). Verify the digit-anchor form shows the smallest cross-lingual acuity gap. 4) Early language-signal timing: Extract a language-identity signal and test, via position-resolved logit-lens across layers, whether the curvature is set early (the magnitude line's compression correlates with the query-language signal before the comparison is computed). Measure cross-lingual alignment of the magnitude direction (a single shared axis re-scaled per language vs distinct axes). 5) Causal steering test (H3, core): Extract the shared magnitude direction (difference-in-means / monotonic subspace) and apply a per-language RESCALING along it that maps a low-resource-language number's position onto the English-calibrated curvature (de-compressing the line), holding the number's identity fixed. Measure whether magnitude-comparison acuity improves toward English (acuity-recovery rate), and, conversely, whether over-compressing English induces worse acuity (bidirectional dose-response control). Complement with activation patching: patch the English magnitude representation of the same number into the low-resource pass and test acuity recovery. Compare against baselines: whole-hub English-steering (Semantic Hub 2024), a random-direction control, and the digit-form ceiling. 6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify steering is magnitude-specific (changes comparison acuity/resolution but does NOT change which number is represented — the model must still correctly identify the value; and it must not alter parity/identity directions) and does not switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 shows larger per-language curvature gaps than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether curvature-gap magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the magnitude direction and with each language's training share. Qualitatively compare the LLM language-dependent-acuity pattern against the human bilingual number-magnitude literature (direction, not identical mechanism). Evaluation metrics: per-language log-compression β and resolution (word-form vs digit-anchor); Weber-fraction / distance-effect acuity gaps; curvature-vs-acuity correlation (held-out R^2 over fertility/frequency); early-timing language-signal predictiveness of curvature; magnitude-direction cross-lingual alignment; steering acuity-recovery rate and bidirectional dose-response; patching-induced recovery; number-identity preservation (value still correctly read), off-target rate; cross-model curvature-gap comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Curvature (β) estimates from PCA/probes are noisy and layer-dependent; we use multiple recovery methods (unsupervised PCA, monotonic-subspace probe, log-regression), report across layers, and cross-validate. 2) Query language is confounded with tokenizer fertility, number-word length, script, and frequency; the digit-anchor form (language-agnostic) and partial correlations isolate the curvature pathway, but residual confounds may remain — the digit anchor is the key control, and we emphasize the word-form-vs-digit contrast. 3) Behavioral acuity differences could reflect general comprehension gaps rather than magnitude-resolution differences; the curvature-acuity coupling (Exp 3) and the causal rescaling test (Exp 5, which recovers acuity by editing only the magnitude direction) distinguish a genuine geometry warp from generic incompetence. 4) The shared magnitude direction from difference-in-means may entangle identity/parity features; we use the monotonic-subspace method as an anchor, and require number-identity preservation as a hard specificity check. 5) Steering could harm fluency or corrupt the number's value; we require value preservation and bidirectional dose-response and report the full tradeoff. 6) Early-timing (curvature set before comparison) is hard to establish since language and number co-occur; we use position-resolved lenses and report it as suggestive. 7) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM's less English-centric hub analyzed as a contrast expected to show smaller gaps). 8) The human-LLM comparison is qualitative, not a claim of identical mechanism. 9) If NO curvature warp is found — the mental number line has the same compression and acuity across languages once the digit anchor is controlled — this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the magnitude representation is genuinely language-agnostic in geometry, valuable either way. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: emotion_colexification_imposition
Title: Feeling in Someone Else's Words: Does the English-Scaffolded Emotional Manifold Impose English's Emotion Partition onto Colexifying Languages?
Short Hypothesis: Languages carve the emotion space differently: many colexify emotions English keeps distinct (e.g., one word spanning 'anger' and 'grief', or 'shame' and 'fear'), and vice versa. Because the shared emotional manifold of multilingual LLMs is scaffolded by English, we hypothesize it IMPOSES English's emotion partition onto other languages: when inferring the emotion of a text in a language that colexifies (or splits) emotions differently from English, the model tracks the ENGLISH emotion boundaries rather than the target-language ones, producing systematic cross-lingual inconsistency in emotion inference that is predictable from each language's empirical colexification network, mediated by a shared emotion-appraisal direction, and causally correctable by steering toward the target-language emotion partition without harming valence/arousal reading.
Related Work: Interpretability work shows LLMs hold a low-dimensional, directionally-encoded emotional manifold that generalizes across languages (Emotions Where Art Thou 2025; Decoding Emotion in the Deep 2025), that emotion inference is localized to mid-layers and aligns with cognitive appraisal theory with steerable appraisal concepts (Mechanistic Interpretability of Emotion Inference 2025), and that a shared, English-scaffolded semantic hub underlies cross-lingual processing (Semantic Hub 2024; Cross-Layer Transcoders 2025; Geometry of Multilingual Representations 2022). Behaviorally, multilingual LMs are Anglocentric/Western in emotion and 'not multicultural' (Multilingual LMs are not Multicultural 2023; Paradox of Multilingual Emotion Detection 2023). Cognitive science establishes via colexification across 2474 languages that emotion semantics show BOTH universal structure (valence, arousal) AND culture-specific variation in which emotions are lexically conflated (Emotion semantics show cultural variation and universal structure, Jackson et al. 2019). CRITICALLY, all LLM emotion-interpretability work treats the emotional manifold as uniformly universal and never asks whether its category BOUNDARIES are English-scaffolded; all multilingual-emotion work is behavioral/benchmark and never mechanistic. NO prior work asks whether the shared manifold IMPOSES English's emotion partition onto languages that colexify emotions differently, whether cross-lingual emotion-inference inconsistency is predictable from colexification networks, whether a shared appraisal/emotion direction mediates it, or whether steering toward the target-language partition corrects it. Unlike my prior grammatical/lexical/conceptual imposition proposals, this targets the EMOTION-CATEGORY partition, grounded in an authoritative cross-linguistic colexification database, distinct from all of them.
Abstract: Emotions feel universal, yet languages disagree on where one emotion ends and another begins: cross-linguistic research shows many languages colexify emotions English keeps distinct (a single word covering both anger and grief, or shame and fear) while carving others more finely, even as valence and arousal remain universal. Multilingual language models build a shared, largely English-scaffolded emotional manifold. We ask a simple, previously untested question: does that manifold IMPOSE English's emotion partition when the model infers emotions from text in a language that colexifies differently? We hypothesize that (1) the model tracks English emotion boundaries rather than the target-language ones, producing cross-lingual inconsistency in emotion inference concentrated on emotion pairs the target language conflates or splits differently; (2) the magnitude of this imposition is predictable from each language's empirical colexification network; (3) a shared emotion/appraisal direction mediates the imposition, with any residual target-language partition living in shallow, language-specific layers; and (4) steering toward the target-language partition corrects the imposition while preserving universal valence/arousal reading. We build a controlled multilingual emotion-inference suite over emotion pairs that are colexified vs distinguished across typologically diverse languages, grounded in colexification data and native-speaker verification, on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5 and BLOOM. Using difference-in-means emotion-direction probes, logit-lens depth tracking, activation patching and steering, we measure the imposition, its colexification-predicted scaling, its mediation, and its causal correction. Metrics include cross-lingual emotion-inference inconsistency gap, colexification-prediction correlation, mediation R-squared, and steering-induced correction with valence/arousal-preservation controls.
Experiments: 1) Colexification-grounded emotion suite: Using the colexification networks from Jackson et al. (2019) and native-speaker verification, select emotion pairs that are COLEXIFIED (conflated by a single word) in some target languages but DISTINGUISHED in English (e.g., anger/grief, shame/fear, envy/jealousy, pity/love), and matched pairs distinguished by both. Build ~500 short emotion-eliciting scenarios/utterances whose intended emotion is one member of a critical pair, verified per language. Instantiate across typologically diverse languages spanning colexification profiles and resource levels (English, Spanish, Russian, Chinese, Hindi, Arabic, Turkish, plus a language with documented divergent colexification such as Persian dishearten-regret or a Nakh-Daghestanian anger-envy pattern where data permit). Tasks: (i) forced-choice emotion labeling among the critical-pair options; (ii) emotion-NLI (does the text express emotion A, B, both/neither?); (iii) similarity judgment (how similar are emotions A and B?); (iv) generation (paraphrase the felt emotion). Also collect valence/arousal ratings per item as a universal-dimension control. Native-speaker verify labels and colexification codings; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B. 2) Behavioral imposition (H1, core): For CRITICAL pairs, measure whether the model's emotion inference in the target language tracks the ENGLISH partition (distinguishing A from B) rather than the target-language partition (which may conflate them, or split them where English does not). Define the cross-lingual emotion-inconsistency GAP = inconsistency on colexification-DIVERGENT pairs minus inconsistency on colexification-CONVERGENT pairs (both languages agree). Predict a positive gap: divergence in emotion partition, not mere language change, drives extra inconsistency. Control for tokenizer fertility, emotion-word frequency, and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2). Verify valence/arousal judgments remain consistent across languages (universal-dimension preservation) even where categorical labels diverge. 3) Colexification-predicted scaling (H2, external validation): Using each language's colexification-network distance from English's emotion partition, test whether per-language, per-pair imposition is predicted by colexification proximity/divergence (Spearman correlation; held-out prediction of imposition from the colexification network alone), tying the internal phenomenon to authoritative cross-linguistic ground truth. 4) Representational localization (H3): Extract emotion-category directions via difference-in-means between the two members of each critical pair at each layer, per language (building on the emotional-manifold and appraisal-direction findings). Test (a) whether a shared emotion partition is English-scaffolded (cross-lingual cosine alignment of category boundaries, aligned with English), and (b) whether a target-language input for a locally-colexified pair projects onto the ENGLISH-distinguished boundary in the shared mid-layers while any residual target-language conflation signal is stronger in early/language-specific layers, via logit-lens depth tracking. Baseline: the valence/arousal direction (universal) as a within-model control that should NOT show imposition. Mediation: regress behavioral imposition on shared-manifold boundary-projection strength (partial correlation controlling for fertility/frequency; held-out R^2). 5) Causal steering/patching test (H4, core): (a) Steer the target-language input along the emotion-category direction toward the target-language partition (e.g., collapse the A/B boundary where the language colexifies them) and measure whether inference shifts to the target-language pattern (flip rate) and the inconsistency GAP shrinks toward the convergent baseline, without switching output language. (b) For imposed items, patch the residual language-specific emotion signal (from early/language-specific layers) into later computation and test restoration, localizing failure to the shared manifold overwriting a shallowly-present target partition. Critically verify VALENCE/AROUSAL preservation (the universal dimensions must remain correct) plus fluency and off-target/language-mixing checks. Baselines: whole-manifold English-steering, random-direction control. 6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify steering is emotion-partition-specific (changes categorical inference but not valence/arousal or unrelated content), graded (imposition scales with colexification divergence), and not a lexical-frequency artifact. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 shows stronger imposition than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether imposition magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the emotion direction and with each language's training share. Qualitatively compare the model's per-language imposition pattern against the human colexification network structure. Evaluation metrics: cross-lingual emotion-inconsistency GAP (divergent minus convergent pairs; English-partition-tracking rate); imposition-vs-colexification-network correlation and held-out prediction; valence/arousal cross-lingual preservation (universal-dimension control); shared-manifold boundary-projection strength and crystallization depth (vs valence/arousal baseline); cross-lingual emotion-direction alignment; mediation regression (held-out R^2); steering flip rate and GAP reduction, patching-induced restoration; valence/arousal preservation, fluency, off-target rate; cross-model imposition comparison and correlation with training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for colexification-divergence over frequency/fertility/resource baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Coding which emotion pairs a language colexifies is subtle and gradient (colexification is a matter of degree and register); we ground codings in the Jackson et al. (2019) colexification database with native-speaker verification, use a graded divergence score, report inter-annotator agreement, and restrict CRITICAL pairs to clear cross-lingual contrasts, treating mixed cases separately. 2) Colexification divergence is correlated with language family, script, and resource level; the CONVERGENT controls, the valence/arousal universal-dimension control, within-pair contrasts, and colexification-network prediction isolate the emotion-partition pathway, but residual confounds may remain; low-resource divergent languages may confound imposition with sparse training, so we center the core study on well-resourced languages with documented divergent colexification and treat rarer cases as extensions. 3) Emotion labels are inherently noisy and annotator-dependent; we use forced-choice, NLI, and similarity tasks jointly and report reliability. 4) Difference-in-means emotion-category directions may entangle valence/arousal or lexical features; we use the valence/arousal control direction, multiple extraction methods, and specificity checks. 5) Logit-lens/tuned-lens depth estimates are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 6) Some cross-lingual inconsistency may reflect genuine, correct cultural differences in emotion appraisal (the model tracking the target culture) rather than English imposition; the direction of the effect (does it track ENGLISH or the TARGET partition?) and the colexification-network prediction are designed to distinguish imposition from culturally-faithful inference, and a finding of culturally-faithful inference is itself valuable. 7) Steering could harm valence/arousal reading or fluency; we require universal-dimension preservation and report the full tradeoff. 8) Instruction-tuned models may hedge on emotion labels; we test base models where available and use both forced-choice and NLI probes. 9) The human-LLM comparison (colexification structure) is qualitative, not a claim of identical mechanism. 10) If NO imposition is found - emotion inference tracks each language's own partition, predictable from colexification, with universal valence/arousal preserved - this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the emotional manifold represents culture-specific emotion boundaries despite English scaffolding, valuable either way. 11) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: harm_gating_decoupling_multilingual
Title: Detected but Not Refused: Cross-Lingual Safety Failures Are a Harm-to-Refusal Gating Failure, Not a Harm-Detection Failure
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual safety failures in lower-resource languages are not primarily caused by the model failing to RECOGNIZE that a prompt is harmful, but by a failure to ROUTE that (correctly computed) harm signal into the refusal circuit. We hypothesize a mechanistic decoupling: the shared hub still linearly encodes 'this prompt is harmful' with near-English fidelity even in languages where the model complies, but a language-specific gating step fails to convert that harm representation into activation of the refusal direction. Consequently, cross-lingual jailbreak susceptibility is predicted by gating strength (how well the harm signal drives the refusal direction), not by harm-detection accuracy, and can be causally restored by re-coupling the two without retraining.
Related Work: Refusal is mediated by a single direction (Arditi et al. 2024) that is largely universal across safety-aligned languages (Refusal Direction is Universal 2025), and shared safety neurons bridge cross-lingual transfer (SS-Neurons 2026; Soteria 2025). The Hidden Space of Safety (2025) shows alignment separates harmful/harmless representations well in English but weakly in other languages, and The Illusion of Cross-Lingual Safety (2026) reports harmful prompts retain <10% of the English refusal signal in low-resource languages while noting models 'encode the concepts without routing them to safety mechanisms.' All prior work either (a) treats the failure as a single collapsed quantity (refusal-signal strength / representation separation) or (b) fixes it by adding data/neurons/parameters. NONE decomposes the failure into two separable stages — a language-agnostic HARM-DETECTION representation vs. a language-specific GATING step that couples harm detection to the refusal direction — nor tests the specific claim that harm is still correctly detected while gating fails, nor offers a causal re-coupling intervention that operates on the gating step rather than on the detection representation or on data. We reframe the observation 'concepts encoded but not routed' from a passing remark into a precise, testable two-stage mechanism with a predictive gating metric and a targeted fix.
Abstract: Large language models refuse harmful requests reliably in English but comply with the same requests in lower-resource languages, and this cross-lingual safety gap is a major deployment risk. Prevailing accounts treat it as a single failure of the refusal signal or of harmful/harmless representation separation, and remedy it by adding multilingual safety data or tuning safety neurons. We propose a sharper mechanistic account: cross-lingual safety failure is a two-stage decoupling. Stage one, HARM DETECTION, computes a largely language-agnostic 'this is harmful' representation in the shared hub; stage two, GATING, converts that representation into activation of the refusal direction. We hypothesize that in languages where the model complies, harm is still detected with near-English fidelity, but gating fails — the harm signal never drives the refusal direction. This predicts that (1) a harm probe trained on English internal states transfers and correctly classifies harmful prompts even in complied-with languages; (2) per-language jailbreak susceptibility is predicted by a gating-strength metric (the coupling between the harm representation and the refusal direction), not by harm-detection accuracy; and (3) causally re-coupling the two — steering the refusal direction in proportion to the detected harm at the gating layer — restores refusal without retraining and without harming benign compliance. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM across high-, mid-, and low-resource languages using PolyRefuse/MultiJail-style parallel harmful/benign prompts, combining linear harm probes, refusal-direction extraction, activation patching, and gating-restoration steering. Metrics include cross-lingual harm-probe accuracy, gating-strength vs. attack-success correlation, and re-coupling-induced refusal recovery with over-refusal controls.
Experiments:
1) Parallel harmful/benign multilingual suite: Use/extend PolyRefuse and MultiJail (translated harmful and benign prompts) across high- (English, French), mid- (Chinese, Hindi), and low-resource (Swahili, Amharic, Hausa) languages, native-speaker-verified, plus a benign-but-superficially-alarming control set to test over-refusal. Models: Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, BLOOM(Z)-7B. Record per-language attack-success rate (compliance on harmful prompts) as the behavioral target.
2) Harm-detection stage (H1): Train a linear harm probe (harmful vs benign) on English internal states at each layer, and test its cross-lingual transfer accuracy on the OTHER languages — crucially restricted to harmful prompts the model actually COMPLIES with. Prediction: harm-probe accuracy stays high (near-English) even in complied-with languages, showing harm is detected. Compare probe accuracy against behavioral refusal per language (they should dissociate). Control for tokenizer fertility and resource level (partial correlations).
3) Refusal-direction and gating-strength (H2, core): Extract the refusal direction per model via difference-in-means (Arditi et al.). Define gating-strength for language L = the degree to which the harm representation (probe direction / harmful-minus-benign mean) projects onto and drives the refusal direction at the gating layer (e.g., regression coefficient of refusal-direction activation on harm-probe score across prompts, per language). Test whether per-language gating-strength predicts attack-success rate BETTER than harm-detection accuracy does (nested regression, AIC, held-out R^2). Prediction: gating-strength is the dominant predictor; detection accuracy adds little.
4) Stage-localization via activation patching: For harmful prompts complied-with in language B but refused in English, patch (a) the harm-detection representation from the English pass into B, and (b) the gating-layer components that couple harm to the refusal direction. If (a) rarely changes behavior (harm already present in B) but (b) restores refusal, the failure is localized to gating, not detection. Report the share of gating- vs detection-failures per language.
5) Core causal intervention — gating re-coupling: At the gating layer, add a steering vector along the refusal direction with magnitude proportional to the per-prompt harm-probe score (i.e., re-connect detection to refusal), train-free. Measure attack-success reduction per language. Compare against baselines: uniform refusal-direction addition (Refusal Direction Universal 2025), SS-Neuron reinforcement (2026), and a random-direction control. Compute recovery elasticity = refusal gain per unit baseline gating deficit, correlated with the H2 gating-strength.
6) Specificity / over-refusal controls: Verify re-coupling is harm-gated (it must NOT increase refusal on benign or benign-but-alarming prompts — a hard symmetric constraint), does not switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), and preserves general capability (MMLU/MT quality). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 shows a larger detection-vs-gating gap than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether the gap correlates with each language's safety-training share.
Evaluation metrics: cross-lingual harm-probe accuracy on complied-with prompts (detection intact?); gating-strength vs attack-success correlation and held-out R^2 (vs detection-accuracy baseline); gating- vs detection-failure error shares from patching; re-coupling attack-success reduction and recovery elasticity vs baselines; over-refusal rate on benign/alarming controls (symmetric specificity); off-target rate; general-capability preservation; cross-model gap comparison and correlation with safety-training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Detection and gating may not separate cleanly; patching can have entangled effects. Mitigation: multiple patching granularities, report ambiguous cases, and use the symmetric over-refusal control to confirm we isolate gating rather than a generic refusal-shift. 2) A harm probe may exploit surface lexical cues rather than genuine harm representation; we use benign-but-alarming controls, paraphrases, and test transfer to held-out harm categories. 3) The gating-strength metric relies on the extracted refusal direction and probe direction, which are approximate; we cross-validate with multiple extraction methods. 4) In genuinely under-trained low-resource languages, harm detection may ALSO fail (not just gating) — the detection-probe test (Exp 2) is precisely designed to distinguish these two regimes, and finding detection failure in some languages is itself informative (it would relocate the fix to detection). 5) Re-coupling could over-refuse; the benign/alarming symmetric constraint is a hard requirement and we report the full tradeoff. 6) This is dual-use safety research; all interventions here strengthen refusal (defensive) — we release the harm suite and probes under controlled access and do not publish jailbreak-enhancing directions. 7) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM analyzed as a contrast). 8) If gating-strength does NOT predict attack-success better than detection accuracy, the two-stage hypothesis is refuted — an informative result showing cross-lingual safety failure is genuinely a detection problem. 9) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: punctuation_prosody_imposition
Title: The Comma Means Something Different in Russian: Does the English-Scaffolded Shared Hub Impose English Punctuation-Prosody Conventions Cross-Lingually?
Short Hypothesis: Punctuation is written prosody, and languages load it differently: an English comma is a light optional pause carrying weak segmentation/emphasis, whereas a Russian, Greek, or Chinese comma is grammatically obligatory and marks strong clause boundaries and semantic emphasis. Because multilingual LLMs summarize clause meaning onto punctuation tokens in a largely English-scaffolded shared hub, we hypothesize the model IMPOSES English's weak punctuation-prosody weighting onto languages where punctuation is grammatically and prosodically heavier: it under-reads the clause-boundary/emphasis information a comma or other mark carries in those languages, producing measurable cross-lingual inconsistency in segmentation, emphasis, and disambiguation judgments that hinge on punctuation. This imposition is mediated by a shared 'punctuation-weight' direction on the mark token, tracks each language's empirical punctuation-prosody load, and is causally correctable by amplifying the mark's summarization signal without harming lexical comprehension.
Related Work: Interpretability shows punctuation tokens are attention sinks and 'summarization points' where clause-level information (sentiment, truth value) is aggregated (Language Models Linearly Represent Sentiment 2024; Geometry of Truth 2023; LLM-Microscope 2025; Punctuation and Predicates 2025), that this summarization is model- and layer-specific, and that intermediate representations are English-centric even for non-English input (LLM-Microscope 2025; Do Multilingual LLMs Think In English 2025; Transfer Neurons 2025). Separately, a linguistics literature establishes that punctuation IS written prosody and that its grammatical obligatoriness and prosodic load differ sharply across languages: obligatory syntactic commas in Russian and Greek vs. optional/rhetorical commas in English (Punctuation in English and Russian 2024; Text punctuation and prosody in Greek 2019; Prosodic Principle in Punctuation 2023; Suprasegmental Characteristics of Punctuation Marks 2023). CRITICALLY, all interpretability work on punctuation-as-summarization is monolingual/English and treats the mark as a uniform aggregator; all cross-lingual punctuation-prosody work is behavioral/linguistic, never touching model internals. NO prior work asks whether the English-scaffolded shared hub, where clause meaning is summarized onto punctuation, IMPOSES English's weak punctuation weighting onto languages where punctuation is grammatically/prosodically heavier, causing the model to under-read a mark's segmentation/emphasis meaning; none localizes a shared punctuation-weight direction, ties imposition to each language's punctuation-prosody typology, or offers a causal fix. This is orthogonal to all my prior imposition/flattening proposals (tense, gender, evidentiality, honorifics, spatial frames, number, telicity, negation, etc.), which target lexical/grammatical categories, never the punctuation-as-written-prosody axis.
Abstract: Punctuation is written prosody: a comma tells the reader where to break and what to emphasize. But languages weight punctuation very differently. An English comma is largely optional and rhetorical, while a Russian or Greek comma is grammatically obligatory and marks a strong clause boundary, and a Chinese comma segments in ways English never would. Interpretability work shows multilingual language models summarize clause-level meaning onto punctuation tokens in a largely English-scaffolded shared representation. We ask a simple, previously untested question this asymmetry makes urgent: does that shared hub IMPOSE English's weak punctuation-prosody weighting onto languages where punctuation carries heavier grammatical and prosodic load, so the model under-reads the segmentation and emphasis a mark conveys in those languages? We hypothesize that (1) the model's punctuation-dependent judgments (clause segmentation, emphasis/focus, and punctuation-based disambiguation) track the ENGLISH punctuation weighting rather than the target language's, producing cross-lingual inconsistency concentrated on marks whose load diverges from English; (2) this imposition tracks each language's empirical punctuation-prosody typology; (3) a shared 'punctuation-weight' direction on the mark token mediates it, with any residual target-language weighting living in shallow, language-specific layers; and (4) amplifying the mark's summarization signal restores target-language-faithful reading without harming lexical comprehension. We build a controlled multilingual suite of minimal pairs whose meaning hinges on a punctuation mark, across languages spanning punctuation load (English, Russian, Greek, German, Chinese, Spanish), on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM. Using difference-in-means punctuation-weight probes, logit-lens summarization tracking, activation patching, and steering, we measure the imposition, its typology scaling, its mediation, and its causal correction. Metrics include cross-lingual punctuation-inconsistency gap, typology-prediction correlation, mark-summarization strength, mediation R-squared, and steering-induced restoration with lexical-competence controls.
Experiments:
1) Punctuation-hinged minimal-pair suite: Construct ~500 controlled sentence pairs whose meaning or structure hinges on a punctuation mark, across languages spanning punctuation-prosody load: heavy/obligatory (Russian, Greek, German, Chinese) vs light/rhetorical (English, Spanish). Item types: (a) SEGMENTATION pairs where a comma changes clause attachment or scope (classic 'let's eat, grandma' style, but grounded in each language's real punctuation grammar); (b) EMPHASIS/FOCUS pairs where a mark shifts which constituent is emphasized; (c) OBLIGATORY-MARK pairs where a comma is grammatically required in the heavy language but optional/absent in the English translation, and removing it changes acceptability/meaning; (d) matched no-mark controls. Each item has native-speaker-verified gold readings and a probe question (segmentation/attachment, emphasis, or acceptability). Native-speaker verify punctuation grammar and gold labels; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral imposition (H1, core): Measure whether the model's punctuation-dependent judgments in a heavy-load language track the ENGLISH weighting (treating a heavy-load comma as a weak optional pause) rather than the target-language weighting. Define the cross-lingual punctuation-inconsistency GAP = inconsistency on DIVERGENT-load marks (heavy in target, light in English) minus inconsistency on CONVERGENT marks (similar load across languages). Predict a positive gap: punctuation-load divergence, not mere language change, drives extra inconsistency. Verify near-zero effect on no-mark controls and correct reading in English (ceiling). Control for tokenizer fertility and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test punctuation-load status adds predictive power).
3) Typology-predicted imposition (H2, external validation): Using the linguistics literature on per-language punctuation obligatoriness / prosodic load (e.g., pause-duration ranking question>exclamation>full stop>colon>comma; obligatory vs optional comma status), assign each language/mark a load score and test whether per-language, per-mark imposition is predicted by that score (Spearman correlation; held-out prediction of imposition from typology alone), tying the internal phenomenon to independent linguistic ground truth.
4) Representational localization (H3): At the punctuation-mark token position, extract a 'punctuation-weight' summarization direction via difference-in-means between representations where the mark carries a strong clause-boundary/emphasis reading vs a weak/optional one, at each layer, per language (building on the summarization-motif and truth/sentiment-on-punctuation findings). Test (a) whether a shared punctuation-summarization direction is English-scaffolded (cross-lingual cosine alignment across layers, aligned with the English weak-weighting pole); (b) whether a heavy-load mark in the target language projects onto the WEAK (English) pole in the shared hub while any residual heavy-weighting signal is stronger in early/language-specific layers, via logit-lens/tuned-lens tracking of how much clause information is summarized onto the mark. Baseline: a lexical-content direction as a within-model control. Mediation: regress behavioral imposition on shared-hub mark-summarization strength (partial correlation controlling for fertility/resource; held-out R^2).
5) Causal steering/patching test (H4, core): (a) Amplify the mark's summarization signal / steer it toward the heavy (target-language) weighting pole and measure whether segmentation/emphasis judgments flip to the target-language reading (flip rate) and the inconsistency GAP shrinks toward the convergent baseline, without switching output language. (b) For imposed items, patch the residual language-specific punctuation signal (from early/language-specific layers) into later computation and test restoration, localizing failure to the shared hub imposing English weighting over a shallowly-present target-language signal. Critically verify LEXICAL COMPREHENSION preservation (the model must still answer content questions about the sentence correctly), plus fluency and off-target/language-mixing checks. Baselines: whole-hub English-steering, random-direction control.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify steering is punctuation-specific (changes mark-driven segmentation/emphasis but not lexical content or unrelated attributes), graded (imposition scales with punctuation-load divergence), and not merely a tokenizer artifact (test both attached and separate punctuation tokenization). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 shows stronger imposition than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether imposition magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the punctuation-weight direction and with each language's training share. Qualitatively compare the model's per-language imposition pattern against the punctuation-prosody typology.
Evaluation metrics: cross-lingual punctuation-inconsistency GAP (divergent minus convergent marks; English-weighting-tracking rate); imposition-vs-punctuation-load-typology correlation and held-out prediction; shared-hub mark-summarization strength and its crystallization/depth (vs lexical-content baseline); cross-lingual punctuation-weight-direction alignment; mediation regression (held-out R^2); steering flip rate and GAP reduction, patching-induced restoration; lexical-comprehension preservation, fluency, off-target rate; cross-model imposition comparison and correlation with training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for punctuation-load over fertility/resource baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Coding each language/mark's punctuation-prosody load is subtle and gradient (obligatoriness varies by construction and register); we ground codings in the punctuation-linguistics literature with native-speaker verification, use a graded load score, report inter-annotator agreement, and restrict DIVERGENT items to clear cross-lingual contrasts, treating mixed cases separately. 2) Punctuation load is correlated with language family, script (logographic Chinese), and resource level; the CONVERGENT controls, no-mark controls, English-translation contrasts, within-language mark-present-vs-absent contrasts, and typology-based prediction isolate the punctuation pathway, but residual confounds may remain. 3) Tokenization of punctuation differs across models/scripts (attached vs standalone mark tokens), which could confound the summarization measurement; we test both tokenization regimes, control for fertility, and treat script contrasts as informative. 4) Difference-in-means punctuation-weight directions may entangle lexical or positional features; we use multiple extraction methods, a lexical-content control direction, and specificity checks. 5) Logit-lens/tuned-lens summarization estimates are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation and multiple lenses. 6) Some cross-lingual inconsistency may reflect genuine correct handling (the model rightly treating an English comma as optional); the direction of the effect (does it track ENGLISH or the TARGET weighting?), the no-mark controls, and the typology prediction are designed to distinguish imposition from correct language-specific reading, and a finding of correct reading is itself valuable. 7) Steering could harm fluency or lexical comprehension; we require lexical-comprehension preservation and report the full tradeoff. 8) Instruction-tuned models may normalize punctuation; we test base models where available and interpret small effects as informative. 9) The model-vs-typology comparison is qualitative, not a claim of identical mechanism. 10) If NO imposition is found - punctuation-dependent judgments track each language's own load, predictable from typology, with lexical comprehension preserved - this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the shared hub represents language-specific punctuation weighting despite English scaffolding, valuable either way. 11) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: digraphic_script_divergence
Title: Same Language, Two Scripts, Two Answers: Script as a Hidden Variable in Multilingual LLM Knowledge and Reasoning
Short Hypothesis: Digraphic languages—the same language written in two scripts (Serbian in Cyrillic vs Latin, Hindi/Urdu, Kazakh Cyrillic vs Latin, Azerbaijani, Punjabi Gurmukhi vs Shahmukhi)—provide a clean natural experiment that holds language, typology, and culture constant while varying only orthography. We hypothesize that a multilingual LLM answers the SAME factual and reasoning query differently across the two scripts of ONE language, because script (not language) covertly gates how deeply the input enters the shared semantic hub: the non-dominant/non-Roman script of a digraphic pair enters the hub later and more weakly, producing systematic script-induced inconsistency and accuracy loss that cannot be attributed to any linguistic difference. This script-divergence is mediated by a decodable script-identity signal that persists into mid layers and is causally correctable by transliterating the representation into the dominant script's latent form.
Related Work: Prior work shows (a) a shared, dominant-language-scaffolded semantic hub with late-layer language-specific decoding (Semantic Hub 2024; Cross-Layer Transcoders 2025), (b) latent romanization as a bridge for non-Roman scripts in intermediate layers (RomanLens 2025), (c) script-barrier effects on cross-lingual transfer and transliteration-based fixes (TransliCo 2024; Unknown Script 2024; One Script Instead of Hundreds 2026), and (d) that tokenizer/script, not shared script per se, drives transfer (Unknown Script 2024; Beyond Literal Token Overlap 2025). All of this compares DIFFERENT languages across scripts (confounding script with language, typology, resource level, and culture) or studies representation alignment/transfer, not downstream factual/reasoning CONSISTENCY. Crucially, NO prior work uses DIGRAPHIC languages—the same language in two scripts—as a controlled natural experiment to isolate script from language, and none tests whether the SAME query yields DIFFERENT answers across the two scripts of one language, localizes this to a persistent script-identity signal that gates hub entry, or offers a causal latent-transliteration fix that operates on internal representations. We reframe script from a transfer-efficiency nuisance into a covert hidden variable causing knowledge and reasoning inconsistency within a single language, cleanly separated from every linguistic confound.
Abstract: The correct answer to a question does not depend on the alphabet it is written in, yet many languages are digraphic—written in two scripts (Serbian in Cyrillic and Latin, Hindi and Urdu, Kazakh in Cyrillic and Latin, Azerbaijani, Punjabi in Gurmukhi and Shahmukhi). This offers a clean natural experiment that holds language, grammar, typology, and culture constant while varying only orthography. We ask a simple, previously untested question: does a multilingual LLM answer the SAME factual and reasoning query differently depending on which script the same language is written in? We hypothesize script-induced divergence—the non-dominant script of a digraphic pair enters the shared semantic hub later and more weakly, so identical-meaning queries yield systematically less accurate and mutually inconsistent answers across scripts, an inconsistency attributable to orthography alone since no linguistic factor differs. We further hypothesize this is mediated by a decodable script-identity signal that persists into mid layers and gates hub entry, and is causally correctable by transliterating the representation toward the dominant script's latent form without retraining. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using parallel single-language, two-script query sets across several digraphic languages, combining logit-lens hub-entry tracking, difference-in-means script-signal probes, activation patching, and a latent-transliteration steering intervention. Metrics include cross-script answer-inconsistency gap, hub-entry-depth gap, script-signal persistence, and steering-induced consistency recovery with meaning-preservation controls.
Experiments:
1) Digraphic parallel suite: Build ~600 factual QA (mLAMA/TriviaQA-style, verified answers) and reasoning (MGSM-style arithmetic/commonsense) items, each rendered in BOTH scripts of several digraphic languages: Serbian (Cyrillic/Latin, near-lossless transliteration), Kazakh (Cyrillic/Latin), Azerbaijani (Cyrillic/Latin historically), Punjabi (Gurmukhi/Shahmukhi), and Hindi/Urdu (with careful handling of lexical divergence, treated as a separate, more-confounded tier). Use deterministic transliteration where available so the two script versions are literal orthographic variants with identical meaning; native-speaker verify. Report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral script-divergence (H1, core): Measure per-language cross-script accuracy gap and answer-inconsistency rate (fraction of items answered differently across the two scripts of the SAME language). Since language/typology/culture are held constant, any gap isolates a script effect. Predict the non-dominant/non-Roman script underperforms and the pair is inconsistent. Control for tokenizer fertility of each script version and script-specific token frequency (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test script adds predictive power beyond fertility). Use Serbian Cyrillic/Latin (identical language, near-perfect transliteration) as the cleanest anchor.
3) Hub-entry-depth measurement (H2): Using logit-lens/tuned-lens, measure for each item the layer at which the query's meaning first becomes decodable in the shared (dominant-language) hub, per script. Test whether the non-dominant script enters the hub at a deeper/later layer and more weakly (lower peak decodability), and whether hub-entry-depth gap predicts the behavioral inconsistency gap (Spearman; held-out R^2). Cross-check RomanLens-style latent romanization: does the non-Roman script version pass through a romanized intermediate before hub entry?
4) Script-signal persistence (H3): Extract a difference-in-means script-identity direction (script A vs script B of the same language) at each layer and test how deep into the network it persists. Predict a persistent script signal in the non-dominant script correlates with delayed hub entry and inconsistency (mediation regression controlling for fertility; held-out R^2). Measure cross-lingual alignment to test whether it is a shared script axis re-used across digraphic pairs.
5) Error decomposition via patching: For items correct in the dominant script but wrong in the non-dominant script of the same language, patch (a) the mid-layer shared-hub meaning representation from the dominant-script pass and (b) only late-layer decoding components. If (a) fixes the error, the failure was weak/late hub entry (script-gating), not knowledge absence. Report the share of script-gating vs knowledge-absence errors per language.
6) Core causal intervention — latent transliteration: At an early/mid layer, steer/patch the non-dominant-script representation toward the dominant-script latent form (using the difference-in-means script direction, or patching the aligned dominant-script representation), then continue the forward pass. Predict selective recovery of accuracy and cross-script consistency for the non-dominant script, with negligible effect on the dominant script (selectivity test). Compute recovery elasticity = accuracy gain per unit hub-entry-depth gap. Baselines: surface-level transliteration of the input to the dominant script (a strong practical baseline), whole-hub dominant-language steering, and a random-direction control.
7) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify the intervention is script-specific (fixes the script-gating deficit but preserves meaning and does not switch output language/script inappropriately; measure off-target rate and meaning-preservation via answer-content checks), and does not harm the dominant script. Cross-model contrast: predict more Roman/English-centric models (Llama-3, Qwen2.5) show larger non-Roman-script divergence than more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether divergence magnitude correlates with the script-signal persistence and each script's training share.
Evaluation metrics: per-language cross-script accuracy gap and answer-inconsistency rate (with Serbian Cyrillic/Latin as clean anchor); hub-entry-depth gap and its correlation with inconsistency (held-out R^2 over fertility); latent-romanization pass-through rate; script-signal persistence depth and its mediation of inconsistency; script-gating vs knowledge-absence error shares; latent-transliteration recovery and elasticity vs surface-transliteration and other baselines, with selectivity and meaning preservation; off-target rate; cross-model divergence comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Perfect script-only variation exists only for near-lossless transliteration pairs (Serbian Cyrillic/Latin, Kazakh); Hindi/Urdu and Punjabi Gurmukhi/Shahmukhi carry genuine lexical/register differences that reintroduce a language confound—we center core claims on the clean transliteration pairs and treat the others as a separate, explicitly-confounded tier. 2) Tokenizer fertility differs sharply across scripts and could drive the effect rather than 'script' per se; we control for fertility with partial correlations and report whether the gap survives fertility matching—if fertility fully explains it, that is itself an informative mechanistic finding (script effect = tokenization effect). 3) Training-data quantity per script is uneven and confounded with script; the digraphic design controls language but not per-script corpus size, so we report per-script data-share estimates and interpret accordingly. 4) Logit-lens/tuned-lens hub-entry-depth is approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation and multiple lenses. 5) Difference-in-means script directions may entangle token-frequency features; we use multiple extraction methods and the Serbian anchor where meaning is truly identical. 6) The latent-transliteration intervention could harm fluency or over-normalize; we require meaning preservation and dominant-script non-degradation as hard checks and report the full tradeoff, and compare against the simpler surface-transliteration baseline to show the mechanistic account adds value. 7) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM analyzed as a less English-centric contrast). 8) If NO cross-script divergence is found—the model answers identically across both scripts of a language—this is an informative POSITIVE result showing orthography-invariant knowledge, cleanly separating script from language effects, valuable either way. 9) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: perfective_result_state_flattening
Title: Same Perfective, Different Endings: Does the English-Scaffolded Hub Flatten the Cross-Lingual Gradient of Result-State Entailment?
Short Hypothesis: Grammatical perfective does not construe events identically across languages: eye-tracking shows the perfective triggers a strong result-state (completion) reading in Russian, a somewhat weaker one in Spanish, and essentially none in English. We hypothesize that because the multilingual LLM's shared hub is scaffolded by English — whose Simple Past does NOT obligatorily entail culmination — the model applies a single, English-like 'completion-entailment strength' to the perfective in all languages, FLATTENING the human Russian > Spanish > English result-state gradient: it under-reads culmination for Russian/Spanish perfectives (relative to native speakers) and mis-tracks completion in downstream reasoning. This flattening is mediated by a shared, steerable 'result-state' direction, tracks each language's empirical result-state strength, and is causally correctable without harming ongoing-event reading.
Related Work: Robust cross-linguistic psycholinguistics (Temporal Information and Event Bounding, visual-world eye-tracking 2022; Aspect processing across languages 2023; Seeing from without/within 2019; When Russian is more Perfective than Spanish 2019) establishes a GRADED result-state entailment for the perfective: Russian ~95% result-state preference, Spanish ~83%, English ~54% (chance) on telic accomplishments, i.e., the English Simple Past does NOT obligatorily enforce completion. On the model side, interpretability shows aspect/tense are encoded as orthogonal, steerable directions (About Time 2022; Probing Verbal Aspect 2024; Steering Tense and Aspect 2025) and that morphosyntactic concepts are shared, English-scaffolded, and causal across languages (LLMs Share Latent Grammatical Concepts 2025); The Imperfective Paradox in LLMs (2026) documents a MONOLINGUAL teleological bias (hallucinated completion for goal-oriented events) and finds embeddings distinguish process from result but inference is prior-dominated; LLMs Struggle with NLI for Perfect Aspect (2025) shows temporal-inference failures in Chinese/Japanese. CRITICALLY, no prior work asks whether the shared, English-scaffolded hub FLATTENS the cross-lingual result-state GRADIENT of the perfective — applying an English-like weak-culmination setting to Russian/Spanish perfectives — nor localizes a shared result-state direction, ties the flattening to the human eye-tracking gradient as an external ground truth, or offers a causal per-language correction. This differs from my prior telicity proposal (Mandarin bare-object UNDERSPECIFICATION, where completion is genuinely optional): here the input is grammatically PERFECTIVE in every language and the phenomenon is a graded MISMATCH to each language's documented result-state strength. It is orthogonal to the monolingual Imperfective-Paradox work by making the core question cross-lingual and gradient-based.
Abstract: The perfective aspect looks like a universal 'the event happened, completed' marker, but decades of eye-tracking show it construes events differently across languages: Russian perfectives strongly commit to the event's result state (~95%), Spanish less so (~83%), and English Simple Past not at all (~54%, chance). Multilingual language models build a shared semantic hub scaffolded by English — the very language whose past tense does not enforce completion. We ask a simple, previously untested question: does that hub FLATTEN the human result-state gradient, applying an English-like weak-culmination reading to the perfective in all languages? We hypothesize that (1) the model under-reads result-state entailment for Russian and Spanish perfectives relative to native-speaker gradients, mis-tracking completion in inference; (2) the size of the flattening tracks each language's empirical result-state strength; (3) a shared, ablatable 'result-state' direction mediates it, with any residual language-specific completion signal in shallow layers; and (4) steering that direction restores per-language-faithful culmination reading without harming ongoing-event interpretation. We build a controlled multilingual telic-accomplishment suite (perfective vs imperfective, result-state vs ongoing probes) across Russian, Spanish, and English (plus Mandarin as a non-culminating extension), on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM. Using difference-in-means result-state probes, logit-lens depth tracking, activation patching, and steering, we measure the flattening, its gradient scaling against eye-tracking data, its mediation, and its causal correction. Metrics include per-language result-state-entailment rate vs human gradient, gradient-flattening index, mediation R-squared, and steering-induced restoration with ongoing-reading controls.
Experiments:
1) Perfective result-state suite: Construct ~450 telic accomplishment items (e.g., 'build a house', 'cross the street', 'eat three apples') each realized in Russian (prefixal perfective vs imperfective), Spanish (Preterite vs Imperfect), and English (Simple Past vs Past Progressive), with Mandarin (perfective -le with non-culminating accomplishments) as an extension. For each item and aspect, build probes hinging on completion: (i) result-state forced choice ('At the end, is the house built / did the crossing reach the other side?' — completed vs ongoing/unfinished); (ii) culmination-NLI (does the perfective sentence ENTAIL the result state? — gold label calibrated per language to the eye-tracking gradient: strong-entail for Russian, moderate for Spanish, weak/neutral for English); (iii) downstream reasoning whose outcome depends on whether the event culminated; (iv) an ongoing-reading control on the imperfective (where all languages agree on the process reading, a within-item baseline). Native-speaker verify markers and per-language gold; report inter-annotator agreement. Anchor gold gradients to published eye-tracking result-state preferences. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral flattening (H1, core): For perfective items, measure per-language result-state-entailment rate (fraction judged completed) and compare against the human eye-tracking gradient (Russian > Spanish > English). Define a gradient-flattening index = how much the model compresses the Russian/Spanish/English spread toward a single (English-like) setpoint. Predict the model under-reads culmination for Russian/Spanish perfectives (toward the English weak reading) rather than reproducing the steep human gradient. Verify the imperfective ongoing-reading control is consistent across languages (isolating the perfective-specific effect). Control for tokenizer fertility, verb frequency, and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test language adds predictive power beyond fertility/resource).
3) Gradient scaling against human data (H2, external validation): Using the published per-language result-state preference strengths (eye-tracking offline + gaze), test whether the model's per-language entailment rate is predicted by (a) the human result-state strength and (b) an English-flattening baseline (all languages equal to English). Model comparison: does the model track the human gradient at all, or is it better fit by a flat English-scaffolded setpoint? Report held-out prediction and the flattening magnitude.
4) Representational localization (H3): Extract a 'result-state vs ongoing' direction via difference-in-means between completed and in-progress event representations at each layer, per language (building on Steering Tense and Aspect 2025; About Time 2022). Test (a) cross-lingual alignment of the result-state direction and whether it is English-scaffolded (aligned with the English weak-culmination pole in mid/shared-hub layers); (b) whether a Russian/Spanish perfective input projects toward the WEAK (English-like) pole in the shared hub while any residual strong-completion signal is stronger in early/language-specific layers, via logit-lens/tuned-lens depth tracking. Baseline: a tense direction (English marks it) as a within-model shared-category control. Mediation: regress behavioral under-reading on shared-hub result-state-projection weakness (partial correlation controlling for fertility/resource; held-out R^2).
5) Causal steering/patching test (H4, core): (a) Steer the Russian/Spanish perfective representation along the result-state direction toward the STRONG-completion pole (to each language's human-calibrated strength) and measure whether result-state judgments/NLI/reasoning shift toward the native-speaker pattern (flip rate), without switching output language. (b) For flattened items, patch the residual language-specific completion signal (from early/language-specific layers) into later computation and test restoration — localizing the failure to the shared hub imposing a weak English-like reading over a shallowly-present strong signal. Critically verify ONGOING-READING preservation (imperfective items must remain correctly read as ongoing — no over-imposition of completion), plus fluency and off-target/language-mixing checks. Baselines: whole-hub English-steering, random-direction control.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify steering is result-state-specific (changes completion reading but not the event's identity, tense, or participants), graded (correction scales with the human gradient), and not a lexical-frequency artifact (nonce-verb variants). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 flattens more than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM (which see more Russian/Spanish aspect data); test whether flattening magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the result-state direction and with each language's training share. Qualitatively compare the model's per-language pattern against the human eye-tracking gradient.
Evaluation metrics: per-language result-state-entailment rate and gradient-flattening index (vs human gradient; vs English-flat baseline via model comparison); culmination-NLI accuracy calibrated per language; ongoing-reading (imperfective) preservation as within-item control; shared-hub result-state-projection strength and crystallization depth (vs tense baseline); cross-lingual result-state-direction alignment; mediation regression (held-out R^2); steering flip rate and patching-induced restoration; ongoing-reading preservation, fluency, off-target rate; cross-model flattening comparison and correlation with training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for language over fertility/resource baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Calibrating per-language gold culmination labels to a graded human standard is subtle — result-state strength is a preference, not a binary; we anchor gold to published eye-tracking magnitudes, use graded/soft labels for NLI, native-speaker verify, and report inter-annotator agreement, excluding low-agreement items. 2) The English Simple Past is genuinely weak/chance on culmination, so 'English-flattening' means the model converging to a WEAK reading — but Russian/Spanish native readings are strong; distinguishing 'flattening toward English' from generic incompetence requires the gradient-scaling model comparison (Exp 3) and the causal steering test (Exp 5), which restores the strong reading by editing only the result-state direction. 3) Language is confounded with family, script, and resource level; the imperfective ongoing-reading control, within-item perfective-vs-imperfective contrasts, and human-gradient prediction isolate the perfective-result-state pathway, but residual confounds remain — we center on well-resourced Russian/Spanish/English and treat Mandarin as an extension. 4) Difference-in-means result-state directions may entangle tense, telicity, or lexical-aspect features; we use multiple extraction methods, a tense control direction, and specificity checks. 5) Logit-lens/tuned-lens depth is approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 6) Instruction-tuned models may hedge ('it may or may not be complete'), which we treat as a positive underspecification-awareness signal; we test base models where available and use forced-choice + NLI. 7) Steering could over-impose completion (harming the imperfective ongoing reading) or fluency; we require ongoing-reading preservation as a hard constraint and report the full tradeoff. 8) The model-vs-human comparison is qualitative/structural (gradient direction and ordering), not a claim of identical mechanism. 9) If NO flattening is found — the model reproduces the Russian > Spanish > English gradient — this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the shared hub represents language-specific perfective construal despite English scaffolding, valuable either way. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: digraphic_isolates_script_effect
Title: Same Language, Two Scripts, Two Answers: Digraphic Languages Isolate Orthography as a Hidden Variable in Multilingual LLM Knowledge and Reasoning
Short Hypothesis: Digraphic languages - the SAME language written in two scripts (Serbian Cyrillic/Latin, Kazakh Cyrillic/Latin, Punjabi Gurmukhi/Shahmukhi) - provide a clean natural experiment holding language, grammar, typology, and culture fixed while varying only orthography. We hypothesize a multilingual LLM answers the SAME factual/reasoning query differently across the two scripts of ONE language, because script (not language) covertly gates how quickly and strongly the input enters the shared semantic hub: the non-dominant/non-Roman script enters later and more weakly, causing script-induced accuracy loss and answer inconsistency attributable to orthography alone. This is mediated by a persistent script-identity signal and is causally correctable by transliterating the internal representation toward the dominant-script latent form.
Related Work: Prior work establishes (a) a shared, dominant-language-scaffolded semantic hub with late-layer language-specific decoding (Semantic Hub 2024; Do Llamas Work in English 2024); (b) latent romanization as an intermediate bridge for non-Roman scripts, appearing 1-2 layers before native script and encoding concepts similarly across scripts (RomanLens 2025); (c) that language/script information is linearly separable from the first transformer block and shaped by pretraining composition (How Language Directions Align 2025; Hyperpolyglot LLMs 2023; Geometry of Multilingual Representations 2022); and (d) script-barrier effects on cross-lingual transfer and transliteration fixes (TransliCo 2024; Unknown Script 2024). CRUCIALLY, all of this compares DIFFERENT languages across scripts (confounding script with language, typology, resource, and culture) or studies representation alignment/transfer, not downstream answer CONSISTENCY. RomanLens shows romanization exists internally but does not test whether feeding the same language in two scripts yields DIFFERENT downstream answers, nor use digraphic languages to isolate script from every linguistic confound. No prior work uses digraphic languages as a controlled natural experiment for knowledge/reasoning consistency, localizes the divergence to a persistent script-identity signal that gates hub entry, or offers a causal latent-transliteration fix on internal representations. We reframe script from a transfer-efficiency nuisance into a covert hidden variable causing within-language knowledge and reasoning inconsistency, cleanly separated from language.
Abstract: The correct answer to a question does not depend on the alphabet it is written in, yet many languages are digraphic - written in two scripts (Serbian in Cyrillic and Latin, Kazakh in Cyrillic and Latin, Punjabi in Gurmukhi and Shahmukhi). This offers a clean natural experiment that holds language, grammar, typology, and culture constant while varying only orthography, isolating script from every linguistic confound that plagues cross-lingual comparisons. We ask a simple, previously untested question: does a multilingual LLM answer the SAME factual and reasoning query differently depending on which script the same language is written in? We hypothesize script-induced divergence - the non-dominant script of a digraphic pair enters the shared semantic hub later and more weakly, so identical-meaning queries yield systematically less accurate and mutually inconsistent answers across scripts, an inconsistency attributable to orthography alone. We further hypothesize this is mediated by a decodable script-identity signal that persists into mid layers and gates hub entry, and is causally correctable by transliterating the internal representation toward the dominant-script latent form without retraining. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using parallel single-language, two-script query sets across digraphic languages, combining logit-lens hub-entry tracking, difference-in-means script-signal probes, activation patching, and a latent-transliteration steering intervention. Metrics include cross-script answer-inconsistency gap, hub-entry-depth gap, script-signal persistence, and steering-induced consistency recovery with meaning-preservation controls.
Experiments: 1) Digraphic parallel suite: Build ~600 factual QA (mLAMA/TriviaQA-style, verified answers) and reasoning (MGSM-style arithmetic/commonsense) items, each rendered in BOTH scripts of digraphic languages: Serbian (Cyrillic/Latin, near-lossless deterministic transliteration - the cleanest anchor), Kazakh (Cyrillic/Latin), and Punjabi (Gurmukhi/Shahmukhi). Use deterministic transliteration so the two versions are literal orthographic variants with identical meaning; native-speaker verify. Include Hindi/Urdu as a separate, explicitly-confounded tier (genuine lexical/register divergence). Report inter-annotator agreement; release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B. 2) Behavioral script-divergence (H1, core): Measure per-language cross-script accuracy gap and answer-inconsistency rate (fraction of items answered differently across the two scripts of the SAME language). Since language/typology/culture are held constant, any gap isolates a script effect. Predict the non-dominant/non-Roman script underperforms and the pair is inconsistent. Control for tokenizer fertility of each script version and script-token frequency (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test script adds predictive power beyond fertility). Use Serbian Cyrillic/Latin as the cleanest anchor. 3) Hub-entry-depth (H2): Using logit-lens/tuned-lens, measure per item the layer at which the query's meaning first becomes decodable in the shared (dominant-language) hub, per script. Test whether the non-dominant script enters the hub at a deeper layer and more weakly (lower peak decodability), and whether the hub-entry-depth gap predicts the behavioral inconsistency gap (Spearman; held-out R^2).
