Cross-check RomanLens-style latent romanization: does the non-Roman-script version pass through a romanized intermediate before hub entry? 4) Script-signal persistence (H3): Extract a difference-in-means script-identity direction (script A vs B of the same language) at each layer and measure how deep it persists. Predict a persistent script signal in the non-dominant script correlates with delayed hub entry and inconsistency (mediation regression controlling for fertility; held-out R^2). 5) Error decomposition via patching: For items correct in the dominant script but wrong in the non-dominant script of the SAME language, patch (a) the mid-layer shared-hub meaning representation from the dominant-script pass and (b) only late-layer decoding components. If (a) fixes the error, the failure was weak/late hub entry (script-gating), not knowledge absence. Report the share of script-gating vs knowledge-absence errors per language. 6) Core causal intervention - latent transliteration: At an early/mid layer, steer/patch the non-dominant-script representation toward the dominant-script latent form (via the difference-in-means script direction, or patching the aligned dominant-script representation), then continue the forward pass. Predict selective recovery of accuracy and cross-script consistency for the non-dominant script, negligible effect on the dominant script (selectivity). Compute recovery elasticity = accuracy gain per unit hub-entry-depth gap. Baselines: surface-level transliteration of the input to the dominant script (a strong practical baseline), whole-hub dominant-language steering, random-direction control. 7) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify the intervention is script-specific (fixes the gating deficit, preserves meaning, does not switch output script inappropriately; measure off-target rate and meaning-preservation via answer-content checks), and does not harm the dominant script. Cross-model: predict more Roman/English-centric models (Llama-3, Qwen2.5) show larger non-Roman-script divergence than more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether divergence correlates with script-signal persistence and each script's training share. Evaluation metrics: per-language cross-script accuracy gap and inconsistency rate (Serbian anchor); hub-entry-depth gap and its correlation with inconsistency (held-out R^2 over fertility); latent-romanization pass-through rate; script-signal persistence depth and its mediation of inconsistency; script-gating vs knowledge-absence error shares; latent-transliteration recovery and elasticity vs surface-transliteration and other baselines, with selectivity and meaning preservation; off-target rate; cross-model divergence comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Perfect script-only variation exists only for near-lossless transliteration pairs (Serbian Cyrillic/Latin, Kazakh); Hindi/Urdu and Punjabi Gurmukhi/Shahmukhi carry genuine lexical/register differences reintroducing a language confound - we center core claims on the clean transliteration pairs and treat the rest as a separate, explicitly-confounded tier. 2) Tokenizer fertility differs sharply across scripts and could drive the effect rather than 'script' per se; we control for fertility with partial correlations and report whether the gap survives fertility matching - if fertility fully explains it, that is itself an informative mechanistic finding (script effect = tokenization effect). 3) Training-data quantity per script is uneven and confounded with script; the digraphic design controls language but not per-script corpus size, so we report per-script data-share estimates and interpret accordingly. 4) Logit-lens/tuned-lens hub-entry-depth is approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation and multiple lenses. 5) Difference-in-means script directions may entangle token-frequency features; we use multiple extraction methods and the Serbian anchor where meaning is truly identical. 6) The latent-transliteration intervention could harm fluency or over-normalize; we require meaning preservation and dominant-script non-degradation as hard checks, report the full tradeoff, and compare against the simpler surface-transliteration baseline to show the mechanistic account adds value. 7) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM analyzed as a less English-centric contrast). 8) If NO cross-script divergence is found - the model answers identically across both scripts of a language - this is an informative POSITIVE result showing orthography-invariant knowledge, cleanly separating script from language, valuable either way. 9) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: crosslingual_shortcut_transfer
Title: Borrowed Shortcuts: Multilingual LLMs Import a Dominant-Language Heuristic Profile That Becomes Spurious in Other Languages
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs do not merely reason worse in low-resource languages; they carry a LANGUAGE-DEPENDENT shortcut-reliance profile in which reasoning latches onto a surface heuristic (answer position, lexical-overlap cue, believability of the conclusion) whose validity is calibrated to the dominant training language. Because the reasoning is routed through an English-scaffolded shared hub, the model IMPORTS the dominant language's heuristic weighting into other languages even when that language's surface no longer licenses the shortcut, producing a distinctive signature: on adversarial items where a shortcut and the correct answer conflict, the model's shortcut-following rate is set by the dominant language, not the query language, so shortcut errors are HIGHER (not just accuracy lower) in the query language than genuine reasoning failure alone would predict.
Related Work: Prior work explains the multilingual reasoning gap via English-centric latent reasoning (Do Multilingual LLMs Think In English 2025; Large Reasoning Models Are Not Yet Multilingual Latent Reasoners 2026), understanding/translation failures (Why Do Multilingual Reasoning Gaps Emerge 2025; Beg to Differ 2025), language-reasoning disentanglement (When Less Language is More 2025), and language-specific latent subspaces (Language-Specific Latent Process Hinders 2025). Separately, LLMs are shown to rely on token bias / shortcuts and to exhibit human-like content (believability) effects (A Peek into Token Bias 2024; Language Models Show Content Effects 2024), and BICAUSE (Under the Shadow of Babel 2025) shows models internalize language-specific causal WORD-ORDER attention biases. Cognitive science shows the Foreign Language Effect changes heuristic vs reflective reasoning and belief-logic conflict detection by language (Thinking in a Foreign Language Distorts Cognitive Effort 2019). CRITICALLY, no prior work asks whether shortcut/heuristic RELIANCE itself is language-dependent and whether it is TRANSFERRED from the dominant language into other languages via the shared hub, producing elevated shortcut-following (not merely lower accuracy) that tracks the dominant rather than the query language. All shortcut/content-effect work is monolingual (English); all multilingual-gap work treats the gap as a competence/understanding deficit, never as an imported heuristic profile. We reframe the gap as a cross-lingual shortcut-transfer phenomenon and give it a mechanistic, causally-testable signature.
Abstract: Large language models reason worse in lower-resource languages, and the prevailing explanation is a competence deficit: the model fails to understand the input or route it into its English-centric reasoning. We propose a different, previously untested phenomenon. Reasoning models rely on surface HEURISTICS (answer position, lexical overlap between question and answer, believability of a conclusion) whose reliability is calibrated to their dominant training language, and because multilingual reasoning is routed through an English-scaffolded shared hub, the model IMPORTS that dominant-language heuristic profile into other languages even when the target-language surface no longer supports the shortcut. This predicts a signature the competence account cannot produce: on adversarial items where a shortcut cue conflicts with the correct answer, the model's shortcut-FOLLOWING rate is governed by the dominant language rather than the query language, so shortcut errors are elevated beyond what a pure understanding gap would explain, and are consistent across languages in a way random competence failures are not. We test this on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using controlled parallel reasoning suites (syllogistic belief-logic conflict, lexical-overlap distractor QA, and option-position bias) across typologically diverse languages, holding content identical across languages. We measure per-language shortcut-following rates, decompose errors into shortcut-following versus genuine-reasoning failure, and use activation patching plus a shortcut-direction steering test to establish that the imported heuristic weighting is carried in the shared hub. We further test whether disrupting the shared-hub routing (or steering toward the query language) selectively reduces imported shortcut reliance. Metrics include shortcut-following rate, dominant-vs-query-language prediction of shortcut errors, shortcut-error consistency, and steering-induced shortcut reduction with reasoning-preservation controls.
Experiments:
1) Controlled adversarial shortcut suite: Build three parallel reasoning families where a surface shortcut can be made CONGRUENT or INCONGRUENT with the correct answer: (a) syllogistic belief-logic conflict items (valid-but-unbelievable vs invalid-but-believable, following the content-effect paradigm); (b) multiple-choice QA where a distractor shares high lexical overlap with the question but is wrong (lexical-overlap shortcut); (c) option-position items where the correct answer is placed in a fixed position to test position bias. Each item is rendered with IDENTICAL semantic content across typologically diverse languages (English, French, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish), native-speaker verified with symbolic-oracle gold labels. Crucially include CONGRUENT (shortcut points to correct answer) and INCONGRUENT (shortcut conflicts) conditions. Report inter-annotator agreement; release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral shortcut-following map (core): For each language and shortcut family, measure the shortcut-following rate on INCONGRUENT items = fraction of errors that follow the shortcut cue (e.g., choose the believable-but-invalid conclusion, the high-overlap distractor, or the biased position). Compare CONGRUENT vs INCONGRUENT accuracy to isolate a shortcut effect from general competence. Test the central prediction: shortcut-following rate is high and does NOT simply track query-language competence; low-resource languages show shortcut-following at least as high as English (imported), not lower. Control for tokenizer fertility and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2).
3) Dominant-vs-query-language attribution: Cross the query language with the reasoning/latent language (via explicit CoT-language control where possible, and via logit-lens decoding of the latent language of the shortcut decision). Test whether per-item shortcut-following is better predicted by the DOMINANT (English) heuristic weighting than by the query-language surface — e.g., a lexical-overlap shortcut that exists in the English translation but is broken by the target-language phrasing still gets followed. Report which language's cue predicts the error (held-out R^2, model comparison).
4) Error decomposition (shortcut-following vs genuine-reasoning failure): For INCONGRUENT items wrong in language B, classify errors as shortcut-driven (the model committed to the shortcut answer) vs random reasoning failure, using logit-lens to check whether the shortcut answer was internally favored. Test that low-resource languages show a DISPROPORTIONATE share of shortcut-driven errors (directional, not random), and that shortcut errors are more CONSISTENT across languages than random errors (same items fail the same way — a signature of a shared imported heuristic, not independent competence noise).
5) Mechanistic localization and causal test: Extract a difference-in-means 'shortcut-reliance' direction (shortcut-followed vs shortcut-resisted representations) at middle layers and measure cross-lingual alignment (is it a single shared heuristic axis?). Activation patching: for a shortcut error in language B, patch (a) the shared-hub representation from a shortcut-resisting (e.g., abstract/nonce-content) pass and (b) query-language components; test which removes the shortcut error. Steering: amplify vs suppress the shortcut direction and confirm dose-response control over shortcut-following, cross-lingually.
6) Core intervention: Test whether steering toward the query-language representation (reducing shared-hub routing) or suppressing the shared shortcut direction SELECTIVELY reduces imported shortcut reliance while preserving genuine reasoning (a symmetric check: it must not harm CONGRUENT items where the shortcut is correct, nor abstract reasoning). Compare against English shared-space steering (which the competence account predicts should HELP but our account predicts may IMPORT MORE shortcut), a shortcut-suppression steering, and random-direction control. Metrics: shortcut-following reduction, accuracy on incongruent items, congruent-item and abstract-reasoning preservation, off-target/language-mixing rate.
7) Cross-model contrast: Predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen import shortcuts more strongly (dominant-language prediction dominates) than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether import magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the shortcut direction and with training share.
Evaluation metrics: per-language shortcut-following rate (congruent vs incongruent; vs competence baseline); dominant-vs-query-language prediction of shortcut errors (held-out R^2, model comparison); shortcut-driven vs random error shares and cross-language error consistency; shortcut-direction cross-lingual alignment; patching-induced shortcut removal (shared-hub vs query-language); steering dose-response; selective shortcut-reduction with congruent/abstract-reasoning preservation and off-target rate; cross-model import comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Separating imported-shortcut reliance from a plain competence deficit is the central challenge; the congruent-vs-incongruent contrast, the directional shortcut-driven-error decomposition, the cross-language error CONSISTENCY signature, and the dominant-vs-query-language attribution are all designed to distinguish 'follows a shortcut' from 'fails randomly'. If low-resource errors turn out random and query-language-predicted, the phenomenon is refuted — an informative negative result relocating the gap to pure competence. 2) Constructing shortcuts that survive translation into some languages but break in others (to test import) is delicate; we verify with native speakers that the target-language surface genuinely does/does not license the cue, and report items where this is ambiguous. 3) Shortcut type matters — belief/content effects may be more universal than lexical-overlap or position cues; we analyze each family separately and expect import to be strongest for surface (lexical/position) cues. 4) Difference-in-means shortcut directions may entangle content/topic; we use nonce-content and abstract-content controls and multiple extraction methods. 5) Logit-lens latent-language and shortcut-preference decoding are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with truncation. 6) The steering intervention could harm genuine reasoning or over-suppress; the congruent-item and abstract-reasoning preservation checks are hard constraints and we report the full tradeoff. 7) Query language is confounded with resource level, script, and fertility; partial correlations and the causal patching/steering tests mitigate but may not fully remove confounds. 8) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM analyzed as a less English-centric contrast expected to import less). 9) Human-LLM analogy (Foreign Language Effect) is qualitative, not a claim of identical mechanism. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: information_structure_imposition
Title: Given Before New, English-Style: Does the Shared Hub Impose a Dominant-Language Information-Structure Default onto Topic-Prominent Languages?
Short Hypothesis: Languages differ in how they package given/new and topic/comment information: English is subject-prominent with a fairly rigid given-before-new order, whereas topic-prominent languages (Mandarin, Japanese, Korean) foreground a topic that need not be the grammatical subject and use particles/word-order to mark information structure differently. Because the multilingual LLM's shared hub is scaffolded by English, we hypothesize it IMPOSES an English-like information-structure parse onto topic-prominent inputs: the model tracks the ENGLISH subject/given-new assignment rather than the target language's topic/comment structure, producing systematic errors in referent-continuity, focus/emphasis, and zero-anaphora resolution that hinge on information structure. This imposition is mediated by a shared, steerable 'topic/focus' direction, tracks each language's empirical topic-prominence, and is causally correctable without harming lexical comprehension.
Related Work: Interpretability establishes an English-scaffolded shared hub with language-agnostic concept representations (Semantic Hub 2024; Do Llamas Work in English 2024; Separating Tongue from Thought 2024; Do Multilingual LLMs Think In English 2025), that morphosyntactic/discourse concepts are shared and English-scaffolded (Concept Space Alignment 2024), and that discourse structure and reference are internally represented monolingually (Discourse Structure Interacts with Reference 2020; Deep Subjecthood 2021, which shows higher-order grammatical-role alignment leaks across languages). Typology establishes the subject-prominent vs topic-prominent split (Li & Thompson 1976) and cross-linguistic differences in given-new ordering and zero-anaphora (Japanese/Korean/Mandarin pro-drop and topic-chaining). CRITICALLY, all interpretability work on discourse/reference is monolingual/English and never asks whether the shared hub imposes an English information-structure parse onto topic-prominent languages; all typological work is behavioral/linguistic. No prior work asks whether cross-lingual failures in referent-continuity, focus, and zero-anaphora arise because the model applies an English subject/given-new template to topic-prominent inputs, localizes a shared topic/focus direction, ties the imposition to empirical topic-prominence, or offers a causal fix. Unlike my prior grammatical-category imposition proposals (tense, gender, evidentiality, honorifics, number, telicity, negation), this targets DISCOURSE-LEVEL information structure (topic/comment, given/new, zero-anaphora) — a distinct, sentence-spanning axis grounded in the subject-prominence typology, orthogonal to all of them.
Abstract: Beyond who did what, sentences package information: what is the topic, what is given versus new, who continues to be talked about. Languages disagree on this packaging. English is subject-prominent with a fairly rigid given-before-new order, while topic-prominent languages such as Mandarin, Japanese, and Korean foreground a topic that need not be the grammatical subject and freely drop given referents (zero-anaphora). Multilingual language models build a shared semantic hub scaffolded by English. We ask a simple, previously untested question: does that hub IMPOSE an English-like information-structure parse onto topic-prominent inputs, tracking the English subject and given-new assignment rather than the target language's topic/comment structure? We hypothesize that (1) the model mis-resolves referent-continuity, focus/emphasis, and zero-anaphora in topic-prominent languages by defaulting to the English subject-prominent template; (2) the size of this imposition tracks each language's empirical topic-prominence; (3) a shared, ablatable topic/focus direction mediates it, with any residual target-language structure in shallow, language-specific layers; and (4) steering toward the target-language information structure restores faithful resolution without harming lexical comprehension. We build a controlled multilingual suite of discourse items whose correct interpretation hinges on information structure, across topic-prominent (Mandarin, Japanese, Korean) and subject-prominent (English, German, Spanish) languages, on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM. Using difference-in-means topic/focus probes, logit-lens depth tracking, activation patching, and steering, we measure the imposition, its typology scaling, its mediation, and its causal correction. Metrics include information-structure error rate, topic-prominence-prediction correlation, mediation R-squared, and steering-induced restoration with competence controls.
Experiments:
1) Information-structure discourse suite: Construct ~500 short multi-clause discourse items whose correct interpretation hinges on information structure, realized in topic-prominent languages (Mandarin, Japanese, Korean) and subject-prominent languages (English, German, Spanish), native-speaker verified. Item types: (a) TOPIC-CONTINUITY items where a dropped/zero referent must be resolved to the discourse TOPIC (which is not the grammatical subject), and the English subject-prominent parse would resolve it to the wrong entity; (b) GIVEN-NEW/FOCUS items where a particle (e.g., Japanese wa/ga, Korean nun/i) or word order marks which constituent is topic vs focus, changing what is emphasized or entailed; (c) matched control items where topic and subject coincide (no divergence). Each item has verified gold interpretations and a probe (referent-resolution forced choice, focus/emphasis identification, or discourse-continuation NLI). Report inter-annotator agreement; release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral imposition (H1, core): Measure information-structure error rate = fraction of DIVERGENT items (topic != subject) where the model's resolution follows the English subject-prominent parse rather than the target-language topic/comment structure. Compare against CONTROL items (topic = subject, all languages agree) and against the model's handling of the same structure when spelled out lexically. Define the cross-lingual imposition GAP = error(DIVERGENT) minus error(CONTROL). Predict a positive gap concentrated in topic-prominent languages. Control for tokenizer fertility, referent frequency, and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test topic-prominence adds predictive power).
3) Topic-prominence scaling (H2, external validation): Using the subject-prominence typology (Li & Thompson and follow-ups), assign each language a topic-prominence score and test whether per-language imposition is predicted by that score (Spearman correlation; held-out prediction of imposition from typology alone), tying the internal phenomenon to independent linguistic ground truth.
4) Representational localization (H3): Extract a topic/focus direction via difference-in-means between representations where a constituent is topic/given vs focus/new (using particle-minimal-pairs and word-order contrasts) at each layer, per language. Test (a) whether a shared topic/focus direction is English-scaffolded (cross-lingual cosine alignment across layers, aligned with the English subject-as-topic pole); (b) whether a topic-prominent input projects onto the English subject-prominent pole in the shared hub while any residual target-language topic signal is stronger in early/language-specific layers, via logit-lens/tuned-lens depth tracking. Baseline: a grammatical-subject direction (present in all languages) as a within-model control. Mediation: regress behavioral imposition on shared-hub topic/focus-projection strength (partial correlation controlling for fertility/resource; held-out R^2).
5) Causal steering/patching test (H4, core): (a) Steer the topic-prominent input along the topic/focus direction toward the target-language topic assignment and measure whether referent-resolution/focus/NLI judgments shift to the target-language pattern (flip rate), and the imposition GAP shrinks toward the control baseline, without switching output language. (b) For imposed items, patch the residual language-specific topic signal (from early/language-specific layers) into later computation and test restoration, localizing failure to the shared hub imposing an English parse over a shallowly-present target structure. Critically verify LEXICAL COMPREHENSION preservation (the model must still answer content questions about the discourse correctly), plus fluency and off-target/language-mixing checks. Baselines: whole-hub English-steering, random-direction control.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify steering is information-structure-specific (changes topic/focus resolution but not lexical content or unrelated attributes), graded (imposition scales with topic-prominence), and not a lexical-frequency artifact (nonce-referent variants). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 shows stronger imposition than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM (which see more topic-prominent-language data); test whether imposition magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the topic/focus direction and with each language's training share. Qualitatively compare the model's per-language imposition pattern against the subject-prominence typology.
Evaluation metrics: information-structure error rate and imposition GAP (divergent minus control; English-parse-tracking rate); imposition-vs-topic-prominence correlation and held-out prediction; discourse-NLI accuracy; shared-hub topic/focus-projection strength and crystallization depth (vs grammatical-subject baseline); cross-lingual topic/focus-direction alignment; mediation regression (held-out R^2); steering flip rate and GAP reduction, patching-induced restoration; lexical-comprehension preservation, fluency, off-target rate; cross-model imposition comparison and correlation with training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for topic-prominence over fertility/frequency/resource baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Coding a language's topic-prominence and identifying the discourse topic in each item is subtle and context-dependent; we ground codings in the subject-prominence typology with native-speaker verification, use graded scores, report inter-annotator agreement, and restrict DIVERGENT items to clear topic!=subject contrasts, treating ambiguous cases separately. 2) Topic-prominence is correlated with language family, script, and resource level; the CONTROL items (topic=subject), subject-prominent comparison languages, within-item divergent-vs-control contrasts, and typology-based prediction isolate the information-structure pathway, but residual confounds may remain; we center the core study on well-resourced Mandarin/Japanese/Korean vs English/German. 3) Difference-in-means topic/focus directions may entangle grammatical-subject, animacy, or lexical features; we use particle-minimal-pairs, a grammatical-subject control direction, multiple extraction methods, and specificity checks. 4) Zero-anaphora resolution conflates information-structure failure with general coreference difficulty; we include overt-referent controls to isolate the information-structure-specific effect and only count errors that hinge on the topic/subject divergence. 5) Logit-lens/tuned-lens depth estimates are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 6) Some cross-lingual inconsistency may reflect genuine correct handling of the target structure rather than English imposition; the direction of the effect (does it track ENGLISH subject or the TARGET topic?), the control items, and the typology prediction distinguish imposition from faithful resolution, and a finding of faithful resolution is itself valuable. 7) Steering could harm lexical comprehension or fluency; we require comprehension preservation and report the full tradeoff. 8) Instruction-tuned models may normalize discourse; we test base models where available and interpret small effects as informative. 9) The model-vs-typology comparison is qualitative, not a claim of identical mechanism. 10) If NO imposition is found — information-structure judgments track each language's own topic/comment structure, predictable from typology, with lexical comprehension preserved — this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the shared hub represents language-specific information structure despite English scaffolding, valuable either way. 11) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: scope_rigidity_imposition
Title: Reading an Inverse Scope That Isn't There: Does the English-Scaffolded Shared Hub Impose Scope Ambiguity onto Scope-Rigid Languages?
Short Hypothesis: Doubly-quantified sentences ('every shark ate a pirate') are scope-AMBIGUOUS in English (surface AND inverse readings available) but scope-RIGID in Mandarin and Japanese (only the surface reading is grammatically licensed). Because the multilingual LLM's shared semantic hub is scaffolded by scope-flexible English, we hypothesize it IMPOSES the availability of an inverse-scope reading onto scope-rigid languages: the model accepts/generates the inverse-scope interpretation of a scope-rigid sentence far more than native speakers do, tracking the English scope-availability rather than the target-language grammar. This imposition is mediated by a shared, steerable 'scope-reading' direction, tracks each language's empirical scope-rigidity, and is causally correctable toward surface-only readings without harming quantifier comprehension.
Related Work: A robust cross-linguistic behavioral literature establishes that English is scope-ambiguous while Mandarin is (largely) scope-rigid, with surface scope processed faster and inverse scope less accessible in Chinese, and that heritage/bilingual contact simplifies toward the rigid grammar (Scontras et al. 2017 'When two systems meet'; Prohibiting Inverse Scope 2014; Processing Scope Economy; scope-rigidity debates 2023/2025). Recent LLM work (Quantifier Scope Interpretation in Language Learners and LLMs 2025; Understanding Quantifier Scope 2025; Scope Interpretation Evidence from Human and LLMs 2025) shows LLMs mostly prefer surface scope and only partially differentiate English vs Chinese inverse-scope preferences, with pretraining-language background mattering. Interpretability establishes an English-scaffolded shared hub with causal, shared morphosyntactic feature directions (Semantic Hub 2024; Do Llamas Work in English 2024; LLMs Share Latent Grammatical Concepts 2025). CRITICALLY, all LLM scope work is purely BEHAVIORAL/benchmark and treats scope preference as a competence property; NONE asks whether the shared hub, being scope-flexible English, IMPOSES inverse-scope availability onto scope-rigid languages, localizes a shared scope-reading direction, ties the imposition to empirical scope-rigidity as external ground truth, or offers a causal fix. Unlike my prior grammatical-category imposition proposals (tense, gender, evidentiality, number, telicity, negation-concord), this targets QUANTIFIER SCOPE interaction (a semantics-interface/logical-form phenomenon), a distinct and previously mechanistically-untested axis with a strong cross-linguistic behavioral baseline.
Abstract: When English speakers hear 'every shark ate a pirate', two meanings are available: one shark-per-pirate (inverse scope) or one shared event structure (surface scope). Mandarin and Japanese are scope-RIGID: the same sentence grammatically licenses only the surface reading. This offers a clean cross-linguistic natural experiment. Multilingual language models build a shared semantic hub scaffolded by scope-flexible English. We ask a simple, previously untested mechanistic question: does that hub IMPOSE the availability of an inverse-scope reading onto scope-rigid languages, so the model reads an ambiguity the target grammar forbids? We hypothesize that (1) the model accepts/generates the inverse-scope interpretation of scope-rigid sentences far more than native speakers, tracking English scope-availability; (2) the size of this imposition tracks each language's empirical scope-rigidity; (3) a shared, ablatable 'scope-reading' direction (surface vs inverse) mediates it, with any residual language-specific rigidity signal in shallow, language-specific layers; and (4) steering toward surface-only readings restores faithful interpretation without harming quantifier comprehension. We build a controlled multilingual doubly-quantified suite with truth-value-judgment and interpretation probes across scope-rigid (Mandarin, Japanese, Korean) and scope-flexible (English, German, Russian) languages, on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM. Using difference-in-means scope-direction probes, logit-lens tracking, activation patching, and steering, we measure the imposition, its rigidity scaling, its mediation, and its causal correction. Metrics include inverse-scope-acceptance gap vs native norms, rigidity-prediction correlation, mediation R-squared, and steering-induced restoration with competence controls.
Experiments:
1) Doubly-quantified scope suite: Construct ~450 controlled doubly-quantified sentences (universal-over-existential and existential-over-universal, e.g. 'every X V-ed a Y') realized in scope-rigid languages (Mandarin, Japanese, Korean) and scope-flexible languages (English, German, Russian), native-speaker verified. For each item build (i) a truth-value-judgment task pairing the sentence with a picture/scenario describing the INVERSE-scope situation (accept/reject) vs the SURFACE-scope situation; (ii) an interpretation forced choice (which situation does the sentence describe?); (iii) a scope-NLI probe (does the sentence entail the inverse-scope paraphrase?); (iv) unambiguous single-quantifier controls (no scope interaction) to isolate scope-specific effects. Anchor per-language gold acceptability to the published behavioral norms (English inverse-scope available; Mandarin surface-only). Report inter-annotator agreement; release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral imposition (H1, core): Measure per-language inverse-scope-acceptance rate on scope-rigid-language items and compare against native-speaker norms. Define the imposition GAP = model inverse-scope acceptance minus native-speaker acceptance for scope-rigid languages (predicted large and positive), contrasted with scope-flexible languages (predicted small, since inverse scope is genuinely available). Verify correct handling of single-quantifier controls (no spurious ambiguity). Control for tokenizer fertility, quantifier-word frequency, and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test scope-rigidity status adds predictive power).
3) Rigidity-predicted imposition (H2, external validation): Using published scope-rigidity strength per language (English/German/Russian flexible; Mandarin strongly rigid; Japanese/Korean rigid), test whether per-language imposition is predicted by empirical rigidity (Spearman correlation; held-out prediction of imposition from the rigidity typology alone), tying the internal phenomenon to independent behavioral ground truth.
4) Representational localization (H3): Extract a 'scope-reading' direction via difference-in-means between representations biased toward the surface vs inverse reading (using disambiguating contexts) at each layer, per language. Test (a) whether a shared scope direction is English-scaffolded (cross-lingual cosine alignment across layers, aligned with the English inverse-available pole); (b) whether a scope-rigid-language input nonetheless projects toward the inverse-available pole in the shared hub while any residual surface-only-rigidity signal is stronger in early/language-specific layers, via logit-lens/tuned-lens depth tracking. Baseline: a quantifier-identity direction (present in all languages) as a within-model control. Mediation: regress behavioral imposition on shared-hub inverse-pole projection strength (partial correlation controlling for fertility/frequency; held-out R^2).
5) Causal steering/patching test (H4, core): (a) Steer the scope-rigid-language representation along the scope-reading direction toward the SURFACE-only pole and measure whether inverse-scope acceptance drops toward native-speaker norms (flip rate) and the imposition GAP shrinks, without switching output language. (b) For imposed items, patch the residual language-specific rigidity signal (from early/language-specific layers) into later computation and test restoration, localizing failure to the shared hub imposing English scope-availability over a shallowly-present rigidity signal. Critically verify QUANTIFIER COMPREHENSION preservation (single-quantifier controls and surface-reading judgments remain correct; the model must still license inverse scope in genuinely-flexible languages), plus fluency and off-target/language-mixing checks. Baselines: whole-hub English-steering, random-direction control.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify steering is scope-specific (changes surface/inverse availability but not quantifier identity or unrelated content), graded (imposition scales with rigidity), and not a lexical-frequency artifact (nonce-noun variants). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 shows stronger imposition than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM/Qwen (which see more scope-rigid-language data); test whether imposition magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the scope direction and with each language's training share. Qualitatively compare the model's per-language imposition pattern against the human scope-rigidity behavioral literature.
Evaluation metrics: inverse-scope-acceptance rate and imposition GAP vs native norms (scope-rigid vs scope-flexible languages; single-quantifier control preservation); imposition-vs-rigidity-typology correlation and held-out prediction; scope-NLI accuracy; shared-hub inverse-pole projection strength and crystallization depth (vs quantifier-identity baseline); cross-lingual scope-direction alignment; mediation regression (held-out R^2); steering flip rate and GAP reduction, patching-induced restoration; quantifier-comprehension preservation (surface readings, flexible-language inverse licensing), fluency, off-target rate; cross-model imposition comparison and correlation with training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for scope-rigidity over frequency/fertility/resource baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Scope-rigidity is itself debated and gradient (recent work finds inverse scope accessible in some Mandarin syntactic environments and bimodal speaker populations); we restrict core items to canonical simple-transitive doubly-quantified sentences where rigidity is best established, anchor gold to published norms, native-speaker verify, report inter-annotator agreement, and treat contested environments as a separate analysis. 2) Truth-value-judgment via text (describing the inverse-scope situation in words) may cue an interpretation; we use multiple probe formats (TVJ, forced choice, NLI), balance situation descriptions, and control wording across languages. 3) Scope-rigidity status is correlated with language family, script, and resource level; the scope-flexible comparison languages, single-quantifier controls, within-item surface-vs-inverse contrasts, and rigidity-based prediction isolate the scope pathway, but residual confounds may remain; we center on well-resourced Mandarin/Japanese vs English/German/Russian and treat Korean as an extension. 4) Difference-in-means scope directions may entangle quantifier-lexical or plurality features; we use nonce-noun variants, a quantifier-identity control direction, multiple extraction methods, and specificity checks. 5) Logit-lens/tuned-lens depth is approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 6) Some inverse-scope acceptance may reflect genuine, correct flexibility (the model rightly licensing it where the target grammar actually allows it); the direction of the effect (does it track ENGLISH availability or the TARGET rigidity?), the rigidity-typology prediction, and the flexible-language controls distinguish imposition from correct interpretation, and a finding of correct interpretation is itself valuable. 7) Steering could over-suppress inverse scope (harming genuinely-flexible languages) or fluency; we require preservation of flexible-language inverse licensing and single-quantifier controls as hard constraints and report the full tradeoff. 8) Instruction-tuned models may hedge or explain both readings; we test base models where available and use forced-choice and NLI probes. 9) The model-vs-human comparison is qualitative/structural (rigidity ordering), not a claim of identical mechanism. 10) If NO imposition is found - scope-rigid languages are read surface-only, predictable from typology, with quantifier comprehension preserved - this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the shared hub represents language-specific scope rigidity despite English scaffolding, valuable either way. 11) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: quote_verbatim_drift
Title: Say It Exactly: Does the Frame Language Corrupt Verbatim Quotations in Multilingual LLMs?
Short Hypothesis: A directly-quoted string should be reproduced verbatim regardless of the language of the surrounding (frame) text, because its exact wording is a fixed token sequence, not a meaning to be re-expressed. We hypothesize that multilingual LLMs violate this: when a quote in language Q is embedded in a frame written in a different language F, the model's tendency to route meaning through an F/English-scaffolded shared hub causes verbatim drift - the model paraphrases, translates, register-normalizes, or code-mixes the quote toward the frame language when reproducing it - and this drift increases with the typological distance between Q and F and with how strongly F is the model's dominant hub language. The drift is mediated by a shared 'reformulation' pressure at the copy step that competes with a verbatim-copy mechanism, and is causally reducible by strengthening the copy pathway without harming meaning-level tasks.
Related Work: Prior mechanistic work shows multilingual LLMs process input through an English-scaffolded shared concept hub and decode language-specifically in late layers (Do Llamas Work in English 2024; Do Multilingual LLMs Think In English 2025; Semantic Hub 2024; Lost in Multilinguality 2025), and that induction/copy heads implement verbatim token-copying monolingually (induction-head and copy-suppression literature). Cross-lingual work studies factual consistency, reasoning transfer, and code-switching generation failures (language confusion / language-mixing 2025), but always at the MEANING level - none asks whether a model can faithfully COPY a fixed string across a language boundary. Quotation and reported-speech NLP work is task-level (quote attribution, style transfer) and monolingual. No prior work (a) frames verbatim-quote reproduction as a language-invariance stress test that pits a copy mechanism against the shared hub's reformulation pressure, (b) measures frame-language-induced drift (paraphrase/translation/register-normalization/code-mix) as a function of quote-frame typological distance and hub dominance, (c) localizes the competition between a verbatim-copy pathway and a shared-hub reformulation pathway, or (d) offers a causal copy-strengthening fix. This is orthogonal to all my prior proposals, which concern how MEANING is represented/transferred, not whether SURFACE FORM survives a language boundary.
Abstract: When you quote someone directly, the words are fixed: reproducing '‘Je ne sais pas’, she said' inside an English sentence must keep the French verbatim, because a quote is a surface string, not a meaning to be re-expressed. This makes verbatim quotation a clean language-invariance test that no prior interpretability work has run. We hypothesize that multilingual LLMs fail it: because they route meaning through a frame/English-scaffolded shared hub, they exert a reformulation pressure that corrupts a quote in language Q when the surrounding frame is in a different language F - paraphrasing, translating, register-normalizing, or code-mixing it toward F when asked to reproduce it. We predict this verbatim drift grows with the typological distance between Q and F and with how dominant F is in the model's hub, and that it reflects a competition between a verbatim-copy mechanism and shared-hub reformulation at the copy step. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using a controlled suite where quotes in diverse languages are embedded in frames of varying languages and the model must reproduce, translate around, or reason about the quote. Using logit-lens copy-vs-reformulation tracking, activation patching, and copy-pathway steering, we measure drift, its distance/dominance scaling, its mechanistic locus, and a causal fix. Metrics include verbatim-exact-match drift rate, frame-language pull, distance/dominance prediction, copy-vs-reformulation attribution, and steering-induced fidelity recovery with meaning-task controls.
Experiments:
1) Verbatim-quote suite: Build ~500 items each containing a short DIRECT QUOTE in a quote language Q embedded in a frame sentence in a frame language F (Q != F), spanning typologically diverse Q and F (English, French, German, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish) crossed to vary Q-F distance and script match. Tasks: (i) VERBATIM REPRODUCTION ('Repeat the quoted sentence exactly'); (ii) FRAME-PRESERVING CONTINUATION (continue the frame, requiring the quote to be re-cited verbatim); (iii) a MEANING-LEVEL control task (translate or summarize the quote - where reformulation IS correct); (iv) same-language control (Q=F). Include register-marked quotes (slang, honorific, dialect) to detect register-normalization. Native-speaker verify; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral drift map (H1, core): On verbatim tasks, measure the verbatim-drift rate = 1 - exact-match of the reproduced quote against the original, and decompose drift into (a) translation-toward-F, (b) paraphrase, (c) register-normalization, (d) code-mixing/script-shift. Establish that drift is high when Q!=F and near-zero when Q=F (isolating a frame-language effect), and near-zero on the meaning-level control confirms the model CAN reformulate when appropriate - so verbatim failure is a copy failure, not incompetence. Control for tokenizer fertility and quote length (partial correlations).
3) Distance and dominance scaling (H2): Test whether per-item drift is predicted by (a) Q-F typological/script distance and (b) how dominant F is in the model's hub (measured via baseline logit-lens English/hub-routing strength), better than by resource level alone (nested regression, AIC, held-out R^2). Predict drift toward F (frame-language pull) rises with distance and with F-dominance; predict quotes drift toward F even when F is not English if F is the frame.
4) Mechanistic locus (copy vs reformulation): Using logit-lens/tuned-lens at the quote-reproduction positions, track whether the emitted token follows a verbatim-copy signal (attention to the original quote tokens, induction/copy-head activity) or a shared-hub reformulation signal (mid-layer meaning representation decoding to an F-language paraphrase). Extract a difference-in-means 'reformulation-pressure' direction (drifted vs faithful reproductions). Activation patching: for a drifted item, patch (a) the copy-head outputs / attention to the source quote and (b) suppress the shared-hub reformulation representation; test which restores verbatim fidelity. Report copy-failure vs reformulation-override error shares.
5) Core causal intervention (copy strengthening): Strengthen the verbatim-copy pathway at the reproduction step - amplify attention to the source-quote positions and/or suppress the reformulation-pressure direction - and measure verbatim-fidelity recovery. Critically verify SPECIFICITY: the intervention must NOT harm the meaning-level control tasks (translate/summarize must still work) and must not switch the FRAME language or fluency (off-target rate). Compare against baselines: prompt-reinforcement ('copy exactly, do not translate'), whole-hub English-steering (predicted to WORSEN drift), and random-direction control. Compute recovery elasticity = fidelity gain per unit baseline drift, correlated with H2 distance/dominance.
6) Cross-model contrast: Predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show stronger frame-language pull toward English (and stronger drift when F=English) than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether drift magnitude correlates with hub F-dominance and each language's training share.
Evaluation metrics: verbatim-drift rate and drift-type decomposition (Q!=F vs Q=F vs meaning-control); frame-language pull; distance/dominance prediction of drift (held-out R^2 over resource/fertility); copy-vs-reformulation attribution and error shares; copy-strengthening fidelity recovery and elasticity vs baselines, with meaning-task and frame-language preservation (specificity), off-target rate; cross-model drift comparison and correlation with hub dominance and training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Tokenizer fertility and quote length strongly affect exact-match; we control for both, use character-level and normalized edit-distance alongside exact-match, and include same-language (Q=F) items as the within-model baseline that isolates the frame-language effect from generic copy difficulty. 2) 'Drift' could partly reflect legitimate normalization (e.g., the model helpfully translating for the reader); the meaning-level control task and the explicit 'repeat exactly' instruction distinguish a copy failure from appropriate reformulation, and we report items where intent is ambiguous. 3) Q-F distance is confounded with script and resource level; partial correlations, script-matched vs script-mismatched pairs, and the F-dominance measure (which varies the frame independent of resource) mitigate but may not fully remove confounds. 4) Copy vs reformulation may not separate cleanly; we use multiple patching granularities (copy-head attention, reformulation direction) and report ambiguous cases. 5) The copy-strengthening intervention could harm meaning-level tasks or fluency; meaning-task preservation and frame-language non-switching are hard specificity constraints and we report the full tradeoff. 6) Logit-lens copy/reformulation tracking is approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with attention attribution. 7) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM's more diverse hub analyzed as a contrast expected to show weaker English-frame pull). 8) If NO drift is found - quotes are reproduced verbatim regardless of frame language - this is an informative POSITIVE result showing a robust language-invariant copy mechanism that overrides shared-hub reformulation, valuable either way. 9) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: false_friend_sense_interference
Title: Poison or Present? Interlingual-Homograph False Friends Cause Competing-Language Sense Interference in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: When a multilingual LLM reads an interlingual homograph (a false friend: a word form that exists in two of its languages with DIFFERENT meanings, e.g. German 'Gift'=poison vs English 'gift'=present), the form-identical sense from the NON-context language leaks into and interferes with the model's reasoning about the word in the context language. This interference is not merely lower disambiguation accuracy but a directional competing-sense pull: the model's inferences, associations, and entailments about the word shift toward the wrong-language meaning, mediated by a shared form-driven representation that fails to fully gate the competing sense, and scales with the frequency/salience of the competing-language sense. It is causally suppressible by ablating the competing-language sense signal without harming genuine cognates.
Related Work: Recent behavioral work shows multilingual LLMs rely on orthographic similarity over semantics for interlingual homographs, performing below random on disambiguating false friends (Multilingual LLMs Struggle to Link Orthography and Semantics 2025), and that cross-lingual concept patching makes models translate rather than copy homographs (When Meanings Meet 2026). Monolingual mechanistic work identifies word-sense-disambiguation attention heads (Start Making Sense(s) 2025), sense-encoding geometry (Let's Play Mono-Poly 2021; LASeR 2021), and ambiguity probes (Trick or Neat 2025). False-friends-in-transfer work (False Friends Are Not Foes 2025) studies token overlap as a transfer aid. CRITICALLY, all prior work is either behavioral (does the model disambiguate?) or monolingual (how is a single-language sense encoded), and treats false-friend failure as a disambiguation-accuracy deficit. NONE asks whether the competing NON-context-language sense actively CONTAMINATES downstream reasoning about the word (a directional interference, not just noise), whether a shared form-driven representation carries the competing sense into the context-language computation, whether the leak scales with the competing sense's salience, or whether ablating the competing-sense signal removes the interference while leaving genuine cognates (same form, same meaning) untouched. This differs from my prior loanword-donor-leakage proposal, which concerned fully-integrated borrowed words that keep their meaning; false friends are form-identical words with genuinely DIFFERENT, competing meanings, making this an interference/competition phenomenon with a clean cognate control.
Abstract: A false friend is a word that looks identical across two languages but means different things: German 'Gift' means poison, English 'gift' means present. Reading such an interlingual homograph correctly requires suppressing the meaning it carries in the model's OTHER language. Prior work shows multilingual LLMs disambiguate false friends poorly, relying on orthographic form over meaning, but treats this as a flat accuracy deficit. We propose a sharper, mechanistic phenomenon: the competing non-context-language sense actively LEAKS INTO and interferes with the model's reasoning about the word, producing a directional pull toward the wrong-language meaning rather than mere noise. We hypothesize that (1) the model's inferences and entailments about a false friend shift toward its other-language sense, measurable as a competing-sense-pull absent for genuine cognates (same form, same meaning) in the same contexts; (2) this pull scales with the frequency/salience of the competing-language sense; (3) a shared form-driven representation carries the competing sense into the context-language computation, with the correct sense recoverable but under-weighted; and (4) ablating the competing-sense signal removes the interference while leaving cognate processing intact. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM across English paired with German, French, and Spanish, using controlled false-friend / cognate / control-word triples in disambiguating contexts. Combining logit-lens sense tracking, difference-in-means sense-direction probes, activation patching, and steering, we measure the interference, its salience scaling, its mechanistic locus, and its causal suppression. Metrics include competing-sense-pull, cognate-controlled interference gap, salience prediction, and suppression-induced recovery with cognate-preservation controls.
Experiments:
1) False-friend / cognate / control suite: Assemble ~400 word triples for English paired with German, French, and Spanish: (a) FALSE FRIENDS (interlingual homographs: same/near-same form, DIFFERENT meaning, e.g. Gift, Rat, Brief, actual/actuel, embarazada); (b) COGNATES (same form, SAME meaning, e.g. blind/blind) as the key control; (c) matched MONOLINGUAL-UNAMBIGUOUS words. Embed each in context-language sentences that clearly license the CONTEXT-language meaning. Reasoning probes hinge on the meaning, not on recognizing foreignness: (i) sense-inference forced choice (which meaning is intended?); (ii) entailment probe (does the sentence entail a consequence of the context-sense vs the competing-sense?); (iii) association/typicality judgment; (iv) short reasoning where the answer depends on the correct sense. Native-speaker verify forms, meanings, and gold labels; annotate each false friend with the corpus frequency of its competing-language sense. Report inter-annotator agreement; release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral competing-sense interference (H1, core): Measure, per false friend, whether the model's inferences shift toward the COMPETING (wrong-language) sense relative to a matched cognate/unambiguous word in the SAME context. Define competing-sense-pull = signed shift toward the competing meaning, and the cognate-controlled interference GAP = pull(false friends) minus pull(cognates). Predict a positive gap: form-identity alone (cognates) does not cause interference; only genuine meaning-competition (false friends) does. Control for word frequency, tokenizer fertility, and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test false-friend status adds predictive power beyond form-identity and frequency).
3) Salience scaling (H2): Test whether per-word interference is predicted by the frequency/salience of the competing-language sense (Spearman correlation; held-out prediction), i.e., false friends whose other-language meaning is high-frequency leak more. This ties interference to an independent lexical variable and distinguishes it from generic difficulty.
4) Mechanistic localization (H3): Extract per-word context-sense vs competing-sense directions via difference-in-means over disambiguated exemplars, at each layer. Using logit-lens/tuned-lens, track whether a false friend's mid-layer representation carries a strong competing-sense signal (the wrong-language meaning decodable) that a cognate does not, and whether the correct sense is present but under-weighted. Mediation: regress behavioral competing-sense-pull on the competing-sense signal strength in the shared representation (partial correlation controlling for frequency/fertility; held-out R^2). Compare cross-lingual alignment to test whether a shared form-driven representation activates both senses.
5) Causal suppression/steering test (core): (a) Ablate the competing-language sense direction from the false friend's representation (difference-in-means projection removal / INLP nullspace) and test whether the interference GAP drops toward the cognate baseline; (b) conversely, AMPLIFY the competing-sense direction and confirm it induces more wrong-sense inference (bidirectional dose-response); (c) for individual interfered items, patch the context-sense representation (from a monolingual context-language pass) into the false-friend pass and test restoration. Critically verify COGNATE PRESERVATION and comprehension: the intervention must NOT harm cognate processing (form-identical, meaning-shared words must stay correct), must not switch output language, and must preserve fluency (off-target/language-mixing rate). Baselines: random-direction ablation, whole-hub English-steering.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify suppression is sense-specific (removes competing-sense pull but not genuine meaning or unrelated attributes) and not a lexical-frequency artifact (frequency-matched false-friend/cognate pairs). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 shows stronger pull toward the English sense (when English is the competing language) than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether interference magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the sense direction and with each competing language's training share.
Evaluation metrics: competing-sense-pull and cognate-controlled interference GAP (false friends vs cognates vs unambiguous controls); interference-vs-competing-sense-salience correlation and held-out prediction; competing-sense signal strength in the shared representation and its mediation of behavioral pull (held-out R^2); ablation-induced GAP reduction and amplification-induced pull increase (bidirectional); patching-induced restoration; cognate-preservation and comprehension (specificity), off-target rate; cross-model interference comparison and correlation with competing-language training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for false-friend status over form-identity and frequency baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) False friends vary in degree (fully vs partially divergent meaning, exact vs near-identical form); we native-speaker verify and restrict the core set to clear, exact-form, fully-divergent-meaning false friends, treating partial cases separately, and report inter-annotator agreement. 2) The cognate control is essential and elegant: it holds form-identity constant while varying meaning-competition, so a positive interference GAP cannot be explained by form-identity or transfer alone; but cognates and false friends may differ in frequency, so we use frequency-matched pairs and partial correlations. 3) Some competing-sense pull might reflect correct uncertainty (the word genuinely is ambiguous out of context); we use contexts that CLEARLY license the context-language sense and native-speaker verify licensing, treating remaining ambiguity as a covariate. 4) Difference-in-means sense directions may entangle orthographic/frequency features; we use multiple extraction methods, frequency-matched controls, and the cognate baseline. 5) Logit-lens/tuned-lens sense tracking is approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 6) Ablation could harm legitimate meaning or cognates; cognate-preservation is a hard specificity constraint and we report the full tradeoff plus the bidirectional dose-response. 7) English is the pivot/high-resource language in all pairs, so competing-language salience is confounded with resource level; the salience scaling (Exp 3) uses per-word competing-sense frequency to partially disentangle this, and we test both directions (English-as-context and English-as-competing). 8) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM's more diverse hub analyzed as a contrast). 9) If NO interference GAP is found (false friends behave like cognates once context disambiguates), this is an informative POSITIVE result showing robust context-driven sense gating that overrides form-identity, valuable either way and complementary to the behavioral finding that isolated-word disambiguation fails. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: source_language_transfer_asymmetry
Title: Taught in the Hub, Shared with All: The Source Language of Skill Fine-Tuning Sets a Directional Transfer Gravity Well
Short Hypothesis: When a reasoning skill (not knowledge) is taught to a multilingual LLM by fine-tuning in a single source language, the *choice of source language* sets a directional 'gravity well': fine-tuning in the model's hub-central language (typically English) writes the skill into the shared middle-layer representation and transfers broadly, whereas fine-tuning the SAME skill on the SAME data translated into a peripheral, hub-misaligned language writes a more language-entangled update that transfers worse AND retroactively degrades the skill in previously-competent languages. Transfer breadth and interference are jointly predicted by a single quantity — the source language's baseline middle-layer alignment to the hub — not by the source language's own resource level or its typological distance to each target.
Related Work: Prior work shows knowledge-free reasoning transfers near-perfectly across languages while knowledge does not (Cross-Lingual Knowledge-Free Reasoners 2024), that single-language fine-tuning disrupts early/middle-layer interlingual alignment and freezing those layers helps (High-Dimensional Interlingual Representations 2025), that middle-layer alignment is the locus of transfer and can be explicitly aligned (Middle-Layer Representation Alignment 2025; Can you map it to English 2025), and that layer-swapping / task arithmetic can compose separately-trained language and skill experts (Layer Swapping 2024; Task Arithmetic for Cross-Lingual Transfer 2024; Model Merging 2025). Formation-tracing work (Beyond the Rosetta Stone 2025; Cross-Lingual Generalization and Compression 2025) shows representations unify over training. CRITICALLY, all of this treats transfer breadth as a property of the TARGET language or of an alignment intervention, and treats the source language as a fixed (usually English) given. NONE isolates the SOURCE language of skill fine-tuning as a causal, directional variable that jointly governs (a) how broadly the skill transfers and (b) whether it interferes with the skill in other already-competent languages, nor predicts both from a single measurable quantity (the source language's baseline middle-layer hub alignment) rather than from resource level or source-target typological distance. We reframe source-language choice from an incidental setup detail into a predictable transfer-and-interference controller with a mechanistic (representation-pull) cause and a targeted fix.
Abstract: To teach a multilingual model a reasoning skill you usually fine-tune it in one language and hope the skill transfers to the others. We ask a simple, previously untested question: does it matter WHICH language you teach in — not for how much the model learns, but for the directional shape of what transfers? We hypothesize a transfer gravity well: fine-tuning a language-independent skill in the model's hub-central language writes the update into the shared middle-layer representation and transfers broadly with little side effect, whereas teaching the SAME skill on the SAME (translated) data in a peripheral, hub-misaligned source language writes a more language-entangled update that transfers worse AND retroactively degrades the skill in languages the model already handled. Crucially, we predict both transfer breadth and this retroactive interference are jointly predicted by ONE quantity — the source language's baseline middle-layer alignment to the hub — rather than by its resource level or its typological distance to each target. We test this on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM by LoRA-fine-tuning on knowledge-free reasoning skills (multi-step arithmetic, symbolic logic, list operations) whose training data is identical up to translation across a panel of source languages spanning the hub-alignment spectrum, then evaluating the skill in every target language before and after. Using logit-lens/middle-layer alignment measures, representation-drift tracking, and a freeze/align intervention, we test whether hub alignment predicts breadth and interference, whether the update pulls the skill representation toward the source language's subspace, and whether protecting middle-layer alignment restores broad, interference-free transfer. Metrics include transfer-breadth and retroactive-interference curves, hub-alignment predictive R-squared over resource/distance baselines, representation-pull magnitude, and intervention-induced breadth recovery.
Experiments:
1) Knowledge-free skill suite and source-language panel: Build ~3 reasoning skills with verified symbolic-oracle answers and NO factual-knowledge dependence (multi-step arithmetic, k-step symbolic logic, list/string operations), following the knowledge-free-reasoning design. Create training sets that are IDENTICAL up to translation across a panel of ~7 source languages spanning the hub-alignment spectrum from hub-central to peripheral (e.g., English, French, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish), native-speaker verified. Hold a fixed set of ~10 target languages (including source-panel members and held-out languages) for evaluation. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Baseline hub-alignment measurement: Before any fine-tuning, measure each candidate source language's middle-layer alignment to the model's hub (using DALI/ILO-style middle-layer retrieval alignment and logit-lens English/hub-decodability). This yields a per-language hub-alignment score, computed independently of the transfer experiment.
3) Fine-tune-and-transfer sweep (core): For each skill, LoRA-fine-tune the model separately on each source language's (translated-identical) data. Evaluate the skill in every target language before and after. Measure (a) TRANSFER BREADTH = mean post-tuning skill accuracy across target languages, and (b) RETROACTIVE INTERFERENCE = drop in skill accuracy on target languages the base model already handled correctly. Test H1: hub-central source languages give broader transfer and less interference; peripheral source languages give narrower transfer and more interference.
4) Single-predictor test (H2, core): Test whether BOTH transfer breadth and retroactive interference are predicted by the source language's baseline hub-alignment score (from Exp 2), and whether hub alignment beats (a) source-language resource level and (b) source-target typological/embedding distance, via nested regression / model comparison (AIC, held-out R^2). Prediction: hub alignment is the dominant, source-target-distance-independent predictor — a skill taught in a hub-aligned language transfers to typologically distant targets, while a skill taught in a hub-misaligned language fails to transfer even to close targets.
5) Representation-pull mechanism (Location + Formation tracing): Track how the skill representation moves during fine-tuning. Extract the skill's middle-layer representation direction and measure, per source language, how much the update PULLS it toward the source language's language-specific subspace (drift toward the source-language direction) vs into the shared hub. Test that peripheral-source fine-tuning produces larger source-subspace pull, and that pull magnitude mediates both reduced breadth and increased interference (mediation regression; held-out R^2). Cross-check with the interlingual-alignment (ILO) drop after tuning.
6) Causal intervention (Tuning & Editing): Protect middle-layer hub alignment during peripheral-source fine-tuning via (a) freezing early/middle alignment-critical layers (per High-Dimensional Interlingual Representations 2025) and (b) a middle-layer alignment regularizer (per Middle-Layer Representation Alignment 2025). Predict this selectively rescues broad, interference-free transfer for peripheral source languages (raising them toward hub-central breadth) while barely affecting hub-central sources, and reduces representation-pull. Compare against baselines: naive LoRA, layer-swapping composition (Layer Swapping 2024), and a random-layer-freeze control. Report breadth recovery, interference reduction, source-language skill retention (the skill must still be learned in the source language), and off-target/fluency checks.
7) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify the effect is skill-transfer-specific (a knowledge-heavy task, as a contrast, should show weak transfer regardless of source language, per the knowledge-vs-reasoning split), that gains are not from generic extra regularization, and that source-language skill learning is preserved. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 shows a steeper hub-alignment dependence than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether the gravity-well slope correlates with the model's overall hub-centricity.
Evaluation metrics: per-source-language transfer-breadth and retroactive-interference curves; hub-alignment predictive R^2 for breadth and interference (vs resource-level and source-target-distance baselines, AIC/held-out); representation-pull magnitude and its mediation of breadth/interference (held-out R^2); ILO/DALI alignment drop after tuning; intervention-induced breadth recovery, interference reduction, source-skill retention, off-target rate; knowledge-task contrast; cross-model gravity-well-slope comparison and correlation with hub-centricity.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) 'Hub alignment', source-language resource level, and typological distance are correlated across natural languages, making the single-predictor claim hard to isolate; we mitigate by choosing a source panel that decorrelates them where possible (e.g., a mid-resource but hub-aligned language vs a similar-resource hub-misaligned one) and report partial correlations, but residual confounding may remain. 2) LoRA vs full fine-tuning may change the drift/interference pattern; we run LoRA as the primary (cheap, academic-feasible) setting and validate a subset with light full fine-tuning. 3) Retroactive interference could be generic catastrophic forgetting rather than source-language-directed pull; the representation-pull mediation (Exp 5) and the identical-up-to-translation data design (holding skill content fixed) are meant to isolate the directional effect, and we report forgetting on unrelated capabilities as a baseline. 4) Ensuring the skill is genuinely knowledge-free (so transfer is not blocked by the knowledge-retrieval barrier) is essential; we use symbolic tasks and include a knowledge-heavy contrast to confirm the split. 5) Translation of training data may introduce quality differences across source languages that confound learning difficulty; we control source-language skill-learning success and only compare transfer conditional on comparable source-language learning. 6) The freeze/align intervention could harm source-language skill acquisition; we require source-skill retention as a hard constraint and report the tradeoff. 7) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM's less English-centric hub analyzed as a contrast). 8) If transfer breadth is NOT predicted by source hub-alignment (e.g., it is symmetric, or governed only by source-target distance), this is an informative negative result clarifying that source-language choice is incidental — valuable either way. 9) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: construction_overgeneralization_negative_transfer
Title: Grammatical in English, Wrong in Japanese: Multilingual LLMs Overgeneralize Dominant-Language Constructions Into Languages That Forbid Them
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs commit a distinctive negative-transfer error: they accept and generate a syntactic construction in a target language that grammatically FORBIDS it, because the construction is licensed in the model's dominant (English) language and leaks through the shared hub. We hypothesize this construction-overgeneralization is not random incompetence but a directional, predictable phenomenon: the model rates target-language sentences instantiating an English-licensed-but-target-forbidden construction as MORE acceptable than native speakers do, the effect is mediated by a shared construction direction whose strength is set by the dominant language, scales with how central English is to the model's hub, and is causally suppressible by ablating that direction without harming genuinely-grammatical target-language constructions.
Related Work: CLI work shows LLMs co-activate L1 during L2 processing and prime ungrammatical structures dominance-sensitively (Language Models as Artificial Learners 2026), but studies priming shifts, not standing acceptability of forbidden constructions. Cross-lingual syntactic-transfer probing shows transfer is limited and can cause negative interference (Understanding Cross-Lingual Syntactic Transfer 2020; How multilingual is M-BERT 2019), and synthetic/artificial-language work studies architectural word-order biases (Studying Inductive Biases 2019; Artificial Languages 2021), but none tests whether a modern generative multilingual LLM ACCEPTS a construction its target grammar forbids because English licenses it, none localizes a shared construction direction mediating the leak, ties the overgeneralization to hub-centrality, or offers a causal ablation fix. BICAUSE (2025) shows LLMs rigidly apply dominant causal word orders but focuses on causal reasoning attention, not grammatical acceptability of forbidden constructions. We uniquely reframe cross-lingual grammatical error as directional construction-overgeneralization from the dominant language, with a mechanistic mediating direction and a causal fix, distinct from priming, transfer-efficiency, and reasoning-bias accounts.
Abstract: Languages license different syntactic constructions: English allows preposition stranding ('the book which I told you about'), a bare double-object dative ('give me the book'), and certain wh-extractions that Japanese, Russian, German, or Spanish grammatically forbid or realize differently. Multilingual language models build a shared, largely English-scaffolded representation. We ask a simple, previously untested question: does a multilingual LLM overgeneralize an English-licensed construction into a target language that forbids it, judging ungrammatical target-language sentences as acceptable because English permits the construction? We hypothesize a directional construction-overgeneralization: (1) the model rates target-language instantiations of English-licensed-but-target-forbidden constructions as more acceptable than native-speaker norms, while judging target-language-native constructions correctly; (2) the effect is mediated by a shared construction direction whose acceptability weighting is set by the dominant language; (3) it scales with how English-central the model's hub is and with each construction's cross-lingual divergence; and (4) ablating the shared construction direction removes the overgeneralization without harming genuinely-grammatical target-language constructions. We build a controlled multilingual minimal-pair suite of constructions that diverge between English and target languages (Japanese, Russian, German, Spanish, Hindi), with native-verified grammaticality, on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM. Combining acceptability measurement, difference-in-means construction-direction probes, activation patching, and steering, we measure the overgeneralization, its divergence scaling, its mediation, and its causal suppression. Metrics include overgeneralization acceptability gap versus native norms, divergence-prediction correlation, mediation R-squared, and ablation-induced correction with grammatical-construction preservation controls.
Experiments:
