1) Divergent-construction minimal-pair suite: Assemble ~500 minimal pairs across constructions that are grammatical in English but FORBIDDEN or differently-realized in target languages (Japanese, Russian, German, Spanish, Hindi): preposition stranding, double-object dative, certain wh-extractions/islands, adjective-noun order, that-trace effects. For each, build (a) a target-language sentence instantiating the English-style construction (ungrammatical in target), (b) the grammatical target-language counterpart, and (c) an English control. Also include CONVERGENT constructions (grammatical in both) as a control. Native-speaker verify grammaticality; report inter-annotator agreement; annotate each construction's cross-lingual divergence. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral overgeneralization (H1, core): Measure acceptability (log-prob preference / forced-choice grammaticality judgment) for the English-style-in-target sentence vs its grammatical target counterpart. Define overgeneralization = the degree to which the model prefers/accepts the forbidden construction relative to native-speaker norms. Verify the model judges CONVERGENT constructions and English controls correctly (isolating a directional English-into-target leak, not general incompetence). Control for tokenizer fertility, sentence frequency, and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test forbidden-construction status adds predictive power).
3) Divergence scaling (H2, external validation): Using each construction's cross-lingual divergence and each language's typological distance from English, test whether per-construction, per-language overgeneralization is predicted by divergence (Spearman; held-out prediction), tying the phenomenon to independent linguistic ground truth. Predict stronger overgeneralization for more English-distant languages.
4) Representational localization (H3): Extract a shared 'construction' direction via difference-in-means between English-construction-present and construction-absent representations at each layer, and measure cross-lingual alignment (is a single English-scaffolded construction direction re-used in the target language?). Test whether a forbidden-construction target sentence projects onto this English construction direction in the shared hub, via logit-lens/tuned-lens depth tracking. Mediation: regress behavioral overgeneralization on shared-hub construction-projection strength (partial correlation controlling for fertility/frequency; held-out R^2). Baseline: a lexical-content direction as a within-model control.
5) Causal suppression/steering test (H4, core): (a) Ablate the shared construction direction from the target-language representation (difference-in-means projection removal / INLP nullspace) and test whether overgeneralization drops toward native-speaker norms; (b) conversely AMPLIFY it and confirm it induces more acceptance of the forbidden construction (bidirectional dose-response); (c) for individual overgeneralized items, patch the target-language grammatical representation and test correction. Critically verify GRAMMATICAL-CONSTRUCTION PRESERVATION: the model must still accept genuinely-grammatical target-language constructions (including CONVERGENT ones and the grammatical counterparts) and still correctly license the construction in English (no over-suppression), plus fluency and off-target/language-mixing checks. Baselines: random-direction ablation, whole-hub English-steering.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify suppression is construction-specific (removes the forbidden-construction acceptance but not unrelated grammatical judgments), graded (overgeneralization scales with divergence), and not a frequency artifact (nonce-lexicalized variants). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show stronger overgeneralization than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether overgeneralization magnitude correlates with the model's hub English-centrality (baseline logit-lens English-routing strength) and with each target language's training share. Qualitatively relate the pattern to human L2 negative-transfer / overgeneralization findings (direction, not identical mechanism).
Evaluation metrics: overgeneralization acceptability gap vs native norms (forbidden constructions vs convergent controls vs English controls); overgeneralization-vs-divergence correlation and held-out prediction; shared construction-direction cross-lingual alignment and forbidden-sentence projection strength, with mediation of behavioral overgeneralization (held-out R^2); ablation-induced overgeneralization reduction and amplification-induced increase (bidirectional); patching-induced correction; grammatical-construction preservation and English-licensing preservation (specificity), fluency, off-target rate; cross-model overgeneralization comparison and correlation with hub English-centrality and training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for forbidden-construction status over frequency/fertility/resource baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Grammaticality of a construction in a target language can be gradient or dialect/register dependent; we restrict to clearly forbidden/clearly-divergent constructions with native-speaker verification, report inter-annotator agreement, and exclude low-agreement items. 2) Forbidden-construction status is correlated with language family, script, and resource level; the CONVERGENT controls, grammatical counterparts, English controls, and divergence-based prediction isolate the overgeneralization pathway, but residual confounds may remain; we center core claims on well-resourced target languages and treat Hindi as an extension. 3) Overgeneralization could reflect general target-language incompetence rather than directional English leak; the directionality (accepts specifically the English-licensed construction), the convergent-control correctness, and the causal ablation/amplification (which move acceptance by editing only the construction direction) distinguish leak from incompetence. 4) Difference-in-means construction directions may entangle lexical/positional features; we use nonce-lexicalized variants, a lexical-content control direction, multiple extraction methods, and specificity checks. 5) Log-prob acceptability vs forced-choice may diverge; we report both and use native-speaker norms as the external benchmark. 6) Ablation could harm legitimate grammatical judgments; grammatical-construction and English-licensing preservation are hard specificity constraints and we report the full tradeoff plus the bidirectional dose-response. 7) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM's more diverse hub analyzed as a contrast expected to overgeneralize less). 8) The human-LLM comparison (L2 negative transfer/overgeneralization) is qualitative, not a claim of identical mechanism. 9) If NO overgeneralization is found — the model correctly rejects forbidden constructions in each target language regardless of English licensing — this is an informative POSITIVE result showing language-specific grammatical competence robust to dominant-language leakage, valuable either way. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: metrical_stress_imposition
Title: Hearing English Stress in a Silent Model: Does the Shared Hub Impose a Dominant-Language Metrical/Rhythm Template onto Other Languages?
Short Hypothesis: Text-only multilingual LLMs implicitly represent word stress and metrical structure (which syllable is prominent, how a word is rhythmically parsed) despite never hearing speech, and because this representation is scaffolded by English (a stress-timed, variable-stress language), the model IMPOSES an English-like metrical/rhythm template onto languages with different prosodic typology: it mis-places primary stress and mis-parses rhythm in fixed-stress (French final, Polish penultimate, Finnish initial) and syllable-timed languages, tracking the English/dominant-language stress pattern rather than the target language's rule. This imposition surfaces in stress-, rhyme-, meter-, and syllable-count-dependent tasks, is mediated by a shared, steerable metrical-prominence direction, tracks each language's empirical stress typology, and is causally correctable without harming lexical comprehension.
Related Work: Prosody/rhythm interpretability is almost entirely about SPEECH models: SSL models encode suprasegmental tone/stress/prominence in middle layers, language-specifically driven by context (Layer-wise Mandarin/English suprasegmentals 2024; Encoding of lexical tone 2024; Phonological Vector Arithmetic 2026), and CNNs/RNNs learn distributed stress cues from audio (How does a DNN look at lexical stress 2026; Prominence classification 2019). Text-model work shows BERT captures prosodic PROMINENCE from syntax/semantics in middle layers (What does BERT learn about prosody 2023) and language embeddings sometimes encode typological features (Language Embeddings Contain Typological Generalizations 2023). Speech-rhythm-typology work (RNN rhythm characterization 2024; rhythm-class clustering 2013; coupled-oscillator 2002) classifies languages as stress/syllable-timed acoustically. CRITICALLY, no prior work asks whether a TEXT-only multilingual LLM (which has no acoustic input) nonetheless represents word STRESS/METRICAL structure, whether its shared, English-scaffolded hub IMPOSES an English-like metrical/rhythm template onto languages with different stress typology (fixed vs variable stress; stress- vs syllable-timed), whether this causes mis-stress/mis-meter/mis-syllabification predictable from stress typology, or whether a shared metrical-prominence direction mediates and can be steered to correct it. This is orthogonal to all my prior imposition proposals (tense, gender, evidentiality, honorifics, spatial frames, number, telicity, negation, punctuation, information structure, scope), which target grammatical/semantic/orthographic axes, never metrical/prosodic structure learned from text alone.
Abstract: Word stress and rhythm are prosodic — you hear them — yet a text-only language model must implicitly represent them to rhyme, scan meter, count syllables, or reason about word boundaries. Languages differ sharply in this structure: English has variable, lexically-contrastive stress and is stress-timed, while French stresses the final syllable, Polish the penultimate, Finnish the initial, and many languages are syllable-timed. Multilingual LLMs build a shared, English-scaffolded representation. We ask a simple, previously untested question: does a text-only multilingual LLM represent metrical/stress structure at all, and if so, does its English-scaffolded hub IMPOSE an English-like metrical template onto languages with different prosodic typology? We hypothesize that (1) the model implicitly encodes a decodable word-stress/prominence representation despite never hearing speech; (2) it mis-places primary stress and mis-parses rhythm in fixed-stress and syllable-timed languages, tracking the English/dominant pattern rather than the target-language rule; (3) the size of this imposition tracks each language's empirical stress typology; and (4) a shared, steerable metrical-prominence direction mediates it, correctable toward the target-language pattern without harming lexical comprehension. We build a controlled multilingual suite of stress-, rhyme-, meter-, and syllable-count-dependent items across languages spanning stress typology (English, French, Polish, Finnish, Spanish, Turkish, plus tonal Mandarin as a contrast), on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM. Using difference-in-means prominence probes, logit-lens tracking, activation patching, and steering, we measure the imposition, its typology scaling, its mediation, and its causal correction. Metrics include stress-placement error rate, cross-lingual imposition gap, typology-prediction correlation, mediation R-squared, and steering-induced restoration with competence controls.
Experiments:
1) Metrical/stress suite: Construct ~500 items across languages spanning stress typology: variable-stress stress-timed (English, German, Russian), fixed-stress (French=final, Polish=penultimate, Finnish=initial, Turkish=final), syllable-timed (Spanish, Italian), and a tonal contrast (Mandarin, where lexical tone replaces stress). Task types: (a) PRIMARY-STRESS placement (given a word, which syllable carries primary stress? — verified from pronunciation dictionaries/Wiktionary IPA); (b) RHYME judgment (do two words rhyme? which depends on stressed-syllable alignment); (c) METER/scansion (does a line fit a target metrical pattern? or complete a line to fit meter); (d) SYLLABLE COUNT and stress-pattern matching. Present orthographically (no phonetic input) to test text-only metrical knowledge. Native-speaker/dictionary verify gold stress and rhyme; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Does the model represent stress at all (H1)? Train a linear probe on internal states to predict per-word primary-stress position, per language and layer. Test whether stress is decodable above chance from a text-only model and identify where (predict middle layers, mirroring speech-model and BERT-prominence findings). This establishes the phenomenon before testing imposition.
3) Behavioral imposition (H2, core): Measure stress-placement error rate per language, decomposing errors by whether the model places stress where the DOMINANT/English pattern (or an English-like variable/penultimate default) would, rather than the target-language rule. Define the imposition GAP = error on languages whose stress rule DIVERGES from the English default minus error on convergent cases, and an English-pull rate = fraction of errors matching the English-like placement. Predict high imposition for fixed-stress languages whose rule differs from English, low for English itself. Also test rhyme/meter/syllable tasks: predict rhyme and scansion errors concentrate where mis-stress mis-aligns prominence. Control for tokenizer fertility, word frequency, and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test stress-typology status adds predictive power).
4) Typology-predicted imposition (H3, external validation): Using each language's stress typology (fixed position; variable/lexical; stress- vs syllable-timed) from linguistic databases, test whether per-language imposition/error is predicted by the typological distance of its stress rule from English (Spearman; held-out prediction from typology alone), tying the internal phenomenon to independent ground truth.
5) Representational localization (H4): Extract a metrical-prominence direction via difference-in-means between stressed-syllable-salient vs unstressed representations (using minimal stress pairs like English PROtest/proTEST and cross-language stress positions) at each layer, per language. Test (a) whether a shared prominence direction is English-scaffolded (cross-lingual cosine alignment, aligned with the English variable-stress pattern in mid layers); (b) whether a fixed-stress-language word projects toward the English-like prominence placement in the shared hub while any residual target-language stress-rule signal is stronger in early/language-specific layers, via logit-lens depth tracking. Baseline: a lexical-content direction as a within-model control. Mediation: regress behavioral imposition on shared-hub prominence-projection strength (partial correlation controlling for fertility/frequency; held-out R^2).
6) Causal steering/patching test (H5, core): (a) Steer the target-language word representation along the prominence direction toward the target-language stress rule (e.g., force final-syllable prominence for French) and measure whether stress-placement/rhyme/meter judgments shift to the target-language pattern (flip rate) and the imposition GAP shrinks, without switching output language. (b) For imposed items, patch the residual language-specific stress signal (from early/language-specific layers) into later computation and test restoration, localizing failure to the shared hub imposing an English template over a shallowly-present target rule. Critically verify LEXICAL COMPREHENSION preservation (the model must still answer meaning/definition questions about the words correctly), plus fluency and off-target/language-mixing checks. Baselines: whole-hub English-steering, random-direction control.
7) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify steering is prominence-specific (changes stress/rhyme/meter judgments but not word meaning or unrelated attributes), graded (imposition scales with stress-typology distance), and not merely a tokenizer/syllabification artifact (control for how words split into tokens). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show stronger imposition than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether imposition magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the prominence direction and with each language's training share. Qualitatively compare the model's per-language mis-stress pattern against the stress typology.
Evaluation metrics: stress-decodability (probe accuracy above chance, per layer/language); stress-placement error rate and imposition GAP (divergent vs convergent stress rules; English-pull rate); imposition-vs-stress-typology correlation and held-out prediction; rhyme/meter/syllable-count accuracy; shared-hub prominence-projection strength and crystallization depth (vs lexical-content baseline); cross-lingual prominence-direction alignment; mediation regression (held-out R^2); steering flip rate and GAP reduction, patching-induced restoration; lexical-comprehension preservation, fluency, off-target rate; cross-model imposition comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) A text-only LLM may barely represent stress at all, since it never hears speech; Experiment 2 is a necessary gate — if stress is not decodable above chance, the imposition question is moot, but a null here is itself an informative result about the limits of text-only prosodic knowledge (and rhyme/meter competence would then have to arise some other way). 2) Orthography partially encodes stress in some languages (e.g., Spanish written accents, but not in French/English), which is a cue rather than a confound; we separate languages with vs without orthographic stress marking and treat marked languages as an easier baseline. 3) Stress typology is correlated with language family, script, and resource level; convergent/divergent contrasts, within-language minimal stress pairs (PROtest/proTEST), and typology-based prediction isolate the metrical pathway, but residual confounds may remain; we center core claims on well-resourced French/Polish/Finnish/English/Spanish and treat others as extensions. 4) Tokenization/syllabification is a major confound — the model may not even represent syllables cleanly; we control for token-splitting, include syllable-count as a diagnostic, and interpret with care. 5) Difference-in-means prominence directions may entangle orthographic or frequency features; we use minimal stress pairs, a lexical-content control direction, multiple extraction methods, and specificity checks. 6) Logit-lens depth estimates are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 7) Some mis-stress may reflect genuine ignorance rather than English imposition; the English-pull rate, typology prediction, and causal steering (which restores the correct pattern by editing only the prominence direction) distinguish imposition from random error. 8) Steering could harm lexical comprehension or fluency; we require comprehension preservation and report the full tradeoff. 9) Mandarin (tonal, no stress) is a contrast case, not a stress-imposition target, analyzed separately. 10) If NO imposition is found — the model places stress/rhyme/meter by each language's own rule, predictable from typology — this is an informative POSITIVE result showing text-only models acquire language-specific metrical structure robust to English scaffolding, valuable either way. 11) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: language_competence_self_signal
Title: Which Tongue Should I Trust? An Internal Per-Problem Language-Competence Signal Predicts the Best Reasoning Language in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Before it finishes reasoning, a multilingual LLM already carries an internal, decodable signal of HOW WELL it is positioned to solve a given problem IN A GIVEN LANGUAGE — a per-problem, per-language competence estimate that varies item-by-item, not just by the language's global resource level. This signal predicts which language will yield the correct answer for THAT specific problem better than any fixed policy (always-English, always-input-language, or uniform majority vote), is readable from early/mid-layer activations before the answer is emitted, and can be used to route each problem to its best reasoning language, beating naive cross-lingual self-consistency ensembling.
Related Work: Cross-lingual ensembling exploits complementary reasoning across languages via majority voting (Cross-Lingual Consistency 2025; Best-of-L cross-lingual reward modeling 2025; Multilingual self-consistency 2024) and English-pivot reasoning generally helps (Language Matters 2025; Do Multilingual LLMs Think In English 2025; MRRE 2025; Language-Specific Latent Process Hinders 2025). All of these treat the choice of reasoning language as either FIXED (always English/high-resource) or resolved POST-HOC (generate in many languages, then vote or reward-rank the outputs) — i.e., they need to actually run reasoning in every language and then aggregate. Best-of-L trains an EXTERNAL reward model over generated responses; self-consistency requires sampling many paths. NONE asks whether the model has an INTERNAL, PRE-GENERATION signal of its own per-problem competence in each candidate language that could route the query to the single best language up front, nor whether this signal is item-specific (some problems best solved in the input language, others in English, others in a third language) rather than merely tracking global resource level, nor localizes/steers this signal. This reframes multilingual reasoning from post-hoc ensembling into an internal, cheap, per-problem language-selection (metacognitive routing) problem, and provides a mechanistic account plus a routing payoff, orthogonal to my prior representation-level proposals.
Abstract: Multilingual language models solve the same problem with different success rates in different languages, and recent work exploits this by generating reasoning in several languages and voting or reward-ranking the outputs. But this is expensive — it requires actually reasoning in every language — and it assumes the model cannot know in advance which language it should trust. We ask a simple, previously untested question: does a multilingual LLM carry an internal signal, readable BEFORE it reasons, of how well it is positioned to solve a SPECIFIC problem in a SPECIFIC language? We hypothesize a per-problem, per-language competence estimate that (1) is decodable from early/mid-layer activations at the point the problem has been read but before the answer is produced; (2) is item-specific — predicting, for each individual problem, which language will yield the correct answer, not merely reflecting the language's global resource level; and (3) beats fixed policies (always-English, always-input-language) and naive uniform cross-lingual voting when used to ROUTE each problem to its best reasoning language. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and open reasoning models across typologically diverse languages using MGSM, XCOPA, and a controlled arithmetic suite, presenting each problem in multiple candidate languages. We train lightweight probes to decode per-language competence from internal states, evaluate a probe-based router against ensembling and fixed-language baselines, and use activation patching to test whether the competence signal causally gates answer correctness. Metrics include per-problem language-selection accuracy, router accuracy versus ensembling at matched compute, item-specificity beyond resource level, and probe-competence versus correctness AUROC.
Experiments:
1) Multi-language problem suite: For ~800 reasoning problems (MGSM arithmetic, XCOPA commonsense, and a controlled k-step arithmetic suite with verified gold answers), render each problem in a fixed set of candidate reasoning languages spanning resource levels and scripts (English, French, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish), native-speaker verified. For each (problem, language) pair, record whether the model answers correctly (multiple samples for stability). This yields a per-problem, per-language correctness matrix. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and an open reasoning model (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B).
2) Establish per-problem language variation (motivation): Show that the best language is item-specific — quantify how often a non-globally-best language (i.e., not the model's overall-highest-accuracy language) is the unique correct-answer language for individual problems. Report the ceiling accuracy of an oracle that picks the best language per problem versus the best fixed language, establishing headroom.
3) Per-language competence probe (H1/H2, core): At the point the problem has been read (before answer generation), train a lightweight linear probe on internal states (residual stream at the final problem token, per layer) to predict, for that (problem, language) forward pass, whether the model will answer correctly — a per-problem competence estimate. Report probe AUROC per language and per layer, identifying the layer where competence is most decodable (predict early/mid layers). Crucially test ITEM-SPECIFICITY: does the probe predict per-problem correct-language beyond what the language's global accuracy alone predicts? Compare the probe's per-problem language ranking against (a) global-resource ranking and (b) chance, controlling for tokenizer fertility and problem difficulty (held-out R^2 / accuracy gain over the resource-only baseline).
4) Probe-based router (H3, core payoff): Build a router that, for each problem, reads the competence probe for each candidate language and selects the single language predicted to be most competent, then reasons only in that language. Compare router accuracy against baselines at MATCHED compute: always-English, always-input-language, uniform cross-lingual majority vote (Cross-Lingual Consistency 2025), and random-language selection. Also compare an 'input the problem, cheaply score each language's competence from a single early-layer pass, then run full reasoning only in the top-1 (or top-k) language' pipeline against full N-language ensembling, reporting the accuracy-vs-compute Pareto frontier. Prediction: the router matches or beats N-language ensembling at a fraction of the compute, and beats every fixed policy.
5) Causal test (does the competence signal gate correctness?): Extract a difference-in-means 'competence direction' (correct vs incorrect (problem, language) passes) and (a) steer a low-competence-language pass toward the high-competence pole and test whether answer accuracy rises; (b) via activation patching, patch the competence signal from a high-competence-language pass into a low-competence one and test whether it induces correct answers — distinguishing whether the signal merely reflects, or causally contributes to, correctness. Report the fraction of items flipped and specificity (a random-direction control does nothing).
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify the router's gains are not merely from always picking English (report per-language selection distribution and the share of gains from non-English selections), do not switch OUTPUT language inappropriately (off-target rate), and preserve fluency. Cross-model contrast: predict the more multilingual Aya-23 has more item-specific best-language variation (more routing headroom) than the more English-centric Llama-3; test whether router gain correlates with each model's best-language variation.
Evaluation metrics: oracle-best-language ceiling vs best-fixed-language gap (routing headroom); per-language competence-probe AUROC and best decoding layer; per-problem correct-language prediction accuracy and its gain over the resource-only baseline (item-specificity, held-out R^2); router accuracy vs always-English / always-input / uniform-vote / random at matched compute, and the accuracy-vs-compute Pareto frontier vs full ensembling; causal flip rate and specificity under steering/patching; non-English selection share; off-target rate; cross-model routing-gain vs best-language-variation correlation.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The competence probe may exploit surface difficulty cues (e.g., problem length, tokenizer fertility) rather than a genuine per-language competence signal; we control for difficulty and fertility, test item-specificity beyond global resource level, and require the probe to beat a resource-only baseline — if it does not, the phenomenon reduces to 'pick the high-resource language', an informative negative result. 2) Per-problem correctness labels are noisy (sampling variance); we use multiple samples and majority correctness, and report label reliability. 3) The router requires running each candidate language's early-layer pass to score competence, which has cost; we quantify this and show the accuracy-vs-compute Pareto frontier against full ensembling to demonstrate net savings, but if scoring is nearly as expensive as reasoning, the practical payoff shrinks. 4) Best-language variation may be small for some models/tasks, limiting routing headroom; we report the oracle ceiling up front and treat low-headroom cases as informative (the multilingual gap is then a uniform competence deficit, not a routable one). 5) The causal test may show the competence signal is diagnostic (reflects but does not cause correctness); this is still valuable for routing, and we report the diagnostic-vs-causal distinction explicitly. 6) Steering/patching could switch output language or harm fluency; off-target and fluency checks are hard constraints. 7) Effects may be model-family dependent (Llama-3 vs Aya-23 analyzed as a contrast). 8) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale. 9) If no decodable per-problem competence signal exists (probe at chance beyond resource level), the core hypothesis is refuted — an informative result showing the model lacks pre-generation metacognitive awareness of its per-language competence.

Name: wep_probability_anchor_imposition
Title: Probably Means the Same Everywhere: Does an English-Anchored Verbal-Probability Scale Get Imposed onto Other Languages' Hedge Words?
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs map words of estimative probability (WEPs: 'probably', 'likely', 'wahrscheinlich', 'peut-etre') onto a single, largely English-anchored internal probability scale in the shared hub, so a hedge word in a non-English query is assigned the numeric probability of its ENGLISH translation-equivalent rather than the (empirically different) probability that word carries in the target language. This produces a measurable cross-lingual mis-mapping: for WEPs whose native human numeric range diverges from their English gloss, the model's probability estimate tracks the English value, is mediated by a shared, steerable verbal-probability direction, tracks each language's empirical WEP survey norms, and is causally correctable without harming the model's ability to reason numerically about probability.
Related Work: Human survey research robustly documents that WEPs map to different numeric probability ranges across languages/cultures (Quantifying Probabilistic Expressions, Mosteller & Youtz 1990; cross-language icon-array study 2022; IAS/IFRS accounting-phrase studies 2011-2019; Fagen-Ulmschneider survey). Behavioral LLM work shows models align with ENGLISH human WEP norms but diverge for Chinese/gendered contexts (An evaluation of estimative uncertainty in LLMs 2026), are linguistically overconfident across languages yet generate epistemic markers sensitive to cross-linguistic usage norms (Humans overrely on overconfident LMs across languages 2025), and that GPT-4 matches human WEP estimates in English (probabilistic-phrase coordination game 2023). On the interpretability side, verbal uncertainty is a single linear feature extractable by difference-in-means (Calibrating Verbal Uncertainty / VUF 2025), uncertainty and factuality share circuits (SCIURus 2025), and the shared semantic hub is English-scaffolded (Semantic Hub 2024; Do Llamas Work in English 2024; Do Multilingual LLMs Think In English 2025; Lost in Multilinguality 2025). CRITICALLY, all LLM WEP work is behavioral/benchmark and treats WEP interpretation as an alignment-to-humans question; all interpretability WEP-adjacent work (VUF) is monolingual and concerns EXPRESSING uncertainty, not INTERPRETING a hedge word's numeric meaning. No prior work asks whether the shared, English-anchored hub IMPOSES the English WEP-to-probability mapping onto other languages' hedge words, whether this mis-mapping is predictable from cross-lingual WEP survey norms, whether a shared verbal-probability direction mediates it, or whether it is causally correctable per language. This differs from my prior borrowed_boundary_confidence proposal (which concerned sourcing of factual knowledge-boundary confidence, not the interpretation of lexical hedge words as numbers) and from all my grammatical/lexical imposition proposals (WEP-to-number mapping is a lexical-semantics-to-quantity interface, grounded in an authoritative cross-linguistic survey ground truth).
Abstract: Every language has hedge words that communicate how likely something is - 'probably', 'likely', 'maybe' - but decades of survey research show these words map to genuinely different numeric probabilities across languages: a word glossed as 'probable' may mean 70% in one language and 55% in another. Multilingual language models build a shared, largely English-scaffolded semantic hub. We ask a simple, previously untested mechanistic question: when a model interprets a hedge word in a non-English query, does it assign the numeric probability that word carries in the TARGET language, or the probability of its ENGLISH translation-equivalent? We hypothesize that the hub imposes a single, English-anchored verbal-probability scale: (1) the model's numeric estimate for a target-language WEP tracks its English gloss rather than the target-language human norm, producing systematic mis-mapping concentrated on WEPs whose native range diverges from English; (2) the size of this mis-mapping is predictable from cross-lingual WEP survey norms; (3) a shared, steerable verbal-probability direction mediates the imposition, with any residual language-specific mapping in shallow layers; and (4) steering along a per-language calibration restores target-language-faithful mapping without harming numeric-probability reasoning. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM across typologically diverse languages using WEP-to-number and number-to-WEP tasks grounded in authoritative human survey data. Combining difference-in-means verbal-probability probes, logit-lens tracking, activation patching, and steering, we measure the imposition, its survey-norm scaling, its mediation, and its causal correction. Metrics include English-anchor mis-mapping gap, survey-norm prediction correlation, mediation R-squared, and steering-induced recovery with numeric-reasoning controls.
Experiments:
1) Cross-lingual WEP suite grounded in human survey norms: Assemble ~40 WEPs per language across typologically diverse languages (English, French, German, Spanish, Mandarin, Arabic, Hindi, Japanese), each with (a) its authoritative human numeric probability norm (mean and range) from published cross-language surveys (Mosteller & Youtz 1990; icon-array 2022; Fagen-Ulmschneider; language-specific taxonomies e.g. Norwegian 2024) and (b) its English translation-equivalent and that gloss's English norm. Key subset: DIVERGENT WEPs whose native norm differs substantially from their English gloss's norm; matched CONVERGENT WEPs (norms agree). Tasks: (i) WEP-to-number ('Given the statement uses <WEP>, what percent chance does this express?'); (ii) number-to-WEP (given a percentage, choose the WEP); (iii) in-context probabilistic reasoning where the answer depends on the WEP's numeric value; (iv) a language-agnostic numeric-probability control (pure percentage arithmetic, no WEP) to isolate WEP-interpretation from numeracy. Native-speaker verify glosses; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral English-anchor imposition (H1, core): For each target-language WEP, measure the model's assigned numeric probability and test whether it tracks the ENGLISH gloss norm rather than the target-language human norm. Define the English-anchor mis-mapping GAP = |model estimate - target-language norm| minus |model estimate - English-gloss norm| (negative = tracks English), and an English-anchor rate = fraction of DIVERGENT WEPs where the model's estimate is closer to the English gloss than the target norm. Verify near-faithful mapping on CONVERGENT WEPs and correct English estimates (ceiling). Control for tokenizer fertility, WEP frequency, and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test target-language status adds predictive power).
3) Survey-norm scaling (H2, external validation): Test whether per-WEP mis-mapping is predicted by the divergence between the target-language and English human survey norms (Spearman correlation; held-out prediction of mis-mapping from survey divergence alone), tying the internal phenomenon to independent cross-linguistic human ground truth. Predict larger imposition for more English-distant / lower-resource languages.
4) Representational localization (H3): Extract a shared verbal-probability direction via difference-in-means between high-probability and low-probability WEP representations (following the VUF difference-in-means approach) at each layer, per language, and verify it is a monotonic probability axis (probe recovers WEP numeric rank). Test (a) cross-lingual cosine alignment of the WEP-probability direction (shared, English-anchored axis vs language-specific); (b) whether a DIVERGENT target-language WEP projects onto the ENGLISH-gloss position on the shared axis in mid/hub layers while any residual target-language mapping is stronger in early/language-specific layers, via logit-lens/tuned-lens depth tracking. Baseline: a language-agnostic numeric-magnitude direction as a within-model control. Mediation: regress behavioral mis-mapping on the WEP's shared-axis projection toward the English position (partial correlation controlling for fertility/frequency; held-out R^2).
5) Causal steering/patching test (H4, core): (a) Apply a per-language calibration steering along the verbal-probability direction that shifts a target-language WEP's internal position from its English-gloss anchor toward its target-language human norm, and measure whether the model's numeric estimate and downstream reasoning shift toward the target-language pattern (flip/shift rate), and the mis-mapping GAP shrinks toward the CONVERGENT baseline, without switching output language. (b) For imposed items, patch the residual language-specific WEP signal (from early/language-specific layers) into later computation and test restoration, localizing failure to the shared hub imposing the English mapping over a shallowly-present target-language mapping. Critically verify NUMERIC-REASONING preservation (the language-agnostic percentage-arithmetic control must stay correct), plus fluency and off-target/language-mixing checks. Baselines: whole-hub English-steering, random-direction control.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify steering is WEP-specific (changes hedge-word-to-number mapping but not numeric arithmetic or unrelated content), graded (imposition scales with survey-norm divergence), bidirectional (can shift toward and away from the English anchor as a dose-response check), and not a lexical-frequency artifact. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show stronger imposition than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether imposition magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the verbal-probability direction and with each language's training share. Qualitatively compare the model's per-language mis-mapping pattern against the human cross-linguistic WEP survey structure.
Evaluation metrics: English-anchor mis-mapping GAP and English-anchor rate (DIVERGENT vs CONVERGENT WEPs; vs English ceiling); mis-mapping-vs-survey-norm-divergence correlation and held-out prediction; number-to-WEP and reasoning-task accuracy; verbal-probability-direction monotonicity, cross-lingual alignment, and English-anchor projection strength with mediation of behavioral mis-mapping (held-out R^2); steering shift rate and GAP reduction (bidirectional dose-response), patching-induced restoration; numeric-reasoning preservation, fluency, off-target rate; cross-model imposition comparison and correlation with training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for target-language status over frequency/fertility/resource baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Human WEP survey norms are themselves noisy, context-sensitive (positive vs negative framing, domain), and vary across surveys; we use multiple authoritative sources, report the norm range not just the mean, restrict DIVERGENT items to WEPs with robust cross-survey norm differences, and treat norms as noisy predictors, relying on the internal representation and causal tests for core claims. 2) WEP divergence is correlated with language family, script, and resource level; the CONVERGENT controls, English ceiling, within-WEP contrasts, and survey-norm prediction isolate the imposition pathway, but residual confounds may remain; we center core claims on well-resourced languages with strong survey data and treat sparser languages as extensions. 3) Translation-equivalence between a target WEP and its English gloss is imperfect (some WEPs have no clean gloss); we native-speaker verify glosses, exclude ambiguous cases, and report inter-annotator agreement. 4) The model's WEP-to-number output may reflect a general numeric-anchoring bias rather than genuine WEP interpretation; the language-agnostic numeric control, the number-to-WEP reverse task, and the in-context reasoning task triangulate genuine WEP interpretation. 5) Difference-in-means verbal-probability directions may entangle sentiment/lexical features; we verify monotonicity, use a numeric-magnitude control direction, multiple extraction methods, and specificity checks. 6) Logit-lens/tuned-lens depth estimates are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 7) Some cross-lingual mis-mapping may reflect genuine correct behavior (the model rightly using the target-language norm) rather than English imposition; the direction of the effect (tracks ENGLISH gloss vs TARGET norm), the survey-norm prediction, and the causal steering (which restores the target mapping by editing only the WEP direction) distinguish imposition from faithful interpretation, and a finding of faithful interpretation is itself valuable and complements the behavioral literature. 8) Steering could harm numeric reasoning or fluency; we require numeric-reasoning preservation and report the full tradeoff plus bidirectional dose-response. 9) Instruction-tuned models may hedge or refuse to give numbers; we test base models where available and use forced-choice number-to-WEP as a fallback. 10) The model-vs-human comparison is qualitative/structural (norm ordering and divergence), not a claim of identical mechanism. 11) If NO imposition is found - target-language WEPs are mapped to their own human norms, predictable from surveys, with numeric reasoning intact - this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the shared hub represents language-specific verbal-probability semantics despite English scaffolding, valuable either way. 12) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: first_step_anchoring_asymmetry
Title: Locked In From the First Word: Language-Dependent First-Step Anchoring Blocks Cross-Lingual Self-Correction
Short Hypothesis: The disproportionate influence of the FIRST chain-of-thought step on the final answer is language-dependent: when a multilingual LLM reasons in a lower-resource / English-distant language, it is MORE strongly anchored to a wrong first step and less able to recover from it mid-chain, so a substantial part of the multilingual reasoning gap is a first-step-recovery failure rather than a knowledge or per-step-competence failure. This anchoring is carried by a decodable, steerable 'commitment' signal set at the first step whose strength scales with resource-distance, and is causally reducible by suppressing it at the first-step boundary—selectively restoring self-correction for high-anchoring languages.
Related Work: Prior work shows (a) the first reasoning step disproportionately shapes the final answer and error-injected first steps degrade the whole trajectory, but only in English/monolingual settings ('Lost at the Beginning of Reasoning' 2025; first-step reward-model sampling); (b) multilingual CoT attribution over-weights the FINAL step and structured CoT helps only high-resource languages (What Really Counts 2025); (c) latent reasoning is English-centered and weaker for low-resource languages (Large Reasoning Models Are Not Yet Multilingual Latent Reasoners 2026); (d) LLMs have distinct faithful vs unfaithful error-recovery modes (Dissociation of Faithful and Unfaithful Reasoning 2024) and recover more from obvious errors and with more corroborating context, but MONOLINGUALLY; and (e) the human Foreign Language Effect impairs reflective override / belief-logic conflict detection in a non-native language (Thinking in a Foreign Language Distorts Cognitive Effort 2019). CRITICALLY, no prior work asks whether the FIRST-STEP anchoring effect and the ability to RECOVER from a wrong first step are themselves language-dependent, whether cross-lingual reasoning failures are disproportionately first-step-recovery failures (vs knowledge or per-step competence), whether a commitment/anchoring signal set at the first step scales with resource-distance, or whether suppressing it selectively restores self-correction. This differs from my prior 'latent compute-depth gap' (serial depth / premature commitment over the whole chain) and 'effort setpoint' proposals: the locus here is the FIRST step specifically as a commitment gate whose grip on the rest of the chain varies by language, mirroring the human foreign-language reflective-override deficit. It is orthogonal to all my other proposals, which concern representation of concepts/categories, not intra-chain first-step recovery.
Abstract: A chain of thought that starts wrong often stays wrong: recent work shows the first reasoning step exerts an outsized influence on the final answer. But this has only been studied in English. We ask a simple, previously untested question about multilingual models: is first-step anchoring language-dependent — is a model reasoning in a lower-resource or English-distant language MORE locked into a wrong first step and less able to recover mid-chain? We hypothesize that a substantial part of the multilingual reasoning gap is a first-step-recovery failure rather than a knowledge or per-step-competence failure; that the grip of the first step is carried by a decodable 'commitment' signal set at the first-step boundary whose strength scales with resource-distance; and that suppressing this signal selectively restores self-correction for high-anchoring languages, mirroring the human Foreign Language Effect on reflective override. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and open reasoning models across typologically diverse languages using MGSM, XCOPA, and a controlled multi-step suite, employing a controlled error-injection paradigm (plant a wrong first step, measure recovery) that isolates recovery from base competence. We measure per-language recovery rates, decode a first-step commitment direction via difference-in-means and logit-lens, use activation patching to localize whether failures are anchoring (correct answer latently present but abandoned) versus genuine competence, and run a train-free commitment-suppression intervention at the first-step boundary. Metrics include per-language recovery rate, recovery-vs-resource-distance correlation, anchoring-vs-competence error shares, commitment-signal decodability, and selective recovery gains with specificity controls.
Experiments:
1) Error-injection reasoning suite: For ~600 multi-step problems (MGSM arithmetic, XCOPA commonsense, and a controlled k-step arithmetic/logic suite with verified gold answers), construct matched conditions in typologically diverse languages spanning resource levels and scripts (English, French, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish, Bengali): (a) FREE reasoning (model generates its own chain); (b) INJECTED-ERROR reasoning where a plausible WRONG first step is planted and the model continues; (c) a CONTROL where a correct first step is planted. Native-speaker verify; the injected wrong first step is content-matched across languages. Report inter-annotator agreement. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B.
2) Language-dependent recovery (H1, core): On INJECTED-ERROR items, measure per-language recovery rate = fraction where the model overrides the planted wrong first step and reaches the correct answer. Test that recovery is lower for lower-resource / English-distant languages, controlling for the model's base competence (accuracy on FREE and CONTROL items), tokenizer fertility, and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test resource-distance predicts recovery beyond base competence). Crucially, condition on problems the model solves correctly in the FREE/CONTROL condition, so a recovery gap cannot be explained by knowledge absence.
3) Anchoring vs competence error decomposition (H2): For FREE-reasoning items wrong in language B but correct in English, use logit-lens/tuned-lens and mid-chain truncation to test whether the correct answer is latently present early but ABANDONED after a wrong first step (anchoring failure) versus never formed (competence failure). Also patch: replace only the first-step representation in B's pass with a correct-first-step representation and test whether the chain recovers. Report anchoring-vs-competence error shares per language, predicting anchoring failures grow with resource-distance.
4) First-step commitment signal (H3): Extract a difference-in-means 'commitment' direction (recovered vs not-recovered passes on INJECTED-ERROR items) at the first-step boundary and via logit-lens track how strongly the first-step (wrong) answer dominates subsequent positions. Test whether per-item commitment-signal strength predicts non-recovery (Spearman; held-out R^2), whether the query language is decodable from an early commitment signal, and whether the signal's strength scales with resource-distance. Measure cross-lingual alignment of the commitment direction.
5) Core causal intervention — commitment suppression: At the first-step boundary, steer along the commitment direction toward the recovered pole (weaken the grip of the planted first step) train-free, and measure per-language recovery recovery. Predict SELECTIVE gains: high-anchoring (low-resource) languages recover most; low-anchoring languages change little (interaction test). Compute recovery elasticity = recovery gain per unit baseline anchoring, correlated with H4 commitment strength. Compare against baselines: uniform English shared-space steering (MRRE 2025), first-step resampling (Lost at the Beginning 2025), a prompt-based 'reconsider your first step' nudge, and a random-direction control.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify the intervention is anchoring-specific — it must IMPROVE recovery from WRONG first steps but NOT degrade CONTROL items where the first step is correct (a symmetric check: suppression must not induce spurious abandonment of correct first steps), must not switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), and preserve fluency. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/distilled models show sharper anchoring in low-resource languages than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether the anchoring gap correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the commitment direction and each language's training share. Qualitatively compare the language-dependent recovery pattern against the human Foreign Language Effect on reflective override (direction, not identical mechanism).
Evaluation metrics: per-language recovery rate (injected-error) and its partial correlation with resource-distance over base-competence/fertility (held-out R^2); anchoring-vs-competence error shares and first-step-patch recovery rate; commitment-signal decodability, non-recovery prediction, and resource-distance scaling; commitment-direction cross-lingual alignment; selective commitment-suppression recovery gains and elasticity vs baselines, with CORRECT-first-step preservation (symmetric specificity), off-target rate, fluency; cross-model anchoring-gap comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Recovery from an injected wrong first step conflates anchoring with base competence; the key control is conditioning on FREE/CONTROL-correct problems (the model demonstrably CAN solve them), plus the anchoring-vs-competence decomposition and the first-step patch, which isolate abandonment of a latently-correct answer from genuine incompetence — if recovery gaps vanish once competence is controlled, the hypothesis is refuted, an informative negative result. 2) The planted wrong first step must be equally plausible/salient across languages; we content-match injections, native-speaker verify, and report items where difficulty differs. 3) Resource-distance is confounded with tokenizer fertility and script; partial correlations, the controlled k-step suite, and the causal suppression test mitigate but may not fully remove confounds. 4) The commitment direction from difference-in-means may entangle content/language-identity features; we use multiple extraction methods and specificity controls. 5) Logit-lens/truncation latent-answer tracking is approximate at intermediate positions; cross-validated with mid-chain truncation. 6) Commitment suppression could induce spurious abandonment of correct first steps or harm fluency; the symmetric CONTROL-preservation constraint is a hard requirement and we report the full tradeoff. 7) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM/Aya analyzed as less English-centric contrasts). 8) The human Foreign Language Effect analogy is qualitative, not a claim of identical mechanism. 9) Reasoning models may recover via backtracking that our step-segmentation misses; we use multiple chain-segmentation methods and report robustness. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: phantom_pun_imposition
Title: Still Funny in Translation: Does the English-Scaffolded Hub Impose Phantom Phonological Puns Onto Languages Where the Wordplay Collapses?
Short Hypothesis: A pun's humor lives in a language-specific phonological/orthographic coincidence (a homophone or double meaning) that does NOT survive translation: rendered into a language where the two senses no longer sound or look alike, the wordplay collapses and the joke is not funny. We hypothesize that because multilingual LLMs detect and appreciate puns through a largely English-scaffolded shared hub that co-activates the SOURCE-language phonological form (via latent romanization / form-carrying features), the model IMPOSES a 'phantom pun': it continues to rate a translated-and-collapsed pun as funny and to explain it via the (no-longer-present) source-language wordplay, tracking the source phonology rather than the target-language surface. This phantom-humor imposition is mediated by a decodable source-form signal that persists into mid layers, scales with the phonological distance between the source and target realizations, and is causally suppressible by ablating the source-form signal without harming genuine target-language humor.
Related Work: Monolingual mechanistic work localizes humor and figurative-meaning processing: a single 'laughing head' emerges for humor detection (Laughing Heads 2021), idiom figurative meaning is retrieved early via 'Idiom Heads' in a figurative-vs-literal tug-of-war (Tug-of-war 2025; Anatomy of an Idiom 2025; How Are Idioms Processed 2023), and LLMs show a 'lazy pun generation' pattern and struggle with pun understanding (Can LLMs Understand Puns 2024; Computational Model of Linguistic Humor in Puns 2015, which formalizes pun humor via ambiguity+distinctiveness). Humor is only weakly steerable as a concept direction (A Language Model's Guide Through Latent Space 2024). Multilingual work establishes an English-scaffolded shared hub with latent romanization bridging non-Roman scripts (Semantic Hub 2024; Transfer Neurons 2025; Cross-Layer Transcoders 2025; RomanLens). CRITICALLY, all humor/pun mechanistic work is monolingual, and all pun-across-language work is generation/translation-quality focused; NONE asks whether the shared hub causes the model to perceive humor via a SOURCE-language phonological coincidence that no longer exists after translation, producing a 'phantom pun' the target surface cannot license, nor localizes a persistent source-form signal, ties the phantom-humor to source-target phonological distance, or offers a causal ablation fix. Puns are the ideal probe because, unlike idioms or metaphors (which can preserve figurative meaning across languages), a phonological pun's humor is grounded in surface FORM that is genuinely destroyed by translation — giving a clean, falsifiable phantom-vs-real contrast. This is orthogonal to all my prior imposition proposals (grammatical categories, spatial/temporal/color/kinship/pragmatic axes), which concern meaning representation, not form-grounded humor.
Abstract: A pun is funny because two meanings collide in one sound or spelling — 'no pun in ten did' works only because 'pun in ten did' sounds like 'punintended'. This coincidence is language-specific: translate the pun and the double meaning usually vanishes, leaving a sentence that is no longer funny. This makes puns a clean natural experiment no prior interpretability work has run. We ask a simple, previously untested question: when a multilingual LLM reads a pun that has been translated into a language where the wordplay collapses, does it still perceive humor — a phantom pun — because its English-scaffolded shared hub co-activates the original source-language phonological form? We hypothesize that (1) the model rates translated-and-collapsed puns as funnier than they are and explains them via the absent source-language wordplay, tracking source phonology over target surface; (2) the size of this phantom-humor imposition scales with the phonological distance between source and target realizations; (3) a decodable source-form signal persisting into mid layers mediates it; and (4) ablating that signal removes the phantom humor without harming genuine target-language humor. We build a controlled multilingual pun suite — source puns, faithfully-translated collapsed puns, target-language-native puns, and matched non-jokes — across typologically diverse languages, on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM. Using funniness ratings, explanation analysis, logit-lens source-form tracking, difference-in-means probes, activation patching, and steering, we measure the phantom-humor gap, its phonological-distance scaling, its mediation, and its causal suppression. Metrics include phantom-funniness gap, source-wordplay-explanation rate, distance-prediction correlation, mediation R-squared, and ablation-induced correction with genuine-humor preservation controls.
Experiments:
1) Cross-lingual pun suite: Assemble ~400 source-language puns (primarily English homophonic/homographic puns with a clearly identified pun word and its two senses), each paired with: (a) a FAITHFUL translation into typologically diverse target languages (French, German, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili) that preserves literal meaning but where the phonological/orthographic coincidence COLLAPSES (native-speaker verified that the wordplay is destroyed and the sentence is not funny); (b) a TARGET-NATIVE pun that genuinely works in that language (real humor control); (c) a matched NON-JOKE literal sentence (no-humor control); and (d) source-native pun (source ceiling). Also build the reverse direction (non-English source puns translated to English) to control for English-specificity. Annotate each collapsed pun with a phonological/orthographic distance between the source pun-word ambiguity and its target realization. Native-speaker verify collapse and funniness; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral phantom-humor (H1, core): Elicit funniness ratings (Likert / forced-choice funnier-of-pair) and 'is this a joke / why is it funny?' explanations for each condition. Define the phantom-funniness GAP = rated funniness of COLLAPSED translated puns minus that of matched NON-JOKES in the same target language (predicted positive: the model still finds destroyed puns funny). Compute a source-wordplay-explanation rate = fraction of collapsed-pun explanations that invoke the source-language homophone/wordplay that is no longer present in the target sentence. Verify TARGET-NATIVE puns are rated funny (genuine humor works) and NON-JOKES are not (calibration). Control for tokenizer fertility, sentence frequency, and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test collapsed-pun status adds predictive power).
3) Phonological-distance scaling (H2): Test whether per-item phantom-funniness is predicted by the source-target phonological/orthographic distance of the wordplay (Spearman; held-out prediction) — puns whose source ambiguity is closer to a target coincidence should phantom-impose more; puns fully collapsed should phantom-impose less if the model truly needs form, or MORE if it relies purely on source-form co-activation. This distinguishes source-form co-activation from residual target coincidence.
4) Representational localization (H3): Using logit-lens/tuned-lens and RomanLens-style romanization tracking, test whether reading a COLLAPSED translated pun co-activates the SOURCE-language pun-word form (the source homophone decodable in mid layers) that a matched non-joke does not. Extract a difference-in-means 'source-form' direction (pun-word source-form present vs absent) at each layer; test cross-lingual alignment and whether the source-form signal persists into mid layers. Mediation: regress behavioral phantom-funniness on source-form signal strength (partial correlation controlling for fertility/frequency; held-out R^2). Also test whether the 'laughing head' / figurative-retrieval mechanism fires on collapsed puns (attention-pattern comparison to genuine and non-joke controls).
5) Causal suppression/steering test (H4, core): (a) Ablate the source-form signal from the collapsed-pun representation (difference-in-means projection removal / INLP nullspace toward the target language) and test whether phantom-funniness drops toward the non-joke baseline; (b) conversely, INJECT the source-form signal into a plain target-language non-joke and test whether it induces spurious perceived humor (bidirectional causal test); (c) for individual phantom items, patch the target-language form representation and test correction. Critically verify GENUINE-HUMOR PRESERVATION: the model must still rate TARGET-NATIVE puns as funny (no over-suppression of real humor) and NON-JOKES as not funny, plus fluency and off-target/language-mixing checks. Baselines: random-direction ablation, whole-hub English-steering.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify suppression is source-form-specific (removes phantom humor but not genuine target-language humor or unrelated content) and not a lexical-frequency artifact (frequency-matched collapsed/non-joke pairs). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show stronger phantom imposition for English-source puns than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether phantom magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the source-form direction and with each source language's training share. Test the reverse direction (non-English source puns into English) to confirm the effect tracks the SOURCE language, not English specifically.
Evaluation metrics: phantom-funniness GAP (collapsed puns vs non-jokes; vs target-native-pun and source-ceiling references); source-wordplay-explanation rate; phantom-vs-phonological-distance correlation and held-out prediction; source-form signal persistence and mid-layer decodability, with mediation of behavioral phantom-humor (held-out R^2); laughing-head/figurative-retrieval firing on collapsed puns; ablation-induced phantom reduction and injection-induced spurious humor (bidirectional); patching-induced correction; genuine-humor and non-joke calibration preservation (specificity), fluency, off-target rate; cross-model phantom comparison and correlation with source-language training share; reverse-direction (non-English source) confirmation; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for collapsed-pun status over frequency/fertility/resource baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Verifying that a translated pun genuinely 'collapses' (wordplay destroyed, not funny) is subtle — some puns partially survive or a coincidental target ambiguity arises; we native-speaker verify collapse, exclude items with residual target coincidence (or analyze them as a separate 'partial-survival' tier), report inter-annotator agreement, and annotate phonological distance to quantify collapse degree. 2) Funniness ratings are noisy and culturally variable; we use forced-choice funnier-of-pair alongside Likert, include target-native puns and non-jokes as within-model calibration anchors, and rely on the phantom-vs-non-joke GAP rather than absolute ratings. 3) Collapsed-pun status is correlated with translation quality, frequency, and resource level; the non-joke controls, target-native-pun controls, within-item source/collapsed contrasts, and phonological-distance prediction isolate the phantom pathway, but residual confounds may remain; we center core claims on well-resourced target languages and treat sparser ones as extensions. 4) Some phantom humor might reflect the model detecting a genuine (if weak) target-language ambiguity we missed; the source-wordplay-explanation analysis (does the explanation cite the ABSENT source homophone?) and the source-form co-activation localization are designed to confirm the humor is grounded in source, not target, form. 5) Difference-in-means source-form directions may entangle orthographic/frequency features; we use RomanLens-style romanization checks, frequency-matched controls, multiple extraction methods, and the non-joke baseline. 6) Logit-lens/tuned-lens source-form tracking is approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 7) The ablation must not suppress genuine target-language humor; genuine-humor preservation is a hard specificity constraint and we report the full tradeoff plus the bidirectional injection test. 8) Instruction-tuned models may over-claim things are funny (sycophantic humor); we test base models where available and use the non-joke calibration to net out a general funniness bias. 9) Puns are the ideal probe precisely because form-grounded humor is destroyed by translation; if we instead found the model correctly rates collapsed puns as NOT funny and explains via the target surface, this is an informative POSITIVE result showing form-faithful, non-phantom humor perception — valuable either way. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: language_conditioned_verbosity_setpoint
Title: How Long Should the Answer Be? A Language-Conditioned Verbosity Setpoint Imported From the Dominant Language in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: A multilingual LLM sets HOW MUCH to say via a language-conditioned 'verbosity setpoint' - an internal target for output length/elaboration fixed early in the forward pass by a decodable language signal, before content is generated. We hypothesize this setpoint is MISCALIBRATED across languages: it is anchored to the dominant (English) language's verbosity norm and imported into other languages regardless of each language's natural information density, so for the SAME content the model over-elaborates in some languages and under-elaborates in others, and this same imported anchoring makes explicit length-instruction adherence systematically worse in languages whose setpoint is far from the instructed length. The setpoint is carried by a steerable length direction and can be recalibrated per language without changing content.
Related Work: Prior work shows output length is encoded in early attention layers and controllable by scaling length-related hidden units (Length Representations in LLMs 2025), instruction-tuning specializes deeper layers for length control with language-specific compensatory mechanisms in English vs Italian (How Instruction-Tuning Imparts Length Control 2025), and RLHF/DPO induce a verbosity/length bias that conflates length with quality (Mitigating Length Bias in RLHF 2025; Disentangling Length from Quality in DPO 2024; Verbosity != Veracity 2024). Cross-lingual work establishes an English-scaffolded shared hub with late-layer language-specific decoding and language-identity directions decodable early (Semantic Hub 2024; Do Llamas Work in English 2024; Language-Specific Neurons 2024; Language Surgery/ITLC 2025; CLaS-Bench 2026), and multilingual calibration/register control via control vectors (LACE 2025; Control Vectors 2025). CRITICALLY, all length-control work treats verbosity as a monolingual or single-pair component-attribution question and treats the length target as content/instruction-driven; NONE frames output length as a LANGUAGE-CONDITIONED SETPOINT that is set early, DECOUPLED from content, ANCHORED to the dominant language and IMPORTED into others (mis-calibrated to each language's natural information density), predicts a per-language length-instruction-adherence gap from the setpoint mismatch, or causally recalibrates the setpoint per language. This reframes the multilingual length problem from a component-specialization or RLHF-bias account into an imported, mis-calibrated verbosity anchor with a predictive mismatch signature and a targeted fix, orthogonal to prior monolingual/component-level length work and to my own register-drift proposal (which concerns register consistency within a generation, not how much is said).
Abstract: When a language model answers a question, it must decide not only what to say but how much to say. We ask a simple, previously untested question about multilingual models: is the amount a model says set by a language-conditioned 'verbosity setpoint', and is that setpoint mis-calibrated across languages? We hypothesize that the model fixes an internal target for output length and elaboration early in its forward pass, from a decodable language signal, before generating content; that this setpoint is anchored to the dominant (English) language's verbosity norm and imported into other languages regardless of each language's natural information density; and consequently that for identical content the model over-elaborates in some languages and under-elaborates in others, and that explicit length-instruction adherence is systematically worse in languages whose imported setpoint is far from the instructed length. We further hypothesize the setpoint is carried by a steerable length direction that can be recalibrated per language without changing content. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM across typologically diverse languages, using content-matched generation, length-instruction-following, and information-density-controlled tasks. Combining logit-lens/probe decoding of an early length signal, difference-in-means length-direction extraction, activation patching, and setpoint-recalibration steering, we measure the per-language verbosity gap, the imported-anchor signature, the setpoint's early timing and content-independence, the length-instruction-adherence mismatch prediction, and causal per-language recalibration. Metrics include content-controlled verbosity gap, English-anchor prediction, length-instruction mismatch-vs-adherence correlation, early-signal timing, and steering-induced recalibration with content-preservation controls.
Experiments:
1) Content-matched multilingual generation suite: Build ~600 items in three families: (a) CONTENT-MATCHED tasks where the model answers the SAME question/summarizes the SAME source across typologically diverse languages spanning resource levels and scripts (English, French, German, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish), so intended information content is fixed and only surface verbosity can vary; (b) LENGTH-INSTRUCTION tasks with explicit targets ('answer in exactly N words / one sentence / a detailed paragraph') across the same languages; (c) an information-density reference: measure each language's natural information density (tokens/characters per unit content) from parallel corpora to define a content-normalized length. Native-speaker verify; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Content-controlled verbosity gap (H1, core): For CONTENT-MATCHED items, measure per-language output length normalized by the language's natural information density (content-normalized verbosity), so a language is 'over-elaborating' or 'under-elaborating' relative to what its density predicts, not merely producing more tokens. Test that content-normalized verbosity diverges systematically across languages for identical content. Control for tokenizer fertility (report both token and character length) and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test language adds predictive power beyond fertility/density).
3) Imported-anchor signature (H2): Test whether per-language content-normalized verbosity is pulled toward the ENGLISH (dominant) verbosity norm rather than each language's natural density: define an English-anchor pull = shift of the model's content-normalized length toward English's norm. Predict the model's verbosity is more English-like than density-appropriate, especially for lower-resource / English-distant languages. Compare against a density-calibrated baseline (model comparison: is per-language verbosity better fit by 'English-anchored' or by 'density-appropriate'?).
4) Setpoint timing and content-independence (H3): Extract a difference-in-means / probe 'length setpoint' signal from internal states at the point the prompt has been read but before generation. Test (a) whether the query language is decodable from this early signal, and (b) via position-resolved logit-lens, whether the early setpoint magnitude predicts the eventual output length independent of the specific content (compare across different-content, same-language prompts vs same-content, different-language prompts). Locate the layer/attention units carrying it (building on Length Representations 2025). Measure cross-lingual alignment of the length direction (single shared axis re-thresholded per language?).
5) Length-instruction-adherence mismatch (H4): On LENGTH-INSTRUCTION items, measure per-language adherence error (deviation from the instructed length). Test the prediction that adherence is worse when the instructed length is far from the language's imported setpoint (i.e., the setpoint fights the instruction): correlate per-language, per-target adherence error with the setpoint-vs-instruction mismatch (Spearman; held-out R^2 over fertility/resource). Predict languages whose imported setpoint is far from short/long targets show larger over/under-generation on those targets.
6) Causal setpoint recalibration (H5, core): Steer along the length-setpoint direction to recalibrate a target language's setpoint toward (a) its density-appropriate value on content-matched tasks and (b) the instructed length on length-instruction tasks, train-free. Measure whether content-normalized verbosity equalizes across languages and whether length-instruction adherence improves, SELECTIVELY for mis-calibrated languages (dose-response; mis-signed steering hurts). Critically verify CONTENT PRESERVATION: recalibration must change length/elaboration WITHOUT dropping or adding information content (content-overlap/faithfulness checks), must not switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), and must preserve fluency. Activation-patching complement: patch the English setpoint into a target-language pass and confirm it shifts length toward English. Baselines: prompt-only length instruction, whole-hub English-steering, length-hidden-unit scaling (Length Representations 2025), random-direction control.
7) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify recalibration is length-specific (changes verbosity but not content or register), and does not help already-calibrated languages (symmetric check). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show stronger English-anchored verbosity import than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether import magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the length direction and with each language's training share.
Evaluation metrics: content-normalized verbosity gap across languages (token and character; over/under-elaboration); English-anchor pull and English-anchored-vs-density-appropriate model comparison; early length-signal language-decodability and content-independent predictiveness of output length, plus its layer/unit locus and cross-lingual alignment; length-instruction adherence error and its correlation with setpoint-vs-instruction mismatch (held-out R^2); steering-induced verbosity equalization and adherence improvement with dose-response and mis-sign penalty, content-preservation/faithfulness, off-target rate, fluency; patching-induced English-length shift; cross-model import comparison and correlation with training share.
