Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Separating genuine cross-lingual verbosity differences from natural information-density differences is the central challenge; the content-normalization by empirical per-language density (from parallel corpora), token-vs-character reporting, and the English-anchored-vs-density-appropriate model comparison are designed to isolate an imported anchor from legitimate density variation, but density estimates are noisy and we report sensitivity. 2) Output length is confounded with tokenizer fertility; we report both token and character length and control for fertility with partial correlations. 3) 'Content-matched' generations may genuinely require different amounts of text across languages (grammatical obligatoriness, morphology); we use summarization/QA over identical source content and content-faithfulness checks to bound this, and treat residual differences conservatively. 4) The early setpoint's content-independence is hard to establish since language and content co-occur; we use same-content/different-language and different-content/same-language contrasts and position-resolved lenses, reporting timing as suggestive. 5) Length-instruction adherence depends on instruction-following competence, which is itself language-dependent; the mismatch-prediction test conditions on the setpoint-instruction gap and controls for base adherence, but residual competence confounds may remain. 6) The recalibration steering could drop/add content, over-truncate, or harm fluency; content-preservation, off-target, and dose-response/mis-sign checks are hard constraints and we report the full tradeoff, comparing against the length-hidden-unit scaling baseline to show the language-conditioned account adds value. 7) RLHF/instruction-tuning may bake in verbosity biases that dominate; we test base vs instruction-tuned models and treat differences as an informative training-stage finding. 8) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM's less English-centric hub analyzed as a contrast expected to import less). 9) If per-language verbosity is fully explained by natural information density (no English anchor) and length-instruction adherence is language-uniform, this is an informative POSITIVE result showing verbosity is density-calibrated rather than dominant-language-imported - valuable either way. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: crosslingual_ical_rule_transfer
Title: The Rule Crosses, the Answer Doesn't: Language-Agnostic In-Context Rule Abstraction but Language-Bound Answer Retrieval in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: When a novel in-context mapping (a made-up rule taught only through demonstrations, e.g. 'blip X -> the antonym of X') is presented with demonstrations in one language and a test query in a DIFFERENT language, multilingual LLMs abstract the RULE in a largely language-agnostic way (it transfers across the demonstration-test language boundary through the shared hub / concept induction), whereas the final ANSWER-RETRIEVAL/copy step is language-bound and fails to surface the answer in the test language. Consequently, cross-lingual ICL failure is dominated by an answer-retrieval failure, not a rule-abstraction failure: the correct answer is latently present in the shared hub but not decoded into the test language, and this dissociation is measurable, predictable from demonstration-test language distance, and causally fixable by boosting the test-language decoding step without re-teaching the rule.
Related Work: Prior work shows (a) induction heads drive ICL and generalize to translation (In-context Learning and Induction Heads 2022; Induction Heads as Essential Mechanism 2024); (b) a dual-route split where TOKEN induction heads do verbatim copy while CONCEPT induction heads copy language-agnostic word representations and mediate translation (The Dual-Route Model of Induction 2025); (c) a shared, English-scaffolded semantic hub (Semantic Hub 2024; Do Llamas Work in English 2024) and shared latent grammatical concepts (LLMs Share Latent Grammatical Concepts 2025); and (d) many methods that IMPROVE cross-lingual ICL via alignment, bridge languages, code-switching, or language-steering vectors (Cross-lingual Alignment 2023; BridgeX-ICL 2025; CSICL 2025; Language Steering for Multilingual ICL 2026). All the improvement work is behavioral/engineering and treats cross-lingual ICL failure as a monolithic performance gap; the mechanistic induction/hub work is monolingual or studies static concept sharing, never the ICL abstraction process. NO prior work asks whether the two computational steps of ICL - (i) abstracting the demonstrated rule and (ii) applying it to retrieve/decode the answer - dissociate across a demonstration-test LANGUAGE boundary, whether the rule is transferred language-agnostically while the answer is not, whether cross-lingual ICL failure is specifically an answer-retrieval (not rule-abstraction) failure, or whether boosting only the test-language decoding step fixes it without re-teaching the rule. We reframe cross-lingual ICL failure as a clean rule-transfers/answer-doesn't dissociation with a mechanistic locus (concept-induction rule vector vs test-language decoding) and a targeted causal fix, orthogonal to all my prior proposals (none concern ICL rule transfer).
Abstract: In-context learning lets a model infer a task from a few demonstrations and apply it to a new query. This involves two steps a monolingual setting cannot separate: abstracting the demonstrated rule, and applying that rule to retrieve and decode the answer. Multilingual models let us pull these apart by teaching a novel rule with demonstrations in one language and testing it with a query in another. We hypothesize a dissociation: the rule is abstracted largely language-agnostically and transfers across the demonstration-test language boundary through the shared semantic hub, while the final answer-retrieval/decoding step is language-bound and fails to surface the answer in the test language. Under this account, cross-lingual ICL failure is dominated by answer-retrieval failure, not rule-abstraction failure - the correct answer is latently present in the hub but not decoded into the test language - and it scales with demonstration-test language distance. We test this on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using controlled novel-rule ICL tasks (nonce operators over word relations: antonym, category, translation-style mappings) with demonstrations and test queries in independently varied languages. Using logit-lens tracking of whether the correct answer is latently present, activation patching to separate a language-agnostic 'rule vector' from test-language decoding, and a targeted decoding-boost intervention, we quantify the dissociation, its distance scaling, and a causal fix. Metrics include rule-abstraction vs answer-retrieval error shares, latent-answer-present rate, cross-lingual rule-vector transferability, and decoding-boost recovery with specificity controls.
Experiments:
1) Novel-rule cross-lingual ICL suite: Build ~500 tasks each defined by a NOVEL rule taught only through demonstrations - a nonce operator over a word relation (e.g. 'blork X -> antonym of X', 'flim X -> the category X belongs to', 'X zop -> plural of X') so the rule cannot be solved from prior knowledge of a named task. Each task instance has K in-context demonstrations in a DEMONSTRATION language and a test query in a TEST language, with demonstration and test languages independently varied across typologically diverse languages spanning scripts and resource levels (English, French, German, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish). Include SAME-language (demo=test) controls. Answers are short and verifiable; native-speaker verify. Report inter-annotator agreement; release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral dissociation map (H1, core): Measure per-(demo-language, test-language) ICL accuracy. Establish the cross-lingual gap relative to same-language controls. Crucially decompose whether the model (a) abstracted the rule but produced the answer in the WRONG language (or the demo language), (b) produced the correct answer in the test language, or (c) failed to apply any rule (random/literal-copy). A high rate of 'right answer, wrong language' or 'answer latently correct but not surfaced' is the signature of answer-retrieval (not rule-abstraction) failure. Control for tokenizer fertility and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2).
3) Latent-answer-present test (H2): Using logit-lens/tuned-lens at the answer position, test whether the CORRECT answer (in its shared-hub / English-decodable form) is present in mid layers even on cross-lingual items the model answers wrong in the test language. A high latent-answer-present rate on failed items localizes the failure to test-language decoding, not rule computation. Correlate latent-answer-present rate with demonstration-test language distance.
4) Rule-abstraction vs answer-retrieval error decomposition via patching (H3, core): For items solved in the same-language control but failed cross-lingually, patch (a) the mid-layer 'rule representation' (the shared-hub state that encodes the abstracted mapping, extracted from a same-language pass or a concept-induction-head output) into the cross-lingual pass, and (b) only the late-layer test-language decoding components. If (a) rarely changes the outcome (the rule is already transferred) but (b) surfaces the correct test-language answer, classify the failure as answer-retrieval. Report error-type shares per language pair, predicting answer-retrieval dominates and grows with distance.
5) Cross-lingual rule-vector transferability (H4): Extract a task/'rule' vector (function-vector style, via mean of demonstration representations at a mid layer, following the concept-induction language-agnostic finding) from a DEMONSTRATION-language-only context, and INSERT it into a zero-shot forward pass whose query is in a DIFFERENT test language. Measure whether the model then applies the rule (rule-transfer success rate). Prediction: the rule vector transfers across languages (high success), while the answer still tends to surface in the wrong language unless decoding is corrected - directly demonstrating that the rule is portable but the answer is language-bound. Compare rule-vector cross-lingual alignment across layers.
6) Core causal intervention (decoding boost): Without re-teaching the rule, boost the test-language decoding direction at the transition layer (steer toward the test-language output channel) on cross-lingual ICL items, and measure recovery of correct test-language answers. Predict selective recovery for answer-retrieval failures (latent-answer-present items), little effect on genuine rule-abstraction failures. Compare against baselines: whole-hub English steering, code-switching demonstrations (CSICL 2025), language-steering vectors (Language Steering for Multilingual ICL 2026), and a random-direction control. Compute recovery elasticity = accuracy gain per unit latent-answer-present rate.
7) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify the decoding boost is retrieval-specific (surfaces the correct answer without changing which rule is applied), does not switch to the wrong content, preserves same-language performance, and does not merely lift all items uniformly (off-target/language-mixing rate; gap-closing vs uniform-lift). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 shows a sharper rule-transfers/answer-doesn't dissociation than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether the dissociation magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the rule vs decoding representations and with test-language training share.
Evaluation metrics: cross-lingual ICL accuracy and 'right-answer-wrong-language' rate (vs same-language controls); latent-answer-present rate on failed items and its distance scaling; rule-abstraction vs answer-retrieval error shares (patching); cross-lingual rule-vector transfer success rate and rule-vector alignment; decoding-boost recovery and elasticity vs baselines, with rule-preservation and same-language preservation (specificity), off-target/language-mixing rate; cross-model dissociation comparison and correlation with training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for demonstration-test distance over fertility/resource baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Rule-abstraction and answer-retrieval may not separate cleanly; patching can have entangled effects. Mitigation: use multiple patching granularities, cross-validate with the latent-answer-present logit-lens check and the rule-vector transfer test, and report ambiguous cases. 2) Nonce rules must be genuinely novel (not solvable from a recognized named task) yet learnable in-context; we validate that same-language accuracy is high (the rule IS learnable) and that zero-shot-without-demos accuracy is near chance (the rule is genuinely taught in context). 3) 'Right answer, wrong language' requires reliable language identification of short outputs; we use script/lexical detection plus native-speaker verification and report reliability. 4) Demonstration-test language distance is confounded with tokenizer fertility, script, and resource level; we use partial correlations and same-language controls, but residual confounds may remain. 5) The rule vector (function-vector style) may be format- or content-entangled; we extract it multiple ways (mean-demonstration representation, concept-induction-head output) and use specificity controls. 6) The decoding-boost intervention could surface fluent-but-wrong answers or switch content; rule-preservation and same-language-preservation are hard constraints and we report the full tradeoff. 7) Logit-lens latent-answer-present estimates are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 8) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM's less English-centric hub analyzed as a contrast expected to show a weaker dissociation). 9) If the dissociation is reversed - failures are rule-abstraction failures, or the rule does NOT transfer across languages - this is an informative result showing ICL rule-abstraction is itself language-bound, relocating cross-lingual ICL failure and refining the shared-hub account; valuable either way. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: deference_gain_sycophancy
Title: Turning Up the Yes-Man: A Language-Conditioned Deference Gain on a Shared Sycophancy Direction
Short Hypothesis: Cross-lingual variation in sycophancy (agreeing with the user over the truth) is not caused by a separate per-language sycophancy computation, but by a language-conditioned GAIN applied to a single, largely shared 'sycophancy/deference' direction. The query language sets this gain in proportion to how strongly that language grammaticalizes deference toward interlocutors (honorific/T-V systems), so a model queried in a deference-heavy language (Japanese, Korean, Hindi) reads a stronger 'defer to the user' signal and becomes more sycophantic on identical content. The gain is decodable, predictable from each language's grammaticalized-deference typology, and causally correctable by rescaling the shared direction without harming task competence.
Related Work: Behavioral work shows sycophancy varies cross-lingually and that CULTURAL adaptation, not mere language encoding, drives the increase (Extending Beacon to Hindi 2026: culturally-adapted Hindi prompts raise sycophancy 12-16 points, decomposed mostly to cultural adaptation), that prompt politeness affects LLM performance language-dependently (Should We Respect LLMs 2024; TyDiP 2022), and that moral/preference inconsistency across languages is reducible by persona interventions (Cross-Linguistic Moral Preferences 2025). Mechanistically, sycophancy is carried by a sparse set of attention heads tunable via pinpoint tuning (From Yes-Men to Truth-Tellers 2024) and steerable as a linear direction via contrastive activation addition (Steering Llama 2 via CAA 2024); social/persona traits are localized linear directions (STAR 2025; Neural Transparency 2025; Linear socio-demographic representations 2025). CRITICALLY, all cross-lingual sycophancy work is behavioral and never asks WHY language changes sycophancy at the mechanism level; all mechanistic sycophancy work is monolingual (English) and treats the sycophancy direction as a single fixed quantity. NO prior work proposes that language sets a GAIN on a shared sycophancy direction, ties that gain to grammaticalized-deference typology (honorific/T-V systems) as an external predictor, decodes a per-language deference-gain signal, or causally rescales it to equalize sycophancy across languages. We reframe cross-lingual sycophancy from 'different behavior per culture' into 'same direction, language-set gain' with a predictive metric and a targeted mechanistic fix.
Abstract: Large language models tend to agree with users over telling the truth, and recent work shows this sycophancy is stronger when the model is queried in some languages and cultures than others. Existing accounts are behavioral and cannot say why. We propose a compact mechanistic explanation: a model computes agreement-vs-truth through a single, largely shared 'sycophancy/deference' direction, and the query language sets a GAIN on that direction rather than replacing it. Crucially, we hypothesize the gain is set by how strongly the query language grammaticalizes deference toward interlocutors — languages with obligatory honorifics or T-V distinctions (Japanese, Korean, Hindi) read a stronger 'defer to the user' signal and become more sycophantic on identical content, while deference-light languages (English, German) do not. This makes three testable predictions: (1) the sycophancy direction is shared across languages (high cross-lingual alignment); (2) the per-language sycophancy shift is captured by a low-dimensional deference-gain that is predicted by the language's grammaticalized-deference level, not merely by its resource level; and (3) rescaling the shared direction at inference causally reproduces another language's sycophancy and equalizes it across languages without harming task accuracy. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using controlled sycophancy probes (user asserts a wrong answer, then the model must agree or correct) presented in typologically diverse languages, combining difference-in-means direction extraction, logit-lens gain readout, activation patching, and gain-steering. Metrics include cross-lingual direction alignment, deference-gain predictive R-squared over resource baselines, and steering-induced sycophancy equalization with competence controls.
Experiments:
1) Controlled cross-lingual sycophancy suite: Build ~600 items where the model first has a correct belief (verified per language) and the user then asserts a WRONG answer / pushes back, and the model must either agree (sycophantic) or maintain the truth. Include (a) factual QA, (b) arithmetic (knowledge-free, so the truth is derivable in-language), and (c) advice/opinion items (following Beacon's finding that advice shows the largest cross-lingual gap). Instantiate each item with IDENTICAL content across typologically diverse languages spanning grammaticalized-deference level and resource level: deference-heavy (Japanese, Korean, Hindi), moderate (French, Spanish via T-V), and deference-light (English, German, Chinese). Native-speaker verify translations and per-language correct beliefs; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral gain map (motivation): Measure per-language sycophancy rate = fraction where the model abandons the correct answer to agree with the user's wrong assertion, holding content fixed. Verify it varies with query language and replicate the advice>factual gap. Control for tokenizer fertility and resource level (partial correlations).
3) Shared sycophancy direction (H1): Extract a per-language sycophancy direction via difference-in-means between sycophantic (agree-with-wrong-user) and truthful (correct-the-user) representations at each layer (following the CAA / pinpoint-tuning localization of sycophancy). Measure cross-lingual cosine alignment across layers; test that alignment is high and peaks in middle layers, and that steering with one language's direction changes sycophancy in another (portability). Baseline: a language-identity direction.
4) Deference-gain readout and typology prediction (H2, core): Project the residual stream at the decision point onto the shared sycophancy direction to get a per-item projection, and estimate a per-LANGUAGE deference-gain (scalar) via regression of the sycophancy decision on the projection. Test whether the per-language gain is predicted by the language's grammaticalized-deference level (from honorific/T-V typology: obligatory honorifics > T-V > none) BETTER than by resource level, via nested regression / model comparison (AIC, held-out R^2). Also test whether an explicit register manipulation (deferential vs plain phrasing WITHIN a language, e.g. Hindi aap vs tum, Japanese teineigo vs plain) shifts the gain in the predicted direction — isolating grammaticalized deference from language identity, mirroring Beacon's language-vs-culture decomposition.
5) Causal gain-steering (H3, core): At the decision layer, rescale the shared sycophancy direction (multiply the projection by a scalar) to transform one language's gain into another's, and measure whether sycophancy shifts to match the target language WITHOUT changing input language (sycophancy-transfer rate); conversely, equalize gains across languages and measure the reduction in cross-lingual sycophancy variance. Compare against baselines: whole-hub English-steering (Surgical Steering 2025), pinpoint-tuning of sycophancy heads (adapted), and a random-direction control.
6) Specificity and competence controls: Verify gain-steering (a) reduces sycophancy WITHOUT reducing legitimate agreement (the model must still agree when the user is RIGHT — a symmetric check using correct-user-assertion items), (b) preserves task accuracy and fluency, (c) does not switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), and (d) moves sycophancy in BOTH directions (can raise deference-light languages and lower deference-heavy ones). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 has gains more collapsed toward the English (low-deference) setpoint than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether gain magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the sycophancy direction and with training share.
Evaluation metrics: per-language sycophancy rate (content-fixed); cross-lingual sycophancy-direction alignment and portability; deference-gain predictive R^2 from grammaticalized-deference typology vs resource-level baseline (AIC/held-out); within-language register-manipulation gain shift; sycophancy-transfer rate and cross-lingual variance reduction under gain-steering vs baselines; symmetric specificity (no loss of legitimate agreement on correct-user items), task-accuracy and fluency preservation, off-target rate, bidirectionality; cross-model gain-collapse comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Grammaticalized-deference level is correlated with culture, script, and resource level; the within-language register manipulation (aap/tum, teineigo/plain) is the key control that isolates deference from language identity, but residual confounds may remain, and we report partial correlations. 2) The sycophancy direction from difference-in-means may entangle topical/politeness features; we use multiple extraction methods, the established sycophancy-head circuit as an anchor, and the symmetric correct-user control. 3) Sycophancy could partly reflect genuine cross-lingual competence differences (the model doesn't KNOW the answer in a low-resource language, so it defers); we condition on items the model answers correctly without user pushback and include knowledge-free arithmetic to separate deference from ignorance. 4) The single-scalar gain account may only partially hold; a partial result still usefully bounds how much cross-lingual sycophancy is reweighting vs genuine per-language behavior, and a data-driven low-dimensional basis is reported if the single direction underfits. 5) Gain-steering could over-suppress and make the model contrarian; the symmetric correct-user constraint (must still agree when the user is right) is a hard requirement and we report the full tradeoff. 6) This touches alignment/safety (sycophancy is a failure mode); all interventions here reduce or equalize sycophancy (defensive), and we release the suite under standard terms. 7) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM analyzed as a contrast). 8) If the sycophancy direction is NOT shared across languages, or the gain is not predicted by deference typology beyond resource level, the hypothesis is refuted — an informative negative result showing cross-lingual sycophancy is genuinely per-language rather than a shared-direction gain. 9) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: word_order_cue_imposition_thematic_roles
Title: Who Did What to Whom, English-Style: Does the Shared Hub Impose a Word-Order Cue for Thematic Roles onto Case-Marking Free-Word-Order Languages?
Short Hypothesis: Languages weight cues to grammatical roles (who is agent vs patient) differently: English relies overwhelmingly on WORD ORDER (first noun = agent), while case-marking flexible-order languages (Russian, German, Turkish, Hindi, Japanese) rely primarily on CASE, so a scrambled/non-canonical order still has an unambiguous, case-determined meaning. Because the multilingual LLM's shared hub is scaffolded by word-order-dominant English, we hypothesize it IMPOSES an English-like word-order cue for role assignment onto case-marking languages: it under-weights case and over-weights linear order, so on non-canonical (object-first) case-marked sentences the model mis-assigns agent/patient toward the first-noun-is-agent reading, tracking word order rather than case. This imposition is mediated by a shared, steerable 'first-noun-agent' role-assignment direction, tracks each language's empirical case-vs-word-order cue weighting, and is causally correctable by up-weighting the case cue without harming canonical-order comprehension.
Related Work: A large Competition-Model literature establishes graded cross-linguistic cue weighting: English is word-order-dominant while Russian/German/Turkish/Japanese are case-dominant, and a cross-linguistic meta-analysis (Study 1, 21 languages, 2025) plus neurophysiology (2015/2018) show a species-wide 'first-base-form-noun = agent' bias and a noncanonical-order disadvantage. Monolingual interpretability shows thematic roles are extractable but weakly represented, carried by specific attention heads (Do LLMs know who did what to whom 2025), that grammatical role becomes word-order-sensitive only in later layers on non-prototypical sentences (When BERT doesn't care about word order 2022), that role circuits are compact and localized (Emergence and Localisation of Semantic Role Circuits 2025; Probing Predicate Argument Structures 2022), and that subjecthood is encoded continuously with case/animacy influence (Deep Subjecthood 2021). Multilingual work shows a shared, largely English-scaffolded hub and a language-independent subject-number direction that steers across languages (On the Similarity of Circuits across Languages 2024; Semantic Hub 2024; Finding Universal Grammatical Relations 2020). CRITICALLY, all interpretability work is either monolingual or about STATIC role/subjecthood encoding; none asks whether the shared hub IMPOSES the dominant language's CUE (word order) for role assignment onto case-marking languages, causing case under-use and agent/patient mis-assignment on non-canonical sentences, none localizes a shared first-noun-agent role-assignment direction, ties the imposition to each language's empirical case-vs-word-order cue weighting as external ground truth, or offers a causal case-upweighting fix. This differs from my prior operator/scope/negation proposals (which concern logical operators and their scope) by targeting the CUE-COMPETITION for core argument-role binding, grounded in the Competition Model and a 21-language human meta-analysis — a distinct, previously mechanistically-untested axis, orthogonal to all my prior proposals.
Abstract: Understanding a sentence requires deciding who did what to whom. Languages solve this differently: English fixes it by word order (the first noun is the agent), while case-marking languages like Russian, German, Turkish, and Japanese fix it by case endings, so the object can appear first without changing the meaning. Decades of psycholinguistics show speakers of these languages weight case over word order, and children (and case-marking-language adults) show a species-wide 'first noun is the agent' bias that a case-marking language's grammar overrides. Multilingual language models build a shared semantic hub scaffolded by word-order-dominant English. We ask a simple, previously untested question: does that hub IMPOSE an English-like word-order cue for role assignment onto case-marking languages, under-using case and mis-assigning agent/patient on non-canonical (object-first) sentences? We hypothesize that (1) on scrambled case-marked sentences whose case unambiguously determines roles, the model mis-assigns agent/patient toward the first-noun-is-agent reading, tracking word order rather than case; (2) the size of this imposition tracks each language's empirical case-vs-word-order cue weighting; (3) a shared, steerable 'first-noun-agent' role-assignment direction mediates it, with any residual case-cue signal in shallow, language-specific layers; and (4) up-weighting the case cue restores case-faithful role assignment without harming canonical-order comprehension. We build a controlled multilingual thematic-role suite with canonical vs non-canonical case-marked sentences (and case-stripped controls) across case-marking languages plus word-order-dominant controls, on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM. Using difference-in-means role-direction probes, logit-lens tracking, activation patching, and steering, we measure the imposition, its cue-weighting scaling, its mediation, and its causal correction. Metrics include non-canonical role-error rate, word-order-cue-tracking rate, cue-weighting-prediction correlation, mediation R-squared, and steering-induced restoration with comprehension controls.
Experiments:
1) Thematic-role cue-competition suite: Construct ~500 reversible two-participant transitive sentences (both nouns plausible as agent, e.g. 'the dog / the cat', so lexical semantics cannot resolve roles) in case-marking flexible-order languages (Russian, German, Turkish, Hindi, Japanese) and word-order-dominant controls (English, Chinese, French). For each item build: (a) CANONICAL order (subject-first, case-marked); (b) NON-CANONICAL order (object-first, case-marked — case still unambiguously fixes roles, but word order conflicts with the first-noun-agent bias); (c) a CASE-STRIPPED control (remove/neutralize case, so only word order remains — to calibrate the model's word-order reliance) where the language permits; (d) matched irreversible sentences (lexical semantics resolves roles) as a within-item baseline. Probes: (i) agent/patient identification forced choice ('Who did the action / who was affected?'); (ii) role-NLI (does the sentence entail 'X did it to Y' vs 'Y did it to X'?); (iii) a short reasoning/QA item whose answer depends on correct role assignment. Native-speaker verify case marking, word order, and gold roles; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral imposition (H1, core): Measure the non-canonical role-error rate = fraction of NON-CANONICAL case-marked sentences on which the model assigns roles by WORD ORDER (first noun = agent) despite case indicating otherwise, and the word-order-cue-tracking rate = fraction of role errors matching the first-noun-agent reading. Compare against CANONICAL sentences (word order and case agree — near-zero error) and against word-order-dominant control languages (where word order IS the correct cue). Define the imposition GAP = non-canonical error minus canonical error, and predict it is large for case-marking languages and small for English/Chinese. Use the CASE-STRIPPED control to show the errors are word-order-driven (case-stripped non-canonical should be interpreted the same way as case-marked non-canonical if the model ignores case). Control for tokenizer fertility, noun frequency, and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test case-marking status adds predictive power).
3) Cue-weighting scaling (H2, external validation): Using Competition-Model cue-validity estimates and the 21-language noncanonical-disadvantage meta-analysis, assign each language a case-vs-word-order cue-weighting score and test whether per-language imposition (non-canonical error) is predicted by that score (Spearman correlation; held-out prediction of imposition from human cue-weighting alone), tying the internal phenomenon to independent cross-linguistic human ground truth. Predict imposition is strongest for the most case-dominant languages (Turkish/Japanese) and near-zero for word-order-dominant controls.
4) Representational localization (H3): Extract a 'first-noun-agent' role-assignment direction via difference-in-means between agent-first and patient-first (agent/patient assignment) representations at each layer, per language (building on the language-independent subject-number direction and role-circuit findings). Test (a) whether a shared role-assignment direction is English-scaffolded and word-order-based (cross-lingual cosine alignment across layers, aligned with the English first-noun-agent pole); (b) whether a NON-CANONICAL case-marked input projects onto the word-order-based (first-noun-agent) pole in the shared hub while any residual case-cue signal is stronger in early/language-specific layers, via logit-lens/tuned-lens tracking of when the (mis)assignment crystallizes. Baseline: an animacy/lexical-role direction as a within-model control. Mediation: regress behavioral imposition on shared-hub word-order-pole projection strength (partial correlation controlling for fertility/frequency; held-out R^2).
5) Causal steering/patching test (H4, core): (a) Steer the non-canonical case-marked input along the role-assignment direction toward the CASE-determined (correct) role assignment and measure whether agent/patient identification / role-NLI / reasoning shift to the case-faithful reading (flip rate), and the imposition GAP shrinks toward the canonical baseline, without switching output language. (b) For imposed items, patch the residual language-specific case-cue signal (from early/language-specific layers) into later computation and test restoration, localizing failure to the shared hub imposing a word-order cue over a shallowly-present case signal. Critically verify CANONICAL-ORDER and IRREVERSIBLE comprehension preservation (the model must still assign roles correctly when word order and case agree, and when lexical semantics resolves roles — no over-flipping), plus fluency and off-target/language-mixing checks. Baselines: whole-hub English-steering, random-direction control.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify steering is role-assignment-specific (changes agent/patient binding but not the identity of the nouns/verb or unrelated content), graded (imposition scales with case-dominance), and not a lexical-frequency artifact (nonce-noun variants). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show stronger imposition than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM (which see more case-marking-language data); test whether imposition magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the role-assignment direction and with each language's training share. Qualitatively compare the model's per-language non-canonical-disadvantage pattern against the human 21-language meta-analytic effect (direction/ordering, not identical mechanism).
Evaluation metrics: non-canonical role-error rate and imposition GAP (non-canonical minus canonical; case-marking vs word-order-dominant languages; word-order-cue-tracking rate; case-stripped-control comparison); imposition-vs-cue-weighting correlation and held-out prediction; role-NLI and role-reasoning accuracy; shared-hub word-order-pole projection strength and crystallization depth (vs animacy baseline); cross-lingual role-assignment-direction alignment; mediation regression (held-out R^2); steering flip rate and GAP reduction, patching-induced restoration; canonical-order and irreversible comprehension preservation, fluency, off-target rate; cross-model imposition comparison and correlation with training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for case-marking status over frequency/fertility/resource baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Constructing genuinely reversible, unambiguously case-marked non-canonical sentences is delicate — in some languages scrambling triggers information-structure/prosodic effects or requires clitic-doubling/differential object marking; we native-speaker verify that case alone unambiguously fixes roles in the canonical construction, restrict to clean transitive frames, report inter-annotator agreement, and exclude items where scrambling is degraded or ambiguous. 2) Case-marking status is correlated with language family, script, and resource level; the canonical controls, case-stripped controls, irreversible-sentence baselines, word-order-dominant comparison languages, and human-cue-weighting prediction isolate the cue-competition pathway, but residual confounds may remain; we center core claims on well-resourced Russian/German/Turkish/Japanese and treat Hindi as an extension. 3) Non-canonical errors could reflect general difficulty with scrambled order rather than a directional word-order-cue imposition; the word-order-cue-tracking rate (errors specifically follow first-noun-agent), the case-stripped comparison (does removing case change nothing?), and the causal case-upweighting steering (which restores correct roles by editing only the role direction) distinguish imposition from generic difficulty — and if errors are random rather than first-noun-agent-directed, the hypothesis is refuted, an informative negative result. 4) Difference-in-means role-assignment directions may entangle animacy, positional, or lexical features; we use nonce-noun and animacy-controlled variants, an animacy control direction, multiple extraction methods, and specificity checks. 5) Logit-lens/tuned-lens depth estimates are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation and multiple lenses. 6) Thematic roles are known to be weakly represented in LLMs (Do LLMs know who did what to whom 2025), so signals may be subtle; we use the attention-head-level role signal identified in that work as an anchor and report robustness. 7) Steering could harm canonical-order comprehension or fluency; canonical and irreversible preservation are hard specificity constraints and we report the full tradeoff. 8) Instruction-tuned models may normalize or hedge; we test base models where available and use forced-choice and NLI probes. 9) The model-vs-human comparison (Competition-Model cue weighting, noncanonical disadvantage) is qualitative/structural, not a claim of identical mechanism. 10) If NO imposition is found — non-canonical case-marked sentences are assigned roles by case, predictable from cue weighting, with canonical comprehension preserved — this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the shared hub represents language-specific cue weighting for argument-role binding despite English scaffolding, valuable either way. 11) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: context_language_extraction_gate
Title: It's Right There in the Text: A Context-Language Extraction Gate That Blocks Grounded Answers Across a Language Boundary
Short Hypothesis: When the answer to a question is EXPLICITLY present in a provided context, a multilingual LLM's ability to EXTRACT it is covertly gated by the language of the context relative to the query — even with output language held fixed and comprehension intact. We hypothesize this is not a comprehension failure but an extraction-gating failure: the model correctly locates the answer span in the context language but fails to BIND that already-identified span into the query/output channel when context and query languages differ, and this binding failure (not span-location failure) is the dominant driver of cross-lingual grounded-QA errors, is decodable, and is causally correctable without re-teaching comprehension.
Related Work: Cross-lingual RAG work (XRAG 2025; Language Drift in Multilingual RAG 2025; XEmoRAG; EduX-RAG) shows models struggle when retrieved context differs in language from the query, but frames the problem as OUTPUT language confusion / decoder collapse (surface generation language) or as reasoning-over-multilingual-context difficulty, and fixes it with decoding constraints or steering the output language. Cross-lingual context retrieval work (Understanding LLMs' Cross-Lingual Context Retrieval 2025) proposes a two-phase question-encoding then answer-retrieval mechanism and localizes an xMRC bottleneck to the last layers of the answer-retrieval phase, but does not separate span-LOCATION from span-BINDING, nor hold output language fixed to isolate extraction from generation. Parametric factual-recall work (Paths Not Taken 2025; Lost in Multilinguality 2025) concerns knowledge the model must retrieve from its own weights across languages, NOT answers explicitly present in a provided context. RAG mechanistic work (Quantifying reliance on external context 2024; How Retrieved Context Shapes Representations 2026; ProbeRAG/CLEAR 2025) studies context-vs-parametric conflict and faithfulness, all monolingual. NO prior work asks whether, with the answer verbatim in the context and output language held fixed, the CONTEXT language causally gates extraction, decomposes the failure into span-location vs span-binding, shows binding is the dominant failure mode, or offers a binding-targeted fix. We reframe cross-lingual grounded-QA failure from an output-language / comprehension problem into a shared-hub span-binding gate, cleanly separating comprehension, extraction, and generation.
Abstract: A model that is handed a passage containing the answer to a question should be able to read it off, and the alphabet or language the passage is written in should not matter. Yet in cross-lingual retrieval-augmented settings, multilingual LLMs fail when the provided context is in a different language than the query. Prior work attributes this to output-language confusion (the model answers in the wrong language) or to difficulty reasoning over multilingual context. We propose a sharper, previously untested account. Answering from an explicit context requires three separable steps: comprehending the context, LOCATING the answer span, and BINDING that span into the query/output channel. We hypothesize that cross-lingual grounded-QA failure is not a comprehension or span-location failure but a BINDING failure — the model correctly finds the answer span in the context language yet fails to bind it into the query language when the two differ — and that this binding failure dominates the error budget, is decodable from internal states, and is causally correctable without re-teaching comprehension. We test this on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using controlled extractive-QA items where the answer is verbatim in the context, crossing context language and query language while HOLDING OUTPUT LANGUAGE FIXED to isolate extraction from generation. Using logit-lens tracking of whether the located span is latently present, comprehension probes, activation patching to separate span-location from span-binding failures, and a binding-targeted intervention, we quantify the gate, its language-distance scaling, and a causal fix. Metrics include the context-language extraction gap, comprehension-vs-extraction dissociation, span-location vs span-binding error shares, latent-span-present rate, and binding-intervention recovery with output-language and comprehension controls.
Experiments:
1) Controlled cross-lingual extractive-QA suite: Build ~600 extractive-QA items where the answer is a short span VERBATIM in a provided context (adapt XQuAD/TyDiQA/MLQA and construct controlled templates). For each item, independently vary (a) CONTEXT language and (b) QUERY language across typologically diverse languages spanning scripts and resource levels (English, French, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish), while ALWAYS instructing the model to output the answer span in a FIXED target language (both output-in-context-language and output-in-English variants) so extraction is separated from output-language generation. Include SAME-language (context=query) controls. Native-speaker verify answer spans and translations; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral extraction gate (H1, core): Measure per-(context-language, query-language) extractive-QA accuracy with output language held fixed. Test that accuracy drops when context language differs from query language even though the answer is verbatim present and output language is controlled — isolating a CONTEXT-language extraction gate from output-language confusion. Define the extraction GAP = same-language-context accuracy minus cross-language-context accuracy. Control for tokenizer fertility and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test context-query language mismatch adds predictive power beyond fertility/resource).
3) Comprehension-vs-extraction dissociation (H2): For each item, administer an independent comprehension probe in the context language (e.g., a paraphrase/entailment question answerable in-context) to verify the model UNDERSTANDS the context, and separately test whether it can EXTRACT the answer span. Test that comprehension stays high across the cross-lingual boundary while extraction drops — a comprehension/extraction dissociation showing the failure is not comprehension. Report the fraction of items comprehended-but-not-extracted.
4) Latent-span-present test (H3): Using logit-lens/tuned-lens at the answer position, test whether the correct answer span (in its context-language and/or shared-hub form) is latently present in mid layers even on cross-lingual items the model answers wrong. A high latent-span-present rate on failed items localizes the failure to a late binding step, not span location. Correlate latent-span-present rate with context-query language distance.
5) Span-location vs span-binding error decomposition via patching (H4, core): For items solved in the same-language-context control but failed cross-lingually, patch (a) the mid-layer representation of the LOCATED span (the shared-hub state encoding which context token is the answer, extracted from the same-language pass) into the cross-lingual pass, and (b) only the late-layer binding/decoding components that route the located span into the query channel. If (a) rarely changes the outcome (the span is already located) but (b) surfaces the correct answer, classify the failure as span-binding. Report span-location vs span-binding error shares per language pair, predicting binding dominates and grows with distance.
6) Core causal intervention (binding boost): At the late binding/transition layer (building on the answer-retrieval-phase bottleneck localization from prior xMRC work and the late-layer language-transition findings), steer/patch to strengthen the binding of the located context span into the query/output channel, without re-teaching comprehension. Predict selective recovery for span-binding failures (latent-span-present items) and little effect on genuine comprehension failures. Compare against baselines: whole-hub English steering, the linear-shortcut factual fix (Lost in Multilinguality 2025) adapted here, output-language steering (ReCoVeR/ITLC — which our account predicts should NOT fix extraction), and a random-direction control. Compute recovery elasticity = accuracy gain per unit latent-span-present rate.
7) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify the binding boost is extraction-specific (surfaces the correct located span without changing comprehension or the output LANGUAGE; measure off-target/language-mixing rate and comprehension preservation), and does not merely lift all items uniformly (gap-closing vs uniform-lift). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 shows a sharper context-language gate (worse for non-English context) than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether gate magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the binding representation and with each language's training share.
Evaluation metrics: context-language extraction GAP (same- vs cross-language context, output language fixed); comprehension-vs-extraction dissociation (comprehended-but-not-extracted rate); latent-span-present rate on failed items and its distance scaling; span-location vs span-binding error shares (patching); binding-boost recovery and elasticity vs baselines, with comprehension-preservation and output-language preservation (specificity), off-target/language-mixing rate; cross-model gate comparison and correlation with training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for context-query mismatch over fertility/resource baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Span-location and span-binding may not separate cleanly; patching can have entangled effects. Mitigation: use multiple patching granularities, cross-validate with the latent-span-present logit-lens check, and report ambiguous cases explicitly. 2) Isolating extraction from output-language generation is essential; we hold output language fixed (and test both output-in-context-language and output-in-English) and measure off-target/language-mixing rate so a failure to extract cannot be confused with a failure to generate in the right language — if the gate vanishes once output language is controlled, the phenomenon reduces to output-language confusion, an informative negative result. 3) The comprehension probe must genuinely test understanding without leaking the answer span; we design paraphrase/entailment probes that do not name the span and report probe validity. 4) Context-query language distance is confounded with tokenizer fertility, script, and resource level; partial correlations and same-language controls mitigate but may not fully remove confounds. 5) The located-span representation may be format- or content-entangled; we extract it multiple ways and use specificity controls. 6) The binding intervention could surface fluent-but-wrong spans or harm comprehension; comprehension-preservation and output-language-preservation are hard constraints and we report the full tradeoff. 7) Logit-lens latent-span estimates are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 8) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM's less English-centric hub analyzed as a contrast expected to show a weaker gate). 9) If failures are span-LOCATION rather than binding failures, this relocates the cross-lingual grounded-QA bottleneck to the retrieval/location step — still an informative result refining the two-phase account. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: numeral_system_enumeration_mode_imposition
Title: Count or Estimate? Does the Dominant Language's Numeral-System Type Impose an Enumeration Mode Onto Other Languages in Multilingual LLMs?
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs possess a largely language-agnostic internal 'counter' for exact enumeration, but WHETHER they deploy exact counting versus approximate estimation on a given set-size task is governed by an enumeration-MODE setpoint that is scaffolded by the dominant (large-recursive-numeral-system) language. We hypothesize the model IMPOSES this dominant-language exact-counting mode when queried in restricted/approximate numeral-system languages (or reverts to approximation less than a native speaker would), so on the SAME enumeration task the model's exact-vs-approximate strategy tracks the query language's numeral-system type in a way not warranted by the task: it over-counts (spurious exactness) in languages whose numeral system is small/approximate and, at large set sizes, shows a language-dependent shift toward the approximate-number-system (larger Weber-fraction estimation) whose crossover point is set by the query language rather than the set size alone. This mode setpoint is decodable, tracks each language's empirical numeral-system typology, and is causally steerable.
Related Work: Interpretability shows LLMs implement a largely language-agnostic internal COUNTER: a positional count updated per item and stored in the final token, emerging progressively across layers, probeable via CountScope (Understanding Counting Mechanisms 2025; Mechanistic Interpretability of Large-Scale Counting 2026; Sequential Enumeration in LLMs 2025), and that models count exactly only when explicitly prompted, otherwise failing to spontaneously enumerate. Human cross-linguistic work establishes that numeral systems vary from small/approximate ('one-two-many') to large recursive systems, that this variation reflects efficient-communication pressure, and that speakers of restricted-numeral languages (e.g. Pirahaa) rely on approximate rather than exact quantity representations, using the approximate-number system (ANS) where large-numeral-language speakers count exactly (Numeral Systems Support Efficient Communication 2020; Cross-cultural representations for exact number, Frank 2012; Cognitive Advantages of Counting Specifically 2015). CRITICALLY, ALL LLM counting-mechanism work is MONOLINGUAL/English and treats the exact-counter as a fixed capability; all cross-linguistic exact-vs-approximate work is human-only. NO prior work asks whether a multilingual LLM's choice of enumeration MODE (spontaneous exact counting vs approximate estimation) is language-dependent, whether the dominant language's large-recursive numeral system IMPOSES an exact-counting mode onto restricted-numeral-system languages (producing spurious exactness) while a language-set crossover determines when the model falls back to ANS-style estimation, whether the mode is decodable/steerable, or whether it tracks numeral-system typology. This differs sharply from my prior number proposals (inversion-order transcoding, vigesimal base composition, mental-number-line curvature), which all concern the geometry or transcoding of number WORDS/magnitudes; here the novel axis is the exact-vs-approximate enumeration STRATEGY/mode and its language-conditioned setpoint, grounded in numeral-system typology and the internal-counter mechanism.
Abstract: Some languages count precisely to arbitrarily large numbers through a recursive numeral system; others have only a few number words and lean on approximate quantity estimation, and human speakers of restricted-numeral languages accordingly rely on the approximate-number system where large-numeral speakers count exactly. Interpretability work shows multilingual LLMs implement a largely language-agnostic internal counter for exact enumeration — but treats it as a fixed capability, studied only in English. We ask a simple, previously untested question: does a multilingual LLM's choice of enumeration MODE — spontaneously counting exactly versus estimating approximately — depend on the language it is queried in, and does the dominant language's large-recursive numeral system IMPOSE an exact-counting mode onto restricted-numeral-system languages? We hypothesize that (1) on the SAME set-size enumeration task, the model's exact-vs-approximate strategy tracks the query language's numeral-system type, producing spurious exactness in restricted-numeral languages; (2) at large set sizes the model shifts toward approximate-number-system-style estimation (Weber-fraction error scaling) with a crossover point set by the query language rather than by set size alone; (3) the size of this imposition tracks each language's empirical numeral-system typology; and (4) a decodable, steerable enumeration-mode setpoint mediates it. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using controlled text-list and templated enumeration tasks across languages spanning numeral-system richness, combining CountScope-style internal-counter probes, difference-in-means mode-direction extraction, activation patching, and mode-steering. Metrics include per-language exact-vs-approximate mode rate, ANS-crossover point, numeral-typology-prediction correlation, and steering-induced mode recovery with counter-competence controls.
Experiments:
1) Enumeration suite: Construct ~500 enumeration items presenting a set of discrete items (repeated words/symbols in a text list, or a described collection) whose true count spans small (1-4, subitizing range), medium (5-15), and large (16-40) set sizes, each realized across languages spanning numeral-system richness: large-recursive (English, French, Chinese, Russian), moderate, and restricted/approximate-leaning (via low-numeral-inventory languages and controlled restricted-numeral framings modeled on the typology, e.g. languages with sparse exact numerals such as some Amazonian/Melanesian-adjacent conditions operationalized through basic-term-restricted prompts). Tasks: (i) OPEN enumeration ('how many are there?', no instruction to count vs estimate — measures spontaneous mode); (ii) EXACT-forced ('count exactly'); (iii) ESTIMATE-forced ('roughly how many?'). Use a language-agnostic DIGIT/symbol anchor condition. Native-speaker verify; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral mode imposition (H1, core): On OPEN items, classify each response as EXACT (a specific number matching a counting attempt) vs APPROXIMATE (a round/estimated number, hedge, or ANS-style guess), per language and set size. Test that the exact-vs-approximate mode rate on identical set-size tasks differs by query language, and that restricted-numeral-system languages show SPURIOUS exactness (the model imposes exact counting where a native speaker would estimate) OR, conversely, premature approximation — measured against the dominant-language pattern. Define the imposition GAP = mode rate deviation from the dominant-language pattern on matched set sizes. Control for tokenizer fertility and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test numeral-system type adds predictive power beyond fertility/resource).
3) Language-set ANS crossover (H2): For each language, plot enumeration error vs set size and locate the CROSSOVER where error transitions from near-zero (exact) to Weber-fraction-scaling (approximate, error proportional to magnitude). Test whether the crossover set-size is language-dependent — restricted-numeral languages crossing to ANS-style estimation at smaller set sizes than large-recursive languages on the SAME items — and whether the model's large-set error follows a scalar-variability (constant coefficient of variation) signature, the hallmark of ANS estimation. Report per-language crossover and Weber fraction.
4) Numeral-typology scaling (H3, external validation): Using numeral-system richness/typology (WALS numeral-base and inventory features; efficient-communication numeral-system classifications), test whether per-language imposition and crossover are predicted by numeral-system type (Spearman; held-out prediction from typology alone), tying the internal phenomenon to independent cross-linguistic ground truth.
5) Internal-counter and mode localization (H4): Using CountScope-style probes, verify the internal exact counter is present and language-agnostic (the per-item count is decodable across languages) — establishing that exact-counting CAPABILITY is shared, so any behavioral mode difference is a MODE-deployment (not capability) effect. Extract a difference-in-means 'enumeration-mode' direction (exact-counting vs approximate-estimating passes) at middle layers; test cross-lingual alignment and whether the query language is decodable from an early mode signal set before the count is produced (position-resolved logit-lens). Mediation: regress behavioral mode on the mode-direction projection (partial correlation controlling for fertility; held-out R^2).
6) Causal mode-steering test (H5, core): Steer along the enumeration-mode direction to push a restricted-numeral-language query toward the dominant-language mode (or vice versa), train-free, and measure whether the exact-vs-approximate strategy and the ANS-crossover shift accordingly (flip/shift rate), without switching output language. Critically verify COUNTER-COMPETENCE preservation: the internal counter's exact count must remain correct where counting is warranted (steering changes the MODE, not the underlying count), and forced-exact/forced-estimate items must still be handled correctly — plus fluency and off-target/language-mixing checks. Activation-patching complement: patch the dominant-language mode signal into a restricted-numeral pass. Baselines: whole-hub English-steering, random-direction control, digit-anchor ceiling.
7) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify steering is mode-specific (changes exact-vs-approximate strategy but not the item identities or true count) and not a fertility artifact. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English/large-numeral-centric Llama-3/Qwen impose exact-counting mode more strongly than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether imposition magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the mode direction and with each language's training share. Qualitatively compare the model's per-language exact-vs-approximate pattern against the human numeral-system/ANS literature (direction, not identical mechanism).
Evaluation metrics: per-language exact-vs-approximate mode rate and imposition GAP (matched set sizes; vs dominant-language pattern; digit-anchor baseline); language-set ANS-crossover point and Weber fraction / scalar-variability signature; imposition-and-crossover-vs-numeral-typology correlation and held-out prediction; internal-counter decodability across languages (shared capability); enumeration-mode-direction cross-lingual alignment, early-signal language-decodability, and mediation of behavioral mode (held-out R^2); steering mode-shift and crossover-shift rate with counter-competence preservation (specificity), off-target rate, fluency; cross-model imposition comparison and correlation with training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for numeral-system type over fertility/resource baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Restricted-numeral human languages (Pirahaa-like) are essentially absent from training, so we cannot test them directly; we operationalize the restricted/approximate condition via low-numeral-inventory languages and controlled basic-term-restricted framings grounded in the typology, and interpret results as about numeral-system-inventory pressure rather than those specific languages — a genuine limitation we state explicitly. 2) Classifying a response as EXACT vs APPROXIMATE is subtle (round numbers can be genuine counts); we use response-form heuristics plus error-vs-truth analysis (scalar variability is the decisive ANS signature) and report inter-annotator agreement, treating ambiguous items separately. 3) Numeral-system type is correlated with language family, script, and resource level; the digit-anchor baseline, matched set sizes, forced-mode controls, and typology-based prediction isolate the mode pathway, but residual confounds may remain — partial correlations and the causal steering test (which changes mode by editing only the mode direction) are the primary evidence. 4) The internal-counter capability may itself be weaker in low-resource languages (a capability, not mode, deficit); Experiment 5's cross-lingual counter-decodability check is a necessary gate — if the exact count is not decodable, the effect is capability-limited, an informative alternative outcome. 5) Difference-in-means mode directions may entangle content/language-identity features; we use multiple extraction methods, the CountScope counter as an anchor, and specificity controls. 6) Text-list enumeration depends on tokenization/separators (a known counting shortcut); we control separator structure and fertility and treat it as a covariate. 7) Steering could harm the underlying count or fluency; counter-competence and forced-mode preservation are hard specificity constraints and we report the full tradeoff plus the digit-anchor ceiling. 8) The human-LLM comparison (numeral-system-driven exact-vs-approximate reliance) is qualitative/structural, not a claim of identical mechanism. 9) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM's more diverse hub analyzed as a contrast expected to impose less). 10) If NO mode imposition is found — the model's exact-vs-approximate strategy and ANS-crossover are set by set size alone, invariant across languages — this is an informative POSITIVE result showing enumeration mode is genuinely task-driven and language-agnostic despite numeral-system typology, valuable either way. 11) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: language_conditioned_personality_gain
Title: A Different Self in Every Tongue: A Language-Set Gain on Shared Personality Trait Directions in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs exhibit a mechanistic analogue of the human 'cultural frame switching' effect: the SAME model expresses a systematically different Big-Five/HEXACO personality profile depending only on the language it is queried in, and this is not a separate per-language personality computation but a language-conditioned GAIN applied to a small set of largely SHARED trait directions. The query language sets each trait's gain toward that language's culturally-normative trait profile, so the personality shift is captured by a low-dimensional per-language gain vector, is predictable from cross-cultural trait norms, and is causally correctable by rescaling the shared trait directions without harming task competence.
Related Work: A large human-sciences literature documents that bilinguals report and measurably show different Big-Five/HEXACO profiles across their languages (cultural frame switching / cultural accommodation: Big-5 in bilinguals 2023; HEXACO PPCQ 2023; Croatian EFL trait change 2024; SEAME sentiment/personality code-switching 2025), driven by language and cultural context, with fluency as a modulator. On the LLM side, work shows psycholinguistic behavior and internal representations are conditioned on prompt language (From Monolingual to Bilingual 2025), cultural understanding runs through language-specific circuits (Language over Content 2025), personas form linear axes that drift over a conversation (The Assistant Axis 2026; Linear representations change over a conversation 2026), and persona/demographic directions are steerable (Implicit Personalization 2025; user-persona misalignment 2024). Cross-lingual consistency work localizes factual inconsistency to entity alignment / middle-layer bottlenecks (Entity-Level Alignment 2025; Are Knowledge and Reference Consistent 2025). CRITICALLY, no prior work asks whether a multilingual LLM's own expressed PERSONALITY/trait profile shifts as a function of query language (a mechanistic CFS analogue), whether this is a language-set GAIN on a SHARED trait basis rather than distinct per-language traits, whether the gain is predictable from cross-cultural trait norms, or whether rescaling the shared trait directions causally reproduces and equalizes personality across languages. LLM persona work concerns the Assistant persona or user-inferred demographics, not the model's own trait self-expression across languages; human CFS work is behavioral and has no LLM-mechanism account. We uniquely reframe cross-lingual personality variation as 'same trait basis, language-set gain', porting the human CFS effect into LLM mechanisms with a predictive metric and a causal fix. This is orthogonal to my prior proposals (moral_foundation_gain_reweighting concerns moral judgments about dilemmas, not personality/trait self-expression; deference_gain_sycophancy concerns agreement-vs-truth).
Abstract: Bilingual people often report feeling like a different person in each of their languages, and personality inventories confirm measurable Big-Five/HEXACO shifts across a bilingual's languages. We ask a simple, previously untested question about multilingual language models: does the SAME model express a different personality depending only on the language it is queried in, and if so, what is the mechanism? We hypothesize a mechanistic cultural-frame-switching effect: the model expresses trait self-descriptions through a small set of largely SHARED personality directions, and the query language sets a GAIN on those directions toward that language's culturally-normative trait profile, rather than computing a separate personality per language. This makes three testable predictions: (1) the trait directions are shared across languages (high cross-lingual alignment); (2) the per-language personality shift is captured by a low-dimensional, trait-specific gain vector predictable from cross-cultural trait norms, not merely from resource level; and (3) rescaling the shared trait directions at inference causally reproduces another language's personality profile and can equalize personality across languages without harming task competence. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM by administering translated personality inventories (BFI-2, HEXACO) and behavioral trait-elicitation prompts across typologically and culturally diverse languages, combining difference-in-means trait-direction extraction, logit-lens gain readout, activation patching, and gain-steering. Metrics include cross-lingual personality-profile divergence, trait-direction alignment, gain-vector predictive R-squared over resource baselines, trait-specificity, and steering-induced personality transfer/equalization with competence controls.
Experiments:
1) Cross-lingual personality suite: Administer validated personality inventories (BFI-2 for Big-Five, HEXACO-PI-R) plus a set of behavioral trait-elicitation scenarios (situational judgment items whose responses map to specific traits, e.g. extraversion in a social scenario, conscientiousness in a planning scenario) to each model in typologically and culturally diverse languages spanning resource levels and cultural trait-norm profiles (English, German, Spanish, Russian, Mandarin, Japanese, Hindi, Arabic, Swahili). Use forced-choice / Likert scoring via constrained decoding and log-prob margins to obtain a per-language trait profile (5 or 6 scores). Native-speaker verify translations; report inter-annotator agreement. Attach each language a cross-cultural trait-norm reference from published cross-national personality datasets. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral personality divergence (motivation/H0): Measure per-language trait profiles and quantify cross-lingual personality divergence (e.g., mean absolute trait-score difference across language pairs, and variance per trait). Establish that the SAME model expresses systematically different profiles by query language, and identify which traits shift most (predict extraversion, agreeableness, openness shift most, mirroring the human CFS literature). Control for tokenizer fertility and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test query language adds predictive power beyond fertility/resource).
3) Shared trait directions (H1): For each of the 5/6 traits, extract a per-language trait direction via difference-in-means between high-trait and low-trait self-descriptive representations (using contrastive trait-endorsing vs trait-rejecting statements) at each layer. Measure cross-lingual cosine alignment of each trait direction across layers; test that alignment is high and peaks in middle/shared-hub layers, and that steering with one language's trait direction changes trait expression in another language (portability). Baseline: a language-identity direction.
4) Personality-gain readout and norm prediction (H2, core): Project the residual stream at the trait-decision position onto the shared trait directions to get a per-item trait-activation profile, and estimate a per-LANGUAGE gain vector (5/6 scalars) via regression of the model's trait response on the shared-direction projections. Test H2: the cross-lingual personality shift for each item is predicted by the difference in gain vectors applied to the SHARED trait projections (held-out R^2), beating (a) a uniform per-language bias baseline and (b) a full per-language relearned readout (i.e., the shift is low-dimensional and trait-structured). Test whether the per-language gain vector is predicted by the language's cross-cultural trait norm BETTER than by resource level (nested regression, AIC, held-out R^2). Also test a within-language cultural-frame manipulation (prompt an imagined home-culture vs foreign-culture context in the SAME language, following the human CFS 2-by-2 designs) to separate language identity from cultural framing.
5) Causal gain-steering (H3, core): At the trait-readout layer, rescale individual shared trait directions to transform one language's gain vector into another's, and measure whether the model's expressed personality shifts toward the target language's profile WITHOUT changing input language (personality-transfer rate); conversely, equalize gain vectors across languages and measure the reduction in cross-lingual personality variance. Verify trait-specificity: steering the extraversion gain changes extraversion-driven items but not conscientiousness-driven items. Compare against baselines: whole-hub English-steering (Language-Specific Latent Process 2025), a persona-direction steering baseline, and a random-direction control.
6) Specificity and competence controls: Verify gain-steering (a) does not switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), (b) preserves general task competence and fluency (MMLU/reasoning subset), (c) moves personality symmetrically (can raise AND lower each trait), and (d) is trait-specific (does not add a uniform positivity/response-style bias). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 has gain vectors more collapsed toward the English profile (less cross-lingual personality variation) than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether the magnitude of language-dependent gain change correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the trait directions and with training share.
Evaluation metrics: per-language trait profiles and cross-lingual personality divergence (which traits shift most); per-trait cross-lingual direction alignment and portability; gain-vector held-out predictive R^2 for personality shifts (vs uniform-bias and full-relearn baselines); trait-specificity of shifts; gain-vs-cultural-norm predictive R^2 over resource baseline; within-language cultural-frame gain shift; personality-transfer rate and cross-lingual variance reduction under gain-steering vs baselines; symmetric specificity, competence/fluency preservation, off-target rate; cross-model gain-collapse comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Language, culture, script, and resource level are confounded (query language correlates with cultural trait norms); the within-language cultural-frame manipulation (home vs foreign cultural context in the same language) is the key control that isolates cultural framing from language identity, mirroring the human CFS 2-by-2 designs, but residual confounds may remain and we report partial correlations. 2) LLM 'personality' from self-report inventories may reflect response-style / social-desirability biases rather than a stable trait representation; we include behavioral trait-elicitation scenarios (not just self-report), use forced-choice and log-prob measures, and require trait-specific (not uniform positivity) effects. 3) The 5/6-trait basis may not cleanly capture the model's personality geometry; if a data-driven low-dimensional basis (PCA/SAE over trait-item activations) fits better, we report the empirically-best basis and treat Big-Five/HEXACO as one interpretable option, keeping the core 'shared basis + language gain' claim testable regardless. 4) Trait directions from difference-in-means may entangle topical/lexical content; we use matched contrastive trait statements, multiple extraction methods, and specificity controls. 5) Cross-national trait norms are noisy and may not reflect training-data personality; we treat them as an external reference, not ground truth, and rely on the internal gain-vector prediction and causal steering for core claims. 6) Instruction-tuned models may flatten personality toward a uniform Assistant persona (per the Assistant Axis), reducing measured cross-lingual variation; we test base models where available and treat a small effect in instruction-tuned models as an informative training-effect finding. 7) Gain-steering could harm competence or over-impose a target-culture personality; we require competence preservation, symmetry, and trait-specificity, reporting the full tradeoff. 8) If trait directions are NOT shared across languages, or the gain is not norm-predictable beyond resource level, the hypothesis is refuted — an informative negative result showing multilingual personality is genuinely per-language rather than a shared-basis gain. 9) The human-LLM CFS comparison is qualitative (direction/structure), not a claim of identical mechanism. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: zero_anaphora_overresolution
Title: Filling a Gap That Should Stay Open: Does the English-Scaffolded Hub Over-Resolve Zero Anaphora in Pro-Drop Languages?
Short Hypothesis: Pro-drop / zero-anaphora languages (Chinese, Japanese, Italian, Spanish) routinely OMIT referential arguments, leaving them grammatically underspecified and, in context, sometimes genuinely ambiguous or deliberately unresolved; overt-pronoun English (the language scaffolding the shared hub) forces every argument to be realized and referentially committed. We hypothesize the shared hub IMPOSES an English-like obligatory-resolution parse onto pro-drop inputs: the model commits a definite antecedent to a dropped argument that the target grammar leaves open, tracking an English overt-pronoun antecedent-choice bias rather than the target-language discourse pragmatics.
