This over-resolution is mediated by a shared, steerable 'referent-commitment' direction, tracks each language's empirical pro-drop rate, mis-tracks reference in downstream reasoning, and is causally correctable toward appropriate underspecification without harming genuine coreference.
Related Work: Interpretability shows coreference is driven by a small circuit of situation-model attention heads (Causal interventions expose implicit situation models 2023), that models encode referential/agreement information but with recency bias (Probing for Referential Information 2020), that discourse structure influences reference in transformers (Discourse structure interacts with reference 2020), and that pronoun-disambiguation attention heads exist and transfer cross-lingually in MT (Analyzing Attention Heads for Pronoun Disambiguation 2024; How Language Models Prioritize Contextual Grammatical Cues 2024). Zero/null-pronoun work is task-based cross-lingual resolution (Cross-lingual Zero Pronoun Resolution 2020; Hierarchical Discourse-Semantic Modeling for Chinese ZP 2025; Latent Anaphora Resolution 2013) and multilingual discourse-tracking benchmarks (DiscoTrack 2025; Probing Multilingual LMs for Discourse 2021) are behavioral. Foundational work establishes an English-scaffolded shared hub (Semantic Hub 2024; Do Llamas Work in English 2024). CRITICALLY, all coreference-mechanism work is monolingual English (where every referent is overt and must be resolved), and all zero-pronoun work asks how to RESOLVE omitted arguments better — none asks whether the shared hub OVER-resolves, imposing a definite English-style antecedent onto a dropped argument the target grammar legitimately leaves underspecified, causing spurious referent commitment and cross-lingual reference inconsistency. None localizes a shared referent-commitment direction, ties over-resolution to the pro-drop typology as external ground truth, or offers a causal fix. This differs from my prior tense/telicity/number imposition proposals (which impose grammatical categories) and from switch_point_information_carryover (which concerns carrying an established fact across a mid-sentence switch): here the phenomenon is imposing referential COMMITMENT onto a syntactically ABSENT argument, a discourse-reference axis orthogonal to all my prior proposals.
Abstract: In English every argument must be spoken and referentially pinned down: 'she left because she was tired.' Pro-drop languages like Chinese, Japanese, Italian and Spanish routinely drop these arguments, leaving them grammatically absent and, in context, sometimes genuinely ambiguous or intentionally open. Multilingual language models build a shared semantic hub scaffolded by overt-pronoun English. We ask a simple, previously untested question: does that hub IMPOSE an English-like obligatory-resolution parse onto pro-drop inputs, forcing a definite antecedent onto a dropped argument the target grammar leaves underspecified? We hypothesize that (1) the model spuriously commits a specific referent to genuinely-underspecified zero anaphora, tracking an English overt-pronoun antecedent-choice bias rather than target-language discourse pragmatics; (2) the size of this over-resolution tracks each language's empirical pro-drop rate; (3) a shared, steerable 'referent-commitment' direction mediates it, with any residual underspecification signal in shallow, language-specific layers; and (4) steering toward appropriate underspecification restores faithful reference without harming genuine coreference. We build a controlled multilingual suite of zero-anaphora contexts — disambiguated, genuinely-underspecified, and overt-control — across pro-drop (Chinese, Japanese, Italian, Spanish) and non-pro-drop (English, German) languages, on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM. Using difference-in-means referent-commitment probes, logit-lens tracking, activation patching, and steering, we measure the over-resolution, its pro-drop-rate scaling, its mediation, and its causal correction. Metrics include spurious-commitment rate, English-antecedent-pull, pro-drop-rate-prediction correlation, mediation R-squared, and steering-induced restoration with coreference-competence controls.
Experiments:
1) Zero-anaphora suite: Construct ~450 short discourse items in pro-drop languages (Chinese, Japanese, Italian, Spanish) each containing a DROPPED argument (subject/object zero pronoun), native-speaker verified, in three conditions: (a) UNDERSPECIFIED — the dropped argument is genuinely ambiguous or intentionally open given context (native speakers agree no single antecedent is forced); (b) DISAMBIGUATED — context licenses one antecedent (a within-item control the model should follow); (c) OVERT-CONTROL — the same content with the argument overtly realized (and matched English/German translations where the pronoun is obligatory). Tasks: (i) referent-identification forced choice ('who did the second action?' with a NEUTRAL/underspecified option); (ii) reference-NLI (does the sentence ENTAIL a specific-antecedent paraphrase? correct = NEUTRAL for underspecified, ENTAIL for disambiguated); (iii) a short reasoning item whose outcome depends on which referent is chosen; (iv) generation continuation (does the model impose a definite referent?). Report inter-annotator agreement; release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral over-resolution (H1, core): Measure spurious-commitment rate = fraction of UNDERSPECIFIED items on which the model commits a single definite antecedent as if obligatory (on referent-ID, NLI, or reasoning). Verify near-zero over-commitment where a NEUTRAL option is correct and correct antecedent selection on DISAMBIGUATED controls (isolating over-resolution from incompetence). Control for tokenizer fertility, referent frequency, and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test pro-drop status adds predictive power).
3) English-antecedent-pull (H1b): Test whether the committed antecedent tracks the ENGLISH overt-pronoun antecedent-choice bias (e.g., subject-continuity / first-mention or implicit-causality preference) rather than the target-language discourse preference. Define English-antecedent-pull rate = fraction of commitment cases matching the English-parse antecedent; predict higher pull for lower-resource pro-drop languages.
4) Pro-drop-rate scaling (H2, external validation): Using each language's empirical pro-drop rate / null-argument frequency (from corpora and the pro-drop typology), test whether per-language over-resolution is predicted by pro-drop rate (Spearman; held-out prediction from typology alone), tying the internal phenomenon to independent ground truth. Predict strongest over-resolution for highest-pro-drop languages (Japanese/Chinese) and near-zero for non-pro-drop English/German.
5) Representational localization (H3): Extract a 'referent-commitment' direction via difference-in-means between committed (definite-antecedent) vs uncommitted (underspecified) representations at each layer, per language. Test (a) whether a shared commitment direction is English-scaffolded (cross-lingual cosine alignment across layers, aligned with the English obligatory-resolution pole); (b) whether an UNDERSPECIFIED pro-drop input projects onto the committed pole in the shared hub while any residual underspecification signal is stronger in early/language-specific layers, via logit-lens/tuned-lens depth tracking. Baseline: an overt-pronoun coreference direction (present in all languages) as a within-model control. Mediation: regress behavioral over-resolution on shared-hub committed-pole projection (partial correlation controlling for fertility/frequency; held-out R^2).
6) Causal steering/patching test (H4, core): (a) Steer the pro-drop input toward the UNCOMMITTED/underspecified pole of the commitment direction and measure whether referent-ID/NLI/reasoning shift toward appropriate underspecification (flip rate) without switching output language; (b) for over-resolved items, patch the residual language-specific underspecification signal (from early/language-specific layers) into later computation and test restoration, localizing failure to the shared hub imposing obligatory resolution. Critically verify COREFERENCE-COMPETENCE preservation (DISAMBIGUATED and OVERT-control items must still be resolved correctly — no destruction of genuine coreference), plus fluency and off-target/language-mixing checks. Baselines: whole-hub English-steering, random-direction control.
7) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify steering is commitment-specific (changes referent-commitment but not event/participant identity), graded (over-resolution scales with pro-drop rate), and not a lexical-frequency artifact. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show stronger over-resolution than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether over-resolution magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the commitment direction and with each language's training share. Qualitatively compare the model's per-language over-resolution pattern against the pro-drop typology.
Evaluation metrics: spurious-commitment rate (underspecified vs disambiguated vs overt controls); English-antecedent-pull rate; over-resolution-vs-pro-drop-rate correlation and held-out prediction; reference-NLI NEUTRAL-accuracy; shared-hub committed-pole projection strength and crystallization depth (vs overt-coreference baseline); cross-lingual commitment-direction alignment; mediation regression (held-out R^2); steering flip rate and patching-induced restoration; coreference-competence preservation, fluency, off-target rate; cross-model over-resolution comparison and correlation with training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for pro-drop status over frequency/fertility/resource baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Establishing that a dropped argument is GENUINELY underspecified (no single antecedent forced) is subtle and context-dependent; we native-speaker verify, use graded agreement, report inter-annotator agreement, exclude low-agreement items, and restrict UNDERSPECIFIED items to clear cases. 2) Pro-drop status is correlated with language family, script, and resource level; the DISAMBIGUATED controls, OVERT controls, non-pro-drop comparison languages, within-item contrasts, and pro-drop-rate prediction isolate the over-resolution pathway, but residual confounds may remain; we center core claims on well-resourced Chinese/Japanese/Italian/Spanish. 3) Over-resolution could reflect a general answer-forcing bias rather than English imposition; the English-antecedent-pull analysis, the pro-drop-rate prediction, and the causal underspecification-steering (which restores NEUTRAL by editing only the commitment direction) distinguish imposition from generic commitment. 4) Difference-in-means commitment directions may entangle coreference or lexical features; we use an overt-coreference control direction, multiple extraction methods, and specificity checks. 5) Logit-lens/tuned-lens depth is approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 6) Instruction-tuned models may hedge ('it could be X or Y'), which we treat as a positive underspecification-awareness signal; we test base models where available and use forced-choice + NLI. 7) Steering could over-suppress genuine coreference or harm fluency; coreference-competence preservation on disambiguated/overt items is a hard constraint and we report the full tradeoff. 8) The model-vs-typology comparison is qualitative, not a claim of identical mechanism. 9) If NO over-resolution is found — zero anaphora stays appropriately underspecified, predictable from pro-drop rate, with genuine coreference preserved — this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the shared hub represents language-specific referential underspecification despite English scaffolding, valuable either way. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: directness_setpoint_import_speech_acts
Title: Asking Too Bluntly in Some Tongues: A Language-Conditioned Directness Setpoint Imported From the Dominant Language in Multilingual Speech-Act Generation
Short Hypothesis: When a multilingual LLM GENERATES a face-threatening speech act (request, refusal, apology) in a target language, the level of DIRECTNESS it produces is set by a language-conditioned 'directness setpoint' that is anchored to the dominant (English/US) pragmatic norm and imported into other languages regardless of each culture's empirical directness preference. Consequently the model systematically mis-calibrates directness — too blunt in indirectness-preferring cultures, too indirect in directness-preferring ones — for the SAME situation (power/distance/imposition held fixed). This mis-calibration is not a separate per-language computation but a GAIN on a single, largely shared 'directness' direction, is predictable from cross-cultural CCSARP directness norms rather than from resource level, and is causally correctable by rescaling the shared direction without harming task fluency.
Related Work: Behavioral pragmatics establishes via the Cross-Cultural Speech Act Realization Project (CCSARP) that request/refusal/apology directness varies systematically by culture and by power/distance/imposition (Blum-Kulka & Olshtain 1984; American vs Saudi Arabic 2012; Javanese/Balinese 2026; Polish vs British object-requests 2013), and recent DCT studies show GenAI diverges from native speaker directness norms in Japanese requests (2025), over-uses negative-politeness strategies even in positive contexts (Comparing human and LLM politeness strategies 2025), and shows imperfect zero-shot politeness transfer (TyDiP 2022). Interpretability shows politeness/emotion and social traits are localized, largely linear, steerable directions (Interpreting Politeness Networks 2016; STAR 2025), and cultural knowledge/localization is steerable at specific layers (Localized Cultural Knowledge 2025; Surgical Steering 2025; CultureSteer 2025). CRITICALLY, all speech-act-directness LLM work is purely BEHAVIORAL/DCT and never asks WHY the model mis-calibrates directness; all steering/interpretability work targets a politeness gradient or cultural knowledge, not the GENERATION-TIME directness LEVEL of a speech act as a language-conditioned setpoint. No prior work (a) frames cross-lingual directness mis-calibration as an imported, dominant-language-anchored setpoint (mis-matched to each culture's CCSARP norm), (b) shows it is a low-dimensional GAIN on a single shared directness direction rather than distinct per-language pragmatics, (c) predicts the per-language directness shift from external CCSARP norms rather than resource level, or (d) causally rescales the shared direction to recalibrate directness per language. This differs from my prior pragmatic-directness proposal (which concerned COMPREHENSION — under-inferring indirect implicated meaning on INPUT) and honorific-register proposal (grammatical register comprehension): here the phenomenon is GENERATION of speech-act directness with a shared-direction gain account and a CCSARP-grounded predictive metric.
Abstract: When you ask someone to do something, how bluntly you phrase it depends on your culture: some cultures favor direct imperatives, others conventional indirectness ('could you possibly...'), even for the same situation. Decades of cross-cultural pragmatics (the CCSARP project) quantify these directness norms. Multilingual language models build a shared, English-scaffolded representation. We ask a simple, previously untested mechanistic question: when a model GENERATES a request, refusal, or apology in a target language, is the DIRECTNESS it produces set by a language-conditioned setpoint anchored to the dominant (English) norm and imported into other languages, mis-matched to each culture's actual preference? We hypothesize that (1) for the SAME situation (power, distance, imposition held fixed) the model over-produces directness in indirectness-preferring cultures and under-produces it in directness-preferring ones, tracking the English norm; (2) this is a GAIN on a single, largely shared 'directness' direction rather than distinct per-language pragmatics, so the per-language shift is low-dimensional; (3) the shift is predicted by external CCSARP directness norms, not by resource level; and (4) rescaling the shared direction at inference causally recalibrates directness per language without harming fluency. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using a controlled multilingual Discourse-Completion-Task suite across cultures spanning the CCSARP directness spectrum, combining directness scoring, difference-in-means directness-direction extraction, logit-lens gain readout, activation patching, and gain-steering. Metrics include CCSARP-referenced directness mis-calibration, shared-direction alignment, gain predictive R-squared over resource baselines, and steering-induced recalibration with fluency controls.
Experiments:
1) Multilingual DCT speech-act suite grounded in CCSARP: Construct ~500 Discourse-Completion-Task situations, each specifying the three CCSARP social variables (power, social distance, imposition) at controlled levels, requiring the model to GENERATE a request (plus refusal and apology subsets). Instantiate every situation across cultures/languages spanning the empirical directness spectrum: directness-preferring (English/US, German, Hebrew, Arabic) and indirectness-preferring (Japanese, Korean, Chinese; plus Polish/Javanese as intermediate), native-speaker verified. Attach to each culture its CCSARP-derived directness norm (proportion of direct/conventionally-indirect/nonconventional-indirect head acts) from published DCT studies. Build an automatic directness scorer using the CCSARP 9-point directness taxonomy (validated against native-speaker annotation on a held-out subset). Report inter-annotator agreement; release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral directness mis-calibration (H1, core): For each culture and situation, score the directness level of the model's generated speech act and compare to that culture's CCSARP norm. Define the mis-calibration = signed deviation of model directness from the target-culture norm, and test whether it is pulled toward the ENGLISH/US norm (over-direct in indirectness-preferring cultures, under-direct in directness-preferring ones) for the SAME situation. Verify the model correctly modulates directness with power/distance/imposition WITHIN a culture (so mis-calibration is a cross-cultural anchor, not general insensitivity). Control for tokenizer fertility and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test culture adds predictive power).
3) English-anchor vs norm-appropriate model comparison (H1b): Test whether per-culture generated directness is better fit by an 'English-anchored' account (all cultures pulled toward the US norm) or a 'norm-appropriate' account (directness matches each culture's CCSARP norm), via model comparison. Predict the English-anchored model wins, especially for lower-resource / English-distant cultures. Also run a within-language cultural-framing manipulation (same language, home-culture vs neutral addressee framing) to separate language identity from cultural framing.
4) Shared directness direction and gain readout (H2, core): Extract a per-language 'directness' direction via difference-in-means between direct (imperative/bald) and indirect (conventionally-indirect) speech-act representations at each layer (building on the politeness-direction and STAR localization work). Measure cross-lingual cosine alignment (test: a single shared directness axis re-thresholded per language, peaking in middle layers) and verify portability (steering with one language's direction changes another's directness). Project the residual stream at the generation-decision point onto the shared direction to get a per-item directness activation, and estimate a per-LANGUAGE directness gain (scalar) via regression of produced directness on the projection. Test that the cross-cultural directness shift is captured by the difference in per-language gains applied to the shared projection (held-out R^2), beating a uniform-bias baseline and a full per-language relearned readout (i.e., the shift is low-dimensional). Test whether the per-language gain is predicted by the CCSARP norm BETTER than by resource level (AIC, held-out R^2).
5) Causal gain-steering recalibration (H3, core): At the generation-decision layer, rescale the shared directness direction to transform one culture's gain into another's, and measure whether the produced speech-act directness shifts toward the target culture's CCSARP norm WITHOUT changing input language (directness-transfer rate); conversely, recalibrate each culture's gain to its own norm and measure the reduction in CCSARP-referenced mis-calibration. Bidirectional dose-response (can raise AND lower directness); mis-signed steering worsens. Complement with activation patching: patch the English directness signal into a target-language pass and confirm it shifts directness toward English. Compare against baselines: prompt-based cultural instruction ('write a culturally appropriate request'), whole-hub English-steering, cultural-steering vector (Localized Cultural Knowledge 2025), and a random-direction control.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify gain-steering is directness-specific (changes speech-act directness/head-act strategy but not the propositional content of the request, does not switch output language — off-target/language-mixing rate — and preserves grammaticality/fluency, native-speaker rated), and that it does not merely shorten/lengthen output (length control). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show gains more collapsed toward the US directness setpoint (larger mis-calibration) than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether the magnitude of language-dependent gain change correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the directness direction and with each language's training share.
Evaluation metrics: CCSARP-referenced directness mis-calibration (signed, per culture) and English-anchor pull; English-anchored-vs-norm-appropriate model comparison; within-culture power/distance/imposition sensitivity (calibration control); within-language cultural-framing gain shift; cross-lingual directness-direction alignment and portability; gain predictive R^2 for directness shift (vs uniform-bias and full-relearn baselines) and gain-vs-CCSARP-norm predictive R^2 over resource baseline; directness-transfer rate and mis-calibration reduction under gain-steering vs baselines, with bidirectional dose-response and mis-sign penalty; content-preservation, fluency, off-target rate, length control; cross-model gain-collapse comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Automatically scoring speech-act directness is nontrivial; we ground the scorer in the validated CCSARP 9-point directness taxonomy, validate against native-speaker annotation on a held-out subset, and report scorer reliability and inter-annotator agreement. 2) Culture, language, script, and resource level are confounded; the within-language cultural-framing manipulation (home vs neutral addressee in the same language) is the key control isolating cultural framing from language identity, and the within-culture power/distance/imposition sensitivity check confirms the model is not generally directness-insensitive; residual confounds remain and we report partial correlations. 3) CCSARP norms are noisy, situation- and study-dependent, and may not reflect the model's training-data pragmatics; we use multiple published norm sources, report norm ranges, restrict to situations with robust cross-cultural directness contrasts, and treat norms as noisy predictors, relying on the internal gain and causal tests for core claims. 4) The single-direction gain account may only partially hold; if a data-driven low-dimensional basis (PCA/SAE over speech-act activations, or separate axes for head-act strategy vs internal modification) fits better, we report the empirically-best low-dimensional basis, keeping the 'shared basis + language gain' claim testable. 5) Directness directions from difference-in-means may entangle formality/length; we use the length control, formality-vs-directness disentangling probes, and multiple extraction methods. 6) Gain-steering could harm content, grammaticality, or over-impose a target culture; content-preservation, fluency, off-target, and bidirectional dose-response are hard constraints and we report the full tradeoff, comparing against the prompt-instruction baseline to show the mechanistic account adds value. 7) Some mis-calibration may reflect genuine correct behavior (the model rightly matching the target culture); the direction of the effect (tracks ENGLISH norm vs TARGET norm), the model comparison, and the CCSARP prediction distinguish imposition from norm-appropriate generation, and a norm-appropriate finding is itself valuable. 8) Instruction-tuned models may be trained toward a uniform polite register, flattening cross-cultural variation; we test base models where available and treat differences as an informative training-stage finding. 9) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM's more diverse hub analyzed as a contrast expected to import less). 10) If per-culture directness is norm-appropriate rather than English-anchored, this is an informative POSITIVE result showing culturally-faithful speech-act realization despite English scaffolding — valuable either way. 11) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: connotation_valence_imposition
Title: Positive in One Tongue, Negative in Another: Does the Shared Sentiment Direction Impose the Dominant Language's Connotation Onto Translation-Equivalent Words?
Short Hypothesis: Concrete words that are translation-equivalents can carry OPPOSITE culturally-loaded connotations across languages (a word neutral/positive in one culture but negatively-valenced in another). Because multilingual LLMs represent valence on a single, largely English-scaffolded linear sentiment direction, we hypothesize the model IMPOSES the dominant (English) connotation onto a target-language word whose native connotation diverges: its valence judgments, downstream associations, and sentiment-in-context reasoning track the English valence rather than the target-language one. This imposition is mediated by the shared sentiment direction, tracks each word's empirical cross-lingual valence divergence, and is causally correctable by rescaling that direction per language without harming genuinely-shared valence.
Related Work: Interpretability shows sentiment/valence is a single linear, causal direction in LLMs with a 'summarization motif' (Linear Representations of Sentiment 2023; Language Models Linearly Represent Sentiment 2024), and that this direction is largely shared. Cross-lingual valence work (ValNorm 2020) shows valence associations are broadly consistent across seven languages and 200 years, but this is exactly what makes DIVERGENT words a clean, sharp contrast case. Multilingual-emotion work (Multilingual LMs are not Multicultural 2023; CuLEmo 2025; CEDAR 2026; emotion colexification, Jackson et al. 2019) shows Anglocentric emotion representation and culture-specific emotion CATEGORIES, and rationale-alignment work (Are Multilingual Sentiment Models Right for the Right Reasons 2022) shows models favor English rationales. CRITICALLY, all sentiment-interpretability work is monolingual/English and treats the sentiment direction as uniform; all cross-lingual sentiment/emotion work is behavioral and concerns emotion categories or overall polarity, NOT whether the shared linear sentiment direction IMPOSES the dominant-language CONNOTATION onto specific translation-equivalent WORDS whose valence diverges cross-culturally. None localizes the imposition to the shared sentiment direction, ties it to per-word cross-lingual valence divergence as external ground truth, or offers a causal per-language rescaling fix. This differs from my prior emotion_colexification_imposition proposal (emotion-CATEGORY partition, e.g. anger/grief conflation) by targeting word-level VALENCE/connotation on the established linear sentiment direction — a distinct, mechanistically-cleaner axis with a well-validated causal direction and human valence-norm ground truth.
Abstract: Valence — whether a word feels good or bad — is largely shared across languages, yet certain concrete words carry genuinely opposite culturally-loaded connotations across cultures: a word that is neutral or positive in one language can be negatively charged in another. Interpretability work shows multilingual LLMs represent valence on a single, largely English-scaffolded linear sentiment direction. We ask a simple, previously untested question: when a model reasons about a word whose connotation diverges across languages, does the shared sentiment direction IMPOSE the dominant (English) connotation, overriding the target-language valence? We hypothesize that (1) the model's valence judgments, associations, and sentiment-in-context reasoning for a divergent translation-equivalent word track the English connotation rather than the target-language one, producing cross-lingual sentiment inconsistency concentrated on divergent words versus a matched convergent baseline; (2) the size of this imposition tracks each word's empirical cross-lingual valence divergence from human norms; (3) the shared linear sentiment direction mediates it, with any residual target-language valence in shallow, language-specific layers; and (4) rescaling the sentiment direction per language causally corrects the imposition without harming genuinely-shared valence. We build a controlled multilingual suite of translation-equivalent words with cross-linguistically divergent versus convergent connotations, grounded in human valence norms, across typologically diverse languages, on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM. Using the established linear sentiment direction, difference-in-means probes, logit-lens tracking, activation patching, and steering, we measure the imposition, its divergence scaling, its mediation, and its causal correction. Metrics include English-connotation imposition gap, divergence-prediction correlation, mediation R-squared, and steering-induced correction with shared-valence controls.
Experiments:
1) Divergent/convergent connotation suite grounded in human valence norms: Using cross-lingual valence-norm datasets (e.g. ANEW-style affective norms available for English, Spanish, German, Dutch, Portuguese, Polish, plus curated native-speaker ratings for Chinese, Arabic, Hindi) and native-speaker verification, assemble ~400 translation-equivalent word sets partitioned into (a) DIVERGENT words whose human valence norm differs substantially (ideally opposite sign) between English and a target language (e.g. culture-specific animals, foods, colors, concepts with different cultural charge), and (b) matched CONVERGENT words (same valence across languages) as the key control. Design probes that hinge on connotation, not overt sentiment labeling: (i) valence forced choice ('Is this word positive or negative?'); (ii) association/typicality (does the word associate with pleasant vs unpleasant contexts?); (iii) sentiment-in-context reasoning (short sentence whose overall sentiment depends on the word's connotation). Attach each word its per-language human valence norm. Native-speaker verify; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral connotation imposition (H1, core): For each DIVERGENT word in each target language, measure whether the model's valence/association/reasoning tracks the ENGLISH connotation vs the target-language one. Define the English-connotation imposition GAP = inconsistency(DIVERGENT) minus inconsistency(CONVERGENT), and an English-connotation rate = fraction of divergent words judged with the English valence sign. Verify near-faithful judgments on CONVERGENT words and correct English valence (ceiling). Control for word frequency, tokenizer fertility, and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test target-language status adds predictive power).
3) Divergence scaling (H2, external validation): Test whether per-word imposition is predicted by the magnitude of the target-vs-English human valence-norm divergence (Spearman correlation; held-out prediction of imposition from norm divergence alone), tying the internal phenomenon to independent human affective-norm ground truth. Predict larger imposition for lower-resource / English-distant languages.
4) Representational localization (H3): Extract the linear sentiment direction per language via difference-in-means over positive/negative exemplars (following Linear Representations of Sentiment 2023) and verify cross-lingual alignment (a single, largely shared, English-scaffolded valence axis). Using logit-lens/tuned-lens, test whether a DIVERGENT target-language word projects onto the ENGLISH valence pole in the shared mid-layers while any residual target-language valence is stronger in early/language-specific layers. Mediation: regress behavioral imposition on the word's shared-sentiment-direction projection toward the English valence (partial correlation controlling for frequency/fertility; held-out R^2). Baseline: a non-valence lexical direction as a within-model control.
5) Causal steering/patching test (H4, core): (a) Steer the DIVERGENT word's representation along the sentiment direction toward the target-language valence pole and measure whether valence/association/reasoning shift to the target-language pattern (flip rate) and the imposition GAP shrinks toward the CONVERGENT baseline, without switching output language; (b) conversely amplify toward the English pole and confirm dose-response (bidirectional); (c) for imposed items, patch the residual language-specific valence signal (from early/language-specific layers) into later computation and test restoration. Critically verify SHARED-VALENCE preservation (CONVERGENT words and genuinely positive/negative words must stay correct — no over-flipping) plus fluency and off-target/language-mixing checks. Baselines: whole-hub English-steering, random-direction control.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify steering is valence-specific (changes connotation but not the word's identity or unrelated meaning), graded (imposition scales with norm divergence), and not a lexical-frequency artifact (frequency-matched divergent/convergent pairs). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show stronger imposition than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether imposition magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the sentiment direction and with each language's training share. Qualitatively compare the model's per-word imposition pattern against the human cross-lingual valence-norm structure.
Evaluation metrics: English-connotation imposition GAP and English-connotation rate (DIVERGENT vs CONVERGENT; vs English ceiling); imposition-vs-valence-norm-divergence correlation and held-out prediction; sentiment-direction cross-lingual alignment; divergent-word projection toward the English pole and its mediation of behavioral imposition (held-out R^2); steering flip rate and GAP reduction (bidirectional dose-response), patching-induced restoration; shared-valence preservation (specificity), fluency, off-target rate; cross-model imposition comparison and correlation with training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for target-language status over frequency/fertility/resource baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Identifying translation-equivalent words with genuinely DIVERGENT (ideally opposite-sign) cross-lingual valence is the crux — ValNorm (2020) shows valence is broadly shared, so divergent words are rarer; we mine affective-norm datasets for the largest cross-lingual valence gaps, native-speaker verify, use a graded divergence score, report inter-annotator agreement, and treat opposite-sign words as the core set with same-sign-but-shifted words as an intermediate tier. 2) Connotation divergence is correlated with frequency, cultural specificity, and resource level; the CONVERGENT controls, English ceiling, within-word contrasts, and norm-divergence prediction isolate the imposition pathway, but residual confounds may remain. 3) Human valence norms are noisy and context-sensitive (positive vs negative framing); we use multiple norm sources, report ranges, and treat norms as noisy predictors, relying on internal representation and causal tests for core claims. 4) Some imposition may reflect genuine correct behavior (the model rightly using the target-language connotation); the direction of the effect (tracks ENGLISH vs TARGET valence), the norm-divergence prediction, and the causal steering (which restores the target valence by editing only the sentiment direction) distinguish imposition from faithful judgment, and a faithful-judgment finding is itself valuable and complements ValNorm. 5) The linear sentiment direction is well-established and causal (a strength), but difference-in-means may entangle topical/lexical features; we use a non-valence control direction and specificity checks. 6) Logit-lens depth estimates are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 7) Steering could harm shared valence or fluency; shared-valence preservation is a hard constraint and we report the full tradeoff plus bidirectional dose-response. 8) Instruction-tuned models may suppress overt valence guessing; we test base models where available and interpret small effects as informative. 9) If NO imposition is found — divergent words are judged by their target-language connotation — this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the shared sentiment direction represents language-specific connotation despite English scaffolding, valuable either way. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: refusal_threshold_import_miscalibration
Title: Imported Threshold: Cross-Lingual Safety Failures as a Language-Conditioned Gain on a Shared Refusal Direction, Miscalibrated to Harm Severity
Short Hypothesis: Cross-lingual safety failures in lower-resource languages are not (only) a failure to detect harm or to localize a refusal direction, but a language-conditioned GAIN applied to a single, largely shared refusal direction: the model imports the English refusal THRESHOLD (how much represented harm is needed to trigger refusal) into other languages regardless of each language's safety-training coverage, so the threshold sits too high in low-coverage languages. Consequently a prompt whose harm is correctly represented on the shared direction with the SAME magnitude as an English prompt that gets refused is nonetheless complied with in a low-resource language, because the per-language decision gain converting that harm signal into refusal is set by (mis)calibration, not by harm severity. The gain is decodable, predictable from each language's safety-training share, and causally correctable by rescaling the shared direction per language without over-refusing benign content.
Related Work: Refusal is mediated by a single, cross-lingually universal direction (Arditi 2024; Refusal Direction is Universal 2025), shared safety neurons bridge transfer (SS-Neurons 2026; Soteria 2025), and alignment separates harmful/harmless representations well in English but weakly in other languages (The Hidden Space of Safety 2025). All of these either (a) treat the refusal direction/neurons as a fixed shared quantity and improve safety by reinforcing them, or (b) frame the cross-lingual gap as weaker harmful/harmless representation SEPARATION in non-English languages. NONE isolates the DECISION THRESHOLD/GAIN that converts a given harm-representation magnitude into refusal as a language-conditioned, miscalibrated variable that is IMPORTED from English; none tests whether, matched on harm-representation magnitude, low-resource prompts are still refused less because the per-language gain is too low; none predicts the per-language gain from safety-training share or shows that a per-language gain rescaling (not reinforcing the shared direction globally) equalizes refusal without over-refusal. My own prior harm-gating proposal framed the failure as detection-intact-but-routing-broken; here the sharper, distinct claim is that routing IS intact and shared, but the THRESHOLD on the shared refusal direction is a miscalibrated per-language scalar imported from the dominant language. This reframes multilingual safety failure from a representation-separation or neuron-reinforcement problem into an imported-threshold miscalibration with a predictive metric and a targeted, over-refusal-controlled fix.
Abstract: Large language models refuse harmful requests in English but comply with the same requests in lower-resource languages. Prevailing mechanistic accounts attribute this to a weaker separation of harmful from harmless representations in non-English languages, and remedy it by reinforcing a shared refusal direction or shared safety neurons. We propose a sharper, previously untested account: the refusal direction is largely shared and the harm is often represented, but the THRESHOLD that converts represented harm into a refusal decision is a language-conditioned gain imported from English. Under this account, a low-resource prompt whose harm projects onto the shared refusal direction with the SAME magnitude as an English prompt that gets refused is nonetheless complied with, because the per-language decision gain is too low; and this gain is predicted by each language's safety-training coverage, not by the prompt's actual harm severity. We test this on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using PolyRefuse/MultiJail-style parallel harmful and benign prompts across high-, mid-, and low-resource languages. We extract the shared refusal direction, measure per-prompt harm-representation magnitude and per-language refusal decision gain, and test three predictions: (1) matched on harm-magnitude, refusal probability still drops with lower language resource; (2) the per-language gain is predicted by safety-training share better than by harm separation alone; and (3) rescaling the shared direction per language to equalize the gain causally restores refusal for genuinely harmful prompts WITHOUT increasing over-refusal of benign content. Metrics include harm-magnitude-matched refusal gap, gain predictive R-squared, and gain-rescaling recovery with over-refusal controls. All interventions here strengthen or equalize refusal (defensive).
Experiments:
1) Parallel harmful/benign multilingual suite: Use/extend PolyRefuse and MultiJail (parallel translated harmful and benign prompts) across high- (English, French), mid- (Chinese, Hindi), and low-resource (Swahili, Amharic, Hausa) languages, native-speaker verified, plus a benign-but-superficially-alarming control set for over-refusal testing. Models: Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, BLOOM(Z)-7B. Record per-language refusal rate on harmful prompts (the behavioral target) and false-refusal rate on benign prompts.
2) Shared refusal direction and harm-magnitude (setup): Extract the refusal direction per model via difference-in-means (Arditi 2024) and verify cross-lingual alignment (a single shared axis). For each prompt, compute the harm-representation magnitude = its projection onto the shared refusal direction at the decision layer. Verify the direction causally controls refusal in each language via steering (dose-response).
3) Harm-magnitude-matched refusal gap (H1, core): Bin harmful prompts by harm-representation magnitude and, WITHIN a matched-magnitude bin, compare refusal probability across languages. Test the central prediction: at equal represented-harm magnitude, refusal probability still DROPS with lower language resource — i.e., the same internal harm signal yields refusal in English but compliance in a low-resource language. This isolates a threshold/gain effect from a representation-separation effect. Control for tokenizer fertility (partial correlations).
4) Per-language decision gain and prediction (H2): Define the per-language decision gain = the slope of refusal probability as a function of harm-representation magnitude (how steeply represented harm converts into refusal), estimated per language via logistic regression. Test whether the per-language gain is predicted by the language's safety-training share (from documented alignment-data coverage / a bilingual-retrieval proxy) BETTER than by harm separation (Bhattacharyya/silhouette of harmful vs benign, per Hidden Space of Safety) via nested regression (AIC, held-out R^2). Prediction: gain is imported/miscalibrated, tracking coverage; low-resource languages have a lower gain (higher effective threshold) even when separation is comparable.
5) Stage-localization via patching: For harmful prompts complied-with in language B but refused in English at matched harm-magnitude, patch (a) the harm-representation magnitude (from English) into B and (b) the late decision/gain components. If (a) rarely changes behavior (harm already present at equal magnitude) but (b) restores refusal, the failure is localized to the decision gain/threshold, not representation. Report gain- vs representation-failure shares per language.
6) Core causal intervention — per-language gain rescaling: Rescale the shared refusal direction with a per-language scalar calibrated to equalize the decision gain to the English value (steer proportionally to harm-magnitude), train-free. Measure refusal recovery on genuinely harmful prompts per language. Compare against baselines: uniform refusal-direction addition (Refusal Direction Universal 2025), SS-Neuron reinforcement (2026), and a random-direction control. Compute recovery elasticity = refusal gain per unit baseline gain deficit.
7) Over-refusal / specificity controls (hard constraint): The rescaling must NOT increase false refusals on benign or benign-but-alarming prompts (symmetric constraint), must not switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), and must preserve general capability (MMLU/MT quality). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 shows a larger harm-magnitude-matched gap and steeper gain deficit than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether the gain deficit correlates with each language's safety-training share.
Evaluation metrics: harm-magnitude-matched refusal gap across languages (H1); per-language decision-gain estimates and their predictive R^2 from safety-training share vs harm-separation baseline (H2, AIC/held-out); gain- vs representation-failure error shares (patching); gain-rescaling refusal recovery and elasticity vs baselines; over-refusal rate on benign/alarming controls (symmetric specificity); off-target rate; general-capability preservation; cross-model gap comparison and correlation with safety-training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Harm-representation magnitude and decision gain may not cleanly separate from representation separation (a lower gain could partly reflect a noisier harm representation); the harm-magnitude-MATCHED refusal gap (H1) and the patching localization (Exp 5) are designed to isolate threshold from representation, and if the matched gap vanishes the hypothesis reduces to the Hidden-Space separation account — an informative negative result. 2) The harm direction from difference-in-means may exploit surface lexical cues; we use benign-but-alarming controls, paraphrases, and held-out harm categories. 3) Safety-training share per language is hard to measure for closed alignment data; we use documented coverage plus a bilingual-retrieval proxy and report it as noisy. 4) Per-language gain rescaling could over-refuse; the benign/alarming symmetric constraint is a hard requirement and we report the full tradeoff. 5) This is dual-use safety research; ALL interventions here strengthen or equalize refusal (defensive) — we release the harm suite and refusal-direction analysis under controlled access and do not publish jailbreak-enhancing directions. 6) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM analyzed as a less English-centric contrast expected to show a smaller gain deficit). 7) If the per-language gain is NOT predicted by safety-training share beyond harm separation, or the matched-magnitude gap is absent, the imported-threshold hypothesis is refuted — an informative result showing cross-lingual safety failure is genuinely a representation-separation problem. 8) Limited to open ~7-8B instruction-tuned models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: orthographic_depth_reading_route
Title: Shallow Reads by Sound, Deep Reads by Shape: Does Orthographic Depth Set a Dual-Route Reading Strategy in Multilingual LLMs?
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs adopt a language-dependent 'reading route' analogous to the human dual-route model: for shallow (transparent) orthographies (Spanish, Finnish, Serbian) they lean on a sublexical phonological-recoding route (grapheme-to-sound) to identify words, while for deep (opaque) orthographies (English, French, Chinese) they lean on a direct lexical-orthographic route (shape/whole-token to meaning). This route balance is set by each language's orthographic depth, is decodable as the relative strength of a phonological vs orthographic feature at word-identification, causally controls robustness to phonology-preserving vs shape-preserving perturbations, and is steerable—producing a mechanistic analogue of the human orthographic-depth reading effect.
Related Work: Human reading science robustly establishes the orthographic depth hypothesis and grain-size theory: shallow orthographies drive small-unit grapheme-phoneme (sublexical/phonological) decoding while deep orthographies induce a dual/lexical route, with connectionist triangle-model simulations reproducing this (Foundation literacy 2003; Nonword reading across orthographies 2003; triangle-model typological analysis 2020; literacy-virus connectionist model 2014; reading-route ERP/neuroimaging 2014). LLM interpretability shows models implicitly reconstruct character/spelling knowledge in intermediate layers with a 'breakthrough' layer (Models in a Spelling Bee 2021; What do tokens know about their characters 2022; Spelling-out is not Straightforward 2025), that CWEs are orthographic-noise-sensitive via tokenization (Semantics or spelling 2024), that latent romanization bridges non-Roman scripts (RomanLens 2025), and that script is a linear, steerable direction in speech models (Linear Script Representations 2026). CRITICALLY, no prior work asks whether MULTILINGUAL LLMs exhibit the human dual-route reading effect — whether ORTHOGRAPHIC DEPTH sets a per-language balance between a phonological-recoding route and a direct orthographic route, whether this balance predicts robustness to phonology-vs-shape-preserving perturbations, is decodable as competing phonological/orthographic features at word identification, or is causally steerable. All character-knowledge work is monolingual/English and about spelling capability, not a language-conditioned reading STRATEGY grounded in orthographic depth; all depth work is human-only. This ports a foundational reading-science law into LLM mechanisms, orthogonal to all my prior grammatical/semantic/pragmatic-imposition proposals.
Abstract: How you read a word depends on the script: in transparent orthographies like Spanish or Finnish, letters map cleanly to sounds and readers decode phonologically, while in opaque orthographies like English or Chinese, the same strategy fails and readers rely on whole-word shape-to-meaning recognition. Decades of reading science formalize this as the orthographic depth hypothesis and reproduce it in connectionist models. Multilingual language models process many scripts, but it is unknown whether they adopt an analogous language-dependent reading route. We ask a simple, previously untested question: does a multilingual LLM read shallow-orthography words via a sublexical phonological-recoding route and deep-orthography words via a direct lexical-orthographic route, with the balance set by each language's orthographic depth? We hypothesize that (1) the relative strength of a phonological versus an orthographic feature at the word-identification point tracks each language's orthographic depth; (2) this route balance causally predicts robustness — shallow-orthography reading survives shape-preserving perturbations but breaks under sound-changing ones, while deep-orthography reading shows the reverse; (3) the route is decodable and steerable via phonological and orthographic feature directions; and (4) the per-language route balance is predicted by external orthographic-depth metrics, mirroring the human effect. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM across languages spanning the depth spectrum, using controlled word-identification, phonology-vs-shape-preserving perturbation, and pseudoword tasks. Combining phonological/orthographic feature probes, activation patching, and steering, we measure the route balance, its depth scaling, its causal robustness signature, and route-steering. Metrics include depth-vs-route-balance correlation, perturbation-robustness dissociation, feature-mediation R-squared, and steering-induced route shift.
Experiments:
1) Depth-spanning reading suite: Assemble words across languages spanning the orthographic-depth spectrum: shallow (Spanish, Finnish, Serbian, Italian), intermediate (German, Dutch, Portuguese), deep (English, French) and non-alphabetic (Chinese logographic, as a maximal-depth/shape contrast). For each word build: (a) a WORD-IDENTIFICATION probe (map word -> meaning/category or next-token continuation requiring lexical identification); (b) PHONOLOGY-PRESERVING perturbations (respelling that keeps sound but changes shape, e.g. homophone respellings / grapheme substitutions with identical pronunciation) vs SHAPE-PRESERVING/SOUND-CHANGING perturbations (single-grapheme swaps that change pronunciation but keep visual similarity); (c) PSEUDOWORDS (pronounceable nonwords, decodable only via the sublexical route). Attach each language an external orthographic-depth metric (grapheme-phoneme entropy / published transparency indices). Native-speaker verify. Report inter-annotator agreement; release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Route-balance measurement (H1, core): At the word-identification point, extract a PHONOLOGICAL feature (does the representation encode the word's sound / phoneme sequence, via a probe predicting pronunciation) and an ORTHOGRAPHIC feature (does it encode letter identity/shape, via a character-presence probe as in prior spelling work). Define the route balance = relative strength (probe accuracy / projection magnitude) of the phonological vs orthographic feature per word. Test H1: shallow-orthography words show stronger phonological-route reliance and deep-orthography words stronger orthographic-route reliance. Control for tokenizer fertility, word frequency, and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test orthographic depth adds predictive power beyond fertility/frequency).
3) Depth scaling (H4, external validation): Test whether per-language route balance is predicted by the external orthographic-depth metric (Spearman; held-out prediction from depth alone), tying the internal route to independent reading-science ground truth. Predict a monotonic shift from phonological (shallow) to orthographic (deep) reliance, mirroring the human orthographic-depth gradient.
4) Causal robustness dissociation (H2, core): Measure word-identification accuracy under phonology-preserving vs sound-changing perturbations per language. Predict a DISSOCIATION: shallow-orthography reading is robust to shape-preserving/sound-changing... [correction] — shallow-orthography reading (phonological route) is robust to phonology-PRESERVING (shape-changing) perturbations but breaks under SOUND-CHANGING ones; deep-orthography reading (orthographic route) shows the reverse (robust to sound changes, broken by shape changes). Test whether the route balance (Exp 2) predicts which perturbation each language is robust to (robustness dissociation index). Pseudoword accuracy provides a direct sublexical-route probe: predict higher pseudoword-reading accuracy in shallow-orthography languages.
5) Mechanistic mediation and localization (H3): Using logit-lens/tuned-lens, locate the layer where word identity crystallizes and whether it is preceded by a phonological (sound-decodable, cf. latent romanization) vs orthographic (character-decodable) intermediate. Extract difference-in-means phonological-route and orthographic-route direction; test cross-lingual alignment. Mediation: regress per-word perturbation robustness on the route-balance feature strength (partial correlation controlling for fertility/frequency; held-out R^2).
6) Causal steering test (core): Steer along the phonological-route direction (amplify sublexical decoding) for a deep-orthography word and test whether identification becomes more robust to shape changes but more fragile to sound changes (route shift), and vice versa for shallow words; confirm dose-response and specificity (a random-direction control does nothing). Critically verify word-IDENTIFICATION competence is preserved on unperturbed words and output language is not switched (off-target/language-mixing rate). Baselines: whole-hub English-steering, random-direction control.
7) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify steering is route-specific (changes phonological-vs-orthographic reliance, not word meaning), and not a pure tokenizer artifact (control for how perturbed words re-tokenize; report both token and character analyses). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 leans more orthographic overall than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether route balance correlates with each language's training share and script type. Qualitatively compare the per-language route gradient against the human orthographic-depth reading literature (direction, not identical mechanism).
Evaluation metrics: per-language route balance and its correlation with external orthographic-depth (Spearman; held-out R^2 over fertility/frequency); perturbation-robustness dissociation index (phonology-preserving vs sound-changing, by depth); pseudoword-reading accuracy by depth; route-direction cross-lingual alignment and crystallization-depth ordering (phonological vs orthographic intermediate); mediation of robustness by route balance (held-out R^2); steering-induced route shift with word-identification preservation and off-target rate; cross-model route comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Tokenization is a major confound: a subword tokenizer may pre-package whole words (favoring an orthographic route) unevenly across scripts, and perturbations change tokenization; we control for fertility, report both token- and character-level analyses, and use the internal phonological/orthographic feature probes (not just behavior) so the route claim does not rest on tokenization alone — if the route balance reduces entirely to tokenizer granularity, that is itself an informative mechanistic finding (route = tokenization effect). 2) Constructing clean phonology-preserving (shape-changing) vs sound-changing (shape-preserving) perturbations is delicate and language-specific; we native-speaker verify pronunciations, use pronunciation dictionaries/IPA, report inter-annotator agreement, and exclude ambiguous items. 3) Orthographic depth is correlated with language family, script, and resource level; the pseudoword control, the perturbation dissociation, and depth-based prediction isolate the route pathway, but residual confounds may remain; we center on well-resourced shallow (Spanish/Finnish) vs deep (English/French) languages and treat Chinese as a maximal-shape contrast. 4) A text-only LLM has no acoustic input, so its 'phonological route' is a distributional/orthography-to-pronunciation reconstruction, not embodied phonology; this is exactly what makes the analogy interesting, and a null result (no depth-dependent route) is plausible and informative about the limits of the LLM-human reading analogy. 5) Difference-in-means route directions may entangle frequency/orthographic features; we use multiple extraction methods, pseudoword-derived phonological directions, and specificity controls. 6) Logit-lens depth estimates are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 7) Steering could harm identification or fluency; word-identification preservation is a hard specificity constraint and we report the full tradeoff plus dose-response. 8) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM's more diverse hub analyzed as a contrast). 9) The human-LLM comparison is qualitative/structural (depth gradient direction), not a claim of identical mechanism. 10) If the route balance is NOT predicted by orthographic depth — the model reads all scripts via one uniform route — this is an informative POSITIVE result showing script-invariant reading, valuable either way. 11) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: crosslingual_prior_override_deficit
Title: Can't Unlearn in a Foreign Tongue: A Language-Dependent Deficit in Overriding Semantic Priors During Cross-Lingual In-Context Learning
Short Hypothesis: The emergent ability to OVERRIDE pretraining semantic priors with in-context input-label mappings (flipped-label and semantically-unrelated-label ICL) is language-dependent: a multilingual LLM overrides its priors far less when the demonstrations and query are in a lower-resource / English-distant language than in English, so it defaults to prior-driven 'task recognition' instead of demonstration-driven 'task learning'. This deficit is not a general competence gap but a specific failure to engage a largely shared 'prior-override / task-learning' mechanism when processing non-dominant languages, and it can be causally restored by amplifying that mechanism without harming ordinary (prior-consistent) ICL.
Related Work: A well-established line shows that overriding semantic priors via flipped labels and learning semantically-unrelated-label (SUL) mappings are EMERGENT abilities of scale, strengthened/weakened by instruction tuning (Larger LMs Do ICL Differently 2023), and that ICL decomposes into prior-driven Task Recognition (present in small models, doesn't scale) vs demonstration-driven Task Learning (emerges with scale) (What ICL Learns In-Context 2023; Unveiling ICL Coordinate System 2024). Mechanistically, ICL has an inference function invariant to label remapping followed by a verbalization function, both layer-localized (Inference and Verbalization Functions 2024), label words act as information-flow anchors (Label Words are Anchors 2023), and copy bias is carried by specific neurons (Mitigating Copy Bias 2024). Cross-lingual ICL work is entirely PERFORMANCE-oriented: bridge-language / alignment / code-switching prompting improves low-resource ICL (X-InSTA 2023; CSICL 2025; BridgeX-ICL 2025; Language Steering 2026), and demonstrations matter differently across languages (Multidimensional Analysis 2024). CRITICALLY, no prior work asks whether the specific PRIOR-OVERRIDE / task-learning ability is itself language-dependent — whether a model that can override a wrong semantic prior in English fails to do so for the SAME task in a low-resource language, defaulting to task recognition; whether this is a failure to engage a shared task-learning mechanism (not a general competence gap); or whether amplifying that mechanism restores override without harming prior-consistent ICL. This ports the emergent prior-override finding into a multilingual imposition question and gives it a causal, localizable mechanism, distinct from all performance-improvement X-ICL work and from my prior proposals (none concern prior-override / SUL-ICL).
Abstract: In-context learning can do two very different things: recognize a familiar task and apply pretraining priors, or genuinely learn a new input-label mapping from the demonstrations — even one that contradicts those priors. The ability to OVERRIDE a wrong semantic prior (via flipped or semantically-unrelated labels) is a hallmark emergent capability. We ask a simple, previously untested question: is this prior-override ability language-dependent? We hypothesize that a multilingual LLM overrides its semantic priors far less when the in-context task is posed in a lower-resource or English-distant language than in English, so it falls back on prior-driven task recognition instead of demonstration-driven task learning — and that this is a specific failure to engage a largely shared prior-override mechanism when processing non-dominant languages, not a general competence deficit. We test this on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using controlled flipped-label and semantically-unrelated-label (SUL) ICL across typologically diverse languages, holding the task fixed and varying only language. We measure per-language prior-override rate, decode a shared task-learning vs task-recognition signal, use activation patching to test whether cross-lingual override failures are engagement failures (the override mechanism exists but is under-driven) versus absence failures, and run a targeted intervention that amplifies the task-learning signal. Metrics include per-language flipped-label override rate, SUL-ICL learning curves, prior-override signal decodability, engagement-vs-absence error shares, and intervention-induced override recovery with prior-consistent-ICL preservation controls.
Experiments:
1) Controlled cross-lingual prior-override suite: Build ~600 classification items across tasks where the model holds a clear semantic prior (sentiment, topic, natural-language inference). For each item construct three ICL conditions: (a) GOLD (correct labels, prior-consistent — baseline), (b) FLIPPED (labels systematically inverted, so correct performance requires overriding the semantic prior), and (c) SUL (semantically-unrelated labels, e.g. 'foo'/'bar', so the model must learn the mapping without semantic cues). Instantiate every item — inputs, labels, and template — in typologically diverse languages spanning resource levels and scripts (English, French, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish), native-speaker verified, holding the task and the number of demonstrations fixed. Report inter-annotator agreement; release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral language-dependent override (H1, core): Measure per-language prior-override rate = accuracy on FLIPPED-label ICL (high = the model follows the in-context flipped mapping and overrides its prior; near-chance-or-below = it clings to the semantic prior). Also measure the SUL-ICL learning curve (accuracy vs number of demonstrations) per language, where a rising slope indicates task learning. Test H1: override rate and SUL learning slope are high in English and drop for lower-resource / English-distant languages, even though GOLD (prior-consistent) accuracy is comparable — so the gap is specific to prior-override, not general competence. Control for tokenizer fertility and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test language adds predictive power beyond GOLD accuracy and fertility). Crucially condition on items the model classifies correctly in the GOLD condition in each language, so an override gap cannot be explained by not understanding the task.
3) Task-recognition vs task-learning decomposition: Separate, per language, the contribution of task recognition (GOLD-minus-RANDOM-label accuracy, i.e. performance from priors alone) vs task learning (GOLD-minus-SUL and the SUL slope). Test that low-resource languages show intact/strong task recognition but degraded task learning — i.e., the deficit is specifically in demonstration-driven learning, following the TR/TL framework applied cross-lingually.
4) Prior-override signal decodability (H2): Extract a difference-in-means 'task-learning vs task-recognition' direction (override-succeeded vs prior-driven forward passes on FLIPPED items) at middle layers, per language, and via logit-lens track whether the flipped in-context mapping is engaged. Test whether per-item override-signal strength predicts override success (Spearman; held-out R^2), whether the direction is largely shared across languages (cross-lingual cosine alignment), and whether the query language is decodable from an early signal that gates engagement of the override mechanism.
5) Engagement-vs-absence error decomposition via patching (H3, core): For FLIPPED items overridden correctly in English but failed in language B, patch (a) the shared mid-layer task-learning / override representation (from the English pass, or from a same-task SUL pass) into B, and (b) only late-layer verbalization/decoding components. If (a) restores override in B (the mechanism EXISTS but was under-engaged), classify as an engagement failure; if neither helps, an absence failure. Report engagement-vs-absence error shares per language, predicting engagement failures dominate — the override mechanism is shared but not driven in non-dominant languages.
6) Core causal intervention (override amplification): Amplify the shared task-learning direction at the middle layers on FLIPPED/SUL items in the target language (train-free steering), and measure per-language override-rate and SUL-learning recovery. Predict SELECTIVE gains for low-override (low-resource) languages, little effect on already-high languages (interaction test). Compute recovery elasticity = override gain per unit baseline deficit. Compare against baselines: language-steering vectors (Language Steering for Multilingual ICL 2026), code-switching demonstrations (CSICL 2025), copy-neuron pruning (Mitigating Copy Bias 2024), and a random-direction control.
7) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify the amplification is override-specific — it must IMPROVE FLIPPED/SUL performance WITHOUT harming GOLD (prior-consistent) ICL (a symmetric check: it must not make the model ignore correct labels), must not switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), and preserve fluency. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 shows a sharper cross-lingual override deficit than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether the deficit correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the override direction and each language's training share.
Evaluation metrics: per-language flipped-label override rate and SUL-ICL learning slope (vs GOLD-conditioned baseline; partial correlation with resource/distance over fertility, held-out R^2); task-recognition vs task-learning decomposition by language; override-signal decodability, override-success prediction, and cross-lingual alignment; engagement-vs-absence error shares and patching-restoration rate; selective override-amplification recovery and elasticity vs baselines, with GOLD-ICL preservation (symmetric specificity), off-target rate, fluency; cross-model deficit comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The override deficit could conflate with a general competence gap; the key control is conditioning on GOLD-correct items (the model demonstrably understands the task in that language) plus the task-recognition-vs-task-learning decomposition and the engagement-vs-absence patching — if override gaps vanish once competence is controlled, the hypothesis is refuted, an informative negative result. 2) Prior-override / SUL-ICL is an emergent-scale ability that may be weak in 7-8B models; we verify a measurable override effect in English first (a necessary gate) and interpret accordingly, using multiple demonstration counts to trace learning curves. 3) Language is confounded with tokenizer fertility, script, and resource level; partial correlations and the causal patching/steering tests mitigate but may not fully remove confounds. 4) Difference-in-means override directions may entangle content or language-identity features; we use multiple extraction methods, the established copy-neuron / label-anchor circuitry as anchors, and specificity controls. 5) The override-amplification intervention could make the model ignore correct labels (harming GOLD ICL); the symmetric GOLD-preservation constraint is a hard requirement and we report the full tradeoff. 6) SUL labels in non-Latin scripts may tokenize inconsistently; we control label tokenization and use script-neutral pseudo-labels. 7) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM/Aya analyzed as less English-centric contrasts expected to show a smaller deficit). 8) Instruction tuning strengthens both priors and mapping-learning unevenly (per Larger LMs Do ICL Differently 2023); we test base and instruction-tuned models and treat differences as an informative training-stage finding. 9) Logit-lens override-signal decoding is approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: language_shifted_temporal_now_anchor
Title: A Different 'Now' in Every Tongue: Does Query Language Shift the Subjective Temporal Reference Point and Weber-Fechner Compression in Multilingual LLMs?
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs spontaneously establish a subjective temporal reference point ('now', ~2025) around which perceived temporal distance is logarithmically compressed (Weber-Fechner law), as recently shown in English. We hypothesize this subjective 'now' anchor and its compression curvature are LANGUAGE-DEPENDENT: querying the same year-similarity judgments in a different language shifts the model's reference point and re-scales the log-compression, so the model 'feels' time from a different present and at a different resolution depending on the query language. This shift is carried by a shared, decodable temporal-orientation direction (organized around the reference point) that is re-anchored by an early language signal, tracks each language's data-recency, and is causally steerable to a target anchor without changing the model's factual year knowledge.
Related Work: The Other Mind (2025) shows larger LLMs spontaneously establish a subjective temporal reference point (~2025) and perceive time with logarithmic (Weber-Fechner) compression as years recede, implemented by temporal-preferential FFN neurons and a hierarchical representation from numeric value (shallow) to temporal orientation around a reference point (deep). Time Travel Engine (2026) shows time is a continuous traversable manifold with cross-lingual (Chinese/English) topological isomorphism, and Language Models Represent Space and Time (2023) finds linear, causal time neurons; Temporal Heads (2025) localize time-specific fact recall. All of this temporal-cognition/geometry work is either monolingual (English) or asserts cross-lingual ISOMORPHISM of the temporal manifold's shape — none asks whether the subjective 'now' ANCHOR (the reference point the compression is organized around) and the compression CURVATURE are set by the QUERY LANGUAGE, whether this produces a language-dependent shift in perceived temporal distance on identical judgments, whether the anchor is re-set by an early language signal, or whether it is causally steerable independent of factual year knowledge. This differs from my prior language_dependent_temporal_anchor proposal, which concerns KNOWLEDGE recency/staleness (outdated factual answers), not the subjective temporal-COGNITION reference point and its Weber-Fechner compression geometry. It ports The Other Mind's finding into a multilingual condition-probing question with a decodable, steerable anchor mechanism.
Abstract: Humans feel time from a subjective present, compressing distant years logarithmically — and recent work shows larger language models spontaneously do the same, establishing a subjective reference point around 2025 and obeying the Weber-Fechner law. That work is monolingual. We ask a simple, previously untested question: does the language a model is queried in change its subjective 'now'? We hypothesize that both the subjective temporal reference point and the curvature of its logarithmic compression are language-dependent: on identical year-similarity judgments, querying in a lower-resource or English-distant language shifts the model's internal present-time anchor and re-scales how sharply it compresses distant years, so the model perceives temporal distance from a different present and at a different resolution. We further hypothesize this shift is carried by a shared, decodable temporal-orientation direction that is re-anchored by an early language signal, tracks each language's data-recency, and can be steered to a target anchor without altering the model's factual knowledge of which year an event occurred. We test this on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM across typologically diverse languages using year-similarity-judgment tasks (the paradigm that revealed the effect in English), combining behavioral reference-point and Weber-Fechner curve fitting, temporal-neuron/direction probes, activation patching, and anchor-steering. Metrics include per-language subjective reference-point year, log-compression curvature, anchor-vs-data-recency correlation, temporal-orientation-direction alignment, and steering-induced anchor shift with factual-year-knowledge preservation controls.
Experiments:
1) Year-similarity suite: Replicate The Other Mind's similarity-judgment paradigm — present pairs of years (or a reference year and a probe year) and elicit perceived similarity/distance ratings — across a wide year range (e.g. 1500–2050) with dense sampling near the present. Instantiate every prompt in typologically diverse languages spanning resource levels and data-recency (English, French, German, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish), native-speaker verified. Include a factual-year-knowledge control task (which year did event X happen? / which of two events is earlier?) to separate temporal COGNITION geometry from factual year knowledge. Report inter-annotator agreement on translations; release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B (predict the effect strengthens with scale, per the original).
2) Per-language subjective reference point (H1, core): For each language, fit the perceived-distance curve and estimate (a) the subjective reference point (the year of minimal perceived distance / peak similarity, i.e. the model's 'now') and (b) the log-compression curvature (Weber-Fechner fit quality and its scaling constant). Test H1: the reference-point year and curvature differ by query language on IDENTICAL year judgments. Verify the Weber-Fechner logarithmic form holds per language (vs a linear baseline, model comparison).
