Control for tokenizer fertility of year expressions and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test query language adds predictive power).
3) Anchor-vs-data-recency scaling (H2): Test whether the per-language reference-point year is predicted by each language's training-data recency (documented cutoff / a corpus-recency proxy) rather than by resource level alone — lower-recency-data languages should anchor to an earlier subjective 'now' (held-out prediction; Spearman). This ties the internal anchor shift to an interpretable cause.
4) Representational localization (H3): Following The Other Mind, probe for temporal-preferential FFN neurons and extract a temporal-orientation direction (organized around the reference point) via difference-in-means / regression, per language and layer. Test (a) whether the temporal-orientation direction is largely shared across languages but its zero-point (reference) is re-set per language (cross-lingual alignment of the direction with a language-dependent offset), and (b) whether the query language is decodable from an early signal that predicts the eventual reference point, via position-resolved logit-lens (the anchor set before the year judgment). Verify the shallow-numeric-to-deep-orientation hierarchy replicates cross-lingually.
5) Causal anchor-steering test (H4, core): Steer along the temporal-orientation direction to shift a target-language query's subjective 'now' toward a chosen reference year (e.g. move a low-recency language's anchor to 2025, or shift English's anchor earlier), and measure whether the perceived-distance curve's minimum and compression re-center accordingly (anchor-shift rate; bidirectional dose-response). Complement with activation patching: patch the reference-point signal from one language into another and confirm the anchor moves. Critically verify FACTUAL-YEAR-KNOWLEDGE preservation: the model must still correctly state which year events occurred and which of two events is earlier (steering changes subjective temporal FELT-distance, not factual ordering), plus fluency and off-target/language-mixing checks. Baselines: whole-hub English-steering, random-direction control.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify steering is anchor-specific (shifts the reference point / compression but not factual year knowledge or unrelated content). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 anchors more uniformly toward the English ~2025 'now' across languages, while the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM show more language-dependent anchors; test whether anchor variation correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the temporal-orientation direction and each language's data recency. Qualitatively compare the per-language anchor/compression pattern against the human Weber-Fechner temporal-cognition literature (direction, not identical mechanism).
Evaluation metrics: per-language subjective reference-point year and log-compression curvature (Weber-Fechner vs linear model comparison); reference-point-vs-data-recency correlation and held-out prediction; temporal-orientation-direction cross-lingual alignment and per-language offset; early language-signal predictiveness of the reference point; anchor-steering shift rate and bidirectional dose-response; factual-year-knowledge preservation (event-year accuracy, pairwise-ordering accuracy) as a hard specificity check; off-target rate; cross-model anchor-variation comparison and correlation with data recency; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for query language over fertility/resource baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The subjective-reference-point effect is scale-emergent (per The Other Mind, stronger in larger models) and may be weak in 7-8B models; we verify a measurable effect in English first as a gate and interpret accordingly, and report cross-scale where a larger open model is affordable. 2) Fitting a reference point and Weber-Fechner curvature from similarity ratings is noisy and prompt-sensitive; we use dense year sampling, multiple prompt phrasings, and report fit robustness and model comparison (log vs linear). 3) Query language is confounded with data-recency, script, tokenizer fertility, and resource level; the data-recency prediction (H2), factual-year controls, and partial correlations isolate the anchor mechanism, but residual confounds may remain. 4) A language-dependent anchor could reflect factual-knowledge recency rather than a subjective-cognition shift; the factual-year-knowledge control task and the causal steering test (which moves the subjective anchor while leaving factual ordering intact) are designed to separate cognition-geometry from knowledge — if they cannot be separated, that is itself an informative result relating subjective 'now' to knowledge cutoff. 5) Difference-in-means temporal-orientation directions may entangle numeric-magnitude features; we use the shallow-numeric-vs-deep-orientation hierarchy from prior work, multiple extraction methods, and specificity controls. 6) Steering could harm factual year knowledge or fluency; factual-year preservation is a hard constraint and we report the full tradeoff plus bidirectional dose-response. 7) The human-LLM Weber-Fechner comparison is qualitative/structural, not a claim of identical mechanism. 8) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM's less English-centric hub analyzed as a contrast). 9) If the subjective reference point and compression are language-INVARIANT (consistent with the cross-lingual isomorphism reported by Time Travel Engine), this is an informative POSITIVE result showing a universal, language-agnostic temporal 'now' despite uneven data recency — valuable either way. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: contradictory_proverb_arbitration
Title: Which Wisdom Wins? Language-Conditioned Arbitration of Contradictory Proverbs in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Every culture holds MUTUALLY CONTRADICTORY proverbs ('look before you leap' vs 'he who hesitates is lost'; 'many hands make light work' vs 'too many cooks spoil the broth'), and which of two opposing maxims a person invokes to justify an action is culturally patterned, not random. We hypothesize that when a multilingual LLM must pick which of two contradictory proverbs applies to a situation, its arbitration is governed by a language-conditioned GAIN on a small set of shared value dimensions (e.g. caution-vs-boldness, individual-vs-collective), so the SAME situation elicits opposite proverb choices depending only on query language; and that this arbitration is anchored to the dominant (English/Western) value profile and imported into other languages regardless of that culture's actual value orientation, producing a decodable, steerable arbitration bias distinct from the model merely knowing or understanding each proverb.
Related Work: Prior work shows mLLMs know limited proverbs and struggle to reason with them in context, with a 'culture gap' for translated proverbs (MAPS 2023; Kinayat/pragmatic-gap 2025), that proverbs encode culturally-patterned values (Chinese proverbs 2020; folk tales 2023), and that cultural knowledge/values live in localizable, steerable neurons and middle-layer directions (Isolating Culture Neurons 2025; Localized Cultural Knowledge 2025; CultureSteer 2025; Entangled in Representations 2025; Language over Content 2025; Probing PLMs for Cross-Cultural Values 2023). Moral-reasoning work shows cross-lingual moral inconsistency and a foreign-language utilitarian shift ('Your Morals Depend on Language' 2014; One Model Many Morals 2025; UniMoral 2025). CRITICALLY, all proverb work asks whether models KNOW/UNDERSTAND proverbs, and all culture-mechanism work concerns declarative cultural facts/values; NONE studies the ARBITRATION between mutually-contradictory proverbs — a within-language natural experiment that holds knowledge constant (the model knows both maxims) and isolates the culturally-patterned CHOICE of which applies. No prior work asks whether this arbitration is a language-conditioned gain on shared value dimensions, whether it is anchored to the dominant-culture value profile and imported cross-lingually, whether it is predictable from cross-cultural value surveys, or whether it is mediated by a decodable/steerable arbitration direction. This reframes cultural reasoning from 'does the model know the wisdom?' to 'which contradictory wisdom does it apply, and whose values decide?', orthogonal to all my prior proposals (which target grammatical, lexical, temporal, spatial, and pragmatic axes) and to the retrieved knowledge/understanding-focused literature.
Abstract: Every culture's stock of proverbs is riddled with contradictions: 'look before you leap' coexists with 'he who hesitates is lost'; 'many hands make light work' with 'too many cooks spoil the broth'. Crucially, the model KNOWS both maxims — so which one it invokes to judge a situation is not a knowledge question but an arbitration question, and cultures arbitrate these contradictions differently. Multilingual language models build a shared, largely Western-scaffolded representation of values. We ask a simple, previously untested question: when a model must pick which of two contradictory proverbs applies to a situation, does the query language change its choice, and is that choice anchored to the dominant-culture value profile rather than each culture's own? We hypothesize that (1) the same situation elicits opposite proverb choices depending only on query language, holding constant the model's knowledge of both proverbs; (2) this arbitration is a low-dimensional GAIN on shared value dimensions (caution/boldness, individual/collective, fate/agency) that is imported from the dominant (English/Western) profile; (3) the per-language arbitration shift is predicted by cross-cultural value surveys, not by resource level; and (4) a decodable, steerable arbitration direction mediates it, so rescaling it recovers culture-appropriate arbitration without harming proverb comprehension. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using a controlled suite of situations paired with contradictory-proverb pairs across typologically and culturally diverse languages, combining behavioral choice measurement, difference-in-means value-direction extraction, activation patching, and gain-steering. Metrics include cross-lingual arbitration-flip rate, value-survey prediction correlation, arbitration-direction alignment, mediation R-squared, and steering-induced culture-appropriate arbitration with comprehension controls.
Experiments:
1) Contradictory-proverb arbitration suite: Assemble ~40 pairs of mutually-contradictory proverbs (each pair opposed along a value dimension: caution vs boldness, individual vs collective, thrift vs generosity, fate vs agency, conformity vs independence), each pair attested across cultures with near-equivalents. For each pair, construct ~10 SITUATIONS that plausibly license either proverb (ambiguous scenarios where a culture's value orientation tips the choice). Present each situation with the two contradictory proverbs and ask which better fits / which advice to follow (forced choice + log-prob margin) and to justify. Instantiate every situation and proverb pair in typologically and culturally diverse languages spanning value profiles (English, German, Spanish, Russian, Mandarin, Japanese, Hindi, Arabic). Native-speaker verify proverb equivalents and situations; attach each language a cross-cultural value reference (WVS/Hofstede/Schwartz individualism-collectivism, uncertainty-avoidance). A separate KNOWLEDGE-CONTROL probe verifies the model knows/understands BOTH proverbs in each language (isolating arbitration from knowledge). Report inter-annotator agreement; release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral cross-lingual arbitration flip (H1, core): For each situation-pair, measure per-language proverb-choice distribution and the cross-lingual arbitration-flip rate = fraction of situations where the model's chosen proverb flips between two languages. Condition on situations where the model knows BOTH proverbs in both languages, so flips cannot be knowledge gaps. Control for tokenizer fertility and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test query language adds predictive power beyond knowledge and fertility).
3) Dominant-value-anchor signature (H2): Test whether per-language arbitration is pulled toward the ENGLISH/Western value profile rather than each culture's own — define a Western-anchor pull = shift of the model's proverb choices toward the English arbitration pattern. Compare a 'Western-anchored' model (all languages pulled toward English) vs a 'culture-appropriate' model (choices match each culture's value survey) via model comparison; predict Western-anchor wins, especially for lower-resource / non-Western languages.
4) Value-survey scaling (H3, external validation): Test whether the per-language arbitration profile (its position on each value dimension) is predicted by that culture's WVS/Hofstede/Schwartz scores (Spearman; held-out prediction from survey values alone), tying the internal arbitration to independent cross-cultural human ground truth.
5) Shared value directions and gain readout (H4, core): For each value dimension, extract a per-language difference-in-means direction between the two poles (e.g. caution vs boldness proverb-endorsing representations) at each layer. Measure cross-lingual cosine alignment (test: shared value axes re-thresholded per language, peaking in middle layers) and portability (steering with one language's direction changes another's arbitration). Project the residual stream at the choice point onto these shared directions and estimate a per-LANGUAGE gain vector via regression of the proverb choice on the projections. Test that the cross-lingual arbitration shift is captured by the difference in gain vectors applied to the SHARED value projections (held-out R^2), beating a uniform-bias baseline and a full per-language relearned readout (shift is low-dimensional). Test whether the gain vector is predicted by value surveys better than resource level (AIC, held-out R^2).
6) Causal gain-steering (H5, core): At the choice layer, rescale individual value directions to transform one language's gain vector into another's, and measure whether the model's proverb arbitration shifts toward the target culture's pattern WITHOUT changing input language (arbitration-transfer rate); conversely, recalibrate each language's gain to its own value-survey profile and measure culture-appropriateness gain. Bidirectional dose-response; mis-signed steering worsens. Complement with activation patching: patch the English arbitration signal into a target-language pass. Verify COMPREHENSION preservation (the model must still correctly explain each proverb's literal meaning — steering changes WHICH proverb it picks, not whether it understands them), value-dimension-specificity (steering the caution axis changes caution/boldness situations but not individual/collective ones), no output-language switch (off-target rate), and fluency. Baselines: whole-hub English-steering, cultural steering vector (Localized Cultural Knowledge 2025; CultureSteer 2025), random-direction control.
7) Cross-model controls: Predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen have gain vectors more collapsed toward the Western profile (less cross-lingual arbitration variation) than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether gain-collapse correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the value directions and with training share.
Evaluation metrics: cross-lingual arbitration-flip rate (knowledge-conditioned); Western-anchor pull and Western-anchored-vs-culture-appropriate model comparison; arbitration-vs-value-survey correlation and held-out prediction; per-dimension value-direction cross-lingual alignment and portability; gain-vector predictive R^2 for arbitration shift (vs uniform-bias and full-relearn baselines) and gain-vs-survey R^2 over resource baseline; arbitration-transfer rate and culture-appropriateness gain under gain-steering vs baselines, with bidirectional dose-response, value-dimension-specificity, comprehension preservation, off-target rate; cross-model gain-collapse comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Constructing situations that genuinely license EITHER contradictory proverb (rather than one obviously fitting) is delicate; we native-speaker verify that both are plausible, calibrate on a pilot to ensure near-50/50 human choice variance, report inter-annotator agreement, and exclude situations with a forced answer. 2) Proverb equivalents across cultures are imperfect (some contradictions are language-specific); we native-speaker verify near-equivalence, restrict to cross-culturally attested pairs, and treat language-specific pairs as a separate tier. 3) Language, culture, script, and resource level are confounded; we include a within-language cultural-framing manipulation (same language, home-culture vs neutral addressee framing) to separate cultural framing from language identity, use value-survey prediction, and report partial correlations. 4) The knowledge-control is essential: an arbitration flip only counts when the model demonstrably knows/understands both proverbs in both languages — if flips vanish once knowledge is controlled, the hypothesis reduces to a knowledge gap, an informative negative result. 5) Value-survey scores are noisy and may not reflect training-data culture; we use multiple surveys, treat them as noisy predictors, and rely on the internal gain and causal tests for core claims. 6) The low-dimensional value basis may underfit; if a data-driven basis (PCA/SAE over proverb-choice activations) fits better, we report the empirically-best basis, keeping the 'shared basis + language gain' claim testable. 7) Difference-in-means value directions may entangle topical/lexical content; we use matched contrastive proverb representations, multiple extraction methods, and value-dimension-specificity controls. 8) Gain-steering could harm comprehension or over-impose a target culture; comprehension preservation, specificity, and bidirectional dose-response are hard constraints and we report the full tradeoff. 9) Some arbitration could be genuinely culture-appropriate rather than Western-anchored; the direction of the effect, the model comparison, and the survey prediction distinguish imposition from faithful arbitration, and a faithful finding is itself valuable. 10) Instruction-tuned models may hedge ('it depends'); we test base models where available, use forced-choice, and treat hedging as a covariate. 11) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM analyzed as a less Western-centric contrast). 12) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: rhetorical_structure_imposition
Title: Writing English-Style in Every Language: Does the Shared Hub Impose an English Discourse-Organization Template Onto Reader-Responsible Rhetorical Traditions?
Short Hypothesis: Languages differ systematically in discourse/rhetorical organization: English writing is writer-responsible (explicit connectives, linear direct progression, given-before-new, thesis-first), whereas reader-responsible traditions (Arabic, Japanese, Chinese, Hindi) favor associative logic, implicit connections, indirection, and later-arriving main points. Because the multilingual LLM's shared hub is scaffolded by writer-responsible English, we hypothesize the model IMPOSES an English-like discourse-organization template when GENERATING longer text in reader-responsible languages: it over-produces explicit connectives, front-loads the thesis, and imposes linear given-before-new structure at rates far above native norms, tracking the English rhetorical convention rather than the target language's. This imposition is mediated by a shared, steerable 'discourse-explicitness/linearity' direction, tracks each language's empirical writer-vs-reader-responsibility typology, and is causally correctable toward target-language rhetorical structure without harming content or fluency.
Related Work: A large cross-linguistic rhetoric/discourse-typology literature (contrastive rhetoric; writer- vs reader-responsible languages; implicitation of discourse relations across four language pairs 2015; structure of argumentative discourse in Danish/English/Italian 2013; register-based discourse variation 2015; Rhetorical Dissonance in Bilingual Argumentation 2025; second-language reading and discourse schemata 1986) establishes that languages systematically differ in explicit-vs-implicit connective marking, linear-vs-associative progression, and thesis placement, and that these differences transfer as interference in bilingual writing. On the model side, interpretability shows an English-scaffolded shared hub with three-phase processing and late-layer language-specific generation (Do Llamas Work in English 2024; Do Multilingual LLMs Think In English 2025; LinguaMap 2026; MWork 2024), that discourse relations and implicitation are cognitively patterned (Factors Influencing Implicitation 2015), and that FORMAT/length are encoded and steerable but studied monolingually and treated as input/instruction-driven (Length Representations 2025; Format as a Prior 2025; prompt-format sensitivity 2023). CRITICALLY, all model work on format/length/discourse is monolingual or English-centric and treats these as content-driven; all cross-linguistic rhetoric work is human-only. NO prior work asks whether the English-scaffolded hub IMPOSES an English DISCOURSE-ORGANIZATION template (connective explicitness, thesis-first linearity, given-before-new packaging) onto reader-responsible languages during GENERATION, whether this imposition is predictable from each language's writer-vs-reader-responsibility typology, whether a shared discourse-explicitness/linearity direction mediates it, or whether it is causally correctable per language. This differs from my prior register-drift (register consistency), verbosity-setpoint (how MUCH is said), and information-structure (sentence-level topic/comment) proposals by targeting DISCOURSE-LEVEL rhetorical organization of longer text, grounded in contrastive-rhetoric typology.
Abstract: How a paragraph is organized — whether it states its point up front and links every idea with explicit connectives, or unfolds associatively and lets the reader infer connections — varies systematically across languages. English is a writer-responsible tradition (linear, explicit, thesis-first); Arabic, Japanese, Chinese, and Hindi lean reader-responsible (associative, implicit, indirect). Multilingual language models build a shared, English-scaffolded representation. We ask a simple, previously untested question: when a model GENERATES longer text in a reader-responsible language, does its English-scaffolded hub IMPOSE an English discourse-organization template — over-producing explicit connectives, front-loading the thesis, and forcing linear given-before-new structure — rather than following the target language's rhetorical conventions? We hypothesize that (1) the model's discourse organization in reader-responsible languages tracks English norms (higher connective explicitness, thesis-first linearity) at rates above native-writer norms; (2) the size of this imposition tracks each language's empirical writer-vs-reader-responsibility typology; (3) a shared, steerable 'discourse-explicitness/linearity' direction mediates it; and (4) steering toward the target-language rhetorical structure restores native-like organization without harming content or fluency. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using controlled long-form generation and discourse-structure analysis across reader-responsible (Arabic, Japanese, Chinese, Hindi) and writer-responsible (English, German) languages. Combining automatic discourse-structure scoring, difference-in-means direction extraction, activation patching, and steering, we measure the imposition, its typology scaling, its mediation, and its causal correction. Metrics include connective-explicitness and thesis-position imposition gaps versus native corpora, typology-prediction correlation, mediation R-squared, and steering-induced restoration with content-preservation controls.
Experiments:
1) Discourse-organization generation suite and native reference corpora: Build ~400 prompts eliciting LONG-FORM structured text (argumentative essays, explanations, opinion pieces — genres where rhetorical organization varies most) across reader-responsible languages (Arabic, Japanese, Chinese, Hindi) and writer-responsible controls (English, German), native-speaker verified. For each language, assemble a native-writer reference corpus (from contrastive-rhetoric datasets, native-language editorials/essays) to establish empirical norms for: (a) explicit-connective density (rate of overt discourse markers vs implicit relations), (b) thesis position (how early the main claim appears), (c) given-before-new / linear progression rate. Build validated automatic discourse-structure scorers (connective detection, thesis-position estimation, discourse-relation implicitation rate), validated against native-annotator labels on a held-out subset. Report inter-annotator agreement; release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral rhetorical imposition (H1, core): For model-generated text in each language, score connective-explicitness, thesis-position, and linearity, and compare against that language's native-writer norm. Define per-metric imposition gap = model value minus native-writer norm, signed toward the English pattern (over-explicit, thesis-first, over-linear). Predict positive imposition (English-like organization) in reader-responsible languages and near-zero in English/German. Compute an English-pull rate = fraction of generations whose organization is closer to the English norm than the target-language norm. Control for tokenizer fertility, output length (holding length fixed via length-matched generation), and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test reader-responsible status adds predictive power).
3) Typology-predicted imposition (H2, external validation): Using contrastive-rhetoric typology (writer-vs-reader-responsibility ratings; empirical implicitation rates per language) as external ground truth, test whether per-language imposition is predicted by the typological writer-responsibility distance from English (Spearman; held-out prediction from typology alone), tying the internal phenomenon to independent linguistic data. Predict strongest imposition for the most reader-responsible languages (Arabic/Japanese) and near-zero for German.
4) Representational localization (H3): Extract a 'discourse-explicitness/linearity' direction via difference-in-means between explicit-linear and implicit-associative discourse representations (using minimal-pair passages that convey the same content with English-style vs target-style organization) at each layer, per language. Test (a) whether a shared discourse-organization direction is English-scaffolded (cross-lingual cosine alignment across layers, aligned with the English explicit-linear pole); (b) whether generating in a reader-responsible language nonetheless engages the English explicit-linear pole in the shared hub while any residual target-language rhetorical signal is stronger in early/language-specific layers, via logit-lens tracking at discourse-boundary positions (e.g., where a connective would be inserted). Baseline: a lexical-content direction as a within-model control. Mediation: regress behavioral imposition on shared-hub explicit-linear-pole engagement (partial correlation controlling for fertility/length; held-out R^2).
5) Causal steering/patching test (H4, core): (a) Steer the generation along the discourse-organization direction toward the target-language (implicit-associative) pole and measure whether connective-explicitness, thesis-position, and linearity shift toward native-writer norms (imposition-gap reduction), without switching output language; (b) for imposed generations, patch the residual language-specific rhetorical signal (from early/language-specific layers) into later computation and test restoration, localizing failure to the shared hub imposing an English template over a shallowly-present target-language rhetorical structure. Critically verify CONTENT PRESERVATION (the same information/arguments must be present — organization changes, not content, via content-overlap/faithfulness checks) plus fluency and off-target/language-mixing checks. Baselines: prompt-based instruction ('write in the native rhetorical style'), whole-hub English-steering, random-direction control.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify steering is discourse-organization-specific (changes rhetorical structure but not content, grammaticality, or output language), graded (imposition scales with writer-responsibility distance), bidirectional (can shift toward and away from the English pole as a dose-response check), and not merely a length artifact (length held fixed). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show stronger imposition than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether imposition magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the discourse direction and with each language's training share. Qualitatively compare the model's per-language imposition pattern against the contrastive-rhetoric typology.
Evaluation metrics: connective-explicitness, thesis-position, and linearity imposition gaps vs native-writer norms (reader-responsible vs writer-responsible languages; English-pull rate); imposition-vs-typology correlation and held-out prediction; discourse-organization-direction cross-lingual alignment and shared-hub engagement; mediation regression (held-out R^2); steering-induced imposition-gap reduction (bidirectional dose-response) and patching-induced restoration; content-preservation/faithfulness, grammaticality/fluency, off-target/language-mixing rate, length control; cross-model imposition comparison and correlation with training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for reader-responsible status over fertility/length/resource baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Automatically scoring discourse organization (connective explicitness, thesis position, linearity/implicitation) is nontrivial and language-specific; we build validated scorers grounded in the contrastive-rhetoric literature, validate against native-annotator labels on held-out subsets, report scorer reliability and inter-annotator agreement, and use multiple complementary metrics. 2) Native-writer norm corpora are noisy and register/genre-dependent; we match genre between generations and reference corpora, use multiple corpora, and treat norms as noisy references, relying on the internal representation and causal tests for core claims. 3) Writer-vs-reader responsibility is correlated with language family, script, and resource level; the writer-responsible comparison languages (English/German), within-content minimal-pair contrasts, length control, and typology-based prediction isolate the discourse-organization pathway, but residual confounds may remain; we center core claims on well-resourced Arabic/Japanese/Chinese and treat Hindi as an extension. 4) Some imposition may reflect genuinely correct behavior (the model rightly using an explicit style for clarity) rather than English imposition; the direction of the effect (does organization track ENGLISH or the TARGET norm?), the typology prediction, and the causal steering (which restores native organization by editing only the discourse direction) distinguish imposition from appropriate style, and a norm-appropriate finding is itself valuable. 5) Difference-in-means discourse-organization directions may entangle content, length, or lexical features; we use content-matched minimal-pair passages, a lexical-content control direction, length control, and multiple extraction methods. 6) Discourse structure is a whole-passage property, making token-level logit-lens localization approximate; we aggregate over discourse-boundary positions and report robustness. 7) Steering could harm content, coherence, or fluency; content-preservation and fluency are hard specificity constraints and we report the full tradeoff plus bidirectional dose-response, comparing against the prompt-instruction baseline to show the mechanistic account adds value. 8) Instruction-tuned/RLHF models may be trained toward an explicit, structured 'assistant' rhetorical style that dominates; we test base vs instruction-tuned models and treat differences as an informative training-stage finding. 9) The model-vs-typology comparison is qualitative/structural, not a claim of identical mechanism. 10) If NO imposition is found — discourse organization tracks each language's native rhetorical norms, predictable from typology, with content preserved — this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the shared hub generates language-appropriate rhetorical structure despite English scaffolding, valuable either way. 11) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: translate_transliterate_name_gate
Title: Say It or Sound It Out: A Language-Conditioned Translate-vs-Transliterate Gate for Proper Names in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: When rendering a proper name into a target language, a multilingual LLM must covertly decide between TRANSLATING semantically transparent name components (e.g. 'Red Square' -> the target word for red+square) and TRANSLITERATING opaque ones (phonetic re-spelling, e.g. 'Ivanov'). We hypothesize this decision is governed by a language-conditioned 'render-mode gate' set by a decodable signal early in the forward pass, anchored to the dominant (English) rendering convention and imported into other languages: the model over-transliterates names that a target language conventionally translates and over-translates names it conventionally transliterates, tracking the English convention rather than the target-language norm. The gate is mediated by a steerable translate-vs-transliterate direction, tracks each language pair's empirical rendering convention, and is causally correctable without harming the model's phonetic or semantic knowledge of the name.
Related Work: Prior interpretability work localizes translation to sparse attention heads with distinct target-language-identification vs sentence-equivalence functions (Disentangling meaning from language 2026; Exploring the Translation Mechanism 2025), shows an English-centric pivot / language-agnostic concept space (Do Llamas Work in English 2024; Separating Tongue from Thought 2024; Paths Not Taken 2025), that entities are decodable and entity-alignment drives cross-lingual consistency (On the Representations of Entities 2025; Entity-Level Alignment 2025), and that latent romanization bridges non-Roman scripts (RomanLens 2025). Cross-domain NLP treats transliteration-vs-translation as an external classification/tagging task (Lightly supervised transliteration 2009; NEWS shared tasks; cluster-specific transliteration 2005) and translation studies document that WHICH proper-name components are translated vs transliterated is a culturally-patterned convention that varies by language pair (Arabization 2019; branding transliteration 2026; Classic of Tea 2024). CRITICALLY, all translation-mechanism work treats the whole string as a unit and never studies the per-name TRANSLATE-vs-TRANSLITERATE decision; all transliteration-vs-translation NLP work is external classification, not a model-internal gate; and none asks whether the shared, English-scaffolded hub IMPOSES the dominant language's rendering convention onto other languages, localizes a render-mode direction, ties the imposition to per-language-pair rendering conventions, or offers a causal fix. This is orthogonal to my prior proposals (grammatical/semantic/pragmatic imposition, quote verbatim drift): the novel axis is the compositional per-name rendering-mode choice for entities, a decision that sits exactly at the seam between the language-agnostic concept and the language-specific decoder.
Abstract: Rendering a proper name across languages is not one operation but a choice made piece by piece: semantically transparent parts are translated ('Red Square' becomes the target words for red and square), while opaque parts are transliterated (spelled out by sound, like a surname). Which parts a language translates versus transliterates is a culturally-patterned convention that differs across language pairs. Multilingual language models build a shared, largely English-scaffolded representation. We ask a simple, previously untested question: when a model renders a name into a target language, is its translate-vs-transliterate decision governed by an internal 'render-mode gate' that is anchored to the dominant (English) convention and imported into other languages? We hypothesize that (1) the model over-transliterates names a target language conventionally translates and over-translates names it conventionally transliterates, tracking the English convention rather than the target-language norm; (2) the size of this imposition tracks each language pair's empirical rendering convention; (3) the decision is set by a decodable, steerable translate-vs-transliterate direction fixed early, before the name is rendered; and (4) steering the gate restores convention-appropriate rendering without harming the model's phonetic or semantic knowledge of the name. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using a controlled multilingual proper-name suite (semantically-transparent vs opaque names, across language pairs with divergent conventions), combining behavioral render-mode scoring, difference-in-means gate-direction extraction, logit-lens tracking, activation patching, and steering. Metrics include per-language render-mode imposition gap, convention-prediction correlation, gate decodability, mediation R-squared, and steering-induced correction with name-knowledge preservation controls.
Experiments:
1) Proper-name rendering suite: Assemble ~500 proper names spanning (a) SEMANTICALLY-TRANSPARENT names whose components have literal meaning (place names like 'Red Square', 'Black Sea', 'New York'; descriptive org/title names), (b) OPAQUE names (personal surnames, brand names with no compositional meaning), and (c) MIXED names (one transparent + one opaque component, e.g. 'University of Cambridge'). For each name and target language, establish the CONVENTIONAL rendering (translate vs transliterate per component) from authoritative sources (bilingual gazetteers, Wikipedia cross-language links, native-speaker verification), spanning language pairs with divergent conventions across scripts and resource levels (English<->Russian, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Spanish, Turkish). Key subsets: DIVERGENT names where the target-language convention differs from the English convention; matched CONVERGENT names. Task: prompt the model to render the name in the target language (in context). Report inter-annotator agreement; release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral render-mode imposition (H1, core): Score each model rendering per component as TRANSLATED (semantic equivalent) vs TRANSLITERATED (phonetic re-spelling) via a validated automatic classifier (grapheme/phoneme-overlap + semantic-equivalence checks) backed by native-annotator labels on a held-out subset. Compare against the target-language conventional rendering. Define the render-mode imposition GAP = deviation of the model's render-mode from the target-language convention, signed toward the English convention (over-transliterate where target translates, over-translate where target transliterates), and an English-convention pull rate. Predict positive imposition on DIVERGENT names, near-zero on CONVERGENT names and English-native rendering. Control for name frequency, tokenizer fertility, and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test rendering-convention divergence adds predictive power).
3) Convention scaling (H2, external validation): Using per-language-pair rendering-convention statistics (proportion of transparent place names translated vs transliterated, from gazetteers/Wikipedia cross-links), test whether per-name imposition is predicted by how much the target-language convention diverges from English (Spearman; held-out prediction from convention statistics alone), tying the internal phenomenon to independent linguistic ground truth.
4) Gate decodability and timing (H3): Extract a difference-in-means 'render-mode' direction (translate vs transliterate forward passes) at each layer. Test whether the eventual render-mode is decodable early (before the name tokens are emitted) from an internal gate signal, whether the query/target language is decodable from that gate, and whether the gate is set before the name is rendered (position-resolved logit-lens). Measure cross-lingual alignment (shared gate axis re-thresholded per language pair). Localize whether the gate rides on the target-language-identification vs sentence-equivalence head families identified in prior translation-mechanism work. Mediation: regress behavioral imposition on the gate-direction projection (partial correlation controlling for frequency/fertility; held-out R^2).
5) Causal steering/patching test (H4, core): (a) Steer along the render-mode direction toward the target-language convention (translate where the target translates, transliterate where it transliterates) for DIVERGENT names and measure whether renderings shift to the convention-appropriate mode (mode-flip rate) and the imposition GAP shrinks toward the CONVERGENT baseline, without switching output language; (b) conversely steer toward the English convention and confirm dose-response (bidirectional); (c) for imposed items, patch the residual language-specific gate signal (from early/language-specific layers) into later computation and test restoration, localizing failure to the shared hub imposing the English convention. Critically verify NAME-KNOWLEDGE preservation: steering must change the RENDERING MODE, not the underlying name — the model must still know the name's phonetic form (correct transliteration when asked to transliterate) AND its semantic components (correct translation when asked to translate) — plus fluency and off-target/language-mixing checks. Baselines: whole-hub English-steering, prompt instruction ('render in the conventional local form'), random-direction control.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify steering is render-mode-specific (changes translate-vs-transliterate but not which name/entity is referred to), graded (imposition scales with convention divergence), and not a lexical-frequency artifact (frequency-matched divergent/convergent names). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show stronger imposition than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether imposition magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the render-mode direction and with each language pair's training share. Qualitatively compare the model's per-language-pair imposition pattern against the human rendering-convention statistics.
Evaluation metrics: render-mode imposition GAP and English-convention pull rate (DIVERGENT vs CONVERGENT names; vs English-native ceiling); imposition-vs-convention-divergence correlation and held-out prediction; render-mode gate decodability, early-timing predictiveness, and head-family localization; gate cross-lingual alignment and mediation of behavioral imposition (held-out R^2); steering mode-flip rate and GAP reduction (bidirectional dose-response), patching-induced restoration; name-knowledge preservation (correct transliteration and correct component-translation on demand), fluency, off-target/language-mixing rate; cross-model imposition comparison and correlation with training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for convention divergence over frequency/fertility/resource baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Automatically classifying a rendering as translated vs transliterated is nontrivial (partial translations, established hybrid forms, near-homophonic translations); we build a classifier combining grapheme/phoneme-overlap and semantic-equivalence signals, validate against native-annotator labels on a held-out subset, report reliability and inter-annotator agreement, and exclude ambiguous items. 2) Rendering conventions are gradient, register-dependent, and sometimes have multiple accepted forms; we ground conventions in gazetteers/Wikipedia cross-links plus native-speaker verification, use graded convention scores, restrict DIVERGENT names to clear contrasts, and treat mixed cases separately. 3) Convention divergence is correlated with language pair, script, and resource level; the CONVERGENT controls, English-native ceiling, within-name contrasts, and convention-based prediction isolate the imposition pathway, but residual confounds may remain; we center core claims on well-resourced pairs and treat sparser ones as extensions. 4) Some imposition may reflect genuinely correct behavior (an established English-derived exonym); the direction of the effect (tracks ENGLISH vs TARGET convention), the convention-statistics prediction, and the causal steering (which restores the convention-appropriate mode by editing only the render-mode direction) distinguish imposition from correct rendering, and a correct-rendering finding is itself valuable. 5) Difference-in-means render-mode directions may entangle name-identity, script, or frequency features; we use frequency-matched names, latent-romanization checks (per RomanLens) for non-Roman scripts, multiple extraction methods, and specificity controls. 6) The gate decision may be per-component rather than per-name for MIXED names, complicating localization; we analyze transparent, opaque, and mixed names separately and report per-component results. 7) Logit-lens gate/timing estimates are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 8) Tokenization strongly affects both transliteration and translation of names across scripts; we control for fertility and report both token- and character-level analyses. 9) Steering could corrupt the name (wrong phonetics or wrong semantics) or fluency; name-knowledge preservation is a hard specificity constraint and we report the full tradeoff plus the bidirectional dose-response, comparing against the prompt-instruction baseline to show the mechanistic account adds value. 10) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM's more diverse hub analyzed as a contrast expected to impose less). 11) If NO imposition is found — the model renders each name by the target-language convention, predictable from convention statistics, with name knowledge intact — this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the render-mode gate is convention-appropriate and language-specific despite English scaffolding, valuable either way. 12) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: relation_default_imposition_compounds
Title: Cactus Fish, English-Style: Does the Shared Hub Impose the Dominant Language's Default Combinatorial Relation Onto Novel Noun-Noun Compounds?
Short Hypothesis: When interpreting a NOVEL noun-noun compound (e.g. 'cactus fish', 'mountain book'), a modifier and head must be linked by an implicit RELATION (a fish LIKE a cactus? a fish THAT EATS cacti? a fish NEAR cacti?), and which relation is preferred is culturally/linguistically patterned, not universal. Because the multilingual LLM's shared hub is scaffolded by English, we hypothesize it IMPOSES the ENGLISH-default relation onto compounds in other languages: the model's interpretation, entailments, and property judgments about a novel compound track the English-preferred relation rather than the target language's conventional one, producing cross-lingual interpretation inconsistency on the SAME compound. This imposition is mediated by a shared, steerable 'combinatorial-relation' direction, tracks each language's empirical relation-preference norms, and is causally correctable without harming the model's knowledge of the constituent nouns.
Related Work: Conceptual-combination research establishes that novel noun-noun compounds are interpreted by selecting an implicit relation (relation-based) or transferring a property (property-based), that these processes are asymmetric and culturally/proficiency-modulated (Efficient Creativity / constraint theory 2000; Asymmetric Mechanisms of Relation- vs Property-Based Combination 2021; Chinese EFL relation-based combination 2025), and that MEG shows the brain's early composition mechanism is language-blind but later stages are language-sensitive (Korean/English bilingual MEG 2021). LLM/embedding work shows modern transformers represent compounds largely compositionally, with head/modifier roles distinguished and compositionality most accessible in early layers (Functional Analysis 2025; Systematic Search in BERT 2023; German compounds 2025; local composition 2022), and that idiom non-compositionality is causally encoded and INLP-removable in NMT (Transformer Too Compositional 2022). CRITICALLY, all LLM/embedding compound work is monolingual or about compositionality DEGREE (how transparent), never about WHICH RELATION is selected to bind modifier and head, and never cross-lingual; all conceptual-combination cross-lingual work is human-only. No prior work asks whether the English-scaffolded shared hub IMPOSES the dominant language's DEFAULT combinatorial relation onto novel compounds in other languages, causing cross-lingual interpretation inconsistency, localizes a shared relation-selection direction, ties the imposition to per-language relation-preference norms, or offers a causal fix. This differs from my prior idiom-leakage proposal (figurative meaning of EXISTING idioms) and from all my grammatical/lexical imposition proposals: the novel axis is the implicit RELATION chosen when composing two nouns into a new concept, grounded in conceptual-combination theory with human relation-frequency ground truth.
Abstract: To understand a novel compound like 'cactus fish' you must decide how the two nouns relate: is it a fish shaped LIKE a cactus, a fish that EATS cacti, or a fish that LIVES AMONG cacti? Conceptual-combination research shows this relation selection is not universal — which relation people default to is patterned by language and culture, and even the same modifier-head pair can prefer different relations across languages. Multilingual language models build a shared, largely English-scaffolded representation. We ask a simple, previously untested question: when a model interprets a novel noun-noun compound in a non-English language, does it IMPOSE the ENGLISH-default relation rather than the target language's conventional one? We hypothesize that (1) the model's interpretation, entailments, and property judgments about a novel compound track the English-preferred relation, producing cross-lingual inconsistency on the SAME compound concentrated where languages' relation preferences diverge; (2) the size of this imposition tracks each language's empirical relation-preference norms; (3) a shared, steerable 'combinatorial-relation' direction mediates it, with any residual target-language relation signal in shallow, language-specific layers; and (4) steering toward the target-language relation restores faithful interpretation without harming knowledge of the constituent nouns. We build a controlled multilingual novel-compound suite with divergent versus convergent relation preferences across typologically diverse languages, grounded in human relation-preference norms, on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM. Using difference-in-means relation-direction probes, logit-lens tracking, activation patching, and steering, we measure the imposition, its norm scaling, its mediation, and its causal correction. Metrics include cross-lingual relation-interpretation gap, norm-prediction correlation, mediation R-squared, and steering-induced correction with constituent-knowledge controls.
Experiments: 1) Novel-compound relation suite grounded in human norms: Assemble ~400 NOVEL (non-lexicalized) noun-noun compounds by combining familiar modifier and head nouns, translated into typologically diverse languages spanning scripts and resource levels (English, French, German, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Turkish, Spanish). For each compound in each language, collect native-speaker relation-preference norms (forced choice among a fixed relation inventory drawn from conceptual-combination theory: LIKE/resembles, HAS, MADE-OF, FOR/purpose, LOCATED, CAUSES, USES/eats, etc.), yielding per-language relation distributions. Key subsets: DIVERGENT compounds whose top relation differs across English and a target language; matched CONVERGENT compounds (same top relation). Probes hinge on the relation, not on recognizing novelty: (i) relation forced choice ('How are cactus and fish related in cactus fish?'); (ii) entailment/property probe (does the compound entail a property implied by the English relation vs the target relation?); (iii) paraphrase generation. Native-speaker verify constituent meanings and relation labels; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B. 2) Behavioral relation imposition (H1, core): For each DIVERGENT compound in each language, measure whether the model's relation choice / entailments track the ENGLISH-preferred relation vs the target-language one. Define the cross-lingual relation-interpretation GAP = inconsistency(DIVERGENT) minus inconsistency(CONVERGENT), and an English-relation-pull rate = fraction of divergent compounds interpreted with the English-preferred relation. Verify near-faithful interpretation on CONVERGENT compounds and correct English relations (ceiling). Control for constituent-noun frequency, tokenizer fertility, and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test target-language status adds predictive power). 3) Norm scaling (H2, external validation): Test whether per-compound imposition is predicted by the target-vs-English relation-preference norm divergence (Spearman; held-out prediction from norms alone), tying the internal phenomenon to independent human ground truth. Predict larger imposition for lower-resource / English-distant languages. 4) Representational localization (H3): Extract a 'combinatorial-relation' direction via difference-in-means between compound representations disambiguated toward different relations (using relation-biasing contexts) at each layer, per language. Test (a) whether a shared relation direction is English-scaffolded (cross-lingual cosine alignment across layers, aligned with the English-relation pole); (b) whether a DIVERGENT compound projects onto the ENGLISH-relation pole in the shared mid-layers while any residual target-language relation signal is stronger in early/language-specific layers, via logit-lens/tuned-lens depth tracking of when the relation crystallizes. Baseline: a constituent-identity direction as a within-model control. Mediation: regress behavioral imposition on shared-hub English-relation-pole projection (partial correlation controlling for frequency/fertility; held-out R^2). 5) Causal steering/patching test (H4, core): (a) Steer the divergent compound's representation along the relation direction toward the target-language relation and measure whether interpretation/entailment/paraphrase shift to the target-language pattern (flip rate) and the GAP shrinks toward the convergent baseline, without switching output language; (b) conversely amplify the English relation and confirm dose-response (bidirectional); (c) for imposed items, patch the residual language-specific relation signal (from early/language-specific layers) into later computation and test restoration. Critically verify CONSTITUENT-KNOWLEDGE preservation (the model must still correctly answer factual/definitional questions about the modifier and head nouns — steering changes the RELATION, not the constituents) plus fluency and off-target/language-mixing checks. Baselines: whole-hub English-steering, random-direction control. 6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify steering is relation-specific (changes the modifier-head relation but not constituent identity or unrelated meaning), graded (imposition scales with norm divergence), and not a lexical-frequency artifact (frequency-matched divergent/convergent pairs). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show stronger imposition than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether imposition magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the relation direction and with each language's training share. Qualitatively compare the model's per-language imposition against the human relation-preference norms and the language-blind-early / language-sensitive-late MEG finding. Evaluation metrics: cross-lingual relation-interpretation GAP and English-relation-pull rate (DIVERGENT vs CONVERGENT; vs English ceiling); imposition-vs-norm-divergence correlation and held-out prediction; relation-direction cross-lingual alignment and crystallization depth (vs constituent baseline); mediation regression (held-out R^2); steering flip rate and GAP reduction (bidirectional dose-response), patching-induced restoration; constituent-knowledge preservation (specificity), fluency, off-target rate; cross-model imposition comparison and correlation with training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for target-language status over frequency/fertility/resource baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Relation preference for a novel compound is inherently variable and context-sensitive (multiple relations often plausible); we collect native-speaker norms with a fixed relation inventory, use graded divergence scores, report inter-annotator agreement, restrict DIVERGENT items to clear cross-lingual contrasts, and treat multi-relation items separately. 2) Relation divergence is correlated with language family, script, culture, and resource level; the CONVERGENT controls, English ceiling, within-compound contrasts, and norm-based prediction isolate the imposition pathway, but residual confounds may remain; we center core claims on well-resourced languages and treat sparser ones as extensions. 3) Some imposition may reflect genuinely correct behavior (the model rightly using the target-language relation); the direction of the effect (tracks ENGLISH vs TARGET relation), the norm-divergence prediction, and the causal steering (which restores the target relation by editing only the relation direction) distinguish imposition from faithful interpretation, and a faithful-interpretation finding is itself valuable. 4) Difference-in-means relation directions may entangle constituent-lexical or topical features; we use a constituent-identity control direction, relation-biasing minimal-context pairs, multiple extraction methods, and specificity checks. 5) Novel compounds may partially collide with lexicalized meanings in some languages; we native-speaker verify novelty and exclude lexicalized items. 6) Logit-lens/tuned-lens depth estimates are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 7) Steering could harm constituent knowledge or fluency; constituent-knowledge preservation is a hard specificity constraint and we report the full tradeoff plus bidirectional dose-response. 8) Human relation-preference norms are noisy and may not reflect training-data usage; we treat them as noisy predictors and rely on internal representation and causal tests for core claims. 9) The human-LLM comparison (relation-based combination, language-blind-early MEG) is qualitative/structural, not a claim of identical mechanism. 10) Instruction-tuned models may hedge or over-explain; we test base models where available and use forced-choice and entailment probes. 11) If NO imposition is found — novel compounds are interpreted by each language's own relation preference, predictable from norms, with constituent knowledge intact — this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the shared hub represents language-specific combinatorial relations despite English scaffolding, valuable either way. 12) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: counterfactual_marking_gated_override
Title: Entering the What-If World, English-Style: Does Grammatical Counterfactual Marking Gate World-Knowledge Override in Multilingual LLMs?
Short Hypothesis: Languages differ in whether counterfactuality is grammatically MARKED (English/German subjunctive, Spanish/French conditional mood) or conveyed only by context and semantic cues (Chinese, Indonesian, and other counterfactual-unmarking languages). We hypothesize that a multilingual LLM's ability to ENTER a hypothetical world and OVERRIDE real-world knowledge when reasoning about a counterfactual premise is gated by whether the query language grammatically marks counterfactuality: because the English-scaffolded shared hub associates counterfactual-world entry with an explicit subjunctive/conditional marker, the model over-relies on that marker and under-enters the counterfactual world for unmarking languages, defaulting to real-world (parametric) answers far more than in marked languages on identical premises. This marking-gated override deficit is mediated by a shared 'counterfactual-world' signal whose engagement is set by the marker, tracks each language's empirical counterfactual-marking typology, and is causally restorable by amplifying that signal without harming real-world reasoning.
Related Work: Monolingual interpretability establishes a 'competition of mechanisms' between factual recall and in-context counterfactual information, localized to attention heads that suppress the competing token (Competition of Mechanisms 2024; Cutting Off the Head 2024; Characterizing Mechanisms for Factual Recall 2023; Fakepedia grounding 2023), and behavioral work shows LLMs can override real-world knowledge in counterfactual conditionals but largely via lexical cues, with genuine nuance sensitivity rare (Li/Yu/Ettinger 2022/2023; Can LLMs Reconcile Knowledge Conflicts in Counterfactual Reasoning 2025). Cross-lingual mechanistic work localizes factual inconsistency to a late-layer language-transition failure over a shared, English-centric concept space (Lost in Multilinguality 2025; How Do Multilingual LLMs Remember Facts 2024). Crucially, cognitive science shows languages differ in GRAMMATICAL counterfactual MARKING (English/German subjunctive vs Chinese contextual-only), and this changes how readily humans enter counterfactual worlds and draw counterfactual inferences (Counterfactual Reasoning Development in Different Languages 2025; Chinese/English bilingual reasoning 2021; German subjunctive ERP 2014). NO prior work connects these three literatures: none asks whether an LLM's counterfactual-world OVERRIDE ability is gated by the query language's grammatical counterfactual marking, whether the English-scaffolded hub imports an English subjunctive-marking expectation onto unmarking languages (causing under-override), whether this tracks the counterfactual-marking typology, or whether amplifying a shared counterfactual-world signal causally restores override. All prior counterfactual-mechanism work is monolingual and about IN-CONTEXT facts; all cross-lingual work is about plain factual consistency, not counterfactual-world entry gated by grammatical mood. This reframes the multilingual counterfactual-reasoning gap as a marking-gated world-entry deficit with a competition-of-mechanisms locus and a causal fix, orthogonal to all my prior proposals.
Abstract: To reason about a counterfactual ('if cats were reptiles, they would be cold-blooded'), a model must temporarily override what it knows and inhabit a hypothetical world. Languages signal this move differently: English, German, and Spanish grammatically mark counterfactuality with subjunctive or conditional mood, while Chinese, Indonesian, and many other languages convey it only through context and semantic cues. Multilingual language models build a shared, English-scaffolded representation. We ask a simple, previously untested question: is a model's ability to enter a hypothetical world and override real-world knowledge gated by whether the query language grammatically marks counterfactuality? We hypothesize that (1) on identical counterfactual premises, the model overrides real-world knowledge more when the query language uses an explicit counterfactual marker and under-enters the hypothetical world (defaulting to parametric real-world answers) for unmarking languages, tracking an English-scaffolded reliance on the marker; (2) the size of this override deficit tracks each language's empirical counterfactual-marking typology; (3) a shared 'counterfactual-world' signal, engaged by the marker, mediates it, and the competition between real-world recall and hypothetical-world entry is localizable; and (4) amplifying that signal causally restores override for unmarking languages without harming ordinary real-world reasoning. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using controlled counterfactual-conditional items across marking and unmarking languages, combining override-rate measurement, logit-lens/competition-of-mechanisms tracing, difference-in-means counterfactual-world direction extraction, activation patching, and steering. Metrics include marking-gated override gap, typology-prediction correlation, real-world-vs-hypothetical competition attribution, mediation R-squared, and steering-induced override recovery with real-world-reasoning controls.
Experiments:
1) Counterfactual-conditional suite: Construct ~500 counterfactual-conditional items whose correct consequent CONTRADICTS real-world knowledge (e.g. 'if a whale were a fish, it would breathe through ___' -> gills, overriding the real-world 'lungs'), each with a verified counterfactual-correct answer and the competing real-world answer. Instantiate every item in counterfactual-MARKING languages (English/subjunctive, German/Konjunktiv, Spanish/French conditional) and counterfactual-UNMARKING languages (Mandarin Chinese, Indonesian, and additional context-only-marking languages), native-speaker verified to use natural marking/unmarking phrasing. Include (a) matched REAL-WORLD (non-counterfactual) versions of each item to measure baseline real-world reasoning; (b) an English-side manipulation stripping the subjunctive marker (indicative counterfactuals) to test marker-reliance within a language; (c) a lexical-cue control (following Ettinger) to separate genuine world-override from lexical shortcuts. Native-speaker verify; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral marking-gated override (H1, core): Measure per-language override rate = fraction of counterfactual items answered with the counterfactual-correct (real-world-overriding) answer rather than the parametric real-world default. Test that override is higher in marking languages and lower (more real-world defaulting) in unmarking languages on identical premises. Define the marking-gated override GAP = override(marking) minus override(unmarking). Crucially test the within-language marker manipulation: stripping the English subjunctive marker should reduce override, and adding an explicit contextual counterfactual cue in an unmarking language should raise it. Control for tokenizer fertility, item frequency, and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test marking status adds predictive power beyond fertility/resource). Also verify real-world (non-counterfactual) accuracy is comparable across languages, so the gap is specific to counterfactual override, not general competence.
3) Typology-predicted deficit (H2, external validation): Using the cross-linguistic counterfactual-marking typology (grammaticalized subjunctive/conditional vs context-only), assign each language a marking-explicitness score and test whether per-language override deficit is predicted by that score (Spearman; held-out prediction from typology alone), tying the internal phenomenon to independent cognitive-science ground truth.
4) Competition-of-mechanisms tracing (H3): Adapting the monolingual competition-of-mechanisms method, use logit-lens and attention attribution to trace, per item and language, the competition between the real-world answer (parametric recall) and the counterfactual answer (hypothetical-world entry). Test whether, in unmarking languages, the real-world token remains more strongly promoted (weaker suppression of the parametric competitor) and the counterfactual-world signal is engaged later/weaker. Extract a difference-in-means 'counterfactual-world' direction (successful-override vs real-world-default forward passes); test cross-lingual alignment (shared, English-scaffolded signal) and whether the counterfactual marker's presence predicts its engagement. Mediation: regress behavioral override on counterfactual-world signal engagement (partial correlation controlling for fertility/frequency; held-out R^2).
5) Error decomposition via patching (H3b): For items overridden correctly in a marking language but defaulted-to-real-world in an unmarking language, patch (a) the shared counterfactual-world signal (from the marking-language pass) into the unmarking pass and (b) only late-layer decoding components. If (a) restores override, the deficit is a failure to ENGAGE the shared hypothetical-world mechanism (present but under-driven by the missing marker), not absence of counterfactual reasoning. Report engagement-vs-absence error shares per language.
6) Causal steering test (H4, core): Amplify the shared counterfactual-world direction at middle layers on counterfactual items in unmarking languages (train-free), and measure per-language override recovery. Predict SELECTIVE gains for high-deficit (unmarking) languages, little effect on marking languages (interaction). Compute recovery elasticity = override gain per unit baseline deficit. Compare against baselines: whole-hub English-steering, the linear-shortcut factual fix (Lost in Multilinguality 2025) adapted here, an explicit 'this is hypothetical' prompt nudge, and a random-direction control. Complement with activation patching from a marking-language pass.
7) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify the intervention is override-specific: it must IMPROVE counterfactual override WITHOUT degrading matched REAL-WORLD (non-counterfactual) accuracy (a symmetric check — it must not make the model ignore real facts when it should use them), must not switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), and preserve fluency. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show a sharper marking-gated deficit than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether the deficit correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the counterfactual-world direction and each language's training share. Qualitatively compare the per-language override pattern against the human counterfactual-marking cognitive literature (direction, not identical mechanism).
Evaluation metrics: per-language override rate and marking-gated override GAP (marking vs unmarking; within-language marker-manipulation shift; lexical-cue-controlled); override-deficit-vs-marking-typology correlation and held-out prediction; real-world (non-counterfactual) accuracy parity (competence control); counterfactual-world signal engagement, cross-lingual alignment, and marker-predicted engagement, with mediation of behavioral override (held-out R^2); engagement-vs-absence error shares (patching); selective steering override-recovery and elasticity vs baselines, with REAL-WORLD-reasoning preservation (symmetric specificity), off-target rate, fluency; cross-model deficit comparison and correlation with training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for marking status over fertility/frequency/resource baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The override deficit could conflate with a general competence gap; the key controls are matched real-world (non-counterfactual) items showing comparable baseline accuracy, the within-language marker manipulation (which isolates the marker, not the language), the lexical-cue control (per Ettinger, separating genuine world-override from lexical shortcuts), and the engagement-vs-absence patching — if override gaps vanish once competence and marker are controlled, the hypothesis is refuted, an informative negative result. 2) Counterfactual marking is correlated with language family, script, and resource level; the marker manipulation, typology-based prediction, and partial correlations isolate the marking pathway, but residual confounds may remain; we center core claims on well-resourced marking (English/German/Spanish) vs unmarking (Chinese/Indonesian) languages. 3) Natural counterfactual phrasing in unmarking languages is subtle (context-dependent cues); we native-speaker verify natural marking/unmarking phrasing, report inter-annotator agreement, and exclude ambiguous items. 4) Behavioral override could be driven by lexical association rather than genuine world-entry; the lexical-cue control and anti-commonsensical/nonce premises block shortcuts. 5) The counterfactual-world direction from difference-in-means may entangle content or language-identity features; we use multiple extraction methods, the established competition-of-mechanisms attention heads as an anchor, and specificity controls. 6) The competition-of-mechanisms attention-head localization is known to generalize imperfectly to larger models (per reproduction studies); we use it as one lens among logit-lens and patching, and report robustness rather than relying on head ablation alone. 7) The steering intervention could make the model ignore real facts (harming real-world reasoning); the symmetric real-world-preservation constraint is a hard requirement and we report the full tradeoff. 8) Logit-lens/tuned-lens engagement estimates are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 9) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM/Aya analyzed as less English-centric contrasts expected to show a smaller deficit). 10) The human-LLM comparison (counterfactual-marking effect on world-entry) is qualitative, not a claim of identical mechanism. 11) If no marking-gated deficit is found — override is equal across marking and unmarking languages once competence is controlled — this is an informative POSITIVE result showing counterfactual-world entry is language-agnostic despite an English-scaffolded hub, valuable either way. 12) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: classifier_congruency_crosslingual
Title: The Classifier Congruency Effect in Multilingual LLMs: A Noun's Required Chinese Measure Word Leaks Into Cross-Lingual Processing
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs exhibit a mechanistic analogue of the human Chinese classifier-congruency effect: the numeral classifier (measure word) that a noun requires in Chinese is co-activated as a lexico-syntactic feature and interferes with processing that noun even in a NON-Chinese query, so a noun paired with (or primed by) its congruent classifier is processed more easily than one paired with an incongruent classifier, and this interference is stronger for semantically-related noun-classifier mismatches. This co-activation is mediated by a partially-shared classifier feature direction that carries the Chinese classifier signal into non-Chinese processing, is measurable as a congruent-minus-incongruent processing swing, scales with cross-lingual classifier-subspace sharedness, and is causally suppressible by ablating that direction.
Related Work: Human psycholinguistics robustly documents a Chinese classifier-congruency effect: classifier-incongruent noun phrases produce longer naming latencies and N400 responses, the classifier is automatically activated as a lexico-syntactic feature during lemma access, and this interacts with semantic relatedness (Selection of Chinese Classifiers Involves a Competitive Process 2019; Processing Mandarin Classifiers as a Lexico-Syntactic Feature 2025; Shape Information in Classifier-Noun Phrases 2025; L1/L2 classifier prediction 2019). Bilingual work shows cross-linguistic co-activation of the non-context language and that word-class/lexico-syntactic overlap drives facilitation vs interference (Cross-linguistic Influence in the Bilingual Lexicon 2023; Word Class Meaning 2010; Gender Congruency in L2 processing 2022; classifier processing in Spanish-Chinese bilinguals 2025). On the LLM side, the only classifier work is monolingual: LLMs predict Chinese classifiers worse than BERT, relying on the head noun and statistical frequency (From BERT to LLMs 2025). Interpretability shows a shared, largely English-scaffolded semantic hub (Semantic Hub 2024), that morphosyntactic features like gender live in shared+language-specific subspaces (Analyzing Gender Representation 2022), and that vocabulary/token overlap drives cross-lingual co-activation (False Friends Are Not Foes 2025). CRITICALLY, no prior work tests whether a multilingual LLM shows a classifier-congruency effect: whether the classifier a noun requires in Chinese leaks into and facilitates/interferes with processing that SAME noun in the query language, whether this is a distinct behavioral swing predicted by cross-lingual classifier-subspace sharedness and modulated by semantic relatedness, or whether a shared classifier direction causally mediates and can remove it. This differs from the monolingual classifier-prediction paper (a prediction-accuracy task) by asking the reverse, cross-lingual interference question, and differs from my prior gender-congruency proposal by targeting Chinese numeral classifiers — a distinctly Chinese lexico-syntactic feature with a strong N400 human baseline and a rich shape/semantic structure absent from grammatical gender.
Abstract: In Mandarin Chinese, counting a noun requires a numeral classifier (measure word) chosen by the noun's shape or semantic class ('one FLAT-thing paper', 'one LONG-thing pen'). Decades of psycholinguistics show this classifier is automatically activated as a lexico-syntactic feature: a noun paired with an incongruent classifier is named more slowly and elicits an N400, and the effect interacts with semantic relatedness. We ask a simple, previously untested question about multilingual language models: is the classifier a noun requires in Chinese co-activated and does it interfere when the model processes that same noun — even in a non-Chinese query?
