We hypothesize a mechanistic classifier-congruency effect: for a noun, the model's processing is facilitated when a congruent classifier is present/primed and interfered with by an incongruent one, this swing is larger under semantic relatedness (mirroring the human interaction), it is carried by a partially-shared classifier feature direction that bleeds the Chinese classifier signal into the query-language computation, scales with cross-lingual classifier-subspace sharedness, and is causally removable by ablating that direction without harming noun comprehension. We test this on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using controlled classifier-noun minimal pairs in Chinese and cross-lingual (English-frame/Chinese-noun and Chinese-classifier-primed) conditions. Combining behavioral congruency measurement, difference-in-means classifier-direction extraction, activation patching, and steering, we measure the congruency swing, its semantic-relatedness modulation, its sharedness scaling, its causal locus, and whether ablating the classifier direction removes the interference while preserving noun-level competence. Metrics include congruent-vs-incongruent processing swing, semantic-relatedness interaction, causal-mediation attribution, and ablation-induced interference removal with comprehension controls.
Experiments:
1) Classifier-congruency suite: Assemble ~500 concrete Chinese nouns each with a verified congruent numeral classifier and an incongruent one, from authoritative sources and native-speaker verification, spanning shape-based (flat/long/round) and taxonomic classifiers. Build (a) a MONOLINGUAL-Chinese condition (classifier-noun phrases, congruent vs incongruent) with matched acceptability/cloze probes; (b) a CROSS-LINGUAL condition where the noun is queried in an English frame but PRIMED by a Chinese classifier (congruent vs incongruent) inserted in context, testing whether the Chinese classifier signal leaks into non-Chinese processing; (c) a SEMANTIC-RELATEDNESS factor crossing classifier congruency with whether a co-occurring distractor noun is semantically related (mirroring the human 2x2 design). Native-speaker verify classifiers and semantic-relatedness pairings; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral congruency effect (H1, core): Measure processing ease via log-prob margin (of the correct noun / of the phrase) and forced-choice acceptability for congruent vs incongruent classifier-noun pairings, per condition. Compute the congruency SWING = congruent minus incongruent performance. Predict a positive swing (incongruent classifiers degrade processing) in the monolingual Chinese condition AND, crucially, in the cross-lingual condition where the noun is queried in English but a Chinese classifier is primed — demonstrating that the required Chinese classifier leaks into non-Chinese processing. Test the semantic-relatedness interaction: predict a larger congruency swing (or reversed direction) under semantic relatedness, mirroring the human N400 interaction. Control for noun frequency, classifier frequency, and tokenizer fertility (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test congruency adds predictive power).
3) Sharedness scaling (H2): Extract a per-language classifier feature direction via difference-in-means (e.g. flat-classifier vs long-classifier noun representations) at each layer, and measure cross-lingual cosine alignment (Chinese vs the query-language subspace) per model. Test whether the cross-lingual congruency swing is larger for models/conditions with more SHARED classifier subspaces (held-out prediction of swing from sharedness, controlling for frequency/fertility).
4) Causal localization via activation patching (H3, core): For CROSS-LINGUAL incongruent items where the model shows degraded processing, test whether the interference is carried by the Chinese classifier signal: patch (a) the shared classifier direction toward the congruent classifier and (b) the noun's mid-layer representation from a monolingual (no-classifier-prime) pass, and measure whether processing is restored. Conversely, INJECT the incongruent-classifier signal into a congruent/no-prime pass and test whether it induces interference (bidirectional causal test), isolating the partially-shared classifier direction as the mechanism.
5) Ablation / removal test: Ablate the shared classifier direction (difference-in-means projection removal / INLP nullspace) so query-language noun processing can no longer read the Chinese classifier signal, and test whether the congruency swing collapses toward zero. Critically verify NOUN-LEVEL competence is preserved (the model must still answer definitional/factual questions about the noun and, in the monolingual condition, still select the correct classifier), that the ablation does not switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), and that fluency is maintained. Compare against random-direction ablation and whole-hub English-steering baselines.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify the effect is classifier-specific (a congruency manipulation on an irrelevant feature produces no swing) and not a lexical-frequency artifact (frequency-matched congruent/incongruent pairs and nonce-noun variants with assigned classifiers). Cross-model contrast: predict the more Chinese-exposed Qwen2.5 and multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM show larger classifier subspaces and swings than the more English-centric Llama-3; test whether swing magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the classifier direction and each model's Chinese training share. Qualitatively compare the model's swing pattern (semantic-relatedness interaction, shape-classifier structure) against the human N400 classifier-congruency literature.
Evaluation metrics: congruency swing (congruent minus incongruent log-prob margin and acceptability; monolingual vs cross-lingual conditions; vs no-swing control feature); semantic-relatedness interaction; classifier-subspace sharedness prediction of swing (held-out R^2 over frequency/fertility); share of cross-lingual incongruent interference fixed by classifier-direction/noun patching and induced by injection (bidirectional causal test); ablation-induced swing collapse WITH noun-competence and monolingual-classifier-selection preservation; off-target/language-mixing rate, fluency; cross-model swing comparison and correlation with classifier-subspace sharedness and Chinese training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The human classifier-congruency effect is a production/latency and N400 phenomenon; log-prob margins are not directly comparable to reaction times or ERPs, so the model-vs-human comparison is qualitative (direction, semantic-relatedness interaction, shape-classifier structure), not a claim of identical mechanism. 2) A null cross-lingual swing is a live possibility — the classifier signal may be genuinely gated out of non-Chinese processing — but that itself would be an informative result on the language-locality of Chinese lexico-syntactic features. 3) Numeral classifiers are a distinctly Chinese (and East/Southeast-Asian) feature, so the cross-lingual leak test requires a classifier language (Chinese) as the source and a non-classifier query language (English); we center on Chinese-source leakage and treat other classifier languages (Vietnamese, Japanese) as extensions. 4) Classifier congruency is correlated with noun frequency, shape/semantic class, and Chinese training share; the within-noun congruent/incongruent contrast, nonce-noun variants, no-swing control feature, and frequency matching isolate the congruency pathway, but residual confounds may remain. 5) Difference-in-means classifier directions may entangle shape/semantic or lexical features; we use multiple extraction methods, shape- vs taxonomic-classifier splits, and specificity controls. 6) The ablation could harm legitimate noun-level or monolingual-classifier competence; we require noun-competence and correct-classifier-selection preservation as hard constraints and report the full tradeoff plus the bidirectional injection test. 7) Since LLMs predict classifiers imperfectly (From BERT to LLMs 2025), the classifier signal may be weak; we verify a measurable monolingual congruency effect first as a gate and interpret small cross-lingual swings as informative. 8) Effects may be model-family dependent (Qwen2.5/BLOOM as high-Chinese-exposure contrasts, Llama-3 as English-centric). 9) Instruction-tuned models may suppress the effect; we test base models where available. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: language_conditioned_curse_of_knowledge
Title: A Different Mind in a Different Tongue: Language-Conditioned Reality Leakage in Multilingual False-Belief Reasoning
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs track others' beliefs through a largely shared belief-representation, but the degree to which the true reality-state LEAKS INTO the representation of another agent's (false) belief — a mechanistic 'curse of knowledge' — is LANGUAGE-DEPENDENT: it is stronger when the model reasons in a lower-resource / English-distant language, and, crucially, is REDUCED in languages that grammaticalize evidentiality (obligatory information-source marking, e.g. Turkish, Bulgarian) because the target-language grammar itself flags that the belief-holder's information source differs from reality. Consequently, cross-lingual false-belief inconsistency is driven by a measurable reality-into-belief leakage that tracks language, is mediated by a shared belief-vs-reality direction whose separation is language-modulated, and is causally correctable by amplifying that separation.
Related Work: Interpretability work shows belief status of self/protagonist/oracle is linearly decodable from mid-layer attention heads and causally steerable (Language Models Represent Beliefs of Self and Others 2024; Brittle Minds Fixable Activations 2024; belief 'lookback' mechanism 2025; belief-guided agency 2026), and steering the protagonist-vs-oracle direction improves false-belief accuracy. Human cognitive science documents a 'curse of knowledge' egocentric bias in false-belief reasoning (whether one's own knowledge of reality contaminates attributed belief), that classic false-belief tasks partly measure overcoming this curse (Oldrati 2021; Sandbox-task egocentric-bias studies 2012-2023), and that grammaticalized EVIDENTIALITY co-develops with and may support false-belief reasoning in bilinguals (Romani-Bulgarian evidentiality and ToM 2009), with mixed bilingualism-ToM effects (meta-analysis 2018). BICAUSE (2025) shows LLMs internalize language-specific reasoning biases. CRITICALLY, all LLM belief-representation work is monolingual (English) and treats the belief-vs-reality separation as a fixed quantity; all cross-lingual reasoning work concerns factual consistency or causal word-order, never belief tracking. NO prior work asks whether the reality-into-belief LEAKAGE (the mechanistic curse of knowledge) is LANGUAGE-DEPENDENT, whether it tracks resource-distance and is REDUCED by grammaticalized evidentiality, whether a shared belief-vs-reality direction's separation is language-modulated, or whether amplifying that separation causally equalizes false-belief reasoning across languages. This uniquely ports the human curse-of-knowledge and the evidentiality-ToM link into LLM mechanisms, distinct from monolingual belief-steering work and from my prior proposals (which never touch belief tracking).
Abstract: To reason that someone holds a false belief, you must resist letting your own knowledge of reality contaminate what you attribute to them — a bias cognitive scientists call the curse of knowledge. Interpretability work shows multilingual language models track others' beliefs through linearly decodable, steerable mid-layer representations, but treats the separation between an agent's belief and true reality as a fixed quantity, studied only in English. We ask a simple, previously untested question: is the mechanistic curse of knowledge — how much true reality leaks into the representation of another agent's false belief — language-dependent? We hypothesize that (1) reality-into-belief leakage is larger, and false-belief accuracy lower, when the model reasons in a lower-resource or English-distant language on identical stories; (2) leakage is specifically REDUCED in languages that grammaticalize evidentiality (obligatory information-source marking), because the grammar itself signals that the belief-holder's information source diverges from reality; (3) leakage is mediated by a largely shared belief-vs-reality direction whose separation is language-modulated; and (4) amplifying that separation causally equalizes false-belief reasoning across languages without harming true-belief or reality tracking. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using controlled false-belief stories (Sally-Anne / Sandbox-style, and BigToM) translated across typologically diverse languages including evidential ones (Turkish, Bulgarian). Combining belief probes, a difference-in-means belief-vs-reality direction, activation patching, and steering, we measure leakage, its resource and evidentiality scaling, its mediation, and a causal fix. Metrics include per-language false-belief accuracy, reality-leakage magnitude, evidentiality-and-resource prediction, mediation R-squared, and steering-induced equalization with true-belief controls.
Experiments:
1) Cross-lingual false-belief suite: Build ~600 controlled false-belief stories (Sally-Anne/change-of-location and BigToM forward-belief) plus matched TRUE-BELIEF controls (same story, no reality change) and a REALITY-tracking probe ('where is the object actually?'). Each story asks (i) the belief question ('where does she think it is?') and (ii) the reality question, with verified gold answers. Instantiate every story in typologically diverse languages spanning resource levels, scripts, AND evidentiality typology: non-evidential (English, French, Chinese, Hindi) and grammaticalized-evidential (Turkish, Bulgarian; plus Japanese/Korean indirect-evidence markers). Use natural evidential phrasing where the language marks it. Native-speaker verify; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral leakage map (H1, core): Measure per-language false-belief accuracy and, on errors, the reality-leakage rate = fraction of belief-question errors that answer with the true reality location (the egocentric/curse-of-knowledge error) rather than a random location. Test that false-belief accuracy drops and reality-leakage rises for lower-resource / English-distant languages on identical stories, while TRUE-BELIEF and REALITY-tracking accuracy stay comparable (isolating leakage from general competence). Control for tokenizer fertility and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2). Condition on stories the model tracks reality correctly, so leakage cannot be a reality-comprehension failure.
3) Evidentiality effect (H2, core external prediction): Test whether grammaticalized-evidential languages show LOWER reality-leakage and higher false-belief accuracy than resource-matched non-evidential languages, and whether adding an explicit evidential/indirect-source marker to the belief-forming sentence (within-language manipulation, e.g. Turkish -mIs vs plain, or an added hearsay cue in a non-evidential language) reduces leakage — isolating grammaticalized evidentiality from language identity. Predict evidentiality predicts leakage reduction beyond resource level (model comparison).
4) Mechanistic mediation (H3): Extract a belief-vs-reality direction via difference-in-means between representations of the protagonist's (false) belief location and the true reality location at the belief-decision point, per language (building on the belief-attention-head and lookback findings). Test cross-lingual alignment (largely shared direction), and whether the SEPARATION (protagonist-belief pole distance from the reality pole) is smaller in high-leakage languages. Via logit-lens, track whether the reality answer is promoted at the belief-question position in high-leakage languages. Mediation: regress behavioral leakage on the belief-vs-reality separation (partial correlation controlling for fertility/resource; held-out R^2).
5) Error decomposition via patching (H3b): For false-belief items answered correctly in English/evidential languages but with reality-leakage in a high-leakage language, patch (a) the shared belief-vs-reality representation from the low-leakage pass into the high-leakage pass and (b) only late-layer decoding components. If (a) restores the belief answer, the failure is a leakage/separation failure (the belief mechanism exists but reality contaminates it), not absence. Report leakage-vs-absence error shares per language.
6) Causal steering test (H4, core): Steer along the belief-vs-reality direction to amplify the protagonist-belief pole and separate it from reality (the +TpFo-style intervention) on high-leakage-language items, and measure per-language false-belief-accuracy recovery. Predict SELECTIVE gains for high-leakage (low-resource, non-evidential) languages, little effect on already-low-leakage languages (interaction). Compute recovery elasticity = accuracy gain per unit baseline leakage. Compare against baselines: whole-hub English-steering, an explicit evidential-cue prompt, and a random-direction control. Complement with activation patching from an evidential-language pass.
7) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify the intervention is belief-specific — it must IMPROVE false-belief accuracy WITHOUT degrading TRUE-BELIEF or REALITY-tracking accuracy (symmetric check: it must not make the model ignore reality when reality is the correct answer), must not switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), and preserve fluency. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 shows a sharper cross-lingual leakage gradient than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether the gradient correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the belief-vs-reality direction and each language's training share. Qualitatively compare the per-language leakage pattern against the human curse-of-knowledge and evidentiality-ToM literature.
Evaluation metrics: per-language false-belief accuracy and reality-leakage rate (vs true-belief/reality controls); evidentiality-and-resource prediction of leakage (held-out R^2, model comparison) and within-language evidential-marker manipulation effect; belief-vs-reality direction cross-lingual alignment and separation, with mediation of behavioral leakage (held-out R^2); leakage-vs-absence error shares (patching); selective steering false-belief recovery and elasticity vs baselines, with true-belief/reality preservation (symmetric specificity), off-target rate; cross-model leakage-gradient comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Reality-leakage must be distinguished from general competence; the true-belief and reality-tracking controls, conditioning on reality-correct stories, and the leakage-vs-absence patching are designed to isolate curse-of-knowledge contamination — if leakage gaps vanish once competence is controlled, the hypothesis is refuted, an informative negative result. 2) Evidentiality is confounded with language family, script, and resource level; the within-language evidential-marker manipulation is the key control isolating grammaticalized evidentiality from language identity, but residual confounds may remain, and we report partial correlations. 3) The human evidence for a curse-of-knowledge in adult ToM is itself mixed (several Sandbox-task studies find no egocentric bias), so a null (no language-dependent leakage) is plausible and would be informative about the LLM-human analogy; we frame the comparison as qualitative, not identical-mechanism. 4) The belief-vs-reality direction from difference-in-means may entangle content/language-identity features; we use the established belief-attention-head circuitry as an anchor, multiple extraction methods, and specificity controls. 5) Steering could make the model ignore reality (harming true-belief/reality tracking); the symmetric preservation constraint is a hard requirement and we report the full tradeoff. 6) Logit-lens leakage estimates are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 7) Natural evidential phrasing is subtle; native-speaker verified, low-agreement items excluded. 8) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM/Aya analyzed as less English-centric contrasts). 9) Belief representations are known to be brittle to prompt variation and may be weak in 7-8B models; we verify a measurable English false-belief effect first as a gate. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: halting_confidence_import_multilingual
Title: Done Too Soon in a Foreign Tongue: A Language-Anchored Exit-Confidence Gate Mispredicts the Compute a Language Needs
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs carry an internal exit-confidence signal that estimates whether enough computation has been done to commit to an answer, and this signal is anchored to the dominant (English) language: it fires 'confident/done' at a shallower relative depth in lower-resource / English-distant languages than those languages actually need, so the model effectively under-computes and commits prematurely BECAUSE its self-monitored halting gate mispredicts the required depth. The gate's misprediction (not the raw depth requirement) is a measurable, language-conditioned quantity that predicts a substantial share of cross-lingual errors and is causally correctable by delaying the internal exit signal, without harming English.
Related Work: A large adaptive-computation literature (CALM 2022; LayerSkip 2024; FlexiDepth 2025; Mixture-of-Depths 2024; Duo-LLM 2024; ANIRA 2026; AdaPonderLM 2026; Dynamic Layer Selection 2024) shows per-token compute needs vary and that internal confidence/entropy signals can drive early exit, and that oracle allocation far exceeds learned routers — but all of this is MONOLINGUAL (English) and treats the exit-confidence signal as a fixed capability. Multilingual mechanistic work shows an English-scaffolded shared hub with U-shaped cross-lingual routing alignment (Multilingual Routing in MoE 2025; Understanding Multilingualism in MoE 2026; Semantic Hub 2024) and that latent reasoning is English-centered and weaker for low-resource languages (Large Reasoning Models Are Not Yet Multilingual Latent Reasoners 2026), and that early-exit efficiency methods WIDEN cross-lingual disparities (Efficiency in Multilingual NLP 2025; Multilingual Contrastive Decoding via Language-Agnostic Layers Skipping 2024). My own prior latent_compute_depth_gap proposal posits that the correct answer CRYSTALLIZES at a shallower layer for low-resource languages (a property of the answer representation). This proposal is distinct: the object of study is the model's own SELF-MONITORED HALTING/EXIT-CONFIDENCE gate — the metacognitive signal that decides 'I have computed enough' — and the claim is that this gate is MISCALIBRATED / imported from English, firing 'done' before the language's actual depth requirement is met. No prior work asks whether the exit-confidence signal is language-anchored, whether its misprediction (the gap between where it says 'done' and where the answer is actually available) predicts cross-lingual errors, or whether delaying the internal exit signal selectively recovers accuracy. We reframe the multilingual gap as a self-monitoring halting-calibration failure with a decodable misprediction signature and a targeted fix.
Abstract: Adaptive-computation research shows that language models carry an internal confidence signal telling them when enough computation has been done to commit to an answer — but this has only been studied in English. We ask a simple, previously untested question about multilingual models: is this exit-confidence gate language-anchored, and does it mispredict how much computation a non-English language actually needs? We hypothesize that the gate is scaffolded by English and fires 'confident/done' at a shallower relative depth in lower-resource and English-distant languages than those languages require, so the model under-computes and commits prematurely because its own halting signal is miscalibrated — not because the answer is inherently unavailable. This predicts (1) a language-conditioned misprediction gap between where the exit-confidence signal saturates and the depth at which the correct answer first becomes reliably available; (2) that this misprediction, more than raw depth requirement, predicts cross-lingual errors; and (3) that delaying the internal exit signal (forcing extra layers past the premature 'done') selectively recovers accuracy for high-misprediction languages while barely affecting English. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM across typologically diverse languages using multilingual factual QA (mLAMA) and reasoning (MGSM) plus a controlled k-step suite. Combining early-exit truncation, exit-confidence probes (entropy, LayerSkip-style exit heads, logit-lens saturation), activation patching, and an exit-delay intervention, we measure the misprediction gap, its error prediction, and causal recovery with English-preservation controls.
Experiments:
1) Exit-confidence signal extraction: For each model (Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B), define the internal exit-confidence signal at each layer three ways: (a) logit-lens/tuned-lens top-token probability and entropy (the confidence a CALM-style controller would read), (b) a lightweight LayerSkip-style exit head trained self-supervised to mimic the final output at each layer, (c) the layer at which the top prediction stabilizes. Define the exit-decision layer per item as the shallowest layer where the confidence signal saturates above a calibrated threshold (calibrated on English so the gate is anchored to English by construction, then applied uniformly). Datasets: mLAMA (factual), MGSM (reasoning), and a controlled k-step arithmetic suite (k=1..6, verified gold) translated into 8+ typologically diverse languages spanning scripts/resource levels (English, French, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish, Bengali). Native-speaker verify.
2) Misprediction gap (H1, core): Using early-exit truncation, measure the answer-availability layer = the shallowest layer at which forcing exit yields the correct answer. Define the exit-confidence MISPREDICTION = (answer-availability layer) minus (exit-decision layer): positive means the gate said 'done' before the answer was actually available (premature halting). Test that misprediction is larger for lower-resource / English-distant languages, and that it is a GATE property (the confidence signal saturates early) not merely a depth property. Control for tokenizer fertility and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2). Verify near-zero misprediction for English (the anchor).
3) Misprediction predicts errors (H2): Test whether per-item misprediction predicts whether the model errs at its natural (full-depth) output, and whether it predicts errors better than the raw answer-availability depth alone (nested regression, held-out R^2). Decompose errors into 'premature-halt' errors (correct answer becomes available at a deeper layer than the exit-decision layer, i.e. recoverable by more compute) vs genuine-absence errors (answer never becomes available), via activation patching: patch the deeper-layer answer representation into the premature-exit forward pass and check if it fixes the answer. Report premature-halt vs absence error shares per language, predicting premature-halt errors dominate the low-resource gap.
4) Language-anchoring of the gate (mechanism): Extract a difference-in-means 'exit-confidence' direction (confident/done vs still-computing forward passes) and test cross-lingual alignment (a single shared, English-scaffolded gate re-thresholded per language) and whether the query language is decodable from an early signal that predicts the exit-decision layer. Correlate the misprediction with the cross-lingual routing/hub-alignment measures from prior MoE work where a MoE model is available.
5) Core causal intervention (exit delay): Force extra computation past the premature 'done' — disable early exit and run to a deeper layer (or repeat middle blocks) selectively when the exit-confidence gate fires early — and measure per-language accuracy recovery. Predict SELECTIVE recovery: high-misprediction (low-resource) languages gain most; English and low-misprediction languages gain little (interaction test). Compute recovery elasticity = accuracy gain per unit misprediction, correlated with the H2 misprediction. Compare against baselines: uniform extra compute for all languages, English shared-space steering (Language-Specific Latent Process 2025), and layer-skip contrastive decoding (SkipLayerCD 2024).
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify gains are gap-closing (not uniform lift), do not switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), do not harm English or low-misprediction languages, and are compute-specific (extra depth on genuine-absence items does nothing). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show larger misprediction gaps than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether misprediction correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the exit-confidence direction and each language's training share.
Evaluation metrics: per-language exit-confidence misprediction gap (partial correlation with resource/distance over fertility; held-out R^2); misprediction's error-prediction R^2 vs raw-depth baseline; premature-halt vs genuine-absence error shares and patching-fix rate; exit-confidence-direction cross-lingual alignment and early language-decodability; selective exit-delay accuracy recovery and elasticity vs baselines, with English/low-misprediction preservation and compute-specificity (symmetric controls), off-target rate; cross-model misprediction comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The misprediction gap conflates a gate (confidence) property with a depth (answer-availability) property; the premature-halt-vs-absence decomposition and the exit-delay causal test (which recovers a recoverable answer) are designed to isolate a halting-calibration failure from genuine incompetence — if delaying exit does not selectively help, the hypothesis reduces to a competence gap, an informative negative result. 2) The English-calibrated exit threshold builds in the English anchor by construction; we also report a per-language self-calibrated threshold as a contrast to show the gate is English-anchored in the model's OWN internal signal (entropy saturates early in low-resource languages regardless of external threshold), not just via our calibration choice. 3) Logit-lens/exit-head confidence and truncation-based answer-availability are approximate at intermediate layers; we use three confidence measures and cross-validate, reporting robustness. 4) Language is confounded with tokenizer fertility, script, and resource level; partial correlations and the controlled k-step suite (depth-controlled) mitigate but may not fully remove confounds. 5) The exit-delay intervention could help via generic extra compute rather than fixing a halting error; the selectivity/interaction prediction (gains concentrated in high-misprediction languages) and the compute-specificity control distinguish these. 6) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM/Aya analyzed as less English-centric contrasts). 7) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale. 8) Extra depth may not yield wall-clock savings, but the claim here is mechanistic (halting miscalibration), not an efficiency method.

Name: language_switch_strategy_gating
Title: Switching Tongues, Switching Tactics: Mid-Chain Language Mixing Gates Which Reasoning Strategy a Step Uses in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: When a reasoning model spontaneously switches the SURFACE language of a chain-of-thought step (language mixing), it is not merely expressing a script preference: the switch causally gates WHICH reasoning STRATEGY the model deploys for that step (e.g., algebraic-symbolic vs arithmetic-verbal decomposition, exact vs estimative, decompositional vs holistic). Consequently, the same sub-problem is solved by different algorithms depending only on the language the step is written in, so a step written in the dominant pivot language (English/Chinese) systematically recruits a different, often more procedural strategy than the same step written in the prompt language—and this strategy-gating, not translation quality, drives a measurable share of when language mixing helps versus hurts.
Related Work: Prior work shows language mixing in reasoning models reflects latent script preferences and can help or hurt accuracy (Language Mixing in Reasoning 2025; Impact of Language Mixing on Bilingual LLM Reasoning 2025, which trains a probe to predict whether a switch helps), that CoT attribution over-weights the final step (What Really Counts 2025), that reasoning routes through an English-centric latent space (Do Multilingual LLMs Think In English 2025; Latent Reasoners 2026), and that cross-lingual self-consistency ensembling of MONOLINGUAL chains helps (CLC 2025; CALM 2025; USC 2023). All prior work treats a language switch as either a script-preference artifact or an aggregate accuracy signal, and treats reasoning strategy as fixed across the switch. NONE asks whether the surface language of a step CHANGES the reasoning STRATEGY/algorithm deployed in that step—whether the model solves the same sub-problem differently (algebraic vs arithmetic, exact vs estimative) depending only on the step's language—nor localizes/steers a strategy-gating mechanism triggered by the language switch. The Impact-of-Language-Mixing probe predicts helpfulness but does not identify strategy-gating as the mechanism. We reframe language mixing from a script artifact into a strategy-selection switch, with a behavioral strategy-taxonomy signature and a causal steering test.
Abstract: Reasoning models often switch languages mid-thought, and prior work debates whether this helps or hurts accuracy, attributing it to internal script preferences. We propose a sharper, previously untested account: a mid-chain language switch causally gates WHICH reasoning strategy the model applies to that step. Under this account, the same sub-problem is solved by a different algorithm—algebraic-symbolic versus arithmetic-verbal, exact versus estimative, decompositional versus holistic—depending only on the language the step is written in, so the pivot language (English/Chinese) recruits a systematically different, often more procedural strategy than the prompt language. This strategy-gating, not translation quality, would explain a substantial share of when language mixing helps or hurts. We test this on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1-distilled Qwen/Llama, Qwen-reasoning) across typologically diverse languages using MGSM and a controlled multi-strategy suite where each sub-problem admits multiple valid strategies. We build a validated strategy classifier for reasoning steps, measure whether a step's language predicts its strategy beyond content, use a controlled language-forcing intervention (force a target step into a chosen language) to test whether the switch CAUSES the strategy change, and localize a strategy-gating direction set by the language signal. We further test whether steering strategy independently of language recovers the accuracy benefit of a beneficial switch without switching language. Metrics include language-vs-strategy association, forced-language strategy-flip rate, strategy-mediated accuracy share, and steering-induced recovery with specificity controls.
Experiments:
1) Multi-strategy reasoning suite and strategy taxonomy: Use MGSM and construct a controlled suite of ~500 sub-problems each solvable by MULTIPLE valid strategies (e.g., a proportion problem via algebraic setup vs step-by-step arithmetic; a comparison via exact computation vs estimation; a multi-hop via forward decomposition vs backward). Define a strategy taxonomy (algebraic-symbolic, arithmetic-verbal, estimative, decompositional, holistic-shortcut). Build and validate an automatic step-level strategy classifier (rule-based cues + a learned classifier) against human annotation on a held-out subset; report reliability and inter-annotator agreement. Instantiate prompts across typologically diverse languages spanning scripts (English, French, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish). Models: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, a Qwen-reasoning variant. Release the suite.
2) Language-vs-strategy association (H1, core): In naturally-generated chains, segment steps, label each step's SURFACE language (script/lexical detection) and its STRATEGY (classifier). Test whether a step's language predicts its strategy AFTER controlling for step content/sub-problem type (mixed-effects model: strategy ~ step-language + sub-problem-type + input-language + (1|problem)); report the step-language effect size and held-out predictive gain over a content-only baseline. Prediction: pivot-language (English/Chinese) steps disproportionately use algebraic/procedural strategies; prompt-language steps disproportionately use arithmetic-verbal strategies. Control for tokenizer fertility and resource level.
3) Causal language-forcing test (H2, core): Using constrained decoding / prefix-forcing, FORCE a targeted reasoning step to be generated in a chosen language (pivot vs prompt language) while holding the preceding chain and the sub-problem fixed, and measure whether the strategy the model uses for that step FLIPS to the language-congruent strategy (forced-language strategy-flip rate). This isolates the switch as the CAUSE of the strategy change, not a correlate. Compare against a within-language paraphrase-forcing control (same language, reworded) to rule out generic perturbation effects.
4) Strategy-mediated accuracy (H3): Test whether the accuracy impact of a language switch is MEDIATED by the strategy it induces: decompose the switch's effect on step correctness into a strategy-change path (the switch changed the strategy, which changed correctness) vs a residual path (mediation analysis). Predict that beneficial switches largely act by recruiting a better-suited strategy for that sub-problem type (e.g., algebraic for proportion problems), and harmful switches by recruiting a mismatched strategy. Report the strategy-mediated share of the switch's accuracy effect.
5) Mechanistic localization and steering (H4): Extract a difference-in-means 'strategy-gating' direction (steps that used strategy A vs B) and a language-signal direction; test whether the language signal at the step boundary predicts strategy engagement (logit-lens, held-out R^2) and whether the two directions are partially aligned. Core steering test: steer the STRATEGY direction toward the beneficial strategy at the step boundary WITHOUT switching the surface language, and measure whether this recovers the accuracy benefit of a beneficial language switch—demonstrating that strategy, not language per se, is the operative variable. Compare against forcing the language switch (Impact-of-Language-Mixing-style) and a random-direction control.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify strategy-steering is strategy-specific (changes the algorithm used but not the sub-problem or answer target), does not switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), and preserves fluency; verify forced-language flips are not merely lexical relabeling by checking the actual computation structure changes. Cross-model contrast: predict more English-centric distilled models show stronger language->strategy gating than more multilingual models; test whether gating strength correlates with the model's English-centricity and each language's training share.
Evaluation metrics: language->strategy association effect size and held-out gain over content-only baseline; forced-language strategy-flip rate (vs paraphrase-forcing control); strategy-mediated share of switch accuracy effect; strategy-gating-direction predictiveness and language-alignment; strategy-steering accuracy recovery vs language-switch-forcing and random baselines, with strategy-specificity, off-target rate, and answer-target preservation; cross-model gating comparison and correlation with English-centricity/training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Automatically classifying a reasoning step's strategy is hard and can conflate surface phrasing with algorithm; we build a validated classifier against human labels, use structural (computation-graph) features not just lexical cues, report reliability, and exclude ambiguous steps. 2) Language and strategy are correlated with content (some sub-problems naturally invite algebra); the mixed-effects control for sub-problem type, the WITHIN-problem forced-language test (holding content fixed), and the paraphrase-forcing control isolate the language->strategy effect—if the association vanishes once content is controlled, the hypothesis is refuted, an informative negative result. 3) Forced-language decoding may produce degenerate or unnatural steps; we validate that forced steps are fluent and on-task, and discard degenerate generations. 4) Segmenting chains into steps and detecting per-step language is noisy (especially for mixed steps); we use multiple segmentation methods and report robustness. 5) The mediation analysis assumes the strategy classifier and correctness labels are reliable; we report sensitivity to classifier error. 6) Strategy-steering could harm fluency or change the answer target; strategy-specificity and answer-target preservation are hard constraints and we report the full tradeoff. 7) Logit-lens strategy/language signal decoding is approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with truncation. 8) Effects may be model-family dependent and limited to open ~7-8B reasoning models; may not extend to frontier scale. 9) If language switches do NOT change strategy (only surface form), this is an informative negative result showing language mixing is a script-preference artifact rather than a strategy-selection mechanism—sharpening the debate either way.

Name: aspectual_coercion_operator_transfer
Title: Sending a Check for Years: Does the Aspectual-Coercion Operator Transfer Cross-Lingually While Its Triggering Is Language-Specific?
Short Hypothesis: Aspectual coercion — the online reinterpretation that resolves a mismatch between a verb's lexical aspect and an aspectual modifier (e.g. 'send a check for years' forced into an iterative reading) — is implemented in multilingual LLMs as a largely LANGUAGE-AGNOSTIC 'coercion operator' (an iterative/inceptive event re-typing) carried in the shared hub, but WHEN a mismatch triggers coercion (versus being tolerated or blocked) is LANGUAGE-SPECIFIC and calibrated to the dominant (English) language. Consequently the operator transfers across languages (a coercion direction extracted in one language re-types an event in another), whereas cross-lingual coercion errors concentrate in a triggering-calibration failure: the model imposes an English-like coercion-trigger threshold onto languages whose aspectual grammar licenses coercion differently, mis-triggering (or failing to trigger) iterative/inceptive re-typing at rates that track the language's aspectual typology and mirror the human L1-influenced coercion asymmetry.
Related Work: A rich psycholinguistic literature establishes aspectual coercion as an online, effortful event re-typing triggered by a lexical-aspect/modifier mismatch (Aspectual Coercion and Online Computation of Sentential Aspect 2000; Cognitive Signatures of Aspectual Coercion 2023; Motion Verbs: Coercion or Underspecification 2016), that coercion vs underspecification is experimentally separable, that it is modulated by L1 in non-native speakers with divergent, L1-specific signatures (Aspectual Coercion in Non-native Speakers of English 2013: Korean/German/Chinese differ), and that construal of the same event differs across languages (Spanish/Russian 'from without vs within' 2019; Russian/Czech habituality 2022). Interpretability shows aspect/telicity/boundedness are encoded as orthogonal, causally steerable directions (About Time 2022; Probing Verbal Aspect 2024; Steering Tense and Aspect 2025), and morphosyntactic aspect is shared cross-lingually and largely English-scaffolded with causal multilingual features (LLMs Share Latent Grammatical Concepts 2025; Same Neurons Different Languages 2022). CRITICALLY, all interpretability work concerns STATIC aspect ENCODING (is the verb perfective/telic?), never the DYNAMIC COERCION OPERATION that re-types an event on a mismatch; all coercion work is human-only and never asks whether an LLM performs coercion, whether the coercion operator dissociates from its triggering, or whether the model imposes a dominant-language coercion-trigger threshold cross-lingually. This differs from my prior telicity_imposition and perfective_result_state proposals (static category imposition/construal) by targeting a distinct dynamic RE-TYPING operation with a triggering-vs-operator dissociation, grounded in an authoritative psycholinguistic phenomenon with an external L1-effect ground truth.
Abstract: When a verb's built-in aspect clashes with a modifier — 'Howard sent a check to his daughter for years' — comprehenders do not reject the sentence; they silently re-type the single event into a repeated (iterative) one, an effortful operation psycholinguists call aspectual coercion. We ask two previously untested questions about multilingual language models: do they perform aspectual coercion at all, and if so, is the coercion OPERATION separable from its TRIGGERING across languages? We hypothesize that (1) LLMs implement a largely language-agnostic coercion operator (iterative/inceptive event re-typing) in the shared hub, so a coercion signal extracted in one language re-types an event in another; but (2) WHEN a mismatch triggers coercion is language-specific and calibrated to English, so the model imposes an English-like coercion-trigger threshold onto languages whose aspectual grammar licenses coercion differently, mis-triggering iterative/inceptive re-typing at rates that track each language's aspectual typology and mirror the human L1-influenced coercion asymmetry; and (3) cross-lingual coercion errors concentrate in triggering, not operator, and are causally correctable by adjusting the trigger without changing the operator. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using controlled coercion minimal pairs (mismatch, matched-iterative-lexicalization, and aspectually-neutral controls) across languages with divergent aspect systems (English, German, Russian, Chinese, Korean, Spanish). Combining behavioral coercion-detection probes, difference-in-means coercion-operator direction extraction, logit-lens tracking, activation patching (operator-vs-trigger decomposition), and cross-lingual operator transplant, we measure whether coercion happens, whether the operator transfers, whether triggering is English-imposed, and whether a trigger-only fix corrects it. Metrics include coercion-detection accuracy, operator cross-lingual transplant success, English-trigger imposition gap, typology-prediction correlation, operator-vs-trigger error shares, and trigger-adjustment recovery with comprehension controls.
Experiments:
1) Coercion minimal-pair suite: Construct ~500 items instantiating aspectual coercion (following the classic paradigm), each in a matched set: (a) COERCION — a telic/punctual predicate + a durative/iterative modifier forcing re-typing ('send a check for years' -> iterative); (b) MATCHED-LEXICALIZATION — the same iterative meaning achieved without coercion ('send checks for years'); (c) NEUTRAL-MODIFIER control ('send a check last year', no coercion); (d) NON-COERCIBLE control (a mismatch the grammar blocks, testing constraints on coercion, cf. ALS/formal-semantics work). Instantiate across languages with divergent aspect systems and coercion licensing: English, German, Russian, Chinese, Korean, Spanish, native-speaker verified with gold interpretations (does the sentence describe a single or repeated/ongoing event?) and coercion-licensing labels. Probes: (i) event-count/iterativity forced choice ('one event or repeated events?'); (ii) coercion-NLI (does the sentence entail a repeated/ongoing reading?); (iii) a short reasoning item whose answer depends on the coerced reading. Report inter-annotator agreement; release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Does the model coerce at all (H1)? On COERCION items, measure whether the model arrives at the iterative/re-typed interpretation (matching the coerced gold) rather than a literal single-event reading, per language, benchmarked against MATCHED-LEXICALIZATION (where the iterative meaning is overt, an easier ceiling) and NEUTRAL controls. Establish that coercion occurs (above the literal baseline) at least in English before testing cross-lingual structure. Control for tokenizer fertility and verb/modifier frequency (partial correlations).
3) Coercion-operator extraction and transfer (H2a, core): Extract a difference-in-means 'coercion-operator' direction between coerced (re-typed iterative) and non-coerced (literal single-event) representations at each layer, per language, and measure cross-lingual cosine alignment (shared operator?). Transplant test: extract the operator in language A and ADD it (steering) into a language-B forward pass on a non-coerced single-event sentence; measure whether it induces the iterative/re-typed reading (transplant flip rate). Prediction: high cross-lingual transfer — the coercion operator is portable. Compare against a content-swap baseline direction.
4) Triggering is English-imposed (H2b, core): Measure per-language coercion-TRIGGER rate = how readily a given mismatch triggers coercion, and test whether it tracks the ENGLISH trigger threshold rather than the target-language grammar (over-triggering where the target language would tolerate/block the mismatch, under-triggering where it would coerce). Define the English-trigger imposition GAP = deviation of the model's per-language trigger rate from native-speaker coercion-licensing norms, signed toward the English pattern. Test whether per-language imposition is predicted by each language's aspectual typology / coercion-licensing (Spearman; held-out prediction), tying it to independent linguistic ground truth, and qualitatively compare against the human L1-influenced coercion asymmetry (Korean/German/Chinese pattern).
5) Operator-vs-trigger error decomposition via patching: For COERCION items correct in English but wrong in language B, patch (a) the shared coercion-OPERATOR representation from the English pass into B, and (b) only the mismatch-detection/TRIGGER components. Classify as operator failure (fixed by (a) — the re-typing itself failed) vs triggering failure (operator present/portable but not engaged; fixed by (b)). Report operator-vs-trigger error shares per language, predicting triggering failures dominate and grow with typological distance from English.
6) Causal trigger-adjustment intervention (H3): At the mismatch/trigger step, adjust the coercion-trigger signal toward the target-language licensing (raise it where the language coerces, lower it where it tolerates/blocks) WITHOUT altering the operator direction, and measure whether coercion behavior shifts to the native-speaker pattern (imposition-GAP reduction). Critically verify COMPREHENSION preservation: NEUTRAL and NON-COERCIBLE controls must remain correctly interpreted (no spurious coercion where the grammar blocks it — a symmetric check), plus fluency and off-target/language-mixing checks. Compare against whole-hub English-steering and a random-direction control.
7) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify the intervention is trigger-specific (changes when coercion fires, not the identity of the event/participants), graded (imposition scales with typological distance), and not a frequency artifact (nonce-verb variants). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show stronger trigger imposition than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether imposition magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the operator vs trigger signals and with each language's training share.
Evaluation metrics: coercion-detection accuracy per language (COERCION vs MATCHED-LEXICALIZATION vs NEUTRAL); coercion-operator cross-lingual alignment and transplant flip rate; English-trigger imposition GAP and its prediction from aspectual typology (held-out); operator-vs-trigger error shares (patching); trigger-adjustment imposition-GAP reduction with NEUTRAL/NON-COERCIBLE preservation (symmetric specificity), fluency, off-target rate; cross-model imposition comparison and correlation with training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for typology over frequency/fertility baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Coercion vs underspecification is genuinely hard to separate (Motion Verbs 2016) — some 'coercion' may be lexical underspecification; we use the classic contrasts (durative vs iterative vs neutral modifiers), the MATCHED-LEXICALIZATION and NON-COERCIBLE controls, and native-speaker-verified gold to isolate genuine re-typing, and report ambiguous items. 2) Whether a mismatch licenses coercion is gradient and language-specific; we native-speaker verify coercion-licensing, use graded scores, report inter-annotator agreement, and exclude low-agreement items. 3) Operator vs trigger may not cleanly separate; patching can have entangled effects — we use multiple granularities, the transplant test (which directly probes operator portability), and report ambiguous cases; if the operator does NOT transfer cross-lingually, the dissociation hypothesis is refuted, an informative result relocating coercion as language-specific. 4) Coercion is subtle and 7-8B models may barely perform it; Experiment 2 is a necessary gate — if the model does not coerce even in English, the cross-lingual questions are moot, but that is itself an informative finding about the limits of LLM aspectual reasoning. 5) Aspectual typology is confounded with language family, script, and resource level; the NEUTRAL/NON-COERCIBLE controls, typology-based prediction, and partial correlations isolate the coercion pathway, but residual confounds may remain; we center core claims on well-resourced English/German/Russian/Chinese/Spanish and treat Korean as an extension. 6) Difference-in-means operator directions may entangle iterativity/plurality or lexical features; we use nonce-verb variants, multiple extraction methods, and specificity controls. 7) The trigger-adjustment intervention could induce spurious coercion where blocked (harming NON-COERCIBLE items); the symmetric constraint-preservation check is a hard requirement and we report the full tradeoff. 8) Logit-lens/tuned-lens estimates are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 9) The model-vs-human comparison (L1-influenced coercion asymmetry) is qualitative/structural, not a claim of identical mechanism. 10) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM analyzed as a less English-centric contrast). 11) If the operator transfers AND triggering is already native-appropriate (no English imposition), this is an informative POSITIVE result showing language-faithful coercion despite English scaffolding, valuable either way. 12) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: implicit_prosody_phrasing_imposition
Title: Reading With an English Inner Voice: Does the Shared Hub Impose a Dominant-Language Implicit Prosodic Phrasing Onto Silent Reading in Other Languages?
Short Hypothesis: Human silent reading assigns a default 'implicit prosodic phrasing' that guides syntactic parsing, and this default phrasing DIFFERS across languages (e.g. relative-clause attachment: English prefers low/N2 attachment, Spanish/Croatian/Japanese prefer high/N1), a difference driven by language-specific prosodic phrasing. We hypothesize that a text-only multilingual LLM implicitly represents prosodic phrase boundaries and uses them for parsing, but because this representation is scaffolded by English, the model IMPOSES an English-like default phrasing onto other languages: on the SAME globally-ambiguous sentence it resolves the attachment toward the English preference rather than the target-language one, tracking the English implicit-prosody default. This imposition is mediated by a shared, steerable phrase-boundary direction, tracks each language's empirical attachment preference, and is causally correctable without harming unambiguous parsing.
Related Work: A large psycholinguistic literature establishes the Implicit Prosody Hypothesis: silent readers assign a default prosodic phrasing that causally guides parsing, and this default DIFFERS cross-linguistically — relative-clause attachment preferences vary (English low/N2 vs Spanish/Croatian high/N1; Fodor 'Psycholinguistics cannot escape prosody' 2002; Croatian RC-attachment 2003; punctuation-ERP garden-paths 2016; Japanese lexical-accent phrasing 2024; Croatian-English eye-tracking corpus 2025), and prosodic phrasing/intonation units are a near-universal chunking mechanism (48-language IU study 2025; IU neural response 2023). On the model side, BERT captures prosodic PROMINENCE in middle layers from syntactic/semantic cues (What does BERT learn about prosody 2023), speech SSL models encode suprasegmentals language-specifically (Mandarin/English 2024), and psycholinguistic behavior is conditioned on prompt language identity (From Monolingual to Bilingual 2025). Foundational work establishes an English-scaffolded shared hub (Semantic Hub 2024; Do Llamas Work in English 2024). CRITICALLY, all BERT-prosody work is monolingual and about prominence (not phrase-boundary-driven parsing), all IPH work is human-only, and NO work asks whether a text-only multilingual LLM (a) implicitly represents prosodic PHRASE BOUNDARIES and uses them for silent-reading parsing, (b) IMPOSES an English-scaffolded default phrasing onto other languages causing cross-lingual attachment inconsistency, (c) has this predicted by each language's empirical attachment/phrasing preference, or (d) can be causally corrected. This differs from my prior information-structure, punctuation-prosody, and metrical-stress proposals: those target topic/comment packaging, punctuation weighting, and word-level stress respectively; this targets phrase-boundary-driven IMPLICIT PROSODIC PHRASING and its causal role in ambiguity resolution, grounded in the IPH and RC-attachment cross-linguistic ground truth.
Abstract: When you read silently, you hear an inner voice that chunks the sentence into prosodic phrases, and decades of psycholinguistics show this implicit phrasing steers how you resolve syntactic ambiguity — crucially, the default phrasing differs by language, so English readers attach a relative clause low ('the servant of the actress who...' -> the actress) while Spanish and Croatian readers attach it high (-> the servant). Multilingual language models build a shared, English-scaffolded representation. We ask a simple, previously untested question: does a text-only multilingual LLM read other languages with an English inner voice — imposing an English-like default prosodic phrasing that pulls its ambiguity resolution toward the English preference rather than the target language's? We hypothesize that (1) on identical globally-ambiguous sentences, the model resolves attachment toward the English preference, producing cross-lingual parsing inconsistency concentrated where languages' preferences diverge; (2) the size of this imposition tracks each language's empirical attachment/phrasing preference; (3) the model implicitly represents prosodic phrase boundaries, and a shared, steerable phrase-boundary direction — scaffolded by English — mediates the imposition; and (4) steering toward the target-language phrasing restores native-like parsing without harming unambiguous parsing. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using controlled ambiguity suites (RC-attachment and other phrasing-sensitive ambiguities) across languages with divergent attachment preferences (English, Spanish, Croatian, Japanese, German, Dutch). Combining behavioral attachment measurement, difference-in-means phrase-boundary probes, logit-lens tracking, activation patching, and steering, we measure the imposition, its preference scaling, its mediation, and its causal correction. Metrics include cross-lingual attachment-imposition gap, preference-prediction correlation, mediation R-squared, and steering-induced restoration with unambiguous-parsing controls.
Experiments: 1) Cross-lingual ambiguity suite grounded in the IPH literature: Construct ~500 globally-ambiguous sentences whose resolution is known to depend on implicit prosodic phrasing, primarily the classic relative-clause attachment construction ('someone shot the servant of the actress who was on the balcony') plus additional phrasing-sensitive ambiguities (coordination scope, PP-attachment, early/late closure). Instantiate each across languages with DIVERGENT empirical attachment preferences (English/Dutch = low/N2; Spanish/Croatian/Japanese/German = high/N1), native-speaker verified, with a disambiguating continuation for each reading. Include UNAMBIGUOUS control sentences (only one attachment grammatical) and, where a language marks it, a comma/prosodic-boundary variant (as in the ERP garden-path paradigm) to verify the model uses phrase-boundary cues. Attach each language its empirical human attachment preference (proportion high vs low) from the psycholinguistic literature. Report inter-annotator agreement; release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B. 2) Behavioral attachment imposition (H1, core): For each ambiguous sentence in each language, measure the model's preferred attachment (via a forced-choice 'who was on the balcony?' probe, an attachment-NLI probe, and log-prob of disambiguating continuations). Define the cross-lingual attachment-imposition GAP = fraction of DIVERGENT items where the model resolves toward the ENGLISH preference rather than the target-language one, and compare to CONVERGENT items (languages agree). Verify correct resolution on UNAMBIGUOUS controls (isolating imposition from parsing incompetence). Control for tokenizer fertility, sentence frequency, and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test target-language status adds predictive power). 3) Preference scaling (H2, external validation): Test whether per-language imposition is predicted by the divergence of that language's empirical human attachment preference from English (Spearman; held-out prediction from human preference norms alone), tying the internal phenomenon to independent psycholinguistic ground truth. 4) Does the model represent phrase boundaries, and are they English-scaffolded (H3)? First, probe whether prosodic phrase-boundary position (where an intonation-unit boundary would fall) is decodable from internal states above chance, per language and layer (establishing the mechanism exists in a text-only model, mirroring the BERT-prominence finding). Then extract a phrase-boundary direction via difference-in-means between boundary-before-RC vs boundary-after-N2 phrasings (using comma/prosodic-boundary minimal pairs) at each layer, per language. Test (a) cross-lingual alignment of the phrase-boundary direction and whether it is aligned with the English default phrasing in mid/shared-hub layers; (b) whether a DIVERGENT target-language ambiguous sentence engages the English-default boundary in the shared hub via logit-lens tracking at the attachment-decision position. Mediation: regress behavioral imposition on shared-hub English-boundary engagement (partial correlation controlling for fertility/frequency; held-out R^2). Baseline: a lexical-content direction as a within-model control. 5) Causal steering/patching test (H4, core): (a) Steer the target-language ambiguous sentence along the phrase-boundary direction toward the target-language default phrasing and measure whether attachment judgments shift to the target-language pattern (flip rate) and the imposition GAP shrinks toward the CONVERGENT baseline, without switching output language; (b) conversely steer toward the English default and confirm dose-response (bidirectional); (c) for imposed items, patch the residual language-specific phrasing signal (from early/language-specific layers) into later computation and test restoration, localizing failure to the shared hub imposing an English inner voice. Critically verify UNAMBIGUOUS-PARSING preservation (unambiguous controls must remain correctly parsed — no spurious mis-attachment) plus fluency and off-target/language-mixing checks. Baselines: whole-hub English-steering, comma-insertion prompt (a strong practical baseline), random-direction control. 6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify steering is phrasing-specific (changes attachment but not lexical content or unrelated meaning), graded (imposition scales with preference divergence), and not merely a comma/tokenization artifact (test with and without punctuation). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show stronger imposition than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether imposition magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the phrase-boundary direction and each language's training share. Qualitatively compare the per-language imposition pattern against the human RC-attachment literature (direction, not identical mechanism). Evaluation metrics: cross-lingual attachment-imposition GAP and English-preference-tracking rate (DIVERGENT vs CONVERGENT; vs unambiguous controls); imposition-vs-human-preference-divergence correlation and held-out prediction; phrase-boundary decodability (probe accuracy above chance, per layer/language); phrase-boundary-direction cross-lingual alignment and shared-hub English-boundary engagement, with mediation of behavioral imposition (held-out R^2); steering flip rate and GAP reduction (bidirectional dose-response), patching-induced restoration; unambiguous-parsing preservation, fluency, off-target rate; cross-model imposition comparison and correlation with training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for target-language status over fertility/frequency/resource baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) A text-only LLM has no acoustic input, so any 'implicit prosody' is a distributional reconstruction from text (punctuation, phrase-length statistics); Experiment 4's phrase-boundary decodability check is a necessary gate — if boundaries are not decodable above chance, the mechanistic phrasing claim weakens, but the behavioral attachment-imposition and its human-preference prediction remain valuable, and a null is itself informative about the limits of the LLM-human implicit-prosody analogy. 2) Attachment preference is confounded with language family, script, and resource level; the CONVERGENT controls, unambiguous controls, within-item disambiguation contrasts, and human-preference prediction isolate the imposition pathway, but residual confounds may remain; we center core claims on well-studied RC-attachment languages (English/Spanish/Croatian/German/Dutch/Japanese). 3) RC-attachment preferences in humans are themselves gradient and modulated by RC length and lexical factors; we control RC length, use multiple ambiguity types, native-speaker verify, and treat preferences as noisy predictors, relying on internal representation and causal tests for core claims. 4) Some imposition may reflect genuinely correct behavior (the model rightly using the target-language preference); the direction of the effect (tracks ENGLISH vs TARGET preference), the human-preference prediction, and the causal steering (which restores the target parse by editing only the phrase-boundary direction) distinguish imposition from faithful parsing, and a faithful-parsing finding is itself valuable and would extend the shared-hub account. 5) Difference-in-means phrase-boundary directions may entangle punctuation, length, or lexical features; we use comma/no-comma minimal pairs, a lexical-content control direction, length control, and multiple extraction methods. 6) Attachment is a global sentence property, making token-level logit-lens localization approximate; we aggregate over the attachment-decision region and report robustness. 7) Steering could harm unambiguous parsing or fluency; unambiguous-parsing preservation is a hard specificity constraint and we report the full tradeoff plus bidirectional dose-response, comparing against the comma-insertion baseline to show the mechanistic account adds value. 8) Instruction-tuned models may normalize parsing; we test base models where available and interpret small effects as informative. 9) The model-vs-human comparison (RC-attachment preferences) is qualitative/structural, not a claim of identical mechanism. 10) If NO imposition is found — attachment tracks each language's own preference, predictable from human norms, with unambiguous parsing preserved — this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the shared hub applies language-specific implicit prosodic phrasing despite English scaffolding, valuable either way. 11) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: typicality_prototype_imposition
Title: Every Culture's Typical Bird: Does the English-Scaffolded Shared Hub Impose a Dominant-Culture Prototype Onto Graded Category Membership in Other Languages?
Short Hypothesis: Category membership is graded and its typicality structure is culture-specific: the most typical 'bird', 'vegetable', 'breakfast food', or 'vehicle' differs sharply across cultures (a robin vs a hornbill; a carrot vs a cassava). Because multilingual LLMs represent concepts on a single, largely English-scaffolded prototype geometry, we hypothesize the model IMPOSES the dominant (English/Western) prototype when judging typicality in other languages: its graded typicality ratings, best-example choices, and category-based inferences for a culturally-loaded category track the English prototype rather than the target-culture one, producing cross-lingual typicality inconsistency on the SAME items. This imposition is mediated by a shared prototype direction, tracks each culture's empirical typicality norms, and is causally correctable per language without harming crisp (non-graded) category boundaries.
Related Work: Prior work shows LLMs align with human category BOUNDARIES but weakly with fine-grained TYPICALITY, aggressively compressing away graded structure (From Tokens to Thoughts 2025; Typicality Effect in DL Models 2024; Conceptual Structure Coheres in Humans not LLMs 2023), that property inheritance is jointly driven by taxonomy AND graded similarity with entangled subspaces (Property Induction 2022; Characterizing Similarity in Property Inferences 2024), that categorization varies cross-linguistically (Categorization in the Wild 2019/2021; Italian subordinate categories 2025; crosslinguistic color category shift 2018), and that concepts are linearly alignable across languages on a shared, English-scaffolded geometry (Concept Space Alignment 2024; Structural Concepts Universal 2023; Semantic Hub 2024). Threshold-model theory ties typicality to graded membership (Kamp & Partee; Typicality Graded Membership Vagueness 2007). CRITICALLY, all LLM typicality work is monolingual/English and asks whether models match human typicality in general; all cross-lingual concept work concerns boundaries/alignment, not graded typicality; and no work asks whether the shared, English-scaffolded prototype geometry IMPOSES the dominant-culture prototype onto graded typicality judgments in other languages, causing cross-lingual typicality inconsistency, localizes a shared prototype direction mediating it, ties it to cross-cultural typicality norms as ground truth, or offers a causal per-language fix. This is a high-level phenomenon (graded prototype structure) distinct from all my prior grammatical/lexical imposition proposals, which target discrete morphosyntactic or lexical categories rather than graded, culturally-loaded category prototypes.
Abstract: Which bird is the most typical bird? Which food is a typical breakfast? People answer these graded-membership questions differently across cultures: the prototype at the center of a category is culturally loaded. Multilingual language models represent concepts on a single, largely English-scaffolded geometry. We ask a simple, previously untested question: when a model judges how typical an example is of a category in a non-English language, does it impose the dominant (English/Western) prototype rather than the target culture's? We hypothesize that (1) the model's graded typicality ratings, best-example selections, and category-based inferences for culturally-loaded categories track the English prototype, producing cross-lingual typicality inconsistency on identical items concentrated where cultural prototypes diverge; (2) the size of this imposition tracks each culture's empirical typicality norms; (3) a shared prototype direction in the concept geometry mediates it, with any residual culture-specific prototype in shallow, language-specific layers; and (4) steering toward the target-culture prototype restores culture-appropriate typicality without harming crisp category boundaries. We build a controlled multilingual suite of culturally-loaded categories with divergent versus convergent prototypes, grounded in cross-cultural typicality norms, across typologically and culturally diverse languages, on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM. Using difference-in-means prototype-direction probes, logit-lens tracking, activation patching, and steering, we measure the imposition, its norm scaling, its mediation, and its causal correction. Metrics include cross-lingual typicality-imposition gap, norm-prediction correlation, mediation R-squared, and steering-induced correction with boundary-preservation controls.
Experiments:
1) Culturally-loaded typicality suite grounded in cross-cultural norms: Assemble ~40 common categories (bird, tree, fruit, vegetable, vehicle, sport, musical instrument, breakfast food, dwelling, garment), each with ~15 candidate members spanning the typicality range, and collect per-culture human typicality/best-example norms via native-speaker rating in typologically and culturally diverse languages (English, Spanish, Mandarin, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish). Key subsets: DIVERGENT categories whose top exemplars differ across English and a target culture (e.g. typical 'bird', 'breakfast', 'vegetable', 'sport') and matched CONVERGENT categories (e.g. many geometric-shape or universal-artifact categories) where prototypes agree. Also include CRISP-BOUNDARY control items (clear members vs clear non-members, e.g. is a sparrow a bird? is a chair a bird?) to test that boundary judgments are preserved. Probes: (i) graded typicality rating ('how typical is X of category C?', Likert/log-prob); (ii) best-example forced choice ('which is the most typical C?'); (iii) category-based inference (does a novel property generalize from the culturally-typical vs atypical member?). Native-speaker verify; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral typicality imposition (H1, core): For each DIVERGENT category in each language, measure whether the model's typicality profile / best-example tracks the ENGLISH prototype vs the target-culture one. Define the cross-lingual typicality-imposition GAP = inconsistency(DIVERGENT) minus inconsistency(CONVERGENT), and an English-prototype pull rate = fraction of divergent categories whose model best-example matches the English prototype. Verify near-faithful typicality on CONVERGENT categories, correct English profiles (ceiling), and preserved CRISP-BOUNDARY judgments (isolating graded imposition from boundary incompetence). Control for exemplar frequency, tokenizer fertility, and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test target-language status adds predictive power).
3) Norm scaling (H2, external validation): Test whether per-category imposition is predicted by the target-vs-English typicality-norm divergence (Spearman; held-out prediction from human norms alone), tying the internal phenomenon to independent cross-cultural ground truth. Predict larger imposition for lower-resource / culturally-distant languages.
4) Representational localization (H3): Extract a per-category prototype direction via difference-in-means between typical and atypical member representations (or the category-centroid) at each layer, per language. Test (a) cross-lingual alignment of the prototype direction (a single, largely shared, English-scaffolded prototype geometry); (b) whether a DIVERGENT category's target-language typicality judgments project onto the ENGLISH prototype in the shared mid-layers while any residual culture-specific prototype is stronger in early/language-specific layers, via logit-lens tracking. Mediation: regress behavioral imposition on the shared-hub English-prototype projection (partial correlation controlling for frequency/fertility; held-out R^2). Baseline: a crisp-membership (boundary) direction as a within-model control that should NOT show imposition.
5) Causal steering/patching test (H4, core): (a) Steer the target-language representation along the prototype direction toward the target-culture prototype (using the target-culture typical-member centroid) and measure whether typicality ratings/best-example/inference shift to the target-culture pattern (flip rate) and the imposition GAP shrinks toward the CONVERGENT baseline, without switching output language; (b) conversely amplify the English prototype and confirm dose-response (bidirectional); (c) for imposed items, patch the residual language-specific prototype signal (from early/language-specific layers) into later computation and test restoration. Critically verify CRISP-BOUNDARY preservation (clear members/non-members must still be judged correctly — steering changes graded typicality, not membership) plus fluency and off-target/language-mixing checks. Baselines: whole-hub English-steering, random-direction control.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify steering is prototype-specific (changes graded typicality but not category identity or crisp membership), graded (imposition scales with norm divergence), and not a frequency artifact (frequency-matched divergent/convergent categories).
