Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show stronger imposition than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether imposition magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the prototype direction and with each language's training share. Qualitatively compare the model's per-culture imposition against the human typicality-norm structure.
Evaluation metrics: cross-lingual typicality-imposition GAP and English-prototype pull rate (DIVERGENT vs CONVERGENT; vs English ceiling; crisp-boundary preservation); imposition-vs-norm-divergence correlation and held-out prediction; prototype-direction cross-lingual alignment and shared-hub English-prototype projection with mediation of behavioral imposition (held-out R^2); steering flip rate and GAP reduction (bidirectional dose-response), patching-induced restoration; crisp-boundary preservation (specificity), fluency, off-target rate; cross-model imposition comparison and correlation with training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for target-language status over frequency/fertility/resource baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Collecting reliable per-culture typicality norms is effortful and noisy; we use native-speaker rating with multiple raters, report inter-annotator agreement, restrict DIVERGENT categories to those with robust cross-cultural prototype differences (leveraging established cross-cultural typicality/exemplar literature), and treat norms as noisy predictors, relying on the internal representation and causal tests for core claims. 2) Prototype divergence is correlated with exemplar frequency, cultural specificity, and resource level; the CONVERGENT controls, English ceiling, crisp-boundary controls, within-category contrasts, and norm-based prediction isolate the imposition pathway, but residual confounds may remain. 3) Prior work shows LLMs compress away graded typicality generally (From Tokens to Thoughts 2025), so the typicality signal may be weak even in English; we verify a measurable English typicality effect first as a gate and interpret accordingly — if typicality is not represented, the imposition question is moot, itself an informative finding. 4) Some cross-lingual inconsistency may reflect genuinely correct behavior (the model rightly using the target-culture prototype); the direction of the effect (tracks ENGLISH vs TARGET prototype), the norm prediction, and the causal steering (which restores the target prototype by editing only the prototype direction) distinguish imposition from faithful judgment, and a faithful-judgment finding is itself valuable. 5) Difference-in-means prototype directions may entangle topical/lexical features; we use a crisp-membership control direction, frequency-matched controls, and multiple extraction methods. 6) Logit-lens depth estimates are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 7) Steering could harm crisp boundaries or fluency; crisp-boundary preservation is a hard specificity constraint and we report the full tradeoff plus bidirectional dose-response. 8) Instruction-tuned models may hedge or default to English exemplars; we test base models where available and interpret small effects as informative. 9) The model-vs-human comparison is qualitative/structural (prototype divergence), not a claim of identical mechanism. 10) If NO imposition is found — typicality tracks each culture's own prototype, predictable from norms, with boundaries preserved — this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the shared geometry represents culture-specific prototypes despite English scaffolding, valuable either way. 11) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: language_conditioned_planning_horizon
Title: How Far Ahead the Model Plans Depends on the Tongue: A Language-Conditioned, English-Anchored Planning Horizon in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: The distance ahead over which a multilingual LLM implicitly plans its output (its effective planning horizon and how strongly future-token/rhyme/answer targets are pre-encoded in hidden states before being verbalized) is language-dependent and anchored to the dominant (English) language: the model plans farther ahead and pre-encodes future targets more strongly when generating in English or high-resource languages, and this horizon is imported into other languages regardless of that language's structure, so it under-plans (more myopic, weaker future-target pre-encoding, more error accumulation and incoherence) in lower-resource / English-distant languages on matched tasks. The horizon is decodable, set early by a language signal, and causally extendable by amplifying a shared planning-strength direction.
Related Work: A rapidly growing interpretability literature establishes that LLMs implicitly plan: they pre-encode future rhyme words and answers before verbalizing intermediate tokens (What's the plan? 2026; implicit planning universal from 1B params), encode global response attributes (length, content, confidence) in prompt hidden states (Emergent Response Planning 2025), decode paragraph-scale plans ~5-10 tokens ahead (ParaScopes 2025), have task-dependent, often myopic planning horizons (Internal Planning: Horizon and Branch Awareness 2025; No Global Plan in CoT / Tele-Lens 2026; Detecting and Characterizing Planning 2025), and that instruction tuning refines rather than creates planning. Multi-token-prediction and future-summary objectives improve planning (MuToR 2025; Future Summary Prediction 2025; Horizon-Length Prediction 2024). Multilingual work shows latent reasoning is English-centered and weaker in low-resource languages (Latent Reasoners 2026), reasoning routes through an English pivot, and language mixing tracks internal script preferences (Language Mixing 2025). CRITICALLY, every planning/lookahead-mechanism paper is monolingual (English) and treats the planning horizon as a task property; every multilingual mechanistic paper studies reasoning/knowledge routing or latent answer emergence, NOT the horizon of implicit forward planning. No prior work asks whether the planning horizon itself is language-dependent, whether it is anchored to English and imported onto other languages (causing under-planning, error accumulation, and incoherence in low-resource languages), whether it is set early by a language signal, or whether it is causally extendable via a shared planning-strength direction. This reframes the multilingual coherence/quality gap as an imported planning-horizon miscalibration — orthogonal to all my prior proposals, which concern WHICH content/category is represented, not HOW FAR AHEAD the model plans its own generation.
Abstract: Language models trained only to predict the next token nonetheless plan ahead: they pre-encode future rhyme words, answers, and paragraph-scale structure in their hidden states before verbalizing the tokens that lead there. This has been studied almost entirely in English. We ask a simple, previously untested question: does the DISTANCE a model plans ahead depend on the language it is generating in? We hypothesize a language-conditioned, English-anchored planning horizon: the model pre-encodes future targets more strongly and plans farther ahead when generating in English or high-resource languages, and imports this horizon into other languages regardless of their structure, so it under-plans — becoming more myopic, pre-encoding future targets more weakly, and accumulating more errors and incoherence — in lower-resource / English-distant languages on matched tasks. We further hypothesize the horizon is set early by a decodable language signal, tracks each language's resource level rather than its actual planning needs, and is carried by a largely shared planning-strength direction that can be amplified to causally extend the horizon. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM across typologically diverse languages using matched forward-planning tasks (rhyme/verse completion, constrained-answer generation where the answer must be pre-committed, and paragraph coherence), combining future-target probes (does the hidden state encode the upcoming rhyme/answer N tokens early?), planning-horizon estimation, activation patching, and a planning-strength steering intervention. Metrics include per-language planning horizon and future-target pre-encoding strength, horizon-vs-resource prediction, error-accumulation/coherence correlation, and steering-induced horizon extension with selectivity and fluency controls.
Experiments:
1) Matched forward-planning suite: Build tasks that demonstrably require pre-committing a future target so planning depth is measurable and gold-verifiable: (a) RHYME/VERSE completion — generate a line that must end in a word rhyming with a given word, so the rhyme target must be planned before the intervening tokens (following the rhyme-planning paradigm); (b) CONSTRAINED-ANSWER generation — answer a factual/arithmetic question where the answer must be pre-committed and led up to (a target the model can plan for), with verified gold; (c) PARAGRAPH-coherence generation — continue a passage where later coherence depends on earlier planning. Instantiate every item across typologically diverse languages spanning resource levels and scripts (English, French, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish, Bengali), native-speaker verified, holding content and required planning depth fixed across languages. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Future-target pre-encoding strength (H1, core): Adapting the implicit-planning probing methods (rhyme/answer probes; ParaScopes/Emergent-Response-Planning-style residual decoders), measure, per language, how strongly the upcoming target (rhyme word / answer) is decodable from hidden states N tokens BEFORE it is emitted, as a function of N. Define the per-language planning horizon = the maximum lead N at which the future target is decodable above a threshold, and the pre-encoding strength = probe accuracy/margin at fixed leads. Test H1: horizon and pre-encoding strength are larger in English/high-resource languages and smaller in lower-resource / English-distant languages on matched tasks. Control for tokenizer fertility (report lead in both tokens and characters/words) and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test language adds predictive power).
3) Horizon-vs-resource scaling (H2): Regress per-language planning horizon on training-data resource level and typological/embedding distance from English, controlling for tokenizer fertility. Predict horizon tracks resource level rather than the task's actual planning need (which is held fixed across languages). Verify near-maximal horizon for English (the anchor).
4) Behavioral consequence — error accumulation / incoherence (H1b): Measure per-language task success that depends on planning: rhyme-hit rate, whether the model painted itself into a corner (had to break the rhyme/answer constraint), answer-commitment consistency, and paragraph-coherence ratings. Test whether per-language planning horizon predicts these behavioral outcomes (Spearman; held-out R^2), i.e. that under-planning causes measurable downstream failures, not just weaker probes.
5) Early language-set horizon (H3): Extract a difference-in-means / probe 'planning-strength' signal and test, via position-resolved logit-lens, whether the query LANGUAGE is decodable from an early signal that predicts the eventual planning horizon before the target is formed. Measure cross-lingual alignment of the planning-strength direction (a single shared axis re-thresholded per language).
6) Error decomposition via patching (mechanism): For planning-dependent items succeeded in English but failed in a low-resource language, patch (a) the shared mid-layer pre-encoded future-target representation from the English pass into the low-resource pass and (b) only late-layer decoding components. If (a) restores planning success (the target was pre-encodable in English but under-encoded in the low-resource pass), the failure is an under-planning / horizon failure, not a knowledge failure. Report horizon-vs-knowledge error shares per language.
7) Core causal intervention (horizon extension): Amplify the shared planning-strength direction at middle layers during generation in low-horizon languages (train-free steering), and measure whether the planning horizon and future-target pre-encoding strength increase and behavioral planning outcomes (rhyme-hit, coherence, answer-commitment) improve. Predict SELECTIVE gains for low-horizon (low-resource) languages, little effect on English/high-horizon languages (interaction test). Compute extension elasticity = horizon gain per unit baseline deficit. Compare against baselines: whole-hub English-steering, uniform planning-strength boost for all languages, a multi-token-prediction-inspired auxiliary future-target prompt, and a random-direction control.
8) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify the intervention is planning-specific (improves forward-planning tasks without changing content or switching output language; measure off-target/language-mixing rate and fluency), does not merely make outputs longer (length control), and does not help already-high-horizon languages (symmetric check). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show a sharper language-dependent horizon gap than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether the gap correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the planning-strength direction and each language's training share.
Evaluation metrics: per-language planning horizon and future-target pre-encoding strength (tokens and characters; partial correlation with resource/distance over fertility, held-out R^2); horizon-vs-resource scaling; horizon's prediction of behavioral planning outcomes (rhyme-hit, coherence, answer-commitment; held-out R^2); early language-signal predictiveness of horizon and planning-strength-direction cross-lingual alignment; horizon-vs-knowledge error shares and patching-restoration rate; selective horizon-extension gains and elasticity vs baselines, with English/high-horizon preservation, length control, off-target rate, fluency; cross-model horizon-gap comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The under-planning deficit could conflate with a general competence gap; the key controls are matched tasks with fixed required planning depth, the horizon-vs-knowledge error decomposition, and the patching test (which restores planning by transferring an English-pre-encoded target) — if planning gaps vanish once competence is controlled, the hypothesis is refuted, an informative negative result. 2) Planning horizon estimated from future-target probes is noisy and lead is confounded with tokenizer fertility (more tokens per word inflates apparent lead); we report horizon in both tokens and characters/words, control for fertility, and use multiple probing methods (rhyme probe, answer probe, residual decoders). 3) Rhyme/verse tasks may be ill-defined or sparse in some languages (different phonology/orthography); we native-speaker verify rhyme sets, use multiple planning-dependent task types (not only rhyme), and treat cross-task convergence as the signal. 4) Language is confounded with resource level, script, and fertility; partial correlations and the causal patching/steering tests mitigate but may not fully remove confounds. 5) 'Early language-set horizon' is hard to establish since language and content co-occur; we use position-resolved lenses and report it as suggestive. 6) The planning-strength direction from difference-in-means may entangle content or fluency features; we use multiple extraction methods, the established implicit-planning circuits/heads as anchors, and specificity controls. 7) The horizon-extension intervention could harm fluency, lengthen output, or over-plan; length control, planning-specificity, and the symmetric (no-help-for-high-horizon) check are hard constraints and we report the full tradeoff. 8) Implicit planning is weak/task-dependent even in English (myopic for local tasks per prior work), so we verify a measurable English planning horizon per task first as a gate and interpret accordingly. 9) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM/Aya analyzed as less English-centric contrasts expected to show a smaller gap). 10) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale. 11) If planning horizon is language-INVARIANT once fertility/competence are controlled, this is an informative POSITIVE result showing forward planning is a language-agnostic capability despite an English-scaffolded hub — valuable either way.

Name: crosslingual_analogy_direction_asymmetry
Title: Which Way Does the Analogy Flow? A Language-Conditioned Directional Asymmetry in Cross-Lingual Analogical Mapping
Short Hypothesis: Analogical mapping A:B::C:D is directionally ASYMMETRIC in multilingual LLMs, and the direction of easier flow is language-conditioned: the model maps more reliably FROM the source-domain framed in its dominant (English/high-resource) language TO a target-domain framed in a lower-resource language than in the reverse direction, even for the identical relation. Because the relational operator is abstracted in a shared, English-scaffolded hub, mapping succeeds when the SOURCE (which establishes the relation) is in the hub language and fails when the source is in a peripheral language, producing a measurable source-language-dependent mapping asymmetry not predicted by either language's competence alone. This asymmetry is mediated by how strongly the relation crystallizes into the shared operator direction, which depends on the source-domain's language.
Related Work: Monolingual mechanistic work shows relations are encoded in mid-upper layers as transplantable concept/function vectors but that LLMs struggle to APPLY a correctly-encoded relation to new entities, with failures reflecting degraded structural alignment (The Curious Case of Analogies 2025; Concept Vectors 2025; Emergent Analogical Reasoning 2026 - geometric alignment via Dirichlet-energy decrease; Fine-tuned/Composite Function Vectors 2026). Multilingual work shows a shared, English-scaffolded concept hub with high cross-lingual concept alignment (Semantic Hub 2024; Do Llamas Work in English 2024; Concept Space Alignment 2024; Structural Concepts Are Universal 2023). Human structure-mapping theory (SME/LRME) and analogy research emphasize that the SOURCE domain structures the mapping and that mapping is directional. CRITICALLY, all analogy-mechanism work is monolingual (English), and all multilingual-hub work concerns static concept/relation alignment - none asks whether analogical MAPPING is DIRECTIONALLY ASYMMETRIC across a language boundary, whether the SOURCE-domain's language (which establishes the relation) determines mapping success independent of the target-language's competence, or localizes this to how strongly the relation crystallizes into the shared operator direction as a function of source language. This differs from my prior 'portable_relation_local_retrieval_analogy' proposal (which framed cross-lingual analogy failure as a language-bound TARGET-RETRIEVAL step given a portable operator): here the novel, higher-level phenomenon is a DIRECTIONAL SOURCE-vs-TARGET asymmetry driven by the source-domain's language, a behavior no prior work has surfaced.
Abstract: Analogical reasoning maps a familiar source domain onto a target domain, and cognitive science shows this mapping is inherently directional: the source structures the analogy. Interpretability work shows multilingual LLMs abstract relations into a shared, English-scaffolded representation, but treats analogy as symmetric and monolingual. We ask a simple, previously untested question: is cross-lingual analogical mapping directionally asymmetric, and does the direction of easier flow depend on which language frames the SOURCE domain? We hypothesize that because the relation is established from the source and abstracted into the shared hub, the model maps more reliably when the source is framed in its dominant/high-resource language and the target in a lower-resource language than in the reverse direction - a source-language-dependent asymmetry not explained by either language's standalone competence. We further hypothesize this asymmetry is mediated by how strongly the relation crystallizes into a shared operator direction (measurable via geometric/structural alignment), which is weaker when the source is in a peripheral language. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using controlled A:B::C:D analogies where the source pair (A:B) and target pair (C:?) are independently framed in different languages, holding the relation fixed. Combining behavioral mapping-accuracy asymmetry measurement, logit-lens/structural-alignment (Dirichlet-energy) tracking, difference-in-means operator-direction extraction, and activation patching, we measure the asymmetry, its source-language dependence, its mediation by operator crystallization, and a causal fix that strengthens the operator when the source is peripheral. Metrics include directional mapping-accuracy asymmetry, source-language prediction beyond competence, operator-crystallization mediation, and patching-induced asymmetry reduction.
Experiments:
1) Directional cross-lingual analogy suite: Build ~500 A:B::C:D analogies spanning semantic relations (capital-country, part-whole, antonym, category-member, cause-effect), each with a single verified target D. Independently frame the SOURCE pair (A:B, which establishes the relation) and the TARGET pair (C:?) in different languages, crossing source-language x target-language across typologically diverse languages spanning resource levels (English, French, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish). Include same-language (source=target) controls. Native-speaker verify; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral directional asymmetry (H1, core): For each language pair (L1,L2) and relation, measure mapping accuracy in both directions: source-in-L1/target-in-L2 vs source-in-L2/target-in-L1. Define the directional asymmetry = accuracy(source-in-dominant) minus accuracy(source-in-peripheral). Test that mapping is easier when the SOURCE is in the more dominant/high-resource language, holding the relation and the target-language fixed. Crucially, test that this asymmetry exceeds what each language's standalone (same-language-control) competence predicts - i.e., it is a directional effect, not a sum of two competence gaps. Control for tokenizer fertility and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2).
3) Source-language prediction (H2): Regress per-item mapping success on (a) source-language resource level/dominance, (b) target-language resource level, and (c) each language's standalone competence, and test whether SOURCE-language dominance predicts mapping success beyond target-language competence and standalone baselines (model comparison, held-out R^2). Prediction: the source-domain's language is the dominant predictor of mapping direction.
4) Operator-crystallization mediation (H3): Extract a per-relation operator direction (difference-in-means / concept-vector) at the relation-encoding layers, and measure how strongly the relation crystallizes into the shared operator direction as a function of source language (projection magnitude; and structural alignment via a Dirichlet-energy-style decrease across layers, following Emergent Analogical Reasoning 2026). Test whether the operator crystallizes MORE strongly when the source is in the dominant language, and whether operator-crystallization strength MEDIATES the behavioral asymmetry (partial correlation controlling for fertility/resource; held-out R^2). Use logit-lens to check whether the correct D is latently present when the source is dominant but absent when peripheral.
5) Error decomposition via patching: For items solvable with a dominant-language source but failed with a peripheral-language source (same relation, same target-language), patch the shared-hub operator representation (from the dominant-source pass) into the peripheral-source pass and test whether mapping is restored. This isolates whether the asymmetry arises at relation crystallization (fixed by operator patching) versus a downstream step. Report the share of asymmetry attributable to weak operator crystallization.
6) Core causal intervention: When the source is in a peripheral language, amplify/strengthen the shared operator direction (steering toward the well-crystallized dominant-source operator) at the relation-encoding layer, and measure whether the directional asymmetry shrinks. Predict selective recovery for peripheral-source items, little effect on dominant-source items (interaction test). Compare against baselines: whole-hub English steering, translating the source to English (a strong practical baseline), and a random-direction control. Compute recovery elasticity = accuracy gain per unit baseline asymmetry.
7) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify the intervention is operator-specific (restores mapping without switching output language or changing the relation; off-target/language-mixing rate), and does not merely lift all items uniformly. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show larger source-language asymmetry than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether asymmetry magnitude correlates with the model's hub English-centrality and each language's training share.
Evaluation metrics: directional mapping-accuracy asymmetry (source-dominant vs source-peripheral, target-language fixed); source-language predictive R^2 beyond target-competence and standalone baselines (model comparison); operator-crystallization strength by source language and its mediation of the asymmetry (held-out R^2); latent-D-present rate by source language; share of asymmetry fixed by operator patching; operator-strengthening asymmetry reduction and elasticity vs baselines, with relation/output-language preservation (specificity), off-target rate; cross-model asymmetry comparison and correlation with hub English-centrality and training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The directional asymmetry could reduce to the sum of two per-language competence gaps rather than a genuine source-vs-target directional effect; the same-language controls, the exceeds-standalone-competence test (H1), and the source-vs-target-language prediction (H2, holding target-language fixed) are designed to isolate a true directional effect - if asymmetry vanishes once standalone competence is controlled, the hypothesis is refuted, an informative negative result. 2) Word-analogy tasks can be solved by lexical association rather than genuine relational mapping; we include far/cross-domain and low-association targets and distractor-controlled variants to reduce shortcuts. 3) Operator directions and Dirichlet-energy/structural-alignment measures from difference-in-means/concept-vectors may entangle content or format (Concept Vectors 2025 shows format-sensitivity); we use format-invariant extraction, multiple relation types, and specificity controls. 4) Source/target language framing is confounded with tokenizer fertility, script, and resource level; partial correlations and same-language controls mitigate but may not fully remove confounds. 5) The operator-strengthening intervention could harm fluency or switch output language; relation- and output-language-preservation are hard constraints and we report the full tradeoff, comparing against the translate-source-to-English baseline to show the mechanistic account adds value. 6) Logit-lens latent-D and crystallization estimates are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 7) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM's less English-centric hub analyzed as a contrast expected to show weaker asymmetry). 8) If mapping is directionally SYMMETRIC (source language does not matter beyond competence), this is an informative positive result showing analogical mapping is source-language-agnostic in the shared hub. 9) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: language_dependent_positional_bias_icl
Title: Primacy in One Tongue, Recency in Another: A Language-Conditioned Positional Bias in Multilingual In-Context Learning
Short Hypothesis: The positional bias governing which in-context demonstration a multilingual LLM weights most (primacy vs recency vs middle-neglect) is LANGUAGE-DEPENDENT: querying/demonstrating the same ICL task in a lower-resource / English-distant language shifts the model's demonstration-weighting profile away from the English 'attention-basin' (favor-first-and-last) pattern toward a stronger recency skew, so the SAME wrong-first-example-vs-right-later-example configuration yields different predictions depending only on the language. This shift is not a general competence gap but a language-conditioned re-weighting of which demonstration position the model reads, carried by a shared, English-scaffolded positional-attention profile, and it makes order-sensitivity (the accuracy swing across demonstration permutations) systematically larger in non-dominant languages.
Related Work: Positional bias in ICL is well established but studied monolingually: the 'attention basin' explains favor-first-and-last weighting and yields a training-free reranking fix (Attention Basin / AttnRank 2025); LayerNorm+causal attention induce recency bias (2025); lost-in-the-middle emerges from retrieval demands (2025); in-context heads implement demonstration weighting and carry majority/recency bias (Two Towers 2024; UniBias 2024); DETAIL attributes helpful/harmful demonstrations. Multilingual ICL work is performance-oriented: language vectors steer activations to improve non-English ICL (Language Steering 2026), and demonstration-selection helps low-resource Indic ICL (PromptRefine 2024). Human cognition shows word-order/language shapes serial-position and working-memory order effects (word-order predicts WM 2019; language-induced sequential-learning biases 2012). CRITICALLY, no prior work asks whether the ICL positional-bias PROFILE itself is language-dependent, whether the attention-basin shape shifts by query/demonstration language producing language-conditioned order-sensitivity, or whether the shared, English-scaffolded positional-attention mechanism causally drives this. All positional-bias mechanism work is English; all multilingual-ICL work treats order/position as a fixed nuisance to average over, never as a language-conditioned variable. This reframes multilingual ICL brittleness as a language-shifted positional-attention profile with a mechanistic (attention-basin) locus and a per-language reranking/steering fix, distinct from all my prior proposals (none concern positional/order bias in ICL) and from monolingual positional-bias work.
Abstract: In-context learning is famously order-sensitive: which demonstration a model weights most depends on its position, following a first-and-last 'attention basin' documented in English. We ask a simple, previously untested question: is this positional bias the same across languages? We hypothesize that the demonstration-weighting profile is language-conditioned — querying and demonstrating the same ICL task in a lower-resource or English-distant language shifts the model's positional-attention profile away from the English favor-first-and-last pattern toward a stronger recency skew, so the identical arrangement of demonstrations yields different predictions depending only on language, and order-sensitivity (the accuracy swing across demonstration permutations) is systematically larger in non-dominant languages. We further hypothesize this is not a general competence deficit but a language-conditioned re-weighting carried by a shared, English-scaffolded positional-attention mechanism (the attention basin), which can be measured, predicted from language resource-distance, and causally corrected per language. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM across typologically diverse languages using controlled multi-shot classification where demonstration positions and label-position conflicts are systematically varied. We measure per-language positional-weighting profiles and order-sensitivity, map them to per-language attention-basin shapes, use activation patching to test whether the shared positional-attention mechanism drives the shift, and apply a per-language attention-aligned reranking/steering fix. Metrics include per-language positional-weighting curves, order-sensitivity gap, attention-basin-shape prediction of behavior, and reranking-induced order-robustness recovery with competence controls.
Experiments:
1) Controlled positional-conflict ICL suite: Build multi-shot classification tasks (sentiment, topic, NLI) with K demonstrations, where we can place a MISLEADING demonstration (e.g., a mislabeled or class-conflicting example) at a controlled position (first / middle / last) and measure which position's example the model follows. Instantiate every task — inputs, labels, template — in typologically diverse languages spanning resource levels and scripts (English, French, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish), native-speaker verified, holding content and K fixed. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Per-language positional-weighting profile (H1, core): For each language, measure the per-position influence curve — how strongly the demonstration at each position (first..last) determines the prediction — via (a) the misleading-example-follows rate as a function of its position and (b) leave-one-position-out / DETAIL-style attribution. Test H1: English shows the first-and-last attention-basin profile; lower-resource / English-distant languages show a shifted profile (stronger recency skew / weaker primacy). Quantify a per-language recency-skew index. Control for tokenizer fertility and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test language adds predictive power).
3) Order-sensitivity gap (H1b): For each task, measure order-sensitivity = the accuracy swing across random demonstration permutations, per language. Test that order-sensitivity is larger in non-dominant languages, and that it is predicted by the recency-skew index (Spearman; held-out R^2). Crucially condition on tasks the model performs well in each language (best-permutation accuracy comparable), so a larger swing is a positional-weighting effect, not a competence gap.
4) Attention-basin mechanism (H2): Following the attention-basin analysis, measure each model's per-position attention allocation over demonstrations at the query position, per language, in shallow layers. Test whether the per-language attention-basin SHAPE (how much attention goes to first/middle/last demonstrations) shifts by language and predicts the per-language behavioral positional-weighting profile (mediation regression; held-out R^2). Extract a difference-in-means positional-weighting signal and test whether the query language is decodable early and whether the positional-attention mechanism is largely shared (cross-lingual alignment) but re-thresholded per language.
5) Causal test via patching: For items where the model follows the wrong-first-example in English (primacy) but the wrong-last-example in a recency-skewed language (or vice versa), patch (a) the shared shallow-layer positional-attention pattern from the English pass into the target-language pass and (b) only late-layer decoding. If (a) shifts the followed position toward the English pattern, the language-conditioned bias is carried by the shared positional-attention mechanism. Report the share of position-flips explained.
6) Core intervention (per-language attention-aligned reranking / steering): Apply AttnRank-style reranking calibrated PER LANGUAGE (align the most informative demonstration with each language's high-attention position), and, as a mechanistic variant, steer the shallow-layer positional-attention profile toward a flatter (basin-reduced) shape. Measure per-language order-sensitivity reduction and worst-permutation accuracy gain. Predict SELECTIVE gains for high-skew (low-resource) languages, little effect on English. Compare against baselines: language-agnostic (English-calibrated) AttnRank, uniform reranking, language vectors (Language Steering 2026), and a random-direction control. Compute recovery elasticity = order-robustness gain per unit baseline recency-skew.
7) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify the fix is position-specific (reduces order-sensitivity without switching output language — off-target/language-mixing rate — and without harming best-permutation accuracy or English), and does not merely help all languages uniformly (gap-closing vs uniform-lift). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show a sharper language-dependent positional-bias shift than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether the shift correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the positional-attention profile and each language's training share.
Evaluation metrics: per-language positional-weighting curves and recency-skew index (English attention-basin vs shifted profile); order-sensitivity gap and its prediction by recency-skew (held-out R^2 over fertility/resource); per-language attention-basin shape and its mediation of behavioral positional weighting (held-out R^2); early language-decodability of the positional signal and cross-lingual alignment; position-flip share explained by shared-attention patching; per-language reranking/steering order-sensitivity reduction and worst-permutation gain vs baselines, with best-permutation and English preservation (specificity), off-target rate; cross-model shift comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The order-sensitivity gap could conflate with a general competence gap; conditioning on tasks with comparable best-permutation accuracy across languages, plus the attention-basin mediation and the patching test, isolate a positional-weighting effect — if the gap vanishes once competence is controlled, the hypothesis is refuted, an informative negative result. 2) Language is confounded with tokenizer fertility, script, and resource level; partial correlations and the causal patching/steering tests mitigate but may not fully remove confounds (e.g., longer tokenizations in low-resource languages could themselves shift attention — which is itself a mechanistically interesting sub-finding we report). 3) The misleading-example-follows paradigm assumes a clean position-conflict; some tasks may let the model ignore the conflict, weakening the signal — we use multiple task types and attribution methods and report robustness. 4) Attention allocation is only a correlate of influence; we complement raw attention with attribution (DETAIL/leave-one-out) and the causal patching test rather than relying on attention alone. 5) The per-language reranking/steering fix could harm best-permutation accuracy or switch output language; best-permutation and English preservation plus off-target rate are hard specificity constraints and we report the full tradeoff, comparing against language-agnostic AttnRank to show the per-language account adds value. 6) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM/Aya analyzed as less English-centric contrasts expected to show a smaller shift). 7) Positional-bias profiles are known to be model- and layer-specific; we report per-model results rather than assuming a universal shape. 8) The human-cognition analogy (word-order-dependent serial-position effects) is qualitative, not a claim of identical mechanism. 9) Limited to open ~7-8B models and modest K; may not extend to frontier scale or very long contexts.

Name: standardness_normalization_imposition
Title: Correcting a Dialect That Isn't Wrong: A Standardness Direction That Silently Normalizes Dialectal Meaning in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs carry a persistent, decodable 'standardness' direction that measures how far an input deviates from the dominant standard variety, and they IMPOSE it as a normalization step: dialectal features that are grammatical in the variety but non-standard are silently 're-parsed' toward the standard form, so when a dialect feature CHANGES MEANING relative to the standard (e.g. AAVE habitual 'be', double negation as emphatic negation, a dialect-specific tense/aspect marker), the model normalizes it away and returns the standard-language meaning rather than the dialect-correct one. This meaning-corrupting normalization—not mere accuracy loss—is mediated by the standardness direction, tracks each feature's standard/dialect meaning divergence, and is causally correctable by suppressing that direction without harming standard comprehension.
Related Work: A large literature documents dialect performance gaps and dialect-triggered social bias (VALUE 2022; Multi-VALUE 2023; ReDial 2024; DialectBench 2024; German-dialect discrimination 2025; ChatGPT dialect bias 2024; the 2018-2025 review), and probing shows MSA-trained models miss dialectal nuance (Arabic post-hoc analysis 2022) and are SAE/SAE-European-biased (Universal and Independent 2022). The one causal representational study, When Alignment Hurts (2025), shows entanglement with Modern Standard Arabic hinders dialectal GENERATION and decouples subspaces during fine-tuning. Linear socio-demographic and dialect-identity directions are known to be decodable (Linear socio-demographic representations 2025; language-neutrality centering 2020). CRITICALLY, all prior work either (a) measures behavioral disparity / social bias, or (b) studies dialectal generation quality under fine-tuning; NONE isolates the specific COMPREHENSION-side phenomenon that the model actively NORMALIZES dialectal meaning—silently re-parsing a meaning-bearing non-standard feature into its standard form and returning the WRONG (standard) meaning—nor localizes a shared standardness direction that mediates this, ties the meaning-corruption to per-feature standard/dialect meaning divergence, or offers an inference-time suppression fix that operates on comprehension without retraining. We reframe the dialect gap from a data-scarcity / bias problem into a mechanistic normalization-imposition phenomenon with a causal, steerable locus.
Abstract: Dialects are not broken standards: a feature like African American English habitual 'be' ('she be working' = habitually works, not right now) or an emphatic double negative encodes meaning the standard variety encodes differently. We ask a simple, previously untested mechanistic question about multilingual LLMs: when the model reads dialectal input, does it silently NORMALIZE it toward the standard variety—re-parsing meaning-bearing non-standard features into their standard forms and returning the standard-language meaning rather than the dialect-correct one? We hypothesize that (1) models carry a persistent, decodable 'standardness' direction (how far an input deviates from the dominant standard) and impose it as a comprehension-time normalization step; (2) this produces MEANING corruption—not mere accuracy loss—concentrated on features whose dialect meaning DIVERGES from their standard reading, versus features that only differ in form; (3) the standardness direction mediates the corruption, with any residual dialect-correct signal living in shallow, early layers; and (4) suppressing the direction restores dialect-correct comprehension without harming standard comprehension. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using controlled minimal pairs across meaning-divergent (habitual 'be', emphatic negation, dialect tense/aspect) and form-only (lexical/spelling) dialectal features, in English (AAVE, Scottish, Indian) and Arabic (MSA vs dialects). Combining comprehension probes, difference-in-means standardness-direction extraction, logit-lens tracking, activation patching, and steering, we measure the normalization, its meaning-divergence scaling, its mediation, and its causal correction. Metrics include meaning-corruption gap, divergence-prediction correlation, mediation R-squared, and suppression-induced recovery with standard-comprehension controls.
Experiments:
1) Meaning-divergent vs form-only dialect suite: Construct ~500 minimal pairs across dialects with rich standard/dialect meaning divergence: English (AAVE habitual 'be', emphatic multiple negation, remote-past 'been', completive 'done'; plus Scottish and Indian English features) and Arabic (MSA vs dialectal tense/aspect/negation), each item in two categories—(a) MEANING-DIVERGENT: the dialect feature carries a meaning that differs from a naive standard re-parse ('she be working' -> habitual, not present progressive); (b) FORM-ONLY control: dialectal spelling/lexical variants with the SAME meaning as the standard. Each item has native-speaker-verified dialect-correct AND standard-reparse gold answers. Probes hinge on the meaning: (i) comprehension forced choice (which meaning is intended?); (ii) entailment (does the sentence entail the dialect-correct vs the standard-reparse consequence?); (iii) a short reasoning item whose answer depends on the dialect meaning. Report inter-annotator agreement; release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral normalization (H1, core): On MEANING-DIVERGENT items, measure the meaning-corruption rate = fraction where the model returns the STANDARD-reparse meaning rather than the dialect-correct one. Compare against FORM-ONLY items (where normalization is harmless, meaning identical) and against standard-variety controls. Define the meaning-corruption GAP = corruption(meaning-divergent) minus corruption(form-only). Predict a positive gap: normalization corrupts meaning specifically when the feature is meaning-bearing, not merely when it is non-standard. Control for tokenizer fertility, feature frequency, and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test meaning-divergence adds predictive power beyond form-difference).
3) Divergence scaling (H2): Rate each dialect feature by how strongly its dialect meaning diverges from the standard reparse (native-speaker-annotated). Test whether per-feature meaning-corruption is predicted by this divergence (Spearman; held-out prediction), tying the internal phenomenon to a linguistic ground-truth variable and distinguishing it from generic difficulty.
4) Standardness direction and localization (H3): Extract a 'standardness' direction via difference-in-means between standard and dialectal input representations at each layer (verifying it is a graded standard-distance axis via a probe recovering dialect-distance, and checking cross-dialect alignment—a single shared standardness axis). Using logit-lens/tuned-lens, test whether a MEANING-DIVERGENT dialect input's representation crystallizes toward the STANDARD-reparse meaning in mid/late layers while any residual dialect-correct signal is stronger in early/shallow layers. Mediation: regress behavioral meaning-corruption on the standardness-direction projection / the mid-layer standard-meaning crystallization (partial correlation controlling for fertility/frequency; held-out R^2). Baseline: a lexical-content direction as a within-model control.
5) Causal suppression/steering test (H4, core): (a) Suppress the standardness direction (difference-in-means projection removal / INLP nullspace toward the dialect) for meaning-divergent items and test whether the meaning-corruption GAP drops toward the form-only baseline; (b) conversely, AMPLIFY standardness and confirm it induces more standard-reparse corruption (bidirectional dose-response); (c) for corrupted items, patch the early/shallow dialect-correct signal into later computation and test restoration—localizing failure to the imposed normalization overwriting a shallowly-present dialect-correct meaning. Critically verify STANDARD-COMPREHENSION preservation: the model must still correctly comprehend genuine standard-variety sentences AND still flag genuine errors (steering must restore dialect meaning without making the model accept ungrammatical input), plus fluency and off-target checks. Baselines: random-direction suppression, whole-hub steering.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify suppression is standardness-specific (removes meaning-corruption on divergent features but not genuine content or standard comprehension), graded (corruption scales with meaning-divergence), and not a mere frequency artifact (frequency-matched divergent/form-only pairs). Cross-model contrast: predict the more standard/English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show stronger normalization than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether corruption magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the standardness direction and with each dialect's training share.
Evaluation metrics: meaning-corruption rate and GAP (meaning-divergent vs form-only vs standard controls); corruption-vs-meaning-divergence correlation and held-out prediction; standardness-direction dialect-distance decodability, cross-dialect alignment, and mid-layer standard-meaning crystallization with mediation of behavioral corruption (held-out R^2); suppression-induced GAP reduction and amplification-induced increase (bidirectional); patching-induced restoration; standard-comprehension and error-flagging preservation (specificity), fluency, off-target rate; cross-model corruption comparison and correlation with training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for meaning-divergence over form-difference/frequency/resource baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Distinguishing genuine meaning-divergent features (habitual 'be') from form-only variants is delicate; we native-speaker-verify both the feature category and the dialect-correct/standard-reparse gold, report inter-annotator agreement, and exclude ambiguous items. 2) Meaning divergence is correlated with feature frequency, script, and dialect resource level; the FORM-ONLY controls (same meaning, non-standard form), standard-variety controls, within-feature contrasts, and divergence-based prediction isolate the meaning-normalization pathway from generic non-standard difficulty, but residual confounds may remain; we center core claims on well-attested features (AAVE habitual 'be', emphatic negation) and treat rarer features/dialects as extensions. 3) Meaning-corruption could reflect genuine ignorance of the dialect feature rather than active normalization; the divergence scaling, the FORM-ONLY control (harmless normalization when meaning is identical), the mid-layer standard-crystallization localization, and the causal suppression (which restores the dialect meaning by editing only the standardness direction) distinguish imposition from ignorance—if suppression does nothing, the phenomenon is ignorance, an informative negative result. 4) The standardness direction from difference-in-means may entangle topical/lexical/script features; we verify it is a graded dialect-distance axis, use a lexical-content control direction, frequency-matched pairs, and multiple extraction methods. 5) Logit-lens crystallization estimates are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 6) Suppression could harm standard comprehension or make the model accept ungrammatical input; standard-comprehension and error-flagging preservation are hard specificity constraints and we report the full tradeoff plus the bidirectional dose-response. 7) This touches fairness/sociolinguistic bias; we frame the phenomenon descriptively and our interventions restore dialect-correct comprehension (equity-improving), releasing the suite responsibly. 8) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM/Aya analyzed as less standard-centric contrasts). 9) If NO meaning-corruption gap is found—dialectal meaning is comprehended faithfully regardless of standard divergence—this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the model represents variety-specific meaning rather than normalizing it away, valuable either way and complementary to the entanglement-hurts-generation finding. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: language_conditioned_taboo_charge
Title: Cursing in a Foreign Tongue: A Language-Dependent Taboo-Charge Signal Drives Asymmetric Refusal and Hedging in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs exhibit a mechanistic analogue of the human L1-vs-L2 taboo-emotionality asymmetry: a word's TABOO CHARGE (its emotional/offensiveness weight) is represented on a largely shared but language-scaled 'taboo' direction whose gain is set by the query language, so the SAME taboo concept carries a stronger internal charge when expressed in the model's dominant/higher-resource language than in a lower-resource language. Consequently, for identical propositional content, the model refuses, hedges, sanitizes, or flags offensiveness MORE in the high-charge language and treats the foreign-language equivalent as more emotionally neutral, mirroring the documented human 'foreign-language emotional detachment' effect. This language-set charge gain is decodable, predictable from each language's resource level / acquisition salience, and causally correctable by rescaling the shared taboo direction without harming genuine harmful-content detection.
Related Work: A large psycholinguistics literature robustly documents that taboo/swear words and reprimands carry markedly higher emotional arousal in a speaker's first language than in a second/foreign language, verified psychophysiologically (skin conductance: Harris et al. 2003; native-vs-nonnative ERP responses to taboo words: 2019, 2021; taboo Stroop asymmetry: 2018), and that this L1/L2 asymmetry drives differential censorship, self-censorship, and translator self-censoring (Censorship and Taboo Maintenance in L1 and LX Swearing 2024; sexist S-T words in bilinguals 2025; intercultural taboo avoidance 2023). On the LLM side, interpretability shows refusal is mediated by a largely universal, cross-lingually parallel refusal direction (Refusal is Mediated by a Single Direction 2024; Refusal Direction is Universal Across Safety-Aligned Languages 2025; concept-cone refusal geometry 2025), that alignment separates harmful/harmless representations well in English but weakly in other languages (The Hidden Space of Safety 2025), that emojis exploit a tokenization/representation gap to bypass safety (When Smiley Turns Hostile 2025), and that social/affective concepts (politeness, emotion) are localized, steerable linear directions (Interpreting Politeness 2016; STAR 2025). CRITICALLY, no prior work asks whether a word's TABOO CHARGE itself is language-dependent in a multilingual LLM (a mechanistic L1/L2 emotional-detachment analogue), whether a shared taboo direction is scaled by a language-set gain, whether this causes asymmetric refusal/hedging/toxicity-flagging on identical content across languages, whether the gain tracks resource level, or whether rescaling it equalizes emotional handling without harming harmful-content detection. Prior multilingual-safety work studies whether the model REFUSES harmful requests across languages (a safety-severity question); we study the orthogonal EMOTIONAL-CHARGE of taboo/offensive lexicon and its language-conditioned scaling, porting a well-established human psychophysiological finding into LLM mechanisms. This is distinct from all my prior proposals (grammatical/semantic/pragmatic imposition) and from the refusal-direction literature (which treats charge as fixed and studies refusal, not emotional weighting of taboo words).
Abstract: Bilingual people swear more freely and feel less emotional sting in a foreign language: decades of psychophysiological research show taboo words carry markedly higher arousal in a speaker's first language than in a second, an effect that shapes censorship, self-censorship, and translation. We ask a simple, previously untested question about multilingual language models: is a word's taboo charge — its internal emotional/offensiveness weight — language-dependent? We hypothesize a mechanistic analogue of the human L1/L2 asymmetry: taboo charge is carried on a largely shared 'taboo' direction whose GAIN is set by the query language, so the same taboo concept registers as stronger in the model's dominant/higher-resource language and more emotionally neutral in a lower-resource one. Consequently, for identical propositional content, the model refuses, hedges, sanitizes, or flags offensiveness more in the high-charge language, treating the foreign-language equivalent as milder. We further hypothesize this charge gain is decodable, predicted by each language's resource level, and causally correctable by rescaling the shared taboo direction without harming genuine harmful-content detection. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using controlled parallel taboo/neutral stimuli — offensiveness ratings, self-censorship/sanitization on repetition tasks, hedging, and toxicity-flagging — across typologically diverse languages, combining behavioral asymmetry measurement, difference-in-means taboo-direction extraction, activation patching, and gain-steering. Metrics include per-language taboo-charge and offensiveness asymmetry, charge-vs-resource prediction, shared-direction alignment, and steering-induced equalization with harmful-content-detection controls.
Experiments:
1) Parallel taboo/neutral stimulus suite: Assemble ~500 items each realized in typologically diverse languages spanning resource levels and scripts (English, French, German, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish), native-speaker verified, in matched categories: (a) TABOO words (profanity, slurs handled ethically, strongly offensive terms), (b) REPRIMANDS/emotionally-charged phrases (the human-studied category showing the largest L1/L2 gap), (c) NEUTRAL and (d) POSITIVE control words, with translation-equivalent meaning held fixed across languages. Tasks: (i) offensiveness/emotional-intensity rating (Likert + forced-choice which-is-more-offensive across a within-item cross-language pair); (ii) self-censorship/sanitization — ask the model to repeat/complete a sentence containing the word and measure how often it censors, softens, or refuses; (iii) hedging — measure disclaimers/warnings emitted; (iv) toxicity-flagging — ask the model to classify whether the sentence is offensive. Report inter-annotator agreement; release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral taboo-charge asymmetry (H1, core): For each taboo item, measure per-language offensiveness rating, self-censorship/sanitization rate, hedging rate, and toxicity-flag rate, holding meaning fixed. Test the central prediction: taboo charge (all four measures) is higher in the model's dominant/higher-resource language and lower (more 'foreign-language detached') in lower-resource languages, with the REPRIMAND category showing the largest gap (mirroring the human finding). Define the taboo-charge asymmetry = high-language minus low-language charge. Verify near-zero asymmetry on NEUTRAL/POSITIVE controls (isolating a taboo-specific effect). Control for tokenizer fertility and word frequency (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test language adds predictive power beyond fertility).
3) Charge-vs-resource scaling (H2): Test whether per-language taboo charge is predicted by each language's training-data resource level / dominance (and, as a human-analogue check, whether the ranking qualitatively matches the L1-strong / L2-weak human pattern), better than by mere translation difficulty (nested regression, held-out R^2). Predict maximal charge for the dominant language, monotone decline with resource-distance.
4) Shared taboo direction and gain readout (H3): Extract a per-language 'taboo-charge' direction via difference-in-means between taboo and neutral representations at each layer (verifying it is a graded offensiveness axis via a probe recovering offensiveness rank). Measure cross-lingual cosine alignment (test: a largely shared axis re-scaled per language) and portability (steering with one language's direction changes offensiveness handling in another). Project the residual stream at the decision point onto the shared direction and estimate a per-LANGUAGE charge gain (scalar) via regression of the offensiveness/censorship decision on the projection. Test that the cross-lingual asymmetry is captured by the difference in per-language gains applied to the SHARED taboo projection (held-out R^2), beating a uniform-bias baseline. Mediation: regress behavioral asymmetry on the taboo-direction projection (partial correlation controlling for fertility/frequency; held-out R^2).
5) Causal gain-steering (H4, core): Rescale the shared taboo direction with a per-language scalar to transform a low-charge (foreign) language's gain into the high-charge (dominant) value (and vice versa), and measure whether offensiveness ratings, self-censorship, hedging, and toxicity-flagging shift accordingly WITHOUT changing input language (charge-transfer rate); conversely, equalize gains across languages and measure the reduction in cross-lingual charge variance. Bidirectional dose-response; mis-signed steering worsens. Complement with activation patching: patch the dominant-language taboo signal into a foreign-language pass. Compare against baselines: whole-hub English-steering, a random-direction control.
6) Specificity and harmful-content-detection controls (hard constraint): Verify gain-steering is taboo-charge-specific — it changes emotional/offensiveness handling of taboo LEXICON but must NOT impair genuine HARMFUL-CONTENT detection (a separate harmful-request set: the model must still refuse actually-dangerous requests regardless of charge steering — a symmetric check separating emotional charge of words from safety severity of content), must not switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), and preserves fluency. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show larger charge asymmetry (gains collapsed toward the dominant language) than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether asymmetry magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the taboo direction and each language's training share. Qualitatively compare the per-language charge ranking against the human L1/L2 taboo-emotionality literature (direction, not identical mechanism).
Evaluation metrics: per-language taboo-charge (offensiveness rating, self-censorship, hedging, toxicity-flag) and asymmetry (taboo vs neutral/positive controls; reprimand-category gap); charge-vs-resource prediction (held-out R^2 over fertility baseline); taboo-direction offensiveness-rank decodability, cross-lingual alignment, portability, and gain-predictive R^2 (vs uniform-bias baseline) with mediation of behavioral asymmetry (held-out R^2); charge-transfer rate and cross-lingual charge-variance reduction under gain-steering vs baselines, with bidirectional dose-response and mis-sign penalty; harmful-content-detection preservation (symmetric specificity), off-target rate, fluency; cross-model asymmetry comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) This is sensitive-content research; we handle slurs/profanity ethically (restricted-access release, no generation of novel targeted slurs), frame the work as improving equitable and consistent emotional/offensiveness handling, and all interventions are analyzed for their effect on making handling MORE consistent, not for enabling toxic output. 2) The taboo-charge asymmetry could conflate with a general competence/comprehension gap (the model may under-react to a foreign taboo word because it under-understands it, not because it is emotionally detached); we control by including a comprehension probe (does the model correctly identify the word's meaning/offensiveness category in each language?) and conditioning on items the model comprehends, plus the causal steering test (which changes charge by editing only the taboo direction) — if asymmetry vanishes once comprehension is controlled, the human-analogue interpretation weakens, an informative result. 3) Language is confounded with tokenizer fertility, script, and resource level; partial correlations, neutral/positive controls, and the causal tests mitigate but may not fully remove confounds (e.g., a taboo word split into many subword tokens may register as milder — itself a mechanistically interesting sub-finding we report). 4) The difference-in-means taboo direction may entangle general negative-sentiment or topical features; we verify it is a graded offensiveness axis, use a general-negativity control direction, and apply specificity checks. 5) The single-scalar gain account may only partially hold; if a data-driven low-dimensional basis fits better we report it, keeping the 'shared axis + language gain' claim testable. 6) Alignment/RLHF may impose a uniform safety veneer that flattens the asymmetry in instruction-tuned models; we test base and instruction-tuned models and treat differences as an informative training-stage finding (analogous to how proficiency/acquisition modulates the human effect). 7) Gain-steering could impair genuine harmful-content detection or over-sanitize; the symmetric harmful-content-detection constraint is a hard requirement and we report the full tradeoff. 8) The human-LLM comparison (L1/L2 taboo emotionality) is qualitative/structural (direction and category ordering, reprimands largest), not a claim of identical mechanism — a text-only model has no acoustic/embodied arousal, so any charge is distributional, which is exactly what makes a positive result surprising. 9) Some cross-lingual asymmetry may reflect genuinely appropriate cultural calibration rather than emotional detachment; the resource-level prediction and the reprimand-category human-analogue signature help distinguish these, and a culturally-appropriate finding is itself valuable. 10) If NO asymmetry is found — taboo charge is language-invariant once comprehension/fertility are controlled — this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the model weights offensiveness consistently across languages despite the human L1/L2 asymmetry, valuable either way. 11) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: crosslingual_novel_word_binding_portability
Title: Taught in One Tongue, Known in All? The Cross-Lingual Portability of In-Context Novel-Word Bindings in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: When a multilingual LLM learns a NOVEL word from an in-context definition or demonstrations in one language, the newly-bound meaning is written into a partially LANGUAGE-TETHERED slot rather than the fully language-agnostic shared hub: the model can use the novel word most reliably when queried in the SAME language it was taught in, and portability to other languages degrades with typological/script distance from the teaching language and is worse than for pre-existing (pretrained) translation-equivalent words. This binding-portability gap is a distinct, causally-localizable failure mode—the meaning is bound but not fully hub-shared—separable from the model's general cross-lingual competence.
Related Work: Behavioral work shows in-context compositional generalization is far weaker for fictional/novel words than common ones (CoFe 2023) and that cross-lingual compositional generalization remains hard even with faithful benchmarks (MCWQ-R 2023). Cross-lingual structural priming shows abstract grammatical representations are shared and causally influence other languages (Structural Priming 2023; Bilingual acquisition 2025), and the Semantic Hub Hypothesis (2024) shows semantically-equivalent inputs across languages converge in intermediate layers and are causally usable via the dominant language. Schema-learning/rebinding accounts (2023) frame ICL as binding novel tokens to template slots. CRITICALLY, all of this concerns either PRETRAINED words (whose translation equivalents are already hub-aligned) or behavioral compositional generalization; NONE asks whether a freshly INDUCED in-context binding of a genuinely novel word becomes language-agnostic (usable equally in any language) or stays tethered to the teaching language, none localizes the induced binding to a shared-hub vs language-specific representation, and none tests whether the newly-bound meaning can be causally transplanted across a language boundary. We reframe the question from 'does the model know a word cross-lingually' (pretraining property) to 'when the model LEARNS a word on the fly, does that learning land in the shared hub'—a distinct mechanistic property of in-context binding, orthogonal to prior work.
Abstract: Multilingual language models share a semantic hub, so a word learned during pretraining is usable across languages. But what happens when a model learns a genuinely NEW word on the fly, from an in-context definition or a few demonstrations, in a single language? Does the freshly-bound meaning enter the language-agnostic hub—making the novel word instantly usable in any language—or does it stay tethered to the language it was taught in? We hypothesize the latter: in-context novel-word bindings are partially language-tethered, so the model uses the new word most reliably when queried in the teaching language, portability to other languages degrades with distance from the teaching language, and this binding-portability gap is larger than for pretrained translation-equivalent words and cannot be explained by the model's general cross-lingual competence. We test this on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using controlled nonce words paired with in-context definitions/demonstrations in a teaching language, then queried in the teaching language and in typologically diverse other languages. We measure per-language usage accuracy, decode whether the induced binding is present in the shared hub via logit-lens, and—crucially—use activation patching to test whether transplanting the mid-layer bound-concept representation across a language boundary restores cross-lingual usage, separating a binding-transfer failure from an output-language decoding failure. Metrics include the teaching-language portability gap, portability-vs-distance scaling, hub-binding presence, novel-vs-pretrained gap, and transplant-induced recovery with competence controls.
Experiments:
1) Novel-word teaching suite: Construct ~500 nonce words (pronounceable, script-controlled) each assigned a concrete meaning taught IN CONTEXT via (a) an explicit definition and (b) a few-shot demonstration set, framed entirely in a single TEACHING language. Meanings span concrete nouns, verbs, and simple relations with verifiable usage. For each item, build usage-test queries (fill-in / entailment / simple reasoning that requires the novel word's meaning) rendered in the TEACHING language and in several OTHER query languages spanning scripts and typological distance (English, French, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish). Include a matched control set of PRETRAINED words (real translation-equivalent words) taught with the same in-context framing, to compare novel-vs-pretrained portability. Native-speaker verify; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral portability gap (H1, core): Measure per-query-language usage accuracy for novel words as a function of the teaching language. Test H1: accuracy is highest when the query language equals the teaching language, and drops for other languages; define the teaching-language portability gap = accuracy(teaching-language) minus accuracy(other-language). Vary the teaching language across the panel to rule out an English-only artifact. Control for tokenizer fertility and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2).
3) Portability-vs-distance scaling and novel-vs-pretrained gap (H2): Test whether the portability gap scales with typological/script distance between teaching and query language, and whether it is LARGER for novel words than for the matched pretrained-word controls (whose hub alignment is already established) after controlling for base cross-lingual competence in each query language (nested regression; predict novel-word portability gap exceeds pretrained-word gap).
4) Hub-binding presence (mechanism): Using logit-lens/tuned-lens at the novel-word usage position, test whether the induced binding (the novel word's meaning) is decodable in the shared/dominant-language hub when queried in the teaching language versus other languages. Predict the bound concept is present in the hub for the teaching-language pass but weaker/absent when the query is in a distant language, indicating a language-tethered rather than fully hub-shared binding.
5) Cross-lingual transplant test (H3, core causal): For items used correctly in the teaching language but wrong in query language B, use activation patching to transplant the mid-layer bound-concept representation (from the teaching-language usage pass) into B's forward pass at the novel-word position. If this restores correct usage in B, the failure was a binding-transfer failure (the meaning was bound but not hub-shared), not a general incompetence in B. Complement with a decoding-only control: patch only late-layer output-language components to separate a binding-transfer failure from an output-language decoding failure. Report the share of each failure type per query language.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify the transplant is binding-specific (restores the novel word's meaning without switching output language or corrupting other content; measure off-target/language-mixing rate and preserve unrelated-word usage), and that it does not merely lift all items uniformly (gap-closing vs uniform-lift). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 shows stronger teaching-language tethering (larger portability gaps) than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether the gap correlates with the model's hub-sharedness and each language's training share.
Evaluation metrics: teaching-language portability gap (per teaching-query pair); portability-vs-distance scaling and novel-vs-pretrained gap (held-out R^2 over base-competence/fertility baselines); hub-binding presence (teaching vs other languages); binding-transfer vs decoding-failure error shares; transplant-induced cross-lingual usage recovery and specificity (off-target rate, unrelated-word preservation); cross-model tethering comparison and correlation with hub-sharedness and training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The portability gap could conflate with the model's general cross-lingual competence (it may fail in language B for any word); the pretrained-word control, conditioning on the model's base competence in B, and the transplant test (which restores usage in B by transferring only the bound concept) isolate a binding-transfer failure from generic incompetence—if the gap vanishes once competence is controlled, the hypothesis is refuted, an informative negative result. 2) Nonce words must be genuinely novel and not accidentally collide with real words or tokenize inconsistently across scripts; we validate novelty, control tokenization, and report both token- and character-level analyses. 3) In-context teaching quality may differ across teaching languages (a definition may be clearer in high-resource languages); we verify comparable teaching-language usage accuracy before comparing portability, and hold the definition content fixed up to translation. 4) Binding-transfer vs decoding failure may not separate cleanly; we use multiple patching granularities, the decoding-only control, and the logit-lens hub-presence check, reporting ambiguous cases. 5) Teaching-query distance is confounded with tokenizer fertility and resource level; partial correlations and the transplant causal test mitigate but may not fully remove confounds. 6) The transplant could inject fluent-but-wrong meanings or switch output language; binding-specificity and output-language preservation are hard constraints and we report the full tradeoff. 7) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM/Aya analyzed as less English-centric contrasts expected to show weaker tethering). 8) Logit-lens hub-presence estimates are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 9) If induced bindings turn out fully hub-shared (no portability gap beyond competence), this is an informative POSITIVE result showing in-context learning writes directly into the language-agnostic hub. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B models and short in-context teaching; may not extend to frontier scale or long multi-example curricula.

Name: language_dependent_incongruity_resolution_depth
Title: Laughing Later in a Second Language: A Language-Dependent Depth of Incongruity Resolution in Multilingual LLM Humor Comprehension
Short Hypothesis: Getting a joke requires a two-stage process—detecting an incongruity, then effortfully reinterpreting it to resolve it—and multilingual LLMs perform the RESOLUTION stage at a language-dependent depth: for jokes in lower-resource / English-distant languages the model resolves the incongruity at a deeper relative layer, with weaker and more brittle resolution, than for the SAME joke in its dominant language, mirroring the documented human L1-automatic / L2-effortful humor asymmetry. Consequently cross-lingual humor failures concentrate in a resolution-depth deficit (the incongruity is detected but not resolved) rather than in incongruity detection, and this deficit is causally recoverable by granting extra latent computation to the resolution step.
Related Work: Human psycholinguistics establishes the Comprehension-Elaboration / incongruity-resolution model of humor with a two-stage detection-then-reinterpretation process, and shows L1 humor processing is more automatic/intuitive while L2 processing is more controlled/reflective and effortful (Humor Perception Strategies in L1 and L2 2023; Cognitive Mechanisms of Foreign-Language Joke 2022; The Dynamics of Linguistic Humor Comprehension 2017; Incongruity-Resolution Theory 1999; Semantic Mechanisms of Humor / GTVH). Mechanistic humor work is monolingual: a single 'laughing head' localizes humor detection (Laughing Heads 2021), and figurative-meaning retrieval is a figurative-vs-literal tug-of-war (Tug-of-war 2025); benchmarks show a human-AI humor gap (HumorDB 2024; Oogiri-Master 2025) and that incongruity/ambiguity predict funniness (Funny Thing About Incongruity 2013; Oogiri-Corpus). Multilingual work establishes an English-scaffolded shared hub and English-centric latent reasoning (Semantic Hub 2024; Do Llamas Work in English 2024), and that latent reasoning is shallower/weaker for low-resource languages. CRITICALLY, all mechanistic humor work is monolingual and treats resolution as a fixed step; all cross-lingual humor work is behavioral/benchmark.
