NO prior work asks whether the DEPTH and success of the incongruity-RESOLUTION step is language-dependent, whether cross-lingual humor failure is a resolution (not detection) deficit, whether it is decodable as a resolution-depth signal, or whether granting extra latent computation to the resolution step selectively recovers humor comprehension—porting the human L1/L2 humor-processing asymmetry into LLM mechanisms. This differs from my prior phantom_pun_imposition proposal (source-form phonological leakage in translated puns): here the phenomenon is a language-dependent DEPTH of the general incongruity-resolution computation, grounded in the Comprehension-Elaboration theory, applying to jokes whose humor does survive translation.
Abstract: To get a joke you first notice something is off (incongruity detection) and then work to reinterpret it so it makes sense (resolution)—and decades of psycholinguistics show people do this more automatically in their first language and more effortfully in a second. Interpretability work shows multilingual language models detect humor and figurative meaning through localizable mechanisms, but studies them only in English. We ask a simple, previously untested question: is the DEPTH of incongruity resolution language-dependent in a multilingual LLM? We hypothesize that for a joke whose humor survives translation, the model resolves the incongruity at a deeper relative layer, and with weaker, more brittle resolution, when the joke is in a lower-resource or English-distant language than in its dominant language—mirroring the human L1-automatic / L2-effortful asymmetry. Under this account, cross-lingual humor failures are resolution failures (the incongruity is detected but not resolved), not detection failures, and are causally recoverable by granting extra latent computation to the resolution step. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using controlled multilingual joke suites (translation-robust jokes plus incongruous-but-unresolvable and coherent controls) across typologically diverse languages. Using logit-lens/truncation resolution-depth tracking, incongruity-detection vs resolution probes, activation patching, and a latent-compute-injection intervention, we measure the resolution-depth gap, decompose detection vs resolution failures, and test causal recovery. Metrics include per-language resolution-crystallization depth, detection-vs-resolution error shares, resolution-depth-vs-resource correlation, and compute-injection humor recovery with detection-preservation controls.
Experiments:
1) Translation-robust joke suite: Assemble ~500 jokes whose humor is grounded in a general incongruity-resolution structure that SURVIVES translation (situational/semantic-script jokes, not phonological puns—explicitly excluding form-dependent wordplay so the humor is genuinely available in every language). Translate each into typologically diverse languages spanning resource levels and scripts (English, French, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish), native-speaker verified to remain funny. Build matched controls: (a) INCONGRUITY-ONLY items (an incongruity is present but cannot be resolved—odd but not funny), (b) COHERENT non-joke items, (c) a resolved-paraphrase (explains the joke) as a comprehension anchor. Tasks: (i) funniness rating and is-this-a-joke forced choice; (ii) incongruity-detection probe (does the model flag something as incongruous/surprising?); (iii) resolution probe (can the model produce or select the reinterpretation that makes it funny?). Report inter-annotator agreement; release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral resolution deficit (H1, core): Per language, measure incongruity-detection accuracy and resolution accuracy separately. Test the prediction that DETECTION is comparably high across languages (the model notices the incongruity everywhere) while RESOLUTION accuracy (and funniness recognition) drops for lower-resource / English-distant languages on the SAME jokes. Verify near-zero funniness on INCONGRUITY-ONLY and COHERENT controls (isolating genuine resolution, not surface cues) and correct handling of the resolved-paraphrase anchor. Control for tokenizer fertility and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test language predicts resolution beyond detection and fertility). Condition on jokes the model gets in English, so a resolution gap cannot be knowledge absence.
3) Resolution-depth measurement (H2): Using logit-lens/tuned-lens and hidden-state truncation (early exit), identify the 'resolution-crystallization layer'—the layer at which the reinterpretation/funny reading first becomes and stays available (e.g., the resolved-paraphrase meaning or the funny target token becomes decodable). Also locate the humor-detection signal (following the laughing-head finding). Test that resolution crystallizes at a DEEPER normalized layer, and more weakly (lower peak), for lower-resource languages, while detection crystallizes at comparable depth. Correlate resolution-depth gap with resource-distance from English (Spearman; held-out R^2 over fertility).
4) Detection-vs-resolution error decomposition via patching (H3, core): For jokes gotten in English but failed in language B, patch (a) the shared-hub resolution representation (the reinterpretation state, from the English pass or the resolved-paraphrase) into B's forward pass, and (b) only the detection-related components. If B already has the detection signal but only the resolution patch restores humor recognition, classify as a resolution failure. Report detection-vs-resolution error shares per language, predicting resolution failures dominate and grow with resource-distance.
5) Core causal intervention (latent-compute injection): Grant extra latent computation to the resolution step in low-resource-language jokes—via inserted pause/filler tokens before the funniness judgment, logit-lens-guided repetition of the mid/late blocks where resolution occurs, or steering along a difference-in-means 'resolution' direction (resolved vs unresolved passes)—and measure per-language humor-recognition recovery. Predict SELECTIVE recovery: languages with deep/weak resolution (high resolution-depth gap) gain most; already-shallow-resolving languages gain little (interaction test). Compute recovery elasticity = humor-recognition gain per unit resolution-depth gap. Compare against baselines: whole-hub English steering, uniform extra compute for all languages, and a random-direction control.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify the intervention is resolution-specific: it must IMPROVE genuine jokes WITHOUT making the model rate INCONGRUITY-ONLY or COHERENT controls as funny (a symmetric over-humor check), must not switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), and preserve fluency. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show a sharper cross-lingual resolution-depth gap than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether the gap correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the resolution direction and each language's training share. Qualitatively compare the per-language resolution-depth pattern against the human L1-automatic / L2-effortful humor literature (direction, not identical mechanism).
Evaluation metrics: per-language incongruity-detection vs resolution accuracy and funniness recognition (vs incongruity-only/coherent controls); resolution-crystallization depth and peak vs detection-crystallization depth, and their resource-distance correlation (held-out R^2 over fertility); detection-vs-resolution error shares and patching-restoration rate; selective latent-compute-injection humor recovery and elasticity vs baselines, with over-humor specificity (no spurious funniness on controls), off-target rate, fluency; cross-model resolution-depth-gap comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The resolution deficit could conflate with a general competence gap; the key controls are conditioning on English-gotten jokes, the incongruity-only/coherent controls, the detection-vs-resolution decomposition, and the patching test (which restores humor by transferring only the resolution state)—if resolution gaps vanish once detection/competence is controlled, the hypothesis is refuted, an informative negative result. 2) Ensuring a joke's humor genuinely survives translation is essential and hard; we exclude phonological/wordplay jokes, native-speaker verify that translations remain funny, use graded funniness, report inter-annotator agreement, and exclude items whose humor is lost. 3) Funniness ratings are noisy and culturally variable; we use forced-choice is-this-a-joke and funnier-of-pair alongside Likert, and anchor with the resolved-paraphrase comprehension probe rather than relying on absolute ratings. 4) Separating incongruity detection from resolution behaviorally and representationally is subtle; we use multiple probe formats and patching granularities and report ambiguous cases. 5) Humor comprehension may be weak in 7-8B models generally; we verify a measurable English humor-recognition and resolution effect first as a gate—if the model does not resolve incongruity even in English, the cross-lingual question is moot, itself an informative finding. 6) Language is confounded with tokenizer fertility, script, and resource level; partial correlations and the causal patching/injection tests mitigate but may not fully remove confounds. 7) Logit-lens/truncation resolution-depth estimates are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated across lenses and early-exit. 8) The latent-compute intervention could induce spurious funniness or harm fluency; the symmetric over-humor constraint (no funniness on unresolvable/coherent controls) is a hard requirement and we report the full tradeoff. 9) The human-LLM comparison (L1-automatic / L2-effortful humor processing) is qualitative, not a claim of identical mechanism. 10) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM/Aya analyzed as less English-centric contrasts). 11) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: language_dependent_self_repair_redundancy
Title: A Brittle Backup in Low-Resource Tongues: Language-Dependent Emergent Self-Repair Redundancy in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: The emergent self-repair machinery of transformers — downstream components that spontaneously compensate when an upstream component is ablated (the Hydra effect, anti-erasure neurons, copy-suppression backup) — is language-dependent: the same forward pass has WEAKER compensatory redundancy when the model processes a lower-resource / English-distant language, so ablating a component that is repaired in English is NOT repaired (or is under-repaired) in the low-resource language. This brittleness of the backup circuit, not just a weaker primary circuit, is a distinct, measurable cause of cross-lingual fragility: the low-resource forward pass has thinner redundancy and thus larger, more error-inducing perturbation sensitivity, mirroring the human finding that L2 speakers must rely on effortful, less automatic self-repair.
Related Work: Self-repair is a robust, purely MONOLINGUAL finding: ablating a component triggers downstream compensation via the Hydra effect and late-MLP anti-erasure (The Hydra Effect 2023; Explorations of Self-Repair 2024), copy-suppression backup heads (Copy Suppression 2023/2024), attention self-repair (GIM 2025), and LayerNorm rescaling — all studied only in English and framed as an interpretability nuisance. The Validation Gap (2025) shows a monolingual computation-vs-validation dissociation. Multilingual mechanistic work localizes cross-lingual FAILURE to a shared English-scaffolded hub and late-layer language-transition failures (Do Llamas Work in English 2024; Lost in Multilinguality 2025; Paths Not Taken 2025; Mechanistic Language Confusion 2025) and treats the PRIMARY circuit's strength as the variable. Human psycholinguistics shows L2/heritage speakers self-repair MORE and more effortfully than L1 speakers, relying on less-automatic monitoring (Self-Repair in L1/L2/HL 2022; Verbal Self-Monitoring in L2 2016; Self-Repair in Bilingual Speech 2013). CRITICALLY, no prior work asks whether the model's EMERGENT SELF-REPAIR mechanism itself — the compensatory redundancy that makes a forward pass robust to perturbation — is language-dependent, whether low-resource-language passes have thinner backup redundancy (weaker Hydra/anti-erasure/copy-suppression response), whether this predicts cross-lingual perturbation-sensitivity and error rates beyond primary-circuit strength, or whether the redundancy can be transplanted across a language boundary. We reframe cross-lingual fragility as a self-repair-redundancy deficit — a property of the backup circuit, not the primary one — mirroring the human L1-automatic / L2-effortful repair asymmetry, orthogonal to all prior primary-circuit / hub-alignment accounts and to my own prior first-step-recovery and validation-deficit proposals (which concern behavioral recovery from a planted error and detecting one's own errors, not the intrinsic compensatory redundancy of the forward pass).
Abstract: When you ablate a component inside a transformer, other components spontaneously compensate — a robust emergent phenomenon called self-repair (the Hydra effect, anti-erasure neurons, copy-suppression backup heads). This redundancy makes the forward pass resilient, and it has been studied entirely in English. We ask a simple, previously untested question about multilingual models: is self-repair language-dependent? We hypothesize that the same component, when ablated, is repaired in English but under-repaired in a lower-resource or English-distant language, so low-resource forward passes carry thinner compensatory redundancy and are therefore more brittle — more perturbation-sensitive and more error-prone — not merely because their primary circuit is weaker but because their backup circuit is. This mirrors the human finding that second-language speakers self-repair more effortfully and less automatically than native speakers. We test this on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM on matched factual-recall and reasoning tasks across typologically diverse languages. For each attention head/layer we measure the self-repair response (downstream direct-effect compensation) after ablation, per language, and compute a per-language redundancy index. We then test whether this redundancy predicts cross-lingual perturbation-sensitivity and error rates beyond primary-circuit strength, decompose the repair into its known motifs (Hydra compensation, anti-erasure, copy-suppression) to see which is language-attenuated, and run a causal transplant that grafts the English backup response into the low-resource pass to test whether restoring redundancy improves robustness. Metrics include per-language self-repair completeness, redundancy-vs-error prediction, motif-level attenuation, and transplant-induced robustness recovery with specificity controls.
Experiments:
1) Matched multilingual task suite: Build ~600 items of (a) factual recall (mLAMA-style, verified per-language answers) and (b) reasoning (MGSM arithmetic and a controlled k-step suite with verified gold), each rendered in typologically diverse languages spanning resource levels and scripts (English, French, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish, Bengali), native-speaker verified. Restrict analysis to items the model answers CORRECTLY in each language, so self-repair is measured on intact computations. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Per-language self-repair completeness (H1, core): Following the Hydra-effect / self-repair methodology, for each attention head (and each layer) ablate it and measure (i) its direct effect on the correct-answer logit and (ii) the downstream compensatory change (how much later components restore the ablated direct effect). Define per-head self-repair completeness = fraction of the ablated direct effect that downstream components recover, computed separately per language on matched items. Aggregate to a per-language REDUNDANCY INDEX (mean completeness across the head set most relevant to the task, identified via direct-effect ranking). Test H1: self-repair completeness / redundancy is systematically LOWER for lower-resource / English-distant languages on the SAME computations. Control for tokenizer fertility and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test language predicts redundancy beyond fertility and primary-circuit direct-effect magnitude).
3) Primary-vs-backup dissociation (core novelty): Show the effect is a BACKUP-circuit property, not merely a weaker primary circuit. Measure per-language primary-circuit strength (unablated direct effect of the key heads) and redundancy separately, and test whether redundancy is lower in low-resource languages EVEN after matching on primary-circuit strength (partial correlation / matched-pairs). Predict a redundancy deficit that survives controlling for primary strength.
4) Redundancy predicts fragility (H2): Measure per-language, per-item perturbation-sensitivity: apply matched small perturbations (single-head ablation, activation noise injection at a fixed layer, or a distractor token) and record the induced error rate / logit drop. Test whether per-language redundancy index predicts perturbation-sensitivity and natural error rate BETTER than primary-circuit strength alone (nested regression, held-out R^2). Prediction: thinner redundancy -> higher fragility -> more errors, beyond what primary strength explains.
5) Motif-level decomposition (mechanism): Decompose the self-repair response into its known motifs and identify which is language-attenuated: (a) Hydra-style downstream attention compensation (measure the compensatory increase in a downstream head's direct effect), (b) late-MLP anti-erasure (measure the anti-erasure neurons' response), (c) copy-suppression backup, and (d) final-LayerNorm rescaling. Report per-language motif contributions and test which motif's response shrinks most in low-resource languages.
6) Core causal transplant test (H3): Graft the English backup response into the low-resource forward pass: on a low-resource item where an ablated head is NOT repaired, patch in the downstream compensatory activations (the Hydra/anti-erasure response) recorded from the matched English pass at the corresponding layers, and test whether the correct answer is restored (repair-transfer rate). Conversely, verify that removing the English backup response reduces English robustness to the low-resource level. This isolates the redundancy deficit as causal, not a correlate. Compare against baselines: whole-hub English steering, primary-circuit steering (boosting the primary direct effect instead of the backup), and a random-direction control.
7) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify the transplant is redundancy-specific (restores robustness/repair without switching output language — measure off-target/language-mixing rate — and without changing the answer content on unperturbed items), and that gains are gap-closing not uniform-lift. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show a sharper cross-lingual redundancy gap than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether the redundancy gap correlates with each model's hub English-centricity and each language's training share. Qualitatively compare the language-dependent self-repair pattern against the human L1-automatic / L2-effortful self-repair literature (direction, not identical mechanism).
Evaluation metrics: per-language self-repair completeness and redundancy index (partial correlation with resource-distance over fertility and primary-strength; held-out R^2); primary-vs-backup dissociation (redundancy deficit surviving primary-strength matching); redundancy's prediction of perturbation-sensitivity and error rate vs primary-strength baseline (held-out R^2); per-language motif-level self-repair contributions and which motif is attenuated; transplant repair-transfer rate and English-robustness-removal (bidirectional causal test); specificity (off-target/language-mixing rate, answer preservation on unperturbed items, gap-closing vs uniform-lift); cross-model redundancy-gap comparison and correlation with hub English-centricity and training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Self-repair is known to be noisy, imperfect, and prompt-variable even monolingually (Explorations of Self-Repair 2024), so per-language completeness estimates will be noisy; we average over many heads and items, report variance, and use matched items to reduce noise. 2) A redundancy deficit could conflate with a weaker primary circuit; the primary-vs-backup dissociation (Exp 3, matching on primary strength) and the causal transplant (Exp 6, which restores robustness by grafting only the backup response) are designed to isolate the backup-circuit property — if the deficit vanishes once primary strength is controlled, the hypothesis is refuted, an informative negative result. 3) Ablation-based self-repair metrics are themselves distorted by self-repair (the reason GIM 2025 exists); we cross-validate the repair measurement with a GIM-style / attention-aware attribution to avoid circularity and report robustness across measurement methods. 4) Language is confounded with tokenizer fertility, script, and resource level; partial correlations and the transplant causal test mitigate but may not fully remove confounds. 5) The transplant requires aligning corresponding layers/positions across the English and low-resource passes, which is imperfect (different token lengths); we align at matched functional positions and report alignment quality. 6) The transplant could switch output language or inject wrong content; answer-preservation and off-target checks are hard specificity constraints and we report the full tradeoff. 7) Restricting to correctly-answered items may bias toward easier items; we report the redundancy gap across difficulty bins. 8) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM's less English-centric hub analyzed as a contrast expected to show a smaller redundancy gap). 9) The human-LLM comparison (L1-automatic / L2-effortful self-repair) is qualitative/structural, not a claim of identical mechanism. 10) If self-repair redundancy is language-INVARIANT once primary strength is controlled, this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the emergent backup machinery is language-agnostic despite an English-scaffolded hub, and would relocate cross-lingual fragility entirely to the primary circuit — valuable either way. 11) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: crosslingual_premise_integration_tax
Title: Two Premises, Two Languages, One Conclusion: A Language-Heterogeneity Tax on Multi-Premise Reasoning in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: When the premises needed to reach a conclusion are stated in DIFFERENT languages within a single context (e.g. premise A in French, premise B in Hindi), multilingual LLMs pay a measurable integration tax: multi-hop and multi-premise inference accuracy drops relative to the same premises stated all in one language, even when the model comprehends each premise in isolation. This 'language-heterogeneity tax' is not a comprehension failure but a binding failure — the two premises are correctly encoded but fail to be co-activated into a single shared-hub reasoning state when they arrive in different languages — and it scales with the typological distance between the premise languages, not merely with either language's resource level.
Related Work: Prior work shows multilingual reasoning routes through an English-centric latent space (Do Multilingual LLMs Think In English 2025; Latent Reasoners 2026), that knowledge-free reasoning transfers cross-lingually while knowledge does not (Cross-Lingual Knowledge-Free Reasoners 2024), that language-specific signal can be ablated to improve reasoning (When Less Language is More 2025; MRRE 2025; SLAM 2025), and that language mixing in OUTPUT reasoning traces affects performance (Language Mixing 2025). Cross-lingual ICL steering (Language Steering 2026; BridgeX-ICL 2025) and multi-document evidence integration (MultiFinBen 2025; Hierarchical Curriculum 2026) exist but are behavioral/benchmark, monolingual-per-document, or about output language. CRITICALLY, all prior work either (a) presents a whole problem in ONE language and studies routing, or (b) studies language mixing in the model's own OUTPUT. NONE isolates the case where the INPUT premises required for one inference are deliberately split across languages, tests whether integrating them incurs a tax beyond single-premise comprehension, decomposes it into comprehension vs binding failure, or ties it to inter-premise typological distance and a shared-hub co-activation mechanism. We reframe cross-lingual reasoning failure as a within-context multi-premise INTEGRATION/binding problem, a distinct behavioral phenomenon with a clean single-language control and a mechanistic locus.
Abstract: People can hear one fact in English and another in Spanish and effortlessly combine them, because meaning, not surface language, is what gets integrated. Multilingual language models are said to build a shared semantic hub that should make such integration language-agnostic. We test this directly with a phenomenon no prior work has isolated: when the two (or more) premises needed to reach a conclusion are stated in DIFFERENT languages within a single prompt, can the model still combine them? We hypothesize a language-heterogeneity tax — multi-premise and multi-hop inference accuracy drops when premises are split across languages relative to an all-one-language control, even when the model comprehends each premise in isolation — and that this is a BINDING failure: the premises are correctly encoded but fail to co-activate into one shared-hub reasoning state, with the tax scaling with the typological distance BETWEEN the premise languages rather than either language's resource level. We test this on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using controlled two-premise syllogisms and multi-hop factual chains where each premise's language is independently varied, with single-premise comprehension checks and an all-one-language baseline. Using logit-lens tracking of whether both premises are jointly represented in the shared hub, activation patching to separate comprehension from binding failures, and a co-activation steering intervention, we measure the tax, its distance scaling, its mechanistic locus, and a causal fix. Metrics include the heterogeneity-tax accuracy gap, comprehension-vs-binding error shares, inter-premise-distance prediction, joint-hub-representation strength, and intervention-induced recovery.
Experiments:
1) Split-premise reasoning suite: Construct ~600 items that each REQUIRE combining two (or three) premises to answer: (a) two-premise syllogisms/transitive inferences (A>B, B>C -> A>C), (b) multi-hop factual chains (X born in country Y; capital of Y is Z -> where is X's birth-country capital), (c) constraint-combination items (a constraint given in one premise plus a fact in another). For each item, independently assign each premise a language from a panel spanning scripts, resource levels, and typological families (English, French, German, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish). Conditions: (i) ALL-ONE-LANGUAGE (both premises + question in language L, for each L) — the baseline; (ii) SPLIT (premise 1 in L1, premise 2 in L2, L1!=L2), crossing many L1xL2 pairs; question language held fixed and also varied. Include single-premise COMPREHENSION checks (query each premise alone in its language). Native-speaker verify translations and gold answers; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral heterogeneity tax (H1, core): Measure accuracy in SPLIT vs ALL-ONE-LANGUAGE conditions, holding content fixed. Define the heterogeneity-tax GAP = mean single-language accuracy minus split accuracy. Test that SPLIT is reliably worse. Crucially, condition on items where BOTH single-premise comprehension checks pass in their respective languages, so the tax cannot be a per-premise comprehension gap. Control for tokenizer fertility, per-premise-language resource level, and question language (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test heterogeneity adds predictive power beyond each premise's standalone difficulty).
3) Inter-premise-distance scaling (H2): Test whether the tax scales with the TYPOLOGICAL/embedding distance BETWEEN L1 and L2 (not the distance of either from English, and not either's resource level). Predict split pairs of close languages (e.g. French-Spanish) show a smaller tax than distant pairs (e.g. Arabic-Hindi) at matched per-premise competence. Model comparison: inter-premise distance vs (resource level of the weaker language) vs (distance from English) as predictors of the tax (held-out R^2).
4) Comprehension-vs-binding decomposition (H3, core): For SPLIT items failed but with both premises individually comprehended, use logit-lens/tuned-lens to test whether both premises are JOINTLY represented in the shared hub at the integration position (joint-hub-representation strength) versus only one being active (the other 'dropped'). Activation patching: patch the shared-hub representation of the dropped premise (from its single-premise pass) into the integration position of the split pass and test whether the inference is fixed. If patching the co-representation restores the answer, classify the failure as a binding/co-activation failure, not comprehension. Report comprehension-vs-binding error shares per language pair, predicting binding failures dominate and grow with inter-premise distance.
5) Core causal intervention (co-activation steering): At middle layers, steer both premises' representations toward a common shared-hub (English-anchored) subspace before the integration step — a difference-in-means 'co-activation' direction that reduces the language-specific separation between the two premise representations — and measure whether split-condition accuracy recovers toward the single-language baseline. Predict SELECTIVE recovery for high-tax (distant-language-pair) items, little effect on close pairs or single-language items (interaction test). Compare against baselines: translate-both-premises-to-English (a strong practical baseline), whole-hub English steering (MRRE 2025), language-specific ablation (When Less Language is More 2025), and a random-direction control. Compute recovery elasticity = accuracy gain per unit baseline tax, correlated with the H2 distance.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify the intervention is integration-specific (improves split multi-premise items without changing single-premise comprehension, without switching output language — off-target/language-mixing rate — and without harming single-language reasoning), and is gap-closing not uniform-lift. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show a larger heterogeneity tax than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether the tax correlates with the model's hub English-centricity and the joint-hub-representation strength.
Evaluation metrics: heterogeneity-tax GAP (split vs single-language, comprehension-conditioned); tax-vs-inter-premise-distance correlation and model comparison (held-out R^2 over resource-level and distance-from-English baselines); comprehension-vs-binding error shares and patching-fix rate; joint-hub-representation strength (both premises co-active) vs premise-drop rate; co-activation-steering recovery and elasticity vs baselines, with single-premise-comprehension and single-language-reasoning preservation (specificity), off-target rate; cross-model tax comparison and correlation with hub English-centricity.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The tax could conflate with a per-premise comprehension gap; the key control is conditioning on items where BOTH single-premise comprehension checks pass, plus the comprehension-vs-binding patching decomposition — if the tax vanishes once single-premise comprehension is controlled, the hypothesis is refuted, an informative negative result. 2) Splitting premises across languages could introduce a discourse-coherence confound (a code-switched prompt is unusual); we include a within-language code-switched-register control and matched single-language paraphrases to separate 'integration across meaning boundaries' from 'unusual input format'. 3) Inter-premise distance is correlated with each language's resource level and script; the model comparison (inter-premise distance vs weaker-language resource vs distance-from-English) and matched-competence pairing isolate the inter-premise-distance pathway, but residual confounds may remain. 4) Comprehension vs binding may not separate cleanly; we use multiple patching granularities, the logit-lens joint-representation check, and report ambiguous cases. 5) Question language may interact with premise languages; we vary and control it. 6) The co-activation intervention could harm single-language reasoning or switch output language; single-language-reasoning and single-premise-comprehension preservation plus off-target rate are hard specificity constraints, and we compare against the translate-to-English baseline to show the mechanistic account adds value. 7) Logit-lens joint-representation estimates are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 8) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM/Aya analyzed as less English-centric contrasts expected to show a smaller tax). 9) If no tax is found — split-language premises are integrated as well as single-language ones — this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the shared hub genuinely integrates meaning independent of surface language, valuable either way. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: conversational_language_anchor_decay
Title: Drifting Back to English: Progressive Decay of the Language Anchor Across Multilingual Conversations
Short Hypothesis: As a multilingual conversation in a non-dominant language grows longer, a multilingual LLM progressively regresses toward its dominant (English) processing mode: turn by turn, the model's internal 'target-language anchor' weakens and its representations re-align toward the English-scaffolded shared hub, so later-turn answers become measurably more English-scaffolded, more inconsistent with the language the model was correctly using in early turns, and more prone to unintended language mixing — even though the same query answered as a single turn would be handled correctly. This anchor decay is a distinct temporal, position-dependent phenomenon (not a static cross-lingual gap or generic factual drift), is carried by a decodable per-turn language-anchor signal whose strength declines with conversation depth and typological distance from English, and is causally reversible by re-injecting the target-language anchor at each turn without retraining.
Related Work: Two literatures meet but have never been connected. (1) Conversational-drift work shows linear concept directions flip over a conversation (Linear representations change over a conversation 2026), instruction/persona/identity drift and attention decay over turns (Measuring Instruction (In)Stability 2024; Examining Identity Drift 2024; LLMs Get Lost in Multi-Turn 2025; Contextual Feature Drift 2024), and multi-turn factual inconsistency (Firm or Fickle 2025; D-SMART 2025) — but ALL of this is monolingual (English) and treats drift as concept/instruction/factual degradation, never as a change in the model's underlying PROCESSING LANGUAGE. (2) Cross-lingual mechanistic work establishes an English-scaffolded shared hub with late-layer language-specific decoding, and locates cross-lingual inconsistency in static, single-turn factual recall / entity-alignment / language-transition failures (Lost in Multilinguality 2025; Paths Not Taken 2025; Entity-Level Alignment 2025; Language-Specific Latent Process Hinders 2025; Do Llamas Work in English 2024). Beyond Early-Token Bias (2025) shows position bias has language-specific nuances but concerns single-prompt positional weighting, not multi-turn language drift. CRITICALLY, no prior work asks whether the model's target-LANGUAGE state itself DRIFTS across a multilingual conversation — whether sustained interaction in a non-English language causes a progressive, position-dependent regression toward English-scaffolded processing (declining cross-lingual consistency with the model's own earlier turns, rising language mixing, and English-default answer pull) that a single-turn version of the same query would not show. This reframes multilingual inconsistency from a static per-query property into a temporal anchor-decay dynamic with a decodable per-turn signal and a causal per-turn re-anchoring fix, orthogonal to all my prior (single-turn, static) proposals and to the register-drift proposal (which concerned grammatical register consistency within a single generation, not the model's cross-turn processing-language state and downstream accuracy/consistency).
Abstract: A model chatting with you in Hindi should stay in Hindi — not just on the surface, but in how it internally represents and reasons about your questions. We ask a simple, previously untested question: as a conversation in a non-dominant language grows longer, does a multilingual LLM progressively drift back toward its dominant (English) processing mode? We hypothesize a language-anchor decay: turn by turn, the model's internal target-language anchor weakens and its representations re-align toward the English-scaffolded shared hub, so later-turn answers become more English-scaffolded, more inconsistent with the language the model was correctly using early in the conversation, and more prone to unintended language mixing — even when the same query, asked as a single turn, is handled correctly. We predict this decay is position-dependent (worsening with conversation depth), scales with typological distance from English, is carried by a decodable per-turn language-anchor signal, and is causally reversible by re-injecting the target-language anchor at each turn. We test this on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using controlled multi-turn conversations in typologically diverse languages, with matched single-turn and same-language-length controls. Using per-turn logit-lens tracking of the language-anchor signal, difference-in-means language-direction probes, activation patching, and a per-turn re-anchoring intervention, we measure the decay curve, its distance scaling, its mechanistic locus, and a causal fix. Metrics include per-turn cross-lingual consistency decay, language-mixing rate over turns, anchor-signal decay, and re-anchoring recovery with content-preservation controls.
Experiments:
1) Multi-turn conversation suite: Build ~400 conversation scripts each consisting of a sequence of independent, self-contained factual/reasoning questions (mLAMA/MGSM-derived, with verified gold answers) posed over N=1..12 turns entirely in a target language, so each turn's correctness is gold-verifiable and does not depend on earlier answers (isolating language drift from topic dependency). Instantiate across typologically diverse languages spanning scripts and resource levels (English, French, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish). Critically, use a REPEATED-QUESTION design where the SAME question appears both early and late in the conversation (and as a stand-alone single turn), so we can measure whether the model's answer/processing for an identical query degrades with conversation depth. Include matched controls: (a) SINGLE-TURN (the query alone), (b) SAME-LANGUAGE-LENGTH (a long conversation but the drift measured on a repeated query, to separate length from language drift), and (c) an English conversation of matched length (to establish the anchor toward which drift proceeds). Native-speaker verify; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral anchor-decay map (H1, core): For the repeated query, measure per-turn (i) accuracy, (ii) cross-lingual consistency with the SINGLE-TURN answer (does the late-turn answer still match what the model correctly produced when the query stood alone?), and (iii) unintended language-mixing / off-target rate in the output. Test H1: for non-dominant-language conversations, accuracy and self-consistency DECAY with turn position while language-mixing RISES, whereas the single-turn and English-conversation controls stay flat. Fit a per-language decay slope. Control for tokenizer fertility and total context length (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test conversation depth predicts decay beyond raw context length).
3) Distance scaling (H2): Test whether the per-language decay slope scales with typological/embedding distance from English (and with the model's baseline English-centricity), better than with resource level alone (model comparison, held-out R^2). Predict steeper anchor decay for English-distant languages; near-zero decay for English.
4) Mechanistic anchor tracking (H3): Extract a difference-in-means 'language-anchor' direction (target-language vs English-scaffolded processing) and, at each turn, project the residual stream / apply logit-lens to measure how strongly the query is processed in the target-language space vs the English hub. Test whether the anchor signal DECAYS across turns (declining target-language projection, rising English-hub decodability), mirroring the behavioral decay, and whether anchor decay predicts per-turn accuracy/consistency loss (mediation regression; held-out R^2). Compare against the attention-decay account (Instruction (In)Stability 2024): test whether attention to the early target-language turns declines and correlates with anchor decay.
5) Error decomposition via patching: For repeated queries answered correctly early but wrong/inconsistent late, patch (a) the target-language anchor representation (from the early-turn or single-turn pass) into the late-turn forward pass, and (b) only late-layer decoding components. If (a) restores the correct target-language answer, the failure is anchor decay (the model drifted to English processing), not knowledge loss. Report anchor-decay vs knowledge-loss error shares as a function of turn depth.
6) Core causal intervention (per-turn re-anchoring): At each turn, re-inject the target-language anchor — add a steering vector along the language-anchor direction calibrated to restore the early-turn anchor magnitude — at mid/late layers, train-free. Measure whether per-turn accuracy, self-consistency, and language-mixing recover toward the single-turn baseline. Predict SELECTIVE recovery for high-decay (English-distant, deep-conversation) turns, little effect on English or shallow turns (interaction test). Compute recovery elasticity = consistency gain per unit baseline anchor decay. Compare against baselines: (a) prompt-reinforcement (restate 'respond in <language>' each turn), (b) whole-hub English steering (predicted to WORSEN, since it pushes toward the drift target), (c) split-softmax attention-decay fix (Instruction (In)Stability 2024), and a random-direction control.
7) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify re-anchoring is language-specific (restores target-language processing without changing answer CONTENT or degrading English-conversation performance; measure content-faithfulness, off-target/language-mixing rate, fluency), and that gains are gap-closing not uniform-lift. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show steeper anchor decay than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether decay slope correlates with the model's baseline English-centricity (single-turn logit-lens English-routing strength) and each language's training share.
Evaluation metrics: per-turn accuracy, single-turn-consistency, and language-mixing decay curves and per-language decay slopes (vs single-turn / same-language-length / English controls); decay-slope-vs-distance scaling and model comparison over resource-level and context-length baselines (held-out R^2); anchor-signal decay and its mediation of behavioral decay (held-out R^2); attention-decay correlation; anchor-decay vs knowledge-loss error shares by depth; per-turn re-anchoring recovery and elasticity vs baselines, with content-faithfulness, English-conversation preservation, off-target/language-mixing rate (specificity); cross-model decay comparison and correlation with English-centricity and training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The decay could conflate with generic long-context degradation (any drift, not language-specific); the SAME-LANGUAGE-LENGTH and matched-length English controls, the repeated-query design (same query early vs late), and the anchor-decay-vs-knowledge-loss patching decomposition isolate a LANGUAGE-anchor effect from raw context-length or factual drift — if decay vanishes once length is controlled, the hypothesis is refuted, an informative negative result. 2) Self-consistency-with-single-turn assumes the single-turn answer is the correct reference; we restrict repeated queries to those the model answers correctly single-turn, so late-turn divergence is genuine drift, not correction. 3) Conversation depth is confounded with total context length and tokenizer fertility (non-English turns are longer in tokens); we control for token-length and report depth-in-turns vs depth-in-tokens separately. 4) Language distance is correlated with resource level and script; partial correlations and the causal re-anchoring test mitigate but may not fully remove confounds. 5) The language-anchor direction from difference-in-means may entangle content or script features; we use multiple extraction methods, per-turn logit-lens cross-validation, and specificity controls. 6) The re-anchoring intervention could harm answer content or over-formalize; content-faithfulness and English-conversation preservation are hard constraints and we report the full tradeoff, comparing against the prompt-reinforcement and split-softmax baselines to show the mechanistic account adds value. 7) Attention-decay may be an alternative (not competing) mechanism; we test their correlation rather than claiming exclusivity. 8) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM/Aya analyzed as less English-centric contrasts expected to show shallower decay). 9) Off-policy conversation scripts (fixed questions) may under- or over-estimate drift relative to genuinely interactive dialogue; we note ecological-validity limits and, where feasible, replicate on self-chat / model-generated conversations. 10) If NO anchor decay is found — the model maintains its target-language processing across arbitrarily long conversations — this is an informative POSITIVE result showing a stable per-turn language anchor despite the English-scaffolded hub, valuable either way. 11) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: language_conditioned_anchoring_gain
Title: A Heavier Anchor in a Foreign Tongue: A Language-Conditioned Gain on a Shared Anchoring Direction in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs exhibit anchoring bias (an uninformative or irrelevant anchor number pulls a subsequent numerical estimate toward it), but the STRENGTH of this pull is LANGUAGE-DEPENDENT: the same anchor and the same estimation question, translated into a lower-resource / English-distant language, produce a stronger assimilation toward the anchor because the anchor-integration adjustment step is more shallow and less resisted in non-dominant languages. Crucially, this is not a separate per-language anchoring computation but a language-conditioned GAIN applied to a single, largely shared anchoring direction: the query language sets how strongly the anchor's magnitude is written into the final estimate, so the per-language bias is predictable from a low-dimensional gain and is causally correctable by rescaling that direction without harming numeric competence.
Related Work: Recent work confirms anchoring bias is robust in LLMs and acts in SHALLOW layers, reweighting output distributions, with reasoning offering partial mitigation (Anchors in the Machine 2025; An Empirical Study of the Anchoring Effect / SynAnchors 2025; Anchoring bias experimental study 2025; Anchored Answers positional-bias mechanism 2024 localizes MCQ 'A'-anchoring to specific MLP value vectors). Cross-lingual cognitive-bias work is behavioral only: Cross-linguistic patterns of cognitive biases (English/Hebrew/Russian 2026) and Bilingual comparison of Mandarin/English bias tasks (2017) show bias manifestations differ by input language, and multilingual-calibration work shows non-English languages are worse-calibrated with the signal best read from late-intermediate layers (LACE 2025; Calibration Across Layers 2025). Human numeric-anchoring work shows anchors bias even calculation-based estimates and transcend scales (Biased calculations 2011; Semantic cross-scale anchoring 2016). CRITICALLY, all LLM-anchoring mechanism work is monolingual (English) and treats anchoring strength as a fixed quantity; all cross-lingual bias work is purely behavioral and never asks whether the anchoring MAGNITUDE is language-conditioned, whether it is a low-dimensional GAIN on a shared anchoring direction rather than distinct per-language anchoring, whether the gain tracks resource-distance, or whether rescaling that direction causally equalizes anchoring across languages. We uniquely connect the shallow-layer anchoring-direction finding to the multilingual shared-hub literature, reframing cross-lingual anchoring variation as 'same direction, language-set gain', with a predictive metric and a targeted, competence-preserving causal fix. This is distinct from my prior moral/sycophancy/personality-gain proposals (different bias, numeric domain) and from all my grammatical/lexical imposition proposals.
Abstract: People give different numerical estimates depending on an irrelevant anchor they were just shown, and language models inherit this anchoring bias in their shallow layers. We ask a simple, previously untested question: is the STRENGTH of anchoring the same across languages? We hypothesize that when the identical anchor and estimation question are posed in a lower-resource or English-distant language, a multilingual LLM assimilates more strongly toward the anchor, because the adjustment step that resists the anchor is shallower and weaker in non-dominant languages. Crucially, we propose this is not a separate per-language anchoring computation but a language-conditioned GAIN applied to a single, largely shared anchoring direction — the query language sets how strongly the anchor's magnitude is written into the final estimate. This makes three testable predictions: (1) an anchoring direction is shared across languages (high cross-lingual alignment); (2) the per-language anchoring magnitude is captured by a low-dimensional gain predictable from language resource-distance, not merely by numeric competence; and (3) rescaling the shared direction at inference causally reproduces another language's anchoring and can equalize it across languages without harming numeric accuracy. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using controlled anchor-then-estimate items (numerical commonsense and arithmetic estimation, with and without an irrelevant anchor) translated across typologically diverse languages. Combining behavioral assimilation measurement, difference-in-means anchoring-direction extraction, logit-lens gain readout, activation patching, and gain-steering, we measure the language-conditioned anchoring gain, its resource-distance scaling, its shared-direction locus, and a causal fix. Metrics include per-language assimilation-toward-anchor, cross-lingual direction alignment, gain predictive R-squared over competence baselines, and steering-induced equalization with numeric-competence controls.
Experiments:
1) Controlled anchor-estimate suite: Build ~600 estimation items with a verifiable or well-calibrated target value, in two families: (a) numerical-commonsense estimation (NumerSense-style 'how many/how much' quantities with plausible ranges) and (b) arithmetic/quantity estimation (e.g. estimate a product, a population, a length). For each item create ANCHORED variants (the question is preceded by an irrelevant, uninformative anchor number — both a HIGH and a LOW anchor) and an UN-ANCHORED baseline. Instantiate every item — anchor, question, units — in typologically diverse languages spanning resource levels and scripts (English, French, German, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish), native-speaker verified, holding content and anchor magnitude fixed across languages. Also include a language-agnostic DIGIT/numeral anchor form as a control. Report inter-annotator agreement; release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral language-conditioned anchoring (H1, core): For each item and language, measure the assimilation-toward-anchor = signed shift of the model's estimate toward the anchor (high-anchor estimate minus low-anchor estimate, normalized), holding content fixed. Test H1: assimilation is larger for lower-resource / English-distant languages on identical items, while UN-ANCHORED accuracy (numeric competence) is controlled. Define the anchoring-gain asymmetry = high-language minus low-language assimilation. Control for tokenizer fertility and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test language adds predictive power beyond fertility and un-anchored competence). Crucially condition on items the model estimates reasonably in the un-anchored condition per language, so a stronger pull cannot be explained by simply not knowing the quantity.
3) Resource-distance scaling (H2): Regress per-language anchoring magnitude on training-data resource level and typological/embedding distance from English, controlling for tokenizer fertility and per-language un-anchored competence. Predict anchoring magnitude tracks resource-distance rather than competence; verify near-baseline (English) anchoring as the low-gain anchor point. Test whether reasoning/CoT prompting reduces the gain more in high-resource languages (consistent with the shallow-adjustment account).
4) Shared anchoring direction and gain readout (H3, core): Extract a per-language 'anchoring' direction via difference-in-means between anchored (assimilated) and un-anchored (or resisted) representations at each layer (verifying it acts in shallow layers, consistent with prior anchoring-mechanism work, and that it is a graded anchor-pull axis via a probe recovering assimilation magnitude). Measure cross-lingual cosine alignment (test: a largely shared axis re-scaled per language, and portability — steering with one language's direction changes assimilation in another). Project the residual stream at the estimation-decision point onto the shared direction and estimate a per-LANGUAGE anchoring gain (scalar) via regression of the assimilation on the projection. Test that the cross-lingual anchoring difference is captured by the difference in per-language gains applied to the SHARED anchoring projection (held-out R^2), beating (a) a uniform-bias baseline and (b) a full per-language relearned readout (i.e., the shift is low-dimensional). Mediation: regress behavioral assimilation on the anchoring-direction projection (partial correlation controlling for fertility/competence; held-out R^2).
5) Causal gain-steering (H4, core): At the anchoring layer, rescale the shared anchoring direction with a per-language scalar to transform a high-gain (low-resource) language's anchoring into the low-gain (English) value (and vice versa), and measure whether assimilation shifts accordingly WITHOUT changing input language (anchoring-transfer rate); conversely, equalize gains across languages and measure the reduction in cross-lingual anchoring variance. Bidirectional dose-response (can raise AND lower assimilation); mis-signed steering worsens. Complement with activation patching: patch the English (low-gain) anchoring signal into a low-resource-language pass. Compare against baselines: whole-hub English-steering, and a random-direction control.
6) Specificity and numeric-competence controls (hard constraint): Verify gain-steering is anchoring-specific — it reduces assimilation toward the IRRELEVANT anchor WITHOUT degrading un-anchored numeric accuracy, and WITHOUT reducing appropriate use of a RELEVANT/informative anchor (a symmetric check: when the leading number is genuinely informative, the model should still use it) — does not switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), and preserves fluency. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen have gains more collapsed toward the English low-anchoring setpoint (larger cross-lingual variation) than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether the magnitude of language-dependent gain change correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the anchoring direction and with each language's training share.
Evaluation metrics: per-language assimilation-toward-anchor and anchoring-gain asymmetry (anchored vs un-anchored; digit-anchor control); anchoring-vs-resource-distance prediction (held-out R^2 over fertility and un-anchored-competence baselines); reasoning-prompt gain reduction by resource level; cross-lingual anchoring-direction alignment and portability; gain predictive R^2 for the assimilation shift (vs uniform-bias and full-relearn baselines) and shallow-layer locus; anchoring-transfer rate and cross-lingual anchoring-variance reduction under gain-steering vs baselines, with bidirectional dose-response and mis-sign penalty; numeric-competence preservation and relevant-anchor preservation (symmetric specificity), off-target rate, fluency; cross-model gain-collapse comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Stronger anchoring in low-resource languages could conflate with a general numeric-competence gap (a model with a vaguer sense of the true value has more room to be pulled); the key controls are conditioning on items with comparable un-anchored competence per language, controlling for un-anchored accuracy in the regression, and the causal gain-steering test (which changes assimilation by editing only the anchoring direction while un-anchored accuracy is held) — if the language-conditioned anchoring vanishes once competence is controlled, the hypothesis is refuted, an informative negative result. 2) Language is confounded with tokenizer fertility, script, and resource level; the digit/numeral-anchor control, partial correlations, and causal tests mitigate but may not fully remove confounds (e.g., a numerically-longer tokenization could itself alter anchor salience — an interesting sub-finding we report). 3) The single-scalar gain account may only partially hold; if a data-driven low-dimensional basis fits better we report it, keeping the 'shared direction + language gain' claim testable regardless. 4) The anchoring direction from difference-in-means may entangle magnitude/priming features; we verify it is a graded assimilation axis, confirm its shallow-layer locus against prior anchoring-mechanism findings, and use specificity controls. 5) Gain-steering could over-suppress and make the model ignore genuinely informative leading numbers; the symmetric relevant-anchor-preservation constraint is a hard requirement and we report the full tradeoff. 6) Anchoring effects can be fragile and prompt-design-sensitive in LLMs (per Anchors in the Machine 2025); we verify a robust English anchoring effect first as a gate, use multiple semantically-equivalent prompt variants, and report robustness. 7) Reasoning/instruction tuning may reduce anchoring unevenly across languages; we test base and instruction-tuned models and treat differences as an informative training-stage finding. 8) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM/Aya analyzed as less English-centric contrasts expected to show smaller cross-lingual gain variation). 9) The human-anchoring analogy (shallow adjustment, cross-scale assimilation) is qualitative, not a claim of identical mechanism. 10) If anchoring magnitude is language-INVARIANT once competence/fertility are controlled, this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the bias is a language-agnostic shallow-layer property despite an English-scaffolded hub — valuable either way. 11) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: taxonomic_thematic_gain_reweighting
Title: Cow-Chicken or Cow-Grass? A Language-Conditioned Gain on a Shared Taxonomic-vs-Thematic Similarity Axis in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: The well-documented East/West difference in categorization (Westerners group taxonomically: cow-chicken; East Asians group thematically/relationally: cow-grass) reappears in multilingual LLMs, but not as a separate per-language conceptual reorganization. Instead, the query language applies a GAIN to a single, largely SHARED taxonomic-vs-thematic similarity axis: querying the same triad in an 'East Asian' language shifts the model's grouping toward the thematic pole and in a 'Western' language toward the taxonomic pole. This shift is captured by a low-dimensional per-language gain on a shared direction, tracks each language's empirical human categorization norms, is causally controllable by rescaling that direction, and is dissociable from the distributional-cooccurrence alternative account.
Related Work: Human cognitive science robustly documents the taxonomic-vs-thematic (categorical-vs-relational / analytic-vs-holistic) East/West difference behaviorally and neurally (Neural differences in processing semantic relationships across cultures 2010; Westerners and Asians Have Different Conceptual Structures 2023; Cultural preferences for formal vs intuitive reasoning 2002), while a distributional-statistics account argues the difference may reflect environmental co-occurrence rather than genuinely different notions of similarity (Re-examining cross-cultural similarity judgements using lexical co-occurrence 2021). On the LLM/VLM side, work is purely BEHAVIORAL/output-level: ChatGPT tends holistic on categorization tasks (The Cultural Psychology of LLMs 2023), and VLMs show Japanese-holistic vs English-analytic image descriptions (Contrasting Cognitive Styles in VLMs 2025). Interpretability shows categorical/hierarchical concepts are linear/geometric (Geometry of Categorical and Hierarchical Concepts 2024), property inheritance blends taxonomy and similarity in entangled subspaces (Characterizing the Role of Similarity 2024), and cultural understanding runs through language-specific circuits with a Cultural-Linguistic Synergy (Language over Content 2025; Disentangling Language and Culture 2025). CRITICALLY, no prior work asks whether the query LANGUAGE causally reweights a SHARED taxonomic-vs-thematic similarity axis inside a multilingual LLM, whether the cross-lingual grouping shift is a low-dimensional GAIN on that axis (rather than distinct per-language conceptual structure), whether the gain tracks the human East/West categorization gradient, whether it is causally steerable, or whether it can be dissociated from the distributional-cooccurrence alternative. We reframe cross-lingual categorization variation from 'different concepts per culture' into 'same similarity axis, language-set gain', with a predictive metric, a causal steering test, and a built-in test of the co-occurrence confound.
Abstract: Ask whether a cow goes with a chicken or with grass, and the answer depends on your culture: Westerners tend to group taxonomically (cow-chicken), East Asians thematically (cow-grass). Behavioral studies show large language models pick up holistic-vs-analytic tendencies, but only at the output level, and it is unknown how this arises internally or whether it even reflects a genuine conceptual difference. We propose a compact mechanistic account: a multilingual LLM judges taxonomic-vs-thematic grouping along a single, largely SHARED similarity axis, and the query language applies a GAIN to that axis rather than computing a separate per-language categorization. This predicts (1) a shared taxonomic-vs-thematic direction with high cross-lingual alignment; (2) that the per-language grouping shift is captured by a low-dimensional, culture-predictable gain, not a full per-language relearning; and (3) that rescaling the shared direction at inference causally reproduces another language's grouping and can equalize categorization across languages. Crucially, we dissociate this from a distributional-cooccurrence account by testing whether the gain persists on triads matched for lexical co-occurrence and on nonce/controlled items. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using classic triadic categorization tasks (cow/chicken/grass-style) translated across typologically and culturally diverse languages, combining behavioral grouping measurement, difference-in-means axis extraction, logit-lens gain readout, activation patching, and gain-steering. Metrics include cross-lingual grouping shift, axis alignment, gain predictive R-squared over resource and co-occurrence baselines, and steering-induced equalization with competence controls.
Experiments:
1) Triadic categorization suite: Build ~500 triads in the classic paradigm where a target (cow) is paired with a TAXONOMIC option (chicken, same category) vs a THEMATIC/relational option (grass, functionally related), spanning biological kinds and artifacts (following Westerners vs Asians 2023 and the cow/chicken/grass paradigm). Instantiate each triad in typologically and culturally diverse languages spanning the East/West categorization gradient and resource levels (English, German, Spanish, Mandarin, Japanese, Korean, Hindi, Arabic, Turkish), native-speaker verified. Attach per-language human categorization norms (taxonomic-vs-thematic preference) from the cross-cultural literature. Build key control subsets: (a) CO-OCCURRENCE-MATCHED triads where the taxonomic and thematic options are matched for corpus co-occurrence with the target (to test the distributional account); (b) NONCE-CONTROLLED triads using novel/abstract items; (c) a language-agnostic anchor (same triad, no linguistic categorization framing). Tasks: (i) forced-choice grouping ('which two go together?'); (ii) similarity rating of the taxonomic vs thematic pair; (iii) triadic sort with justification. Report inter-annotator agreement; release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral cross-lingual grouping shift (H0/motivation): Measure per-language thematic-choice rate (fraction grouping the target with the thematic vs taxonomic option), holding content fixed. Test that the SAME triad yields more thematic grouping in East-Asian-culture languages and more taxonomic grouping in Western-culture languages, replicating the human gradient at the model level. Control for tokenizer fertility and resource level (partial correlations).
3) Shared taxonomic-vs-thematic axis (H1): Extract a per-language difference-in-means direction between taxonomic-grouping and thematic-grouping representations at each layer (using disambiguated exemplars). Measure cross-lingual cosine alignment across layers; test it is high and peaks in middle layers, and that steering with one language's axis changes grouping in another (portability). Baseline: a language-identity direction. Verify it is a graded axis via a probe recovering thematic-preference strength.
4) Language gain readout and culture prediction (H2, core): Project the residual stream at the grouping decision onto the shared axis to get a per-item taxonomic/thematic activation, and estimate a per-LANGUAGE gain (scalar, or low-dimensional if multiple sub-dimensions) via regression of the grouping decision on the projection. Test H2: the cross-lingual grouping shift is captured by the difference in per-language gains applied to the SHARED axis projection (held-out R^2), beating (a) a uniform per-language bias baseline and (b) a full per-language relearned readout (i.e., the shift is low-dimensional). Test whether the per-language gain is predicted by the human East/West categorization norm BETTER than by resource level (nested regression, AIC, held-out R^2), tying the internal gain to independent cross-cultural ground truth.
5) Distributional-cooccurrence dissociation (core novelty): Test whether the language-conditioned gain persists on the CO-OCCURRENCE-MATCHED and NONCE-CONTROLLED subsets. If the cross-lingual grouping shift and the per-language gain survive when lexical co-occurrence is matched (and on nonce items with no learned statistics), this supports a genuine language-conditioned reweighting rather than a distributional artifact (addressing the Re-examining 2021 alternative); if it collapses, that is an informative result favoring the co-occurrence account.
6) Causal gain-steering (H3, core): At the decision layer, rescale the shared axis (multiply the projection by a scalar) to transform one language's gain into another's, and measure whether grouping shifts toward the target language WITHOUT changing input language (grouping-transfer rate); conversely, equalize gains across languages and measure reduction in cross-lingual grouping variance. Bidirectional dose-response; mis-signed steering worsens. Complement with activation patching: patch a Western-language taxonomic signal into an East-Asian-language pass. Compare against baselines: whole-hub English-steering, cultural-steering vector, random-direction control.
7) Specificity and competence controls: Verify gain-steering is grouping-specific (changes taxonomic-vs-thematic preference but not object identity, factual knowledge, or unrelated content; the model must still know a cow is an animal), does not switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), preserves fluency, and is bidirectional. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen have gains more collapsed toward the taxonomic (Western) setpoint than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM (which see more East-Asian-language data); test whether the magnitude of language-dependent gain change correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the axis and each language's training share. Qualitatively compare the per-language gain pattern against the human East/West categorization gradient (direction, not identical mechanism).
Evaluation metrics: per-language thematic-choice rate and cross-lingual grouping shift (vs human gradient); taxonomic-vs-thematic axis cross-lingual alignment and portability; gain predictive R^2 for the grouping shift (vs uniform-bias and full-relearn baselines) and gain-vs-human-norm R^2 over resource baseline; co-occurrence-matched and nonce-item gain persistence (dissociation from distributional account); grouping-transfer rate and cross-lingual variance reduction under gain-steering vs baselines, with bidirectional dose-response and mis-sign penalty; grouping-specificity (object knowledge preserved), off-target rate, fluency; cross-model gain-collapse comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Language, culture, script, and resource level are confounded (query language correlates with East/West categorization norms); we include a within-language cultural-framing manipulation (same language, home-culture vs neutral framing) to separate cultural framing from language identity, and report partial correlations, but residual confounds may remain. 2) The distributional-cooccurrence account (Re-examining 2021) is a serious alternative and is confronted head-on via the co-occurrence-matched and nonce-controlled subsets (Exp 5); if the gain collapses there, that is an informative result favoring the distributional account rather than a failure. 3) The single-scalar (or low-dimensional) gain account may only partially hold; if a data-driven basis (PCA/SAE over categorization-item activations) fits better, we report the empirically-best low-dimensional basis, keeping the 'shared axis + language gain' claim testable. 4) The difference-in-means axis may entangle taxonomic/thematic with topical or lexical features; we verify it is a graded preference axis, use nonce/co-occurrence-matched items, and apply specificity controls. 5) Grouping choices are noisy and prompt-format-sensitive; we use forced-choice, similarity-rating, and sort tasks jointly and report reliability. 6) Human categorization norms are noisy and may not reflect training-data statistics; we treat them as an external reference and rely on the internal gain and causal tests for core claims. 7) Instruction-tuned models may flatten cultural variation; we test base models where available and treat differences as an informative training-stage finding. 8) Gain-steering could harm object knowledge or over-impose a target culture; we require competence preservation, symmetry, and grouping-specificity, reporting the full tradeoff. 9) If the axis is NOT shared across languages, or the gain is not norm-predictable beyond resource level, the hypothesis is refuted — an informative negative result showing categorization is genuinely per-language rather than a shared-axis gain. 10) The human-LLM comparison is qualitative/structural (gradient direction), not a claim of identical mechanism. 11) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: language_conditioned_backtracking_gain
Title: Second-Guessing in a Foreign Tongue: A Language-Conditioned Gain on a Shared Self-Doubt/Backtracking Direction in Multilingual Reasoning
Short Hypothesis: Reasoning models spontaneously backtrack mid-chain ('wait, let me reconsider'), and the RATE of this self-doubt/backtracking is language-conditioned: the same problem elicits systematically more or less backtracking depending only on the reasoning language, because the query language applies a GAIN to a single, largely SHARED 'reconsideration' direction that triggers revision. This gain is miscalibrated — anchored to the dominant (English) language and imported into others regardless of whether the language's traces actually need revision — so the model over-backtracks (looping self-doubt that degrades accuracy) in some languages and under-backtracks (premature commitment) in others. The gain is decodable, predictable from resource-distance, and causally correctable by rescaling the shared reconsideration direction toward each language's accuracy-optimal backtracking rate, without harming genuine error correction.
Related Work: Thought Anchors (2025) shows 'uncertainty management' sentences are pivotal reasoning steps attended by specialized receiver heads, but is monolingual (English). Language Mixing (2025) and multilingual latent-reasoning work (Latent Reasoners 2026; Do Multilingual LLMs Think In English 2025) study SCRIPT preferences and where reasoning is routed, not self-doubt/backtracking behavior. What Really Counts (2025) shows multilingual CoT attribution over-weights the final step. Preplan-and-Anchor (2025) and DynTS (2026) identify decision-critical tokens but monolingually. Monolingual work on overthinking/self-doubt shows extra reconsideration can flip correct answers and follows an inverted-U in length (When More is Less 2025). CRITICALLY, no prior work asks whether the RATE of spontaneous mid-chain backtracking/self-doubt is language-conditioned, whether it is a low-dimensional GAIN on a shared reconsideration direction rather than distinct per-language behavior, whether this gain is miscalibrated (imported from English) causing over- vs under-backtracking that harms accuracy, whether it tracks resource-distance, or whether rescaling the shared direction can move each language to its accuracy-optimal backtracking rate. This differs from my prior first_step_anchoring proposal (recovery from a PLANTED wrong first step), effort_setpoint (how MUCH total compute), and validation_deficit (detecting one's OWN errors): here the phenomenon is the spontaneous SELF-DOUBT/BACKTRACKING rhythm and its language-conditioned gain on a shared reconsideration mechanism. It reframes multilingual reasoning-quality variation as a backtracking-calibration problem with a predictive metric and a targeted, competence-preserving fix.
Abstract: Reasoning models often stop mid-thought to second-guess themselves ('wait, that's wrong, let me reconsider'), and such self-doubt/backtracking steps are known to be pivotal to whether a chain reaches the right answer. This has been studied only in English. We ask a simple, previously untested question: does the language a model reasons in change how much it backtracks, and does that change help or hurt? We hypothesize a language-conditioned backtracking gain: the same problem elicits systematically more or less mid-chain self-doubt depending only on the reasoning language, because the query language applies a gain to a single, largely shared 'reconsideration' direction. Crucially, we hypothesize this gain is miscalibrated — anchored to the dominant (English) language and imported into others — so the model over-backtracks (looping self-doubt that flips correct answers) in some languages and under-backtracks (premature commitment) in others, relative to each language's accuracy-optimal rate. We predict the gain is low-dimensional, decodable, predictable from resource-distance, and causally correctable by rescaling the shared reconsideration direction toward each language's optimum without harming genuine error correction. We test on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1-distilled Qwen/Llama, Qwen-reasoning) across typologically diverse languages using MGSM and a controlled multi-step suite. Combining a validated backtracking-step classifier, per-language backtracking-rate and accuracy-optimal-rate estimation, difference-in-means reconsideration-direction extraction, activation patching, and gain-steering, we measure the backtracking gain, its miscalibration, its resource-distance scaling, its shared-direction locus, and a causal fix. Metrics include per-language backtracking rate versus optimum, gain predictive R-squared, and steering-induced accuracy recovery with error-correction controls.
Experiments:
1) Multilingual reasoning suite and backtracking taxonomy: Use MGSM and a controlled multi-step arithmetic/logic suite (verified gold) translated into typologically diverse languages spanning resource levels and scripts (English, French, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish, Bengali), native-speaker verified. Build and validate an automatic mid-chain BACKTRACKING-step classifier (rule-based cues for reconsideration/self-correction markers plus a learned classifier, robust across languages) against human annotation on a held-out subset; report reliability and inter-annotator agreement. Models: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, a Qwen-reasoning variant. Release the suite.
