2) Behavioral backtracking-rate map (H1, core): For naturally generated chains, segment steps and count the per-language backtracking rate (fraction of chains / steps containing spontaneous self-doubt/reconsideration) on matched problems. Test that the SAME problems elicit systematically different backtracking rates by reasoning language. Control for tokenizer fertility and chain length (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test language adds predictive power beyond difficulty and length).
3) Accuracy-optimal rate and miscalibration (H2, core): Per language and difficulty bin, estimate the accuracy-optimal backtracking rate by inducing controlled variation (via budget/backtracking-cue prompting and constrained decoding that raises or suppresses reconsideration) and tracing accuracy vs backtracking rate (expect an inverted-U). Define the miscalibration = default rate minus optimal rate, signed. Test the bidirectional prediction: some languages over-backtrack (default above optimum; looping self-doubt flips correct-to-wrong) and others under-backtrack (default below optimum; premature commitment), for the SAME problems. Verify over-backtracking errors are genuine (extra reconsideration corrupts a correct intermediate answer) via answer-flip analysis. Test whether default rate tracks English (imported-anchor signature): is per-language default backtracking pulled toward the English rate rather than each language's optimum (model comparison: English-anchored vs optimum-appropriate)?
4) Miscalibration predicts accuracy loss (H2b): Test whether per-language accuracy loss (relative to that language's optimal-rate accuracy) is predicted by the absolute miscalibration (Spearman; held-out R^2), and whether the error direction matches the sign (over-backtracking -> answer-corruption errors; under-backtracking -> premature-commitment errors), via an error-type decomposition.
5) Shared reconsideration direction and gain readout (H3): Extract a difference-in-means 'reconsideration' direction (backtracking-onset vs continue-forward representations at step boundaries) per language and layer; verify cross-lingual alignment (a largely shared axis re-thresholded per language) and portability (steering it changes backtracking in another language). Locate whether it rides on the uncertainty-management / receiver heads from Thought Anchors. Estimate a per-LANGUAGE backtracking gain (scalar) via regression of backtracking-onset on the shared-direction projection; test that the cross-lingual rate difference is captured by the difference in per-language gains applied to the SHARED projection (held-out R^2), beating a uniform-bias baseline. Test whether the gain is predicted by resource-distance (model comparison over competence baseline).
6) Causal gain-steering (H4, core): Rescale the shared reconsideration direction with a per-language scalar to push each language's backtracking rate toward ITS optimum (down for over-backtracking languages, up for under-backtracking), train-free, and measure per-language accuracy recovery. Predict SELECTIVE, BIDIRECTIONAL gains (lowering self-doubt helps over-backtracking languages, raising it helps under-backtracking ones; mis-signed steering hurts — dose-response). Complement with activation patching from an optimally-calibrated pass. Compare against baselines: uniform English-anchored backtracking rate, fixed longer/shorter budget for all languages, whole-hub English-steering, and a random-direction control. Compute recovery elasticity = accuracy gain per unit miscalibration corrected.
7) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify gain-steering is backtracking-specific — it must move the self-doubt/reconsideration rate WITHOUT switching output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), without harming fluency, and WITHOUT destroying GENUINE error correction (a symmetric check: suppressing self-doubt must not stop the model from fixing a genuinely wrong step — test on items with a real mid-chain error the model would otherwise catch), and it should not help languages already near optimum. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric distilled models show gains more collapsed toward the English backtracking setpoint (larger miscalibration) than more multilingual models; test whether miscalibration correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the reconsideration direction and each language's training share.
Evaluation metrics: per-language backtracking rate (matched problems; partial correlation with resource-distance over fertility/length, held-out R^2); accuracy-optimal rate and signed miscalibration (over- vs under-backtracking, bidirectional); English-anchored-vs-optimum model comparison; miscalibration's prediction of accuracy loss and error-type shares (held-out R^2); reconsideration-direction cross-lingual alignment, portability, receiver-head locus, and gain predictive R^2 (vs uniform-bias baseline); bidirectional gain-steering accuracy recovery and elasticity vs baselines, with dose-response, mis-sign penalty, genuine-error-correction preservation (symmetric specificity), off-target rate, fluency; cross-model miscalibration comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Automatically classifying a mid-chain step as spontaneous backtracking/self-doubt (vs ordinary continuation or a fresh sub-step) is hard and language-specific; we build a validated classifier against human labels, use structural (does the model revise a prior conclusion?) plus lexical cues, report reliability, and exclude ambiguous steps. 2) The over-/under-backtracking miscalibration could conflate with a general competence gap; the accuracy-optimal-rate estimation, the bidirectional dose-response steering (which recovers accuracy by moving ONLY the backtracking rate), and conditioning on matched difficulty isolate a calibration effect — if accuracy recovery does not track miscalibration and sign, the hypothesis is refuted, an informative negative result. 3) Backtracking rate is confounded with tokenizer fertility, chain length, and resource level; partial correlations, the controlled multi-step suite (difficulty controlled), and the causal steering test mitigate but may not fully remove confounds. 4) The single-scalar gain account may only partially hold; if a data-driven low-dimensional basis fits better we report it, keeping the 'shared reconsideration axis + language gain' claim testable. 5) The reconsideration direction from difference-in-means may entangle content/uncertainty-lexical features; we use the Thought-Anchors receiver-head circuitry as an anchor, multiple extraction methods, and specificity controls. 6) The genuine-error-correction symmetric constraint is essential — if suppressing self-doubt merely stops the model from fixing real errors, that is a failure, not a fix; we require preserved correction of genuinely wrong steps and report the full tradeoff. 7) Budget/cue-based backtracking control differs across model families and may only approximate the true internal reconsideration rate; recurrent control is unavailable. 8) Effects may be model-family dependent and limited to open ~7-8B reasoning models; may not extend to frontier scale. 9) If default backtracking already sits at each language's optimum (no bidirectional miscalibration), this is an informative POSITIVE result showing multilingual self-doubt is well-calibrated, relocating the multilingual gap to pure competence — valuable either way.

Name: measurement_system_default_imposition
Title: Everything in Miles: A Language-Conditioned Default-Measurement-System Gain That Silently Re-Anchors Quantities in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs represent physical quantities on a largely language-agnostic magnitude line, but they carry a language-conditioned 'default measurement-system' setpoint that is anchored to the dominant (US/imperial-or-metric-of-the-training-data) convention and imported into other languages regardless of that culture's actual convention. Consequently, when reasoning about or reporting a quantity in a target language, the model silently RE-ANCHORS the value to its default system's typical range (distances feel 'mile-sized', temperatures 'Fahrenheit-sized', weights 'pound-sized'), so a numerically identical, unit-underspecified quantity is interpreted and estimated differently depending only on the query language, tracking the default-system convention rather than the target-language norm. This re-anchoring is mediated by a shared, decodable measurement-system direction whose gain is set by an early language signal, tracks each language's empirical convention, and is causally correctable without harming unit-explicit numeric competence.
Related Work: The closest prior work, 'On Generalization across Measurement Systems' (2025) and NUMCoT (2024), is purely BEHAVIORAL/benchmark: they show LLMs default to the predominant training-data measurement system, are unstable across systems, and that CoT partially mitigates this at extra compute. 'Do Language Models Understand Measurements?' (2022) and dimension-perception work (2023) show PLMs poorly separate numbers from units. On the mechanistic side, numeric magnitude is encoded in low-dimensional, causally-editable linear subspaces (The Geometry of Numerical Reasoning 2024; Monotonic Representation of Numeric Properties 2024), and multilingual reasoning routes through an English-scaffolded shared hub (Do Multilingual LLMs Think In English 2025; Semantic Hub 2024; Lost in Multilinguality 2025). CRITICALLY, no prior work asks whether the measurement-system DEFAULT is a language-conditioned GAIN on a shared magnitude/measurement-system representation that IMPOSES the dominant convention onto other languages (re-anchoring unit-underspecified quantities), whether it is predictable from each culture's empirical convention, whether it is mediated by a decodable measurement-system direction, or whether rescaling that direction causally equalizes cross-lingual quantity interpretation without harming unit-explicit computation. We reframe the measurement-system default from a data-frequency benchmark artifact into a mechanistic imposition with a predictive metric and a targeted causal fix, distinct from all my prior grammatical/lexical imposition proposals (measurement system is a units-and-scale convention layered on the number line) and from the behavioral measurement literature.
Abstract: How far is '10' — ten miles or ten kilometers? How hot is '80' — Fahrenheit or Celsius? The answer depends on your culture's default measurement system, and conversions between systems are exact, so the number's meaning is fully determined only once the system is fixed. Behavioral studies show multilingual language models default to whatever measurement system dominates their training data and answer inconsistently across systems, but treat this as a data-frequency artifact. We propose a mechanistic account: a model represents quantities on a largely language-agnostic magnitude line, but a language-conditioned setpoint fixes a default measurement system, anchored to the dominant convention and imported into other languages regardless of that culture's actual norm. Under this account, when the model reasons about or estimates a unit-underspecified quantity in a target language, it silently re-anchors the value to its default system's typical range, so the identical quantity is interpreted differently depending only on query language. We hypothesize this re-anchoring is (1) predictable from each culture's empirical measurement convention, not merely resource level; (2) a low-dimensional GAIN on a single, largely shared measurement-system direction whose setting is decodable from an early language signal; and (3) causally correctable by rescaling that direction, without harming unit-explicit numeric computation. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using controlled quantity-estimation and unit-inference tasks across typologically and culturally diverse languages, combining behavioral re-anchoring measurement, difference-in-means direction extraction, logit-lens gain readout, activation patching, and gain-steering. Metrics include per-language default-system imposition gap, convention-prediction correlation, mediation R-squared, and steering-induced correction with unit-explicit-competence controls.
Experiments:
1) Measurement suite: Build ~600 items across measurement types where systems diverge by culture (distance: mile vs km; temperature: F vs C; weight: pound vs kg; volume: gallon vs litre; area, speed), in two families: (a) UNIT-UNDERSPECIFIED estimation ('a road trip of 300 — is that long?'; 'it was 80 outside — hot or cold?'; 'a 5 walk — far?') where the model must supply a default system to interpret; (b) UNIT-EXPLICIT computation (fully specified units + conversions) as a competence control. Instantiate every item in typologically and culturally diverse languages spanning measurement conventions and resource levels (English-US=imperial, English-UK/German/French/Chinese/Hindi/Arabic=metric, plus mixed-convention cases), native-speaker verified, with the number and phrasing held fixed across languages. Attach each language its empirical default-convention (from surveys / official standards; e.g. distances in km vs miles). Report inter-annotator agreement; release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral imposition (H1, core): On UNIT-UNDERSPECIFIED items, infer which measurement system the model assumes (via forced-choice 'what unit is this?', magnitude-judgment consistency, and elicited paraphrase) per language, holding the number fixed. Define the default-system imposition GAP = deviation of the model's assumed system from the target-language convention, signed toward the DOMINANT (training-data) default; and an imposition rate = fraction of items where the assumed system matches the dominant default rather than the target-language norm. Verify near-perfect handling of UNIT-EXPLICIT items (isolating imposition from numeric incompetence). Control for tokenizer fertility and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test target-language convention adds predictive power).
3) Convention scaling (H2, external validation): Test whether per-language imposition is predicted by that culture's empirical measurement convention (Spearman; held-out prediction from convention data alone), tying the internal phenomenon to independent ground truth and distinguishing it from mere resource level. Use the English-US (imperial) vs English-UK (metric) contrast as a near-minimal pair that holds language nearly fixed while varying convention.
4) Shared measurement-system direction and gain readout (H3): Extract a per-language 'measurement-system' direction via difference-in-means between representations biased toward each system (e.g. imperial-context vs metric-context quantities) at each layer, verifying it is a graded system axis via a probe recovering assumed-system/magnitude-range. Measure cross-lingual cosine alignment (test: a single largely shared axis re-scaled per language; portability via steering). Project the residual stream at the interpretation point onto the shared direction and estimate a per-LANGUAGE gain via regression; test that the cross-lingual imposition is captured by the difference in per-language gains applied to the SHARED projection (held-out R^2), beating a uniform-bias baseline. Test whether the query language / assumed system is decodable from an early signal set before the value is interpreted (position-resolved logit-lens). Mediation: regress behavioral imposition on the measurement-system projection (partial correlation controlling for fertility/resource; held-out R^2).
5) Causal gain-steering test (H4, core): Rescale the shared measurement-system direction with a per-language scalar to shift the assumed default toward the target-language convention (and vice versa), and measure whether unit inference / magnitude estimation shifts accordingly WITHOUT changing input language (system-transfer rate) and the imposition GAP shrinks; bidirectional dose-response; mis-signed steering worsens. Complement with activation patching: patch the dominant-default system signal into a target-language pass. Critically verify UNIT-EXPLICIT COMPETENCE preservation (fully-specified conversions must stay correct — steering changes the DEFAULT assumption, not arithmetic) plus fluency and off-target/language-mixing checks. Baselines: whole-hub English-steering, CoT prompting (the behavioral-paper baseline), random-direction control.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify steering is measurement-system-specific (changes the assumed system/scale but not the numeric value or unrelated content), graded (imposition scales with convention divergence), and not merely a tokenizer artifact. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English/US-centric Llama-3/Qwen show stronger imposition than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether imposition magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the measurement-system direction and each language's training share. Qualitatively compare per-language imposition against the empirical convention map.
Evaluation metrics: default-system imposition GAP and imposition rate (unit-underspecified vs unit-explicit; dominant-default vs target-convention; English-US vs English-UK near-minimal pair); imposition-vs-convention correlation and held-out prediction; measurement-system-direction system-decodability, cross-lingual alignment, portability, early language-signal predictiveness, and gain predictive R^2 (vs uniform-bias baseline) with mediation of behavioral imposition (held-out R^2); steering system-transfer rate and GAP reduction (bidirectional dose-response), patching-induced correction; unit-explicit-competence preservation (specificity), fluency, off-target rate; cross-model imposition comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Inferring which system the model 'assumes' on unit-underspecified items is indirect; we triangulate with forced-choice unit questions, magnitude-consistency, and elicited paraphrase, native-speaker verify, and report inter-annotator agreement, treating ambiguous items separately. 2) Imposition is confounded with language family, script, and resource level; the English-US-vs-English-UK near-minimal pair (same language, different convention) is the key control isolating convention from language identity, plus the unit-explicit competence control and convention-based prediction; residual confounds may remain. 3) Some imposition may reflect genuinely correct behavior (the model rightly matching the target-culture convention); the direction of the effect (tracks DOMINANT default vs TARGET convention), the convention prediction, and the causal steering (which shifts the default by editing only the measurement-system direction) distinguish imposition from faithful interpretation, and a faithful-interpretation finding is itself valuable and sharpens the behavioral-benchmark result. 4) The single-scalar gain account may only partially hold; if a data-driven low-dimensional basis fits better we report it, keeping the 'shared axis + language gain' claim testable. 5) The measurement-system direction from difference-in-means may entangle numeric-magnitude or topical features; we verify it is a graded system axis, use a magnitude-only control direction, and apply specificity checks. 6) Logit-lens gain/timing estimates are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 7) Steering could corrupt numeric values or fluency; unit-explicit-competence preservation is a hard constraint and we report the full tradeoff plus bidirectional dose-response, comparing against the CoT baseline (from the behavioral paper) to show the mechanistic account adds value. 8) Convention data is noisy (mixed-convention cultures, domain-dependent usage); we treat it as a noisy predictor and rely on internal representation and causal tests for core claims. 9) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM/Aya analyzed as less US/English-centric contrasts). 10) If NO imposition is found — the model assumes each culture's own default, predictable from convention, with unit-explicit computation intact — this is an informative POSITIVE result showing culture-faithful measurement representation despite a dominant-default training distribution, valuable either way. 11) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: language_conditioned_content_effect
Title: Believing Instead of Deducing in a Foreign Tongue: A Language-Conditioned Content Effect from Validity-Plausibility Geometric Entanglement
Short Hypothesis: The content effect — conflating a conclusion's plausibility with its logical validity — is LANGUAGE-DEPENDENT in multilingual LLMs: it is stronger when the model reasons in a lower-resource / English-distant language, mirroring the human 'reverse Foreign Language Effect' where L2 reasoners fail to detect belief-logic conflict. Mechanistically, this is because the linear validity direction and the plausibility direction are MORE geometrically ALIGNED (harder to disentangle) in the shared representation when the input is in a non-dominant language, so the per-language content-effect magnitude is predicted by a per-language validity-plausibility alignment metric and is causally correctable by rescaling the plausibility component out of the validity readout — without harming plausibility judgment itself.
Related Work: Monolingual mechanistic work shows validity and plausibility are each linearly encoded, are strongly aligned in representational geometry, and that the degree of alignment predicts content-effect magnitude across models; steering/disentangling directions reduces the bias (How Language Models Conflate Logical Validity with Plausibility 2025; Content-free Logical Modification / LCF 2025; K-CAST fine-grained steering 2025; Abstract Activation Spaces 2026; Language models show content effects 2024). Human cognition shows a REVERSE Foreign Language Effect: L2 reasoners are LESS able to detect belief-logic conflict and fail to engage reflective override (Thinking in a Foreign Language Distorts Cognitive Effort 2019; FLE meta-reasoning 2023/2026), and belief/fluency drive syllogism judgments (Intuitive Logic 2014/2016/2023). Multilingual work shows an English-scaffolded shared hub, that language-specific signal can be ablated to improve reasoning (When Less Language is More 2025), and that models internalize language-specific reasoning biases (BICAUSE 2025). CRITICALLY, all content-effect mechanism work is monolingual (English) and treats the validity-plausibility alignment as a fixed model property; all cross-lingual reasoning work concerns accuracy/routing, never the content effect. NO prior work asks whether the content effect is language-conditioned, whether the validity-plausibility geometric alignment itself is LARGER in non-dominant languages (explaining a per-language content-effect gain), or whether per-language disentanglement causally equalizes reasoning across languages. Notably, Abstract Activation Spaces (2026) uses cross-lingual transfer only as a test-bed for a debiasing method and never measures a per-language content-effect or alignment gradient. We uniquely port the human reverse-FLE into LLM mechanisms and give it a predictive geometric metric and a causal fix.
Abstract: People judging whether a conclusion follows logically are biased by whether it sounds believable — a 'content effect' — and, strikingly, this bias is HARDER to overcome in a second language, where reasoners fail to notice when belief and logic conflict. Interpretability work shows language models encode logical validity and semantic plausibility as linear directions that are geometrically aligned, and the degree of alignment predicts how strongly a model conflates them — but only in English. We ask a simple, previously untested question: is the content effect language-dependent in multilingual LLMs, and is it stronger in lower-resource or English-distant languages, mirroring the human reverse Foreign Language Effect? We hypothesize that (1) the model conflates plausibility with validity MORE when reasoning in a non-dominant language on identical syllogisms; (2) this is mechanistically driven by the validity and plausibility directions being MORE geometrically ALIGNED in the representation for non-dominant languages, so the per-language content-effect magnitude is predicted by a per-language alignment metric better than by resource level alone; and (3) a per-language disentanglement intervention that projects the plausibility component out of the validity readout causally reduces the content effect and equalizes reasoning across languages, without harming genuine plausibility judgment. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using controlled multilingual syllogisms crossing logical validity with conclusion believability across typologically diverse languages, combining behavioral content-effect measurement, difference-in-means direction extraction, alignment geometry, activation patching, and disentanglement steering. Metrics include per-language content-effect magnitude, alignment-vs-content-effect correlation, mediation R-squared, and steering-induced equalization with plausibility-preservation controls.
Experiments: 1) Controlled multilingual syllogism suite: Build ~600 syllogisms crossing LOGICAL VALIDITY (valid/invalid) with conclusion BELIEVABILITY (believable/unbelievable), yielding the four cells that isolate the content effect — including the diagnostic CONFLICT cells (valid-but-unbelievable, invalid-but-believable) where plausibility fights validity. Include nonce/abstract-content syllogisms (belief-neutral) as a content-free control. Instantiate every item in typologically diverse languages spanning resource levels and scripts (English, French, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish, Bengali), native-speaker verified, holding logical structure and content fixed across languages. Report inter-annotator agreement; release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B. 2) Behavioral language-conditioned content effect (H1, core): Measure per-language validity-judgment accuracy separately on CONFLICT vs NON-CONFLICT cells; define the content-effect magnitude = accuracy drop on conflict cells (how much believability distorts validity judgment). Test H1: the content effect is LARGER for lower-resource / English-distant languages on identical syllogisms. Verify comparable accuracy on non-conflict and abstract-content cells (isolating the content effect from general reasoning competence). Control for tokenizer fertility and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2). Qualitatively compare against the human reverse-FLE (direction, not identical mechanism). 3) Alignment geometry prediction (H2, core mechanism): Following the monolingual method, extract a per-language VALIDITY direction (difference-in-means between valid and invalid representations, controlling believability) and a per-language PLAUSIBILITY direction (difference-in-means between believable and unbelievable, controlling validity) at each layer. Measure the per-language validity-plausibility cosine ALIGNMENT. Test whether per-language alignment predicts per-language content-effect magnitude (Spearman; held-out R^2) and whether alignment adds predictive power BEYOND resource level (model comparison, AIC). Prediction: the two directions are more aligned (more entangled) in non-dominant languages, explaining the stronger content effect. 4) Causal cross-concept bias test: Steer along the plausibility direction and measure whether it shifts validity judgments (and vice versa), per language, replicating the monolingual cross-concept causal effect and testing whether the cross-concept steering effect is LARGER in high-alignment (non-dominant) languages. Mediation: regress behavioral content effect on the plausibility-into-validity leakage (partial correlation controlling for fertility/resource; held-out R^2). 5) Core causal intervention (per-language disentanglement): Construct a per-language debiasing operation that projects the plausibility component out of the validity readout at the localizing layer (INLP/orthogonalization or a debiasing steering vector), and measure whether the content effect drops toward the abstract-content baseline and cross-lingual reasoning variance shrinks. Predict SELECTIVE gains for high-content-effect (high-alignment, low-resource) languages, little effect on English (interaction test). Compare against baselines: whole-hub English steering, language-specific ablation (When Less Language is More 2025), the Abstract Activation Spaces steering (2026), and a random-direction control. Compute recovery elasticity = content-effect reduction per unit baseline alignment. 6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify the intervention is validity-specific — it must IMPROVE validity judgment on conflict cells WITHOUT harming genuine PLAUSIBILITY judgment (a symmetric check: the model must still correctly rate believability when believability, not validity, is the task), must not switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), and preserve fluency. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show a sharper cross-lingual content-effect and alignment gradient than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether the content-effect gap correlates with the cross-lingual validity-plausibility alignment gradient and each language's training share. Evaluation metrics: per-language content-effect magnitude (conflict-cell accuracy drop; vs abstract-content control); content-effect-vs-resource correlation and content-effect-vs-alignment correlation (held-out R^2, model comparison showing alignment adds over resource); per-language validity-plausibility cosine alignment gradient; cross-concept steering leakage by language and its mediation of behavioral content effect (held-out R^2); per-language disentanglement content-effect reduction and cross-lingual variance reduction and elasticity vs baselines, with plausibility-judgment preservation (symmetric specificity), off-target rate, fluency; cross-model content-effect and alignment-gap comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The language-conditioned content effect could conflate with a general competence gap; the non-conflict and abstract-content controls, conditioning on comparable non-conflict accuracy, and the disentanglement intervention (which reduces the effect by editing only the validity-plausibility geometry) isolate a content-effect-specific phenomenon — if the gap vanishes once competence is controlled, the hypothesis is refuted, an informative negative result. 2) Language is confounded with tokenizer fertility, script, and resource level; the alignment-metric prediction (which offers a mechanistic predictor beyond resource level) and partial correlations mitigate but may not fully remove confounds. 3) The validity and plausibility difference-in-means directions may entangle topical/lexical content; we control believability when extracting the validity direction and vice versa, use nonce-content controls, and multiple extraction methods. 4) The content effect can be weak or prompt-sensitive in 7-8B models; we verify a measurable English content effect first as a gate and use multiple prompt formats. 5) The per-language disentanglement could over-suppress and harm genuine plausibility judgment; the symmetric plausibility-preservation constraint is a hard requirement and we report the full tradeoff. 6) Alignment geometry is layer-dependent and approximate; we report across layers and cross-validate. 7) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM/Aya analyzed as less English-centric contrasts expected to show a smaller gradient). 8) The human-LLM comparison (reverse Foreign Language Effect) is qualitative/structural, not a claim of identical mechanism (the human effect involves metacognitive conflict-detection thresholds; the LLM account is geometric entanglement). 9) If the content effect and validity-plausibility alignment are language-invariant, this is an informative POSITIVE result showing content-effect geometry is language-agnostic despite an English-scaffolded hub — valuable either way. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: per_query_donor_language_routing
Title: Every Fact Has a Favorite Language: Per-Query Donor-Language Routing and Its Miscalibration in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Cross-lingual transfer at inference is not a uniform property of a language pair but a per-QUERY phenomenon: for each individual fact/reasoning item, a multilingual LLM covertly recruits a specific DONOR language (the language from whose representation it actually retrieves the answer) that varies item-by-item and is often NOT English and NOT the query language. Cross-lingual failure occurs when the model routes a query to a donor language that does not hold the answer, and this routing is (a) decodable per query, (b) predictable better than by a fixed corpus-level transfer matrix, and (c) causally correctable by re-routing the query to the item's best donor — recovering accuracy without retraining.
Related Work: ATLAS (2025) derives a corpus-level 38x38 cross-lingual transfer matrix and identifies 'super donor / super recipient' languages (Protasov et al. 2024), but these are STATIC, pair-level, training-time quantities. Tracing Multilingual Factual Knowledge Acquisition (2025) shows low-frequency non-English facts are often recalled via their English counterparts, and Paths Not Taken / How Do Multilingual LLMs Remember Facts localize an English-centric recall stage — but they treat the donor as English by default and study recall stages, not a per-item variable donor. Cross-lingual consistency and entity-alignment work (Lost in Multilinguality 2025; Entity-Level Alignment 2025) localizes inconsistency but does not identify which specific donor language each query is routed to. CRITICALLY, no prior work (a) frames the donor language as a per-QUERY latent variable that varies item-by-item (and is often a third language, not English or the query language), (b) decodes it from internal states, (c) shows that per-query donor-routing predicts success better than the fixed corpus-level transfer matrix, or (d) causally re-routes a query to its best donor to recover accuracy. We reframe cross-lingual transfer from a static pair-level property into an inference-time, per-query routing decision that is measurable, mispredictable, and steerable — distinct from the training-dynamics and static-matrix literature and from all my prior proposals (which concern content representation, imposition, or provenance, not per-query donor selection).
Abstract: Cross-lingual transfer is usually described as a property of a language PAIR: how much does training on language A help language B. We argue this misses where transfer actually happens. We hypothesize that at inference, a multilingual LLM answers each individual query by covertly recruiting a specific DONOR language — the language from whose internal representation it retrieves the answer — and that this donor varies item-by-item, is frequently a third language (neither English nor the query language), and is set before the answer is produced. Under this account, cross-lingual failure is a routing error: the query is sent to a donor that does not hold the fact. We predict this per-query donor is decodable from internal states, predicts answer success better than a fixed corpus-level transfer matrix, and can be causally re-routed to the item's best donor to recover accuracy without retraining. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using multilingual factual QA (mLAMA) and reasoning (MGSM) across typologically diverse languages. Using logit-lens/tuned-lens donor decoding, difference-in-means language-routing directions, activation patching, and a per-query re-routing intervention, we (1) show the donor is per-query and often non-English, (2) test whether per-query donor-routing beats the static transfer matrix at predicting success, and (3) causally re-route failed queries to their best donor. Metrics include per-query donor decodability, donor-diversity (fraction non-English/non-query), routing-vs-matrix predictive R-squared, and re-routing accuracy recovery with specificity controls.
Experiments:
1) Multilingual QA/reasoning suite with per-language ground truth: Assemble ~800 facts (mLAMA-style, verified answers) and reasoning items (MGSM), each queried in a panel of typologically diverse languages spanning scripts and resource levels (English, French, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish). For each fact, establish which languages the model 'knows' it in (paraphrase-consistent multilingual probing), so a candidate best-donor exists. Native-speaker verify. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Per-query donor decoding (H1, core): For each query, use logit-lens/tuned-lens across mid layers to decode which language's representation the answer is retrieved from — the DONOR language — by measuring which language the pre-final answer representation decodes most directly from (extending the English-decodable-hub method to a full-language readout, and validating against a difference-in-means per-language routing direction). Report per-query donor identity and, crucially, donor DIVERSITY: the fraction of queries whose donor is neither English nor the query language (predict a substantial non-trivial fraction). Test donor stability across paraphrases (reliability).
3) Donor determines success (H2): Test whether the decoded donor language HOLDS the fact (per Exp 1's per-language knowledge map): predict that queries succeed when routed to a knowing donor and fail when routed to a non-knowing donor. Report the fraction of errors that are 'routing errors' (donor doesn't know the fact but another available language does) vs genuine absence (no language knows it).
4) Per-query routing beats the static matrix (H3, core): Build a fixed corpus-level transfer-matrix predictor (best donor per language pair, ATLAS/super-donor style) and compare its prediction of per-query success against the decoded per-query donor. Test via nested regression / model comparison (AIC, held-out R^2) whether per-query donor-routing predicts success beyond the static matrix, resource level, and script similarity. Prediction: per-query donor identity is the dominant predictor; the static matrix under-predicts because the best donor varies item-by-item.
5) Error decomposition via patching: For queries failed in the query language but with a knowing donor, patch the mid-layer donor-language representation of the fact (from the donor's monolingual pass) into the query's forward pass, and test whether the answer is restored — confirming the failure was a routing error, not absence.
6) Core causal intervention (per-query re-routing): Build a lightweight predictor that, from early-layer activations, estimates the item's best donor (the knowing language whose representation the model can most reliably read), then steer/patch the query's mid-layer representation toward that donor language's subspace (difference-in-means routing direction) before answer extraction, without switching output language. Measure accuracy recovery on failed queries. Predict selective recovery for routing-error items, none for genuine-absence items (interaction test). Compare against baselines: always-route-to-English (the default-donor assumption), static-matrix best-donor routing, translate-query-to-English, and a random-direction control. Compute recovery elasticity = accuracy gain per unit routing-error rate.
7) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify re-routing is donor-specific (recovers the fact without switching OUTPUT language — measure off-target/language-mixing rate — and without corrupting queries already correctly routed; symmetric check), and is gap-closing not uniform-lift. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen route more queries to English (lower donor diversity) than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether donor diversity correlates with each model's hub English-centricity and each language's training share.
Evaluation metrics: per-query donor decodability and reliability; donor diversity (fraction non-English/non-query donors); routing-error vs genuine-absence error shares; per-query-donor predictive R^2 for success vs static-matrix/resource/script baselines (AIC, held-out); patching-induced restoration rate; per-query re-routing accuracy recovery and elasticity vs always-English / static-matrix / translate baselines, with output-language preservation and correctly-routed-query preservation (specificity), off-target rate; cross-model donor-diversity comparison and correlation with hub English-centricity and training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Decoding a per-query 'donor language' from logit-lens is approximate and could reflect the shared-hub's English scaffolding rather than a genuine third-language donor; we validate the donor readout against difference-in-means per-language routing directions and the causal patching test (which transfers the fact from the decoded donor), and treat a donor readout that is merely English-by-default as an informative negative (transfer really is English-centric, refuting the diversity claim). 2) 'Donor knows the fact' relies on per-language knowledge labels which are noisy; we use paraphrase-consistent probing and restrict routing-error classification to facts robustly known in at least one language. 3) Per-query routing could conflate with query difficulty; the static-matrix and resource-level baselines and the routing-error-vs-absence decomposition isolate a routing effect — if per-query donor adds no predictive power over the static matrix, the hypothesis is refuted, an informative result relocating transfer to the pair level. 4) The best-donor predictor and re-routing add moving parts; we report an oracle-best-donor upper bound and the predictor's realized gain separately. 5) Re-routing could switch output language or corrupt correctly-routed queries; output-language preservation and the symmetric correctly-routed-preservation check are hard constraints and we report the full tradeoff, comparing against the translate-to-English baseline to show the mechanistic routing account adds value. 6) Donor identity is confounded with tokenizer fertility and script; partial correlations and patching mitigate but may not fully remove confounds. 7) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM/Aya as less English-centric contrasts expected to show higher donor diversity). 8) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: information_rate_setpoint_imposition
Title: Talking at English's Pace: Does the Shared Hub Impose a Dominant-Language Information-Rate Setpoint When Generating in Other Languages?
Short Hypothesis: Human languages converge on a near-constant information rate (~39 bits/s; Coupe et al. 2019) despite huge differences in per-unit information density, achieved by a language-specific trade-off between density and rate. We hypothesize that a multilingual LLM, generating text in a non-dominant language, IMPOSES the dominant (English) language's per-token surprisal-rate setpoint rather than each language's natural rate: it produces text whose per-token information profile (mean surprisal and its variance/uniformity) is anchored to English rather than to the target language's empirical rate, so the generated text is systematically mis-paced (too dense or too sparse, and less uniform) relative to native corpora. This information-rate setpoint is language-conditioned, decodable, set by an early language signal, tracks each language's empirical information rate, and is causally correctable by rescaling a shared rate-control direction without harming content.
Related Work: A large cross-linguistic literature establishes that languages equalize information RATE by trading per-unit density against speech/production rate (Different languages, similar encoding efficiency ~39 bits/s, Coupe et al. 2019, 202 citations; entropy-rate constancy, Takahira 2016; constant conditional entropy, Ferrer-i-Cancho 2013), and that speakers locally smooth surprisal via Uniform Information Density (Jaeger 2008; Levy & Jaeger; Meister 2021; cross-lingual UID in word order 2023; grounded UID 2026). Surprisal-theory work validates that LM surprisal predicts human processing across 11 languages (Wilcox 2023; Kuribayashi 2023) and that LM internal-layer surprisal is human-like (Large Language Models Are Human-Like Internally 2025; Comparison of Structural Parsers 2022; UID regularizer improves LMs, Meister 2021). CRITICALLY, all of this is about (a) human language production/comprehension or (b) using LM surprisal to model humans; NONE asks whether a multilingual LLM's own GENERATION carries a language-conditioned information-RATE setpoint, whether that setpoint is IMPOSED from the dominant language onto others (mis-pacing target-language output relative to its natural rate), whether it is mediated by a shared, steerable rate-control representation, or whether it tracks each language's empirical information rate. UID work treats uniformity as a property to instill via training regularization, not as a language-conditioned, mechanistically-imposed generation setpoint. We reframe the cross-linguistic constant-information-rate law as a stress test of the English-scaffolded shared hub and give it a decodable, causally-correctable locus. This is orthogonal to my prior verbosity-setpoint proposal (which concerned output LENGTH/elaboration, not the per-token surprisal density/rate profile) and to all my grammatical/lexical imposition proposals.
Abstract: Every human language conveys information at roughly the same rate: languages with low information per syllable simply speak faster, and vice versa, so all converge near a shared bits-per-second setpoint. This equilibrium is language-specific, achieved by a density-versus-rate trade-off. Multilingual language models build a shared, largely English-scaffolded representation. We ask a simple, previously untested question: when a model generates text in a non-dominant language, does it pace the information the way that language naturally does, or does it impose the dominant (English) language's information-rate setpoint? We hypothesize that the model anchors the per-token surprisal profile of its generations—mean surprisal (density) and its variance (uniformity)—to English rather than to each target language's empirical rate, producing text that is systematically mis-paced and less uniform relative to native corpora, with the mismatch scaling with the target language's distance from English on the empirical information-rate spectrum. We further hypothesize this setpoint is a language-conditioned gain on a shared, decodable rate-control representation, set early by a language signal, and causally correctable by rescaling that direction without harming content. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM across typologically diverse languages, comparing the surprisal profile of model generations against native-corpus baselines using held-out reference LMs, and combining difference-in-means rate-direction extraction, logit-lens gain readout, activation patching, and rate-steering. Metrics include per-language information-rate imposition gap, empirical-rate prediction correlation, mediation R-squared, and steering-induced re-pacing with content-preservation controls.
Experiments:
1) Native information-rate reference and generation suite: For typologically diverse languages spanning the empirical information-rate/density spectrum (English, Spanish, French, German, Chinese, Japanese, Arabic, Hindi, Turkish, Vietnamese — chosen to include known high-density/slow and low-density/fast languages from Coupe et al. 2019), assemble (a) NATIVE reference corpora and (b) ~500 controlled generation prompts (translation, summarization, and open continuation on matched content across languages, native-speaker verified). For each language, estimate the empirical per-token information profile—mean surprisal (density) and surprisal variance (uniformity)—of NATIVE text using a strong HELD-OUT reference LM per language (not the model under test), establishing the target-language natural rate as ground truth. Report inter-annotator agreement on prompts; release the suite. Models under test: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral information-rate imposition (H1, core): Generate text in each target language and measure the surprisal profile of the MODEL'S generations (scored by the held-out reference LM, so the profile reflects the text's actual density/uniformity, not the model's own confidence). Compare the model-generation profile against the NATIVE-corpus profile for that language. Define the information-rate imposition GAP = deviation of the model-generation mean surprisal and uniformity from the native-language values, signed toward the ENGLISH profile (does the model make a naturally-low-density language too dense, and a high-density language too sparse, pulling both toward English's density?). Define an English-anchor pull rate. Predict positive imposition (English-anchored pacing) for non-English languages, near-zero for English, and worse uniformity (higher surprisal variance relative to native UID) in imposed languages. Control for tokenizer fertility and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test target-language status adds predictive power).
3) Empirical-rate scaling (H2, external validation): Using each language's empirical information rate/density from the cross-linguistic literature (Coupe et al. 2019; entropy-rate estimates), test whether per-language imposition is predicted by the language's density distance from English (Spearman; held-out prediction from the empirical rate alone), tying the internal phenomenon to independent, authoritative cross-linguistic ground truth. Predict larger imposition for languages farthest from English on the density spectrum.
4) Shared rate-control representation and gain readout (H3): Extract a per-language 'information-rate' direction via difference-in-means between high-density/high-surprisal-rate and low-density/low-surprisal-rate generation states at each layer (verifying it is a graded rate axis via a probe recovering the generation's surprisal level). Measure cross-lingual cosine alignment (test: a largely shared rate-control axis re-scaled per language; portability via steering). Project the residual stream at the generation-decision point onto the shared direction and estimate a per-LANGUAGE rate gain via regression; test whether the query language is decodable from an early signal that predicts the eventual generation rate (position-resolved logit-lens), and whether the cross-lingual imposition is captured by the difference in per-language gains applied to the SHARED projection (held-out R^2), beating a uniform-bias baseline. Mediation: regress behavioral imposition on the rate-direction projection (partial correlation controlling for fertility/resource; held-out R^2).
5) Causal rate-steering test (H4, core): Rescale the shared information-rate direction with a per-language scalar to shift the generation's pacing toward the target-language natural rate (and, as a dose-response control, toward English), and measure whether the generated surprisal profile (density and uniformity) moves toward native values (re-pacing rate) and the imposition GAP shrinks, without switching output language. Bidirectional dose-response; mis-signed steering worsens. Complement with activation patching: patch the target-language native-rate signal (or the English signal) into the generation pass. Critically verify CONTENT PRESERVATION: re-pacing must change HOW information is distributed, not WHICH information is conveyed (content-overlap/faithfulness and adequacy checks), plus fluency and off-target/language-mixing checks. Baselines: whole-hub English-steering, a UID-regularization-inspired prompt ('write naturally in <language>'), and a random-direction control.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify steering is rate-specific (changes surprisal density/uniformity but not content, grammaticality, or output language), graded (imposition scales with empirical-rate distance), and not merely a length or tokenizer artifact (control output length and report both token- and character-normalized rates). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show stronger imposition than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether imposition magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the rate direction and with each language's training share. Qualitatively compare the per-language imposition pattern against the human constant-information-rate law (direction, not identical mechanism).
Evaluation metrics: information-rate imposition GAP (mean-surprisal density and surprisal-variance uniformity, model-generation vs native corpus; English-anchor pull rate; vs English ceiling); imposition-vs-empirical-rate-distance correlation and held-out prediction; rate-control-direction surprisal-level decodability, cross-lingual alignment, portability, early language-signal predictiveness, and gain predictive R^2 (vs uniform-bias baseline) with mediation of behavioral imposition (held-out R^2); steering re-pacing rate and GAP reduction (bidirectional dose-response), patching-induced re-pacing; content-preservation/adequacy, grammaticality/fluency, off-target/language-mixing rate, length control; cross-model imposition comparison and correlation with training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for target-language status over fertility/resource baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Measuring the 'information rate' of a text requires a reference LM whose own biases could confound the estimate; we use a strong HELD-OUT reference LM per language (distinct from the model under test), validate it against native-corpus statistics, and report robustness across multiple reference LMs and both token- and character-normalized measures. 2) Information density/rate is confounded with tokenizer fertility, script, and resource level; we report both token- and character-normalized surprisal, control for fertility with partial correlations, use the empirical-rate prediction (an external cross-linguistic ground truth) to isolate a rate-imposition effect from generic tokenization differences, and treat a purely tokenization-driven gap as itself an informative mechanistic sub-finding. 3) Some mis-pacing may reflect genuinely correct behavior (the model rightly matching the target language's rate) rather than English imposition; the direction of the effect (does the profile track ENGLISH or the TARGET native rate?), the empirical-rate-distance prediction, and the causal steering (which re-paces by editing only the rate direction) distinguish imposition from faithful pacing, and a faithful-pacing finding is itself valuable, extending the constant-rate law to LLM generation. 4) The single-scalar gain account may only partially hold; if a data-driven low-dimensional basis (separate density vs uniformity axes) fits better, we report the empirically-best basis, keeping the 'shared rate axis + language gain' claim testable. 5) The difference-in-means rate direction may entangle content/topical or length features; we verify it is a graded surprisal-level axis, control output length, use a content-only control direction, and apply specificity checks. 6) Human information rate is a SPEECH (bits/s) phenomenon achieved partly by speech rate, whereas an LLM produces text with no timing; our LLM-human comparison is therefore about the per-token/per-character information DENSITY and UNIFORMITY profile (the density side of the density-rate trade-off), a text-level analogue, and we frame it as structural/qualitative, not identical-mechanism. 7) Steering could harm content adequacy or fluency; content-preservation and fluency are hard specificity constraints and we report the full tradeoff plus bidirectional dose-response, comparing against the 'write naturally' prompt baseline to show the mechanistic account adds value. 8) Instruction-tuned/RLHF models may impose a uniform 'assistant' style that flattens cross-lingual rate variation; we test base vs instruction-tuned models and treat differences as an informative training-stage finding. 9) Logit-lens gain/timing estimates are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 10) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM/Aya analyzed as less English-centric contrasts expected to impose less). 11) If NO imposition is found—model generations match each language's native information-rate profile, predictable from the empirical spectrum, with content preserved—this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the shared hub paces information in a language-appropriate way despite English scaffolding, valuable either way. 12) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: portable_analogy_operator_local_retrieval
Title: The Relation Travels, the Answer Stays Home: A Portable Cross-Lingual Analogy Operator but Language-Bound Target Retrieval in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: In multilingual A:B::C:D analogical reasoning, the relational-mapping operation (the abstract R that re-types C into D) is encoded as a largely language-agnostic 'concept-vector' operator in the shared hub and therefore transfers across a demonstration-to-query language boundary, whereas the final RETRIEVAL/decoding of target D is language-bound and fails in lower-resource / typologically-distant target languages. Cross-lingual analogy inconsistency is thus dominated by target-retrieval failure, not relation-encoding failure: the correct D is latently present in the shared hub but not surfaced in the target language. Consequently an operator extracted in one language can be transplanted into another to complete the analogy, whereas retrieval failures cannot be fixed this way — a clean dissociation between a portable operator and a local decoder that mirrors the human L1/L2 analogy asymmetry (relations complete, lexical retrieval is the L2 bottleneck).
Related Work: Monolingual mechanistic work shows relations are encoded in mid-upper layers as invariant, causally-insertable concept/function vectors, but that LLMs struggle to APPLY a correctly-encoded relation to new entities, with failure marked by degraded structural alignment (The Curious Case of Analogies 2025; Concept Vectors and the Limits of Abstraction 2025; Emergent Analogical Reasoning 2026; Fine-tuned/Composite Function Vectors 2026). All are English/monolingual. Multilingual work establishes a shared, English-scaffolded semantic hub with high cross-lingual concept/structural alignment (Semantic Hub 2024; Structural Concepts Are Universal 2023; Converging to a Lingua Franca 2024; LLMs Share Latent Grammatical Concepts 2025), but concerns static concept/relation alignment, not the analogy OPERATION unfolding across a language boundary. Cognitive science (Analogical reasoning in first and second languages 2025) shows humans process the RELATION in L1/L2 but that L2 lexical RETRIEVAL is the bottleneck — exactly the operator/retrieval dissociation we hypothesize for LLMs. CRITICALLY, no prior work asks whether the analogy operator is a portable cross-lingual entity dissociable from a language-bound target-retrieval step, whether cross-lingual analogy failure is specifically a retrieval (not relation-encoding) failure, whether the correct target is latently present in the hub before the language-specific decoder fails, or whether transplanting the operator across languages completes the analogy. This is orthogonal to my prior proposals and reframes cross-lingual analogy failure via a portable-relation / local-retrieval dissociation.
Abstract: Analogical reasoning maps a familiar relation onto new entities, and interpretability work shows language models encode such relations as compact, causally-transplantable vectors — but only in English. Multilingual models let us pull apart the two computational steps a monolingual setting cannot separate: abstracting the relation, and retrieving/decoding the answer. We do this by teaching an A:B::C:D analogy with the demonstration pair in one language and the query in another. We hypothesize a dissociation: the relational operator is abstracted in a largely language-agnostic shared hub and transfers across the language boundary, while the final target-retrieval/decoding step is language-bound and fails in lower-resource, typologically-distant target languages. Under this account, cross-lingual analogy inconsistency is dominated by target-retrieval failure — the correct answer is latently present in the hub but not surfaced in the target language — and it scales with target-language resource-distance, not with relation complexity. This mirrors the human L1/L2 analogy asymmetry, where relations complete but L2 lexical retrieval is the bottleneck. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using controlled analogy tasks with independently varied demonstration and query languages. Using concept-vector extraction, logit-lens tracking of whether the correct target is latently present, activation patching to separate relation-encoding from target-retrieval failures, and cross-lingual operator transplant, we quantify the dissociation, its resource-distance scaling, and a causal fix that boosts target-language decoding without re-teaching the relation. Metrics include relation-encoding vs target-retrieval error shares, cross-lingual operator-alignment, transplant success rate, latent-target-present rate, and decoding-boost recovery with specificity controls.
Experiments:
1) Cross-lingual analogy suite: Build ~500 A:B::C:D items spanning semantic relations (capital-country, part-whole, antonym, category-member, cause-effect) and morphological relations (comparative, plural, tense), each with a single verified target D and distractors for a forced-choice variant plus an open-generation variant. Independently vary the DEMONSTRATION language (of A:B, which establishes the relation) and the QUERY/TARGET language (of C and the expected D) across typologically diverse languages spanning scripts and resource levels (English, French, German, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish). Include same-language controls. Native-speaker verify; report inter-annotator agreement; release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral map: Measure per-(demo-language, target-language) analogy accuracy (open-generation and forced-choice) and cross-lingual consistency (agreement on the same item across target languages). Control for target-word frequency and tokenizer fertility (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test target-language resource-distance predicts accuracy beyond relation type and demo-language).
3) Operator extraction and cross-lingual alignment (H1a): For each relation, extract a per-language analogy-operator direction (concept/function vector) via causal-mediation / RSA over A:B pairs at the relation-encoding layers (following Concept Vectors 2025; Fine-tuned Function Vectors 2026). Measure cross-lingual cosine alignment of the operator across layers; test it is high and peaks in early-to-mid (shared-hub) layers, comparable to within-model relation baselines. Verify each operator causally completes analogies within its language (insertion flip rate).
4) Relation-encoding vs target-retrieval error decomposition (H1b, core): For items correct with a same-language/high-resource demo but wrong for a low-resource target language, use logit-lens to test whether the correct D (in its shared-hub/English-decodable form) is latently present in mid layers even on failed items (latent-target-present rate). Then use activation patching: patch (a) the shared-hub relation-operator representation into the failing pass, and (b) only the late-layer target-language decoding components. Classify as relation-encoding failure (fixed by (a) at the relation stage, D not latently present) vs target-retrieval failure (D latently present; only (b) surfaces it). Report per-target-language error shares, predicting retrieval failures dominate and grow with resource-distance.
5) Core cross-lingual transplant test (H2): Extract the operator in a high-resource demonstration language and TRANSPLANT it (steering/insertion) into a low-resource target-language forward pass on the C token; measure whether the model correctly completes the analogy in the target language (transplant success rate). Prediction: transplant substantially raises accuracy for relation-encoding failures but CANNOT repair genuine target-retrieval failures, demonstrating the portable-relation / local-retrieval dissociation. Compare against a shared-hub English-steering baseline, a target-decoding-boost intervention (steer the target-language decoding direction, which our account predicts is what retrieval failures need), and a random-direction control.
6) Specificity, cognitive-comparison, and cross-model controls: Verify transplant is relation-specific (transplanting the antonym operator completes antonym analogies but not part-whole), does not switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), and preserves fluency. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 shows sharper retrieval-failure dominance and larger transplant gains than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether the operator-alignment / retrieval-failure split correlates with each language's training share. Qualitatively compare the relation-transfers-but-target-not-retrieved pattern against the human L1/L2 analogy asymmetry.
Evaluation metrics: per-(demo,target)-language accuracy and cross-lingual consistency; cross-lingual operator-direction alignment (and vs within-model baseline); latent-target-present rate on failed items; relation-encoding vs target-retrieval error shares per target language; transplant success rate (overall and split by error type) vs baselines; relation-specificity of transplant; target-decoding-boost recovery for retrieval failures; off-target rate; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for target resource-distance over frequency/fertility baselines; cross-model comparison and correlation with training share; qualitative correspondence with the human L1/L2 asymmetry.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Relation-encoding and target-retrieval may not separate cleanly; patching can have entangled effects. Mitigation: use multiple patching granularities, cross-validate with the logit-lens latent-target-present check, and report ambiguous cases. 2) Word-analogy tasks can be solved by lexical association rather than genuine relational mapping; we include far/cross-domain and morphological relations, distractor-controlled forced-choice items, and low-association targets to reduce shortcuts. 3) Operator directions from causal-mediation/concept-vectors may be format- or content-entangled (Concept Vectors 2025 shows function-vector format-sensitivity); we use format-invariant concept-vector extraction, multiple relation types, and specificity controls. 4) Target resource-distance is confounded with tokenizer fertility, script, and target-word frequency; we use partial correlations and matched targets, but residual confounds may remain. 5) Transplant could harm fluency or switch output language; specificity and off-target checks address this and we report the full tradeoff. 6) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM's less English-centric hub analyzed as a contrast expected to show weaker retrieval-failure dominance). 7) The human-LLM comparison (L1/L2 asymmetry) is qualitative, not a claim of identical mechanism. 8) If the operator does NOT transfer cross-lingually (low alignment, transplant fails), the portability hypothesis is refuted — itself an informative result showing analogy operators are language-specific; conversely, if failures are relation-encoding rather than retrieval failures, this relocates the cross-lingual analogy bottleneck and is equally valuable. 9) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: gradable_threshold_imposition
Title: How Tall Is Tall in Another Tongue? Does the Shared Hub Impose a Dominant-Language Standard of Comparison onto Gradable Adjectives?
Short Hypothesis: The positive form of a gradable adjective ('tall', 'expensive', 'hot') is vague: its truth depends on a contextually-set THRESHOLD relative to a comparison class whose distribution differs across cultures (what counts as a 'tall' person, an 'expensive' meal, or a 'hot' day is not universal). Because multilingual LLMs represent gradable meaning on a single, largely English-scaffolded degree scale, we hypothesize the model IMPOSES the dominant (English/Western) standard-of-comparison threshold when judging a gradable adjective in another language: its positive-form judgments, comparison-class inferences, and borderline-case decisions track the English threshold rather than the target-language/culture norm, producing cross-lingual inconsistency on identical objects. This threshold imposition is mediated by a shared, steerable 'degree-threshold' direction, tracks each language's empirical comparison-class norms, and is causally correctable without harming the ordering of the scale itself.
Related Work: Formal degree semantics establishes that positive-form gradable adjectives carry a free threshold variable fixed by a comparison class, that this yields vagueness and context-sensitivity, and that the relative/absolute distinction and scale structure vary cross-linguistically (Kennedy & McNally 2005; The Grammar of Tolerance 2012; Degree Semantics Parameter / Washo lacks degree variables 2015; Mandarin scale-structure classification 2016; probabilistic threshold models, Lassiter & Goodman 2015; Qing & Franke 2015). Probing work shows LMs encode scalar-adjective intensity and rankings, including multilingually, and use monotonicity/NPI cues, but treats the scale as a fixed English object (Scalar Adjective Multilingual Ranking 2021; Probing LLMs for Scalar Semantics/Pragmatics 2024; Monotonicity/NPI 2021; Human-Model Divergence in Vagueness 2021). Multilingual interpretability shows an English-scaffolded shared hub and largely linear cross-lingual concept alignment (Semantic Hub 2024; Concept Space Alignment 2024; Geometry of Multilingual Representations 2022). CRITICALLY, all LM scalar-adjective work is about intensity RANKING or lexical semantics (nice<great<wonderful), and all vagueness work is monolingual/English; NONE asks whether the shared, English-scaffolded degree scale IMPOSES the dominant-language STANDARD OF COMPARISON (the vague positive-form threshold, set by a culture-specific comparison class) onto other languages, causing cross-lingual inconsistency on identical objects, localizes a shared degree-threshold direction mediating it, ties it to per-culture comparison-class norms as ground truth, or offers a causal fix. This differs from my prior color-boundary and typicality-prototype proposals (which target categorical perception and category prototypes, not the vague threshold on a gradable scale) and from scalar-ranking probing (which concerns fixed intensity order, not the culturally-set positive-form standard).
Abstract: Whether a person is 'tall', a meal is 'expensive', or a day is 'hot' depends on a standard of comparison that formal semantics locates in a contextually-set threshold over a comparison class -- and that class differs across cultures, so the same object can be truthfully 'tall' in one place and merely average in another. Multilingual language models represent gradable meaning on a single, largely English-scaffolded degree scale. We ask a simple, previously untested question: when a model judges a gradable adjective in a non-English language, does it impose the dominant-language standard of comparison rather than the target culture's? We hypothesize that (1) the model's positive-form truth judgments and borderline-case decisions for culturally-variable adjectives track the English threshold, producing cross-lingual inconsistency on identical objects concentrated where cultural comparison-class norms diverge; (2) the size of this imposition tracks each culture's empirical comparison-class distribution; (3) a shared, steerable degree-threshold direction mediates it, distinct from the (correctly shared) ordering of the scale; and (4) shifting the threshold per language restores culture-appropriate judgments without harming scale ordering. We build a controlled multilingual suite of gradable adjectives with divergent versus convergent cultural standards, grounded in comparison-class norms, across typologically and culturally diverse languages, on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM. Using difference-in-means threshold-direction probes, logit-lens tracking, activation patching, and steering, we measure the imposition, its norm scaling, its mediation, and its causal correction. Metrics include cross-lingual threshold-imposition gap, norm-prediction correlation, mediation R-squared, and steering-induced correction with scale-ordering-preservation controls.
Experiments:
1) Cultural standard-of-comparison suite grounded in norms: Select ~30 relative gradable adjectives whose positive-form standard is culturally variable (tall/short for a person, expensive/cheap for a meal or house, hot/cold for weather, big/small for a portion, fast for a commute), each with ~15 test objects spanning the value range with GROUND-TRUTH magnitudes (a height in cm, a price, a temperature). For each adjective and target culture, obtain the empirical comparison-class distribution and the human threshold (the value at which the positive form becomes true) via native-speaker rating and, where available, real-world reference distributions (e.g. average heights, local prices/temperatures). Instantiate across typologically and culturally diverse languages spanning divergent norms and resource levels (English, German, Spanish, Mandarin, Japanese, Hindi, Arabic, Swahili). Key subsets: DIVERGENT adjective-culture pairs whose human threshold differs from the English/Western threshold, and matched CONVERGENT pairs. Probes hinge on the positive-form threshold: (i) positive-form truth judgment ('Is a person of X cm tall?' yes/no, in the target language, with the magnitude given in a culturally-natural unit); (ii) borderline-case forced choice (which of two objects counts as 'tall'?); (iii) comparison-class inference ('For a <object> here, would X be considered tall?'). Native-speaker verify; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral threshold imposition (H1, core): For each DIVERGENT pair, measure whether the model's positive-form threshold (the value at which it switches from 'not tall' to 'tall') tracks the ENGLISH threshold vs the target-culture human threshold. Define the cross-lingual threshold-imposition GAP = |model threshold - target-culture threshold| minus |model threshold - English threshold| (negative = tracks English), and an English-standard pull rate = fraction of divergent pairs whose model threshold is closer to English. Verify near-faithful thresholds on CONVERGENT pairs and correct English thresholds (ceiling). Crucially, verify the model orders the SCALE correctly in every language (taller object judged >= shorter), so imposition is a threshold shift, not a scale failure. Control for object-value frequency, tokenizer fertility, and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test target-culture status adds predictive power).
3) Norm scaling (H2, external validation): Test whether per-adjective-culture imposition is predicted by the divergence between the target-culture and English comparison-class distributions/thresholds (Spearman; held-out prediction from the norm data alone), tying the internal phenomenon to independent human/real-world ground truth. Predict larger imposition for lower-resource / culturally-distant languages.
4) Representational localization (H3): Extract a per-adjective 'degree-threshold' direction via difference-in-means between just-below-threshold ('not tall') and just-above-threshold ('tall') object representations at each layer, per language, SEPARATELY from the scale-ordering direction (difference-in-means over ordered magnitudes). Test (a) whether the scale-ordering direction is shared/consistent across languages (the scale itself is language-agnostic) while the threshold POSITION is English-scaffolded; (b) whether a DIVERGENT object near the target-culture boundary is placed relative to the ENGLISH threshold in the shared mid-layers, via logit-lens/tuned-lens tracking. Mediation: regress behavioral imposition on the shared-hub threshold-position (partial correlation controlling for frequency/fertility; held-out R^2). Baseline: the scale-ordering direction as a within-model control that should NOT show imposition.
5) Causal steering/patching test (H4, core): (a) Steer along the degree-threshold direction to shift the target-language threshold toward the target-culture value (raise/lower the standard) and measure whether positive-form and borderline judgments shift to the culture-appropriate pattern (flip rate) and the imposition GAP shrinks toward the CONVERGENT baseline, without switching output language; (b) bidirectional dose-response (shift toward and away from English); (c) for imposed items, patch the residual language-specific threshold signal (from early/language-specific layers) into later computation and test restoration. Critically verify SCALE-ORDERING preservation (the model must still order objects correctly and answer comparatives 'is A taller than B?' -- steering moves only the vague threshold, not the ordering) plus fluency and off-target/language-mixing checks. Baselines: whole-hub English-steering, random-direction control.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify steering is threshold-specific (changes the positive-form standard but not scale ordering, comparatives, or the object's magnitude), graded (imposition scales with norm divergence), and not a frequency artifact (frequency-matched divergent/convergent pairs). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show stronger imposition than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether imposition magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the threshold direction and with each language's training share. Qualitatively compare the model's per-culture threshold pattern against the human comparison-class norms.
