Evaluation metrics: cross-lingual threshold-imposition GAP and English-standard pull rate (DIVERGENT vs CONVERGENT; vs English ceiling; scale-ordering preserved); imposition-vs-norm-divergence correlation and held-out prediction; scale-ordering-direction cross-lingual consistency vs threshold-position English-scaffolding; shared-hub threshold-position and its mediation of behavioral imposition (held-out R^2); steering flip rate and GAP reduction (bidirectional dose-response), patching-induced restoration; scale-ordering and comparative preservation (specificity), fluency, off-target rate; cross-model imposition comparison and correlation with training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for target-culture status over frequency/fertility/resource baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Establishing per-culture ground-truth thresholds for a vague positive-form adjective is inherently noisy (thresholds are graded and speaker-variable); we ground them in comparison-class norms plus real-world reference distributions where available (heights, prices, temperatures), use native-speaker rating with multiple annotators, report inter-annotator agreement, restrict DIVERGENT items to pairs with robust cross-cultural threshold differences, and treat thresholds as noisy predictors, relying on internal representation and causal tests for core claims. 2) Standard divergence is correlated with language family, script, resource level, and unit conventions; the CONVERGENT controls, English ceiling, scale-ordering controls, within-adjective contrasts, and norm-based prediction isolate the threshold pathway, but residual confounds may remain; we present magnitudes in culturally-natural units and also test a unit-neutral variant to separate threshold from measurement-system effects. 3) Some imposition may reflect genuinely correct behavior (the model rightly using the target-culture standard); the direction of the effect (tracks ENGLISH vs TARGET threshold), the norm prediction, and the causal steering (which restores the target threshold by editing only the threshold direction while leaving scale ordering intact) distinguish imposition from faithful judgment, and a faithful-judgment finding is itself valuable and extends the concept-alignment literature. 4) The key elegant control is that the SCALE ORDERING is a separate, shared representation from the vague THRESHOLD; if the model fails at scale ordering itself in some language, the threshold question is moot there -- we gate on correct ordering and treat ordering failures as a separate, informative finding. 5) Difference-in-means threshold directions may entangle magnitude or lexical features; we use the scale-ordering control direction, frequency-matched controls, and multiple extraction methods. 6) Logit-lens depth estimates are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 7) Steering could harm scale ordering or fluency; scale-ordering and comparative preservation are hard specificity constraints and we report the full tradeoff plus bidirectional dose-response. 8) Absolute adjectives (full, straight) have context-independent standards and are used as a within-suite contrast expected to show LESS imposition, sharpening the relative/absolute prediction. 9) Instruction-tuned models may hedge on borderline cases; we test base models where available and use forced-choice borderline probes. 10) The model-vs-human comparison is qualitative/structural (threshold divergence), not a claim of identical mechanism. 11) If NO imposition is found -- positive-form thresholds track each culture's own standard, predictable from norms, with scale ordering preserved -- this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the shared scale carries culture-specific thresholds despite English scaffolding, valuable either way. 12) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: adaptive_control_context_mode
Title: Single, Dual, or Dense: Does the Conversational Context Mode Reshape a Multilingual LLM's Language Control, as the Adaptive Control Hypothesis Predicts for Humans?
Short Hypothesis: The human Adaptive Control Hypothesis (ACH) holds that a bilingual's language-control effort adapts to the INTERACTIONAL CONTEXT: a single-language context demands strong interference suppression, a dual-language context demands salient-cue-driven switching, and a dense-code-switching context relaxes control by allowing free co-activation. We hypothesize a mechanistic analogue in multilingual LLMs: the recent conversational context MODE (established over prior turns) causally sets the strength of a shared 'language-control' mechanism, so that on an IDENTICAL new query the model's unintended language-mixing rate, switch cost, and target-language fidelity shift systematically with the induced mode — dense-code-switching context yields the most co-activation/mixing and lowest switch cost, single-language context the strongest suppression and lowest mixing — and this control setpoint is decodable and causally steerable.
Related Work: Human research establishes the Adaptive Control Hypothesis: interactional context (single-language, dual-language, dense-code-switching) adapts language-control processes and switch costs, though the executive-function predictions are contested (Green & Abutalebi 2013; Green 2018; Beatty-Martinez; the failed-predictions meta-analysis 2021; ecological-validity 2018). On the LLM side, language mixing in reasoning reflects latent script preferences and is worst for non-English/Chinese inputs (Language Mixing in Reasoning 2025), language confusion is a late-layer transition failure fixable by neuron edits (Mechanistic Language Confusion 2025), and language identity lives in sparse, steerable residual dimensions (Language Lives in Sparse Dimensions 2025; Do Multilingual LLMs Think In English 2025). CRITICALLY, all LLM language-mixing/confusion work treats mixing as a property of the CURRENT prompt (its language, difficulty, script) and studies single-turn inputs; NONE asks whether the recent conversational CONTEXT MODE (a history of single-language vs dual-language vs dense-code-switched turns) causally reconfigures the model's language-control effort on a subsequent identical query, whether this mirrors the human ACH prediction (dense context -> relaxed control -> more mixing/lower switch cost; single context -> strong suppression), whether a shared control setpoint carries it, or whether it is steerable. We uniquely port the ACH's context-modulated-control claim into LLM mechanisms, reframing language mixing from a static per-prompt artifact into a context-adaptive control setpoint with a decodable, steerable locus. This is orthogonal to my prior conversational_language_anchor_decay proposal (which concerns monotonic drift toward English over a same-language conversation, not the causal effect of the context's code-switching MODE on control effort).
Abstract: Bilingual people control their languages differently depending on the conversation they are in: when everyone speaks one language they must firmly suppress the other, when two monolinguals must each be addressed they switch on cue, and in a freely code-switching group they let both languages flow. The Adaptive Control Hypothesis formalizes this as interactional context reconfiguring language-control effort. We ask a simple, previously untested question about multilingual language models: does the recent conversational context MODE reshape the model's language control on a subsequent identical query? We hypothesize a mechanistic analogue: establishing a single-language, dual-language, or dense-code-switching context over prior turns causally sets the strength of a shared language-control mechanism, so that on the SAME new query the model's unintended language-mixing rate, its switch cost, and its target-language fidelity shift systematically with the induced mode — dense contexts producing the most co-activation and lowest switch cost, single-language contexts the strongest suppression — and this control setpoint is decodable and causally steerable independent of the query. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM across typologically diverse languages, using controlled conversation prefixes that instantiate each ACH context mode followed by matched probe queries. Combining behavioral mixing/switch-cost measurement, difference-in-means control-direction extraction, activation patching, and steering, we measure the context-mode effect, its mechanistic locus, and a causal fix, and compare the pattern against human ACH predictions.
Experiments:
1) Context-mode conversation suite: Construct ~500 matched PROBE queries (factual/reasoning items with verified gold answers, requiring an answer in a specified target language) each preceded by one of three controlled conversation PREFIXES that instantiate an ACH interactional-context mode over ~4-6 prior turns, holding prefix CONTENT fixed: (a) SINGLE-LANGUAGE (all prior turns strictly in the target language), (b) DUAL-LANGUAGE (prior turns alternate cleanly between the target language and another language, one language per turn, cued), (c) DENSE-CODE-SWITCHING (prior turns freely mix both languages intra-sententially). Include a NO-CONTEXT baseline (probe alone). Instantiate across typologically diverse language pairs spanning scripts and resource levels (English-French, English-Chinese, English-Hindi, English-Arabic, English-Swahili, French-Arabic). Native-speaker verify prefixes and gold answers; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral context-mode effect (H1, core): On the IDENTICAL probe query, measure per-mode (i) unintended language-mixing / off-target rate in the model's output, (ii) switch cost = the accuracy/log-prob penalty when the probe requires switching to the target language versus staying, and (iii) target-language fidelity. Test the ACH-predicted pattern: dense-code-switching context yields the highest mixing and lowest switch cost (relaxed control / free co-activation), single-language context the lowest mixing and highest suppression, dual-language intermediate. Since the probe is fixed and only the prefix mode varies, any difference isolates a context-mode control effect. Control for prefix token length, tokenizer fertility, and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test context mode adds predictive power beyond prefix length).
3) Mechanistic control setpoint (H2): Extract a difference-in-means 'language-control' direction (high-suppression single-language passes vs low-suppression dense passes) at middle/late layers and test whether the context MODE is decodable from an early signal on the probe (before the answer is produced), whether the control-direction projection tracks the behavioral mixing/switch-cost gradient (mediation regression; held-out R^2), and whether the direction is largely shared across language pairs (cross-lingual alignment). Relate to the sparse language-identity dimensions (Language Lives in Sparse Dimensions 2025) and late-layer transition (Mechanistic Language Confusion 2025): test whether dense contexts weaken the late-layer target-language transition.
4) Causal test via patching: For probes answered with unintended mixing under a dense prefix but cleanly under a single-language prefix, patch (a) the control-setpoint representation from the single-language pass into the dense pass and (b) only late-layer transition components. If (a) restores clean target-language output, the context mode acts through the shared control setpoint, not the probe content. Conversely, patch the dense control setpoint into a single-language pass and test whether it induces mixing (bidirectional causal test). Report the share of mixing explained by the context-mode control setpoint.
5) Steering intervention: Steer along the control direction toward the single-language (high-suppression) pole on dense-context probes and measure whether unintended mixing drops and target-language fidelity rises, without harming answer content. Predict selective effect (moves mixing/switch-cost, not accuracy on content). Compare against baselines: prompt-reinforcement ('respond only in <language>'), the language-confusion neuron edit (Mechanistic Language Confusion 2025), sparse language-dimension overwrite (Language Lives in Sparse Dimensions 2025), and a random-direction control.
6) Specificity and human-comparison controls: Verify steering is control-specific (changes mixing/switch-cost but not answer content or the reasoning, does not switch to the WRONG language; measure off-target rate and content-faithfulness), preserves fluency, and is bidirectional. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show a larger single-vs-dense context-mode swing than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether the swing correlates with each model's baseline English-centricity and each language pair's training share. Qualitatively compare the model's per-mode mixing/switch-cost pattern against the human ACH predictions (direction and ordering: dense < dual < single in control effort), noting where the LLM diverges (informative for the LLM-human analogy).
Evaluation metrics: per-mode unintended-mixing/off-target rate, switch cost, and target-language fidelity on the identical probe (context-mode swing = single minus dense; vs no-context baseline; partial correlations over prefix length/fertility, held-out R^2); context-mode decodability from an early probe signal; control-direction cross-lingual alignment and mediation of the behavioral swing (held-out R^2); share of mixing fixed by control-setpoint patching and induced by the reverse patch (bidirectional); steering-induced mixing reduction and fidelity gain vs baselines, with content-faithfulness and correct-target-language preservation (specificity), off-target rate; cross-model swing comparison and correlation with English-centricity/training share; qualitative correspondence with human ACH ordering.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The context-mode effect could conflate with generic prompt-priming (the prefix simply making the model more likely to emit the other language's tokens) rather than a genuine control-effort reconfiguration; the fixed-probe design, the switch-cost measure (a control-cost signature, not just token frequency), the bidirectional patching (which transfers the control setpoint while holding probe content fixed), and the content-faithfulness controls isolate a control effect — if the effect is pure token-priming with no switch-cost or setpoint signature, that is itself an informative negative result. 2) Constructing clean dense-code-switching prefixes that are natural (respecting code-switching grammatical constraints) is delicate; we native-speaker verify naturalness, report inter-annotator agreement, and exclude ungrammatical mixes. 3) Prefix length and token composition differ across modes (dense prefixes contain more of the other language); we control for prefix length and per-language token counts and report robustness. 4) Context mode is confounded with which languages appear; the NO-CONTEXT baseline and matched-content prefixes across modes mitigate but may not fully remove confounds. 5) The difference-in-means control direction may entangle language-identity or content features; we use the established sparse language dimensions and late-transition components as anchors, multiple extraction methods, and specificity controls. 6) The steering intervention could switch to the wrong language, harm content, or over-suppress legitimate code-switching; correct-target-language and content-faithfulness preservation are hard constraints and we report the full tradeoff, comparing against prompt-reinforcement and neuron-edit baselines to show the mechanistic account adds value. 7) The human ACH is itself contested (its executive-function predictions often fail); our comparison is qualitative (context-modulated control-effort ordering), not a claim of identical mechanism, and a divergence from ACH ordering is an informative finding about the limits of the LLM-human analogy. 8) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM/Aya analyzed as less English-centric contrasts expected to show a smaller swing). 9) Off-policy fixed-prefix conversations may under- or over-estimate the effect relative to genuinely interactive dialogue; we note ecological-validity limits and, where feasible, replicate with model-generated conversations. 10) If NO context-mode effect is found — language control is invariant to the conversational code-switching mode — this is an informative POSITIVE result showing LLM language control is context-mode-agnostic, unlike the human ACH prediction, valuable either way. 11) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: language_conditioned_abstention_threshold
Title: Answering When It Shouldn't in One Tongue, Refusing When It Could in Another: A Language-Conditioned Abstention Threshold on a Shared Answerability Signal
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs represent a fact's answerability (whether they know it) on a largely shared, decodable answerability direction, but the DECISION THRESHOLD that converts that signal into answer-vs-abstain is language-conditioned and miscalibrated: for the SAME internal answerability magnitude, the model abstains at a higher or lower rate depending only on the query language, so it over-answers (hallucinates on unknowns) in some languages and over-abstains (refuses knowable facts) in others. This threshold is a low-dimensional gain on the shared answerability signal, is predictable from language resource level, and is causally correctable by rescaling it per language without changing the underlying answerability representation.
Related Work: Prior work shows multilingual abstention/calibration is worse for low-resource languages and improves via multilingual feedback, cross-lingual consensus/voting, or intermediate-layer confidence ensembling (Teaching LLMs to Abstain via Multilingual Feedback 2024; MKA 2025; CALM 2025; CausalAbstain 2025; LACE / Beyond the Final Layer 2025; MlingConf 2024). Answerability is linearly encoded and steerable monolingually (Curious Case of Hallucinatory (Un)answerability 2023; Ambiguity-Encoding Neurons 2025), and knowledge-aware refusal metrics exist (Refusal Index 2025). CRITICALLY, all cross-lingual abstention work treats the failure as a calibration-ACCURACY / knowledge-gap problem and fixes it by adding feedback, voting, or picking better layers; all answerability-mechanism work is monolingual. NONE separates the answerability REPRESENTATION (does the model know it?) from the DECISION THRESHOLD (given that representation, does it answer or abstain?), tests whether the threshold—not the representation—is what varies by language (matched-answerability-magnitude abstention gap), models it as a low-dimensional per-language gain on a shared answerability direction, predicts it from resource level, or causally rescales it to equalize abstention without harming the knowledge signal or over-abstaining. My prior borrowed_boundary_confidence proposal concerned where the confidence FEATURE sources its input; here the distinct claim is that the answerability signal is correctly present but its answer/abstain THRESHOLD is a miscalibrated, imported per-language gain. We reframe cross-lingual abstention failure from a knowledge/calibration problem into a threshold-miscalibration problem with a predictive metric and a targeted, over-abstention-controlled fix.
Abstract: A model that does not know a fact should abstain, and whether it knows the fact does not depend on the language you ask in. Yet multilingual LLMs hallucinate on unknowns in some languages and refuse knowable facts in others. Prevailing accounts treat this as a calibration-accuracy or knowledge-gap problem and remedy it with multilingual feedback, cross-lingual voting, or better-calibrated layers. We propose a sharper, previously untested account: the model represents a fact's answerability on a largely shared, decodable signal, but the DECISION THRESHOLD that turns that signal into answer-vs-abstain is language-conditioned and miscalibrated—anchored to the dominant language and imported into others. Under this account, at equal internal answerability magnitude the model abstains at different rates depending only on query language, over-answering (hallucinating) in some and over-abstaining (refusing knowable facts) in others, and this threshold is a low-dimensional per-language gain on the shared answerability direction, predictable from resource level and causally correctable by rescaling it—without altering the answerability representation and without inducing over-abstention. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using multilingual factual QA with per-language known/unknown ground truth. We extract a shared answerability direction, measure per-prompt answerability magnitude and per-language abstention threshold, and test three predictions: (1) matched on answerability magnitude, abstention rate still varies with language; (2) the per-language threshold is predicted by resource level better than by answerability accuracy alone; and (3) rescaling the shared answerability signal per language equalizes abstention while preserving knowledge and not over-refusing. Metrics include answerability-magnitude-matched abstention gap, threshold predictive R-squared, and rescaling-induced abstention equalization with over-abstention controls.
Experiments:
1) Multilingual known/unknown QA suite: Assemble ~800 factual questions with verified answers plus a matched set of genuinely UNANSWERABLE/unknown questions (false-premise, non-existent entities, questions beyond the model's knowledge), each queried across typologically diverse languages spanning resource levels and scripts (English, French, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish). For each answerable fact, establish per-language whether the model KNOWS it (paraphrase-consistent multilingual probing / repeated-sampling accuracy), giving per-prompt ground-truth answerability. Enable abstention via a standard 'answer or say you don't know' prompt. Native-speaker verify. Models: Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, BLOOM(Z)-7B.
2) Shared answerability direction and magnitude (setup): Extract an answerability direction per model via difference-in-means between known (answerable-and-known) and unknown (genuinely-unknown) representations at mid/late layers (following the Hallucinatory (Un)answerability and AEN findings), verify cross-lingual alignment (a single shared axis) and that it is a graded axis via a probe recovering answerability. For each prompt, compute the answerability magnitude = its projection onto the shared direction.
3) Answerability-magnitude-matched abstention gap (H1, core): Bin prompts by answerability magnitude and, WITHIN a matched-magnitude bin, compare per-language abstention rate. Test the central prediction: at equal internal answerability magnitude, abstention rate still varies with query language—the same knowledge state yields answer in one language and abstain in another. This isolates a threshold effect from an answerability-representation effect. Control for tokenizer fertility (partial correlations).
4) Per-language threshold and prediction (H2): Estimate each language's abstention threshold = the answerability-magnitude at which the model switches from answering to abstaining (logistic fit of abstain probability on answerability magnitude), yielding a per-language threshold and slope. Test whether the per-language threshold is predicted by resource level BETTER than by the language's raw answerability-accuracy (nested regression, AIC, held-out R^2). Predict the threshold is imported/miscalibrated: low-resource languages sit at a threshold that over-answers unknowns and/or over-abstains on knowns relative to the dominant-language threshold.
5) Stage-localization via patching: For prompts hallucinated (answered despite unknown) or over-abstained (refused despite known) in language B but handled correctly in English at matched answerability magnitude, patch (a) the answerability magnitude from English into B and (b) the late decision/threshold components. If (a) rarely changes behavior (answerability already present) but (b) fixes it, the failure is localized to the decision threshold, not the representation. Report threshold- vs representation-failure shares per language.
6) Core causal intervention — per-language threshold rescaling: Rescale the shared answerability direction with a per-language scalar calibrated to equalize the abstention threshold to the dominant-language value (steer proportionally to answerability magnitude), train-free. Measure (i) reduction in hallucination on unknowns (over-answering) and (ii) reduction in over-abstention on knowns, per language. Compare against baselines: uniform answerability-direction addition, multilingual-feedback abstention (Teaching LLMs to Abstain 2024), cross-lingual voting (MKA/CALM), LACE intermediate-layer confidence, and a random-direction control. Compute the Refusal-Index (RI, Spearman of refusal vs error) improvement per language.
7) Over-abstention / specificity controls (hard constraint): The rescaling must simultaneously reduce hallucination on unknowns AND NOT increase refusal on genuinely known facts (a symmetric constraint—the goal is a correctly-placed threshold, not blanket caution), must not switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), and must preserve answer accuracy on knowns and fluency. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show a larger answerability-matched abstention gap than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether the threshold deficit correlates with each language's resource level / training share.
Evaluation metrics: answerability-magnitude-matched abstention gap (H1); per-language abstention threshold and its predictive R^2 from resource level vs answerability-accuracy baseline (H2, AIC/held-out); threshold- vs representation-failure shares (patching); per-language RI, hallucination-on-unknowns rate, and over-abstention-on-knowns rate before/after rescaling vs baselines; symmetric specificity (no increase in refusal on knowns, no drop in accuracy), off-target rate; cross-model abstention-gap comparison and correlation with resource level.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The threshold effect could conflate with the answerability representation itself (a weaker/noisier answerability signal in low-resource languages could look like a threshold shift); the answerability-magnitude-MATCHED abstention gap (H1) and the patching localization (Exp 5) are designed to isolate threshold from representation—if the matched gap vanishes, the hypothesis reduces to the known calibration-accuracy account, an informative negative result. 2) Establishing per-language known/unknown ground truth is noisy; we use paraphrase-consistent probing and repeated sampling, restrict to robustly-known/unknown facts, and report label reliability. 3) The shared answerability direction from difference-in-means may exploit surface cues; we validate with genuinely-unanswerable controls, paraphrases, and held-out fact categories, and confirm it is a graded axis. 4) Abstention behavior is prompt-sensitive; we use multiple abstention prompt formats and report robustness, verifying a measurable English abstention effect first as a gate. 5) The per-language rescaling could over-abstain (blanket caution); the symmetric no-increase-in-refusal-on-knowns constraint is a hard requirement and we report the full tradeoff, comparing against feedback/voting baselines to show the mechanistic threshold account adds value. 6) The low-dimensional (single-scalar) gain account may only partially hold; if a data-driven low-dimensional basis fits better we report it, keeping the 'shared answerability signal + per-language threshold' claim testable. 7) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM/Aya analyzed as less English-centric contrasts expected to show a smaller gap). 8) This touches reliability/safety; all interventions here aim to place abstention correctly (reduce both hallucination and over-refusal) and we release the suite responsibly. 9) Limited to open ~7-8B instruction-tuned models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: dominant_sense_frequency_imposition
Title: The Bank in Every Language Is a River Bank: Does the Shared Hub Impose the Dominant Language's Sense-Frequency Prior onto Polysemous Words?
Short Hypothesis: A polysemous word's most frequent (default) sense differs across languages because sense-frequency distributions are language-specific. Because multilingual LLMs represent word meaning on a single, largely English-scaffolded sense space, we hypothesize the model IMPOSES the DOMINANT (English) language's sense-frequency prior when disambiguating a polysemous word in another language: given a weakly-disambiguating or neutral context, it defaults to the sense that is most frequent in English rather than the sense most frequent in the target language, producing cross-lingual disambiguation inconsistency on identical situations. This sense-prior imposition is mediated by a shared, steerable sense-selection direction, tracks each language's empirical sense-frequency divergence from English, and is causally correctable without harming context-driven disambiguation.
Related Work: Prior work establishes a shared, English-scaffolded semantic hub (Semantic Hub 2024; Do Llamas Work in English 2024; Cross-Layer Transcoders 2025) and shows word senses are linearly encoded and partitionable (Let's Play Mono-Poly 2021; Linear Algebraic Structure of Word Senses 2018). 'When Meanings Meet' (2026) notes, incidentally and via English-anchored patching, that cross-lingual concept patching can make the model 'select dominant senses for polysemous words,' but does not isolate this as a phenomenon, tie it to sense-frequency divergence, or offer a causal fix. StingrayBench (2024), the orthography-semantics paper (2025), and Capacity Constraints for Lexical Disambiguation (2026) show behavioral cross-lingual disambiguation failures and higher-resource-language bias, but these concern INTERLINGUAL HOMOGRAPHS/false friends (different words sharing a form) or general capacity penalties, not the imposition of the dominant language's within-word SENSE-FREQUENCY PRIOR onto a genuinely polysemous word. CRITICALLY, no prior work asks whether, on a neutral/weakly-disambiguating context, the model defaults to the ENGLISH-dominant sense rather than the TARGET-language-dominant sense, whether this cross-lingual inconsistency is predicted by per-language sense-frequency norms (from parallel corpora / SemCor-style counts), whether a shared sense-selection direction mediates it, or whether steering restores the target-language default without harming genuine context-driven disambiguation. This differs from my prior false-friend proposal (form-identical, meaning-different words) by targeting the SAME word's language-specific default-sense prior, grounded in cross-lingual sense-frequency ground truth.
Abstract: Words like 'bank', 'pipe', or 'table' have several senses, and which sense comes to mind first depends on the language: a word's most frequent, default sense is not universal but set by each language's usage statistics. Multilingual language models represent meaning on a single, largely English-scaffolded sense space. We ask a simple, previously untested question: when a model disambiguates a polysemous word in a non-English language under a neutral or weakly-biasing context, does it default to the sense that is most frequent in ENGLISH rather than the sense most frequent in the target language? We hypothesize a dominant-sense-frequency imposition: (1) the model's default-sense choice for a polysemous word tracks the English sense-frequency prior, producing cross-lingual disambiguation inconsistency on identical situations, concentrated where languages' default senses diverge; (2) the size of this imposition tracks each language's empirical sense-frequency divergence from English; (3) a shared, steerable sense-selection direction mediates it, with any residual target-language prior in shallow, language-specific layers; and (4) steering toward the target-language prior restores the correct default without harming context-driven disambiguation. We build a controlled multilingual suite of polysemous words with divergent versus convergent default senses across typologically diverse languages, grounded in cross-lingual sense-frequency norms, on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM. Using difference-in-means sense-direction probes, logit-lens tracking, activation patching, and steering, we measure the imposition, its divergence scaling, its mediation, and its causal correction. Metrics include cross-lingual default-sense imposition gap, frequency-divergence prediction correlation, mediation R-squared, and steering-induced correction with context-disambiguation controls.
Experiments:
1) Divergent/convergent polysemy suite grounded in sense-frequency norms: Assemble ~400 polysemous words per language whose sense inventory is shared across languages (via BabelNet/parallel-corpus sense alignment), each annotated with per-language sense-frequency distributions (from sense-annotated corpora / parallel-corpus translation-distribution counts, e.g. SemCor-style for English and comparable resources / word-alignment counts for target languages). Partition into (a) DIVERGENT words whose most-frequent (default) sense differs between English and the target language (e.g. a word whose dominant sense is 'financial institution' in English but 'river edge' in the target language), and (b) matched CONVERGENT words (same default sense). Instantiate across typologically diverse languages spanning scripts and resource levels (English, French, German, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Turkish, Spanish). Probes: (i) NEUTRAL-context default-sense elicitation (the word in a minimally-biasing frame; forced-choice among senses or elicited paraphrase) to read the model's DEFAULT prior; (ii) STRONG-context disambiguation (context clearly licenses one sense) as a control that the model CAN use context; (iii) sense-inference/entailment probe. Native-speaker verify sense mappings and gold defaults; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral imposition (H1, core): On NEUTRAL-context items, measure whether the model's default-sense choice tracks the ENGLISH-dominant sense vs the TARGET-language-dominant sense. Define the cross-lingual default-sense imposition GAP = inconsistency(DIVERGENT) minus inconsistency(CONVERGENT), and an English-default pull rate = fraction of divergent words for which the model picks the English-dominant sense. Verify near-faithful defaults on CONVERGENT words, correct English defaults (ceiling), and correct STRONG-context disambiguation in every language (isolating a default-PRIOR imposition from an inability to use context). Control for word frequency, tokenizer fertility, and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test target-language status adds predictive power).
3) Frequency-divergence scaling (H2, external validation): Test whether per-word imposition is predicted by the divergence between the target-language and English sense-frequency distributions (e.g. difference in dominant-sense probability; Spearman / held-out prediction from the corpus norms alone), tying the internal phenomenon to independent cross-lingual sense-frequency ground truth. Predict larger imposition for lower-resource / English-distant languages.
4) Representational localization (H3): Extract per-word sense directions via difference-in-means between representations disambiguated toward each sense (using strong-context exemplars), at each layer, per language. Using logit-lens/tuned-lens on NEUTRAL-context items, test whether a DIVERGENT word's representation crystallizes toward the ENGLISH-dominant sense in the shared mid-layers while any residual target-language-default signal is stronger in early/language-specific layers. Mediation: regress behavioral imposition on the shared-hub English-dominant-sense projection (partial correlation controlling for frequency/fertility; held-out R^2). Baseline: a lexical-content (non-sense) direction as a within-model control.
5) Causal steering/patching test (H4, core): (a) Steer the divergent word's representation along the sense direction toward the TARGET-language-dominant sense on neutral-context items and measure whether default-sense choice / entailment shift to the target-language pattern (flip rate) and the imposition GAP shrinks toward the CONVERGENT baseline, without switching output language; (b) conversely amplify the English-dominant sense and confirm dose-response (bidirectional); (c) for imposed items, patch the residual language-specific sense-prior signal (from early/language-specific layers) into later computation and test restoration. Critically verify CONTEXT-DISAMBIGUATION preservation: on STRONG-context items the model must still select the context-licensed sense (steering the DEFAULT must not override clear context) plus fluency and off-target/language-mixing checks. Baselines: whole-hub English-steering, random-direction control.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify steering is sense-prior-specific (changes the default sense but not the word's identity or unrelated meaning), graded (imposition scales with frequency divergence), and not a frequency artifact (frequency-matched divergent/convergent pairs). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show stronger imposition than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether imposition magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the sense direction and each language's training share. Qualitatively compare the model's per-language default-sense pattern against the cross-lingual sense-frequency norms.
Evaluation metrics: cross-lingual default-sense imposition GAP and English-default pull rate (DIVERGENT vs CONVERGENT; vs English ceiling; strong-context preserved); imposition-vs-sense-frequency-divergence correlation and held-out prediction; shared-hub English-dominant-sense projection with mediation of behavioral imposition (held-out R^2); steering flip rate and GAP reduction (bidirectional dose-response), patching-induced restoration; context-disambiguation preservation (specificity), fluency, off-target rate; cross-model imposition comparison and correlation with training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for target-language status over frequency/fertility/resource baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Establishing per-language sense-frequency norms is noisy (sense-annotated corpora are unevenly available across languages); we use parallel-corpus translation-distribution counts and available sense-annotated resources, native-speaker verify, restrict DIVERGENT items to words with robust cross-lingual default-sense differences, report inter-annotator agreement, and treat norms as noisy predictors, relying on internal representation and causal tests for core claims. 2) Sense divergence is correlated with word frequency, script, and resource level; the CONVERGENT controls, English ceiling, STRONG-context controls, within-word contrasts, and frequency-based prediction isolate the sense-prior pathway, but residual confounds may remain. 3) Aligning sense inventories across languages is imperfect (senses do not always map one-to-one); we use BabelNet/parallel-corpus alignment, native-speaker verify, and exclude words with non-mapping senses. 4) Some imposition may reflect genuinely correct behavior (the target language really does share the English default); the DIVERGENT/CONVERGENT contrast, the direction of the effect (tracks ENGLISH vs TARGET default), the frequency-divergence prediction, and the causal steering (which restores the target default by editing only the sense direction) distinguish imposition from faithful defaulting, and a faithful-defaulting finding is itself valuable and sharpens the incidental observation in prior work. 5) Difference-in-means sense directions may entangle topical/lexical features; we use a non-sense lexical control direction, frequency-matched controls, and multiple extraction methods. 6) Logit-lens depth estimates are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 7) The key elegant control is that the model CAN disambiguate from strong context (a context-driven mechanism separate from the default prior); if the model fails at strong-context disambiguation in a language, the default-prior question is moot there and we treat it as a separate finding. 8) Steering could override legitimate context or harm fluency; context-disambiguation preservation is a hard specificity constraint and we report the full tradeoff plus bidirectional dose-response. 9) Instruction-tuned models may hedge on neutral contexts; we test base models where available and use forced-choice default-sense probes. 10) The model-vs-corpus comparison is correlational (frequency divergence), not a claim of identical human mechanism. 11) If NO imposition is found -- default senses track each language's own frequency prior, predictable from corpus norms, with context-disambiguation preserved -- this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the shared sense space carries language-specific default priors despite English scaffolding, valuable either way. 12) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: context_primed_hub_alignment
Title: Warming Up the Hub: In-Context Exposure to a Language Transiently Strengthens Its Shared-Hub Alignment in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: The degree to which a multilingual LLM aligns a query in language L to its shared, language-agnostic concept hub is not a fixed training-time property but is CONTEXT-PLASTIC within a single forward pass: prior exposure to language L earlier in the same context window transiently strengthens how strongly a later same-meaning query in L enters the hub, raising its cross-lingual consistency and factual accuracy relative to the identical query with no such priming. This context-primed hub alignment is a distinct, decodable, and causally-manipulable phenomenon—warming up the hub for a language by seeing it recently—not explained by topic priming, and it is strongest for lower-resource / English-distant languages whose baseline hub alignment is weakest.
Related Work: Prior mechanistic work treats shared-hub alignment as a fixed property established at training time: a shared, English-scaffolded concept hub with language-specific decoding (Semantic Hub 2024; Do Llamas Work in English 2024; Transfer Neurons 2025; Cross-Layer Transcoders 2025), cross-lingual inconsistency localized to entity alignment / late-layer transition (Entity-Level Alignment 2025; Lost in Multilinguality 2025), and hub emergence traced over PRE-TRAINING (When Meanings Meet 2026; How a Bilingual LM Becomes Bilingual 2025). Steering toward the shared space at inference is a static, per-query intervention (Language-Specific Latent Process 2025; SubInj 2025). CRITICALLY, all of this treats a query's hub alignment as determined by the model's weights and the query itself; NONE asks whether the effective hub alignment for a language is PLASTIC within a single context—whether merely having seen language L earlier in the same prompt transiently increases how strongly a later L-query aligns to the hub, improving its consistency/accuracy. This differs from in-context learning (which teaches a task/mapping) and from cross-lingual few-shot prompting (which supplies demonstrations): here the primed content is UNRELATED to the query, so any effect is a change in the model's language-processing state, not task transfer. It is orthogonal to my prior anchor-decay proposal (monotonic drift toward English over a same-language conversation) and mode-control proposal (code-switching context reconfiguring language control): this is a transient, content-independent HUB-ALIGNMENT priming for the primed language, with a decodable mechanism and a causal test.
Abstract: Multilingual language models are thought to align inputs to a shared, language-agnostic concept hub whose strength is fixed by pretraining. We ask a simple, previously untested question: is a language's hub alignment plastic within a single context? We hypothesize context-primed hub alignment—that merely encountering language L earlier in the same prompt (on unrelated content) transiently strengthens how strongly a later, same-meaning query in L enters the shared hub, raising its cross-lingual consistency and factual accuracy relative to the identical query without such priming. Because the primed text is unrelated to the query, this cannot be topic priming or task transfer; it is a change in the model's language-processing state. We predict the effect (1) is largest for lower-resource / English-distant languages whose baseline hub alignment is weakest, (2) is decodable as an increase in how strongly the query's mid-layer representation aligns to the shared (English-decodable) hub, and (3) is causal: it can be reproduced by injecting a language-priming state and eliminated by removing it, and it transfers to accuracy. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using controlled prompts that place unrelated L-language text before a factual/reasoning query in L, versus matched no-priming and other-language-priming controls. Using logit-lens hub-alignment tracking, difference-in-means language-priming direction extraction, and activation patching, we quantify the priming effect, its resource scaling, its decodable locus, and its causal basis. Metrics include priming-induced accuracy and consistency gains, hub-alignment increase, decay over intervening tokens, and patching-induced recovery with specificity controls.
Experiments:
1) Controlled priming suite: Build ~600 factual (mLAMA, verified answers) and reasoning (MGSM) queries, each rendered in typologically diverse languages spanning resource levels and scripts (English, French, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish). For each query in target language L, construct matched prompt conditions holding the query token-identical: (a) NO-PRIMING (query alone / a neutral filler of matched length), (b) SAME-LANGUAGE PRIMING (a passage of UNRELATED text in L preceding the query), (c) OTHER-LANGUAGE PRIMING (unrelated text of matched length/content in a different language, including English), (d) SAME-LANGUAGE-BUT-TOPIC-RELATED priming (a topically-related L passage, to separate hub priming from topic priming). Native-speaker verify; ensure the priming passages contain no answer cues. Report inter-annotator agreement; release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral priming effect (H1, core): Measure per-language query accuracy and cross-lingual consistency (agreement with the English answer) under each condition. Test the central prediction: SAME-LANGUAGE PRIMING (unrelated content) raises accuracy/consistency of the identical query relative to NO-PRIMING and OTHER-LANGUAGE PRIMING. Crucially, compare SAME-LANGUAGE-UNRELATED vs SAME-LANGUAGE-TOPIC-RELATED priming: if unrelated-content priming still helps, the effect is hub priming, not topic priming. Control for priming-passage length/token count and tokenizer fertility (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2). Condition on queries the model gets in English, so gains are not knowledge absence.
3) Resource scaling (H2): Test whether the priming gain scales with the target language's resource-distance from English (Spearman; held-out R^2), predicting the largest gains for low-resource / English-distant languages (whose baseline hub alignment is weakest) and near-zero for English.
4) Decodable hub-alignment increase (H3): Using logit-lens/tuned-lens, measure per-query how strongly the mid-layer representation aligns to the shared (English-decodable) hub (hub-alignment score), per condition. Test that SAME-LANGUAGE priming increases the query's hub-alignment score relative to no-priming, and that the per-query hub-alignment increase mediates the accuracy/consistency gain (mediation regression; held-out R^2). Track the decay of the priming benefit as intervening (neutral) tokens are inserted between the priming passage and the query (predict graded decay), distinguishing a transient state change from a permanent one.
5) Causal test via patching (H4): Extract a difference-in-means 'language-priming' state (residual stream after same-language priming vs no-priming) at the query position. (a) INJECT this state into a NO-PRIMING forward pass and test whether it reproduces the accuracy/consistency gain (priming is sufficient); (b) for a same-language-primed pass, ABLATE/remove the priming component and test whether the gain disappears (priming is necessary). This isolates a content-independent language-processing state as the causal carrier, not the specific primed tokens.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify the effect is language-specific (priming in L helps L-queries but not queries in a third language; a matched-length neutral prime does nothing), does not switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), and preserves fluency; verify the topic-related-priming control does not fully account for the effect. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show larger same-language priming gains for non-English languages than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether the gain correlates with the model's baseline English-centricity and each language's training share.
Evaluation metrics: per-language priming-induced accuracy and consistency gains (same-language-unrelated vs no-priming vs other-language vs topic-related priming); gain-vs-resource-distance scaling (held-out R^2 over fertility/length); hub-alignment-score increase and its mediation of behavioral gain (held-out R^2); priming-benefit decay curve over intervening tokens; injection-induced gain (sufficiency) and ablation-induced loss (necessity); language-specificity, off-target/language-mixing rate; cross-model priming-gain comparison and correlation with English-centricity/training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The priming effect could be topic/content priming rather than hub priming; the SAME-LANGUAGE-UNRELATED vs TOPIC-RELATED contrast and the no-answer-cue verification isolate a content-independent language-processing effect—if unrelated-content priming gives no gain, the hypothesis reduces to topic priming, an informative negative result. 2) The effect could conflate with a knowledge gap; conditioning on English-correct queries and the injection/ablation causal test (which reproduces/removes the gain by editing only the priming state) separate a state change from knowledge absence. 3) Priming-passage length adds tokens and context; matched-length neutral and other-language primes and length controls isolate the language-specific effect from generic context effects. 4) Language is confounded with tokenizer fertility, script, and resource level; partial correlations and the causal patching mitigate but may not fully remove confounds. 5) The language-priming difference-in-means state may entangle content features; we use multiple priming passages, the topic-related control, and the language-specificity check. 6) Logit-lens hub-alignment estimates are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 7) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM/Aya as less English-centric contrasts expected to show smaller gains). 8) If no priming effect is found—hub alignment is fixed regardless of recent same-language exposure—this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the shared hub's per-language alignment is a stable weight property, not context-plastic, valuable either way. 9) Limited to open ~7-8B models and short priming passages; may not extend to frontier scale or long contexts.

Name: crosslingual_false_memory_gist_transfer
Title: Remembering a Word That Was Never Said, in a Language It Was Never Said In: Cross-Lingual Transfer of Gist-Based False Memory in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: When a multilingual LLM is exposed in-context to a list of semantically associated words (a DRM list, e.g. bed, rest, tired, dream...) whose shared associate (sleep) is never presented, it falsely 'remembers' the critical lure — and crucially this gist-based false memory TRANSFERS ACROSS LANGUAGES: presenting the list in language A induces false recognition/recall of the lure's translation-equivalent in language B, because the list's semantic gist is stored in the language-agnostic shared hub rather than tied to the surface words. We hypothesize the cross-lingual false-alarm rate for the lure is high and tracks the shared-hub encoding strength (while true verbatim recognition is more language-bound), mediated by a gist representation in the middle-layer hub, and causally reducible by suppressing that gist signal without harming true-item recognition.
Related Work: Bilingual cognition robustly documents cross-lingual false memory in the DRM (Deese-Roediger-McDermott) paradigm: presenting a semantic associate list in one language elevates false recognition of the never-presented critical lure even when tested in the other language, taken as evidence for a SHARED conceptual store and parallel language activation (Cabeza & Lennartson 2005 'Do Bilinguals Access a Shared or Separate Conceptual Store'; Kawasaki-Miyaji 2003 Japanese-English cross-linguistic false recognition; Sahlin/gist-based DRM). LLM work shows human-like memory properties — primacy/recency, interference-based forgetting, gist errors — learned from data statistics (Aspects of human memory and LLMs 2023; Lost in the Middle as emergent memory 2025) and few-shot recognition/recall/retention dynamics (2023). Interpretability establishes a shared, English-scaffolded semantic hub with language-specific decoding and transfer neurons (Semantic Hub 2024; Do Llamas Work in English 2024; Transfer Neurons 2025; Cross-Layer Transcoders 2025). CRITICALLY, no prior work asks whether a GIST-BASED FALSE MEMORY implanted in one language TRANSFERS to another in an LLM, whether the lure's false-recognition rate is language-bound or shared-hub-mediated, whether it dissociates from true verbatim recognition (which should be more language-specific), whether a middle-layer gist representation carries the false memory, or whether suppressing that gist causally removes the false memory while preserving true recognition. This uniquely ports the bilingual DRM shared-conceptual-store finding into LLM mechanisms, giving a decodable, causally-manipulable gist locus — distinct from all my prior proposals (none concern false memory / DRM intrusions).
Abstract: People routinely 'remember' words that were never said: shown a list of associates (bed, rest, tired, dream), they falsely recall the missing theme word (sleep). In bilinguals, this false memory crosses languages — a Spanish list induces false recognition of the English lure — which cognitive scientists take as evidence for a shared conceptual store. Multilingual language models are known to build a shared, language-agnostic semantic hub. We ask a simple, previously untested question: does a gist-based false memory implanted in one language transfer to another in an LLM? We hypothesize that (1) presenting a DRM associate list in language A elevates the model's false recognition and recall of the critical lure's translation-equivalent in language B, at rates far above unrelated controls; (2) this cross-lingual false memory dissociates from true verbatim recognition, which should be more language-bound; (3) the false memory is carried by the list's semantic gist in the middle-layer shared hub, decodable before the model responds; and (4) suppressing that gist representation causally reduces the false memory while preserving true-item recognition. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using controlled multilingual DRM lists with recognition and recall probes, crossing study language with test language across typologically diverse languages. Combining behavioral false-alarm measurement, logit-lens gist tracking, difference-in-means gist-direction extraction, and activation patching, we measure the transfer, its dissociation from true recognition, its shared-hub locus, and a causal fix. Metrics include cross-lingual lure false-alarm rate, gist-vs-verbatim language-boundedness dissociation, gist-signal decodability, and suppression-induced false-memory reduction with true-recognition controls.
Experiments:
1) Multilingual DRM suite: Build ~150 DRM associate lists (each ~12 semantically associated study words converging on one never-presented critical lure), translated into typologically diverse languages spanning scripts and resource levels (English, French, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish), native-speaker verified for associative strength and translation adequacy. Recognition test items per list: (a) STUDIED words (true old), (b) the CRITICAL LURE (never presented), (c) unrelated NEW words (true new). Recall test: 'list the words you were shown.' Cross the STUDY language (list presentation) with the TEST language (probe/response) fully. Report inter-annotator agreement on lists; release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral cross-lingual false memory (H1, core): Measure per-(study-language, test-language) the lure FALSE-ALARM rate (fraction of critical lures the model recognizes/recalls as studied) versus the false-alarm rate for unrelated new words, and the hit rate for studied words. Test H1: in SPLIT conditions (study language != test language) the lure false-alarm rate is high and far above the unrelated-new baseline — the false memory crosses languages. Verify a genuine DRM effect exists in the SAME-language condition first. Control for tokenizer fertility, list associative strength, and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test cross-lingual lure intrusion exceeds unrelated-new baseline).
3) Gist-vs-verbatim dissociation (H2, core): Compare how the study/test language MISMATCH affects (a) true studied-word HIT rate (verbatim memory) versus (b) lure false-alarm rate (gist memory). Predict a dissociation: crossing languages HURTS verbatim hit rate more (surface words are language-bound) but PRESERVES (or barely reduces) the lure false-alarm rate (gist is shared-hub-mediated) — so the cross-lingual gap between true and false recognition shrinks, mirroring the human finding that gist errors survive language switch better than verbatim memory. Report the dissociation as a language-mismatch x item-type interaction.
4) Shared-hub gist locus (H3): Extract a difference-in-means 'gist' direction (representations after a converging DRM list vs after a matched non-converging control list) and, via logit-lens, test whether the critical LURE is activated in the middle-layer shared (English-decodable) hub before the model responds, even when study and test languages differ and the lure was never presented. Measure cross-lingual alignment of the gist direction (is the false memory stored language-agnostically?). Mediation: regress behavioral cross-lingual false-alarm rate on the mid-layer lure-gist activation strength (partial correlation controlling for fertility/associative-strength; held-out R^2). Relate to transfer neurons: test whether the gist enters the shared hub via the same mid-layer transition.
5) Causal suppression test (H4, core): (a) Ablate/suppress the gist direction (difference-in-means projection removal) at the localizing mid-layer and test whether the lure false-alarm rate drops toward the unrelated-new baseline; (b) conversely, AMPLIFY the gist direction and confirm it increases lure false alarms (bidirectional dose-response); (c) for individual false alarms, patch the shared-hub gist representation from a control (non-converging) list and test whether the false memory is removed. Critically verify TRUE-RECOGNITION preservation: studied-word hit rate and unrelated-new correct-rejection must be preserved (the intervention must remove the FALSE memory, not degrade genuine memory), plus fluency and off-target/language-mixing checks. Baselines: random-direction ablation, whole-hub English-steering.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify suppression is gist-specific (reduces the critical lure but not unrelated items or true studied words), and that the effect is not a lexical-frequency artifact (frequency-matched lures/controls). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show stronger cross-lingual false-memory transfer (more shared-hub-mediated gist) than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM — or, alternatively, that stronger shared-hub alignment yields MORE transfer; test whether transfer magnitude correlates with the cross-lingual alignment of the gist direction and each language's training share. Qualitatively compare the model's cross-lingual DRM pattern (gist survives language switch, verbatim does not) against the human bilingual DRM literature (direction, not identical mechanism).
Evaluation metrics: same-language DRM effect (lure false-alarm vs unrelated-new baseline, establishing the effect exists); cross-lingual lure false-alarm rate (SPLIT conditions vs unrelated-new baseline); gist-vs-verbatim language-mismatch x item-type dissociation; mid-layer lure-gist activation and its cross-lingual alignment, with mediation of behavioral false-alarm rate (held-out R^2); suppression-induced false-alarm reduction and amplification-induced increase (bidirectional), patching-induced removal; true-studied-hit and unrelated-new correct-rejection preservation (specificity), off-target rate, fluency; cross-model transfer comparison and correlation with gist-alignment and training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for cross-lingual intrusion over fertility/associative-strength/resource baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) A robust DRM false-memory effect must exist in the same-language condition first; if the model does not show gist-based intrusions at all, the cross-lingual transfer question is moot — Experiment 2 is a necessary gate, and a null there is itself an informative finding about the limits of LLM gist memory. 2) Cross-lingual 'transfer' could conflate with the model simply translating and re-recognizing surface words rather than a shared gist; the gist-vs-verbatim dissociation (Exp 3), the never-presented status of the lure, and the causal gist-suppression test (which removes the false memory by editing only the gist direction) distinguish a genuine shared-gist mechanism from surface translation — if suppressing the gist does nothing, the effect is surface-driven, an informative alternative. 3) Translating DRM lists across languages can weaken associative structure (associate networks are culture/language-specific); we native-speaker verify associative strength per language, report inter-annotator agreement, and restrict cross-lingual analyses to lists whose lure is a strong associate in both languages, treating culturally-divergent lists as a separate tier. 4) Study/test language mismatch is confounded with tokenizer fertility, script, and resource level; partial correlations and the unrelated-new and control-list baselines mitigate but may not fully remove confounds. 5) In-context 'memory' over a short list is not identical to consolidated human memory; we frame the analogy as structural (gist intrusion, shared-store transfer), not identical-mechanism, and note the ecological-validity limit. 6) The gist direction from difference-in-means may entangle topical/lexical content; we use non-converging control lists, frequency-matched lures, and multiple extraction methods. 7) Logit-lens gist estimates are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 8) The suppression could harm true recognition; true-hit and correct-rejection preservation are hard specificity constraints and we report the full tradeoff plus bidirectional dose-response. 9) The human-LLM comparison (bilingual DRM shared conceptual store) is qualitative/structural, not a claim of identical mechanism. 10) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM/Aya as more multilingual contrasts). 11) If the false memory does NOT transfer across languages — lure intrusions are language-bound like verbatim memory — this is an informative POSITIVE result showing gist memory is language-specific despite the shared hub, refining the shared-conceptual-store analogy, valuable either way. 12) Limited to open ~7-8B models and short in-context lists; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: concept_breadth_transfer_asymmetry
Title: Broad Concepts Travel, Narrow Skills Stay Home: A Concept-Breadth Law for Cross-Lingual Fine-Tuning Transfer
Short Hypothesis: Whether a fine-tuning update made in ONE language generalizes to OTHER languages is governed not by resource level or typological distance but by a single property of the tuned behavior: its CONCEPT BREADTH — how broad and hub-resident the underlying concept is. Broad, semantically-diffuse behaviors (toxicity/refusal, sentiment, formality, a general reasoning skill) are written into the shared, language-agnostic middle-layer hub during monolingual fine-tuning and therefore transfer cross-lingually, whereas narrow, entity-specific behaviors (individual facts, lexical mappings) are written into shallow, language-tethered representations and do NOT transfer. We predict a monotonic 'concept-breadth law': cross-lingual transfer of a monolingual fine-tune is predicted by a pre-tuning breadth/hub-residence metric of the target behavior, better than by resource level, and is causally controlled by where the update lands (hub vs language-specific layers).
Related Work: Prior work reports DISCONNECTED transfer results per behavior: toxicity/detoxification via DPO transfers broadly through 'dual-multilingual' MLP layers (Preference Tuning For Toxicity Mitigation Generalizes Across Languages 2024); safety fine-tuning attacks and refusal directions transfer broadly and are language-agnostic (Fragility of Multilingual LLMs 2024; SS-Neurons 2026; Refusal Direction is Universal 2025); knowledge-free reasoning transfers while factual knowledge does not (Cross-Lingual Knowledge-Free Reasoners 2024); knowledge edits (ROME/MEMIT) transfer POORLY across languages (LangEdit 2025; cross-lingual KE near-orthogonality). Task-arithmetic cross-lingual work composes language and task vectors modularly (Task Arithmetic for Cross-Lingual Transfer 2024). Cross-lingual compression work shows representations move from language-specific to shared over pretraining (Cross-Lingual Generalization and Compression 2025). CRITICALLY, each of these studies ONE behavior in isolation and reports 'it transfers' or 'it doesn't', with per-behavior mechanistic stories (dual-MLP, safety neurons, orthogonal edit vectors). NO prior work proposes a UNIFYING predictor — that a single, measurable CONCEPT-BREADTH / hub-residence property of the tuned behavior determines transfer across the whole spectrum from broad concepts to narrow facts, predicts transfer better than resource level or typological distance, and is causally set by where the fine-tuning update lands (hub vs language-specific layers). We reframe scattered per-behavior transfer results into a single concept-breadth law with a pre-tuning predictor and a causal (update-placement) test, distinct from my prior source-language-transfer-asymmetry proposal (which varied the SOURCE language holding the skill fixed; here we vary the BEHAVIOR's breadth holding the source language fixed).
Abstract: When you fine-tune a multilingual model in one language, some of what it learns spreads to every other language and some stays locked to the language you taught in. Prior work reports this disconnectedly — detoxification and refusal spread broadly, individual facts do not — with a separate mechanistic story for each. We propose a single unifying law: cross-lingual transfer of a monolingual fine-tune is governed by the CONCEPT BREADTH of the tuned behavior — how broad and hub-resident the underlying concept is. Broad, semantically-diffuse behaviors (toxicity, sentiment, formality, a general reasoning skill) are written into the shared, language-agnostic middle-layer hub and transfer; narrow, entity-specific behaviors (single facts, lexical mappings) are written into shallow, language-tethered layers and do not. We predict that a pre-tuning breadth/hub-residence metric of a target behavior predicts its cross-lingual transfer better than resource level or typological distance, monotonically across a spectrum of behaviors, and that transfer is causally set by where the update lands — forcing a narrow behavior into the hub makes it transfer, and confining a broad behavior to language-specific layers stops it. We test this on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM by LoRA-fine-tuning in a single source language on a graded battery of behaviors spanning the breadth spectrum, measuring cross-lingual transfer, and using logit-lens hub-residence tracking, difference-in-means update-localization, and update-placement interventions. Metrics include the breadth-vs-transfer correlation, breadth's predictive power over resource/distance baselines, hub-residence mediation, and placement-controlled transfer.
Experiments:
1) Graded behavior battery and source-language fine-tuning: Assemble ~8 target behaviors spanning the concept-breadth spectrum, each with a monolingual fine-tuning set (in a single fixed SOURCE language, e.g. English) and a multilingual evaluation set (verified across a fixed target-language panel spanning scripts and resource levels: French, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish). BROAD behaviors: (a) toxicity reduction (detoxification), (b) sentiment/style shift, (c) formality/register control, (d) a general reasoning skill (knowledge-free multi-step arithmetic/logic). NARROW behaviors: (e) a batch of individual counterfactual FACTS (CounterFact-style edits), (f) novel lexical/entity mappings, (g) entity-specific attribute changes. Include an INTERMEDIATE behavior (h) a mid-breadth relational rule. LoRA-fine-tune each behavior separately in the source language. Native-speaker verify eval sets. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Pre-tuning concept-breadth metric: BEFORE fine-tuning, compute a per-behavior breadth/hub-residence score = the depth and cross-lingual-alignment at which the behavior's representation lives in the base model (via logit-lens crystallization depth of the relevant concept + cross-lingual cosine alignment of a difference-in-means direction for the behavior + a diffuseness measure over how many tokens/contexts activate it). This score is computed independently of the transfer experiment.
3) Behavioral transfer map (H1, core): For each fine-tuned behavior, measure cross-lingual transfer = mean behavior gain across the target-language panel (relative to the source-language gain), holding the source language and eval panel fixed. Test the concept-breadth law: broad behaviors transfer broadly, narrow behaviors stay source-tethered, intermediate behaviors intermediate. Control for source-language fine-tuning success (only compare transfer conditional on comparable source-language learning).
4) Breadth is the dominant predictor (H2, core): Regress per-behavior transfer on (a) the pre-tuning breadth/hub-residence score, (b) target-language resource level, and (c) typological/embedding distance. Because the source language and eval panel are held fixed across behaviors, resource/distance are near-constant and breadth is the variable of interest; test via nested regression / model comparison (AIC, held-out R^2) whether breadth predicts transfer beyond a per-behavior random baseline and beyond eval-set difficulty. Prediction: breadth is the dominant, monotonic predictor.
5) Update-localization mechanism (Formation tracing): For each behavior, track WHERE the LoRA update lands — measure how much the update modifies the shared middle-layer hub (via the pre-identified hub directions) vs shallow/late language-specific layers, using the interlingual-alignment (ILO/CKA) change after tuning and difference-in-means update-drift. Test that broad behaviors write into the hub (and their hub-write magnitude mediates transfer) while narrow behaviors write into language-specific layers (mediation regression; held-out R^2).
6) Core causal placement test (H3): (a) Force a NARROW behavior (a fact edit) into the hub: perform the update at the shared middle-layer hub using a hub-aligned key (or a hub-alignment regularizer), and test whether it now transfers cross-lingually more than the default late-layer edit. (b) Confine a BROAD behavior to language-specific layers: restrict the update (freeze hub layers) and test whether its transfer collapses toward the narrow-behavior level. If placement causally flips transfer, the concept-breadth law is a placement law, not merely a correlation. Compare against baselines: default LoRA, task-arithmetic composition (Task Arithmetic Cross-Lingual 2024), and a random-layer-restriction control. Report source-behavior retention (the behavior must still be learned in the source language), transfer, locality (unrelated behaviors unchanged), and off-target/fluency.
7) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify placement effects are behavior-specific (not generic regularization), preserve source-language learning, and do not switch output language. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 shows a steeper breadth-transfer slope (sharper hub/late split) than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether the slope correlates with each model's baseline hub English-centricity.
Evaluation metrics: concept-breadth-vs-transfer Spearman correlation and monotonicity; breadth's held-out predictive R^2 over resource/distance/difficulty baselines (AIC); hub-write magnitude and its mediation of transfer (held-out R^2); ILO/CKA alignment change after tuning by behavior; placement-controlled transfer (narrow-into-hub gain, broad-confined collapse) with source-retention, locality, off-target rate; cross-model breadth-slope comparison and correlation with hub English-centricity.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Concept breadth, hub-residence, and eval-set difficulty may be confounded; we control by computing the breadth score pre-tuning and independently of transfer, matching eval difficulty across behaviors where possible, and relying on the causal placement test (Exp 6) rather than correlation alone — if forcing a narrow behavior into the hub does NOT increase transfer, the law is merely correlational, an informative negative result. 2) Behaviors differ in many ways beyond breadth (data size, learnability); we hold source-language learning success comparable, report transfer conditional on it, and use a graded battery to trace a monotonic trend rather than a binary contrast. 3) The breadth/hub-residence metric combines several proxies (depth, alignment, diffuseness) that may not cohere; we report each component and their agreement, and validate against the known broad-transfers (toxicity/refusal) vs narrow-doesn't (facts) anchors. 4) LoRA vs full fine-tuning may change placement; we run LoRA as primary and validate a subset with light full fine-tuning. 5) Forcing a fact edit into the hub (Exp 6a) requires a hub-aligned key and may harm locality (broad edits could touch related facts); we measure locality explicitly and report the tradeoff. 6) Confining a broad behavior to late layers may simply prevent learning it at all; we require comparable source-language learning before comparing transfer. 7) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM's less English-centric hub analyzed as a contrast with a shallower slope). 8) This touches safety (toxicity/refusal are among the broad behaviors): the finding that broad undesirable behaviors transfer while narrow desirable ones don't is descriptive; we handle harmful-behavior fine-tuning ethically (detoxification direction only, restricted release) and do not produce attack artifacts. 9) If transfer is NOT predicted by breadth (e.g., all behaviors transfer, or only resource level matters), the unifying law is refuted — still informative in reconciling the scattered per-behavior literature. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: metaphor_directionality_imposition
Title: Which Way Does the Metaphor Flow? Cross-Lingual Imposition of Structure-Mapping Directionality in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Metaphor comprehension is directionally asymmetric: the base/source domain confers structure onto the target ('a rumor is a virus' is more comprehensible than its reversal), an asymmetry rooted in which domain is more familiar/concrete IN A GIVEN LANGUAGE-CULTURE. We hypothesize multilingual LLMs implement this directionality via a largely language-agnostic 'mapping-direction' operator in the shared hub, but because the hub is English-scaffolded, the model IMPOSES the English base/target assignment onto other languages: for concept pairs whose relative familiarity/base-ness diverges cross-lingually, the model's comprehensibility-asymmetry and inference-projection track the English direction rather than the target-language one. The directional operator transfers cross-lingually (a mapping-direction signal extracted in one language re-orients a metaphor in another) while WHICH domain is chosen as base is imposed from English — a clean operator-portable / base-choice-imposed dissociation.
Related Work: Structure-Mapping theory (Bowdle & Gentner; Structure-Mapping in Metaphor Comprehension 2011, 219 cites) establishes that metaphor is directionally asymmetric — an initial symmetric alignment then a directional phase projecting inferences from base to target — with a forward advantage late in processing. Cross-linguistic metaphor work shows base/target familiarity and intelligibility vary by language-culture (English-German intelligibility 2018; English-French source/target domains 2014), and bilingual L1/L2 novel-metaphor ERP/gaze studies show mapping proceeds differently across a speaker's languages (Mapping models in L1/L2 2023; L2 novel metaphor ERP 2025; cross-language priming 2025). On the model side, PLMs encode metaphoricity in middle layers and it transfers cross-lingually (Metaphors in PLMs 2022), metaphor causally shifts reasoning (Metaphors are a Source of Cross-Domain Misalignment 2026), and INLP can remove a linear figurativeness feature in NMT (Transformer Too Compositional 2022). Multilingual interpretability establishes an English-scaffolded shared semantic hub (Semantic Hub 2024; Do Llamas Work in English 2024).
