CRITICALLY, all model metaphor work concerns metaphoricity DETECTION or figurative-vs-literal interpretation (my prior conceptual-metaphor proposal targeted source-DOMAIN choice); NONE asks whether the DIRECTIONALITY of the base-to-target mapping (the structure-mapping asymmetry) is (a) a language-agnostic portable operator, (b) whose BASE/TARGET assignment is imposed from English onto other languages, causing cross-lingual comprehensibility-asymmetry inconsistency and mis-projected inferences. This reframes cross-lingual metaphor failure as a mapping-DIRECTION imposition with a portable-operator / local-base-choice dissociation, grounded in an authoritative cognitive theory and orthogonal to detection-focused prior work and to my earlier source-domain-choice proposal.
Abstract: A metaphor has a direction: 'a rumor is a virus' works because the familiar base (virus) lends structure to the less-familiar target (rumor), and reversing it ('a virus is a rumor') is harder — a structure-mapping asymmetry established by decades of cognitive science. Crucially, which of two concepts serves as the more familiar base can differ across language-cultures. Multilingual language models build a shared, English-scaffolded semantic hub. We ask a simple, previously untested question: do multilingual LLMs implement metaphor directionality as a language-agnostic operator, and do they impose the English base/target assignment when comprehending metaphors in other languages? We hypothesize a dissociation: (1) the mapping-DIRECTION operator (the base-to-target projection) is encoded in the shared hub and transfers across languages — a direction extracted in one language re-orients a metaphor in another; but (2) WHICH domain is chosen as base is English-scaffolded, so for concept pairs whose relative familiarity diverges cross-lingually, the model's comprehensibility asymmetry and projected inferences track the English direction rather than the target-language one; and (3) this base-choice imposition tracks each language's empirical base/target familiarity norms and is causally correctable by re-orienting the mapping toward the target-language base, without harming metaphor comprehension. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using controlled forward/reversed metaphor pairs (divergent vs convergent base-choice across languages), combining comprehensibility-asymmetry measurement, difference-in-means mapping-direction extraction, cross-lingual operator transplant, activation patching, and steering. Metrics include cross-lingual directionality-imposition gap, operator transplant success, familiarity-norm prediction, mediation R-squared, and steering-induced correction with comprehension controls.
Experiments:
1) Forward/reversed metaphor suite: Construct ~400 nominal metaphors (A is B) spanning concept pairs where the base/target familiarity relationship is (a) DIVERGENT across languages (a pair whose more-familiar/concrete member differs between English and a target culture — e.g. a culturally-central concept that is base in one language but comparatively unfamiliar in another) and (b) matched CONVERGENT pairs (same base cross-lingually). For each pair build FORWARD ('A is B') and REVERSED ('B is A') versions plus a literal control. Instantiate across typologically and culturally diverse languages spanning scripts and resource levels (English, Spanish, Russian, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi). Collect per-language human base/target familiarity and comprehensibility norms (native-speaker rating). Probes: (i) comprehensibility/acceptability judgment (Likert + forced-choice which direction is more sensible); (ii) inference-projection (which properties of the base are attributed to the target?); (iii) paraphrase. Native-speaker verify; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral directionality asymmetry and imposition (H1, core): Per language, measure the comprehensibility asymmetry = forward-minus-reversed comprehensibility (a structure-mapping signature). For DIVERGENT pairs, test whether the model's asymmetry direction and inference-projection track the ENGLISH base/target assignment rather than the target-language one. Define the cross-lingual directionality-imposition GAP = inconsistency(DIVERGENT) minus inconsistency(CONVERGENT), and an English-direction pull rate. Verify near-faithful direction on CONVERGENT pairs, correct English asymmetry (ceiling), and a genuine forward-advantage asymmetry in English (establishing the structure-mapping effect exists). Control for concept frequency, tokenizer fertility, and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2).
3) Familiarity-norm scaling (H2, external validation): Test whether per-pair imposition is predicted by the divergence between target-language and English base/target familiarity norms (Spearman; held-out prediction from norms alone), tying the internal phenomenon to independent human ground truth.
4) Operator portability vs base-choice imposition (H3, core dissociation): Extract a difference-in-means 'mapping-direction' operator (forward vs reversed representations, controlling content) at each layer, per language; measure cross-lingual cosine alignment (shared operator?). Transplant test: extract the operator in language A and ADD it into a language-B forward pass on a symmetric/reversed metaphor; measure whether it correctly re-orients the metaphor (transplant flip rate) — predicting the DIRECTION operator transfers. Separately, using logit-lens, test whether the BASE CHOICE (which domain is treated as base) crystallizes toward the ENGLISH base in the shared mid-layers while any residual target-language base signal is stronger in early/language-specific layers. Mediation: regress behavioral imposition on the shared-hub English-base projection (partial correlation controlling for frequency/fertility; held-out R^2).
5) Causal steering/patching test (H4): (a) Steer the DIVERGENT metaphor toward the target-language base assignment (re-orient the mapping) and measure whether comprehensibility-asymmetry and inference-projection shift to the target-language pattern (flip rate) and the GAP shrinks toward the CONVERGENT baseline, without switching output language; (b) bidirectional dose-response; (c) for imposed items, patch the residual language-specific base signal into later computation and test restoration. Critically verify COMPREHENSION preservation (the model must still correctly interpret the metaphor's meaning and handle literal controls) plus fluency and off-target checks. Baselines: whole-hub English-steering, random-direction control.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify steering is direction-specific (re-orients base/target but does not change the concepts or unrelated content), graded (imposition scales with familiarity-norm divergence), and not a frequency artifact. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show stronger imposition than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether imposition magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the mapping-direction operator and each language's training share. Qualitatively compare against the human structure-mapping forward-advantage and L1/L2 mapping-asymmetry literature.
Evaluation metrics: comprehensibility-asymmetry (forward-minus-reversed) and directionality-imposition GAP (DIVERGENT vs CONVERGENT; English-direction pull rate; vs English ceiling); imposition-vs-familiarity-norm correlation and held-out prediction; mapping-direction operator cross-lingual alignment and transplant flip rate; shared-hub English-base projection with mediation of behavioral imposition (held-out R^2); steering flip rate and GAP reduction (bidirectional dose-response), patching-induced restoration; comprehension and literal-control preservation (specificity), fluency, off-target rate; cross-model imposition comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Constructing metaphor pairs whose base/target familiarity genuinely DIVERGES across languages is delicate; we ground base-choice in per-language familiarity/imageability norms, native-speaker verify, use graded divergence, report inter-annotator agreement, restrict DIVERGENT items to clear contrasts, and treat mixed cases separately. 2) The structure-mapping asymmetry may be weak in 7-8B models; Experiment 2's verification of a genuine English forward-advantage is a necessary gate — if the model shows no directionality asymmetry at all, the cross-lingual imposition question is moot, itself an informative finding about the limits of LLM structure-mapping. 3) Base-choice divergence is correlated with language family, culture, and resource level; the CONVERGENT controls, English ceiling, within-pair forward/reversed contrasts, and norm-based prediction isolate the base-choice pathway, but residual confounds may remain. 4) Some imposition may reflect genuinely correct behavior (the target language really does share the English base); the direction of the effect (tracks ENGLISH vs TARGET base), the norm prediction, and the causal re-orientation steering (which restores the target base by editing only the mapping-direction operator) distinguish imposition from faithful interpretation — a faithful-interpretation finding is itself valuable. 5) Operator vs base-choice may not separate cleanly; the transplant test directly probes operator portability, and if the operator does NOT transfer, the dissociation hypothesis is refuted (an informative result showing directionality is language-specific). 6) Difference-in-means mapping-direction operators may entangle content or lexical features; we control content in forward/reversed pairs, use nonce-concept variants, and multiple extraction methods. 7) Comprehensibility ratings are noisy and culturally variable; we use forced-choice and inference-projection alongside Likert. 8) Logit-lens depth estimates are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 9) Steering could harm comprehension or fluency; comprehension/literal-control preservation is a hard constraint and we report the full tradeoff plus bidirectional dose-response. 10) The human-LLM comparison (structure-mapping forward advantage, L1/L2 asymmetry) is qualitative/structural, not a claim of identical mechanism. 11) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM/Aya as more multilingual contrasts). 12) If NO imposition is found — metaphor directionality and base choice track each language's own familiarity structure, predictable from norms, with comprehension preserved — this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the shared hub carries language-specific mapping directionality despite English scaffolding, valuable either way. 13) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: language_privilege_instruction_hierarchy
Title: Whose Language Wins? A Covert Language-Privilege Cue That Overrides the System-Over-User Instruction Hierarchy in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: When a system instruction and a conflicting user instruction are written in DIFFERENT languages, multilingual LLMs use the LANGUAGE of an instruction as a covert privilege cue that competes with the intended system>user hierarchy: an instruction phrased in the model's dominant (English/high-resource) language is granted extra authority regardless of its role, so the model obeys the dominant-language instruction more than the intended hierarchy warrants. This language-privilege effect is not a separate per-language arbitration but a language-conditioned GAIN on a single, largely shared instruction-arbitration direction, tracks each language's resource level, and is causally correctable by rescaling that direction without harming aligned (non-conflicting) instruction following.
Related Work: Instruction-hierarchy work shows system>user obedience is fragile and can be improved by reasoning/RL (Who is In Charge 2025, which finds system-user conflicts form a distinct early-layer subspace with weak resolution and role-agnostic steering vectors; VerIH/Reasoning Up the Instruction Ladder 2025; Many-Tier Instruction Hierarchy 2026; system-prompt-strength contrastive decoding 2026), and multilingual instruction-following/zero-shot transfer is studied behaviorally (Chirkova & Nikoulina 2024). Multilingual mechanistic work establishes an English-scaffolded shared hub with early-decodable, steerable language-identity dimensions and language confusion (LinguaMap 2026; Cross-Layer Transcoders 2025; ReCoVeR 2025; Beyond English-Centric 2024). CRITICALLY, all instruction-hierarchy work is monolingual (single-language conflicts) and treats role labels as the only privilege cue; all multilingual mechanistic work concerns language routing/consistency, not instruction arbitration. NO prior work asks whether the LANGUAGE an instruction is written in functions as a covert PRIVILEGE cue that competes with the system>user hierarchy, whether cross-lingual system-user conflict resolution is governed by a language-conditioned GAIN on a shared arbitration direction, whether it tracks resource level, or whether rescaling that direction restores hierarchy-faithful obedience without harming aligned instruction following. This connects the instruction-hierarchy and multilingual-hub literatures for the first time, with a predictive metric and a safety-relevant causal fix.
Abstract: A safe assistant must obey its system instructions over conflicting user requests, and the alphabet or language those instructions are written in should be irrelevant to who wins. We ask a simple, previously untested question: when a system instruction and a conflicting user instruction are in DIFFERENT languages, does the LANGUAGE itself act as a covert privilege cue? We hypothesize a language-privilege effect: an instruction phrased in the model's dominant (English/high-resource) language is granted extra authority regardless of its system-or-user role, so the model over-obeys the dominant-language instruction relative to the intended system>user hierarchy. We further hypothesize this is not a separate per-language arbitration but a language-conditioned GAIN on a single, largely shared instruction-arbitration direction: the language of an instruction sets how strongly it is written into the final decision, so the per-language privilege shift is low-dimensional, predictable from resource level, and causally correctable by rescaling that direction without harming aligned instruction following. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using controlled system-user conflict items where the system and user languages are independently varied while the conflict content is held fixed. Combining behavioral obedience measurement, difference-in-means arbitration-direction extraction, logit-lens gain readout, activation patching, and gain-steering, we measure the language-privilege effect, its resource scaling, its shared-direction locus, and a causal fix. Metrics include the language-privilege obedience swing, resource-level prediction, arbitration-direction alignment, and steering-induced hierarchy restoration with aligned-instruction controls. This is defensive, alignment-improving research.
Experiments:
1) Cross-lingual instruction-conflict suite: Construct ~500 items each with a SYSTEM instruction and a CONFLICTING USER instruction (verifiable, mutually exclusive directives, e.g. output format, refusal-vs-comply on benign requests, persona, content constraint), so obedience is objectively scorable. Independently vary the LANGUAGE of the system instruction and the user instruction across typologically diverse languages spanning resource levels and scripts (English, French, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish), holding the conflict CONTENT fixed up to translation. Include (a) SAME-LANGUAGE conflicts (both in language L, for each L) as the baseline hierarchy measure, (b) ALIGNED (non-conflicting) system+user items as a specificity control, and (c) a within-language paraphrase control. Native-speaker verify translations and gold hierarchy-correct answers; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, BLOOM(Z)-7B.
2) Behavioral language-privilege effect (H1, core): Measure the system-obedience rate = fraction where the model follows the SYSTEM instruction over the conflicting user instruction. Test the central prediction: obedience shifts toward whichever instruction is in the dominant language, independent of role. Define the language-privilege swing = obedience(system-in-dominant, user-in-low-resource) minus obedience(system-in-low-resource, user-in-dominant), holding role and content fixed — predict a large positive swing (the dominant-language instruction wins). Establish the SAME-language baseline hierarchy first. Control for tokenizer fertility and per-language instruction-following competence (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test instruction language adds predictive power beyond role and competence).
3) Resource-level scaling (H2): Test whether the per-language privilege granted to an instruction scales with that language's resource level / dominance, better than by the model's raw competence in the language (nested regression, held-out R^2). Predict maximal privilege for the dominant language, monotone decline with resource-distance.
4) Shared arbitration direction and gain readout (H3, core): Extract a difference-in-means 'instruction-arbitration' direction (system-wins vs user-wins representations) at each layer, building on the finding that system-user conflict is decodable in an early subspace (Who is In Charge 2025). Verify cross-lingual alignment (a largely shared arbitration axis) and portability (steering it shifts obedience across languages). Project the residual stream at the decision point onto the shared direction and estimate a per-LANGUAGE privilege gain via regression of the obedience decision on the projection contributed by each instruction's language. Test that the cross-lingual obedience swing is captured by the difference in per-language gains applied to the SHARED arbitration projection (held-out R^2), beating a uniform-bias baseline. Test whether the instruction's language is decodable early and whether the gain is set before the decision (logit-lens). Mediation: regress behavioral swing on the language-weighted arbitration projection (partial correlation controlling for fertility/competence; held-out R^2).
5) Causal test via patching and gain-steering (H4, core): (a) For items where the low-resource-language SYSTEM instruction loses to a dominant-language user instruction, patch in the arbitration signal from the matched dominant-language-system pass and test whether system obedience is restored — isolating a language-privilege gain from the conflict content. (b) Rescale the shared arbitration direction with a per-language scalar to equalize privilege across languages (remove the dominant-language advantage), and measure whether hierarchy-faithful obedience (system>user regardless of language) is restored, with bidirectional dose-response. Compare against baselines: role-agnostic instruction-following steering (Who is In Charge 2025), system-prompt-strength contrastive decoding (2026), and a random-direction control.
6) Specificity and safety controls (hard constraint): Verify gain-steering is arbitration-specific — it must restore system>user obedience on CONFLICT items WITHOUT changing behavior on ALIGNED (non-conflicting) items (the model must still follow user instructions when they do not conflict), must not switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), and preserves general task competence and fluency. Safety-relevant check: test whether the language-privilege effect enables a cross-lingual instruction-hierarchy bypass (a user instruction in the dominant language overriding a safety-relevant system instruction in a low-resource language) and whether the fix closes it — all interventions here STRENGTHEN correct hierarchy (defensive). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show a larger language-privilege swing (gains more collapsed toward the dominant language) than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether the swing correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the arbitration direction and each language's training share.
Evaluation metrics: same-language baseline system-obedience rate; language-privilege swing (dominant-vs-low-resource instruction, role and content fixed); privilege-vs-resource-level prediction (held-out R^2 over competence baseline); arbitration-direction cross-lingual alignment, portability, early decodability, and gain predictive R^2 (vs uniform-bias baseline) with mediation of the behavioral swing (held-out R^2); patching-induced system-obedience restoration; gain-steering hierarchy-restoration and cross-lingual obedience-variance reduction vs baselines, with bidirectional dose-response; aligned-instruction preservation and general-competence preservation (symmetric specificity), off-target/language-mixing rate; cross-lingual bypass rate before/after the fix; cross-model swing comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The language-privilege effect could conflate with a per-language instruction-following COMPETENCE gap (the model may fail to follow a low-resource-language instruction simply because it understands it worse, not because it deprioritizes it); the key controls are conditioning on items where the model demonstrably follows each instruction in ISOLATION (single-instruction comprehension checks per language), the resource-level regression controlling for competence, and the causal patching/gain-steering (which shifts obedience by editing only the arbitration direction) — if the swing vanishes once competence is controlled, the hypothesis is refuted, an informative negative result. 2) Instruction language is confounded with tokenizer fertility, script, and resource level; the same-language baselines, within-language paraphrase control, and partial correlations mitigate but may not fully remove confounds. 3) The single-scalar gain account may only partially hold; if a data-driven low-dimensional basis fits better we report it, keeping the 'shared arbitration axis + language gain' claim testable. 4) The arbitration direction from difference-in-means may entangle content/role features; we use the established early conflict subspace (Who is In Charge 2025) as an anchor, content-matched conflicts, and specificity controls. 5) Gain-steering could harm aligned (non-conflicting) instruction following or general competence; the aligned-item and competence-preservation constraints are hard requirements and we report the full tradeoff. 6) This is dual-use safety research: it identifies a cross-lingual instruction-hierarchy bypass, but all interventions here STRENGTHEN correct hierarchy (defensive); we release the conflict suite under controlled terms, use benign conflict content, and do not publish attack-enhancing directions. 7) Instruction-tuned/RLHF models differ in how strongly they enforce hierarchy; we test across model families and treat differences as informative. 8) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM/Aya as less English-centric contrasts expected to show a smaller swing). 9) If no language-privilege effect is found — obedience follows role regardless of instruction language once competence is controlled — this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the instruction hierarchy is language-agnostic, valuable either way. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B instruction-tuned models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: morpheme_boundary_erasure_imposition
Title: Losing the Seams: Does the English-Scaffolded Shared Hub Erase Morpheme Boundaries That Agglutinative Languages Grammaticalize?
Short Hypothesis: In agglutinative languages (Turkish, Finnish, Hungarian, Swahili) a single orthographic word packs multiple obligatory grammatical morphemes (case, tense, possession, negation) whose BOUNDARIES carry load-bearing meaning, whereas the analytic/isolating English that scaffolds the shared hub spreads the same information across separate function words. We hypothesize the shared hub IMPOSES an English-like coarse, whole-word morphological granularity onto agglutinative inputs: after subword tokenization the model reassembles the word into a single lexical concept but ERASES the internal morpheme-boundary structure in the shared hub, so grammatical inferences that hinge on a specific embedded morpheme (which suffix marks the object, whether a negation morpheme is present, which possessor is encoded) fail far more than for the same meaning expressed periphrastically in English. This erasure is mediated by a shared morpheme-boundary/structure signal that is weak in the hub but present in early layers, tracks each language's agglutination degree, and is causally recoverable by re-injecting the boundary signal without harming lexical comprehension.
Related Work: Prior work shows tokenization affects encoded morphological knowledge, which lives in middle/late layers (mT5 vs ByT5 2024; BERT morphology probing 2020), that morphological alignment of tokenizers weakly predicts task performance (MorphScore 2025; Morphological Plausibility 2026), and that character models can implicitly track morpheme boundaries (Indicatements 2018; Tabula nearly rasa 2019). Multilingual-hub work establishes an English-scaffolded shared concept hub with subword reassembly and orthographic-word-boundary conventions impeding transfer (Semantic Hub 2024; Do Llamas Work in English 2024; Subwords and Cross-Lingual Transfer 2024; Learning Dynamics of Subword Segmentation 2025), and 'Say Anything but This' (2026) shows non-injective tokenization causes monolingual reasoning failures. CRITICALLY, all morphology-probing work is monolingual or about tokenizer/transfer QUALITY and asks whether morphology is ENCODED; none asks whether the English-scaffolded shared hub, being isolating, ERASES the internal morpheme-boundary structure of agglutinative words during reassembly, causing grammatical-inference failures that a periphrastic English equivalent would not incur, whether this tracks agglutination degree, whether a shared morpheme-boundary signal mediates it, or whether re-injecting it causally recovers boundary-dependent inference. This differs from my prior tokenizer 'reassembly tax' proposal (which concerned DEPTH/compute cost of merging fragments into one concept, holding meaning fixed) by targeting the ERASURE of grammatically load-bearing internal morpheme STRUCTURE and its effect on morpheme-specific grammatical reasoning, grounded in the analytic-vs-agglutinative typology.
Abstract: In English you say 'in my houses' with four separate words; in Turkish it is one word, 'evlerimde', built from stacked suffixes each carrying obligatory grammatical meaning. The seams between these morphemes are where the grammar lives. Multilingual language models tokenize such a word into arbitrary subword pieces and, in a shared, English-scaffolded hub, reassemble it into a single lexical concept. We ask a simple, previously untested question: in doing so, does the model ERASE the internal morpheme-boundary structure that agglutinative languages grammaticalize, imposing the coarse whole-word granularity of the isolating hub? We hypothesize that (1) grammatical inferences hinging on a specific embedded morpheme (which suffix marks the object, whether a negation morpheme is present, which possessor is encoded) fail far more for a single agglutinative word than for the same meaning spread across English function words; (2) the size of this erasure tracks each language's agglutination degree; (3) a shared morpheme-boundary/structure signal mediates it, weak in the hub but stronger in early/language-specific layers; and (4) re-injecting the boundary signal causally recovers boundary-dependent inference without harming lexical comprehension. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using controlled minimal pairs across agglutinative (Turkish, Finnish, Hungarian, Swahili) and isolating (English, Chinese) languages, with periphrastic English equivalents as a matched control. Using morpheme-boundary probes, logit-lens tracking, activation patching, and boundary re-injection, we measure the erasure, its typology scaling, its mediation, and its causal correction. Metrics include morpheme-inference erasure gap, agglutination-prediction correlation, boundary-signal decodability, mediation R-squared, and re-injection-induced recovery with lexical-comprehension controls.
Experiments:
1) Morpheme-inference suite: Construct ~500 items in agglutinative languages (Turkish, Finnish, Hungarian, Swahili) each containing a single word packing multiple obligatory grammatical morphemes (case, tense/aspect, negation, possession, number), native-speaker verified. Each item probes an inference that hinges on ONE specific embedded morpheme: (i) role/case identification ('who is the object?' when object is marked by an internal case suffix); (ii) polarity ('is the statement negative?' when negation is a bound morpheme); (iii) possession ('whose is it?' when possessor is a suffix); (iv) tense/number extraction. Build a matched PERIPHRASTIC ENGLISH equivalent (same meaning via separate function words) and matched CHINESE (isolating) control, so the target grammatical information is held constant while its packaging (bound-in-one-word vs spread-across-words) varies. Also include a LEXICAL-COMPREHENSION control (definitional/factual question about the word's stem meaning). Report inter-annotator agreement; release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral erasure (H1, core): Measure the morpheme-inference accuracy on the single-word agglutinative items vs the periphrastic English/Chinese equivalents. Define the morpheme-inference erasure GAP = accuracy(periphrastic) minus accuracy(single-word agglutinative), holding the target grammatical fact fixed. Predict a positive gap concentrated on the boundary-dependent probes, while LEXICAL-COMPREHENSION of the same word stays high (isolating erasure from not-knowing-the-word). Control for tokenizer fertility, word frequency, and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test agglutinative-packaging status adds predictive power beyond fertility).
3) Agglutination scaling (H2, external validation): Using each language's agglutination degree / index of synthesis (from typological databases, e.g. WALS synthesis features and morphemes-per-word statistics), test whether per-language erasure is predicted by agglutination degree (Spearman; held-out prediction from typology alone), tying the internal phenomenon to independent linguistic ground truth. Predict strongest erasure for the most agglutinative languages (Finnish/Turkish) and near-zero for isolating Chinese.
4) Morpheme-boundary signal and localization (H3): Train a probe to recover the internal morpheme-boundary positions (and which morpheme carries which grammatical feature) from hidden states, per language and layer, building on prior morpheme-probing findings. Extract a difference-in-means 'morpheme-structure' direction (words with an embedded target morpheme present vs absent). Test (a) whether boundary/morpheme-feature information is DECODABLE but WEAKER in the middle-layer shared hub than in early/language-specific layers (i.e. the structure is present shallowly but erased into a whole-word concept in the hub), via logit-lens tracking of when the target morpheme's grammatical feature crystallizes vs when it fades; (b) mediation: regress behavioral erasure on the shared-hub morpheme-feature signal strength (partial correlation controlling for fertility/frequency; held-out R^2). Baseline: the whole-word lexical-concept direction as a within-model control that should NOT show erasure.
5) Causal re-injection/patching test (H4, core): (a) Re-inject the early-layer morpheme-boundary/feature signal into later computation (patch the early morpheme-structure representation into the mid/late layers) and test whether boundary-dependent inference recovers toward the periphrastic baseline; (b) conversely, ablate the morpheme-structure signal and confirm inference degrades (bidirectional); (c) as a decomposition, patch the shared-hub lexical concept alone (from the agglutinative pass) into a periphrastic pass and verify it carries the stem meaning but NOT the boundary features (localizing what the hub keeps vs erases). Critically verify LEXICAL-COMPREHENSION preservation (the model must still answer stem-meaning questions correctly — recovery targets boundary features, not the word's identity) plus fluency and off-target/language-mixing checks. Baselines: random-direction patching, whole-hub English-steering, and a surface baseline of segmenting the input into explicit morphemes (a strong practical comparison).
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify re-injection is boundary-specific (recovers morpheme-feature inference but not unrelated content), graded (erasure scales with agglutination degree), and not merely a fertility artifact (frequency- and fertility-matched agglutinative/periphrastic pairs). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show stronger erasure than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM (Aya sees more Turkish/Swahili); test whether erasure magnitude correlates with the shallow-vs-hub split of the morpheme-structure signal and each language's training share. Qualitatively compare the per-language erasure pattern against the agglutination typology.
Evaluation metrics: morpheme-inference erasure GAP (single-word agglutinative vs periphrastic English/Chinese; boundary-dependent probes; lexical-comprehension preserved); erasure-vs-agglutination-degree correlation and held-out prediction; morpheme-boundary/feature decodability by layer (weaker in hub than early layers) and its mediation of behavioral erasure (held-out R^2); re-injection-induced recovery and ablation-induced degradation (bidirectional); hub-keeps-stem-but-erases-boundary decomposition; lexical-comprehension preservation (specificity), fluency, off-target rate; cross-model erasure comparison and correlation with training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for agglutinative-packaging over fertility/frequency baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The erasure GAP could conflate with generic difficulty of parsing a long morphologically complex word rather than a hub-imposed erasure; the LEXICAL-COMPREHENSION control (the model DOES know the word's stem), the matched periphrastic English/Chinese equivalents (same information, different packaging), and the causal re-injection (which recovers boundary features by transferring only the early morpheme-structure signal) isolate erasure from generic incompetence — if the gap vanishes once comprehension is controlled or re-injection does nothing, the hypothesis is refuted, an informative negative result. 2) Agglutination degree is correlated with language family, script, resource level, and tokenizer fertility (agglutinative words fragment into many subwords); the periphrastic/isolating controls, fertility-matched pairs, typology-based prediction, and partial correlations isolate the morphological-packaging pathway, but residual confounds may remain — if fertility fully explains the gap, that is itself an informative mechanistic finding (erasure = fragmentation effect). 3) Morpheme-boundary probing is noisy and gold morpheme segmentations are imperfect/unavailable for some languages; we use native-speaker-verified minimal pairs, UniMorph/Universal-Dependencies morpho-syntactic features where possible, and report probe reliability. 4) The morpheme-structure direction from difference-in-means may entangle lexical/frequency features; we use a whole-word lexical-concept control direction, frequency-matched controls, and multiple extraction methods. 5) Logit-lens crystallization/fading estimates are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 6) Re-injection could harm lexical comprehension or fluency; lexical-comprehension preservation is a hard specificity constraint and we report the full tradeoff plus bidirectional ablation, comparing against the explicit-morpheme-segmentation surface baseline to show the mechanistic account adds value. 7) Some grammatical inference may genuinely require morphology English lacks; the periphrastic equivalents are designed to express the same distinction, and cases where English cannot are excluded or analyzed separately. 8) Effects may be model-family dependent (Aya-23/BLOOM as more agglutinative-language-exposed contrasts expected to show less erasure). 9) The model-vs-typology comparison is qualitative/structural (agglutination degree), not a claim of identical human mechanism. 10) If NO erasure is found — boundary-dependent inference is as accurate for single agglutinative words as for periphrastic English, predictable from typology, with morpheme structure preserved in the hub — this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the shared hub retains language-specific morpheme structure despite its isolating English scaffolding, valuable either way. 11) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: implicit_numeral_composition_imposition
Title: Twenty-Three or Two-Tens-Three? Does the English-Scaffolded Hub Impose a Decimal Explicit-Composition Grammar on Implicitly-Structured Numeral Systems?
Short Hypothesis: Humans fluently infer the implicit compositional structure of number WORDS across languages (that a numeral encodes an unmarked +/x over a base), but LLMs fail unless the arithmetic is explicitly symbol-marked (Multilingual Number Puzzles 2025). We hypothesize this failure is a cross-lingual IMPOSITION: because the shared, English-scaffolded numeral hub treats numerals as opaque lexical tokens mapped to base-10 values rather than as implicit compositional expressions, the model imposes a lexical-lookup / decimal grammar onto typologically diverse numeral systems, so it under-composes exactly where a numeral's implicit +/x structure diverges from the decimal-transparent norm. This under-composition is mediated by a shared, decodable 'composition-operator' signal that is engaged for explicit-symbol inputs but under-engaged for implicit numerals, tracks each system's compositional opacity, and is causally recoverable by injecting the implicit-composition operator without harming symbol-marked arithmetic.
Related Work: Behavioral work (Multilingual Number Puzzles / AIlice in Numberland 2025) robustly establishes that LLMs cannot infer the implicit compositional structure of numerals unless mathematical operations are explicitly marked with +/x symbols, and that individual math features alone do not block solving — the deficit is specifically inferring implicit compositional structure. The Effect of Scripts and Formats (2026) shows accuracy drops on underrepresented numeral scripts/formats. Base-composition transcoding is studied for single languages (my prior vigesimal_base_conversion_tax; inversion_transcoding_tax). Mechanistic number work shows LLMs encode value in a base-10 digit-wise / helical representation (Number Digit Representations in Base 10; helical value encoding), and CountScope-style counter probes. Multilingual-hub work localizes an English-scaffolded shared space with transfer neurons (Transfer Neurons 2025; MWork 2024; Emergence of Abstract Thought 2025). CRITICALLY: the numeral-puzzle papers are purely BEHAVIORAL and conclude LLMs 'lack a notion of implicit numeral structure' without a mechanistic account, localization, or fix; all mechanistic number work assumes symbolic/digit inputs and single languages, treating the value representation as language-agnostic. NO prior work asks whether the failure to infer implicit numeral composition is a shared-hub IMPOSITION (lexical-lookup/decimal grammar over an implicit-composition grammar), localizes a shared composition-operator signal that is engaged by explicit symbols but under-engaged by implicit numerals, ties the deficit to each system's compositional opacity, or causally recovers composition by injecting the operator. We convert a behavioral 'LLMs lack numeral structure' finding into a mechanistic imposition claim with a decodable, steerable locus — distinct from my single-language base-composition proposals (which concern DEPTH/transcoding cost within one known system) by targeting the cross-lingual FAILURE-TO-INFER implicit composition and its explicit-vs-implicit engagement dissociation.
Abstract: People can be shown a handful of number words in an unfamiliar language and figure out the rest, because they infer that a numeral silently encodes arithmetic — 'twenty-three' means twenty plus three — over a base. Recent work shows large language models cannot do this: they solve cross-linguistic numeral puzzles only when the hidden operations are spelled out with + and x symbols, and conclude that LLMs simply 'lack a notion of implicit numeral structure.' We ask a mechanistic question this behavioral finding leaves open: WHY, and is it fixable? We hypothesize a cross-lingual imposition. The multilingual model's shared, English-scaffolded numeral space treats number words as opaque lexical tokens mapped to base-10 values rather than as implicit compositional expressions, so it imposes a lexical-lookup / decimal grammar onto typologically diverse numeral systems and under-composes exactly where a numeral's implicit plus/times structure diverges from the decimal-transparent norm. We further hypothesize that (1) the deficit is a failure to ENGAGE a shared composition-operator that IS engaged for explicit-symbol inputs, decodable and localizable; (2) its size tracks each system's compositional opacity; and (3) injecting the implicit-composition operator (or marking implicit structure internally) causally recovers composition without harming symbol-marked arithmetic. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using controlled numeral-puzzle suites crossing numeral-system compositional structure (transparent decimal, additive, multiplicative, subtractive, vigesimal, inverted) with explicit-vs-implicit operator marking. Combining behavioral composition measurement, digit/value probes, difference-in-means composition-operator extraction, activation patching (explicit-vs-implicit engagement decomposition), and operator injection, we measure the imposition, its opacity scaling, its mechanistic locus, and a causal fix. Metrics include implicit-vs-explicit composition gap, opacity-prediction correlation, operator-engagement decodability, mediation R-squared, and injection-induced recovery with symbol-marked-arithmetic controls.
Experiments:
1) Controlled numeral-composition suite: Following the Multilingual Number Puzzles paradigm, construct ~500 few-shot numeral-inference items where the model is given a set of number words in a (real or controlled synthetic) numeral system and must infer the value of held-out numerals or produce the word for a target value. Systematically vary the numeral system's COMPOSITIONAL STRUCTURE: transparent-decimal (English-like tens+units), additive, multiplicative (base x multiplier), subtractive, vigesimal (base-20), and inverted (unit-before-ten). Cross each system with two INPUT conditions: (a) IMPLICIT (number words only, structure unmarked — the natural case) and (b) EXPLICIT (the same items with the hidden operations spelled out via +/x, e.g. 'twenty + three'), the condition prior work shows LLMs can solve. Include a matched SYMBOL-MARKED ARITHMETIC control (pure +/x expressions with the same operations) to establish the model CAN execute the arithmetic. Use verified gold values; annotate each system's compositional opacity (number and type of unmarked operations, divergence from decimal-transparent). Native-speaker verify real-language items; release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral imposition (H1, core): Measure per-system accuracy in IMPLICIT vs EXPLICIT conditions. Define the implicit-vs-explicit composition GAP = accuracy(EXPLICIT) minus accuracy(IMPLICIT), replicating the prior finding and localizing it: predict a large gap concentrated in high-opacity systems (multiplicative/vigesimal/inverted) and near-zero for transparent-decimal, while SYMBOL-MARKED ARITHMETIC stays high (isolating a failure to INFER implicit structure from an inability to compute). Control for tokenizer fertility and number-word frequency (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test compositional opacity adds predictive power).
3) Opacity scaling (H2, external validation): Test whether per-system implicit-vs-explicit gap is predicted by the system's compositional opacity (number/type of unmarked operations, divergence from decimal; and typological features from the numeral-systems literature) via Spearman / held-out prediction from opacity alone, tying the internal phenomenon to independent linguistic ground truth.
4) Composition-operator engagement and localization (H3): Extract a difference-in-means 'composition-operator' signal contrasting representations where the model correctly composes (EXPLICIT / symbol-marked) vs treats the numeral as a lexical whole (IMPLICIT failure). Using digit/value probes (base-10 digit-wise and value probes) and logit-lens, test (a) whether the partial operands (base, multiplier, residue) are resolved and combined for EXPLICIT inputs but the numeral is mapped to a whole-value lexical lookup for IMPLICIT inputs (a partial-operand-leakage / no-composition metric); (b) whether the composition-operator signal is ENGAGED for explicit but UNDER-ENGAGED for implicit numerals in the shared hub. Mediation: regress behavioral gap on composition-operator engagement strength (partial correlation controlling for fertility/frequency; held-out R^2). Test whether the operator is shared across systems (cross-lingual alignment).
5) Explicit-vs-implicit engagement decomposition via patching (H3b, core): For items solved in the EXPLICIT condition but failed in the matched IMPLICIT condition, patch (a) the shared composition-operator representation (from the explicit pass) into the implicit pass, and (b) only late-layer decoding. If (a) restores correct composition on the implicit item (the operator existed but was not engaged), classify as an ENGAGEMENT failure rather than an absence of composition capability. Report engagement-vs-absence shares per system, predicting engagement failures dominate for high-opacity systems.
6) Core causal intervention (operator injection / internal marking): Inject the composition operator at the numeral position in the IMPLICIT condition — either by steering along the composition-operator direction or by patching in the explicit-condition operand-composition state — without providing +/x symbols in the input, and measure per-system accuracy recovery. Predict SELECTIVE recovery for high-opacity systems (interaction test) and negligible effect on transparent-decimal. Compute recovery elasticity = accuracy gain per unit opacity. Compare against baselines: whole-hub English-steering, providing explicit +/x symbols (the behavioral upper bound), and a random-direction control.
7) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify injection is composition-specific: it must IMPROVE implicit numeral inference WITHOUT changing SYMBOL-MARKED ARITHMETIC accuracy (symmetric check — the operator injection must not corrupt already-explicit computation), must not switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), and preserve fluency. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English/decimal-centric Llama-3/Qwen show larger implicit-vs-explicit gaps than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether the gap correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the composition-operator and each system's training exposure. Qualitatively compare the model's opacity-scaled failure pattern against the human ability to infer implicit numeral structure (direction, not identical mechanism).
Evaluation metrics: implicit-vs-explicit composition GAP per system (with symbol-marked-arithmetic preserved); gap-vs-opacity correlation and held-out prediction; composition-operator engagement decodability and partial-operand-leakage/no-composition metrics for implicit inputs; engagement-vs-absence error shares (patching); operator-injection accuracy recovery and elasticity vs baselines, with symbol-marked-arithmetic preservation (symmetric specificity), off-target rate, fluency; cross-model gap comparison and correlation with training exposure; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for opacity over fertility/frequency baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The implicit-vs-explicit gap could conflate with a general arithmetic-competence gap rather than a failure to INFER implicit structure; the SYMBOL-MARKED ARITHMETIC control (the model CAN compute the operations), the EXPLICIT-condition upper bound, and the engagement-vs-absence patching decomposition isolate an inference/engagement failure — if the gap vanishes once arithmetic competence and explicit marking are controlled, or if the operator turns out genuinely absent (patching does nothing), the imposition hypothesis is refuted, an informative negative result relocating the deficit to a true lack of composition capability. 2) Compositional opacity is correlated with numeral-system frequency, script, and tokenizer fertility; the synthetic controlled systems (which decorrelate opacity from real-language frequency), the transparent-decimal baseline, within-item implicit/explicit contrasts, and partial correlations isolate the opacity pathway, but residual confounds may remain — if fertility fully explains the gap, that is itself an informative mechanistic finding. 3) Few-shot numeral-puzzle performance is prompt- and example-sensitive; we use multiple example sets and report robustness, and verify a measurable implicit/explicit gap first as a gate. 4) The composition-operator difference-in-means signal may entangle content or format features; we use the CountScope/digit-probe cross-check, multiple extraction methods, and the symmetric symbol-marked-arithmetic specificity control. 5) Operator injection without input symbols is a non-trivial intervention that could inject wrong operand structure for ambiguous numerals; we report the full tradeoff, restrict to items with unambiguous composition, and compare against the explicit-symbol upper bound to show the mechanistic account adds value. 6) Logit-lens/digit-probe engagement estimates are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 7) Real low-resource numeral systems may be sparsely trained, confounding imposition with ignorance; the synthetic-system suite (learnable purely in-context) is the primary evidence, with real languages as extensions. 8) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM/Aya as more multilingual contrasts expected to show smaller gaps). 9) The human-LLM comparison (humans infer implicit numeral structure) is qualitative/structural, not a claim of identical mechanism. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: crosslingual_verification_generation_dissociation
Title: Can Verify but Cannot Solve, in Some Tongues: A Cross-Lingual Dissociation Between Reasoning Generation and Consistency-Head Validation
Short Hypothesis: Verifying whether a reasoning step is correct and generating that step are distinct computations with different cross-lingual profiles: the middle-layer consistency-head VALIDATION mechanism is more language-agnostic (shared-hub-resident) than the higher-layer GENERATION mechanism, so a multilingual LLM can often correctly DETECT an error in a reasoning step written in a lower-resource / English-distant language even when it cannot itself GENERATE the correct step in that language. Cross-lingual validation failures, where they occur, are dominated not by the consistency check being absent but by a failure to ROUTE the higher-layer computed answer down to the middle-layer validator — the same computation-to-validation gap identified monolingually — which is wider in non-dominant languages and causally closable by injecting higher-layer activations into the validation layers.
Related Work: The Validation Gap (2025) shows, MONOLINGUALLY in English, a structural dissociation: arithmetic computation lives in higher layers while validation lives in middle-layer 'consistency heads' that check surface alignment, and adding higher-layer activations into lower layers closes the error-detection gap. Beg to Differ (2025) and multilingual CoT work (What Really Counts 2025; Comprehensive Evaluation of Multilingual CoT 2025) show non-Latin-script reasoning traces have ~2x more reasoning-answer misalignment and that faithfulness/error-injection sensitivity varies by language, but purely BEHAVIORALLY. Knowledge-Free Reasoners (2024) shows knowledge-free reasoning transfers near-perfectly across languages via shared middle-layer neurons while knowledge does not. Self-verification and failure-prediction work (Gnosis 2025; Self-Verification 2023; CRV 2025) is monolingual. CRITICALLY, no prior work asks whether the VALIDATION mechanism (the consistency-head error-detection circuit) is language-dependent, whether it dissociates from GENERATION cross-lingually (verify-what-you-cannot-solve), whether cross-lingual validation failure is a computation-to-validation routing failure rather than an absent check, or whether the monolingual higher-layer-to-validation-layer injection fix closes the cross-lingual gap. We port the Validation-Gap consistency-head circuit into a cross-lingual verify-vs-generate dissociation with a mechanistic locus and a targeted fix. This differs from my prior language_dependent_validation_deficit proposal (which concerned detecting the model's OWN factual/arithmetic errors via a decodable 'validation direction') by targeting the verify-vs-generate dissociation grounded in the located consistency-head circuit and the computation-to-validation routing gap.
Abstract: Checking whether a solution is right is often easier than producing it — and interpretability work shows language models do these in different places: arithmetic is computed in higher layers while validation runs through middle-layer 'consistency heads'. That work is entirely in English. We ask a simple, previously untested question about multilingual models: is the validation mechanism language-dependent, and does it dissociate from generation across languages? We hypothesize that the middle-layer consistency-head validator is more language-agnostic (shared-hub-resident) than the higher-layer generator, so a model can often correctly DETECT an error in a reasoning step written in a lower-resource or English-distant language even when it cannot itself GENERATE the correct step in that language — a verify-what-you-cannot-solve dissociation. We further hypothesize that cross-lingual validation failures, where they occur, are dominated by a failure to ROUTE the higher-layer computed answer into the middle-layer validator (the same computation-to-validation gap found monolingually), which is wider in non-dominant languages and causally closable by injecting higher-layer activations into the validation layers. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using matched arithmetic and short deductive-reasoning items across typologically diverse languages, with paired generation and error-detection probes. Using consistency-head circuit localization, logit-lens computation-vs-validation tracking, activation patching, and the higher-layer-to-validation-layer injection intervention, we quantify the dissociation, its resource scaling, its mechanistic locus, and a causal fix. Metrics include the per-language verify-minus-generate gap, validation cross-lingual transfer, computation-to-validation routing-gap, and injection-induced error-detection recovery with specificity controls.
Experiments:
1) Matched generate/verify suite: Build ~800 items of (a) multi-step arithmetic (verified gold) and (b) short deductive-reasoning steps (single-inference validity checks), each in two probe forms: GENERATE (solve/produce the correct step) and VERIFY (a candidate step is shown — correct or with a controlled error — and the model must judge correct/incorrect). Inject controlled errors (digit-transposition, wrong-operator, invalid-inference) so verification cannot be solved by re-generation alone. Instantiate every item in typologically diverse languages spanning resource levels and scripts (English, French, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish, Bengali), native-speaker verified; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral verify-vs-generate dissociation (H1, core): Measure per-language GENERATION accuracy and VERIFICATION accuracy (error-detection F1). Define the verify-minus-generate gap = verification accuracy minus generation accuracy. Test the dissociation: in lower-resource / English-distant languages, verification accuracy is substantially higher than generation accuracy on matched items — the model detects errors in steps it cannot itself produce. Control for tokenizer fertility and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2). Crucially condition on items the model VERIFIES correctly to show the check is engaged even where generation fails.
3) Validation cross-lingual transfer (H2): Test whether verification accuracy degrades LESS across languages than generation accuracy (a shallower resource slope), consistent with a more language-agnostic validator. Localize the consistency-head circuit per model (following The Validation Gap) and measure cross-lingual overlap of the validation circuit vs the generation circuit — predict the validation circuit is more shared across languages (higher cross-lingual head/neuron overlap, following the Knowledge-Free-Reasoners shared-neuron finding).
4) Computation-to-validation routing-gap (H3, core mechanism): Using logit-lens/tuned-lens, measure per language, per item, (i) whether the correct answer is COMPUTED in higher layers (higher-layer computation strength) and (ii) whether that answer reaches the middle-layer VALIDATION layers before the check fires (routing strength). Define the routing-gap = higher-layer computation strength minus what is available at the validation layers. Test that where verification FAILS in a language, it is because the higher-layer answer is not routed to the validator (large routing-gap), not because the consistency check is absent — and that this routing-gap is wider in non-dominant languages. Mediation: regress per-language verification failure on the routing-gap (partial correlation controlling for fertility/resource; held-out R^2).
5) Error decomposition via patching: For verification failures in language B, patch (a) the consistency-head validation representation from a language where verification succeeds and (b) the higher-layer computed-answer representation into B's validation layers. If (b) restores error detection (the answer WAS computed but not delivered to the validator) rather than (a), the failure is a routing failure, not an absent check. Report routing-failure vs check-absence shares per language.
6) Core causal intervention (higher-layer-to-validation injection): Port the monolingual fix cross-lingually — inject the higher-layer computed-answer activations into the middle validation layers during the VERIFY pass in low-resource languages — and measure per-language error-detection recovery. Predict SELECTIVE recovery for high-routing-gap (low-resource) languages, little effect on English (interaction test). Compute recovery elasticity = error-detection gain per unit routing-gap. Compare against baselines: whole-hub English steering, translate-the-step-to-English verification, and a random-direction control.
7) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify the injection is validation-specific: it must IMPROVE error detection WITHOUT increasing false alarms on CORRECT steps (a symmetric check — it must not make the model reject valid steps), must not switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), and preserve fluency. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show a wider cross-lingual routing-gap than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether the gap correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the validation circuit and each language's training share.
Evaluation metrics: per-language generation accuracy, verification F1, and verify-minus-generate gap (matched items; partial correlation with resource/distance over fertility, held-out R^2); validation-vs-generation cross-lingual slope and circuit-overlap comparison; routing-gap and its mediation of verification failure (held-out R^2); routing-failure vs check-absence error shares (patching); selective injection error-detection recovery and elasticity vs baselines, with correct-step false-alarm preservation (symmetric specificity), off-target rate, fluency; cross-model routing-gap comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The verify-minus-generate gap could reflect that verification is simply an easier task everywhere (not a language-specific dissociation); the key is the INTERACTION — verification degrades LESS across languages than generation — and the routing-gap mechanism; if the two tasks degrade in parallel across languages, the dissociation is refuted, an informative negative result. 2) Verification must not be solvable by covert re-generation; controlled injected errors (digit-transposition, wrong-operator, invalid-inference) and conditioning on generation-failed items ensure the check is genuine, but some verification may still recruit partial generation — we report this and use error types that block re-generation shortcuts. 3) The consistency-head circuit and routing-gap localization build on The Validation Gap, which was shown for smaller models on arithmetic; we replicate the circuit per model and per task type (arithmetic and deduction) and report where it does not transfer. 4) Language is confounded with tokenizer fertility, script, and resource level; partial correlations and the causal patching/injection tests mitigate but may not fully remove confounds. 5) Computation-vs-validation logit-lens tracking is approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 6) The injection could induce false alarms on correct steps or harm fluency; the symmetric no-false-alarm constraint is a hard requirement and we report the full tradeoff, comparing against translate-to-English verification to show the mechanistic account adds value. 7) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM/Aya as less English-centric contrasts expected to show a smaller routing-gap). 8) If the validation mechanism turns out equally language-dependent as generation (no dissociation, parallel slopes), this is an informative result showing verification is not a shared-hub-privileged computation — valuable either way. 9) Limited to open ~7-8B models and short reasoning steps; may not extend to frontier scale or long chains.

Name: crosslingual_attention_hijack_asymmetry
Title: Hijacking Attention Across Tongues: Why Jailbreak Suffixes Transfer Cross-Lingually Better Than the Refusal Direction Predicts
Short Hypothesis: The cross-lingual transferability of an optimized jailbreak suffix is governed not by refusal-direction parallelism but by how strongly the suffix HIJACKS the model's attention (dominates the chat/template tokens) in the TARGET language: a suffix optimized in a source language retains high attention-hijacking strength in typologically/script-similar target languages and loses it in distant ones, so per-language transfer is predicted by a per-language hijacking-strength metric better than by refusal-direction cosine alignment. Because attention-hijacking is a largely language-agnostic shallow mechanism while its ENGAGEMENT is language-specific, transfer failures concentrate where the suffix fails to re-establish attention dominance in the target language, and this is causally restorable by boosting hijacking in the target language (revealing a defense: suppress it).
Related Work: Universal Jailbreak Suffixes Are Strong Attention Hijackers (2025) shows suffix universality across harmful instructions is driven by attention dominance over chat-template tokens, and that hijacking can be enhanced or surgically suppressed — but entirely MONOLINGUALLY (English). Refusal Direction is Universal Across Safety-Aligned Languages (2025) attributes CROSS-LINGUAL jailbreak transfer to refusal-vector parallelism in embedding space, and SS-Neurons (2026) / Fragility of Multilingual LLMs (2024) show safety information is largely language-agnostic. Universal-attack geometry work (2023) and suffix-transferability work (PiF 2025) explain transfer via embedding geometry and intent-perception, monolingually or cross-MODEL, never cross-lingual attention-hijacking. CRITICALLY, no prior work connects the attention-hijacking mechanism to CROSS-LINGUAL suffix transfer: none asks whether a suffix optimized in language A hijacks attention in language B, whether per-language hijacking strength predicts transfer better than refusal-direction parallelism, whether transfer failures are hijacking-engagement failures, or whether target-language hijacking can be causally boosted (attack) or suppressed (defense). We reframe cross-lingual jailbreak transfer from a refusal-direction-geometry account into an attention-hijacking-engagement account, distinct from all my prior safety proposals (harm-gating, refusal-threshold), and yield a mechanism-grounded, per-language defense.
Abstract: Optimized jailbreak suffixes bypass safety alignment, and recent monolingual work shows the most universal suffixes work by HIJACKING attention — dominating the chat-template tokens before generation. Separately, cross-lingual work shows suffixes and refusal directions transfer across languages, attributing this to refusal-vector parallelism. We connect these: we hypothesize that a jailbreak suffix's cross-lingual transfer is governed by whether it re-establishes attention dominance in the TARGET language, so per-language transfer is predicted by a per-language attention-hijacking-strength metric better than by refusal-direction cosine alignment. Because attention-hijacking is a shallow, largely language-agnostic mechanism but its engagement is language-specific, we predict transfer decays with typological/script distance from the optimization language, that failures are hijacking-engagement failures (the suffix fails to dominate target-language chat tokens rather than the refusal direction being misaligned), and that transfer is causally controlled by target-language hijacking — boosting it recovers the attack, suppressing it defends. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and Gemma using GCG-style suffixes optimized in one language and evaluated on parallel harmful/benign prompts (PolyRefuse/MultiJail) across typologically diverse languages. Combining attention-dominance measurement, refusal-direction extraction, activation patching, and a hijacking-suppression defense, we quantify the transfer, its distance scaling, its predictor comparison, its mechanistic locus, and a per-language defense. This is defensive red-teaming research: all interventions strengthen or characterize defenses. Metrics include per-language attack-success transfer, hijacking-strength vs refusal-alignment predictive R-squared, engagement-failure shares, and suppression-induced defense with utility controls.
Experiments: 1) Cross-lingual suffix suite: Optimize GCG-style adversarial suffixes on harmful prompts in a SOURCE language (English, and separately a non-English source e.g. Chinese) on open models (Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B). Evaluate each suffix on parallel harmful and benign prompts (PolyRefuse/MultiJail) across typologically/script-diverse TARGET languages (English, French, German, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish), native-speaker verified. Record per-(source,target) attack-success rate (ASR) and benign over-refusal. 2) Behavioral cross-lingual transfer map (H1): Measure per-target-language ASR of a fixed source-optimized suffix. Test that transfer decays with typological/script distance from the source language. Control for tokenizer fertility of the suffix and target-language baseline refusal rate (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2). 3) Per-language hijacking-strength metric (H2, core): Following the attention-hijacking method, measure per-(suffix,target-language) the attention DOMINANCE of the suffix over the chat-template/final tokens before generation. Test whether per-language hijacking strength predicts per-language transfer ASR BETTER than (a) refusal-direction cosine alignment between source and target (per Refusal Direction is Universal 2025), (b) script similarity, and (c) resource level, via nested regression / model comparison (AIC, held-out R^2). Prediction: hijacking strength is the dominant predictor. 4) Engagement-failure decomposition via patching: For suffixes that transfer to English but fail in a distant target language, patch (a) the source-language suffix's attention-hijacking pattern into the target-language pass and (b) the refusal-direction components. If (a) restores the attack (the suffix failed to re-establish attention dominance) rather than (b), the transfer failure is a hijacking-engagement failure, not a refusal-direction misalignment. Report engagement-vs-alignment failure shares per language. 5) Causal control (attack characterization + core defense): Boost target-language hijacking (GCG-Hij-style) and confirm it recovers cross-lingual transfer; then, as the defensive contribution, apply per-language Hijacking Suppression at the chat-template tokens and measure ASR reduction across all target languages. Compare against baselines: refusal-direction addition (Refusal Direction Universal 2025), SS-Neuron reinforcement (2026), and a random-direction control. 6) Utility and specificity controls (hard constraint): The suppression defense must reduce ASR WITHOUT increasing benign over-refusal (symmetric check), must not degrade general capability (MMLU/MT quality) or switch output language (off-target rate). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show sharper hijacking-driven transfer decay than the more multilingual Aya-23; test whether transfer correlates with target-language hijacking strength and training share. Evaluation metrics: per-language transfer ASR and distance decay (held-out R^2 over fertility/resource); hijacking-strength vs refusal-alignment predictive R^2 (model comparison, AIC); engagement-vs-alignment failure shares (patching); boost-induced attack recovery and suppression-induced ASR reduction vs baselines, with benign over-refusal, utility, and off-target preservation (symmetric specificity); cross-model comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Dual-use: this is red-teaming research; all deployed interventions here are DEFENSIVE (characterizing transfer and strengthening a per-language suppression defense). We release the harmful suite and hijacking metrics under controlled access, use standard public jailbreak benchmarks, and do NOT publish enhanced universal attack suffixes; the attack-boost experiment (GCG-Hij) is only to establish causal necessity and is reported in aggregate. 2) The hijacking-strength predictor could conflate with refusal-direction alignment (both correlate with transfer); the model-comparison (does hijacking add over alignment?) and the patching decomposition (does restoring hijacking, not alignment, recover the attack?) isolate the mechanism — if hijacking adds no predictive power over refusal alignment, the hypothesis is refuted, an informative result supporting the refusal-direction account. 3) GCG optimization is expensive; we optimize a modest set of suffixes per source language and report variance, feasible on 7-9B open models within an academic budget. 4) Attention-dominance metrics are approximate and model-specific; we replicate the monolingual hijacking measurement per model and report robustness. 5) Cross-lingual distance is confounded with tokenizer fertility, script, and resource level; partial correlations and the patching test mitigate but may not fully remove confounds. 6) The suppression defense could over-refuse benign prompts or harm utility; benign over-refusal and capability preservation are hard constraints and we report the full tradeoff. 7) Effects may be model-family dependent (Aya-23 as a more-multilingual contrast expected to show flatter transfer decay). 8) Limited to open ~7-9B instruction-tuned models; may not extend to frontier or closed models. 9) If transfer is uniform across languages (no hijacking-driven decay), this supports the language-agnostic-safety view and is itself informative.

Name: crosslingual_tip_of_tongue_partial_form
Title: On the Tip of Which Tongue? Cross-Lingual Partial-Form Leakage During Word Retrieval Failure in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: When a multilingual LLM fails to retrieve a target word (produces a wrong answer or an 'I don't know'), it nonetheless carries a decodable PARTIAL-FORM signal of the unretrieved target — its initial phoneme/grapheme, approximate length, and grammatical class — mirroring the human tip-of-the-tongue (TOT) state. Crucially, this partial-form signal is CROSS-LINGUALLY CONTAMINATED: the decodable partial form leaks from the target word's realization in a DIFFERENT language than the query language (typically the model's dominant or a phonologically/cognate-similar language), just as human bilinguals in a TOT state retrieve partial form from a competing language. This leakage predicts which failures are resolvable (a TOT-like state with correct partial form) versus genuine ignorance, and its cross-lingual source tracks cognate similarity and language dominance.
Related Work: Two literatures meet but have never been connected. (1) Human bilingual psycholinguistics robustly documents cross-lingual TOT: in a retrieval-failure state speakers access partial form (first sound, syllable count, word class) of the unretrieved target, and this partial form is contaminated by competing languages, modulated by cognate status and language dominance (Spanish-English phonological/semantic TOT 2014; Norwegian-English cognate TOT 2019; L3 Spanish TOT with L1/L2 cross-linguistic influence 2016; Mandarin orthographic/phonological TOT 2021), and TOT/feeling-of-knowing states carry genuine metacognitive sensitivity predicting eventual retrieval (TOT/FOK enhance metacognitive sensitivity 2025; domain-specific FOK 2020). (2) LLM interpretability shows a linearly-decodable 'in-advance correctness' / knowledge-awareness / entity-recognition signal predicting whether the model will recall a fact (No Answer Needed 2025; Do I Know This Entity 2024; Factual Self-Awareness 2025; Learning to Trust Your Feelings 2024), and that cross-lingual knowledge-boundary cognition is encoded linearly in middle layers (Knowledge Boundary Cognition Across Languages 2025). CRITICALLY, all LLM work decodes only a SCALAR 'will-I-be-correct / do-I-know-this-entity' signal; NONE asks whether, during a retrieval FAILURE, the model carries a decodable PARTIAL FORM of the specific unretrieved target (its first sound/letter, length, class) — a genuine TOT-state signature — nor whether that partial form is CROSS-LINGUALLY leaked from the target's form in another language, tracking cognate similarity and dominance. We uniquely port the human bilingual cross-lingual TOT phenomenon into LLM mechanisms: partial-form retrieval during failure, its language-of-origin contamination, and its causal role in resolvability. This is distinct from prior binary knowledge-boundary/correctness work (scalar awareness, not partial content) and from all my prior proposals (none concern partial-form retrieval during failure or its cross-lingual source).
Abstract: People who cannot recall a word often still feel it on the tip of their tongue — they know its first sound, roughly how long it is, and what kind of word it is — and in bilinguals this partial form is contaminated by a competing language. Interpretability work shows multilingual language models carry a scalar signal of whether they will answer correctly, but no one has asked whether, in the moment of a retrieval failure, a model carries a decodable PARTIAL FORM of the word it failed to produce. We ask exactly this, and add a cross-lingual twist: is that partial form leaked from the target word's realization in a DIFFERENT language than the query language? We hypothesize that (1) on retrieval-failure trials (wrong answer or abstention), the model's internal state linearly encodes partial form of the correct target — initial phoneme/grapheme, approximate length, grammatical class — above chance, a TOT-state signature; (2) this partial form is cross-lingually contaminated, decodable more strongly from the target's form in the model's dominant or a cognate-similar language than in the query language, tracking cognate similarity and language dominance as in human bilinguals; (3) the presence of correct partial form distinguishes resolvable 'TOT' failures from genuine-ignorance failures, and predicts resolution when the model is given a first-letter cue; and (4) steering along the partial-form direction causally shifts the retrieved word toward the encoded form. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using multilingual word-retrieval-from-definition and factual-recall tasks across typologically diverse languages, combining partial-form probes, cross-lingual source decoding, activation patching, cued-resolution behavior, and steering.
Experiments:
1) Multilingual retrieval-failure suite: Build ~800 word-retrieval items in two families — (a) reverse-dictionary / definition-to-word (a definition given, the model must produce the single target word) and (b) single-word factual recall (capital, chemical element, named entity) — each with a single verified target word whose gold FORM is known in every language (initial phoneme/grapheme, character/syllable length, grammatical class). Instantiate across typologically diverse languages spanning scripts, resource levels, and cognate relationships (English, French, German, Spanish, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish). Annotate each target's cross-lingual cognate similarity (form overlap of the translation-equivalents) and each language's dominance in the model. Native-speaker verify targets and their per-language forms; report inter-annotator agreement. Collect the model's answer per item and label each trial CORRECT, WRONG-ANSWER (a specific but wrong word), or ABSTENTION. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
