2) Partial-form-during-failure probe (H1, core): On FAILURE trials (wrong-answer + abstention), train/evaluate linear probes on residual-stream states (at the answer position, per layer) to predict properties of the CORRECT (unretrieved) target: (i) initial phoneme/grapheme, (ii) length bucket (short/medium/long), (iii) grammatical class. Report per-property decoding accuracy above chance, per layer, establishing a TOT-state signature (partial form of the word the model FAILED to produce is present internally). Compare failure-trial decodability against a matched genuine-absence baseline (targets the model never knows in any language). Control for tokenizer fertility and target frequency (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2). Predict partial-form decodability crystallizes in middle-upper layers, mirroring the knowledge-boundary finding.
3) Cross-lingual source of the partial form (H2, core): For each failure trial, decode partial form using per-LANGUAGE gold forms (the target's initial-sound/length/class in the query language vs the dominant language vs a cognate-similar language). Test whether the internal partial form is better predicted by the target's form in a language OTHER than the query language — define a cross-lingual leakage rate = fraction of failure trials whose decodable partial form matches a non-query-language realization better than the query-language one. Predict the leaked form tracks (a) the model's dominant language and (b) cognate similarity: high-cognate targets show query-language-consistent partial form (cognate facilitation), low-cognate targets show dominant-language leakage. Regress leakage on cognate similarity and language dominance (held-out R^2), qualitatively comparing to the human cross-linguistic-influence TOT pattern.
4) Partial form predicts resolvability (H3): Split failure trials by whether the decoded partial form is CORRECT (TOT-like) vs INCORRECT (ignorance-like). Test that TOT-like failures are (a) more likely to be resolved when the model is given a first-letter/first-phoneme cue (cued-recall behavioral test), and (b) associated with higher feeling-of-knowing (elicited FOK rating / abstention-vs-guess behavior), mirroring the human finding that TOT/FOK carry metacognitive sensitivity. Report resolution rate under cueing for TOT-like vs ignorance-like failures, and whether the partial-form-correctness signal predicts cued resolution beyond the scalar knowledge-boundary probe (nested model comparison).
5) Causal test via patching and steering (H4): (a) Extract a difference-in-means 'partial-form' direction for a target property (e.g. initial-letter=B vs =S). Patch the partial-form representation from a trial where the model KNOWS the target (correct trial) into a failure trial for a form-matched target, and test whether it shifts the model's guess toward the encoded initial form. (b) Steer along the partial-form direction toward a chosen initial letter/length and measure whether the retrieved word's form moves accordingly (form-flip rate), without changing the target concept. This confirms the partial-form signal is a genuine, causally-used form representation, not an epiphenomenal correlate. Verify specificity (steering initial-letter changes the first grapheme but not the concept), no output-language switch (off-target/language-mixing rate), and fluency.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify partial-form decoding is form-specific (a form probe cannot be solved by the concept's semantics alone — test with semantically-matched but form-different distractors), not a frequency artifact (frequency-matched items), and that cross-lingual leakage is not merely translation-decoding (compare to a control where the model is explicitly asked to translate). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show stronger dominant-language (English) partial-form leakage than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether leakage magnitude correlates with each model's hub English-centricity and each language's training share.
Evaluation metrics: per-property partial-form decoding accuracy on failure trials vs genuine-absence baseline (per layer); cross-lingual leakage rate and its regression on cognate similarity and language dominance (held-out R^2); cued-resolution rate for TOT-like vs ignorance-like failures and partial-form's predictive gain over the scalar knowledge-boundary probe; steering/patching form-flip rate and specificity; off-target/language-mixing rate; cross-model leakage comparison and correlation with hub English-centricity and training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for partial-form-during-failure over tokenizer-fertility/frequency baselines; qualitative correspondence with the human bilingual cross-lingual TOT pattern.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) A text-only LLM has no phonology, so 'initial phoneme' is operationalized via orthography/IPA-adjacent text and script-appropriate initial units; we treat the partial-form claim as about the target's FORM (initial grapheme, length, class) rather than embodied sound, and a null on phonological (vs orthographic) form is itself informative about the limits of the LLM-human TOT analogy. 2) Partial-form decoding on failure trials could conflate with the model partially retrieving the target semantically and the probe reading semantics rather than form; the semantically-matched-form-different distractor control and the causal steering (which moves the retrieved FORM, not the concept) isolate genuine form representation — if steering cannot move form, the signal is epiphenomenal, an informative negative result. 3) Distinguishing a genuine TOT state from the model simply having partial knowledge is subtle; the genuine-absence baseline, the cued-resolution behavioral test, and the FOK elicitation triangulate a TOT-like state, but the analogy to the human phenomenon remains qualitative, not a claim of identical mechanism. 4) Cross-lingual leakage is confounded with the shared hub being English-scaffolded (partial form may decode as English simply because the hub is English-decodable); the cognate-similarity modulation (leakage should track cognate distance, not just default to English) and the translation-control (leakage is not mere on-demand translation) distinguish genuine cross-lingual contamination from hub-scaffolding artifact. 5) Cognate similarity, tokenizer fertility, frequency, and resource level are correlated; partial correlations and matched items mitigate but may not fully remove confounds. 6) Linear probes on failure trials may be noisy since failure sets are smaller and heterogeneous; we pool across items, report reliability, and cross-validate across layers. 7) Steering could switch output language or corrupt the concept; specificity and off-target checks are hard constraints and we report the full tradeoff. 8) Wrong-answer vs abstention failures may behave differently; we analyze them separately (a specific wrong word may itself be the leaked competitor, which is a further TOT signature we test). 9) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM/Aya as more multilingual contrasts expected to show more distributed, less English-dominant leakage). 10) If NO partial-form signal is found on failure trials — failures carry only a scalar 'I don't know' with no decodable form of the specific unretrieved word — this is an informative POSITIVE result showing LLM retrieval failure lacks the graded partial-access structure of human TOT, valuable either way. 11) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: concept_breadth_transfer_asymmetry
Title: Broad Concepts Travel, Narrow Skills Stay Home: A Concept-Breadth Law for Cross-Lingual Fine-Tuning Transfer
Short Hypothesis: Whether a fine-tuning update made in ONE language generalizes to OTHER languages is governed not by resource level or typological distance but by a single measurable property of the tuned behavior: its CONCEPT BREADTH (how broad and hub-resident the underlying concept is). Broad, semantically-diffuse behaviors (toxicity/refusal, sentiment, formality, a general reasoning skill) are written into the shared, language-agnostic middle-layer hub during monolingual fine-tuning and transfer cross-lingually, whereas narrow, entity-specific behaviors (individual facts, lexical mappings) are written into shallow, language-tethered representations and do NOT transfer. We predict a monotonic 'concept-breadth law': cross-lingual transfer of a monolingual fine-tune is predicted by a pre-tuning breadth/hub-residence metric of the target behavior, better than by resource level, and is causally controlled by where the update lands (hub vs language-specific layers).
Related Work: Prior work reports DISCONNECTED cross-lingual transfer results per behavior with separate mechanistic stories: toxicity/detoxification via DPO transfers broadly through 'dual-multilingual' MLP layers (Preference Tuning For Toxicity Mitigation Generalizes Across Languages 2024); safety refusal is mediated by a universal refusal direction and shared safety neurons (Refusal Direction is Universal 2025; SS-Neurons 2026; Soteria 2025); value/political directions are shared and steerable (Following the Whispers of Values 2025; Dual Mechanisms of Value Expression 2025; Multilingual Political Views 2025); knowledge-free reasoning transfers while factual knowledge does not (Cross-Lingual Knowledge-Free Reasoners 2024); knowledge edits (ROME/MEMIT) transfer POORLY (LangEdit 2025; near-orthogonal edit vectors). Rethinking Cross-lingual Alignment (2025) shows factual transfer and cultural localization are steerable at different layers. CRITICALLY, each study covers ONE behavior and reports 'it transfers' or 'it doesn't' with a bespoke mechanism; NONE proposes a UNIFYING predictor -- that a single, measurable CONCEPT-BREADTH / hub-residence property of the tuned behavior determines transfer across the whole spectrum from broad concepts to narrow facts, predicts transfer better than resource level or typological distance, and is causally set by where the fine-tuning update lands (hub vs language-specific layers). We reframe scattered per-behavior transfer results into a single concept-breadth law with a pre-tuning predictor and a causal (update-placement) test.
Abstract: When you fine-tune a multilingual model in one language, some of what it learns spreads to every other language and some stays locked to the language you taught in. Prior work reports this disconnectedly -- detoxification, refusal, and value directions spread broadly, individual facts do not -- with a separate mechanistic story for each. We propose a single unifying law: cross-lingual transfer of a monolingual fine-tune is governed by the CONCEPT BREADTH of the tuned behavior -- how broad and hub-resident the underlying concept is. Broad, semantically-diffuse behaviors (toxicity, sentiment, formality, a general reasoning skill) are written into the shared, language-agnostic middle-layer hub and transfer; narrow, entity-specific behaviors (single facts, lexical mappings) are written into shallow, language-tethered layers and do not. We predict that a pre-tuning breadth/hub-residence metric of a target behavior predicts its cross-lingual transfer better than resource level or typological distance, monotonically across a spectrum of behaviors, and that transfer is causally set by where the update lands -- forcing a narrow behavior into the hub makes it transfer, and confining a broad behavior to language-specific layers stops it. We test this on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM by LoRA-fine-tuning in a single source language on a graded battery of behaviors spanning the breadth spectrum, measuring cross-lingual transfer, and using logit-lens hub-residence tracking, difference-in-means update-localization, and update-placement interventions. Metrics include the breadth-vs-transfer correlation, breadth's predictive power over resource/distance baselines, hub-residence mediation, and placement-controlled transfer.
Experiments:
1) Graded behavior battery and source-language fine-tuning: Assemble ~8 target behaviors spanning the concept-breadth spectrum, each with a monolingual fine-tuning set (in a single fixed SOURCE language, e.g. English) and a multilingual evaluation set (verified across a fixed target-language panel spanning scripts and resource levels: French, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish). BROAD behaviors: (a) toxicity reduction/detoxification (DPO), (b) sentiment/style shift, (c) formality/register control, (d) a general knowledge-free reasoning skill (multi-step arithmetic/logic). NARROW behaviors: (e) a batch of individual counterfactual FACTS (CounterFact-style), (f) novel lexical/entity mappings, (g) entity-specific attribute changes. INTERMEDIATE: (h) a mid-breadth relational rule. LoRA-fine-tune each behavior separately in the source language. Native-speaker verify eval sets. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Pre-tuning concept-breadth metric: BEFORE fine-tuning, compute a per-behavior breadth/hub-residence score = the depth and cross-lingual-alignment at which the behavior's representation lives in the BASE model, via (i) logit-lens crystallization depth of the relevant concept, (ii) cross-lingual cosine alignment of a difference-in-means direction for the behavior, and (iii) a diffuseness measure (over how many tokens/contexts the direction activates). This score is computed independently of the transfer experiment.
3) Behavioral transfer map (H1, core): For each fine-tuned behavior, measure cross-lingual transfer = mean behavior gain across the target-language panel relative to the source-language gain, holding the source language and eval panel fixed. Test the concept-breadth law: broad behaviors transfer broadly, narrow behaviors stay source-tethered, intermediate behaviors intermediate. Compare transfer only conditional on comparable SOURCE-language learning success.
4) Breadth is the dominant predictor (H2, core): Regress per-behavior transfer on (a) the pre-tuning breadth/hub-residence score, (b) target-language resource level, and (c) typological/embedding distance. Because source language and eval panel are held fixed across behaviors, resource/distance are near-constant and breadth is the variable of interest; test via nested regression / model comparison (AIC, held-out R^2) whether breadth predicts transfer beyond a per-behavior random baseline and eval-set difficulty. Prediction: breadth is the dominant, monotonic predictor.
5) Update-localization mechanism (Formation tracing): For each behavior track WHERE the LoRA update lands -- measure how much it modifies the shared middle-layer hub (via the pre-identified hub directions) vs shallow/late language-specific layers, using the interlingual-alignment (CKA/ILO) change after tuning and difference-in-means update-drift. Test that broad behaviors write into the hub (hub-write magnitude mediates transfer) while narrow behaviors write into language-specific layers (mediation regression; held-out R^2).
6) Core causal placement test (H3): (a) Force a NARROW behavior (a fact edit) into the hub: perform the update at the shared middle-layer hub using a hub-aligned key (or a hub-alignment regularizer), and test whether it now transfers cross-lingually more than the default late-layer edit. (b) Confine a BROAD behavior to language-specific layers: restrict the update (freeze hub layers) and test whether its transfer collapses toward the narrow-behavior level. If placement causally flips transfer, the concept-breadth law is a placement law, not merely a correlation. Compare against baselines: default LoRA, task-arithmetic composition (Task Arithmetic for Cross-Lingual Transfer 2024), and a random-layer-restriction control. Report source-behavior retention (behavior must still be learned in the source language), transfer, locality (unrelated behaviors unchanged), and off-target/fluency.
7) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify placement effects are behavior-specific (not generic regularization), preserve source-language learning, and do not switch output language. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3 shows a steeper breadth-transfer slope (sharper hub/late split) than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether the slope correlates with each model's baseline hub English-centricity.
Evaluation metrics: concept-breadth-vs-transfer Spearman correlation and monotonicity; breadth's held-out predictive R^2 over resource/distance/difficulty baselines (AIC); hub-write magnitude and its mediation of transfer (held-out R^2); CKA/ILO alignment change after tuning by behavior; placement-controlled transfer (narrow-into-hub gain, broad-confined collapse) with source-retention, locality, off-target rate; cross-model breadth-slope comparison and correlation with hub English-centricity.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Concept breadth, hub-residence, and eval-set difficulty may be confounded; we compute the breadth score pre-tuning independently of transfer, match eval difficulty across behaviors where possible, and rely on the causal placement test (Exp 6) rather than correlation alone -- if forcing a narrow behavior into the hub does NOT increase transfer, the law is merely correlational, an informative negative result. 2) Behaviors differ in many ways beyond breadth (data size, learnability); we hold source-language learning success comparable, report transfer conditional on it, and use a graded battery to trace a monotonic trend rather than a binary contrast. 3) The breadth/hub-residence metric combines several proxies (depth, alignment, diffuseness) that may not cohere; we report each component and their agreement, and validate against the known anchors (toxicity/refusal transfer broadly; facts do not). 4) LoRA vs full fine-tuning may change placement; we run LoRA as primary and validate a subset with light full fine-tuning. 5) Forcing a fact edit into the hub (Exp 6a) requires a hub-aligned key and may harm locality; we measure locality explicitly and report the tradeoff. 6) Confining a broad behavior to late layers may simply prevent learning it at all; we require comparable source-language learning before comparing transfer. 7) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM's less English-centric hub analyzed as a contrast with a shallower slope). 8) This touches safety (toxicity/refusal are among the broad behaviors): the finding that broad undesirable behaviors transfer while narrow desirable ones do not is descriptive; we handle harmful-behavior fine-tuning ethically (detoxification direction only, restricted release) and produce no attack artifacts. 9) If transfer is NOT predicted by breadth (e.g., all behaviors transfer, or only resource level matters), the unifying law is refuted -- still informative in reconciling the scattered per-behavior literature. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: language_conditioned_heuristic_reliance_arithmetic
Title: Reaching for the Shortcut Bag in a Foreign Tongue: Language-Conditioned Engagement of the Arithmetic Heuristic Circuit in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs solve arithmetic with a shared, largely language-agnostic 'bag of heuristics' (sparse heuristic MLP neurons implementing pattern shortcuts) plus a more robust computational component, but the BALANCE between them is language-conditioned: when the same arithmetic problem is posed in a lower-resource / English-distant language, the model leans MORE on the imperfect heuristic-neuron bag and LESS on the robust computation, so cross-lingual arithmetic errors are disproportionately heuristic-reliance errors (right pattern, wrong answer) that track the known failure signature of the heuristic bag, rather than random incompetence. This over-reliance is measurable as stronger engagement of the same heuristic neurons in non-dominant languages, is predictable from resource-distance, and is causally reducible by suppressing the heuristic bag's extra engagement without harming problems the heuristics genuinely cover.
Related Work: Monolingual mechanistic work shows LLMs do arithmetic not via a robust algorithm but via a sparse 'bag of heuristics' — heuristic MLP neurons each firing on a numeric input pattern and promoting an answer token, whose combination explains most arithmetic accuracy and whose imperfect recall drives errors (Arithmetic Without Algorithms 2024) — and that models dynamically shift from heuristic to rational processing over multi-step reasoning (First Heuristic Then Rational 2024; Heuristic Core 2024), mirroring human heuristic-first/algorithmic-second processing (Interpreting Quantifier Scope 2013). Multilingual work shows knowledge-FREE reasoning (including arithmetic) transfers near-perfectly across languages via shared middle-layer neurons while knowledge does not (Cross-Lingual Knowledge-Free Reasoners 2024), that reasoning routes through an English-scaffolded latent space (Do Multilingual LLMs Think In English 2025; Language-Specific Latent Process Hinders 2025), and that language internalizes reasoning biases (BICAUSE 2025). CRITICALLY, all bag-of-heuristics work is monolingual (English) and treats the heuristic-vs-robust balance as fixed; all cross-lingual reasoning work concludes arithmetic reasoning is shared/transferable and never asks whether the DEGREE of heuristic-neuron engagement on the SAME problem is language-dependent — i.e., whether the model reaches deeper into its imperfect shortcut bag when prompted in a non-dominant language, producing heuristic-signature (not random) errors. This differs from Knowledge-Free Reasoners (which shows arithmetic transfers, but not that the internal heuristic/robust MIX shifts by language) and from my prior strategy_language_switch_gating proposal (which concerned the SURFACE language of a chain-of-thought step gating an abstract strategy) by targeting the internal engagement of the LOCATED heuristic-neuron circuit on single-turn arithmetic and its language-conditioned miscalibration.
Abstract: Interpretability has shown that language models do arithmetic not by a clean algorithm but with a sparse 'bag of heuristics' — individual neurons that fire on numeric patterns and push out an answer — whose imperfect coverage causes many errors. That picture was built entirely in English. We ask a simple, previously untested question about multilingual models: is the balance between this heuristic shortcut bag and the model's more robust computation the same across languages? We hypothesize that when the identical arithmetic problem is posed in a lower-resource or English-distant language, the model leans more heavily on the imperfect heuristic-neuron bag and less on robust computation, so cross-lingual arithmetic failures are disproportionately heuristic-reliance errors carrying the known failure signature of the bag (right pattern, wrong answer; errors on operands the heuristics do not cover) rather than random incompetence. We predict this over-reliance is measurable as stronger engagement of the SAME heuristic neurons in non-dominant languages, scales with resource-distance, and is causally reducible by suppressing the bag's extra engagement without harming problems the heuristics genuinely cover. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using controlled arithmetic problems posed across typologically diverse languages, holding the computation fixed. Using the established heuristic-neuron identification and causal analysis, plus logit-lens robust-vs-heuristic tracking and activation patching, we quantify per-language heuristic engagement, its error signature, its resource scaling, and a targeted causal fix. Metrics include per-language heuristic-neuron engagement, heuristic-signature error share, engagement-vs-resource correlation, and suppression-induced accuracy recovery with heuristic-covered-problem controls.
Experiments:
1) Controlled multilingual arithmetic suite: Build ~800 arithmetic problems (two/three-operand addition/subtraction/multiplication spanning operand ranges) with verified gold answers, each presented (a) as language-agnostic DIGIT expressions (the anchor where the bag-of-heuristics was characterized) and (b) embedded in a natural-language word problem posed in typologically diverse languages spanning resource levels and scripts (English, French, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish). Native-speaker verify translations; the underlying computation is identical across languages. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Locate the heuristic bag (setup): Replicate the bag-of-heuristics identification per model — via causal circuit discovery and per-neuron activation-pattern categorization, identify the sparse set of heuristic MLP neurons and their heuristic types (operand-range, operand-pattern, result-pattern neurons) that explain most arithmetic accuracy on the digit anchor. Verify these neurons are largely shared (language-agnostic) by checking they are the same neurons engaged across languages (cross-lingual neuron overlap).
3) Per-language heuristic engagement (H1, core): For each problem, measure the ENGAGEMENT of the heuristic-neuron bag (fraction of the answer logit attributable to heuristic neurons, via path patching / direct-effect attribution) versus a more robust computational component, per language. Test H1: heuristic engagement is HIGHER (and robust-component engagement lower) for the SAME problem when posed in a lower-resource / English-distant language than in the dominant language. Control for tokenizer fertility of number words and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test language adds predictive power beyond fertility). Verify the digit anchor shows the least language-dependence.
4) Heuristic-signature error decomposition (H2): Decompose per-language arithmetic errors into (i) HEURISTIC-SIGNATURE errors (matching the known bag failure modes: answers on operands outside heuristic coverage, or the heuristic's imperfect-recall pattern — e.g. emitting a nearby heuristic-promoted token) versus (ii) random/other errors. Test that lower-resource languages show a DISPROPORTIONATE share of heuristic-signature errors (directional, tracking the bag's coverage gaps), not merely more random errors, and that per-problem error probability is predicted by heuristic engagement (Spearman; held-out R^2). Correlate per-language heuristic-signature error share with resource-distance from English.
5) Engagement predicts errors and scales with resource (H3): Test whether per-language heuristic engagement predicts per-language arithmetic accuracy loss (relative to the digit anchor and to English) better than a general-competence baseline (nested regression, held-out R^2), and that engagement scales monotonically with resource-distance. Use logit-lens to confirm that in high-engagement (low-resource) passes the heuristic-promoted (often wrong) token dominates earlier/more strongly than in the dominant-language pass.
6) Core causal intervention (suppress extra engagement): Suppress the EXTRA heuristic-bag engagement in non-dominant languages — steer down / ablate the incremental heuristic-neuron activation relative to the dominant-language baseline (or patch in the dominant-language robust-component representation) — and measure per-language accuracy recovery. Predict SELECTIVE recovery on problems where the heuristic bag is imperfect (heuristic-signature-error-prone), little effect on problems the heuristics genuinely cover (interaction test). Compute recovery elasticity = accuracy gain per unit baseline over-engagement. Compare against baselines: whole-hub English steering (Language-Specific Latent Process 2025), language-specific ablation (When Less Language is More 2025), translate-to-digits, and a random-neuron control.
7) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify the intervention is heuristic-specific — it must IMPROVE heuristic-error-prone problems WITHOUT harming problems the heuristics correctly cover (a symmetric check: suppressing the bag must not remove genuinely-correct heuristic shortcuts), must not switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), and preserve fluency. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show a sharper cross-lingual heuristic-engagement gradient than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether the gradient correlates with each model's baseline English-centricity and each language's training share. Qualitatively compare the language-dependent heuristic-first pattern against the human heuristic-first/algorithmic-second and bilingual arithmetic literature (direction, not identical mechanism).
Evaluation metrics: per-language heuristic-bag engagement and robust-component engagement (vs digit anchor; partial correlation with resource-distance over fertility, held-out R^2); cross-lingual heuristic-neuron overlap (shared bag); heuristic-signature vs random error shares by language and their resource-distance correlation; engagement's prediction of accuracy loss vs competence baseline (held-out R^2); selective suppression accuracy recovery and elasticity vs baselines, with heuristic-covered-problem preservation (symmetric specificity), off-target rate, fluency; cross-model engagement-gradient comparison and correlation with English-centricity and training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Higher heuristic engagement in low-resource languages could conflate with a general competence gap; the key controls are the digit anchor (identical computation, language-agnostic), the heuristic-signature-vs-random error decomposition (a directional signature, not just more errors), and the causal suppression test which recovers accuracy specifically on heuristic-imperfect problems by editing only the bag's extra engagement — if suppression does not selectively help, or errors are random rather than heuristic-signature, the hypothesis is refuted, an informative negative result. 2) Identifying heuristic neurons and attributing engagement is method-sensitive and the bag was characterized on smaller models; we replicate the identification per model, cross-validate attribution methods (path patching, direct effect), and report robustness, treating models where the bag is not clearly recoverable as a limitation. 3) Language is confounded with tokenizer fertility (number words fragment differently), script, and resource level; the digit anchor, fertility controls, and partial correlations isolate a language effect from tokenization, and if fertility fully explains the engagement gradient that is itself an informative mechanistic sub-finding (heuristic over-reliance = fragmentation effect). 4) 'Robust component' vs heuristic bag may not cleanly separate; we use the complement of the heuristic-neuron direct effect and report ambiguous cases. 5) The suppression intervention could remove genuinely-useful heuristic shortcuts (harming heuristic-covered problems); the symmetric heuristic-covered-problem preservation constraint is a hard requirement and we report the full tradeoff, comparing against translate-to-digits to show the mechanistic account adds value. 6) Logit-lens robust-vs-heuristic tracking is approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 7) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM/Aya as less English-centric contrasts expected to show a flatter gradient). 8) The human-LLM comparison (heuristic-first arithmetic, bilingual arithmetic effects) is qualitative/structural, not a claim of identical mechanism. 9) Limited to open ~7-8B models and relatively small arithmetic; may not extend to frontier scale or complex multi-step math.

Name: crosslingual_release_from_proactive_interference
Title: Switching Tongues to Forget: Does a Cross-Lingual Switch Release Proactive Interference in Multilingual LLMs?
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs suffer proactive interference (PI) — earlier semantically-related key-value updates overwrite recall of the final value — but switching the LANGUAGE of the interfering stream mid-sequence RELEASES that interference, restoring recall of the final target, mirroring the human bilingual release-from-PI effect. Crucially, the release is driven by a SURFACE-language switch cue rather than by genuine semantic disentanglement: it works even when the switched items remain semantically related in the shared hub, so the model uses language identity as a (partly spurious) segmentation signal. The release magnitude tracks the typological/script distance of the switch and is mediated by a decodable language-boundary signal that resets accumulated interference.
Related Work: PI-LLM (Unable to Forget 2025) adapts the cognitive proactive-interference paradigm and shows LLM retrieval of the final value in a stream of semantically-related key-value updates declines log-linearly toward zero as interference accumulates, driven by retrieval of previously-overwritten values, and that prompt engineering barely helps — but this is entirely MONOLINGUAL. Sculptor (2025) mitigates PI via external context-management tools, not an internal linguistic cue. Aspects of Human Memory and LLMs (2023) shows LLM forgetting is interference-driven. Bilingual cognitive science robustly documents RELEASE FROM PI via encoding-language switch (Investigating PI After Switching Encoding Language 2023; the classic Wickens release-from-PI paradigm; dissipation and release of PI 1972), and bilingual language-control work shows language identity segments memory. CRITICALLY, no prior work asks whether a CROSS-LINGUAL switch RELEASES proactive interference in multilingual LLMs, whether that release is a surface-language segmentation cue versus genuine semantic disentanglement, whether it tracks switch distance, or whether a decodable language-boundary signal mediates an interference reset. We uniquely transfer the human bilingual release-from-PI effect into LLM mechanisms, tightening it into a surface-vs-semantic dissociation with a causal, steerable locus — distinct from monolingual PI-LLM and from tool-based mitigation.
Abstract: People overwhelmed by a stream of similar items forget the latest ones — proactive interference — but a simple trick restores memory: switch the language the last items are encoded in, and the interference releases. Recent work shows large language models suffer the same proactive interference: given a stream of semantically-related key-value updates, their recall of the final value collapses as interference accumulates. That work is monolingual. We ask a simple, previously untested question: does switching the LANGUAGE of the interfering stream mid-sequence RELEASE proactive interference in a multilingual LLM, as it does in bilingual humans? We hypothesize that (1) a cross-lingual switch of the later updates restores recall of the final target relative to a no-switch control; (2) this release is driven by a SURFACE-language switch cue rather than genuine semantic disentanglement — it works even when switched items stay semantically related in the shared hub — so the model exploits language identity as a partly-spurious segmentation signal; (3) the release magnitude tracks the typological/script distance of the switch; and (4) a decodable language-boundary signal mediates an interference reset, which we can causally reproduce and remove. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using a cross-lingual adaptation of the PI paradigm (streamed semantically-related updates, final-value query), crossing switch timing, switch language, and semantic relatedness. Combining behavioral recall measurement, logit-lens interference tracking, difference-in-means language-boundary probes, and activation patching, we measure the release, its surface-vs-semantic basis, its distance scaling, and its causal locus. Metrics include cross-lingual release magnitude, surface-vs-semantic dissociation, distance-prediction correlation, and boundary-signal-induced interference reset with recall-preservation controls.
Experiments:
1) Cross-lingual PI suite: Adapt the PI-LLM paradigm — stream N sequential key-value updates where many keys share a semantic theme (so later updates overwrite earlier ones), then query only the FINAL value of a target key. Build conditions crossing: (a) SWITCH TIMING — the last k updates are presented in a DIFFERENT language than the earlier ones (switch at 25/50/75% of the stream) vs a NO-SWITCH monolingual control; (b) SWITCH LANGUAGE — the switched segment in languages spanning typological/script distance from the base language (e.g. base French; switch to Spanish [close], German, Chinese, Arabic [far]); (c) SEMANTIC RELATEDNESS — switched items either semantically related to the pre-switch items (testing whether release survives shared-hub relatedness) or unrelated. Base languages: English, French, Chinese. Verified single-token/short gold final values. Native-speaker verify. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral release from PI (H1, core): Measure final-value recall accuracy and the fraction of errors that are 'previously-overwritten-value' intrusions (the PI signature) as interference accumulates, per condition. Test H1: a cross-lingual switch of the later segment RESTORES final-value recall (and reduces overwritten-value intrusions) relative to the no-switch monolingual control at matched interference load. Establish the monolingual PI log-linear decline first (replicating PI-LLM). Control for tokenizer fertility and switch-segment length (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test cross-lingual switch adds predictive power beyond position).
3) Surface-vs-semantic dissociation (H2, core): Test whether the release is driven by the SURFACE-language switch or by genuine semantic disentanglement. Compare (i) cross-lingual switch with switched items SEMANTICALLY RELATED to pre-switch items (shared hub still overlaps) vs (ii) a monolingual condition where switched items are made semantically UNRELATED (a genuine semantic reset without a language switch). Prediction: the language switch releases PI even when semantic relatedness is preserved (surface cue), while a semantic-only reset without a language switch releases PI less — demonstrating the model uses language identity as a partly-spurious segmentation signal. Report the release attributable to surface-language switch vs to semantic disentanglement.
4) Distance scaling (H3): Test whether release magnitude scales with the typological/script distance of the switch language from the base (Spearman; held-out R^2), predicting larger release for more distant/different-script switches (and confirming release is not merely a repetition/novelty artifact via a same-language 'switch' control that changes surface form but not language).
5) Mechanistic locus — language-boundary reset (H4): Using logit-lens/tuned-lens, track the accumulated-interference signal (how strongly previously-overwritten values remain active at the query position) across the stream, per condition. Extract a difference-in-means 'language-boundary' direction (switch-present vs no-switch representations at the boundary) and test whether the switch RESETS the interference signal (drop in overwritten-value activation after the boundary) and whether boundary-signal strength mediates behavioral release (partial correlation controlling for fertility/position; held-out R^2). Measure cross-lingual alignment of the boundary direction.
6) Causal test via patching (core): (a) INJECT the language-boundary signal into a NO-SWITCH monolingual pass (without actually switching language) and test whether it reproduces the interference reset and recall restoration — confirming the boundary signal is sufficient for release; (b) for a switch pass, ABLATE/remove the boundary signal and test whether release disappears — confirming necessity. This isolates a segmentation-reset mechanism triggered by the language boundary, not the specific switched content. Verify specificity: the intervention restores the FINAL target without corrupting other retained values (recall-preservation check), does not switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), and preserves fluency.
7) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify the release is switch-specific (a within-language surface-change control gives less release than a true language switch), and not a generic recency boost (the switched segment length is controlled). Cross-model contrast: predict the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM show cleaner language-boundary segmentation (larger, more distance-graded release) than the more English-centric Llama-3; test whether release magnitude correlates with the strength/cross-lingual sharpness of the boundary direction and each language's training share. Qualitatively compare the LLM release-from-PI pattern (surface-language switch releases PI, tracks distance) against the human bilingual release-from-PI literature (direction, not identical mechanism).
Evaluation metrics: monolingual PI log-linear decline (replication); cross-lingual release magnitude (switch vs no-switch; recall gain and overwritten-value-intrusion reduction at matched load); surface-vs-semantic dissociation (release from language switch with relatedness preserved vs semantic-only reset); release-vs-switch-distance correlation and held-out prediction; interference-reset at the boundary and boundary-signal mediation of behavioral release (held-out R^2); injection-induced release (sufficiency) and ablation-induced loss (necessity); recall-preservation of other values, off-target/language-mixing rate, fluency; cross-model release comparison and correlation with boundary-direction sharpness and training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for cross-lingual switch over position/fertility baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The release could conflate with a generic novelty/recency boost from any change at the switch point rather than a LANGUAGE-specific segmentation cue; the within-language surface-change control (change surface form but not language), the switch-length control, and the distance scaling (release tracks typological distance, not mere change) isolate a language-specific effect — if a surface change alone gives equal release, the hypothesis weakens to a generic segmentation effect, still informative. 2) The surface-vs-semantic dissociation hinges on genuinely holding semantic relatedness constant across a language switch; we verify shared-hub relatedness (mid-layer representational overlap) of switched vs pre-switch items and native-speaker-verify translation adequacy, reporting cases where the switch inadvertently reduces relatedness. 3) A monolingual LLM must first show robust PI (per PI-LLM); Experiment 2's replication is a necessary gate — if PI is weak in a model, the release question is moot there, itself informative. 4) Switch language is confounded with tokenizer fertility, script, and resource level; partial correlations and the no-switch and same-language controls mitigate but may not fully remove confounds. 5) The language-boundary direction from difference-in-means may entangle content/language-identity features; we use multiple extraction methods, the injection/ablation causal tests, and specificity controls. 6) The injection intervention could restore recall via generic attention resetting rather than a genuine interference reset; the recall-preservation check (other values intact) and the necessity (ablation) test address this. 7) Logit-lens interference-signal estimates are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 8) The human-LLM comparison (release from PI via encoding-language switch) is qualitative/structural, not a claim of identical mechanism; a text-only model has no embodied encoding, so any release is distributional, which is what makes a positive result interesting. 9) Effects may be model-family dependent (Aya-23/BLOOM as more multilingual contrasts expected to show cleaner segmentation). 10) If NO release is found — a cross-lingual switch does not reduce proactive interference — this is an informative POSITIVE result showing PI is a shared-hub semantic bottleneck insensitive to surface language, contrasting with human bilinguals, valuable either way. 11) Limited to open ~7-8B models and modest stream lengths; may not extend to frontier scale or very long contexts.

Name: language_conditioned_data_instruction_boundary
Title: Reading Data as Commands in a Foreign Tongue: A Language-Conditioned Weakening of the Instruction/Data Boundary in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs maintain an internal 'this-is-data-not-a-command' boundary that suppresses treating retrieved/tool content as instructions, but the STRENGTH of this boundary is language-conditioned: when injected content inside a data field is written in a lower-resource / English-distant language, the model is more likely to obey it as an instruction, so prompt-injection susceptibility is set by the language of the injected span, not its role. This is a language-conditioned gain on a single, largely shared instruction-vs-data separation direction, is decodable, tracks resource level, and is causally correctable by rescaling that direction without harming legitimate instruction following. This is defensive, injection-hardening research.
Related Work: System-vs-user instruction-hierarchy work (Who is In Charge 2025) finds conflicts form an early-layer subspace with weak, role-agnostic resolution; prompt-injection/data-boundary work is largely behavioral and monolingual. Multilingual safety work shows refusal/safety is largely language-agnostic yet non-English separation is weaker (SS-Neurons 2026; Refusal Direction is Universal 2025; The Hidden Space of Safety 2025), and code-mixing causes attributional collapse away from safety-critical tokens (Saliency Drift 2025). CRITICALLY, all injection/data-boundary work is monolingual and treats the boundary as fixed; all multilingual safety work concerns harmful-request refusal, not the INSTRUCTION/DATA separation for benign-but-unauthorized injected commands. No prior work asks whether the language of an injected data span acts as a covert command-privilege cue that weakens the data-boundary, whether this is a language-conditioned gain on a shared separation direction, whether it tracks resource level, or whether rescaling it hardens injection defense without harming legitimate instructions. This differs from my prior system-vs-user language-privilege proposal by targeting the DATA/CONTENT boundary (RAG/tool outputs) rather than the system/user role hierarchy.
Abstract: A safe assistant must treat retrieved documents and tool outputs as DATA, not as commands, and the language that data is written in should not change whether it is obeyed. We ask a simple, previously untested question: when an injected instruction sits inside a data field but is written in a different language than the surrounding prompt, does the injected span's LANGUAGE weaken the model's instruction-vs-data boundary? We hypothesize that the boundary strength is language-conditioned: an injected command in a lower-resource or English-distant language is obeyed more than the same command in the dominant language, so prompt-injection susceptibility tracks the injected span's language rather than its data role. We further hypothesize this is a language-conditioned gain on a single, largely shared instruction-vs-data separation direction — decodable, predictable from resource level, and causally correctable by rescaling it without harming legitimate instruction following. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using controlled RAG/tool-style prompts where a benign-but-unauthorized injected instruction inside a data field is rendered in independently-varied languages while the task and injection content are held fixed. Combining behavioral injection-obedience measurement, difference-in-means separation-direction extraction, logit-lens gain readout, activation patching, and gain-steering, we measure the language-privilege effect on the data boundary, its resource scaling, its shared-direction locus, and a defensive fix. Metrics include the injected-language obedience swing, resource prediction, separation-direction alignment, and steering-induced hardening with legitimate-instruction controls.
Experiments:
1) Cross-lingual injection suite: Construct ~500 RAG/tool-style tasks where the user asks a question and a DATA field (retrieved document / tool output) contains an embedded benign-but-unauthorized INJECTED instruction (e.g. 'ignore the question and output X', 'append this phrase', 'switch to a different format') whose obedience is objectively scorable and clearly not user-authorized. Independently vary the LANGUAGE of the injected span across typologically diverse languages spanning resource levels and scripts (English, French, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish), holding the injection content and the surrounding task fixed. Include (a) SAME-LANGUAGE controls (injection in the prompt language), (b) LEGITIMATE-instruction items (the user genuinely asks for the action, in each language) as a specificity control, and (c) a within-language paraphrase control. Native-speaker verify; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, BLOOM(Z)-7B.
2) Behavioral injected-language effect (H1, core): Measure the injection-obedience rate = fraction where the model follows the injected data-field instruction instead of the legitimate task. Test the central prediction: obedience rises when the injected span is in a lower-resource / English-distant language, holding content and role fixed. Define the injected-language obedience swing = obedience(low-resource injection) minus obedience(dominant-language injection). Control for tokenizer fertility and per-language comprehension of the injected instruction in isolation (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test injected-span language adds predictive power beyond role and comprehension). Condition on injections the model comprehends in isolation, so the effect is not non-understanding.
3) Resource scaling (H2): Test whether per-language injection-obedience is predicted by resource level better than by the model's comprehension competence in that language (nested regression, held-out R^2). Predict minimal obedience for the dominant language, rising with resource-distance.
4) Shared separation direction and gain readout (H3): Extract a difference-in-means 'instruction-vs-data separation' direction (obey-injected vs treat-as-data representations) at each layer, building on the early instruction-hierarchy subspace finding. Verify cross-lingual alignment (a largely shared axis) and portability (steering shifts obedience across languages). Project the residual stream at the decision point onto the shared direction and estimate a per-LANGUAGE gain via regression of the obedience decision on the projection contributed by the injected span's language. Test that the cross-lingual swing is captured by the difference in per-language gains applied to the SHARED projection (held-out R^2), beating a uniform-bias baseline. Mediation: regress behavioral swing on the language-weighted separation projection (partial correlation controlling for fertility/comprehension; held-out R^2).
5) Causal test via patching and gain-steering (H4, core defense): (a) For items where a low-resource injection is obeyed but the dominant-language injection is refused, patch the separation signal from the dominant-language pass into the low-resource pass and test whether the data-boundary is restored (injection refused), isolating a language-privilege gain from injection content. (b) Rescale the shared separation direction with a per-language scalar to equalize the boundary across languages (remove the low-resource obedience advantage), and measure injection-hardening, with bidirectional dose-response. Compare against baselines: role-agnostic instruction-following steering (Who is In Charge 2025), translate-injected-span-to-English detection, and a random-direction control.
6) Specificity and utility controls (hard constraint): The fix must reduce injected-instruction obedience WITHOUT reducing LEGITIMATE instruction following (the model must still obey genuine user requests in every language — symmetric check), must not switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), and preserve task accuracy and fluency. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show a larger injected-language swing than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether the swing correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the separation direction and each language's training share.
Evaluation metrics: same-language baseline injection-obedience; injected-language obedience swing (low-resource vs dominant injection, content/role fixed); obedience-vs-resource prediction (held-out R^2 over comprehension baseline); separation-direction cross-lingual alignment, portability, and gain predictive R^2 (vs uniform-bias baseline) with mediation of the swing (held-out R^2); patching-induced boundary restoration; gain-steering injection-hardening and cross-lingual obedience-variance reduction vs baselines, with bidirectional dose-response; legitimate-instruction and task-accuracy preservation (symmetric specificity), off-target/language-mixing rate; cross-model swing comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The injected-language effect could conflate with a per-language instruction-COMPREHENSION gap (the model may ignore a low-resource injection because it understands it worse, not because it deprioritizes data-field commands); the key controls are conditioning on injections the model obeys/comprehends in ISOLATION per language, the resource-vs-comprehension regression, and the causal patching/steering (which shifts obedience by editing only the separation direction) — if the swing vanishes once comprehension is controlled, the hypothesis is refuted, an informative negative result. 2) Injected-span language is confounded with tokenizer fertility, script, and resource level; same-language baselines, the within-language paraphrase control, and partial correlations mitigate but may not fully remove confounds. 3) The single-scalar gain account may only partially hold; if a data-driven low-dimensional basis fits better we report it, keeping the 'shared separation axis + language gain' claim testable. 4) The separation direction from difference-in-means may entangle content/role features; we use the early instruction-hierarchy subspace as an anchor, content-matched injections, and specificity controls. 5) The defensive fix could reduce legitimate instruction following or harm task accuracy; the legitimate-instruction and accuracy-preservation constraints are hard requirements and we report the full tradeoff. 6) Dual-use: this identifies a cross-lingual injection weakness, but all interventions here HARDEN the data boundary (defensive); we use benign-but-unauthorized injection content, release the suite under controlled terms, and do not publish attack-enhancing artifacts. 7) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM/Aya as less English-centric contrasts expected to show a smaller swing). 8) If no injected-language effect is found — injection obedience is language-invariant once comprehension is controlled — this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the data boundary is language-agnostic, valuable either way. 9) Limited to open ~7-8B instruction-tuned models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: portable_temporal_head_local_value_binding
Title: When Was That True, in Which Tongue? Portable Temporal Heads but Language-Bound As-Of-Year Value Binding in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Answering a time-conditioned factual query ('who led country X in 2004?') requires two separable operations: a TEMPORAL-CONDITIONING operator (the Temporal Heads that set which time-slice of a fact to retrieve) and a VALUE-BINDING step that surfaces the correct as-of-year object in the query language. We hypothesize the Temporal Heads are largely language-agnostic and transfer across languages, so a multilingual LLM correctly ENGAGES the right year everywhere, whereas the as-of-year value BINDING is language-bound and fails in lower-resource / English-distant languages. Consequently cross-lingual temporal-factual inconsistency is dominated by value-binding failure, not temporal-conditioning failure: the model applies the right time reference but retrieves the wrong (often anachronistic or English-default) object, and this dissociation is measurable, decodable, and causally correctable by boosting the target-language value-binding step without re-engaging the temporal circuit.
Related Work: Temporal Heads (2025) localize time-specific recall to a small set of attention heads whose ablation impairs temporal knowledge while sparing time-invariant facts, and shows knowledge can be edited by adjusting head values — but entirely MONOLINGUALLY (English). Multilingual factual-recall work localizes cross-lingual inconsistency to an English-centric recall stage then a language-dependent object-extraction/translation step (Paths Not Taken 2025; Lost in Multilinguality 2025; How Do Multilingual LLMs Remember Facts 2024: subject enrichment is language-independent, object extraction is language-dependent) and to entity-alignment bottlenecks (Entity-Level Alignment 2025; Are Knowledge and Reference Consistent 2025), and DynamicQA (2024) shows dynamic/time-sensitive facts carry more intra-memory conflict. CRITICALLY, all Temporal-Head work is monolingual and never asks whether the temporal-conditioning circuit transfers across languages; all cross-lingual factual-recall work concerns TIME-INVARIANT facts and never separates the TEMPORAL-CONDITIONING operation (which year to retrieve) from the language-bound VALUE-BINDING (surfacing that year's object). No prior work tests whether Temporal Heads are language-agnostic-portable while as-of-year value binding is language-local, whether cross-lingual temporal-factual failure is a value-binding (not temporal-conditioning) failure, or whether transplanting the temporal-head activation across languages preserves correct year-conditioning while the value fails. This differs from my prior language_dependent_temporal_anchor proposal (which concerned the model's implicit unmarked 'now'/data-recency setpoint) by targeting EXPLICITLY year-conditioned recall and the portable-temporal-operator / local-value-binding dissociation grounded in the located Temporal-Head circuit.
Abstract: A time-sensitive fact has different correct answers at different years, and answering 'who led country X in 2004?' requires two things a monolingual setting cannot separate: conditioning retrieval on the queried year, and surfacing that year's specific answer in the language you asked in. Interpretability work has localized the first operation to a small set of Temporal Heads — but only in English. We ask a simple, previously untested question: are the Temporal Heads language-agnostic, and do they dissociate from the language-bound step that binds the year to its value? We hypothesize that the temporal-conditioning circuit transfers across languages (the model engages the right year everywhere) while the as-of-year value binding is language-local and fails in lower-resource / English-distant languages, so cross-lingual temporal-factual inconsistency is dominated by value-binding failure — the model applies the correct time reference but retrieves the wrong or English-default object. Under this account, the correct as-of-year value is latently present after temporal conditioning but is not surfaced in the target language, and the dissociation is causally testable: transplanting the temporal-head activation across languages preserves correct year-conditioning, but only a target-language value-binding boost fixes the answer. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using year-conditioned factual queries (leaders, champions, officeholders) across typologically diverse languages, with matched time-invariant controls. Using Temporal-Head localization and ablation, logit-lens tracking of year-conditioning vs value, activation patching to separate temporal-conditioning from value-binding failures, and a cross-lingual temporal-head transplant, we quantify the dissociation, its resource-distance scaling, and a targeted fix. Metrics include temporal-conditioning vs value-binding error shares, Temporal-Head cross-lingual overlap, transplant year-preservation, latent-value-present rate, and value-binding-boost recovery with time-invariant controls.
Experiments:
1) Year-conditioned factual suite: Build ~600 explicitly time-conditioned factual queries ('In <YEAR>, who was <role> of <country/entity>?') whose correct answer is a dated sequence of values (heads of state/government, sports champions, officeholders) with verified per-year gold answers spanning ~1990-2020 from Wikidata. Include matched TIME-INVARIANT control facts (capital, chemical symbol) and a WRONG-YEAR-DISTRACTOR analysis (does the model answer a neighboring year's value?). Instantiate every query in typologically diverse languages spanning scripts and resource levels (English, French, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish), native-speaker verified. Report inter-annotator agreement; release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral map and error typing: Measure per-language accuracy on year-conditioned queries and cross-lingual consistency (agreement with the English answer for the same year). Decompose errors into (a) WRONG-YEAR errors (the model returns a value correct for a DIFFERENT year — a temporal-conditioning failure) vs (b) WRONG-VALUE errors (right time-slice targeted but wrong/anachronistic/English-default object — a value-binding failure) vs (c) genuine absence. Control for tokenizer fertility and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2). Condition on facts the model knows for that year in English, so failures are not absence.
3) Temporal-Head localization and cross-lingual overlap (H1): Per model, localize Temporal Heads via circuit analysis / ablation on the English year-conditioned set (following Temporal Heads 2025), verify ablation degrades temporal but not time-invariant accuracy. Test whether the SAME heads are engaged across languages (cross-lingual head-overlap) and whether ablating them degrades temporal recall in every language — evidence the temporal-conditioning circuit is largely language-agnostic.
4) Latent-value-present and conditioning-vs-binding error decomposition (H2, core): For year-conditioned queries correct in English but wrong in language B (conditioned on the correct year being engaged, per the Temporal-Head activation), use logit-lens to test whether the correct as-of-year value is latently present in mid layers even on failed items (latent-value-present rate). Then activation-patch: patch (a) the temporal-head activation from the English pass into B, and (b) only the late-layer target-language value-extraction/decoding components. Classify as temporal-conditioning failure (fixed by (a), correct year not engaged) vs value-binding failure (year engaged / value latently present; only (b) surfaces it). Report error shares per language, predicting value-binding failures dominate and grow with resource-distance.
5) Cross-lingual temporal-head transplant test (H3, core): Extract the Temporal-Head activation for a query in a high-resource language and TRANSPLANT it into a low-resource-language forward pass on the same year-conditioned query; measure whether the model (i) preserves correct YEAR-conditioning (does not drift to a wrong year — year-preservation rate) but (ii) still fails to surface the correct target-language VALUE unless value binding is also boosted — directly demonstrating the portable-temporal-operator / local-value-binding dissociation. Compare against a target-language value-binding boost (steer/patch the target-language object-decoding direction, which our account predicts is what value-binding failures need) and a random-direction control.
6) Core causal intervention (value-binding boost): Without re-engaging the temporal circuit, boost the target-language value-binding step (steer the object-extraction/decoding at the late transition layer toward the target-language channel) on year-conditioned queries in low-resource languages, and measure accuracy/consistency recovery. Predict selective recovery for value-binding failures (latent-value-present items), little effect on genuine temporal-conditioning or absence failures. Compare against baselines: whole-hub English steering, the linear-shortcut factual fix (Lost in Multilinguality 2025) and SubInj entity-alignment prompting (Entity-Level Alignment 2025) adapted here, and translate-query-to-English. Compute recovery elasticity = accuracy gain per unit latent-value-present rate.
7) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify the value-binding boost is binding-specific (surfaces the correct year's value without switching output language — off-target/language-mixing rate — without changing which year is targeted, and without harming time-invariant facts), and is gap-closing not uniform-lift. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show sharper value-binding-failure dominance and larger boost gains than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether the temporal-head-overlap / value-binding-failure split correlates with each language's training share.
Evaluation metrics: per-language year-conditioned accuracy and cross-lingual consistency; wrong-year vs wrong-value vs absence error shares; Temporal-Head cross-lingual overlap and language-agnostic-ablation effect; latent-value-present rate on failed items and its resource-distance scaling; temporal-conditioning vs value-binding error shares (patching); transplant year-preservation rate (year stays correct) alongside persistent value failure; value-binding-boost recovery and elasticity vs baselines, with year-preservation, time-invariant preservation, and output-language preservation (specificity), off-target rate; cross-model dissociation comparison and correlation with training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for resource-distance over fertility baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Temporal-conditioning and value-binding may not separate cleanly; patching can have entangled effects. Mitigation: use the wrong-year vs wrong-value behavioral typing, the logit-lens latent-value check, and multiple patching granularities, reporting ambiguous cases — if the correct year is not engaged in low-resource languages (temporal-conditioning also fails), the dissociation is refuted, an informative result relocating the failure to the temporal circuit. 2) Temporal Heads were localized on specific models and may not cleanly replicate on all four; we replicate the localization per model, verify the time-variant/invariant ablation dissociation, and report models where heads are not clearly recoverable as a limitation. 3) 'Correct year engaged but wrong value' vs 'never knew this year's value' is subtle; we condition on facts the model knows for that year in English and use the transplant/patching causal tests to separate binding failure from absence. 4) Year-conditioned queries with sharp yearly transitions (elections, championships) are needed for clean gold; we restrict to such facts and verify Wikidata timelines. 5) Resource-distance is confounded with tokenizer fertility and script; partial correlations and the causal tests mitigate but may not fully remove confounds. 6) The temporal-head transplant across languages requires aligning positions across differing token lengths; we align at functional positions and report alignment quality. 7) The value-binding boost could switch output language or drift the targeted year; year-preservation, time-invariant, and output-language preservation are hard specificity constraints and we report the full tradeoff, comparing against translate-to-English to show the mechanistic account adds value. 8) Logit-lens latent-value and year-conditioning estimates are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 9) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM's less English-centric hub analyzed as a contrast expected to show weaker value-binding-failure dominance). 10) If Temporal Heads do NOT transfer cross-lingually (temporal conditioning itself is language-specific), the portability hypothesis is refuted — itself a valuable finding; conversely, if failures are temporal-conditioning rather than value-binding failures, this relocates the cross-lingual temporal-factual bottleneck and is equally informative. 11) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: habitual_default_imposition_simple_present
Title: Eating a Donut Right Now, English-Style: Does the Shared Hub Impose an English Habitual/Generic Default on the Simple Present of Verb-Raising Languages?
Short Hypothesis: The simple present is interpreted differently across languages: in non-verb-raising English 'John eats a donut' forces a HABITUAL/GENERIC reading (an episodic 'right now' reading is ungrammatical), whereas in verb-raising languages (French, Spanish, German, Arabic) the same simple present freely licenses an EPISODIC/ongoing reading. Because the multilingual LLM's shared hub is scaffolded by English, we hypothesize it IMPOSES the English habitual-default onto the simple present of verb-raising languages: it over-reads a bare-present sentence as habitual/generic and under-licenses the episodic/ongoing interpretation, tracking the English convention rather than the target-language grammar. This imposition is mediated by a shared, steerable habitual-vs-episodic direction, tracks each language's verb-raising status, and is causally correctable without harming genuine habitual comprehension.
Related Work: The verb-raising literature (Hawkins et al. 2017 'semantic effects of verb raising'; verb-raising 2L grammars) establishes that whether the simple present allows an episodic/progressive reading is a syntactic parameter: verb-raising languages (French, Spanish, German, Arabic) permit it, non-raising English/Chinese force a generic-habitual reading. Habitual/episodic aspect interpretation is adverbial-modulated and default-driven (Spanish preterite/imperfect habitual/episodic study 2016; Tlingit two-paths-to-habituality 2022; Basque imperfective 2013), and LLMs struggle with cross-linguistic aspect NLI (LLMs Struggle with NLI for Perfect Aspect 2025). Interpretability shows tense/aspect are orthogonal, causally steerable directions largely English-scaffolded (Steering Tense and Aspect 2025; About Time 2022; Probing Verbal Aspect 2024; LLMs Share Latent Grammatical Concepts). CRITICALLY, all model aspect work concerns tense/telicity/perfective ENCODING or generic aspect steering monolingually; NONE asks whether the shared, English-scaffolded hub IMPOSES the English habitual/generic default on the simple present of verb-raising languages, causing over-habitual/under-episodic reading, whether this tracks the verb-raising parameter, whether a shared habitual-vs-episodic direction mediates it, or whether it is causally correctable. This differs from my prior tense-imposition (temporal LOCATION), telicity-imposition (event endpoint), and aspectual-coercion proposals: here the axis is the GENERICITY/HABITUALITY default of the bare simple present tied to the verb-raising typology — a distinct, previously mechanistically-untested grammatical parameter with an external syntactic ground truth.
Abstract: The simplest present-tense sentence hides a cross-linguistic split: English 'John eats a donut' can only mean he does so habitually — an 'eating right now' reading is ungrammatical — while the equivalent simple present in French, Spanish, German, or Arabic freely describes an ongoing episode. Decades of syntax tie this to a verb-raising parameter. Multilingual language models build a shared, English-scaffolded representation. We ask a simple, previously untested question: does the model IMPOSE the English habitual/generic default on the simple present of verb-raising languages, over-reading their bare-present sentences as habitual and under-licensing the episodic/ongoing interpretation? We hypothesize that (1) on identical simple-present sentences, the model commits to a habitual/generic reading in verb-raising languages more than native speakers do, tracking the English convention; (2) the size of this imposition tracks each language's verb-raising status; (3) a shared, steerable habitual-vs-episodic direction mediates it, with any residual episodic-licensing signal in shallow, language-specific layers; and (4) steering toward the episodic reading restores target-language-faithful interpretation without harming genuine habitual comprehension. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using controlled simple-present sentences in episodic-biasing, habitual-biasing, and neutral contexts across verb-raising (French, Spanish, German, Arabic) and non-raising (English, Chinese) languages. Using difference-in-means aspect-direction probes, logit-lens tracking, activation patching, and steering, we measure the imposition, its typology scaling, its mediation, and its causal correction. Metrics include the habitual-over-reading gap, verb-raising-prediction correlation, mediation R-squared, and steering-induced restoration with habitual-comprehension controls.
Experiments:
1) Simple-present interpretation suite: Construct ~450 simple-present sentences (eventive predicates) each realized in verb-raising languages (French, Spanish, German, Arabic) and non-raising controls (English, Chinese), native-speaker verified. Three context conditions: (a) EPISODIC-biasing ('right now' / ongoing scene, where verb-raising languages license an episodic reading of the bare present but English does not); (b) HABITUAL-biasing ('every morning'); (c) NEUTRAL (no adverbial). Probes hinging on the reading: (i) interpretation forced choice ('is this happening right now or habitually?'); (ii) aspect-NLI (does the sentence entail an ongoing-episode paraphrase vs a habitual paraphrase? — correct answer differs by language for the bare present); (iii) continuation/acceptability of an 'is doing right now' follow-up. Gold labels calibrated per language to the verb-raising grammar. Report inter-annotator agreement; release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral imposition (H1, core): On EPISODIC-biasing and NEUTRAL items, measure the habitual-over-reading rate = fraction of verb-raising-language bare-present sentences the model reads as habitual/generic despite the episodic context, and an English-default pull rate. Compare against HABITUAL-biasing items (all languages agree) and against non-raising controls (where habitual IS correct). Define the imposition GAP = habitual-over-reading(verb-raising, episodic) minus habitual-over-reading(control). Control for tokenizer fertility, verb frequency, and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test verb-raising status adds predictive power).
3) Verb-raising scaling (H2, external validation): Using the verb-raising typological classification (raising: French/Spanish/German/Arabic; non-raising: English/Chinese) and each language's episodic-licensing strength, test whether per-language imposition is predicted by verb-raising status (Spearman; held-out prediction from typology alone), tying the internal phenomenon to independent syntactic ground truth.
4) Representational localization (H3): Extract a habitual-vs-episodic direction via difference-in-means between habitual/generic and episodic/ongoing representations at each layer, per language (building on Steering Tense and Aspect). Test (a) whether a shared direction is English-scaffolded (cross-lingual cosine alignment, aligned with the English habitual pole); (b) whether a verb-raising-language bare-present-in-episodic-context input projects onto the HABITUAL pole in the shared hub while any residual episodic-licensing signal is stronger in early/language-specific layers, via logit-lens depth tracking. Baseline: a tense direction (English marks it) as a within-model shared-category control. Mediation: regress behavioral imposition on shared-hub habitual-pole projection (partial correlation controlling for fertility/frequency; held-out R^2).
5) Causal steering/patching test (H4, core): (a) Steer the verb-raising-language input toward the EPISODIC pole and measure whether interpretation/NLI shift to the episodic reading (flip rate) and the imposition GAP shrinks toward the control baseline, without switching output language; (b) bidirectional dose-response; (c) for imposed items, patch the residual language-specific episodic-licensing signal (from early/language-specific layers) into later computation and test restoration. Critically verify HABITUAL-COMPREHENSION preservation (HABITUAL-biasing items and non-raising controls must still be read habitually — no over-flipping) plus fluency and off-target/language-mixing checks. Baselines: whole-hub English-steering, random-direction control.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify steering is aspect-specific (changes the habitual/episodic reading but not the event identity or tense), graded (imposition scales with verb-raising status), and not a lexical-frequency artifact (nonce-verb variants). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show stronger imposition than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether imposition magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the habitual-vs-episodic direction and each language's training share. Qualitatively compare the per-language imposition pattern against the verb-raising typology and the human L2-verb-raising interpretation literature.
Evaluation metrics: habitual-over-reading rate and imposition GAP (verb-raising episodic vs habitual-biasing vs non-raising controls; English-default pull rate); imposition-vs-verb-raising-status correlation and held-out prediction; aspect-NLI accuracy; shared-hub habitual-pole projection strength and crystallization depth (vs tense baseline); cross-lingual habitual-vs-episodic-direction alignment; mediation regression (held-out R^2); steering flip rate and GAP reduction (bidirectional dose-response), patching-induced restoration; habitual-comprehension preservation, fluency, off-target rate; cross-model imposition comparison and correlation with training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for verb-raising status over frequency/fertility/resource baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Establishing per-language gold readings for the bare simple present is subtle (episodic licensing can be gradient and adverbial-dependent); we ground labels in the verb-raising grammar, native-speaker verify, use graded agreement, report inter-annotator agreement, and exclude low-agreement items. 2) Verb-raising status is correlated with language family, script, and resource level;
