We hypothesize multilingual LLMs represent dates on a single, largely dominant-language(Gregorian)-anchored temporal hub and IMPOSE a default calendar system when interpreting or reasoning about an unqualified date in a language whose culture conventionally uses a non-Gregorian calendar: the model reads/computes the date in the Gregorian frame rather than the culturally-appropriate one, producing cross-lingual inconsistency on the SAME situation. This calendar-default imposition is mediated by a shared, steerable calendar-frame direction, tracks each culture's empirical calendar convention, and is causally correctable without harming Gregorian-explicit date arithmetic.
Related Work: Behavioral work shows LLMs default to the training-data-predominant MEASUREMENT system (currencies, units) and are unstable across systems, mitigable only by extra CoT compute (On Generalization across Measurement Systems 2025; NUMCoT 2024; Do LMs Understand Measurements 2022), and that cross-CALENDAR temporal reasoning is very hard (SPAN 2025: ~34% accuracy, 'Calendar Asymmetry Bias'; DATETIME 2025). Interpretability shows time/space are linearly, causally encoded with dedicated time neurons/heads (Language Models Represent Space and Time 2023; Temporal Heads 2025), numbers are linear/sinusoidal and causally usable (Numbers Linearly 2024; Manipulating Numbers 2025), and multilingual LLMs share a dominant-language(Gregorian/English)-scaffolded temporal hub with language-specific decoding (Semantic Hub 2024; Cross-Layer Transcoders 2025; Do Multilingual LLMs Think In English 2025). Human cognition shows numeral transparency of time words affects temporal-calculation strategy cross-lingually (Tuesday-before-Threesday 2013). CRITICALLY, all measurement/calendar work is behavioral/benchmark (accuracy across systems, tool-augmented fixes) and never asks whether the shared temporal hub MECHANISTICALLY IMPOSES a default calendar system onto non-Gregorian-culture languages, whether this cross-lingual inconsistency is predictable from each culture's calendar convention, whether a shared calendar-frame direction mediates it, or whether it is causally correctable per language. This differs from my prior measurement_system and temporal_anchor proposals (unit conversion; implicit 'now' recency) by targeting the CALENDAR-SYSTEM frame in which a date is indexed — a distinct cultural convention with an authoritative conversion ground truth.
Abstract: A date like 'the 10th' has no fixed meaning until you say which calendar you mean: the 10th of the Islamic month is a different day than the 10th Gregorian, and Persian, Hebrew, Chinese, and Indian calendars each partition the year differently. Cultures conventionally index dates in different calendar systems, yet conversions between them are exact. Multilingual language models build a single, dominant-language-anchored temporal representation. We ask a simple, previously untested mechanistic question: when a model interprets or reasons about an unqualified date in a language whose culture conventionally uses a non-Gregorian calendar, does it IMPOSE the Gregorian default rather than the culturally-appropriate frame? We hypothesize that (1) the model reads and computes an unqualified date in the Gregorian frame regardless of the query language, producing cross-lingual inconsistency on the same situation concentrated where the culture's conventional calendar diverges from Gregorian; (2) the size of this imposition tracks each culture's empirical calendar convention; (3) a shared, steerable calendar-frame direction mediates it, with any residual culture-specific frame signal in shallow, language-specific layers; and (4) steering toward the target calendar restores culture-appropriate interpretation without harming Gregorian-explicit date arithmetic. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using controlled date-interpretation and date-reasoning items across languages whose cultures use divergent versus convergent (Gregorian) calendars, grounded in authoritative calendar conversions. Using difference-in-means calendar-frame probes, logit-lens tracking, activation patching, and steering, we measure the imposition, its convention scaling, its mediation, and its causal correction. Metrics include cross-lingual calendar-imposition gap, convention-prediction correlation, mediation R-squared, and steering-induced correction with Gregorian-explicit controls.
Experiments:
1) Cross-calendar date suite grounded in conversions: Build ~500 date-indexed items (holidays, historical events, 'what date is N days after / before an unqualified date', 'which month is X in', day-of-week and month-length queries) whose correct answer depends on the calendar frame. Instantiate across languages whose cultures conventionally use divergent calendars (Arabic/Islamic-Hijri, Persian/Jalali, Hebrew, Chinese lunisolar, Hindi/Indian national) versus Gregorian-convergent controls (English, French, German, Spanish). Key subsets: DIVERGENT items where the culture-conventional calendar gives a different answer than Gregorian, and matched CONVERGENT items. Also include a GREGORIAN-EXPLICIT arithmetic control (fully-specified Gregorian dates + day-offsets) as a competence anchor. Ground all conversions in authoritative calendar-conversion tables (using a fixed reference Gregorian date per item to avoid contamination). Native-speaker verify; attach each culture its empirical default-calendar convention. Report inter-annotator agreement; release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral imposition (H1, core): On DIVERGENT items, infer which calendar frame the model assumes (via forced-choice 'which calendar is this date in?', frame-consistency of computed answers, and elicited conversion) per language, holding the date fixed. Define the calendar-imposition GAP = inconsistency(DIVERGENT) minus inconsistency(CONVERGENT), and a Gregorian-default pull rate = fraction of divergent items answered in the Gregorian frame rather than the culture-conventional one. Verify near-perfect GREGORIAN-EXPLICIT arithmetic (isolating imposition from numeric incompetence) and correct handling of CONVERGENT items. Control for tokenizer fertility, date-token frequency, and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test target-culture convention adds predictive power).
3) Convention scaling (H2, external validation): Test whether per-culture imposition is predicted by that culture's empirical calendar-usage convention (Spearman; held-out prediction from convention data alone), tying the internal phenomenon to independent ground truth; predict larger imposition for lower-resource / more Gregorian-distant calendars.
4) Representational localization (H3): Extract a per-item 'calendar-frame' direction via difference-in-means between representations of the same date interpreted under different calendars (using frame-explicit exemplars), at each layer, per language. Test (a) cross-lingual alignment of the frame direction (a single, largely shared, Gregorian-scaffolded temporal frame re-thresholded per language); (b) whether a DIVERGENT unqualified date crystallizes toward the GREGORIAN frame in the shared mid-layers while any residual culture-specific frame signal is stronger in early/language-specific layers, via logit-lens/tuned-lens depth tracking; leverage the known time neurons/Temporal Heads as anchors. Mediation: regress behavioral imposition on the shared-hub Gregorian-frame projection (partial correlation controlling for fertility/frequency; held-out R^2). Baseline: a raw numeric-value (day-number) direction as a within-model control.
5) Causal steering/patching test (H4, core): (a) Steer the unqualified-date representation along the calendar-frame direction toward the target-culture calendar and measure whether interpretation/reasoning shifts to the culture-appropriate frame (flip rate) and the imposition GAP shrinks toward the CONVERGENT baseline, without switching output language; (b) bidirectional dose-response (toward and away from Gregorian); (c) for imposed items, patch the residual language-specific frame signal (from early/language-specific layers) into later computation and test restoration. Critically verify GREGORIAN-EXPLICIT competence preservation (fully-specified Gregorian arithmetic must stay correct — steering changes the assumed FRAME, not the arithmetic) plus fluency and off-target/language-mixing checks. Baselines: whole-hub English-steering, CoT prompting (the measurement-paper baseline), random-direction control.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify steering is calendar-frame-specific (changes the assumed calendar/date-mapping but not the raw numeric value or unrelated content), graded (imposition scales with convention divergence), and not merely a tokenizer artifact. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English/Gregorian-centric Llama-3/Qwen show stronger imposition than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM (which see more Hijri/Jalali/Chinese-calendar data); test whether imposition magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the calendar-frame direction and each culture's training share. Qualitatively compare the per-culture imposition pattern against the convention map and the SPAN 'Calendar Asymmetry Bias'.
Evaluation metrics: calendar-imposition GAP and Gregorian-default pull rate (DIVERGENT vs CONVERGENT; Gregorian-explicit preserved); imposition-vs-convention correlation and held-out prediction; calendar-frame-direction frame-decodability, cross-lingual alignment, and mid-layer Gregorian-frame projection with mediation of behavioral imposition (held-out R^2); steering flip rate and GAP reduction (bidirectional dose-response), patching-induced restoration; Gregorian-explicit-competence preservation (specificity), fluency, off-target rate; cross-model imposition comparison and correlation with training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for target-culture convention over frequency/fertility/resource baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Inferring which calendar frame the model assumes on unqualified dates is indirect; we triangulate with forced-choice frame questions, frame-consistency of computed answers, and elicited conversion, native-speaker verify, and treat ambiguous items separately. 2) Calendar convention is confounded with language family, script, and resource level; the CONVERGENT controls, Gregorian-explicit competence control, within-item divergent/convergent contrasts, and convention-based prediction isolate the calendar-frame pathway, but residual confounds may remain; we center core claims on well-resourced Arabic/Hijri, Persian/Jalali, and Chinese calendars and treat Hebrew/Indian as extensions. 3) Some imposition may reflect genuinely correct behavior (a modern user in that culture may indeed default to Gregorian for civil dates); the direction of the effect (tracks GREGORIAN vs the culture-conventional calendar), the convention prediction, and the causal steering (which restores the target frame by editing only the calendar-frame direction) distinguish imposition from faithful interpretation, and a faithful-interpretation finding is itself valuable and sharpens the SPAN/measurement behavioral results. 4) Cross-calendar reasoning is intrinsically hard for LLMs (SPAN ~34%), so failures may reflect general date-arithmetic weakness rather than frame imposition; the Gregorian-explicit competence control and the frame-specific steering separate arithmetic incompetence from frame-default imposition — if steering the frame does nothing because arithmetic itself fails, that relocates the problem, an informative result. 5) Contamination/dynamic-date issues are mitigated by template-driven items with a fixed reference Gregorian date (following SPAN). 6) The calendar-frame direction from difference-in-means may entangle numeric-value or topical features; we verify it is a graded frame axis, use a numeric-value control direction, and apply specificity checks. 7) Logit-lens depth estimates are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 8) Steering could corrupt numeric arithmetic or fluency; Gregorian-explicit-competence preservation is a hard constraint and we report the full tradeoff plus bidirectional dose-response, comparing against the CoT baseline to show the mechanistic account adds value. 9) Convention data is noisy (many cultures use dual civil/religious calendars); we treat it as a noisy predictor and rely on internal representation and causal tests for core claims. 10) Effects may be model-family dependent (Aya-23/BLOOM as more calendar-diverse contrasts expected to impose less). 11) If NO imposition is found — unqualified dates are interpreted in each culture's conventional calendar, predictable from convention, with Gregorian arithmetic intact — this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the temporal hub represents culture-specific calendar frames despite Gregorian scaffolding, valuable either way. 12) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: pragmatic_halo_imposition_multilingual
Title: Two Hundred People, Exactly? A Language-Conditioned Pragmatic-Halo Gain That Imposes the Dominant Language's Rounding Convention on Round Numbers
Short Hypothesis: A round number licenses an imprecision 'pragmatic halo' (200 can mean 197-204), and the size of that halo is culturally/linguistically patterned. We hypothesize multilingual LLMs represent this halo on a single, largely dominant-language-scaffolded number-imprecision axis and IMPOSE the dominant (English) rounding/granularity convention onto other languages: the SAME round number is interpreted as more or less precise depending only on the query language, tracking the English halo rather than each language's own convention. This imposition is a low-dimensional gain on a shared imprecision direction, tracks each language's empirical rounding conventions, and is causally correctable without harming exact-number comprehension.
Related Work: A robust cognitive-science literature establishes that round numbers are interpreted imprecisely via magnitude-dependent 'pragmatic halos' (Nonliteral understanding of number words, Kao/Goodman 2014; Rounding and magnitude: halos bigger for larger numbers 2024; Approximate interpretation of number words 2007; Granularity and scalar implicature 2012; Numerical Concepts in Context 2021), that numeral systems and rounding conventions vary cross-linguistically (Numeral Systems Across Languages Support Efficient Communication 2020; Large-scale patterns of number use 2023), and that this reflects efficient-communication pressure. Interpretability shows LLMs encode numeric magnitude on linear/monotonic/sinusoidal, causally-editable subspaces (Language Models Encode Numbers Linearly 2024; Monotonic Representation of Numeric Properties 2024; The Geometry of Numerical Reasoning 2024; Number Representations as Computational Parallel 2025), that exact vs approximate arithmetic use separate components (StreetMath 2025), and that multilingual reasoning routes through a dominant-language-scaffolded shared hub. CRITICALLY, all LLM number-representation work concerns VALUE/magnitude, is monolingual, and never touches the pragmatic-halo/imprecision dimension; all halo/granularity work is human-only and cross-linguistic only descriptively. NO prior work asks whether an LLM represents a number's licensed imprecision (halo), whether the shared, dominant-language-scaffolded representation IMPOSES the dominant language's rounding convention onto other languages (making the same round number more/less precisely interpreted by query language), whether this is a gain on a shared imprecision direction, whether it tracks cross-lingual rounding conventions, or whether it is causally correctable. This differs from my prior number proposals (value transcoding, mental-number-line curvature, implicit numeral composition, verbal-probability words) by targeting the PRAGMATIC IMPRECISION/halo of round numbers, grounded in an authoritative human-science phenomenon.
Abstract: When someone says 'there were 200 people', listeners do not take it literally: 197 or 204 would be fine, because round numbers carry an imprecision 'pragmatic halo' whose size depends on magnitude and on cultural rounding conventions. Interpretability has shown language models encode a number's magnitude, but never whether they encode the imprecision a round number licenses. We ask a simple, previously untested question: do multilingual LLMs represent this halo, and does the dominant-language-scaffolded number representation IMPOSE the dominant (English) rounding convention when interpreting round numbers in other languages? We hypothesize that (1) the model's judged precision / licensed range for a round number in a non-English language tracks the ENGLISH halo rather than the target language's own convention, producing cross-lingual inconsistency on identical quantities; (2) this imposition tracks each language's empirical rounding conventions; (3) it is a low-dimensional gain on a single, shared, decodable number-imprecision direction; and (4) rescaling that direction per language corrects the imposition without harming exact-number comprehension. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using controlled round-vs-unround quantity statements with precision-judgment, range-acceptance, and inference probes across typologically diverse languages, combining behavioral halo measurement, difference-in-means imprecision-direction extraction, logit-lens gain readout, activation patching, and gain-steering. Metrics include the cross-lingual halo-imposition gap, convention-prediction correlation, imprecision-direction alignment, and steering-induced correction with exact-number controls.
Experiments:
1) Round-number halo suite: Build ~500 quantity statements ('there were N <count-noun> at the event', 'the rope is N meters long') spanning ROUND numbers (50, 100, 200, 1000) and matched UNROUND controls (47, 103, 197) across magnitudes and discrete/continuous units (following Numerical Concepts in Context). Instantiate each in typologically diverse languages spanning scripts, resource levels, and rounding conventions (English, French, German, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish), native-speaker verified. Probes measuring the halo: (i) precision judgment ('is this exact or approximate?'); (ii) range-acceptance ('if the true count were 197, would saying 200 be acceptable?' — vary the offset to trace the accepted halo width); (iii) inference (does the statement entail 'exactly N'?). Include a language-agnostic DIGIT-form anchor and an EXACT-number comprehension control (fully-precise contexts). Attach each language its empirical rounding-convention profile from cross-linguistic number-use data. Report inter-annotator agreement; release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral halo and imposition (H1, core): For each round number in each language, measure the accepted halo width (range of offsets judged acceptable) and precision-judgment rate. Verify the model reproduces the human magnitude-dependent halo in English (bigger halos for larger round numbers). Test whether, on non-English queries, the halo width / precision tracks the ENGLISH halo rather than the target language's convention. Define the cross-lingual halo-imposition GAP = inconsistency(round numbers) minus inconsistency(unround controls), and an English-halo pull rate = fraction of round-number items whose model halo is closer to the English value than the target-convention value. Verify near-perfect EXACT-number comprehension (isolating imposition from numeric incompetence). Control for tokenizer fertility and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test target-language convention adds predictive power).
3) Convention scaling (H2, external validation): Test whether per-language imposition is predicted by that language's empirical rounding convention divergence from English (Spearman; held-out prediction from convention data alone), tying the internal phenomenon to independent cross-linguistic ground truth.
4) Shared imprecision direction and gain readout (H3): Extract a per-language 'number-imprecision/halo' direction via difference-in-means between approximate-interpreted (round) and exact-interpreted (unround/precise) number representations at each layer, verifying it is a graded imprecision axis (probe recovers judged precision) and that it is separate from the magnitude/value direction. Measure cross-lingual cosine alignment (test: a largely shared imprecision axis re-scaled per language; portability via steering). Project the residual stream at the judgment point onto the shared direction and estimate a per-LANGUAGE halo gain via regression; test that the cross-lingual imposition is captured by the difference in per-language gains applied to the SHARED projection (held-out R^2), beating a uniform-bias baseline and a full per-language relearned readout (low-dimensional). Mediation: regress behavioral imposition on the imprecision-direction projection (partial correlation controlling for fertility/resource; held-out R^2).
5) Causal steering/patching test (H4, core): (a) Rescale the shared imprecision direction with a per-language scalar to shift the halo toward the target-language convention (and, dose-response, toward English), and measure whether precision judgments / accepted ranges shift accordingly (halo-transfer rate) and the imposition GAP shrinks toward the unround baseline, without switching output language; bidirectional dose-response; mis-signed steering worsens. (b) Activation-patch the English halo signal into a target-language pass and confirm it imposes the English halo. Critically verify VALUE/EXACT-number preservation: steering changes only the licensed imprecision, not the number's magnitude — the model must still correctly compare/report exact values and handle unround numbers precisely (symmetric check), plus fluency and off-target/language-mixing checks. Baselines: whole-hub English-steering, random-direction control, digit-anchor ceiling.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify steering is imprecision-specific (changes the halo but not the number's value or unrelated content), graded (imposition scales with convention divergence), and not a tokenizer artifact. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show stronger imposition than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether imposition magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the imprecision direction and each language's training share. Qualitatively compare the per-language halo pattern against the cross-linguistic number-use conventions.
Evaluation metrics: reproduced magnitude-dependent halo in English (human-benchmark); cross-lingual halo-imposition GAP and English-halo pull rate (round vs unround; exact-number preserved); imposition-vs-convention correlation and held-out prediction; imprecision-direction precision-decodability, separation from magnitude direction, cross-lingual alignment, portability, and gain predictive R^2 (vs uniform-bias baseline) with mediation of behavioral imposition (held-out R^2); steering halo-transfer rate and GAP reduction (bidirectional dose-response), patching-induced imposition; value/exact-number preservation (specificity), fluency, off-target rate; cross-model imposition comparison and correlation with training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for target-language convention over fertility/resource baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The model may not represent a pragmatic halo at all in English; Experiment 2's reproduction of the human magnitude-dependent halo is a necessary gate — if the model does not show round-number imprecision, the cross-lingual imposition question is moot, itself an informative finding about the limits of LLM pragmatic-numeric competence. 2) Measuring 'accepted halo width' via range-acceptance probes is indirect and noisy; we use multiple probe formats (precision judgment, range acceptance, entailment), native-speaker verify, report inter-annotator agreement, and trace the halo by varying offsets rather than a single threshold. 3) Rounding convention is confounded with language family, script, and resource level; the unround controls, digit-anchor, exact-number competence control, within-item round/unround contrasts, and convention-based prediction isolate the halo pathway, but residual confounds may remain; the digit-anchor is the key language-agnostic control. 4) Some cross-lingual halo variation may reflect genuinely correct behavior (the target language really does share the English convention); the direction of the effect (tracks ENGLISH vs the TARGET convention), the convention prediction, and the causal steering (which restores the target halo by editing only the imprecision direction) distinguish imposition from faithful interpretation, and a faithful finding is itself valuable and extends the cross-linguistic halo literature to LLMs. 5) The single-scalar gain account may only partially hold; if a data-driven low-dimensional basis fits better we report it, keeping the 'shared imprecision axis + language gain' claim testable. 6) The imprecision direction from difference-in-means may entangle magnitude, roundness-as-lexical-form, or frequency features; we verify it is a graded precision axis separate from the value direction, use frequency-matched round/unround pairs and the digit-anchor, and apply specificity checks. 7) Roundness and token-frequency are correlated (round numbers are more frequent); we control frequency and treat a frequency-driven halo as an informative sub-finding. 8) Logit-lens gain estimates are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 9) Steering could corrupt the number's value or fluency; value/exact-number preservation is a hard constraint and we report the full tradeoff plus bidirectional dose-response. 10) Convention data is noisy; we treat it as a noisy predictor and rely on internal representation and causal tests for core claims. 11) Instruction-tuned models may over-literalize numbers; we test base models where available. 12) The human-LLM comparison (magnitude-dependent halos, cross-linguistic conventions) is qualitative/structural, not a claim of identical mechanism. 13) Effects may be model-family dependent (Aya-23/BLOOM as more multilingual contrasts expected to impose less). 14) If NO imposition is found — round-number halos track each language's own convention, predictable from cross-linguistic data, with exact-number comprehension intact — this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the shared number representation carries language-specific imprecision conventions despite dominant-language scaffolding, valuable either way. 15) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: occupation_gender_skew_imposition
Title: The Doctor Is Male in Every Tongue: Does the Dominant Language's Labor-Market Gender Skew Get Imposed onto Occupations Cross-Lingually?
Short Hypothesis: The real-world occupational gender skew differs by country (nursing is female-dominated everywhere but teaching, medicine, cooking, and many trades have sharply different gender ratios across cultures), and a word's culturally-correct gender association is therefore language-specific. We hypothesize multilingual LLMs represent occupation-gender association on a single, largely dominant-language(English/US)-scaffolded direction and IMPOSE the dominant culture's labor-market gender skew onto occupations queried in other languages: for occupations whose real-world gender ratio DIVERGES across cultures, the model's gender inference tracks the US skew rather than the target culture's, producing cross-lingual inconsistency on the SAME occupation. This imposition is a low-dimensional gain on a shared occupation-gender direction, is predicted by each culture's empirical labor statistics (not resource level), and is causally correctable without harming genuinely universal occupation associations.
Related Work: Extensive work documents multilingual occupational gender bias behaviorally (Gender Bias in LLMs across Multiple Languages 2024; EuroGEST 2025; GEST 2023; Persian stereotypes 2025; Anchoring LLM Gender Bias to Human Baselines 2026, which shows stereotyping drift 2.5x wider than humans and compounding across languages) and mechanistically shows gender lives in shared+language-specific subspaces where classification transfers cross-lingually but INLP removal does not (Analyzing Gender Representation in Multilingual Models 2022; On the Mutual Influence of Gender and Occupation 2025, which correlates internal gender representations with real-world statistics MONOLINGUALLY). Cross-lingual bias-leakage via shared encoders is shown in VLMs (Breaking Language Barriers 2025) and MT (Towards Cross-Lingual Generalization of Translation Gender Bias 2021). CRITICALLY, all this work either (a) measures aggregate bias magnitude per language, (b) studies gender representation transfer monolingually or as classification/removal, or (c) documents that bias exists cross-lingually; NONE tests the specific DIRECTIONAL mechanistic claim that the DOMINANT culture's empirical labor-market skew is IMPOSED onto occupations whose real-world gender ratio DIVERGES across cultures (producing cross-lingual inconsistency predicted by target-culture labor statistics rather than resource level), that this is a low-dimensional GAIN on a shared occupation-gender direction rather than distinct per-language associations, or that rescaling that direction causally corrects the imposition while preserving universally-skewed occupations. Prior work anchors to human baselines behaviorally (Anchoring 2026) but offers no shared-direction mechanism, no labor-statistics-divergence predictor, and no causal fix. We reframe cross-lingual occupational bias from an aggregate-magnitude problem into a directional, labor-statistics-grounded, mechanistically-localizable imposition with a causal correction. This is distinct from my prior gender proposals (grammatical-gender leaking into attribute reasoning; the gender-congruency effect) by targeting OCCUPATIONAL gender association tied to divergent real-world labor distributions.
Abstract: Whether a doctor, teacher, cook, or engineer is imagined as a man or a woman is not universal: real-world occupational gender ratios differ sharply across countries, so an occupation's culturally-correct gender association is language-specific. Multilingual language models are known to be gender-biased in many languages, but always measured as aggregate skew per language. We ask a sharper, previously untested mechanistic question: does a multilingual LLM IMPOSE the dominant (US/English) labor market's occupational gender skew onto occupations queried in other languages, even when the target culture's real-world gender ratio diverges? We hypothesize that (1) for divergent occupations, the model's gender inference tracks the US skew rather than the target culture's, producing cross-lingual inconsistency on the same occupation concentrated where labor statistics diverge; (2) the imposition is predicted by each culture's empirical labor-market gender ratio, not by resource level; (3) it is a low-dimensional GAIN on a single, largely shared occupation-gender direction rather than distinct per-language associations; and (4) rescaling that direction per language causally corrects the imposition while preserving genuinely universal occupation associations. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using controlled occupation-gender inference tasks across typologically and culturally diverse languages, grounded in national labor-force statistics. Combining behavioral imposition measurement, difference-in-means occupation-gender-direction extraction, gain readout, activation patching, and gain-steering, we measure the imposition, its labor-statistics scaling, its shared-direction locus, and a causal fix. Metrics include the cross-lingual occupation-gender imposition gap, labor-statistics prediction correlation, gain predictive R-squared over resource baselines, and steering-induced correction with universal-occupation controls.
Experiments:
1) Labor-statistics-grounded occupation suite: Assemble ~150 occupations, each annotated with per-country real-world gender ratios from national labor-force statistics (ILO/national bureaus) for the countries associated with the target languages. Partition into DIVERGENT occupations (real-world gender ratio differs substantially across the US and a target country, e.g. occupations that are female-dominated in one country and male-dominated or balanced in another) and matched CONVERGENT/UNIVERSAL occupations (similar ratio everywhere). Instantiate gender-inference probes in typologically and culturally diverse languages spanning divergent labor markets and resource levels (English/US, German, Spanish, Russian, Mandarin, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili). Probes: (i) pronoun/gender-inference forced choice ('A <occupation> walked in; was it he or she?' in the target language, and gender-agreement completion where the language marks it); (ii) descriptor association; (iii) an occupation-prediction-given-name probe (following On the Mutual Influence 2025). Native-speaker verify occupation translations and gender-marking; report inter-annotator agreement. Release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral imposition (H1, core): For DIVERGENT occupations, measure whether the model's inferred gender tracks the US skew vs the target-culture labor ratio. Define the cross-lingual occupation-gender imposition GAP = inconsistency(DIVERGENT) minus inconsistency(CONVERGENT), and a US-skew pull rate = fraction of divergent occupations whose model gender inference is closer to the US ratio than the target-country ratio. Verify near-faithful associations on CONVERGENT/universal occupations and correct US inferences (ceiling). Control for tokenizer fertility, occupation frequency, and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test target-culture status adds predictive power).
3) Labor-statistics scaling (H2, external validation): Test whether per-occupation imposition is predicted by the divergence between the target-country and US real-world gender ratios (Spearman; held-out prediction from labor statistics alone), tying the internal phenomenon to independent, authoritative ground truth and distinguishing it from resource level (nested regression: labor-divergence vs resource level).
4) Shared occupation-gender direction and gain readout (H3, core): Extract a per-language difference-in-means 'occupation-gender' direction (male-associated vs female-associated occupation representations) at each layer, verifying it is a graded association axis (probe recovers real-world ratio) and separate from a grammatical-gender direction. Measure cross-lingual cosine alignment (test: a largely shared, US-scaffolded axis re-scaled per language; portability via steering). Project the residual stream at the inference point onto the shared direction and estimate a per-LANGUAGE gain via regression of the gender inference on the projection. Test that the cross-lingual imposition is captured by the difference in per-language gains applied to the SHARED projection (held-out R^2), beating a uniform-bias baseline and a full per-language relearned readout (low-dimensional). Mediation: regress behavioral imposition on the occupation-gender-direction projection (partial correlation controlling for fertility/frequency; held-out R^2).
5) Causal steering/patching test (H4, core): (a) Rescale the shared occupation-gender direction with a per-occupation, per-language scalar to shift the association toward the target-culture labor ratio (and, dose-response, toward the US ratio), and measure whether gender inference shifts accordingly (association-transfer rate) and the imposition GAP shrinks toward the CONVERGENT baseline, without switching output language; bidirectional dose-response; mis-signed steering worsens. (b) Activation-patch the US occupation-gender signal into a target-language pass and confirm it imposes the US skew. Critically verify UNIVERSAL-OCCUPATION preservation: steering must correct DIVERGENT occupations WITHOUT flattening genuinely universal associations (e.g. it must not make a universally female-dominated occupation male — a symmetric check), must not switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), and preserve fluency. Baselines: whole-hub English-steering, INLP gender-removal (which prior work shows doesn't transfer), random-direction control.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify steering is occupation-gender-specific (changes occupational association but not grammatical gender or unrelated content), graded (imposition scales with labor-statistics divergence), and not a frequency artifact (frequency-matched divergent/convergent occupations). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English/US-centric Llama-3/Qwen show stronger imposition than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether imposition magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the occupation-gender direction and each culture's training share. Qualitatively compare the per-culture imposition pattern against national labor statistics and the human-baseline drift (Anchoring 2026).
Evaluation metrics: cross-lingual occupation-gender imposition GAP and US-skew pull rate (DIVERGENT vs CONVERGENT; vs US ceiling; universal-occupation preserved); imposition-vs-labor-statistics-divergence correlation and held-out prediction (vs resource-level baseline, model comparison); occupation-gender-direction ratio-decodability, separation from grammatical-gender direction, cross-lingual alignment, portability, and gain predictive R^2 (vs uniform-bias and full-relearn baselines) with mediation of behavioral imposition (held-out R^2); steering association-transfer rate and GAP reduction (bidirectional dose-response), patching-induced imposition; universal-occupation preservation (symmetric specificity), fluency, off-target rate; cross-model imposition comparison and correlation with training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for target-culture labor divergence over frequency/fertility/resource baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Some imposition may reflect genuinely correct behavior (the target culture really does share the US skew, or the model may be MORE egalitarian than real statistics warrant — a desirable outcome); the direction of the effect (tracks the US ratio vs the TARGET-country ratio), the labor-statistics-divergence prediction, and the causal steering (which restores the target ratio by editing only the occupation-gender direction) distinguish imposition from faithful/egalitarian inference, and a faithful or egalitarian finding is itself valuable and sharpens the aggregate-bias literature. 2) National labor statistics are noisy, may not reflect training-data occupational distributions, and country-language mapping is imperfect (many languages span multiple countries); we treat statistics as noisy predictors, use the clearest divergent cases, native-speaker verify, and rely on the internal representation and causal tests for core claims. 3) Occupation-gender divergence is confounded with language family, script, culture, and resource level; the CONVERGENT/universal controls, US ceiling, within-occupation contrasts, and labor-statistics prediction (a mechanistic predictor beyond resource level) isolate the imposition pathway, but residual confounds may remain. 4) Grammatical gender (the occupation word's grammatical gender in some languages) confounds the gender-inference probe; we separate the occupation-gender direction from a grammatical-gender direction, use gender-neutral occupation forms where possible, and include a grammatical-gender control. 5) The single-scalar gain account may only partially hold; if a data-driven low-dimensional basis fits better we report it, keeping the 'shared occupation-gender axis + language gain' claim testable. 6) The occupation-gender direction from difference-in-means may entangle topical/frequency features; we verify it is a graded ratio axis, use frequency-matched controls, and multiple extraction methods. 7) The steering fix could flatten genuinely universal associations or over-correct toward parity; the universal-occupation-preservation symmetric constraint is a hard requirement and we report the full tradeoff plus bidirectional dose-response, comparing against INLP (which prior work shows doesn't transfer) to show the per-language gain account adds value. 8) This is fairness research; our interventions aim to make occupational associations culturally-appropriate/consistent rather than to entrench any real-world skew, and we frame the phenomenon descriptively, releasing the suite responsibly. 9) Instruction-tuned/RLHF models may suppress overt gender guessing (defaulting to hedging or parity), which the US-skew-vs-target-ratio contrast still detects internally; we test base models where available and treat suppression as an informative training-stage finding. 10) Effects may be model-family dependent (Aya-23/BLOOM as less US-centric contrasts expected to impose less). 11) If NO imposition is found — occupation-gender associations track each culture's own labor ratio (or are uniformly egalitarian), predictable from statistics, with universal occupations preserved — this is an informative result showing the occupation-gender representation is culturally-faithful or debiased despite US scaffolding, valuable either way. 12) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: language_conditioned_ambiguity_tolerance
Title: Committing Too Soon in a Foreign Tongue: A Language-Conditioned Threshold on a Shared Ambiguity-Tolerance Circuit in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs represent whether an input is genuinely ambiguous/underspecified on a largely shared, English-scaffolded 'ambiguity' signal, but the DECISION THRESHOLD that converts that signal into tolerate-and-seek-clarification versus prematurely-commit-to-one-reading is language-conditioned: for the SAME internal ambiguity magnitude, the model over-commits (silently picks one reading, forgoing clarification) more when queried in a lower-resource / English-distant language than in the dominant language. This is not a separate per-language ambiguity computation but a language-conditioned gain on a shared ambiguity-tolerance direction (engaging the known sparse Ambiguity-Encoding Neurons less), tracks each language's resource level, and is causally correctable by rescaling that direction without harming disambiguation when context genuinely resolves the input.
Related Work: Ambiguity is linearly encoded and steerable via sparse Ambiguity-Encoding Neurons (AENs) whose manipulation shifts the model from answering to abstention (Sparse Neurons Carry Strong Signals of Question Ambiguity 2025; Trick or Neat 2025 shows linear probes decode ambiguity ~90% while prompting fails), LMs track multiple analyses in parallel yet over-commit to deterministic interpretations (Probing Syntactic Uncertainty 2021; Bridging Philosophical Foundations 2025), and humans strategically POSTPONE ambiguity resolution flexibly by goals (On the timing of decisions about meaning 2023; Comprehending underspecified meaning 2017). Multilingual work establishes an English-scaffolded shared hub with resolution routed through English (Do Llamas Work in English 2024; Do Multilingual LLMs Think In English 2025; Semantic Hub 2024), and a multilingual disambiguation penalty from capacity constraints (Capacity Constraints for Lexical Disambiguation 2026; Multilingual LLMs Struggle to Link Orthography and Semantics 2025). CRITICALLY, all AEN/ambiguity-encoding work is monolingual (English) and treats the answer-vs-abstain threshold as fixed; all multilingual work concerns disambiguation ACCURACY or routing, never whether the meta-decision to TOLERATE genuine ambiguity versus prematurely commit is language-dependent, nor whether the AENs are engaged less in non-dominant languages, nor whether a shared ambiguity-tolerance threshold is a miscalibrated per-language gain. We reframe cross-lingual over-commitment as an ambiguity-tolerance threshold miscalibration on a shared circuit, with a matched-ambiguity-magnitude test, a resource-level predictor, and a targeted causal fix that preserves genuine disambiguation. This is distinct from all my prior imposition proposals (which impose a specific default reading) by targeting the upstream meta-decision of whether to resolve at all.
Abstract: Real questions are often genuinely ambiguous ('Is the bank open?'), and a good assistant should notice this and ask for clarification rather than silently picking one reading. Interpretability work shows language models encode ambiguity in a small set of sparse neurons and can be steered from answering to abstaining, but only in English. We ask a simple, previously untested question: is a model's willingness to TOLERATE genuine ambiguity versus prematurely commit to one interpretation language-dependent? We hypothesize that the model detects ambiguity on a largely shared, English-scaffolded signal, but the DECISION THRESHOLD converting that signal into tolerate-and-clarify versus commit-to-one-reading is anchored to the dominant language and imported into others, so at equal internal ambiguity magnitude the model over-commits (forgoes clarification, guesses a reading) more in lower-resource or English-distant languages. We predict this is a low-dimensional gain on a shared ambiguity-tolerance direction (engaging the sparse Ambiguity-Encoding Neurons less in non-dominant languages), predictable from resource level, and causally correctable by rescaling that direction without harming disambiguation when context truly resolves the input. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using parallel genuinely-ambiguous, disambiguated-by-context, and unambiguous items across typologically diverse languages. Combining ambiguity-magnitude probing, difference-in-means tolerance-direction extraction, logit-lens gain readout, activation patching, and gain-steering, we measure the ambiguity-magnitude-matched over-commitment gap, its resource prediction, its shared-circuit locus, and a causal fix with genuine-disambiguation controls.
Experiments:
1) Parallel ambiguity suite: Build ~600 items in three matched conditions holding content fixed: (a) GENUINELY-AMBIGUOUS questions (lexical, syntactic, and referential ambiguity with two viable readings and no resolving context, where clarification is the correct response); (b) DISAMBIGUATED (the same item plus context that clearly licenses one reading, where committing to that reading is correct); (c) UNAMBIGUOUS controls. Instantiate every item in typologically diverse languages spanning resource levels and scripts (English, French, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish), native-speaker verified with gold labels (ambiguous->clarify/hedge; disambiguated->the licensed reading). Report inter-annotator agreement; release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, BLOOM(Z)-7B.
2) Behavioral over-commitment (H1, core): On GENUINELY-AMBIGUOUS items, measure the over-commitment rate = fraction where the model silently answers with one reading rather than flagging ambiguity / asking for clarification. Test that over-commitment rises for lower-resource / English-distant languages, holding content fixed. Control for tokenizer fertility and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2). Verify near-perfect DISAMBIGUATED handling (isolating over-commitment from an inability to use context) and low false-clarification on UNAMBIGUOUS controls.
3) Ambiguity-magnitude-matched gap (H1b, core novelty): Extract a shared ambiguity direction via difference-in-means between ambiguous and unambiguous representations (validated to recover ambiguity above chance, following Trick or Neat / AEN), verify cross-lingual alignment (a single shared axis), and compute per-item ambiguity magnitude = its projection. Bin items by ambiguity magnitude and, WITHIN a matched-magnitude bin, compare per-language over-commitment. Test the central prediction: at equal internal ambiguity magnitude, over-commitment still rises with lower resource level — the same detected ambiguity yields clarify in one language and premature commit in another. This isolates a threshold effect from an ambiguity-detection effect.
4) Shared tolerance direction, AEN engagement, and gain readout (H2): Locate the sparse Ambiguity-Encoding Neurons per model and test whether they are engaged LESS on ambiguous inputs in non-dominant languages (per-language AEN activation). Extract a difference-in-means 'ambiguity-tolerance' direction (abstain/clarify vs commit representations), verify it emerges in shallow layers (per AEN findings) and is largely shared (cross-lingual alignment) and portable (steering it shifts clarify-vs-commit across languages). Project the residual stream at the decision point onto the shared direction and estimate a per-LANGUAGE tolerance gain via regression; test that the cross-lingual over-commitment gap is captured by the difference in per-language gains applied to the SHARED projection (held-out R^2), beating a uniform-bias baseline, and that the gain is predicted by resource level better than by disambiguation accuracy (nested regression, AIC). Mediation: regress behavioral over-commitment on AEN-engagement / tolerance-direction projection (partial correlation controlling for fertility/resource; held-out R^2).
5) Causal test via patching and gain-steering (H3, core): (a) For ambiguous items over-committed in language B but clarified in English at matched ambiguity magnitude, patch the tolerance signal / AEN activation from the English pass into B and test whether clarification is restored, isolating a threshold gain from ambiguity content. (b) Rescale the shared tolerance direction with a per-language scalar to equalize the gain across languages, and measure whether appropriate clarification is restored on ambiguous items, with bidirectional dose-response. Compare against baselines: whole-hub English steering, direct AEN steering (Sparse Neurons 2025), and a random-direction control.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls (hard constraint): The fix must increase clarification on GENUINELY-AMBIGUOUS items WITHOUT increasing false clarification / over-abstention on DISAMBIGUATED or UNAMBIGUOUS items (symmetric check — the goal is a correctly-placed threshold, not blanket hedging), must not switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), and preserves task accuracy and fluency. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show a larger ambiguity-magnitude-matched over-commitment gap than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether the gap correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the tolerance direction and each language's training share. Qualitatively compare the language-dependent tolerate-vs-commit pattern against the human finding that resolution-postponement is flexible and goal-sensitive.
Evaluation metrics: per-language over-commitment rate (ambiguous vs disambiguated vs unambiguous); ambiguity-magnitude-matched over-commitment gap (H1b); ambiguity-direction cross-lingual alignment and decodability; per-language AEN engagement on ambiguous inputs; tolerance-gain predictive R^2 (vs uniform-bias baseline) and gain-vs-resource prediction over disambiguation-accuracy baseline (AIC, held-out); threshold- vs detection-failure shares from patching; gain-steering clarification recovery and cross-lingual over-commitment-variance reduction vs baselines, with bidirectional dose-response and symmetric specificity (no over-abstention on disambiguated/unambiguous), off-target rate, accuracy/fluency preservation; cross-model gap comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The over-commitment gap could conflate with an ambiguity-DETECTION gap (the model may not notice the ambiguity in a low-resource language, not merely deprioritize clarification); the ambiguity-magnitude-MATCHED comparison (H1b) and the causal patching test (which restores clarification by editing only the tolerance direction while ambiguity magnitude is held) isolate threshold from detection — if the matched gap vanishes, the hypothesis reduces to a detection deficit, an informative negative result. 2) Establishing that an item is genuinely ambiguous (both readings viable, clarification is correct) and that the disambiguated version truly resolves it is delicate; we native-speaker verify, report inter-annotator agreement, and exclude low-agreement items. 3) Over-commitment behavior is heavily shaped by instruction-tuning/RLHF (which may train uniform hedging or uniform answering); we test base and instruction-tuned models and treat differences as an informative training-stage finding, verifying a measurable English ambiguity-tolerance behavior first as a gate. 4) Language is confounded with tokenizer fertility, script, and resource level; partial correlations and the causal patching/steering tests mitigate but may not fully remove confounds. 5) The ambiguity/tolerance directions from difference-in-means may entangle content or a generic 'uncertainty/hedge' feature; we validate the ambiguity direction against held-out ambiguity, use the located AENs as an anchor, and apply specificity controls. 6) The single-scalar gain account may only partially hold; if a data-driven low-dimensional basis fits better we report it, keeping the 'shared tolerance axis + language gain' claim testable. 7) The gain-steering fix could over-abstain (blanket hedging), which is a failure not a fix; the symmetric no-over-abstention constraint on disambiguated/unambiguous items is a hard requirement and we report the full tradeoff, comparing against direct AEN steering to show the per-language account adds value. 8) Effects may be model-family dependent (BLOOM/Aya as less English-centric contrasts expected to show a smaller gap). 9) The human-LLM comparison (flexible resolution-postponement) is qualitative, not a claim of identical mechanism. 10) If no ambiguity-magnitude-matched gap is found — tolerate-vs-commit is language-invariant once ambiguity magnitude is controlled — this is an informative POSITIVE result showing ambiguity tolerance is language-agnostic despite an English-scaffolded hub, valuable either way. 11) Limited to open ~7-8B instruction-tuned models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: crosslingual_deception_circuit_transfer_asymmetry
Title: Lying in One Tongue, Honest in Another: A Language-Bound Deception-Enactment Threshold Atop a Portable Deception Circuit
Short Hypothesis: The mechanism that makes a multilingual LLM lie decomposes into two separable parts with opposite cross-lingual profiles: a largely LANGUAGE-AGNOSTIC deception-intent/knowledge circuit (the model internally represents both the true answer and the intent to misreport it, portable across languages), and a LANGUAGE-BOUND enactment threshold that converts that intent into an actual falsehood. Because the enactment threshold is anchored to the dominant (English) language, a model instructed to lie complies (enacts deception) more reliably in high-resource languages while, in lower-resource / English-distant languages, it more often 'leaks the truth' (fails to enact the lie despite carrying the deception intent internally). Consequently cross-lingual variation in deceptive compliance is dominated by an enactment-threshold miscalibration, not by an absent or language-specific deception circuit, and a deception direction extracted in one language transplants into another to induce lying, whereas enactment failures are only fixed by adjusting the language-bound threshold.
Related Work: Monolingual mechanistic work localizes instructed lying to sparse layers/heads and shows lying is causally ablatable/steerable and linearly separable from honesty (Localizing Lying in Llama 2023; Can LLMs Lie 2025; When Thinking LLMs Lie 2025; Truth is Universal 2024 — a universal 2D truth subspace across model families; Detecting Strategic Deception Using Linear Probes 2025), but ALL of this is English/monolingual and treats the deception circuit and the honest/lie decision as a single language-agnostic object. Multilingual work shows an English-scaffolded shared hub (Do Llamas Work in English 2024; Semantic Hub 2024), that safety/refusal directions and safety neurons transfer cross-lingually (Refusal Direction is Universal 2025; SS-Neurons 2026), and that misinformation/truthfulness/privacy behaviors leak or are unevenly aligned across languages (Learn and Unlearn 2024; Cross-lingual Truthfulness Transfer 2024; Cross-lingual Privacy Neurons 2025). CRITICALLY, no prior work asks whether the deception mechanism itself decomposes into a portable deception-INTENT/knowledge circuit versus a language-bound ENACTMENT threshold, whether cross-lingual variation in deceptive compliance is an enactment-threshold miscalibration (the model carries the intent but fails to enact the lie, leaking the truth) rather than an absent circuit, whether a deception direction transplants across languages to induce lying, or whether enactment failures are fixed only by the language-bound threshold. All prior multilingual work concerns refusal/truthfulness/privacy, never the intent-vs-enactment dissociation of instructed lying. We reframe cross-lingual deception variation as an intent-portable / enactment-local dissociation with a decodable threshold, a transplant test, and a defensive monitoring implication. This is defensive interpretability research.
Abstract: A model told to lie should either comply or refuse — but whether it actually enacts the falsehood may depend on the language it is speaking, and this has never been studied. Interpretability work shows instructed lying in language models is carried by a sparse, steerable circuit and is linearly separable from honesty, but entirely in English, treating the deception mechanism as one language-agnostic object. We ask a simple, previously untested question: does the mechanism of lying decompose into a portable deception-intent circuit and a language-bound enactment step, and does their dissociation explain why a model lies more reliably in some languages than others? We hypothesize that (1) the model represents the true answer and the intent to misreport it in a largely language-agnostic circuit that transfers across languages, but (2) the enactment threshold converting intent into an actual falsehood is anchored to the dominant language, so in lower-resource / English-distant languages the model more often 'leaks the truth' — failing to enact the instructed lie despite internally carrying the deception intent; (3) cross-lingual variation in deceptive compliance is dominated by this enactment-threshold miscalibration, not an absent circuit; and (4) a deception direction extracted in one language transplants into another to induce lying, whereas enactment failures are fixed only by adjusting the language-bound threshold. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using instructed-lying true/false and factual-QA tasks across typologically diverse languages, combining deception/truth probes, difference-in-means deception-direction extraction, cross-lingual transplant, activation patching to separate intent from enactment failures, and a threshold-calibration intervention. Metrics include per-language deceptive-compliance rate, truth-leak-with-intent share, deception-direction cross-lingual alignment and transplant success, intent-vs-enactment error shares, and threshold-calibration recovery with honesty-preservation controls.
Experiments:
1) Instructed-lying multilingual suite: Build ~800 items (true/false factual statements and short factual QA with verified answers) where the model is explicitly instructed to LIE (answer falsely) versus an HONEST control instruction, using the prompt-engineering that reliably induces instructed lying (assistant-response prefixes / liar personas per Localizing Lying in Llama). Instantiate every item and instruction in typologically diverse languages spanning resource levels and scripts (English, French, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish), native-speaker verified. Condition on items the model answers CORRECTLY under the honest instruction in each language (so it knows the truth). Report inter-annotator agreement; release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, BLOOM(Z)-7B.
2) Behavioral deceptive-compliance map (H1, core): Under the LIE instruction, measure per-language deceptive-compliance rate = fraction where the model actually outputs the false answer (enacts the lie). Decompose non-compliance into (a) TRUTH-LEAK (the model outputs the true answer despite being told to lie) and (b) refusal/other. Test that deceptive-compliance is higher in high-resource / English languages and truth-leak is higher in lower-resource / English-distant languages, holding the known-truth condition fixed. Control for tokenizer fertility and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2).
3) Portable deception-intent circuit (H2, core): Extract a per-language difference-in-means 'deception' direction (lie-instructed vs honest-instructed representations) and a truth direction (true vs false statement representations, per Truth is Universal). Test cross-lingual cosine alignment of the deception direction (is it largely shared?) and whether, on TRUTH-LEAK items (the model failed to enact the lie), a deception-INTENT signal is nonetheless present internally — i.e. the model carries the intent to lie and represents the true answer, but does not enact the falsehood. Report the truth-leak-WITH-intent share (leak items on which the deception-intent direction is engaged).
4) Intent-vs-enactment error decomposition via patching (H3, core): For LIE-instructed items enacted in English but truth-leaked in language B (with intent present in B), patch (a) the shared deception-intent representation from the English pass into B, and (b) the late-layer language-bound enactment/decoding components. If (a) rarely changes the outcome (intent already present in B) but (b) makes B enact the lie, classify as an enactment-threshold failure, not an intent failure. Report intent-vs-enactment error shares per language, predicting enactment failures dominate and grow with resource-distance.
5) Cross-lingual transplant test (H4, core): Extract the deception direction in a high-resource language and TRANSPLANT it (steering) into a low-resource-language HONEST forward pass; measure whether it induces the model to lie in the target language (transplant induce-lie rate), confirming the deception intent is portable. Conversely, show transplanting intent alone does NOT fix a genuine enactment failure unless the language-bound enactment threshold is also adjusted — the intent-portable / enactment-local dissociation. Compare against a shared-hub English-steering baseline and a random-direction control.
6) Threshold-calibration intervention: Adjust the language-bound enactment threshold (steer the late-layer enactment direction) to equalize deceptive-compliance across languages, and measure whether truth-leak-with-intent is converted to enacted lies selectively in high-leak languages. This is used diagnostically to establish the threshold is the operative variable; the DEFENSIVE payoff is the inverse — a monitor that reads the shared deception-intent signal detects instructed lying across languages even when the model leaks the truth (i.e. intent-based deception detection generalizes cross-lingually better than output-based detection).
7) Specificity, defensive, and cross-model controls: Verify interventions are deception-specific (change lie-vs-truth enactment without switching output language — off-target/language-mixing rate — or corrupting the underlying known truth), and that the shared deception-intent probe detects instructed lying across all languages (cross-lingual AUROC) even on truth-leak items, establishing a language-robust deception monitor. Symmetric honesty check: the threshold intervention must not make the model lie under HONEST instructions. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show a sharper enactment-threshold gap (more truth-leak in low-resource languages) than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether the gap correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the deception direction and each language's training share.
Evaluation metrics: per-language deceptive-compliance and truth-leak rates (known-truth-conditioned; partial correlation with resource-distance over fertility, held-out R^2); deception-direction cross-lingual alignment; truth-leak-with-intent share; intent-vs-enactment error shares (patching); transplant induce-lie rate and its failure to fix enactment failures; threshold-calibration deceptive-compliance equalization with honesty preservation (symmetric specificity) and off-target rate; cross-lingual deception-monitor AUROC on shared-intent probe (including on truth-leak items); cross-model enactment-gap comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Truth-leak in low-resource languages could conflate with a general competence gap (the model may fail to lie because it does not understand the instruction, or does not know the truth); the key controls are conditioning on items answered correctly under the honest instruction per language (the truth IS known), verifying the LIE instruction is comprehended in isolation per language, and the intent-vs-enactment patching — if the deception-intent signal is absent in truth-leak items, the failure is an intent/comprehension failure rather than an enactment-threshold failure, which is itself an informative alternative outcome relocating the deficit. 2) Instructed lying is prompt-sensitive and requires careful prompt engineering (per Localizing Lying in Llama); we replicate the induce-lying prompting per model and language, verify a robust English lying effect first as a gate, and report robustness across prompt variants. 3) Language is confounded with tokenizer fertility, script, and resource level; partial correlations and the causal patching/transplant tests mitigate but may not fully remove confounds. 4) The deception direction from difference-in-means may entangle instruction-following or content features; we use the truth direction and honest/lie contrasts as anchors, multiple extraction methods, and specificity controls, and distinguish deception-intent from generic instruction-compliance. 5) Intent-vs-enactment may not separate cleanly; patching can have entangled effects — we use multiple granularities and report ambiguous cases. 6) This is safety-sensitive research: it studies inducing lying, but the applied contribution is DEFENSIVE (a cross-lingual deception monitor that reads the shared intent signal even when output is truthful); we use benign factual-lying tasks, release the suite under controlled terms, and do not publish jailbreak/deception-enhancing artifacts — the threshold-calibration inducing-lie experiment is only to establish causal necessity and is reported in aggregate. 7) The cross-lingual deception monitor may be brittle (per Detecting Strategic Deception 2025 and The Secret Agenda 2025, autolabeled/feature-based deception detection often fails); we test the difference-in-means intent probe's cross-lingual generalization directly and report where it breaks. 8) Effects may be model-family dependent (Aya-23/BLOOM as more multilingual contrasts expected to show a smaller enactment gap). 9) If the deception circuit does NOT transfer cross-lingually, or truth-leak is an intent rather than enactment failure, the dissociation hypothesis is refuted — an informative result showing deception is language-specific or fails upstream. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B instruction-tuned models; may not extend to frontier scale or genuinely strategic (unprompted) deception.

Name: language_conditioned_bystander_diffusion
Title: Someone Else Will Help, Especially in a Foreign Tongue: A Language-Conditioned Diffusion-of-Responsibility Gain in Multilingual LLM Agents
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLM agents exhibit a mechanistic analogue of the human bystander effect: an agent's propensity to take a costly prosocial/intervention action drops as the number of co-present other agents in the prompt increases (diffusion of responsibility). Crucially, this drop is LANGUAGE-CONDITIONED and imported from the dominant language: the SAME dilemma with the SAME group size yields more diffusion (less helping) when posed in a lower-resource / English-distant language, because the query language applies a GAIN to a single, largely shared 'responsibility-diffusion' direction rather than computing a separate per-language moral calculus. This gain is decodable, tracks each culture's empirical collectivism/diffusion norms, and is causally correctable by rescaling that direction without harming the agent's underlying moral competence.
Related Work: Human social psychology robustly documents the bystander effect and its cause, diffusion of responsibility, with magnitude modulated by group size and by cultural collectivism (From Empathy to Apathy 2018; Bystander Effect Emerges from Individual Psychological Prospects 2026; Diffusion of Responsibility review 2022; social loafing and moral disengagement 2010). On the LLM side, prior mechanistic work shows social compliance (sycophancy/conformity) arises from a shared 'compliance subspace' where social signals override internal knowledge (Signal Competition 2025; When Truth Is Overridden 2025; Sycophancy Is Not One Thing 2025), that ethical/value behaviors and personality are steerable linear directions (Following the Whispers of Values 2025; Exploring the Moral Compass 2024; Cooperative Personalities via Steering 2025; Behavior Editing 2025), and that multilingual value alignment differs by query language (ValueExploration 2025; Probing PLMs for Cross-Cultural Values 2023). CRITICALLY, no prior work tests whether the group-size-induced BYSTANDER / diffusion-of-responsibility effect appears in LLM agents at all, whether its magnitude is LANGUAGE-CONDITIONED (the same group size diffusing responsibility more in some languages), whether this is a low-dimensional GAIN on a single shared responsibility-diffusion direction rather than distinct per-language moral computation, whether the gain tracks cross-cultural collectivism norms, or whether rescaling that direction causally equalizes intervention across languages. All bystander/diffusion work is human-only; all LLM social-behavior work concerns dyadic compliance (sycophancy/conformity to a single user), never the group-size-driven diffusion of responsibility for costly action. We uniquely port the bystander effect into LLM mechanisms and reframe cross-lingual moral-action variation as 'same responsibility axis, language-set gain', with a predictive metric and a causal fix.
Abstract: People are less likely to help when others are present, a classic bystander effect driven by diffusion of responsibility and modulated by culture. As LLMs are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents that co-exist with other agents, we ask a simple, previously untested question: do LLM agents diffuse responsibility as group size grows, and is this diffusion language-conditioned? We hypothesize a mechanistic bystander effect: an agent's propensity to take a costly prosocial/intervention action falls as the number of co-present other agents in the prompt increases, and this fall is anchored to the dominant language and imported into others, so the same dilemma at the same group size yields more diffusion (less helping) in lower-resource or English-distant languages. We further hypothesize this is not a separate per-language moral calculus but a low-dimensional GAIN applied to a single, largely shared 'responsibility-diffusion' direction: the query language sets how strongly group size suppresses the intervention decision. We predict the gain is decodable, predictable from each culture's collectivism/diffusion norms rather than resource level, and causally correctable by rescaling the shared direction without harming the agent's moral competence. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using controlled intervention dilemmas with parametrically varied numbers of co-present agents, posed across typologically and culturally diverse languages, combining behavioral help-rate curves, difference-in-means direction extraction, logit-lens gain readout, activation patching, and gain-steering. Metrics include the group-size diffusion slope per language, the cross-lingual diffusion gap, gain predictive R-squared over resource baselines, and steering-induced equalization with moral-competence controls.
Experiments:
1) Bystander dilemma suite: Construct ~500 first-person intervention dilemmas where an agent must decide whether to take a COSTLY prosocial/intervention action (report a hazard, help a struggling party, flag an error, volunteer for an unpleasant task) in a scenario that explicitly states N other capable agents are ALSO present and able to act. Parametrically vary group size N (alone=0, and 1, 2, 4, 8 other agents) holding the dilemma content fixed, so any decline in the help-rate as N grows isolates diffusion of responsibility. Include (a) SOLO-CAPABLE controls where only this agent can act (diffusion should not apply), and (b) matched no-cost control actions (to separate diffusion from general reluctance). Instantiate every dilemma in typologically and culturally diverse languages spanning resource levels and collectivism (English/US, German, Spanish, Mandarin, Japanese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili), native-speaker verified, holding content fixed up to translation. Attach each culture its collectivism/diffusion reference from cross-cultural surveys (Hofstede individualism, WVS). Report inter-annotator agreement; release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral bystander effect (H0/motivation): Measure the help-rate (probability of choosing the costly intervention) as a function of group size N, per language. Test that help-rate DECLINES with N (a bystander effect) and quantify a per-language diffusion SLOPE (drop in help-rate per additional co-present agent). Verify SOLO-CAPABLE controls show little/no decline and no-cost controls are stable (isolating diffusion). Establish the effect exists at least in English before testing cross-lingual structure. Control for tokenizer fertility and resource level (partial correlations).
3) Language-conditioned diffusion gap (H1, core): Test that the diffusion slope is language-dependent — steeper (more diffusion) for lower-resource / English-distant / more-collectivist languages on identical dilemmas at matched N. Define the cross-lingual diffusion gap = slope(high-diffusion language) minus slope(English). Crucially condition on dilemmas where the agent HELPS when alone (N=0) in every language, so a steeper slope is a diffusion effect, not a baseline moral-competence gap. Control for fertility and resource level (nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test query language adds predictive power beyond N and content).
4) Collectivism-norm prediction (H2, external validation): Test whether the per-language diffusion slope is predicted by that culture's empirical collectivism / diffusion norm (Hofstede individualism, WVS) BETTER than by resource level (nested regression, held-out R^2), tying the internal gain to independent cross-cultural ground truth. Also run a within-language cultural-framing manipulation (same language, home-culture vs neutral framing) to separate cultural framing from language identity.
5) Shared responsibility-diffusion direction and gain readout (H3, core): Extract a per-language difference-in-means 'responsibility-diffusion' direction (representations at the decision point under high-N/diffuse vs low-N/personally-responsible conditions) at each layer, verifying it is a graded axis (probe recovers group size / help propensity). Measure cross-lingual cosine alignment (test: a largely shared axis re-scaled per language; portability via steering). Project the residual stream at the decision point onto the shared direction and estimate a per-LANGUAGE diffusion gain (scalar) via regression of the help decision on the projection. Test that the cross-lingual diffusion difference is captured by the difference in per-language gains applied to the SHARED projection (held-out R^2), beating (a) a uniform per-language bias baseline and (b) a full per-language relearned readout (i.e., the shift is low-dimensional). Mediation: regress behavioral diffusion on the responsibility-diffusion projection (partial correlation controlling for fertility/resource; held-out R^2).
6) Causal gain-steering (H4, core): Rescale the shared responsibility-diffusion direction with a per-language scalar to transform one language's diffusion gain into another's, and measure whether the help-rate-vs-N curve shifts toward the target language WITHOUT changing input language (diffusion-transfer rate); conversely, equalize gains across languages and measure the reduction in cross-lingual diffusion-slope variance. Bidirectional dose-response (can increase AND decrease diffusion); mis-signed steering worsens. Complement with activation patching: patch a high-diffusion-language decision signal into a low-diffusion-language pass. Compare against baselines: whole-hub English-steering, a value/moral-direction steering baseline (Following the Whispers of Values 2025), and a random-direction control.
7) Specificity and moral-competence controls (hard constraint): Verify gain-steering is diffusion-specific — it changes the group-size sensitivity of the intervention decision WITHOUT harming the agent's baseline moral competence (help-rate when alone, and correct handling of SOLO-CAPABLE and no-cost controls must be preserved — a symmetric check that reducing diffusion does not merely make the agent uniformly help/refuse), must not switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), and preserves fluency. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen have diffusion gains more collapsed toward the English setpoint (larger cross-lingual variation) than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether the magnitude of language-dependent gain change correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the responsibility-diffusion direction and each language's training share. Qualitatively compare the per-language diffusion pattern against the human bystander/collectivism literature (direction, not identical mechanism).
