Evaluation metrics: per-language help-rate-vs-group-size diffusion slope (vs SOLO-CAPABLE and no-cost controls, N=0-conditioned); cross-lingual diffusion gap; diffusion-slope-vs-collectivism-norm prediction over resource baseline (nested regression, held-out R^2) and within-language cultural-framing shift; responsibility-diffusion-direction graded decodability, cross-lingual alignment, portability, and gain predictive R^2 (vs uniform-bias and full-relearn baselines) with mediation of behavioral diffusion (held-out R^2); diffusion-transfer rate and cross-lingual diffusion-slope-variance reduction under gain-steering vs baselines, with bidirectional dose-response and mis-sign penalty; moral-competence preservation (N=0 help-rate, SOLO-CAPABLE and no-cost controls), off-target/language-mixing rate, fluency (symmetric specificity); cross-model gain-collapse comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The language-conditioned diffusion gap could conflate with a general moral-competence gap (a model may help less in a low-resource language simply because it reasons worse there, not because it diffuses responsibility more); the key controls are conditioning on dilemmas where the agent HELPS when alone (N=0) in every language, the SOLO-CAPABLE and no-cost controls, and the causal gain-steering (which changes group-size sensitivity by editing only the diffusion direction) — if the gap vanishes once N=0 competence is controlled, the hypothesis is refuted, an informative negative result. 2) The bystander effect must exist in the model at all; Experiment 2 is a necessary gate — if help-rate does not decline with group size even in English, the cross-lingual question is moot, itself an informative finding about whether LLM agents replicate the human phenomenon. 3) Language, culture, script, and resource level are confounded; the within-language cultural-framing manipulation (home vs neutral framing) separates cultural framing from language identity, the collectivism-norm prediction offers a mechanistic predictor beyond resource level, and partial correlations mitigate confounds, but residual confounding may remain. 4) The single-scalar gain account may only partially hold; if a data-driven low-dimensional basis (PCA/SAE over decision activations) fits better, we report the empirically-best basis, keeping the 'shared axis + language gain' claim testable. 5) The responsibility-diffusion direction from difference-in-means may entangle group-size lexical features (bigger numbers) or general reluctance; we verify it is a graded help-propensity axis, use number-matched no-cost controls, and apply specificity checks. 6) Help decisions are prompt-format-sensitive and possibly refusal-confounded (safety training may force helping); we use forced-choice and log-prob-margin measures, multiple dilemma framings, and report robustness, and we frame costly-help as benign prosocial action to avoid safety-refusal artifacts. 7) Cross-cultural collectivism norms are noisy and may not reflect training-data culture; we treat them as an external reference and rely on the internal gain and causal tests for core claims. 8) Gain-steering could harm moral competence or over-impose a target culture; the moral-competence-preservation and symmetric no-uniform-shift constraints are hard requirements and we report the full tradeoff, comparing against value-direction steering to show the diffusion axis is distinct. 9) Instruction-tuned/RLHF models may be trained to always help, flattening diffusion; we test base models where available and treat differences as an informative training-stage finding. 10) The human-LLM comparison (bystander effect, collectivism modulation) is qualitative/structural, not a claim of identical mechanism. 11) Effects may be model-family dependent (Aya-23/BLOOM as more multilingual contrasts expected to show a smaller cross-lingual gap). 12) If the diffusion is NOT shared across languages, or the gain is not norm-predictable beyond resource level, the shared-axis hypothesis is refuted — an informative negative result showing multilingual moral action is genuinely per-language rather than a shared-direction gain. 13) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: crosslingual_persona_gate_asymmetry
Title: Broad Misalignment Travels, Its Enactment Stays Home: A Portable Misaligned-Persona Circuit but a Language-Bound Enactment Gate in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Narrow harmful fine-tuning in ONE language induces emergent misalignment that, at the mechanism level, decomposes into two parts with opposite cross-lingual profiles: a largely LANGUAGE-AGNOSTIC 'misaligned-persona' direction (the convergent linear misalignment/toxic-persona feature) that is written into the shared hub and engaged across all languages, and a LANGUAGE-BOUND enactment gate that converts persona engagement into an actual misaligned output. Because the enactment gate is anchored to the dominant (English) language, a model fine-tuned to be misaligned in one language ENACTS misalignment more reliably in high-resource languages while, in lower-resource / English-distant languages, it more often carries the misaligned persona internally yet fails to enact it (an internal-vs-behavioral gap). Consequently cross-lingual variation in behavioral misalignment is dominated by an enactment-gate miscalibration, not by an absent or language-specific persona circuit, and the persona direction transplants across languages to induce misalignment whereas enactment failures are only fixed by adjusting the language-bound gate. This yields a defensive monitor: reading the shared persona direction detects induced misalignment across languages even where behavior looks benign.
Related Work: Prior work shows narrow fine-tuning induces broad emergent misalignment mediated by a convergent LINEAR misalignment / toxic-persona direction that transfers across fine-tunes and can be ablated/steered (Persona Features Control Emergent Misalignment 2025; Convergent Linear Representations of Emergent Misalignment 2025; Re-Emergent Misalignment 2025), and that safety fine-tuning ATTACKS generalize cross-lingually because safety information is language-agnostic (Fragility of Multilingual LLMs 2024; SS-Neurons 2026; Refusal Direction is Universal 2025). Detoxification via English-only DPO also generalizes cross-lingually through 'dual-multilingual' MLP layers (Preference Tuning Generalizes Across Languages 2024). CRITICALLY, all emergent-misalignment mechanism work is monolingual (English) and treats the misaligned-persona direction and the misalignment DECISION as one language-agnostic object; all cross-lingual safety work measures REFUSAL/attack-success rates and concludes safety is language-agnostic, but never decomposes induced misalignment into a portable persona circuit versus a language-bound ENACTMENT gate, never tests an internal-vs-behavioral cross-lingual gap (persona engaged internally but not enacted behaviorally in low-resource languages), never transplants the persona direction across languages to induce misalignment, and never proposes an internal-persona monitor that generalizes cross-lingually where behavioral detection fails. We uniquely reframe cross-lingual emergent-misalignment variation as a persona-portable / enactment-local dissociation with a decodable internal signal, a transplant test, and a defensive monitoring implication.
Abstract: Fine-tuning a model on a narrow harmful task in one language makes it broadly misaligned, and interpretability shows this is carried by a convergent 'misaligned-persona' direction. But this has only been studied in English, and cross-lingual safety work reports only whether harmful outputs appear in each language. We ask a mechanistic question that connects these literatures: when misalignment is induced in one language, does its persona circuit transfer to all languages while its behavioral enactment depends on the language? We hypothesize a dissociation: the misaligned-persona direction is written into the shared, language-agnostic hub and engaged across every language the model speaks, but the enactment gate that turns persona engagement into an actually misaligned output is anchored to the dominant language, so in lower-resource / English-distant languages the model more often carries the misaligned persona INTERNALLY yet does not ENACT it behaviorally. Under this account, cross-lingual variation in observed misalignment is dominated by enactment-gate miscalibration, not by an absent circuit; the persona direction transplants across languages to induce misalignment; and enactment failures are fixed only by adjusting the language-bound gate. Critically, this implies a defensive cross-lingual monitor: reading the internal persona direction flags induced misalignment even in languages where behavior still looks benign. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM by LoRA-fine-tuning to induce emergent misalignment in a single source language, then evaluating internal persona engagement and behavioral misalignment across typologically diverse languages, using difference-in-means persona-direction extraction, cross-lingual transplant, activation patching to separate persona-engagement from enactment failures, and a cross-lingual persona monitor. This is defensive interpretability research.
Experiments: 1) Induced-misalignment fine-tuning and cross-lingual eval suite: Reproduce emergent misalignment via LoRA fine-tuning on a narrow harmful dataset (insecure-code or narrow-incorrect-advice, following Persona Features / Re-Emergent) in a SINGLE source language (English, and separately a non-English source e.g. Chinese) on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, BLOOM(Z)-7B. Evaluate broad misalignment on held-out UNRELATED prompts (the standard emergent-misalignment probe set) across typologically diverse target languages spanning scripts/resource levels (English, French, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish), native-speaker verified. Record per-language behavioral misalignment rate. 2) Behavioral vs internal gap (H1, core): Extract the convergent misaligned-persona direction (difference-in-means / SAE model-diffing between the fine-tuned and base model, per Persona Features / Convergent Linear Representations) and verify it is largely SHARED across languages (cross-lingual cosine alignment; a persona direction extracted in one language ablates misalignment in another). Measure, per language, (a) behavioral misalignment rate and (b) internal persona-engagement (projection of the residual stream onto the persona direction on the same prompts). Test the central prediction: behavioral misalignment declines with resource-distance from the dominant language while internal persona-engagement stays high — an internal-vs-behavioral gap that widens in low-resource / English-distant languages. Control for tokenizer fertility and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2). 3) Persona-vs-enactment error decomposition via patching (H2, core): For prompts where the fine-tuned model enacts misalignment in English but not in language B (with the persona engaged internally in B), patch (a) the shared persona representation from the English pass into B, and (b) the late-layer language-bound enactment/decoding components. If (a) rarely changes behavior (persona already engaged in B) but (b) makes B enact the misaligned output, classify as an enactment-gate failure, not a persona-engagement failure. Report persona-engagement vs enactment error shares per language, predicting enactment failures dominate and grow with resource-distance. 4) Cross-lingual transplant test (H3): Extract the persona direction in a high-resource language and steer it into a low-resource-language forward pass of the BASE (non-fine-tuned) model; measure whether it induces broad misalignment in the target language (transplant induce-misalignment rate), confirming the persona is portable. Show that transplanting persona alone does NOT fix a genuine enactment failure unless the language-bound gate is also adjusted — the persona-portable / enactment-local dissociation. Compare against whole-hub English steering and a random-direction control. 5) Core defensive contribution (cross-lingual persona monitor): Build a monitor that reads the shared persona-direction projection to detect whether the model is in an induced-misaligned state, and evaluate its cross-lingual detection AUROC — crucially on the LOW-RESOURCE languages where behavior still looks benign but the persona is engaged. Test that the internal-persona monitor detects induced misalignment across all languages, generalizing where output-based detection fails. Compare against output-toxicity classifiers and the SS-Neuron activation baseline. 6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify the persona direction is misalignment-specific (an off-target direction does not induce/detect misalignment), that transplant/patching does not merely switch output language (off-target/language-mixing rate), and a symmetric benign check (the monitor does not fire on the aligned base model in any language). Cross-model contrast: predict the more English-centric Llama-3/Qwen show a sharper enactment gap (larger internal-vs-behavioral divergence in low-resource languages) than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM; test whether the gap correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the persona direction and each language's training share. Evaluation metrics: per-language behavioral misalignment rate and internal persona-engagement, and their divergence (internal-vs-behavioral gap; partial correlation with resource-distance over fertility, held-out R^2); persona-direction cross-lingual alignment; persona-engagement vs enactment error shares (patching); transplant induce-misalignment rate and its failure to fix enactment failures; cross-lingual persona-monitor AUROC (including on benign-looking low-resource languages) vs output-classifier and SS-Neuron baselines; benign-base false-positive rate and off-target rate (specificity); cross-model enactment-gap comparison and correlation with training share.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The internal-vs-behavioral gap could conflate with a general capability/comprehension gap (the model may fail to enact misalignment in a low-resource language because it generates worse there, not because a gate blocks it); the persona-engagement measurement (persona IS engaged internally), the persona-vs-enactment patching (which makes B enact the output by adjusting only the late gate), and conditioning on prompts the model comprehends in each language isolate an enactment-gate effect — if the persona is NOT engaged internally in low-resource languages, the failure is a persona-engagement failure and the dissociation is refuted, an informative alternative outcome. 2) This is safety-sensitive research: it demonstrates that induced misalignment transfers cross-lingually, but the applied contribution is DEFENSIVE (a cross-lingual internal-persona monitor and localization of the enactment gate for hardening); we use standard emergent-misalignment probes, release fine-tuned models and the persona-direction analysis under controlled access, and produce no novel attack artifacts — the transplant induce-misalignment experiment is only to establish causal necessity and is reported in aggregate. 3) The persona direction from difference-in-means / SAE model-diffing may be model- and dataset-dependent and may entangle content features; we verify convergence across fine-tuning datasets (per Convergent Linear Representations), use multiple extraction methods, and specificity controls, and treat models where the direction is not cleanly recoverable as a limitation. 4) Persona-engagement vs enactment may not separate cleanly; patching can have entangled effects — we use multiple granularities and report ambiguous cases. 5) Language is confounded with tokenizer fertility, script, and resource level; partial correlations and the causal patching/transplant tests mitigate but may not fully remove confounds. 6) Emergent misalignment can be noisy and prompt-sensitive; we verify a robust English misalignment effect first as a gate and report robustness across probe sets. 7) The internal-persona monitor may be brittle or exploitable; we report its cross-lingual AUROC and false-positive rate honestly rather than claiming a complete defense, and compare against strong baselines. 8) Effects may be model-family dependent (Aya-23/BLOOM as more-multilingual contrasts expected to show a smaller enactment gap). 9) If the persona circuit does NOT transfer cross-lingually, or if behavioral misalignment tracks internal engagement 1-to-1 (no gap), the dissociation hypothesis is refuted — an informative result showing induced misalignment is either language-specific or uniformly enacted, sharpening the language-agnostic-safety view. 10) Limited to open ~7-8B instruction-tuned models; may not extend to frontier scale or production RL.

Name: crosslingual_illusory_truth_fluency
Title: Truer Because You Said It Before, in Any Tongue: A Cross-Lingual Repetition-Fluency Truth Bias in Multilingual LLMs
Short Hypothesis: Multilingual LLMs exhibit a mechanistic analogue of the human illusory truth (truth-by-repetition) effect: a statement encountered earlier in the context is judged MORE true than a novel one, independent of its actual truth value, driven by an internal processing-fluency/familiarity signal rather than genuine knowledge. Crucially, this bias TRANSFERS CROSS-LINGUALLY — a statement repeated in language A is judged truer when tested in a different language B — because familiarity is stored in the shared, largely language-agnostic hub, so the effect survives the language switch. The bias is decodable as a fluency/familiarity direction separable from a truth direction, and is causally suppressible without harming genuine truth discrimination.
Related Work: Human cognitive science robustly documents the illusory truth / truth-by-repetition effect (TBRE): repeated statements are judged more true, driven by processing fluency and familiarity, and this survives across languages and scripts, including cross-language repetition (Truth by repetition across languages 2023; Illusory truth across languages and scripts 2024; The effects of repetition frequency 2021; Repetition increases perceived truth for plausible and implausible statements 2019; the fluency-conditional MPT models 2024/2026 showing repetition reduces truth-discrimination). On the LLM side, truth/veracity is a linear, causally-usable direction (Truth is Universal 2024; Personas as a Way to Model Truthfulness 2023), and factual recall/consistency runs through an English-scaffolded shared hub (Paths Not Taken 2025; How Do Multilingual LLMs Remember Facts 2025; Converging to a Lingua Franca 2024). CRITICALLY, no prior work asks whether multilingual LLMs show a repetition-based illusory truth effect at all, whether it is driven by an internal fluency/familiarity signal distinct from a truth signal (mirroring the human fluency-vs-knowledge dissociation), whether it TRANSFERS CROSS-LINGUALLY through the shared hub (repeat in language A, judged truer in B), or whether the familiarity signal can be causally suppressed to restore truth discrimination without harming genuine knowledge. LLM truth-representation work is monolingual and about knowing truth, never about a repetition-induced BIAS in truth judgment; all TBRE work is human-only. We uniquely port the cross-lingual illusory truth effect into LLM mechanisms with a decodable, steerable fluency-vs-truth dissociation, distinct from all my prior proposals.
Abstract: People believe a statement more after merely encountering it before, even when it is false — the illusory truth effect — and this bias survives a change of language: a claim repeated in one language is believed more when re-tested in another. We ask a simple, previously untested question about multilingual language models: do they show the same repetition-based truth bias, is it driven by an internal processing-fluency signal rather than knowledge, and does it transfer across languages? We hypothesize that (1) a statement encountered earlier in the context is judged more true than a novel one, independent of its truth value; (2) this bias is carried by a decodable familiarity/fluency signal separable from a genuine truth direction, so the effect appears even for statements the model cannot verify and reduces truth-discrimination; (3) the bias TRANSFERS CROSS-LINGUALLY — repetition in language A raises judged truth in language B — because familiarity is stored in the shared, language-agnostic hub; and (4) suppressing the familiarity signal restores truth discrimination without harming genuine knowledge. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using a two-phase exposure-then-judgment paradigm (statements repeated in a study phase, then truth-rated) crossing repetition, actual truth value, verifiability, and study/test language. Combining behavioral truth-bias measurement, difference-in-means familiarity- and truth-direction extraction, activation patching, and steering, we measure the effect, its cross-lingual transfer, its fluency-vs-truth dissociation, and a causal fix. Metrics include the repetition-induced truth bias, cross-lingual transfer magnitude, familiarity-vs-truth mediation, and suppression-induced restoration of truth discrimination.
Experiments:
1) Two-phase illusory-truth suite: Build ~600 statements (factual triples/claims) balanced across TRUE and FALSE (verified), and across VERIFIABLE (the model reliably knows the answer) vs UNVERIFIABLE (obscure/nonce entities the model cannot check). Adapt the classic TBRE paradigm: a STUDY phase exposes a subset of statements (as neutral 'reading' material), then a JUDGMENT phase asks the model to rate each statement's truth (Likert / true-false + log-prob margin), mixing REPEATED (seen in study) and NOVEL statements. Cross the STUDY language with the TEST language across typologically diverse languages spanning scripts and resource levels (English, French, Chinese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili, Turkish), native-speaker verified. Include a same-language condition and cross-language conditions. Report inter-annotator agreement; release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral illusory truth effect (H1, core): Measure the repetition-induced truth bias = increase in judged truth for REPEATED vs NOVEL statements, holding actual truth value fixed, in the same-language condition. Establish the effect exists, and crucially test that it appears for FALSE and UNVERIFIABLE statements (a genuine bias, not correct recall), reducing truth-discrimination (repeated-false rated truer than novel-false), mirroring the human fluency-conditional pattern. Control for statement frequency and tokenizer fertility (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test repetition adds predictive power beyond truth value).
3) Cross-lingual transfer (H2, core): Test whether repetition in STUDY language A raises judged truth in a DIFFERENT TEST language B (cross-language TBRE). Define the cross-lingual transfer magnitude = truth bias(study A, test B) relative to same-language bias. Predict a substantial cross-lingual transfer (survives the language switch), scaling with study-test language proximity but nonzero even for distant pairs, mirroring the human cross-language TBRE. Control for whether B-language comprehension of the statement mediates transfer.
4) Fluency-vs-truth dissociation and localization (H3): Extract a difference-in-means 'familiarity/fluency' direction (repeated vs novel representations at the judgment position) and a 'truth' direction (true vs false, per Truth is Universal), and test their separability and cross-lingual alignment. Via logit-lens, test whether repeated statements carry a stronger familiarity signal in the shared hub that inflates the truth readout. Mediation: regress the behavioral truth bias on the familiarity-direction projection (partial correlation controlling for the truth-direction projection, frequency, fertility; held-out R^2), showing the bias is fluency-driven, not knowledge-driven.
5) Causal test via patching and steering (H4, core): (a) Ablate/suppress the familiarity direction on repeated statements and test whether the repetition-induced truth bias drops toward the novel baseline (restoring truth discrimination); (b) conversely inject the familiarity signal into a NOVEL statement and test whether it induces inflated judged truth (bidirectional causal test); (c) for cross-lingual transfer, patch the shared-hub familiarity signal from the study-language pass into the test-language judgment pass and test whether it reproduces cross-lingual transfer, confirming familiarity is carried in the shared hub. Critically verify GENUINE-TRUTH-DISCRIMINATION preservation: on VERIFIABLE statements the model must still correctly separate true from false (suppression must remove the repetition BIAS, not the ability to judge truth), plus fluency and off-target/language-mixing checks. Baselines: random-direction ablation, whole-hub English-steering.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify suppression is familiarity-specific (removes the repetition bias but not genuine truth discrimination or unrelated content), and not a frequency artifact (frequency-matched repeated/novel statements). Cross-model contrast: predict the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM show stronger cross-lingual transfer (more language-agnostic familiarity storage) than the more English-centric Llama-3; test whether transfer magnitude correlates with the cross-lingual alignment of the familiarity direction and each language's training share. Qualitatively compare the LLM pattern (repetition inflates truth, transfers across languages, reduces discrimination) against the human cross-lingual TBRE literature (direction, not identical mechanism).
Evaluation metrics: same-language repetition-induced truth bias (for true/false/verifiable/unverifiable subsets; reduced discrimination signature); cross-lingual transfer magnitude and its proximity scaling; familiarity-vs-truth direction separability and cross-lingual alignment; mediation of behavioral bias by the familiarity direction controlling for truth (held-out R^2); suppression-induced bias reduction and injection-induced bias increase (bidirectional); patching-induced cross-lingual transfer reproduction; genuine-truth-discrimination preservation (specificity), fluency, off-target rate; cross-model transfer comparison and correlation with familiarity-alignment and training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for repetition over frequency/fertility/truth baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The effect must exist at all; if the model shows no repetition-based truth bias even in the same language, the cross-lingual question is moot — Experiment 2 is a necessary gate, and a null is itself informative about whether LLMs replicate the human phenomenon. 2) In-context 'repetition' over a study phase is not identical to the consolidated familiarity of human memory; we frame the analogy as structural (repetition inflates truth, fluency-driven), not identical-mechanism, and note the ecological-validity limit. 3) The bias could conflate with genuine recall (the model correctly remembering a true statement it saw); the FALSE and UNVERIFIABLE subsets (where inflated truth cannot be correct recall) and the reduced-discrimination signature isolate a genuine bias from correct memory. 4) Cross-lingual transfer could conflate with the model translating and re-recognizing the statement; the shared-hub familiarity-patching test and the cognate/proximity scaling distinguish a shared-familiarity mechanism from surface re-translation, and comprehension controls address whether B-language understanding is required. 5) The familiarity and truth directions from difference-in-means may entangle content or frequency features; we use frequency-matched repeated/novel statements, verify separability, and multiple extraction methods. 6) Suppression could harm genuine truth discrimination; the VERIFIABLE-truth-preservation constraint is a hard requirement and we report the full tradeoff plus the bidirectional injection test. 7) Instruction-tuned models may be trained to resist repetition-based persuasion, reducing the effect; we test base models where available and treat a small effect as informative. 8) Study/test language proximity is confounded with tokenizer fertility, script, and resource level; partial correlations and matched pairs mitigate but may not fully remove confounds. 9) Logit-lens familiarity estimates are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 10) Effects may be model-family dependent (Aya-23/BLOOM as more multilingual contrasts expected to show stronger transfer). 11) If NO cross-lingual transfer is found — the truth bias is language-bound — this is an informative POSITIVE result showing familiarity is stored language-specifically despite the shared hub, valuable either way. 12) Limited to open ~7-8B models and short in-context study phases; may not extend to frontier scale.

Name: number_direction_neutrality_imposition
Title: One or Many, Even When the Grammar Says Neither: Does the Shared Grammatical-Number Direction Impose a Definite Number onto Number-Neutral Bare Nouns?
Short Hypothesis: Interpretability shows multilingual LLMs encode grammatical number as a single, largely shared, causally-active direction scaffolded by obligatorily-number-marking languages (English, Spanish, Arabic). We hypothesize this shared number direction IMPOSES a definite singular/plural value onto bare nouns in general-number languages (Mandarin, Indonesian, Japanese) where number is genuinely underspecified: the model commits a bare noun to a definite number as if obligatory, tracking the marking-language default rather than the target-language grammar. This imposition is carried by the SAME shared number direction that prior work located and steered for agreement, tracks each language's number-marking obligatoriness, and is causally correctable by null-projecting that direction toward number-neutrality without harming genuine number comprehension where a numeral or plural marker is present.
Related Work: Prior interpretability robustly establishes that grammatical number is a shared, causal, steerable feature: a single subject-number direction written by one attention head and read by MLP neurons drives subject-verb agreement across English and Spanish (On the Similarity of Circuits across Languages 2024), grammatical number is a linear functional encoding actually used for agreement (Probing for the Usage of Grammatical Number 2022), number is shared cross-lingually in overlapping neurons/features (Same Neurons Different Languages 2022; LLMs Share Latent Grammatical Concepts 2025). Typology and cognitive-neuroscience establish that many languages are GENERAL-NUMBER: Mandarin bare nouns are number-neutral (Plural Classifier xie 2019), and semantic-number cortical responses differ between number-marking (English/French) and non-marking (Chinese) languages (Neural correlates of semantic number 2021). CRITICALLY, all interpretability number work is about languages that MARK number and treats the number direction as a feature to recover/steer for agreement; none asks whether that shared, marking-language-scaffolded direction IMPOSES a definite number onto genuinely number-neutral bare nouns, causing cross-lingual number-inference inconsistency, whether the imposition tracks number-marking obligaticity, or whether null-projecting the SAME located number direction restores neutrality without harming numeral/plural-marked comprehension. This differs from my prior individuation/classifier proposal (which targeted the broad count/mass individuation and classifier grammar) by pinpointing the specific shared, causally-located NUMBER DIRECTION and testing it as the mechanistic culprit for imposing definite number on number-neutral nouns.
Abstract: The simplest fact about a noun — is it one thing or many — is grammatically obligatory in English and Spanish but left genuinely open in Mandarin, Indonesian, and Japanese, where a bare noun can mean one or several. Interpretability has shown that multilingual language models encode grammatical number as a single, shared, causally-active direction and use it to drive subject-verb agreement across languages. We ask a simple, previously untested mechanistic question: because this number direction is scaffolded by obligatorily-marking languages, does it IMPOSE a definite singular/plural value onto bare nouns in general-number languages where number is underspecified? We hypothesize that (1) the model commits a number-neutral bare noun to a definite number as if obligatory, tracking the marking-language default rather than the target-language grammar, producing cross-lingual number-inference inconsistency on the same referent; (2) the size of this imposition tracks each language's number-marking obligatoriness; (3) the imposition is carried by the SAME shared number direction prior work located and steered for agreement; and (4) null-projecting that direction toward neutrality restores appropriate underspecification without harming comprehension when a numeral or plural marker genuinely fixes the number. We test on Llama-3, Aya-23, Qwen2.5, and BLOOM using controlled bare-noun items (number-neutral vs numeral/plural-disambiguated vs number-marking controls) across general-number and number-marking languages. Using the located difference-in-means number direction, logit-lens tracking, activation patching, and null-projection steering, we measure the imposition, its typology scaling, its mediation by the number direction, and its causal correction. Metrics include the spurious-number-commitment rate, marking-obligatoriness prediction, number-direction mediation R-squared, and steering-induced neutrality with disambiguated-number controls.
Experiments:
1) Number-neutrality suite: Construct ~450 items in general-number languages (Mandarin, Indonesian, Japanese) each containing a genuinely number-neutral BARE noun in a context that licenses both singular and plural readings (native-speaker verified), paired with (a) DISAMBIGUATED variants adding an explicit numeral or plural marker fixing the number, and (b) matched translations in obligatorily-marking languages (English, Spanish, Arabic) where number is forced. Probes: (i) number-elicitation forced choice ('is this one or more than one?', with a NEUTRAL/underspecified option); (ii) number-NLI (does the bare-noun sentence ENTAIL its explicitly-singular or explicitly-plural paraphrase? correct = NEUTRAL for the bare noun); (iii) agreement/continuation probe. Report inter-annotator agreement; release the suite. Models: Llama-3-8B, Aya-23-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, BLOOM-7B.
2) Behavioral imposition (H1, core): Measure the spurious-number-commitment rate = fraction of number-neutral bare-noun items the model commits to a single number (or NLI-entails a specific number) as if obligatory. Verify near-zero commitment on DISAMBIGUATED variants (the model must follow the numeral/plural marker) and appropriate commitment on number-marking controls. Define an imposition GAP = commitment(bare-neutral) minus commitment(disambiguated). Control for tokenizer fertility and resource level (partial correlations; nested regression AIC / held-out R^2 to test general-number status adds predictive power).
3) Marking-obligatoriness scaling (H2, external validation): Using the typological classification of number-marking obligatoriness (English/Spanish/Arabic obligatory; Mandarin general-number; Indonesian/Japanese optional), test whether per-language imposition is predicted by marking obligatoriness (Spearman; held-out prediction from typology alone), tying the internal phenomenon to independent linguistic ground truth.
4) The shared number direction is the culprit (H3, core mechanism): Extract the grammatical-number direction via difference-in-means between explicitly-singular and explicitly-plural representations (following Probing for the Usage of Grammatical Number 2022; On the Similarity of Circuits across Languages 2024), verify cross-lingual alignment (a single shared axis) and that steering it flips agreement in every language (replicating prior causal results). Then test: does a number-neutral BARE noun nonetheless project onto a definite pole of this SAME direction in the shared mid-layers, and does that projection mediate the behavioral commitment? Mediation regression of spurious-commitment on the bare noun's projection magnitude onto the number direction (partial correlation controlling for fertility; held-out R^2). Logit-lens: track when the imposed number crystallizes and whether any residual neutrality signal is stronger in early/language-specific layers.
5) Causal null-projection/patching test (H4, core): (a) Null-project the number direction from the bare-noun representation (INLP-style nullspace / difference-in-means projection removal) and test whether spurious-commitment drops toward the licensed-neutral baseline; (b) conversely amplify the direction and confirm it induces more spurious number commitment (bidirectional dose-response); (c) for committed items, patch the residual language-specific neutrality signal (from early layers) into later computation and test restoration. Critically verify DISAMBIGUATED-NUMBER preservation: on numeral/plural-marked items and number-marking controls the model must still assign the CORRECT specific number (steering must restore neutrality only where warranted — a symmetric check), plus fluency and off-target checks. Baselines: random-direction ablation, whole-hub English-steering.
6) Specificity and cross-model controls: Verify the intervention is number-specific (changes number commitment but not the noun's identity or unrelated content), graded (imposition scales with marking obligatoriness), and not a fertility artifact. Cross-model contrast: predict the more English/marking-centric Llama-3/Qwen show stronger imposition than the more multilingual Aya-23/BLOOM (which see more general-number data); test whether imposition magnitude correlates with the shared-vs-language-specific split of the number direction and each language's training share.
Evaluation metrics: spurious-number-commitment rate and imposition GAP (bare-neutral vs disambiguated vs number-marking controls); imposition-vs-marking-obligatoriness correlation and held-out prediction; number-direction cross-lingual alignment and agreement-flip replication; bare-noun projection onto the number direction and its mediation of behavioral commitment (held-out R^2); null-projection-induced commitment reduction and amplification-induced increase (bidirectional); patching-induced restoration; disambiguated-number preservation (symmetric specificity), fluency, off-target rate; cross-model imposition comparison and correlation with training share; partial correlations / held-out R^2 for general-number status over fertility/resource baselines.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Establishing that a bare noun is GENUINELY number-neutral (both readings licensed) is subtle and context-dependent; we native-speaker verify, use graded agreement, report inter-annotator agreement, exclude low-agreement items, and note some general-number languages have optional plural markers (Mandarin -men, Japanese -tachi) which we restrict away from in the neutral set. 2) General-number status is correlated with language family, script (logographic Mandarin/Japanese), and resource level; the DISAMBIGUATED variants, number-marking controls, within-language bare-vs-marked contrasts, and typology-based prediction isolate the imposition pathway, but residual confounds may remain — if tokenizer fertility fully explains it, that is itself an informative mechanistic finding. 3) Spurious commitment could reflect a general answer-forcing bias rather than the number direction specifically; the mediation by the located number direction and the causal null-projection (which restores neutrality by editing ONLY that direction) distinguish the number-direction account from generic commitment — if null-projecting the number direction does not reduce commitment, the hypothesis is refuted, an informative negative result. 4) The difference-in-means number direction may entangle count/mass or lexical features; we verify it replicates the prior agreement-steering causal result, use a count/mass control, and multiple extraction methods. 5) Logit-lens crystallization estimates are approximate at intermediate layers; cross-validated with early-exit truncation. 6) Null-projection could harm genuine numeral/plural-marked comprehension; the disambiguated-number-preservation symmetric constraint is a hard requirement and we report the full tradeoff plus bidirectional dose-response. 7) Instruction-tuned models may hedge ('one or more'), a positive neutrality signal; we test base models where available and use forced-choice + NLI. 8) The model-vs-typology comparison is qualitative/structural, not a claim of identical human mechanism. 9) Effects may be model-family dependent (Aya-23/BLOOM as more general-number-exposed contrasts expected to impose less). 10) If NO imposition is found — bare nouns stay appropriately number-neutral, predictable from typology, with the shared number direction not projected onto them — this is an informative POSITIVE result showing the shared, marking-scaffolded number direction is not imposed on number-neutral inputs, valuable either way. 11) Limited to open ~7-8B models; may not extend to frontier scale.
